discovered.note: Listed as a double star by John Herschel (HJ 3945)

facts.text: The name comes from Benjamin Gould’s Uranometria Argentina, a southern star atlas made from Córdoba, Argentina. This was his 145th star of Canis Major — hence “145 G. Canis Majoris”.
facts.title: Gould’s 145th

facts.text: The fainter star, HD 56578, is an Am star: a hot star whose spectrum shows unusually strong lines of metals in its outer layers.
facts.title: A metal-lined companion

story: Not every [[double-star|double star]] is a couple. The two stars of the “Winter Albireo” look like partners, but they are strangers. The fainter one, HD 56578, is a much closer and more modest star. The brighter one lies far beyond it, and is a giant on an entirely different scale.

Just how giant has been debated. In 1978 it was classed as a giant; in 1989 it was promoted to a supergiant. The answer hangs on its distance. Hipparcos measurements made it merely a big giant, but the Gaia spacecraft places it farther away — which means it must be brighter, more than 20,000 times the Sun, and bigger. Put it in the Sun’s place and it would reach at least to the orbit of Venus, and probably beyond Earth’s.

Its cool surface, around 4,000 degrees, gives it a warm [[star-colour|colour]]. A 2012 study estimated nearly eight times the Sun’s mass and an age of only about 35 million years: a star that has lived fast and is already in its later years.
145-canis-majoris.tagline: The “Winter Albireo”: a pair of strangers, one of them a supergiant that could swallow Earth’s orbit.

discovered.note: Listed by F. G. W. Struve as STF 1657

facts.text: Coma Berenices means Berenice’s Hair. Queen Berenice II of Egypt offered her locks for her husband’s safe return from war; when they vanished from the temple, the astronomer Conon declared them set among the stars.
facts.title: A queen’s hair

facts.text: Its double-star number, STF 1657, comes from Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve, who measured thousands of double stars at Dorpat — now Tartu, in Estonia — in the 1820s.
facts.title: Struve’s number 1657

facts.text: The system gives off X-rays, most likely from the cooler star of the close pair.
facts.title: An X-ray glow

story: 24 Comae Berenices has a hidden third star. The system shows two stars, but the fainter of them is itself a tight pair: two stars whipping around each other every 7.33 days, far too close for any telescope to split. Only their spectra give them away, revealing a [[multiple-star|triple system]].

The brightest member is an ageing orange giant. It has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 20 times the Sun’s width, shining 173 times as brightly. The close pair is made of an A-type star with unusually strong metal lines in its spectrum and a slightly cooler partner; their spins may have locked in step with their orbit.

The giant and the close pair travel through space together. If they really are bound, one lap around each other takes roughly 28,000 years — the last time they stood in today’s positions, mammoths still roamed Europe.
24-comae-berenices.tagline: A pair of stars with a hidden third — and a 28,000-year orbit, if the two halves are really bound.

discovered.note: Listed by F. G. W. Struve as STF 470

facts.text: Eridanus is the river into which, in Greek myth, Phaethon plunged after losing control of his father’s Sun chariot. It winds a long way across the sky.
facts.title: The river of Phaethon

facts.text: It is also known as STF 470, an entry in the double-star catalogue of Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve, the great 19th-century measurer of double stars.
facts.title: Struve 470

story: Two stars at very different stages of life make up this [[double-star|double star]]. The brighter, 32 Eridani A, is an evolved giant: it has swollen to about 15 times the Sun’s width and shines some 138 times as brightly, its surface cooled to around 5,000 degrees.

Its companion, 32 Eridani B, is still in the prime of life, burning hydrogen in its core, but it is a much hotter star — over 9,000 degrees — and it spins furiously. Its equator whirls at 180 kilometres per second or more, around 90 times faster than the Sun’s. That is enough to squash it: the star is noticeably flattened, bulging at its waist.
The two share a single entry in the Hipparcos catalogue, HIP 18255, while the older Bright Star Catalogue gives each its own number.
32-eridani.tagline: An ageing giant and a furiously spinning young star, paired in the River Eridanus.

discovered.note: Discoverers of its planet, 51 Pegasi b

facts.text: Before it had an official name, the planet was nicknamed Bellerophon, after the Greek hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus.
facts.title: Bellerophon

facts.text: In 2015 the star became Helvetios, after the Celtic Helvetii of ancient Switzerland, and its planet Dimidium, Latin for ‘half’ — names proposed by an astronomy society in Lucerne.
facts.title: Names from Switzerland

story: On 6 October 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet orbiting 51 Pegasi — the first ever found around a Sun-like star. Working at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence in France, they had caught the star wobbling as an unseen companion tugged it back and forth. In 2019 the discovery won them a share of the Nobel Prize in Physics.

The planet, 51 Pegasi b, was a shock. With at least half the mass of Jupiter, it races round its star in just over four days, so close that it is heated to around 1,200 °C. Theory said giant planets should form far from their stars, so this ‘hot Jupiter’ pushed astronomers to accept that planets can migrate.

The [[star]] itself is a near-cousin of the Sun: slightly older at about 4.8 billion years, 9% more massive, 11.5% larger and richer in heavy elements. It seems to be in a quiet spell with few starspots, like the Sun’s own Maunder minimum.
51-pegasi.tagline: An ordinary-looking star that changed astronomy: the first Sun-like star found with a planet.

discovered.note: Catalogued by Flamsteed; first seen as a double by James Bradley in 1753

facts.text: Bessel’s parallax was about a third of an arcsecond — roughly the apparent width of a 2-centimetre coin seen from 13 kilometres away.
facts.title: A coin from 13 kilometres

facts.text: 61 Cygni A is so steady that it serves as an “anchor star” in the Morgan–Keenan system, the standard scheme for classifying stars by their spectra.
facts.title: An anchor for the stars

facts.text: 61 Cygni is approaching us. Its closest pass to the Sun will come around the year 20,000.
facts.title: Still coming closer

story: Most stars hold their places for centuries; this one flies. In 1792 Giuseppe Piazzi compared his measurements of a faint star in Cygnus with James Bradley’s from 40 years earlier, and found it had shifted. No other naked-eye star crosses our sky so quickly. Piazzi dubbed it the “Flying Star” and suggested that anything moving so fast must be near — a prime target for measuring a star’s distance.

Attempt after attempt failed: the errors were bigger than the effect. Then Friedrich Bessel, using a new heliometer by Joseph von Fraunhofer, measured its tiny yearly shift from Königsberg in 1837–38. It was the first reliable distance to any star beyond the Sun, published just ahead of Struve’s result for Vega and Thomas Henderson’s for Alpha Centauri.

What he measured is a [[double-star]] of two small orange dwarfs, cooler, dimmer and older than the Sun, circling each other every 659 years or so. Over the twentieth century several astronomers claimed a giant planet here; better measurements showed every claim was unfounded.
61-cygni.tagline: Piazzi’s “Flying Star” — the fastest-moving star you can see with the naked eye, and a landmark of astronomy.

discovered.note: Catalogued as a binary in the late 18th century; listed by Ptolemy in the 2nd century

facts.text: In 1855 William Stephen Jacob of the Madras Observatory claimed a wobble in the orbit betrayed a planet. It was the first known attempt to find an exoplanet by tracking a star’s position — and it was wrong.
facts.title: The first exoplanet hunt

facts.text: In 1943 Dirk Reuyl and Erik Holberg announced a companion of roughly ten Jupiter masses on a 17-year orbit. It caused a stir at the time, but later observations gradually discredited it.
facts.title: A sensation that faded

facts.text: The pair’s combined light varies by a few hundredths of a magnitude over about 1.9 days. The fainter star is the suspect, but the cause is still uncertain.
facts.title: A faint flicker

story: Imagine two suns, each a little smaller and cooler than ours, circling one another on a stretched-out orbit that takes 88 years — about a human lifetime. At their closest they are a little farther apart than Saturn is from the Sun; at their widest, farther apart than Neptune. 70 Ophiuchi is one of the Sun’s nearer neighbours, and Ptolemy already listed it as an ordinary star in his Almagest in the 2nd century.

William Herschel catalogued it as a [[double-star|binary]] in the late 18th century and showed that its two stars really do orbit each other. Pairs like this helped prove that Newton’s law of gravity works far beyond the Solar System.

Ever since, it has tempted planet hunters. Every claimed discovery so far has fallen apart, yet the door is not quite shut: a world no heavier than Saturn could still be circling the brighter star in its habitable zone.
70-ophiuchi.tagline: Two orange suns on a lopsided orbit — and the star where astronomers first went hunting for an alien planet.

facts.text: In June 2025 the IAU named the brighter star Bodu, after the Chinese asterism Bó Dù, the “Textile Ruler”, which it forms together with 102 Herculis.
facts.title: Bodu, the “Textile Ruler”

facts.text: Together with 93, 102 and 109 Herculis it once made up Cerberus, named after the hound of the underworld. That constellation is now obsolete.
facts.title: A lost constellation

facts.text: The giant looks the fainter of the two, yet it puts out more energy in total — about 172 Suns’ worth against 156 — because much of its light is infrared, which our eyes cannot see.
facts.title: The giant’s hidden light

story: Two stars of almost exactly the same weight — each about three times the Sun’s — and yet they no longer look alike. The slightly heavier one is further along in life. It has already swollen into a yellow giant and begun burning helium in its core, while its partner is a white star only now moving on from the hydrogen-burning prime of its life.

That difference shows up as [[star-colour|colour]]. The white star’s surface is around 8,200 kelvins; the giant’s is closer to 5,000, which is why so many observers see the pair in contrasting tints. The white star also spins fast, its equator turning at more than 230 kilometres a second.
The two are so widely separated that no orbital motion has ever been detected. One lap must take at least 11,000 years.
95-herculis.tagline: Near-twins in mass, caught at different stages of life — one still white, the other already a yellow giant.

facts.text: In Isaac Asimov’s 1951 novel The Stars, Like Dust, a character raised on another planet insists the nebula was named after Horace Hedd, the first man to enter it.
facts.title: Named after Horace Hedd?

facts.text: E. E. Barnard listed it as number 33 in his catalogue of dark nebulae, describing a dark mass on a nebulous strip south of Zeta Orionis.
facts.title: Barnard 33

story: In 1888 Williamina Fleming — a former maid who became one of Harvard College Observatory’s leading astronomers — spotted the Horsehead on a photographic plate. It is a [[dark-nebula]], a dense cloud of cold gas and dust that blocks the light behind it. The horse’s head rises from a larger dark cloud and is silhouetted against the red glow of IC 434, an [[emission-nebula]].
It is not empty. Bright spots at its base are young stars still forming, and the whole cloud is part of the vast Orion molecular cloud complex.
B33.tagline: The most famous dark nebula of all: a cold cloud of dust shaped like a horse’s head, found on a Harvard photograph.

discovered.note: Catalogued by Hipparchus as early as 130 BC

facts.text: NGC 884 holds five red supergiants — RS, AD, FZ, V403 and V439 Persei — and all of them are variable stars, slowly changing in brightness.
facts.title: Red giants among the blue

facts.text: The Double Cluster lies close to the radiant of the Perseid meteor shower, the point from which August’s shooting stars appear to stream each year.
facts.title: Home of the Perseids

facts.text: Both clusters are approaching us, at about 38 and 39 kilometres per second.
facts.title: Heading our way

story: In Greek myth, Perseus holds Medusa’s head in one hand and a sword in the other, and this pair of clusters marks the sword’s jewelled handle. Hipparchus catalogued the glow as early as 130 BC. To Bedouin Arabs it was the tail of a small fish, and it appears in al-Sufi’s Book of Fixed Stars. Only telescopes showed what it really is: two separate [[open-cluster|open clusters]], NGC 869 and NGC 884, still known by their old star-like names h and χ Persei.

Both clusters are young — about 14 million years old, several times younger than the Pleiades — and full of hot blue-white stars. They lie in the Perseus Arm of our galaxy and form the heart of the Perseus OB1 association, a wider family of young, hot stars.
C14.tagline: Two young star clusters side by side — the jewelled hilt of Perseus’s sword, recorded since ancient Greece.

discovered.note: Known since prehistoric times; probably first catalogued by Hodierna in 1654

facts.text: The Hyades are close enough to measure directly by parallax, as Hipparcos and Hubble have done. Other methods agree, making the cluster a key rung on the ladder used to measure distances to other galaxies.
facts.title: A cosmic ruler

facts.text: Epsilon Tauri, known as Ain, the ‘Bull’s Eye’, has a giant planet candidate — the first planet found in any open cluster.
facts.title: First planet in a cluster

facts.text: The Hyades and the Praesepe cluster, M 44, share their age, chemistry and motion, and their paths trace back to the same region of space. They were probably born together.
facts.title: Long-lost sibling

story: In Greek myth the Hyades were five daughters of Atlas and half-sisters of the Pleiades. When their brother Hyas died, they wept so much that they were turned into stars, forever linked with rain. In England the cluster was known as the ‘April Rainers’. Homer placed them on the shield that the god Hephaistos made for Achilles in the Iliad.

This [[open-cluster]] was born from a single cloud about 625 million years ago. Its five brightest members have used up the hydrogen in their cores and swollen into giants, and eight white dwarfs in its core mark heavier siblings that have already died. Most clusters break up within 50 million years. The Hyades has survived, but it is slowly evaporating: about a third of its known members lie in a halo beyond its gravitational edge, probably escaping.
C41.tagline: The weeping sisters of Greek myth, on the shield of Achilles — and a ruler for measuring the cosmos.

discovered.note: First catalogued as an emission nebula

facts.text: ‘Cave Nebula’ was first used for a different object, Ced 201, a brighter reflection nebula elsewhere in Cepheus. The SIMBAD database still gives the name to Ced 201, not to this one.
facts.title: A borrowed name

facts.text: It was first listed as an emission nebula in 1959, in the expanded second edition of Stewart Sharpless’s catalogue of glowing hydrogen clouds — hence its other name, Sh 2-155.
facts.title: Catalogued in 1959

story: Patrick Moore gave this faint cloud in Cepheus its name, probably inspired by photographs showing a curved arc of glowing gas like the mouth of a cave. He made it number 9 in his Caldwell catalogue, and the name ‘Cave Nebula’ has stuck to it ever since.

It is an [[emission-nebula]]: hydrogen gas made to shine by the fierce light of young stars from a family called Cepheus OB3. It sits at the edge of a dark molecular cloud, Cepheus B. One of those stars, the hot O-type star HD 217086, may be compressing that cloud and triggering the birth of a new generation of stars. X-ray and infrared studies with Chandra and Spitzer found a progression of stellar ages in front of the cloud — just what that idea predicts.
C9.tagline: A glowing cloud where one hot young star may be squeezing gas into a new generation of stars.

discovered.note: First European report; long known to southern peoples

facts.text: In Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle’s novel The Mote in God’s Eye, a red supergiant is set against the Coalsack, and a yellow star in front of it is the ‘mote’ of the title.
facts.title: The Mote in God’s Eye

facts.text: In Kenji Miyazawa’s Japanese classic, the boy Giovanni sees only the black emptiness of the Coalsack where his friend Campanella departs for the afterlife.
facts.title: Night on the Galactic Railroad

story: In 1499 the Spanish explorer Vicente Yáñez Pinzón gave the first European report of a dark hole in the southern Milky Way. Amerigo Vespucci called it ‘il Canopo fosco’, the dark Canopus, and others named it Magellan’s Spot or the Black Magellanic Cloud — a dark twin to the bright Magellanic Clouds. It is a [[dark-nebula]], a vast cloud of dust blotting out the stars of the Milky Way behind it.

It had a place in other skies long before. In several Australian Aboriginal cultures it forms the head of the Emu in the sky. To the Wardaman people it is the head and shoulders of a law-man, watching to make sure people do not break traditional law. The Inca called it Yutu, after a partridge-like bird, the tinamou.
C99.tagline: A hole in the Milky Way that Europeans called Magellan’s Spot — and Aboriginal Australians the head of the Emu.

discovered.note: Described in his Book of Fixed Stars

facts.text: Its official name honours Dalmero Brocchi, an amateur who mapped its stars in the 1920s for the American Association of Variable Star Observers, to help calibrate photometers.
facts.title: Brocchi’s map

facts.text: The Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna rediscovered it in the 17th century, and Per Collinder listed it as cluster 399 in his 1931 catalogue.
facts.title: Found again and again

story: The Persian astronomer al-Sufi described this little group in his Book of Fixed Stars in 964, and for most of the 20th century astronomers took it for a genuine star cluster. Then the Hipparcos satellite measured its stars’ distances and motions with new precision. Studies from 1998 onwards gave the verdict: the Coathanger is an [[asterism]], ten unrelated stars at different distances, not a family born together.
Cr399.tagline: The Coathanger: a famous little star pattern that turned out not to be a cluster at all.

story: Pictor began life in the 1750s as the painter’s easel, one of the constellations Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille invented to honour the tools of art and science. ESO 121-6 is one of its galaxies: an Sc [[spiral-galaxy]] whose long, thin outline suggests we see it nearly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]]. Its name comes from a survey of the southern sky made on photographic plates by the European Southern Observatory and Sweden’s Uppsala Observatory.
ESO121-6.tagline: A slender spiral galaxy in Pictor, the painter’s easel, seen nearly edge-on.

facts.text: It is a classic ‘superthin’ galaxy, a flat disc of stars seen nearly edge-on. A compact core of dark matter may help explain how its disc stays so thin.
facts.title: Superthin

facts.text: One idea is that it is what remains of a spiral galaxy pulled apart near Centaurus A, with the spiral’s core surviving as the dwarf galaxy NGC 5237.
facts.title: A lost core?

story: In May 1970, two astronomers photographing the region around the giant galaxy Centaurus A at Cerro Tololo noticed a faint, elongated streak. Fourcade, from Argentina, and Figueroa, from Chile, named it after themselves. At first it was taken for a shred of debris from Centaurus A, but in 1978 it was shown to be a galaxy in its own right: a very thin disc, an [[edge-on-galaxy]] seen almost perfectly side-on.
ESO270-17.tagline: A razor-thin galaxy near Centaurus A that may be the shredded remains of a spiral.

facts.text: AS0039, the most metal-poor star known outside the Milky Way, lives here. Its chemistry hints that it formed from the debris of a hypernova from one of the universe’s very first stars.
facts.title: From the ashes of the first stars

story: In 1937 Harlow Shapley spotted a faint swarm of stars on plates from the Bruce telescope at Boyden Observatory in South Africa. It was the first of a new kind of [[galaxy]]: a dwarf spheroidal, a small, dim satellite orbiting the Milky Way. Its stars hold only about 4% of the heavy elements found in our galaxy, so it resembles the primitive galaxies seen at the edge of the universe. Its two distinct populations of stars may be the scars of an ancient merger with another small galaxy.
ESO351-30.tagline: The first dwarf spheroidal galaxy ever found, home to the most metal-poor star known beyond the Milky Way.

facts.text: Its cluster Fornax 4 is about 3 billion years younger than the others — a sign that small galaxies kept making globular clusters after the Milky Way’s halo had stopped.
facts.title: A latecomer cluster

story: A year after finding the Sculptor Dwarf, Harlow Shapley turned up a second faint companion of the Milky Way on Boyden Observatory plates: the Fornax Dwarf, discovered in 1938. For a small [[galaxy]] it has a surprising entourage of six [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], an unusually high number for its size. The largest, NGC 1049, had been discovered long before anyone knew the galaxy existed. Most of its stars are old, but it also has younger and middle-aged ones.
ESO356-4.tagline: A small satellite of the Milky Way with six globular clusters — one of them found before the galaxy itself.

discovered.note: Known since prehistory; first confirmed written record by Amerigo Vespucci in 1502

facts.text: In 2025 astronomers announced strong evidence for a black hole of about 600,000 Suns at its heart — based on 21 fast stars in our galaxy’s halo that seem to have been flung out of the LMC by it.
facts.title: A black hole’s slingshot

facts.text: Astronomers at Mount Stromlo named one supernova remnant, N86, after the Australian High Court judge Lionel Murphy — for his interest in science, and its supposed likeness to his large nose.
facts.title: Named for a judge’s nose

facts.text: It is often said that al-Sufi recorded it around 964 as al-Bakr, the White Ox. That seems to be a misreading of his note about stars south of Canopus — stars he admitted he had never seen.
facts.title: The White Ox?

facts.text: Measurements with the Hubble Space Telescope in 2014 revealed how fast the LMC spins: it turns once every 250 million years or so.
facts.title: One turn in 250 million years

story: South of the equator, the Large Magellanic Cloud looks like a scrap torn from the Milky Way and left glowing in the dark. It is in fact a whole [[galaxy]], a satellite of our own with about a hundredth of its mass — and still the fourth-largest galaxy in the Local Group. In about 2.4 billion years it is predicted to merge with the Milky Way.

People in the south have watched it since prehistory. The first confirmed written mention comes from Amerigo Vespucci, who in a letter of 1502 described “three Canopi, two bright and one obscure” — the two [[magellanic-clouds|Magellanic Clouds]] and the dark Coalsack. Ferdinand Magellan’s voyage of 1519 made it famous in Europe, and it now bears his name.

It is a treasure-house. It holds the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in the Local Group, along with hundreds of star clusters and planetary nebulae. In 1987 a star here exploded as Supernova 1987A, the closest supernova seen since 1604.
ESO56-115.tagline: A whole galaxy hanging in the southern sky, and home to the closest supernova seen in nearly four centuries.

discovered.note: Hidden by Milky Way dust until then

facts.text: SN 1996cr exploded here unseen. It first showed up in a 2001 Chandra X-ray image as a bright, variable source, and was confirmed as a supernova only years later.
facts.title: A supernova noticed late

facts.text: It is one of twelve large galaxies in the ‘Council of Giants’, a ring of big galaxies surrounding our Local Group.
facts.title: Council of Giants

story: One of the closest active galaxies to us went unnoticed until 1977. The Circinus Galaxy lies just 4° from the plane of the Milky Way, so its light has to fight through our galaxy’s dust and crowded stars. At its heart a supermassive black hole is feeding, making it a Seyfert [[galaxy]], and rings of gas appear to be streaming out of it.
ESO97-13.tagline: One of the nearest active galaxies, hidden behind the Milky Way until 1977.

discovered.note: Édouard Stephan had logged it in 1876 as a single nebula, NGC 6027

facts.text: Simulations suggest the four true members will keep spiralling inwards and eventually merge into a single giant elliptical galaxy.
facts.title: One galaxy, eventually

facts.text: Édouard Stephan spotted the group on 17 June 1876 at Marseille, but logged it as a single nebula, NGC 6027.
facts.title: Stephan saw it first

story: Carl Seyfert counted six members in this tiny [[galaxy-group]] in 1948, and in 1951 described it as the most compact group of galaxies then known. The name stuck; the count did not. Only four of the six are galaxies tangled together by gravity. One ‘member’ is a tidal tail of stars and gas flung out of the central galaxy, NGC 6027, and another is a spiral far in the background, more than four times as distant, lined up purely by chance.
HCG79.tagline: Six members, only four real galaxies: a tiny group where one ‘galaxy’ is a tail and another lies far behind.

facts.text: In July 2022 Stephan’s Quintet was one of five targets in the first science images released from the James Webb Space Telescope.
facts.title: Webb’s first look

facts.text: In the 1946 film It’s a Wonderful Life, the angels discussing George Bailey’s fate are shown as the galaxies of Stephan’s Quintet.
facts.title: A film star

facts.text: The shock wave is bigger than the whole Milky Way, and heats the gas between the galaxies to millions of degrees, making it shine in X-rays.
facts.title: A shock bigger than a galaxy

story: In 1877, at Marseille Observatory, Édouard Stephan found a tight knot of five galaxies in Pegasus — the first compact [[galaxy-group]] ever discovered. Only four are true companions, though. The brightest, NGC 7320, is a foreground galaxy, much closer to us, that simply lies in the same direction.

The other four are locked in a slow-motion collision. One of them, NGC 7318B, is falling into the group at several million kilometres an hour, driving a shock wave through the gas between the galaxies.
HCG92.tagline: The first compact group of galaxies ever found — and one of the first sights the Webb telescope showed us.

story: Sagitta, the Arrow, is one of the smallest constellations, but it holds a neat contrast. M 71 is a [[globular-cluster]], a dense ball of very old stars. Less than half a degree away lies Harvard 20, a loose [[open-cluster]] of the kind that forms in the galaxy’s disc. Its name comes from a list of clusters drawn up at Harvard College Observatory, and Per Collinder included it in his 1931 catalogue as Collinder 408.
Harvard20.tagline: A small star cluster in Sagitta, less than half a degree from the globular cluster M 71.

story: Small clusters like Harvard 21 are easy to overlook among the crowded star fields of the Cassiopeia Milky Way. Its name comes from a short list of clusters drawn up at Harvard College Observatory. It shares its patch of sky with two larger clusters, NGC 7788 and NGC 7790, both within a degree. Like every [[open-cluster]], it is a group of stars that formed together from one cloud and, for now, still travel as a family.
Harvard21.tagline: A tiny star cluster in Cassiopeia, sharing its corner of sky with NGC 7788 and NGC 7790.

story: Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of the 88 constellations, yet it sits in a rich stretch of the southern Milky Way and holds several star clusters. The best known is the Jewel Box. Harvard 5 is a far humbler [[open-cluster]] in the same constellation. Its name comes from a list of clusters drawn up at Harvard College Observatory, and Per Collinder’s 1931 catalogue lists it as Collinder 258.
Harvard5.tagline: A small star cluster in Crux, the Southern Cross — the smallest of all 88 constellations.

facts.text: IC 10 sits inside a huge envelope of hydrogen gas, far larger than the galaxy we see — and the visible galaxy seems to rotate in a different direction from it.
facts.title: Turning the other way

story: Our cosmic neighbourhood holds dozens of galaxies, but only one is in the middle of a starburst: IC 10. It is crowded with Wolf–Rayet stars — rare, very hot, massive stars near the ends of their lives — packed more densely than in either [[magellanic-clouds|Magellanic Cloud]]. Studying it is hard, though, because it lies close to the plane of the Milky Way and we must peer at it through thick dust.
Lewis Swift discovered it on 8 October 1887. Nicholas Mayall suggested in 1935 that it lay beyond our galaxy, but its place in the [[galaxy-group|Local Group]] was only confirmed in 1996.
IC10.tagline: The Local Group’s only starburst galaxy, hiding behind the dust of our own Milky Way.

discovered.note: Rediscovered by George Abell in 1952 as Palomar 7

facts.text: The Palomar Sky Survey revealed 15 faint globular clusters. Only two had been seen before: this one, and Palomar 9, which William Herschel spotted in 1784.
facts.title: Two out of fifteen

story: [[globular-cluster|Globular clusters]] are tight balls of ancient stars, among the oldest things in the Milky Way. IC 1276 is one, but thick dust in the plane of our galaxy dims it badly, so it hides in plain sight. Lewis Swift first saw it in 1889. In 1952 George Abell found it again on plates from the great Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, and it became Palomar 7 — one of the faint Palomar globulars.
IC1276.tagline: A globular cluster found twice — by Lewis Swift in 1889, and again on the Palomar Sky Survey in 1952.

story: On 31 May 1892 E. E. Barnard caught this glow on a photographic plate and at first took it for a “nebulous star”. It is in fact an [[emission-nebula]] — also catalogued as Sh 2-37, and nicknamed the Twiddlebug — partly hidden by dust in the direction of the galaxy’s centre. It lies towards Dias 5, the star cluster whose light makes its gas glow. Beside its red glow sit two small blue [[reflection-nebula|reflection nebulae]], NGC 6589 and NGC 6590.
IC1284.tagline: The Twiddlebug Nebula: a red cloud of glowing gas towards the crowded heart of the Milky Way.

story: In 1684 Johannes Hevelius carved a new constellation out of faint stars below Aquila and named it Scutum Sobiescianum, Sobieski’s Shield, after the Polish king John III Sobieski, who had led the victory at Vienna the year before. Today it is simply Scutum, and IC 1287 lies within it. This [[reflection-nebula]] does not shine by itself: it is a cloud of dust that scatters the light of nearby stars, and because fine dust scatters blue light best, such clouds usually look blue in photographs.
IC1287.tagline: A faint veil of starlit dust in Scutum, the constellation named after a Polish king’s shield.

story: The Sun was once part of a family like IC 1442. Stars are born in batches from collapsing clouds of gas, and for a while each batch travels together as an [[open-cluster]]. Over hundreds of millions of years, the pull of the galaxy and of passing clouds teases them apart, and they scatter among the general crowd of the [[milky-way]]. IC 1442, a small cluster in Lacerta, is still together, a third of a degree from its neighbour NGC 7245.
IC1442.tagline: A small star cluster in Lacerta, keeping company with NGC 7245 a third of a degree away.

facts.text: Allan Sandage noted a glowing cloud here in 1971 using the 200-inch Hale telescope. Now called S8, it is the wreck of a star that exploded only some 2,700 to 4,400 years ago.
facts.title: A young supernova remnant

facts.text: It holds DR1, a WO star — an extremely hot, rare kind of Wolf–Rayet star — which may be the only Wolf–Rayet star in the whole galaxy.
facts.title: A rare kind of star

facts.text: In 1999 astronomers caught the first nova ever detected in IC 1613: a white dwarf flaring up as it pulls in gas from a companion star.
facts.title: Its first nova

story: A galaxy with almost no dust is a gift to astronomers. IC 1613, a faint dwarf on the outskirts of the Local Group, is unusually clean: there is little dust inside it, and little along our line of sight. Its stars shine through undimmed, so their brightness is easy to read.

That made it a key testing ground for the Cepheid period–luminosity rule, the yardstick used to measure the universe. It also holds RR Lyrae stars — rare in a dwarf irregular [[galaxy]] — which provide a second, independent check. Together they allow especially accurate distance estimates. Most of its stars are around 7 billion years old, though some are far older.
Max Wolf, the Heidelberg pioneer of astrophotography, discovered it in 1906.
IC1613.tagline: A dust-free dwarf galaxy that became a testing ground for measuring the universe.

discovered.note: He saw its brightest knot, now catalogued as NGC 896

facts.text: The Heart is the brightest part of the W4 superbubble, a ‘chimney’ through which hot gas is thought to escape from the Milky Way’s disc into its halo.
facts.title: A chimney into the halo

story: At the centre of the Heart Nebula sits a small [[open-cluster|cluster]], IC 1805, and a few of its stars weigh nearly 50 times as much as the Sun. Their intense radiation makes the surrounding hydrogen glow red and sculpts the cloud into the shape seen in photographs — a heart to most people, a running dog to others.

William Herschel saw its brightest knot, on the western edge, on 3 November 1787; that knot still has its own number, NGC 896. In 1958 Gart Westerhout found that the [[emission-nebula|nebula]] gives off radio waves, so it is also called Westerhout 4.
IC1805.tagline: Half of the ‘Heart and Soul’: a glowing cloud shaped by stars nearly 50 times as massive as the Sun.

facts.text: Two galaxies, Maffei 1 and Maffei 2, lie in the same part of the sky but are almost hidden by Milky Way dust. Once thought to be Local Group members, they belong to a group of their own.
facts.title: Hidden galaxies

story: Massive stars do not just light up their birth clouds — they sculpt them. In the Soul Nebula, the brightest stars have blown huge cavities in the gas. Around them, stars grow steadily younger the farther they lie from each cavity’s centre, as if the expanding edges had squeezed new stars into being. It is some of the best evidence yet for ‘triggered’ star formation.

The Soul sits beside the Heart Nebula; together they are the ‘Heart and Soul’ of Cassiopeia. IC 1848 is the [[open-cluster|cluster]] in its body, and lends the whole [[emission-nebula]] its usual catalogue name.
IC1848.tagline: The Soul Nebula, where massive stars set off new generations of stars in waves.

story: M 35 is one of the finest star clusters in Gemini, and it has company. Less than a degree away lies NGC 2158, and a little beyond that sits IC 2157, a much smaller [[open-cluster]]. They look like neighbours, but they are not. IC 2157 lies more than twice as far away as M 35, and NGC 2158 farther still. Seen from Earth the three simply line up — a reminder that the sky is a flat picture of a deep space.
IC2157.tagline: A small cluster in Gemini that lines up with M 35 and NGC 2158 — though all three lie at very different depths.

story: About five billion years from now, the Sun will swell into a red giant, shed its outer layers and leave a small, hot core behind. In IC 2165 that ending is already under way for another star. Its exposed core bathes the cast-off gas in ultraviolet light and makes it glow. Despite the name, a [[planetary-nebula]] has nothing to do with planets: William Herschel coined the term because many of these small round glows reminded him of a planet’s disc.
IC2165.tagline: A small, bright planetary nebula in Canis Major: the cast-off shell of a dying star.

facts.text: Astronomers think the nebula formed when the dying giant interacted with a companion star that was torn apart.
facts.title: A torn-apart companion

facts.text: Its two lobes make an almost symmetrical butterfly, and its filaments curve like the field lines around a bar magnet.
facts.title: Shaped like a magnet’s field

story: Toby jugs are old English pottery mugs shaped like a stout, seated man, and this small nebula has a similar outline. It is made of dust and cool gas thrown off by HR 3126, a red giant near the end of its life, and it shines by reflecting the star’s light — a [[reflection-nebula]]. Clouds like this are rarely seen, because the phase that creates them is brief. The Gemini South telescope in Chile photographed it in detail in 2023.
IC2220.tagline: The Toby Jug Nebula: a dying red giant wrapped in a butterfly of dust it has blown off.

discovered.note: Described as “a nebulous star” around 964; found again by Lacaille

facts.text: Al-Sufi’s Book of Fixed Stars is also the oldest known record of the Andromeda Galaxy, which he described as a small cloud.
facts.title: The Book of Fixed Stars

facts.text: One member of the cluster is a quadruple star: four suns bound together by gravity, born along with the rest of the cluster.
facts.title: Four in one

facts.text: The cluster’s stars formed at about the same time as a nearer, scattered group called the Argus Association, which lies in the same direction of the sky.
facts.title: A wider family

story: More than a thousand years ago, the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi noted “a nebulous star” in the southern sky, in what we now call Vela. He wrote it down around 964, more than six centuries before the first telescope.

Some eight centuries later the Abbé Lacaille found it again from the Cape of Good Hope and listed it as Lac II 5. What both men saw is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] of about 30 hot, young, bluish stars, some of them in pairs.

Astronomers date it with a neat trick. Young, low-mass stars slowly destroy the lithium in their cores, and the smallest take longest. So the faintest cluster stars to have lost their lithium mark its age: for IC 2391, about 50 million years — the same era as its neighbour IC 2602, the Southern Pleiades.
IC2391.tagline: A star cluster first written down more than a thousand years ago by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi.

discovered.note: Probably; Solon Bailey found it independently in 1908

facts.text: One of its stars, HD 74339, is a Beta Cephei variable — a hot, massive star that brightens and fades slightly as it pulsates.
facts.title: A pulsing member

story: On 17 February 1752, observing from the Cape of Good Hope, Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille noted a 6th-magnitude star joined to another, more southerly one by a nebulous trail. His entry is often listed as missing, but it may well be IC 2395. Solon Bailey found the cluster again in 1908, and a misplaced position later led several star atlases to show it twice, as two different clusters.
IC 2395 is a young [[open-cluster]], between 6 and 18 million years old, and may belong to a loose association of hot, massive stars in Vela.
IC2395.tagline: A young cluster in Vela that Lacaille may have glimpsed in 1752, then lost in catalogue confusion.

facts.text: IC 2431 is also Markarian 1224, one of a catalogue of galaxies picked out for their strong ultraviolet light. It may hold an active nucleus that drives out ionised gas.
facts.title: Bright in ultraviolet

story: IC 2431 is a pile-up. At least three galaxies are falling together in Cancer, and as they close in, gravity is tearing each of them apart, twisting their shapes and setting off bursts of star formation. At the centre, a thick cloud of dust blocks the view, though light from a more distant [[galaxy]] peeks through its edges. Collisions like this are how big galaxies grow: the Milky Way owes much of its size to mergers of its own. Stéphane Javelle discovered the group on 24 February 1896.
IC2431-NED2.tagline: A pile-up of at least three galaxies in Cancer, tearing each other apart as they merge.

story: Williamina Fleming found IC 2448 in 1898, one of many nebulae and variable stars she discovered on Harvard’s photographic plates. It is a [[planetary-nebula]] in Carina, lying near the bright star Beta Carinae: a shell of gas thrown off by a dying star. What remains of that star is among the hottest kind known, an O-type core stripped of its outer layers. Gaia data suggest it may not be alone, but one half of a binary system.
IC2448.tagline: A planetary nebula near Beta Carinae, found by Williamina Fleming in 1898 — perhaps around a double star.

facts.text: Studies count about 370 probable member stars, including three blue stragglers and at least three red giants, one of them a spectroscopic binary.
facts.title: A bigger family than it looks

story: On 25 January 1752, during his expedition to South Africa, the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille recorded this [[open-cluster]] as entry III.4 in his southern catalogue. James Dunlop saw it again from Australia in 1826, describing a faint cluster with two or three fairly bright stars. Only in 1908 did it receive its IC number, using a position Solon Bailey had measured on photographs taken at Arequipa in Peru.
IC2488.tagline: A Vela cluster first logged by Lacaille in 1752 — and catalogued again and again over the next 150 years.

story: [[planetary-nebula|Planetary nebulae]] do not last. The glowing shell around a dying star fades into space within some tens of thousands of years — a blink in a stellar life of billions. IC 2501, in the southern constellation Carina, is caught in that brief window: the hot, exposed core of a star not unlike the Sun, lighting up the gas it has shed. In time that gas will mix into the Milky Way’s clouds, carrying carbon and other elements made inside the star into new generations of stars and planets.
IC2501.tagline: A tiny planetary nebula in Carina: a dying star’s glowing breath, caught in a short-lived phase.

story: Carina is the keel of a ship. It was once part of Argo Navis, the vast constellation of Jason’s ship, until the 18th-century French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille divided it into keel, stern and sails. IC 2553 lies in the keel. It is a [[planetary-nebula]]: the glowing gas a dying star threw off as it ran out of fuel. The star left at its centre is a small, hot core that will end its days as a white dwarf.
IC2553.tagline: A small planetary nebula in the keel of the ancient ship Argo, now the constellation Carina.

story: Edwin Coddington found this faint glow in Ursa Major in 1898, and it still carries his name: Coddington’s Nebula. It is really a dwarf [[galaxy]], an outlying member of the M 81 [[galaxy-group|group]]. Most of it cannot be seen. About 90% of its mass is thought to be dark matter, with its stars and gas only a thin sprinkling. It shows no sign of being disturbed by other galaxies, yet it is still forming stars, in clumps scattered through it.
IC2574.tagline: Coddington’s Nebula: a dwarf galaxy in the M 81 group that is about nine-tenths dark matter.

story: Few parts of the sky are as crowded as the Milky Way in Carina. Here our galaxy’s disc is thick with star clusters and glowing clouds, gathered around the great Carina Nebula, one of the largest star-forming regions in the Milky Way. IC 2581 is one of the [[open-cluster|clusters]] in this busy neighbourhood. It lies a little over a degree from NGC 3293, and not far from NGC 3324, whose edge became the ‘Cosmic Cliffs’ in the James Webb Space Telescope’s first images.
IC2581.tagline: A star cluster in one of the busiest stretches of the southern Milky Way, near the great Carina Nebula.

facts.text: Lacaille knew Theta Carinae as Theta Navis, in the giant ship Argo Navis. He later split that unwieldy constellation into three: Carina the keel, Puppis the stern and Vela the sails.
facts.title: The ship that was broken up

facts.text: Theta Carinae is part of the Diamond Cross, a pattern of stars often mistaken for the real Southern Cross in Crux.
facts.title: The Diamond Cross

facts.text: An exoplanet has been found orbiting TOI-837, one of the cluster’s young stars — a planet whose age we know, because we know the cluster’s.
facts.title: A planet of known age

story: The north has its Pleiades; the south has a sister. On 3 March 1751, at the Cape of Good Hope, the Abbé Lacaille noted a bright star in the great ship Argo Navis surrounded by a swarm of fainter ones, and remarked how much the group resembled the Pleiades. The comparison has stuck: this is the Southern Pleiades.

Among [[open-cluster|open clusters]], only the Hyades and the Pleiades themselves outshine it. Its roughly 75 stars are young — probably around 50 million years old, though one method gives an even younger age — and the cluster belongs to a much larger family of young stars, the Lower Scorpius–Centaurus association.
Its brightest member, Theta Carinae, is a hot blue star. Another, p Carinae, lies well outside the main group and varies slightly in brightness.
IC2602.tagline: The third-brightest star cluster in the sky — the southern answer to the Pleiades.

story: Working from Parramatta in New South Wales, James Dunlop catalogued hundreds of southern clusters and nebulae, and IC 2714 was one of his 1826 finds. It is a rich [[open-cluster]] in Carina, with nearly 500 probable members, lying in the Carina–Sagittarius Arm of the Milky Way. Its stars have much the same chemical make-up as the Sun. Eleven red giants show that its heaviest stars — those above about three times the Sun’s mass — have already left the prime of life.
IC2714.tagline: A rich southern cluster of nearly 500 stars, first spotted by James Dunlop in 1826.

facts.text: Infrared images from the 2MASS survey show six stars within the largest of Thackeray’s Globules — though no sign has been found that any are forming there.
facts.title: Stars in the shadows

facts.text: What looks like one cloud in photographs is several catalogue entries: IC 2944 is the cluster and its glow stretching towards Lambda Centauri, while the brighter patch to the south-east is IC 2948.
facts.title: Three nebulae in one

story: Small, dark, ragged blobs float against the glowing gas of IC 2944, like drops of ink on a lit screen. A. David Thackeray spotted them in 1950, and they are now called Thackeray’s Globules: dense clouds of cold gas and dust, silhouetted against the light behind.

Dark globules like these, known as Bok globules, are often places where new stars are being born. Here, so far, none shows any sign of it. Instead they are being worn away by the fierce light of the hot young stars in this [[cluster-nebula|cluster and nebula]].

The region has a sillier name too. A group of its stars is said to resemble a running chicken, so it is also known as the Running Chicken Nebula. Lambda Centauri, which lends it its other name, actually lies just outside.
IC2944.tagline: Dark globules drifting against glowing gas — and a pattern of stars said to look like a running chicken.

facts.text: William Frederick Denning, who found it in 1892, was a British amateur from Bristol best known for his studies of meteors — and the discoverer of several comets.
facts.title: A meteor man’s galaxy

facts.text: Its nucleus is classed as an H II nucleus: a core lit up by young, hot stars and the gas around them, rather than by a feeding black hole.
facts.title: A star-forming heart

story: Few galaxies have been so hard to size up. In 1935 Harlow Shapley measured IC 342 and found it wider than the full Moon — by apparent size the third-largest spiral galaxy then known, beaten only by Andromeda and Triangulum. Modern estimates are more modest, at half to two-thirds of the Moon’s width, but it is still a giant of our sky.

Edwin Hubble first thought it belonged to our own Local Group. It doesn’t: it is one of the brightest members of the IC 342/Maffei [[galaxy-group|Group]], one of the closest galaxy groups to ours. The dust of the Milky Way’s disc dims it so badly that even its distance is hard to pin down.
It is a quiet neighbour, too. Unlike Andromeda, with its swarm of small companions, IC 342 has few dwarf satellite galaxies; the first dwarf spheroidal around it, KKH 32, was only identified in 2020.
IC342.tagline: A great spiral peeking through the Milky Way’s dust — once thought to be one of our own Local Group.

facts.text: In 2023 researchers claimed to have found tryptophan, an amino acid, in IC 348’s gas. Later Webb observations and better laboratory data showed the signal came from instrument artefacts.
facts.title: The amino acid that wasn’t

story: A few million years ago, roughly 400 stars were born here, inside the Perseus molecular cloud. They are still so young that about half are wrapped in the dusty discs from which planets form. IC 348 is a relatively close [[cluster-nebula|star-forming region]], which lets astronomers hunt for the faintest, lightest objects born in it.

In 2023 the James Webb Space Telescope found brown dwarfs here weighing just three or four times as much as Jupiter, among the smallest free-floating ones on record. Objects that light blur the line between stars and planets.
IC348.tagline: A young star cluster in Perseus where the Webb telescope found some of the lightest free-floating brown dwarfs known.

facts.text: E. E. Barnard announced it in 1890 as a comet-like nebula. Charles Pritchard claimed to have caught it on an Oxford photograph in 1889, yet dismissed it as an “apparently insignificant fleck”.
facts.title: Who saw it first?

facts.text: Astronomers searched its bright knot for a hidden newborn star, in visible and infrared light. They found none — only very fine dust scattering Merope’s light.
facts.title: No star inside

story: Most of the blue haze around the Pleiades is a wide veil of dust lit by the cluster’s stars. IC 349 is different: a small, dense knot, a [[reflection-nebula]] lying very close to the star Merope. It is not even travelling with the cluster. Its motion matches the gas of the nearby Taurus clouds, so it is probably a stray that has wandered into Merope’s glare — and the star’s radiation, its wind, or both, are now tearing it apart.
IC349.tagline: A small cloud of dust being torn apart as it drifts past Merope, a star of the Pleiades.

story: Camelopardalis, the Giraffe, is a large, faint constellation of the far northern sky, added to star maps in the early 1600s by the Flemish-born mapmaker Petrus Plancius. Its stars are dim, but it holds a number of galaxies. IC 356 is one: an [[hubble-type|Sb]] [[spiral-galaxy]], with moderately wound arms around a fair-sized central bulge. It lies not far from the band of the Milky Way, so its light reaches us through the dusty outskirts of our own galaxy.
IC356.tagline: A spiral galaxy in the Giraffe, glimpsed through the dusty outskirts of our own Milky Way.

facts.text: AE Aurigae has a partner in flight: Mu Columbae, racing away in the opposite direction. Both seem to have been flung out of the same close encounter between stars in Orion, a few million years ago.
facts.title: Flying apart

facts.text: AE Aurigae is itself a variable star, brightening and dimming irregularly — so the light that sets its nebula aglow is never quite steady.
facts.title: An unsteady flame

story: AE Aurigae is a star on the run. Trace its path back across the sky and it leads towards Orion, where it seems to have been born before being flung out at high speed. Now it is ploughing through a cloud of gas and dust in Auriga, lighting it up as it goes.

The result is the Flaming Star Nebula. Where the star’s ultraviolet light strikes hydrogen, the gas glows as an [[emission-nebula]]; where it meets dust, the light simply bounces off, as in a [[reflection-nebula]]. In long-exposure photographs, the wisps around the star look like curling flames.
It is a chance encounter. AE Aurigae was not born in this cloud, and one day it will move on, leaving the gas to fade back into darkness.
IC405.tagline: A runaway star, flung out of Orion, now setting a cloud of gas and dust aglow as it passes through.

facts.text: In colour images, red marks nitrogen, the coolest gas; green is hydrogen; and the traces of blue are oxygen, the hottest gas, closest to the star.
facts.title: Colour-coded gas

facts.text: Three faint concentric rings surround it, thrown off roughly 630 years apart — a record of the star’s repeated bouts of mass loss.
facts.title: Rings in time

story: A few thousand years ago, a red giant in Lepus shed its outer layers. Its exposed core, the hot star HD 35914, now floods that gas with ultraviolet light and makes it glow. That is IC 418, a [[planetary-nebula]]. In Hubble’s famous portrait its shell is laced with fine, looping lines, like the patterns drawn with a Spirograph toy — which gave it its nickname. What carves that pattern is still unknown.
IC418.tagline: The Spirograph Nebula: a dying star’s shell, etched with a pattern like a child’s drawing toy.

story: Many star clusters have more than one name, and IC 4291’s second one honours a remarkable astronomer. In research catalogues it is Pismis 18, after Paris Pişmiş, who was born in Istanbul and spent most of her working life in Mexico. She catalogued a series of faint clusters in the southern Milky Way, and this [[open-cluster]] in Centaurus is one of them. It lies almost exactly on the plane of our galaxy, among the crowded star fields of the Milky Way.
IC4291.tagline: A star cluster in Centaurus whose other name honours Paris Pişmiş, a pioneer of astronomy in Mexico.

facts.text: IC 434 is one of the youngest glowing regions to form around the hot stars of the Orion OB1 association, the family of massive stars that includes Orion’s Belt.
facts.title: Young as nebulae go

story: Without IC 434 behind it, the Horsehead would be invisible. This sheet of glowing hydrogen, an [[emission-nebula]], stretches south from Orion’s Belt, and the famous horse’s head is a cloud of [[dark-nebula|dark dust]] silhouetted against it. The light comes from Sigma Orionis, a hot multiple star whose ultraviolet radiation makes the gas glow red. William Herschel recorded the nebula on 1 February 1786 — about a century before the Horsehead itself was noticed on a photograph.
IC434.tagline: The glowing curtain behind the Horsehead, lit by the hot stars of Sigma Orionis.

facts.text: Very Large Telescope images reveal at least five faint ring-like arcs to the north and south of the main nebula.
facts.title: Hidden rings

story: From above, IC 4406 would probably look like a ring. We see it from the side instead, almost in the plane of its equator, so the doughnut of gas and dust thrown off by a dying star appears as a rectangle. Across it run dark, lacy knots of dust, which some liken to the retina at the back of an eye — the source of this [[planetary-nebula]]’s nickname. Its central star has a spectrum like a Wolf–Rayet star’s, and Gaia data hint that it may have a companion.
IC4406.tagline: The Retina Nebula: a ring of gas and dust seen almost side-on, so that it looks like a rectangle.

facts.text: IC 443 is one of the best-studied cases of a supernova remnant colliding with dense molecular clouds. A giant cloud in front of it also absorbs much of its light.
facts.title: Ploughing into clouds

facts.text: A third, larger shell once counted as part of IC 443 is now known to be a separate, older remnant, about 100,000 years old.
facts.title: An older ghost

story: A massive star once collapsed and exploded in Gemini, near the star Eta Geminorum at Castor’s foot. The Jellyfish Nebula is the wreckage: a ragged, shell-shaped [[supernova-remnant]] whose curving rim and trailing filaments look like a jellyfish in photographs. The explosion also left behind a neutron star — the crushed core of the star — which still sits near the remnant’s southern rim.
Nobody is sure when it happened. Estimates range from about 3,000 to more than 30,000 years ago.
IC443.tagline: The Jellyfish Nebula: the tattered shell of an exploded star, still crashing into dark clouds.

discovered.by: Max Wolf and E. E. Barnard
discovered.note: Found on photographs between 1888 and 1894; which nebula they recorded is uncertain

facts.text: Wolfgang Steinicke matched IC 444 to the nebulosity around Mu Geminorum; Harold Corwin placed it among the clouds north-east of the Jellyfish Nebula. Others call it simply lost.
facts.title: Other suspects

story: Some objects are lost not because they faded, but because their positions were muddled. J. L. E. Dreyer added IC 444 to his [[ngc-ic|Index Catalogue]] from photographic discoveries by Max Wolf and E. E. Barnard, noting a nebula with a star involved. Yet his position falls on empty sky.

Most people now identify it with LBN 840, a small [[reflection-nebula]] beside the stars 10, 11 and 12 Geminorum. One researcher calls this a bad match, arguing that it is too small and faint for Wolf’s little lens to have recorded.
IC444.tagline: A nebula nobody can quite pin down: astronomers still argue over which cloud in Gemini it really is.

story: Monoceros R1 is a long cloud of cold gas and dust, and IC 447 marks one end of it, with IC 446 at the other. Several massive, hot B-type stars are embedded in the [[nebula]], lighting up its dust and gas. They may belong to the young [[open-cluster]] Collinder 95, whose biggest stars could have shaped the cloud we see. It carries two Index Catalogue numbers: IC 447 and IC 2169.
IC447.tagline: A cloud of gas and dust in Monoceros, lit by hot young stars at one end of a long star-forming cloud.

story: In 1995 IC 4499 looked like a misfit. Measurements suggested this loose [[globular-cluster]] was 3 to 4 billion years younger than most of its kind, which would have made it a rare latecomer among the Milky Way’s oldest citizens. A 2011 study disagreed, putting its age at around 12 billion years — back in line with its siblings. Like other very old globulars, it contains two generations of stars. It lives in the galaxy’s halo, seen in Apus, the Bird of Paradise.
IC4499.tagline: A loose globular cluster near the south celestial pole, once thought to be billions of years too young.

story: Long-exposure photographs show the head of a horse, rendered in blue — the reason IC 4592 is called the Blue Horsehead. Unlike Orion’s famous dark Horsehead, this one shines. It is a [[reflection-nebula]]: dust that scatters the light of Nu Scorpii, a multiple star system. Tiny dust grains scatter blue light more than red, the same physics that makes our daytime sky blue.
IC4592.tagline: The Blue Horsehead: a vast cloud of dust in Scorpius, lit by the multiple star Nu Scorpii.

facts.text: To mark its first year of science in 2023, the James Webb Space Telescope released an image of a small part of this cloud, showing young stars with discs around them.
facts.title: Webb’s first birthday

facts.text: The first brown dwarf ever identified in a star-forming region, Rho Oph J162349.8-242601, was found in this cloud.
facts.title: A brown dwarf first

story: Few places where stars are being born lie closer to us than the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex. IC 4604 is the [[reflection-nebula]] around the star Rho Ophiuchi itself, at the northern end of a great [[dark-nebula|dark cloud]]. Hidden in that dust, infrared telescopes have found hundreds of young stellar objects, many under a million years old and still wrapped in discs that may one day form planets.
IC4604.tagline: One of the nearest star nurseries to the Sun, chosen for the Webb telescope’s first-birthday image.

story: About a degree from Antares, the star 22 Scorpii sits in, or just beside, a faint [[nebula]], IC 4605. The star is a hot B-type star, ten million years old, spinning fast and shining about 600 times as brightly as the Sun, and its light makes the surrounding gas and dust glow. The cloud belongs to the western reaches of the Rho Ophiuchi complex, one of the nearest regions of star birth to the Sun.
IC4605.tagline: A faint glow around the star 22 Scorpii, on the western edge of the Rho Ophiuchi clouds.

discovered.note: First catalogued by J. L. E. Dreyer in the 1895 Index Catalogue

facts.text: One of its stars, IC 4651 9122, shows wobbles that hint at an orbiting planet, though stellar activity cannot yet be ruled out as the cause.
facts.title: A possible planet

story: Star clusters slowly fall apart, and IC 4651 shows how far the process can go. Born about 1.2 billion years ago, this [[open-cluster]] now holds only about 7% of its original mass in shining stars. Roughly a third of that original mass has turned into white dwarfs and other stellar remnants; the rest has drifted off into the Milky Way. Its stars are richer than the Sun in elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.
IC4651.tagline: A billion-year-old cluster in Ara whose shining stars are just 7% of what it was born with.

facts.text: IC 4665 appears to be colliding with the older cluster Collinder 350, about 4° away in our sky. The two formed far apart, and nobody yet knows whether they will merge.
facts.title: A slow-motion collision

story: Charles Messier and William Herschel catalogued hundreds of clusters between them, yet neither included IC 4665 — probably because it is so loose and scattered. It is one of the brightest clusters left off their lists. The Swiss astronomer Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux had found it back in 1745. Nicknamed the Summer Beehive and Poseidon’s Trident, this [[open-cluster]] is young: the lithium in its stars suggests it began to form about 55 million years ago.
IC4665.tagline: The Summer Beehive: one of the brightest star clusters that both Messier and Herschel left out.

story: Sagittarius looks towards the crowded centre of our galaxy, and its Milky Way is full of glowing clouds. The most famous is the Lagoon Nebula, M 8, a stellar nursery bright enough to see without a telescope. IC 4678 is a far more modest [[emission-nebula]] less than a degree away: a patch of hydrogen gas made to glow by the ultraviolet light of hot young stars.
IC4678.tagline: A small cloud of glowing gas in Sagittarius, less than a degree from the Lagoon Nebula.

discovered.note: Found independently by Kasimir Graff in 1922

facts.text: HD 172189 is an eclipsing binary that dims every 5.7 days, and its main star also pulsates as a Delta Scuti variable, so its light flickers to two different rhythms.
facts.title: A star with two rhythms

story: Lewis Carroll’s twins have a home in the sky. IC 4756 and NGC 6633, two bright [[open-cluster|open clusters]] about three degrees apart, are known as Tweedledee and Tweedledum. IC 4756 is also called the Secret Garden Cluster, and Graff’s Cluster: Solon Bailey discovered it, and Kasimir Graff found it again independently in 1922. Its stars have almost exactly the same share of heavy elements as the Sun.
IC4756.tagline: Graff’s Cluster: a bright Serpens cluster paired with NGC 6633 as Tweedledee and Tweedledum.

discovered.note: Unpublished; rediscovered by Hugo Clemens in 1896 and Frank Bellamy in 1903

facts.text: IC 4996 lies 28′ from P Cygni, a restless supergiant star that suddenly brightened in 1600. Gaia data support the idea that IC 4996 and a cluster around P Cygni form a double cluster, though it is not yet proven.
facts.title: A double with P Cygni?

story: William Herschel saw this cluster on 20 September 1786 but never published it, and his find stayed unknown until the catalogue historian Wolfgang Steinicke went through his records. Hugo Clemens discovered it again in 1896, and Frank Bellamy a third time in 1903. Dreyer, unaware of Clemens, credited Bellamy when he added it to the Index Catalogue in 1908.
IC 4996 is a young [[open-cluster]], and seven of its brightest stars form a tight trapezium.
IC4996.tagline: A young Cygnus cluster discovered three times — and perhaps half of a double cluster with P Cygni.

discovered.note: Found independently by Gustav Gruss the same year

story: IC 4997 passes for an ordinary star in smaller telescopes; only its spectrum reveals the glowing gas. Edward Pickering and Williamina Fleming at Harvard identified it in 1896, and Gustav Gruss found it independently the same year.

It is a very young, very dense [[planetary-nebula]], and its gas is unusually hot, about 20,000 degrees — twice that of most nebulae. Stranger still, it changes. In the 1960s its spectrum shifted suddenly, perhaps as the nebula expands or as the dying star’s wind waxes and wanes.
IC4997.tagline: A planetary nebula disguised as a star, whose light changed suddenly in the 1960s.

facts.text: Among the dense filaments of cold gas that remain is Herbig–Haro object HH 555, which shoots out two jets — the outflows of a young star still forming inside.
facts.title: Jets in the dark

story: The Pelican’s likeness is only temporary. This [[emission-nebula]] is part of the same great cloud of hydrogen as the North America Nebula, separated from it by a band of [[dark-nebula|dark, dusty gas]] in the foreground. Young, energetic stars are heating the cold gas and pushing a glowing ionisation front steadily outwards. Millions of years from now, the stars and gas will be so rearranged that the Pelican will look like something else entirely.
IC5070.tagline: The Pelican Nebula: a glowing cloud beside the North America Nebula, slowly being remade by its own stars.

facts.text: The Cocoon is part emission nebula, glowing where its hottest stars ionise the gas, and part reflection nebula, where dust simply scatters their light.
facts.title: Light and shadow

facts.text: The young stars inside form a cluster of their own, catalogued as Collinder 470 — a family still emerging from the cloud that made it.
facts.title: A cluster in a cocoon

story: The star that lights the Cocoon Nebula formed only about 100,000 years ago. When it was born, modern humans were already walking the Earth.

It is not alone. This [[cluster-nebula|cluster and nebula]] is a stellar nursery, and the Spitzer and Chandra space telescopes have together found hundreds of young stars here — some in the glowing gas, others still hidden in the cold, dark cloud that trails away from it like a tail.

Among the heavyweights is BD +46 3474, a hot B-type star of around 14 times the Sun’s mass. Another resident, BD +46 3471, is a Herbig Ae/Be star: a young star of middling mass, still showing strong emission lines from the gas around it.
IC5146.tagline: A star younger than humankind, glowing at the head of a long, dark trail of dust.

story: Not every galaxy with a disc has spiral arms. IC 5267 is [[hubble-type|classed S0-a]], on the border between lenticular galaxies and spirals: a lens-shaped system with a bright central bulge and a broad disc, but only faint hints of the spiral structure and fresh star formation that light up galaxies like the Milky Way. Astronomers see lenticulars as a halfway stage between spirals and ellipticals. IC 5267 lies in Grus, the Crane, a little over two degrees from the spiral NGC 7424.
IC5267.tagline: A smooth, lens-shaped galaxy in Grus, caught between the spirals and the ellipticals.

facts.text: IC 5332 lies towards the south pole of our galaxy, so we see it by looking straight out of the Milky Way’s disc rather than along it.
facts.title: Looking out of the galaxy

story: IC 5332 is a quiet galaxy. Seen almost face-on, this [[spiral-galaxy]] has a tiny central bulge, loose, open arms and a very low [[surface-brightness]], and it makes new stars only slowly. Lewis Swift found it on 19 November 1897. More recently the James Webb Space Telescope’s mid-infrared camera looked straight through the dust in its arms, revealing a tangle of structure that visible and ultraviolet images had never shown.
IC5332.tagline: A wispy, face-on spiral in Sculptor whose hidden dust lanes the Webb telescope laid bare.

facts.text: The Crab was the first object in the sky linked to a supernova recorded in history. The case was built in the 1920s, once photographs showed the cloud was expanding.
facts.title: The first supernova match

facts.text: When the Crab’s pulsar was pinned down in 1968, it settled a debate: pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars, not pulsating white dwarfs as many had suggested.
facts.title: Proof that pulsars spin

facts.text: Because the explosion was dated almost to the day, the Crab Pulsar is the only pulsar from a historical supernova whose age is known for certain — a yardstick for the physics of dead stars.
facts.title: A dead star with a birthday

facts.text: Its radio waves passing through the Sun’s corona were used to map it in the 1950s and 60s. In 2003, Titan’s atmosphere was measured as Saturn’s moon blocked the Crab’s X-rays.
facts.title: A lamp behind the Solar System

story: On 4 July 1054, Chinese astronomers recorded a “guest star” in Taurus, bright enough to see in daylight. At its peak it outshone everything in the night sky except the Moon, and it stayed visible to the naked eye for about two years. The Crab Nebula is what that explosion left behind: a [[supernova-remnant]] still flying apart at about 1,500 kilometres per second, with a neutron star no wider than a city at its heart.

John Bevis found the glowing cloud in 1731. In 1758 Charles Messier, searching for the predicted return of Halley’s Comet, came across it and at first thought he had found the comet. When it refused to move, he realised such fixed smudges would keep fooling comet hunters, so he began listing them. The Crab became number one in the [[messier-catalog|Messier catalogue]].
Its name comes from Lord Rosse, whose drawing in the early 1840s gave it crab-like arms. Looking again in 1848 with a bigger telescope, he could no longer see the likeness — but the name stuck.
M1.tagline: The wreckage of a star that blazed in daylight in 1054 — and the object that started Messier’s list.

facts.text: M 10 circles the Milky Way about every 140 million years on a rosette-shaped path, crossing the galaxy’s disc every 53 million years or so.
facts.title: A looping orbit

facts.text: Among its 35 known variable stars are 16 SX Phoenicis stars, pulsating blue stragglers. The cluster also hosts two millisecond pulsars, each spinning hundreds of times a second.
facts.title: Pulsars and pulsators

facts.text: Harlow Shapley was the first to estimate how far away M 10 lies. His figure turned out to be more than twice the modern value.
facts.title: A first guess, too far

story: On 29 May 1764, Charles Messier described M 10 as a “nebula without stars”. Ten years later Johann Bode agreed, calling it “very pale”. It took William Herschel’s larger telescope to reveal “a beautiful cluster of extremely compressed stars” — a [[globular-cluster]]. Lord Rosse later thought he could see a dark lane crossing part of it.

Inside, gravity sorts the stars. Pairs of stars weigh more than single ones, so they sink towards the centre: about 14% of the stars in the core are binaries, against 1.5% in the outskirts. Crowded together, some of these pairs merge or trade mass, becoming blue stragglers — stars that look younger than their neighbours. Most of M 10’s blue stragglers formed 2–5 billion years ago.
M10.tagline: An ancient star swarm where gravity sorts the stars and old ones are reborn as blue stragglers.

facts.text: Seven supernovae have been found in M 100 since 1901. The first two were spotted by Heber Curtis, who in 1920 argued that spiral nebulae are separate galaxies — and was proved right.
facts.title: Seven supernovae

facts.text: On 15 April 1979 amateur astronomer Gus Johnson discovered SN 1979C in M 100. Its remnant has since been traced at wavelengths from X-rays to radio waves.
facts.title: An amateur’s catch

facts.text: Two small satellite galaxies, NGC 4323 and NGC 4328, accompany M 100. NGC 4323 is linked to it by a bridge of glowing matter.
facts.title: Little companions

story: Deep in the heart of M 100, two tightly wound spiral arms coil around a small central bar, forming a ring of furious star birth. Stars have been forming there in separate bursts for at least 500 million years, and astronomers class M 100 as a starburst galaxy.

Pierre Méchain found it in 1781, and Charles Messier saw it 29 days later, noting a faint nebula without a star. Admiral William Smyth later called it a pearly white nebula. In 1850 Lord Rosse listed it among just fourteen known ‘spiral nebulae’ — at a time when nobody knew these were [[galaxy|galaxies]] in their own right.
M100.tagline: A grand spiral of the Virgo Cluster, where seven exploding stars have been seen since 1901.

facts.text: Six supernovae have been seen in M 101. SN 2011fe reached magnitude 9.9, the brightest of 2011, and in May 2023 Kōichi Itagaki discovered SN 2023ixf.
facts.title: Supernova season

facts.text: The X-ray source M101 ULX-1 is a black hole of just 20 to 30 suns paired with a companion star. It swallows matter faster than theory says it should.
facts.title: A greedy black hole

facts.text: M 101 has about 150 globular clusters — the same number as our own Milky Way.
facts.title: As many globulars as ours

story: Count the stars in M 101 and you would reach around a trillion. Its arms are studded with [[emission-nebula|glowing clouds of gas]] lit by hot young stars — a 1990 study catalogued 1,264 of them, and three are bright enough to carry NGC numbers of their own. The pull of its companion galaxies has made M 101 lopsided, squeezing its gas and setting off bursts of star birth along the arms.

Pierre Méchain found it in 1781, describing a nebula “very obscure and pretty large”. William Herschel suspected its mottled glow might one day be resolved into stars, and in the 19th century Lord Rosse sketched its spiral with his 72-inch reflector. In 2006 Hubble combined 51 exposures into what was then its largest and most detailed image of any galaxy.
M101.tagline: A giant spiral of around a trillion stars, where bright supernovae flared in 2011 and 2023.

discovered.note: Identity disputed; usually taken to be NGC 5866

facts.text: Galaxies near NGC 5866 — NGC 5879, NGC 5907 and NGC 5908 — have been proposed too. None is as bright, or as high in surface brightness, so they are less likely.
facts.title: The other suspects

facts.text: J. L. E. Dreyer, compiler of the New General Catalogue, wondered whether Iota Serpentis had been mixed up with Iota Draconis. That would point to NGC 5928 — but it is far too faint for Messier’s telescopes.
facts.title: A typo theory

story: Every catalogue has its mysteries, and M 102 is the great puzzle of [[messier-catalog|Messier’s list]]. In spring 1781 Pierre Méchain reported a very faint nebula between the stars Omicron Boötis and Iota Draconis, and Messier added it — but without giving its position.

Two years later Méchain took it back. In a letter to the astronomer J. Bernoulli he wrote that numbers 101 and 102 were the same nebula, counted twice because of an error in the star charts. That might have settled it, but Messier’s own handwritten notes give a position that matches NGC 5866, a lens-shaped [[galaxy]] in Draco that also fits Méchain’s description.
NGC 5866, nicknamed the Spindle, is now the favourite, and NASA treats it as M 102. But the case has never been fully closed.
M102.tagline: The Messier entry nobody can pin down — its own discoverer said it was a mistake.

facts.text: Åke Wallenquist first counted 40 member stars in M 103. Antonín Bečvář raised that to 60, and modern estimates put it at about 172.
facts.title: Counting the family

facts.text: Admiral William Smyth noted the cluster’s red giant as a double star on Cassiopeia’s knee — a spot on the figure of the seated queen in the old star maps.
facts.title: On Cassiopeia’s knee

story: On 27 March 1781 Pierre Méchain found a small knot of stars in Cassiopeia, and Charles Messier added it to his catalogue. M 103 was the last entry in the list as Messier published it in 1781; the seven after it were added by later astronomers, working from his notes and Méchain’s letters.

Its stars are young, somewhere between about 13 and 25 million years old. Around 172 are thought to belong to this [[open-cluster]], and near its centre glows a red giant. A bright double star in the same view, Struve 131, is not a member at all — it simply lies in the foreground.
M103.tagline: The last object Messier published himself: a young family of stars, born long after the dinosaurs died.

discovered.note: Found independently by William Herschel in 1784; added to the Messier list in 1921

facts.text: In the 1990s John Kormendy’s team found stars near the centre moving so fast that about a billion suns’ worth of mass must lie hidden there. A 2016 study revised it to about 640 million.
facts.title: A heavyweight black hole

facts.text: The Sombrero has an estimated 1,200 to 2,000 globular clusters — around ten times as many as the Milky Way. Galaxies with big bulges tend to have more of them.
facts.title: A swarm of globulars

facts.text: In 2006 astronomers measured terahertz radiation from the Sombrero’s core that matches none of the usual sources — not warm dust, not hot gas, not fast electrons. Its origin is still unknown.
facts.title: An unexplained signal

story: Tip a galaxy almost edge-on, give it a swollen glowing centre and a dark band of dust, and you get the Sombrero. That dark band is really a ring of dust and cold gas circling the bulge, and it is where this galaxy makes most of its new stars. The whole galaxy weighs about 800 billion suns. Its classification is unclear: the Spitzer Space Telescope found its halo far larger and more massive than expected — more like that of a giant [[elliptical-galaxy]] than a [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]].

Pierre Méchain found it on 11 May 1781, and William Herschel independently in 1784, noting a “dark stratum” — the dust lane. Messier jotted it into his personal list, but only in 1921, when Camille Flammarion came across that handwritten note, did it officially become M 104.
M104.tagline: A galaxy dressed as a hat, with a black hole of hundreds of millions of suns at its heart.

facts.text: M 105 and its neighbour NGC 3384 lie inside an enormous ring of hydrogen holding nearly two billion suns’ worth of gas — and new stars are forming in it.
facts.title: A giant ring of gas

facts.text: Ellipticals are known for old stars, but M 105 hosts a few young stars and star clusters. Even such quiet galaxies, it seems, can still make stars — just very slowly.
facts.title: Not quite retired

facts.text: M 105 belongs to the M 96 Group, one of the richest galaxy groups in our cosmic neighbourhood. Rather than one giant, several large galaxies share the lead.
facts.title: A group with several leaders

story: Some galaxies are all drama; M 105 is the picture of calm. It is a near-perfect oval of old stars, with no spiral arms and barely a ripple in its smooth glow — a textbook [[elliptical-galaxy]], and the biggest one in the Messier catalogue outside the Virgo Cluster. At its heart sits a black hole of between 140 and 200 million suns.

Pierre Méchain found it in 1781, a few days after M 95 and M 96. Messier never checked it himself, so it was left out of his catalogue. It was added only in 1947, after Helen Sawyer Hogg came across a letter in which Méchain described where it lay.
