M105.tagline: A calm, smooth elliptical galaxy that joined Messier’s list only after a forgotten letter came to light.

facts.text: M 106 holds Cepheid variable stars with a range of chemical make-ups, some like the Milky Way’s and some like other galaxies’. That lets astronomers cross-check these ‘standard candles’ and sharpen distances across the universe.
facts.title: Calibrating the cosmos

facts.text: Two supernovae have been seen in M 106, in 1981 and 2014. The first, SN 1981K, was reported by E. Hummel and confirmed by Paul Wild from archive photographs.
facts.title: Found in the archives

story: Close to the core of M 106, a thin, slightly warped disc of gas whirls around a black hole of about 39 million suns. Water molecules in the disc act like a natural microwave laser, a ‘megamaser’, sending out sharp radio signals. By tracking that spinning disc, radio astronomers proved the black hole was there — and measured the galaxy’s distance directly, a first for any galaxy.

Pierre Méchain discovered M 106 in 1781. This [[spiral-galaxy]] is one of the largest and brightest galaxies in our part of the universe, similar in size and luminosity to the Andromeda Galaxy, and its core is an active Seyfert nucleus, lit up by gas falling towards the black hole.
M106.tagline: Where water molecules around a black hole gave astronomers their first direct measure of a galaxy’s distance.

discovered.note: Found independently by William Herschel in 1793

facts.text: M 107 holds 22 known RR Lyrae stars — old stars that swell and shrink, brightening and fading over a cycle of hours — and probably one SX Phoenicis variable.
facts.title: Stars with a heartbeat

facts.text: M 107 is the last globular cluster in the Messier catalogue. The three entries after it, M 108 to M 110, are all galaxies.
facts.title: Last of its kind

story: Picture a ball of ancient stars on a looping path around the Milky Way. M 107 lies close to the plane of our galaxy, but its orbit carries it out towards the halo and back in until it dips into the galactic bar — the long bar of stars across our galaxy’s centre.

Pierre Méchain found it in April 1782, but it never appeared in Messier’s published catalogue, so it waited 165 years for its number. William Herschel found it again on his own in 1793, and his son John later described a large, very rich [[globular-cluster]], “clearly consisting of stars”. It is sometimes called the Crucifix Cluster.
M107.tagline: The last globular cluster in Messier’s list, on a looping orbit that dips into the Milky Way’s central bar.

facts.text: In 2016 the Spitzer Space Telescope caught SPIRITS 16tn, a supernova so buried in dust that it could be seen only in infrared light — one of the most heavily obscured ever observed.
facts.title: A supernova in disguise

facts.text: SN 2023dbc, found in M 108 in March 2023, is among the nearest Type Ic supernovae yet discovered — the explosion of a star that had lost its outer hydrogen.
facts.title: A stripped star’s end

story: Nicknamed the Surfboard, M 108 is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] tipped almost edge-on to us — and something of a loner, an isolated member of the Ursa Major Cloud of galaxies. It weighs around 125 billion suns, and about 290 globular clusters swarm around it.

Its hydrogen gas holds a puzzle: huge expanding shells, perhaps blown out by generations of exploding stars, perhaps by gas falling in from intergalactic space or by jets from its core. Chandra has found 83 X-ray sources in it. The brightest may be an intermediate-mass black hole — heavier than those left by single stars, far lighter than the giants in galaxy cores. Pierre Méchain discovered M 108 in 1781 or 1782.
M108.tagline: The Surfboard Galaxy, where Spitzer caught a supernova so smothered in dust that only infrared could see it.

facts.text: In March 1956 Howard S. Gates spotted supernova SN 1956A in M 109, using the 18-inch Schmidt telescope at Palomar Observatory. It is the only supernova seen there so far.
facts.title: One lone supernova

facts.text: For decades astronomers disagreed over entries past M 103. Sir Patrick Moore stopped at M 104 and listed M 105 to M 109 as extras; by the late 1970s all 110 were in common use.
facts.title: Where does the list end?

story: Of the 110 objects in Messier’s catalogue, M 109 is the most distant. This barred [[spiral-galaxy]], nicknamed the Vacuum Cleaner Galaxy, is the brightest member of the M 109 Group, a gathering in Ursa Major that may hold more than 50 galaxies. At least three small satellite galaxies orbit it.

Radio maps of its hydrogen reveal a hole at the centre, where the bar lies. The bar may have funnelled the gas inwards, and the emptiness of the hole suggests that no large amount of gas has fallen in recently.
Pierre Méchain discovered M 109 in 1781, and Messier later appended it to his catalogue.
M109.tagline: The most distant object in Messier’s catalogue, and the leading light of a family of perhaps fifty galaxies.

facts.text: Scutum, the Shield, was created in the 17th century to honour the Polish king John III Sobieski. In French, M 11 is still called the Amas de l’Écu de Sobieski — the cluster of Sobieski’s Shield.
facts.title: Sobieski’s Shield

facts.text: Despite its youth, M 11 is rich in heavy elements, especially “alpha” elements such as oxygen and magnesium. One explanation is that a nearby supernova enriched the cloud it formed from.
facts.title: Seeded by a supernova?

story: Gottfried Kirch found this cluster in 1681, and Charles Messier added it to his catalogue in 1764. Its popular name comes from its brighter stars, which form a triangle like a flock of wild ducks in flight — or, from another angle, a single duck swimming.

As [[open-cluster|open clusters]] go, the Wild Duck is a heavyweight. Estimates of its mass range from 3,700 to 11,000 Suns, making it one of the most massive known, and it has been studied in great detail. At about 316 million years old, it still lies near its birthplace, close to the plane of the Milky Way.
M11.tagline: One of the most massive open clusters known — named for a flight of wild ducks.

discovered.note: Drawn by Messier but not numbered; found independently by Caroline Herschel in 1783

facts.text: Unlike its neighbour M 32, M 110 shows no evidence of a supermassive black hole at its centre.
facts.title: No giant black hole

facts.text: About half of Andromeda’s satellite galaxies orbit in a single flat plane. One model suggests these 16 once travelled with M 110, until a close pass by Andromeda broke the group apart.
facts.title: Leader of a lost pack?

story: Look closely at Charles Messier’s drawing of the Andromeda ‘nebula’ and you will find two smaller smudges beside it. One is M 32; the other is this galaxy. A label on the drawing shows he first saw it in 1773, yet he never gave it a number. Caroline Herschel found it independently on 27 August 1783, and her brother William described her discovery in 1785. It became M 110 only in the 20th century, at the suggestion of Kenneth Glyn Jones.

M 110 is a dwarf [[elliptical-galaxy]] in orbit around the Andromeda Galaxy. Unusually for its kind, it has patches of dust and young blue stars near its centre, and no one is sure why. Much of its gas seems to have been blown out by exploding stars and then stripped away by Andromeda’s tides.
M110.tagline: Andromeda’s faint companion, sketched by Messier in 1773 but numbered only in the 20th century.

facts.text: M 10 and M 12 are close together in space as well as on the sky. From one, the other would shine at about magnitude 4.5 — an easy naked-eye sight.
facts.title: Neighbours in space

facts.text: M 12 is drifting towards us at about 16 kilometres per second. Thirteen variable stars have been recorded among its members.
facts.title: Heading our way

story: Charles Messier found M 12 on 30 May 1764, the day after its neighbour M 10, and called it a “nebula without stars”. Its stars are so loosely packed for a [[globular-cluster]] that it was once thought to be a tightly concentrated open cluster.

M 12 is missing something. A 2006 study found it has unusually few low-mass stars. The authors suggest the Milky Way is to blame: as the cluster passed through the galaxy’s matter-rich disc, its lightweight stars were stripped away, leaving the heavier ones behind.
M12.tagline: A loose globular cluster that has lost its smallest stars to the Milky Way’s disc.

facts.text: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message towards M 13 describing humans, DNA and Earth’s place in the Solar System. It is still on its way, and will be for many thousands of years.
facts.title: A postcard to the stars

facts.text: M 13 appears inside the dome of St Anne’s Church, Kew, in London, based on a NASA photograph. Halley found the cluster in 1714 — the year the church was first dedicated.
facts.title: Painted on a church dome

facts.text: Its variable stars are still being catalogued: the three most recent, V63, V64 and V65, were found by observers in Spain between 2021 and 2024.
facts.title: Still finding new stars

story: Picture several hundred thousand suns packed into one ball of light. Its stars are packed more than a hundred times more densely than those around the Sun — so close that some collide and merge, forming young-looking “blue stragglers”. It is a [[globular-cluster]] of ancient stars, with only about 4.6% as much iron as the Sun, born when the galaxy was young.

Edmond Halley — of comet fame — came across it in 1714. Charles Messier added it to his list on 1 June 1764, and its individual stars were first resolved in 1779. It is one of more than a hundred globular clusters that orbit the centre of the Milky Way.

Science fiction loves it. Isaac Asimov and Poul Anderson set stories on a world inside it, the Arkonides of Perry Rhodan call it home, and in Doctor Who the Cybermen plotted to make one of its stars go nova.
M13.tagline: The great star ball of Hercules — and the target of humanity’s first message to the stars.

facts.text: About 70 variable stars are known in M 14. Many are W Virginis stars, old pulsating giants that brighten and fade over a matter of days or weeks.
facts.title: A crowd of pulsing stars

facts.text: A nova happens when a white dwarf steals gas from a close companion until the stolen layer ignites in a runaway blast. The star survives, and can flare again.
facts.title: What is a nova?

story: Several hundred thousand stars crowd into M 14, together shining about 400,000 times brighter than the Sun. Charles Messier discovered this [[globular-cluster]] in 1764. Unlike most of its kind, it is not round but decidedly elongated.

In 1938 something happened in M 14 that no one saw. A star suddenly flared up as a nova, briefly outshining every ordinary star in the cluster. The outburst sat unnoticed on photographic plates until 1964, when astronomers studying them finally spotted it — a discovery made 26 years late.
M14.tagline: A nova flared here in 1938 — and nobody noticed for 26 years.

facts.text: M 15 holds eight known pulsars, including M15-C, a pair of neutron stars orbiting each other — the crushed cores of two exploded stars.
facts.title: A nest of pulsars

facts.text: Satellites including Uhuru and Chandra have found two bright X-ray sources in M 15. The first, M 15 X-1, was the first X-ray source detected in Pegasus.
facts.title: X-ray beacons

facts.text: Along with its pulsars, M 15 is home to 112 known variable stars.
facts.title: A pulsing crowd

story: M 15 is a survivor from the dawn of the Milky Way. At around 12.5 billion years old, it is one of the oldest [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known, and more than 100,000 stars crowd into it. Over time its core has shrunk in on itself — a “core collapse” — piling up a huge number of stars around what may be a central black hole.

Jean-Dominique Maraldi discovered it in 1746, and Messier added it to his catalogue in 1764. In 1928 astronomers found a surprise inside: Pease 1, a [[planetary-nebula]] — the shed outer layers of a dying star. Only three others have been found in globular clusters since.
M15.tagline: About 12.5 billion years old, crowded to the point of collapse, and home to eight pulsars.

facts.text: In 2007, Spitzer data hinted that a supernova blast was already sweeping through the nebula and would destroy the pillars. Hubble’s second look in 2014 found no evidence of it: the pillars should last, in some form, at least 100,000 more years.
facts.title: The supernova that wasn’t

facts.text: Hubble photographed the pillars again in 2014, in visible and infrared light. Comparing the two sets of images, taken 20 years apart, let astronomers measure how fast the columns are evaporating.
facts.title: Twenty years apart

facts.text: Chandra X-ray images show young stars dotted across the nebula but not in the pillars: any stars forming inside the EGGs are not yet hot enough to shine in X-rays.
facts.title: Not hot enough yet

story: In 1995 Jeff Hester and Paul Scowen turned the Hubble Space Telescope on the heart of the Eagle Nebula. One of their pictures became famous as the Pillars of Creation: dark columns of hydrogen gas and dust, rising like stalagmites from the floor of a cavern. Inside them are knots of denser gas called EGGs — evaporating gaseous globules — and in some of these, stars are forming.

The light that sculpts the pillars comes from a young [[open-cluster|star cluster]] only 1–2 million years old, with some 8,100 stars. Its brightest member is really a pair of hot stars, about 80 times the Sun’s mass in total and up to a million times more luminous.

Jean-Philippe de Chéseaux discovered the cluster in 1745–46. Robert Burnham Jr. saw the central pillar as a queen in silhouette, which gave the [[emission-nebula|nebula]] its other name: the Star Queen.
M16.tagline: Home of the Pillars of Creation — towers of gas and dust where new stars are still being born.

facts.text: Different observers have seen different shapes in it, so M 17 is known as the Omega, Swan, Checkmark, Lobster and Horseshoe Nebula.
facts.title: A nebula of many names

facts.text: Comparing the nebula with his 1837 drawing, John Herschel suspected part of it had really changed in brightness. Observations by a Yale student, Mr Mason, made two years after that drawing, weakened the case.
facts.title: Had it changed?

story: Turn the Orion Nebula on its side and you have something like M 17. Both are vast stellar nurseries with a similar layout, but we see this one edge-on. It is one of the brightest and most massive star-forming regions in the Milky Way, part of a cloud holding some 30,000 Suns’ worth of gas and dust.

Its glow comes from a cluster of hot young stars — up to 800 of them, nine of the fierce O type — only about a million years old. More than a thousand more are still forming around the edges. In 2020 the airborne SOFIA observatory found nine protostars never seen before, and its images suggest parts of this [[emission-nebula]] formed separately, helping give it its swan-like outline.
Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1745. When John Herschel sketched it in 1833, he wrote that its figure was “nearly that of a Greek capital omega”.
M17.tagline: An Orion Nebula seen from the side — one of the brightest, most massive star nurseries in the galaxy.

facts.text: As of 2022, M 18 was one of the few Messier objects that the Hubble Space Telescope had never photographed.
facts.title: Skipped by Hubble

facts.text: Its brightest member, HD 168352, is a B-type giant: a hot, blue-white star that has begun to swell as it ages.
facts.title: A swelling giant

story: Charles Messier found this little [[open-cluster]] in 1764 and added it to his list of comet-like objects. At about 33 million years old it is young: its stars include 29 hot B-type stars, one of them a definite Be star — a fast-spinning star that sheds a disc of gas — and three supergiants.

M 18 takes about 186.5 million years to circle the Milky Way, on an almost perfectly round orbit. As it travels it bobs gently up and down, crossing the galaxy’s midplane once every 27.4 million years. All told, it holds about 188 times the mass of the Sun.
M18.tagline: A small family of hot young stars, nicknamed the Black Swan Cluster.

facts.text: M 19’s stars include Cepheids and RV Tauri variables — pulsating giants that swell and shrink — plus at least one RR Lyrae star with a known period.
facts.title: Pulsing giants

facts.text: The ROSAT X-ray satellite searched M 19 for faint X-ray sources and found none.
facts.title: Quiet in X-rays

story: M 19 appears to be one of the most flattened [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known. But looks deceive. Gas and dust between us and the cluster strongly absorb its light along the eastern edge, dimming and reddening it. In infrared light, which slips through dust more easily, the cluster looks almost perfectly round.
It lies close to the centre of the Milky Way and is a heavyweight: about 1.1 million times the mass of the Sun, in stars around 11.9 billion years old.
Charles Messier found it on 5 June 1764. William Herschel resolved it into stars in 1784, and his son John later called it “a superb cluster resolvable into countless stars”.
M19.tagline: It looks like one of the most squashed globular clusters — but the squashing may be a trick of dust.

facts.text: Jean-Dominique Maraldi spotted M 2 in 1746 while observing a comet with Jacques Cassini. Messier saw it in 1760 and took it for a starless nebula; William Herschel first resolved its stars in 1783.
facts.title: Found while chasing a comet

facts.text: Most estimates put M 2 at about 12.5 billion years old, but one recent study argues for at least 13.2 billion — close to the age of the universe itself.
facts.title: Older than it looks?

story: Imagine some 150,000 stars, around 12.5 billion years old, crowded into a single ball. M 2 is one of the larger [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known, and it does not sit in the Milky Way’s disc at all. It drifts through the galactic halo, below the galaxy’s southern pole. Its brightest stars are red and yellow giants — suns nearing the end of their lives.

M 2 may not have been born here. It is counted as part of the Gaia Sausage, the suspected remains of a dwarf galaxy that merged with ours long ago. Data from the Gaia spacecraft have also revealed a long stream of stars, stretching about 45 degrees across the sky, that is probably being pulled away from the cluster.
M2.tagline: 150,000 ancient suns — and perhaps a souvenir of a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way swallowed long ago.

facts.text: In 2005 NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope, looking in infrared, found 30 embryonic stars and 120 newborn stars in the Trifid that do not show up in visible-light images.
facts.title: Hidden newborns

facts.text: Jets like the one Hubble found are the exhaust of star formation: gas blasted out as a young star grows, made to glow here by radiation from the nebula’s central star.
facts.title: Exhaust of starbirth

story: The Trifid is four things at once. A pink [[emission-nebula]] glows as hot young stars light up its hydrogen. A blue [[reflection-nebula]] shines with scattered starlight. Dark dust lanes, catalogued as Barnard 85, split it into three lobes — the name means “three-lobed”. And at its heart sits a cluster of about 3,100 young stars.
Charles Messier found it on 5 June 1764. Its most massive star, HD 164492A, has more than 20 times the Sun’s mass, and its radiation powers the whole nebula.

In 1997 Hubble zoomed in on a dense cloud nearby — a nursery full of embryonic stars. A jet of gas shoots from a young star hidden inside, glowing in the central star’s light. Beside it, a finger-like stalk points straight at that star: its dense tip has resisted being eaten away by the radiation.
M20.tagline: Four objects in one: a glowing cloud, a blue mist, dark dust lanes and a cluster of newborn stars.

facts.text: Astronomers picked out 26 likely baby stars in M 21 from two clues in their light: glowing hydrogen and lithium. Stars destroy their lithium as they age, so finding it is a sign of youth.
facts.title: Fingerprints of youth

facts.text: Despite a few blue giants, M 21 is made mainly of small, dim stars — at least 105 members, together weighing nearly 800 times as much as the Sun.
facts.title: Mostly small stars

story: The stars of M 21 are about 6.6 million years old, born long before the first humans walked the Earth but very recently by cosmic standards. They show no real spread in age, which suggests that a single trigger set off the whole [[open-cluster|cluster’s]] birth at once.

Charles Messier discovered and catalogued it on 5 June 1764. It lies near the Trifid Nebula in our sky but is not connected to it; instead it belongs to Sagittarius OB1, a loose family of hot young stars. Some of its smaller members are so young that they are still contracting and have not yet settled into steady hydrogen burning.
M21.tagline: A cluster of stars that seem to have been born all at once, about 6.6 million years ago.

facts.text: M 22 is one of only four globular clusters known to contain a planetary nebula. First noticed by the IRAS satellite in 1986, the shell, GJJC1, is probably only about 6,000 years old.
facts.title: A rare glowing shell

facts.text: M 22 sits in front of the crowded bulge of our galaxy. As its stars pass in front of more distant ones, their gravity can briefly brighten them — so it is a useful place to study microlensing.
facts.title: A natural magnifying glass

facts.text: Its red giants show an unusually wide spread of colours, much like those of Omega Centauri. That puzzle has kept astronomers studying M 22 closely since 1977.
facts.title: A mixed-up family

story: In 1665 Abraham Ihle came across a fuzzy patch in Sagittarius: one of the first [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] ever discovered. Charles Messier added it to his catalogue in 1764. It was also one of the first to be studied carefully: in 1930 Harlow Shapley estimated it held roughly 70,000 stars around a dense core.

M 22 has surprising residents. In 2012 the Very Large Array radio telescope found two black holes, each of 10 to 20 solar masses, later backed up by the Chandra X-ray telescope. Astronomers had expected such black holes to be flung out of clusters. Now they estimate M 22 could hold anywhere from 5 to 100, and their pull on other stars may explain its unusually large core.
M22.tagline: One of the first globular clusters ever found — hiding black holes and a young glowing shell.

facts.text: M 23 lies within 5 degrees of the Sun’s yearly path across the sky, so the Moon can pass in front of it and hide its stars one by one.
facts.title: Hidden by the Moon

facts.text: A 6th-magnitude star at the cluster’s north-western edge, HD 163245, is not a member at all. It lies far in the foreground, much closer to us than M 23.
facts.title: A foreground interloper

story: Charles Messier found this [[open-cluster]] in 1764. Its stars are about 330 million years old and share almost exactly the Sun’s chemical make-up. Counts of its members range from 169 to 414, together weighing around 1,200 times the mass of the Sun.

Age is starting to show. Five members are candidate red giants — stars that have used up the hydrogen in their cores and swollen up. The orange variable VV Sagittarii may already be on the asymptotic giant branch, one of the last stages in a star’s life before it sheds its outer layers.
M23.tagline: A rich, 330-million-year-old cluster that the Moon can pass in front of.

facts.text: M 24 has a counterpart in the Andromeda Galaxy: NGC 206, a large, bright star cloud in our neighbour’s disc.
facts.title: A twin in Andromeda

facts.text: Among its crowded stars lie two planetary nebulae, M 1-43 and NGC 6567 — glowing shells cast off by dying stars.
facts.title: Hidden dying stars

facts.text: Its brightest star, HD 167356, is a white supergiant whose brightness changes slightly as it rotates — an Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum variable.
facts.title: A spotted, spinning star

story: M 24 is not a cluster or a nebula. It is a window. Here a gap in the Great Rift — the dark lanes of dust that split the [[milky-way]] — lets us look deep into our galaxy, through the crowded stars of the Scutum–Centaurus Arm, the major spiral arm between us and the galactic centre. It is a [[star-cloud]]: countless suns at many depths, blended into one glow.

Charles Messier catalogued it in 1764 as “a large nebulosity in which there are many stars of different magnitudes”. Some sources have wrongly identified M 24 with the small cluster NGC 6603 inside it.
Clouds of dust are woven through the star field. Barnard 92, the darker of the two largest, looks like a round hole empty of stars; E. E. Barnard discovered it in 1913.
M24.tagline: Not an object at all, but a window — a gap in the dust that opens a view deep into the Milky Way.

facts.text: New research suggests M 25 may form a triple star cluster with two others, NGC 6716 and Collinder 394.
facts.title: A family of three?

facts.text: Cepheids like U Sagittarii are the stars Henrietta Leavitt showed could measure cosmic distances: the slower one pulses, the brighter it really is.
facts.title: Cosmic yardsticks

story: Philippe Loys de Chéseaux made the first recorded observation of M 25 in 1745, and Charles Messier added it to his list of nebulous objects in 1764. A dark lane of dust passes near its centre.

Its stars are about 67.6 million years old, born around the time the dinosaurs died out. The cluster weighs about 1,937 times the mass of the Sun, and roughly a quarter of that is not stars at all but gas and dust between them. Among its members are two red giants, one of them a binary, and U Sagittarii, a Cepheid [[variable-star]] — the kind of pulsating star whose rhythm reveals its true brightness.
M25.tagline: Stars born as the dinosaurs died out — and perhaps one of three sibling clusters.

facts.text: One of M 26’s stars is a spectroscopic binary — a pair so close that only the spectrum of their light reveals there are two.
facts.title: Two stars in one

facts.text: At about 85 million years old, M 26 is barely a quarter the age of its bright neighbour on the sky, the Wild Duck Cluster (M 11).
facts.title: Younger than its neighbour

story: Charles Messier found this small [[open-cluster]] in 1764. Its stars are about 85 million years old.

M 26 has a puzzle at its heart. Near the centre there are surprisingly few stars. Astronomers first suspected that a dark cloud of dust in front of the cluster was hiding them, but James Cuffey argued that could not be so: there really is a “shell of low stellar space density”. In 2015 Michael Merrifield of the University of Nottingham said there was still no clear explanation.
M26.tagline: A modest star cluster with a mystery at its core: a strange gap where stars should be.

facts.text: The nebula is really shaped like a stretched-out ball, and we see it side-on, looking across its equator — part of why it can look like a dumbbell, or an apple core.
facts.title: Seen from the side

facts.text: M 27 grows on the sky by no more than 2.3 arcseconds per century. From that slow creep, astronomers worked out it can be no older than about 14,600 years.
facts.title: An upper age limit

story: When Charles Messier came across M 27 in 1764, he had found a new kind of object. It was the first [[planetary-nebula]] ever discovered: the outer layers of a dying star, puffed off into space and lit up by the hot core left behind.

That core is becoming a white dwarf. It holds a little over half the Sun’s mass, yet it is larger than most known white dwarfs. The shell around it is expanding at about 31 kilometres per second, which suggests the star began shedding it roughly 10,000 years ago.

Near the centre, the gas is full of dark and bright knots trailing comet-like tails, like those found in the Helix and Eskimo nebulae. Their bright tips mark where the star’s ultraviolet light is eating into them.
M27.tagline: The first planetary nebula ever discovered — the cast-off breath of a dying star.

facts.text: Millisecond pulsars are old neutron stars that have been spun up by pulling gas from a companion star, until they rotate hundreds of times a second.
facts.title: Spun up by a partner

facts.text: Eighteen RR Lyrae variable stars have been found in M 28 — old pulsating stars that brighten and fade in less than a day.
facts.title: Stars with a daily rhythm

story: Charles Messier noted M 28 in 1764 as a round “nebula containing no star”, seen with difficulty. It is in fact a [[globular-cluster]] of ancient stars, roughly 12 billion years old, holding about 551,000 times the mass of the Sun. Its stars contain more than ten times less of the heavier elements than the Sun does — a mark of their great age.

Its place in history came from the Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank in England, which found the pulsar PSR B1821–24 here: the first millisecond pulsar ever discovered in a globular cluster. Eleven more have since been found in M 28 with the Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia. As of 2011, only Terzan 5 and 47 Tucanae had more.
M28.tagline: Where astronomers found the first millisecond pulsar inside a globular cluster.

facts.text: Its four brightest stars form a squat quadrilateral that reminded observers of the curved, hyperboloid cooling towers of power stations.
facts.title: Why the Cooling Tower?

facts.text: Near the cluster lies WR 143, an especially hot Wolf–Rayet star in a binary — a massive star stripping itself bare in a powerful wind.
facts.title: A fierce neighbour

facts.text: Counts vary: an early estimate gave M 29 about 20 member stars, while the Sky Catalogue lists 50.
facts.title: How many members?

story: The brightest stars of M 29 are blue giants of spectral class B0 — very hot, very young stars that put the cluster’s age at only about 10 million years. Together it shines with about 160,000 times the Sun’s light, though much of that is dimmed by dust and faint nebulosity before it reaches us.

Charles Messier found this [[open-cluster]] in 1764. It belongs to Cygnus OB1, a loose association of young, hot stars, and it is moving towards us at about 28 kilometres per second. Its distance is hard to pin down, because the dust of our local spiral arm, the Orion–Cygnus Arm, makes it difficult to tell how much of its light has been lost.
M29.tagline: A young cluster of hot blue giants, half-hidden by the dust of our own spiral arm.

facts.text: In 1913 Solon Bailey began cataloguing M 3’s variable stars. The count now stands at 274 — by far the most of any globular cluster — and new ones were still being found in 2025.
facts.title: Record holder

facts.text: 133 of those variables are RR Lyrae stars, which pulse in a steady rhythm. About a third also show the Blazhko effect, a slower cycle that modulates their pulsing.
facts.title: Stars with a heartbeat

facts.text: For a globular cluster, M 3 is relatively rich in heavier elements. It is the prototype of the Oosterhoff type I clusters, one of two families astronomers use to sort globulars by their pulsating stars.
facts.title: A prototype

story: On 3 May 1764, Charles Messier spotted a small, round glow in Canes Venatici and logged it as a nebula without stars. It was the first entry in his catalogue that he discovered himself; M 1 and M 2 had been found by others. Around 1784, William Herschel’s larger telescopes showed what it really was: a [[globular-cluster]], a vast ball of stars.

Those stars are about 11.4 billion years old. M 3 floats on its own, high above the disc of the Milky Way, and has become one of the best-studied globular clusters of all. Many amateur astronomers rank it second only to M 13 among the globulars of the northern sky.
M3.tagline: The first object Messier discovered himself — and the record holder for variable stars.

facts.text: At roughly 12.9 billion years old, M 30 formed less than a billion years after the universe began.
facts.title: Born soon after the Big Bang

facts.text: Heavier stars have probably sunk towards M 30’s centre, a process called mass segregation. The result is a colour gradient: the cluster grows bluer towards the middle.
facts.title: Bluer at the heart

story: Most of the Milky Way turns in the same direction. M 30 goes the other way. Its retrograde orbit through the inner halo of the galaxy suggests it was not born here at all, but acquired from a smaller satellite galaxy.

At roughly 12.9 billion years old, this [[globular-cluster]] is among the oldest things in the galaxy, with about 160,000 times the mass of the Sun. Its core has gone through “core collapse”, making it one of the densest places in the Milky Way. Packed so close, stars interact constantly, forming new pairs and blue stragglers — stars rejuvenated by stealing mass from a partner.
Charles Messier found it in 1764 and described a circular nebula without a star. The New General Catalogue of the 1880s called it a “remarkable globular, bright, large, slightly oval”.
M30.tagline: An ancient cluster swimming against the galactic current — probably adopted from another galaxy.

discovered.note: Earliest known record, around AD 964; visible to the naked eye

facts.text: In 1885 a “nova” flared in Andromeda. No one realised it was a supernova, far brighter than an ordinary nova. S Andromedae remains the only supernova ever seen there.
facts.title: The supernova of 1885

facts.text: In 1943 Walter Baade resolved stars in Andromeda’s core and sorted them into two populations, young and old. His labels are now used for stars in the Milky Way and beyond.
facts.title: Where star populations got their names

facts.text: In 1912 Vesto Slipher measured Andromeda’s speed relative to the Solar System: about 300 kilometres per second, the largest velocity measured up to then.
facts.title: Record speed

facts.text: Charles Messier catalogued it in 1764 but credited Simon Marius, who had described it through a telescope in 1612 — even though it is visible to the naked eye.
facts.title: Credit where it wasn’t due

story: Around AD 964, the Persian astronomer al-Sufi described a “small cloud” in Andromeda in his Book of Fixed Stars. It is the earliest known record of a [[galaxy]] beyond our own — though for nearly a thousand years, no one knew that is what it was.

Was it a cloud of gas inside the Milky Way, or an “island universe” of its own? Immanuel Kant suspected the latter in 1755. In 1864 William Huggins found that its light looked like starlight, not glowing gas, and in 1920 Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis argued the question in the Great Debate. Then in 1925 Edwin Hubble found Cepheid variable stars in it, measured its distance and settled the matter: Andromeda is a separate galaxy, and ours is just one of many.

It is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] with a mass similar to the Milky Way’s, and the largest galaxy of the Local Group. The two have about a 50% chance of colliding within the next 10 billion years, perhaps merging into one giant elliptical galaxy.
M31.tagline: The galaxy that proved the universe is bigger than the Milky Way — and may one day merge with it.

facts.text: M 32 holds a supermassive black hole of about 1.5 to 5 million Suns. A faint radio and X-ray source at its centre, called M32*, comes from gas falling onto it.
facts.title: A black hole at the heart

facts.text: M 32 lies in front of Andromeda, not behind it: its stars are not reddened by Andromeda’s dust. In 2000, a star in M 32 even briefly magnified a star in Andromeda by gravitational microlensing.
facts.title: In front, not behind

story: M 32 is a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, discovered by Guillaume Le Gentil in 1749. It is the prototype of a rare class, the compact [[elliptical-galaxy]]. Half its stars crowd into its inner core — mostly old red and yellow stars, with almost no gas or dust left to make new ones, although there are hints of star formation in the fairly recent past.

How did it get so compact? One idea is that it was once a disc galaxy whose outer layers were stripped away by Andromeda’s gravity, leaving only its dense centre. A bolder one says M 32 is the core of a lost galaxy, M32p — once the third-largest in the Local Group — that merged with Andromeda about two billion years ago. Others argue it was simply born compact. The puzzle remains open.
M32.tagline: Andromeda’s compact little companion — perhaps all that remains of a once-great spiral galaxy.

discovered.note: Probably recorded before 1654; found again by Messier in 1764

facts.text: Some books and telescope software call M 33 the Pinwheel Galaxy, but professional databases reserve that name for M 101 in Ursa Major.
facts.title: Not the Pinwheel

facts.text: A clumpy stream of hydrogen gas links M 33 with the Andromeda Galaxy, announced in 2004 and confirmed in 2011. The two may have interacted in the past.
facts.title: A bridge of gas

facts.text: NGC 604, M 33’s brightest star-forming cloud, is one of the largest such regions known, with a spectrum like the Orion Nebula’s. William Herschel catalogued it separately from the galaxy.
facts.title: A giant star nursery

facts.text: In 2005, radio astronomers followed two water masers — natural microwave lasers — on opposite sides of M 33, measuring its rotation and motion across the sky for the first time.
facts.title: Tracked by its water

story: Under a very dark sky, some people can pick out M 33 with the naked eye: a faint smudge that is a whole [[spiral-galaxy]] of perhaps 40 billion stars. It is the most distant permanent object visible without optical aid, and one of the reference objects of the [[bortle-scale]] used to rate dark skies.

Giovanni Hodierna probably recorded it before 1654, as a cloud “near the Triangle”. Charles Messier found it independently on the night of 25–26 August 1764. William Herschel, who generally left Messier’s objects out of his own catalogue, made an exception for this one in 1784, and in 1850 Lord Rosse identified it as one of the first “spiral nebulae”.

In 1926 Edwin Hubble showed that 35 of its variable stars were Cepheids, helping prove that spiral nebulae are independent galaxies. M 33 is the third-largest member of the Local Group, after Andromeda and the Milky Way, and may be a satellite of Andromeda.
M33.tagline: A whole spiral galaxy that keen eyes can see without a telescope — farther away than Andromeda.

facts.text: M 34’s stars contain about 17% more iron, relative to hydrogen, than the Sun does — though they are short of nickel.
facts.title: A dash of extra iron

facts.text: White dwarfs in a cluster of known age help astronomers work out how massive a star can be and still end its life quietly, rather than exploding as a supernova.
facts.title: Clues from the dead

story: Giovanni Hodierna probably found this [[open-cluster]] before 1654, and Charles Messier added it to his list in 1764, noting that a 3-foot telescope would separate its stars. It holds about 400 stars of between a tenth and one solar mass.

At 200–250 million years old, M 34 sits between the youthful Pleiades and the older Hyades. That is about how long a star of half the Sun’s mass takes to settle into steady hydrogen burning on the main sequence; a star like the Sun gets there in just 30 million years.
Its heaviest stars have already died. At least 19 members are white dwarfs — the cooling remains of stars of up to eight times the Sun’s mass, with no nuclear fusion left to keep them shining.
M34.tagline: A middle-aged star cluster, with at least 19 burnt-out stars among its members.

discovered.note: Found independently by John Bevis before 1750

facts.text: To belong to a cluster, a star must be held by its gravity — or, if it recently escaped, have been born in the same event as the rest.
facts.title: What makes a member?

facts.text: Four probable members of M 35 are chemically peculiar stars, with unusual amounts of certain elements in their atmospheres. Overall, its stars hold a little less iron than the Sun.
facts.title: Odd ones out

story: Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered M 35 around 1745, and John Bevis found it again on his own before 1750. Sometimes called the Shoe-Buckle Cluster, it is a big, rich [[open-cluster]] — and counting its members is surprisingly hard.

Stars are judged by their motions, distances and spectra: 305 are almost certainly members, while as many as 4,349 have at least an even chance of belonging. Its central region alone holds around 1,600 times the mass of the Sun.
Many of its stars come in pairs. A 2015 study of 418 probable members found 64 whose speed towards or away from us keeps shifting back and forth — the sign of an unseen partner tugging them around.
M35.tagline: The Shoe-Buckle Cluster: a rich swarm in which more than one star in seven hides a partner.

facts.text: A young star with an outflow appears near M 36 and is nicknamed Holoea, Hawaiian for “flowing gas”. It probably lies far behind the cluster, in the star-forming region S235.
facts.title: Holoea, the flowing gas

facts.text: 38 of M 36’s members give off more infrared light than expected — often a sign of warm dust around a star.
facts.title: Glowing in the infrared

story: Move the Pleiades much farther off and you would see something like M 36. The two clusters are very similar: placed at the same distance, they would shine about equally bright. M 36’s stars are young, about 25 million years old. Which of its stars still hold lithium — a fragile element that stars destroy as they age — points to a matching age of about 22 million years.

Giovanni Hodierna described this [[open-cluster]] as a nebulous patch before 1654. Guillaume Le Gentil found it again in 1749, and Charles Messier added it to his catalogue in 1764. All told it holds about 746 times the mass of the Sun, with 178 stars down to 14th magnitude.
M36.tagline: A twin of the Pleiades, seen from much farther away.

facts.text: As of 2022, M 37 held only the third planetary nebula known to be associated with an open cluster — the glowing shell of a dying star.
facts.title: A rare planetary nebula

facts.text: M 37 circles the Milky Way every 219 million years, bobbing gently through the galactic plane every 31.7 million years.
facts.title: Round the galaxy

story: Giovanni Hodierna recorded M 37 before 1654, along with its neighbours M 36 and M 38. When Guillaume Le Gentil rediscovered those two in 1749 he missed this one, and Charles Messier found it independently in September 1764.

It lies in the opposite direction from the centre of the galaxy, still within our own spiral arm. Its 500-plus stars are somewhere between 347 and 550 million years old, and the heavier ones are already ageing. There are at least a dozen red giants, and its hottest surviving main-sequence stars are of type B9 — hotter, more massive stars have long since burned out. This rich [[open-cluster]] weighs about 1,500 times as much as the Sun.
M37.tagline: A crowd of 500 stars with a rare guest: one of only three planetary nebulae known in an open cluster.

facts.text: The small cluster NGC 1907 appears right beside M 38, but the two were born in different parts of the galaxy. They are most likely just passing each other in a fly-by.
facts.title: Ships passing in the night

facts.text: Older reports almost always mention a cross. Yet Walter Scott Houston found that through a 24-inch telescope, the host of stars made any search for a geometric figure fruitless.
facts.title: Patterns that fade

story: Giovanni Hodierna found M 38 before 1654, together with its Auriga neighbours M 36 and M 37, and Guillaume Le Gentil found it again in 1749. Observers have long seen shapes in its stars: the Greek letter pi, or, according to Webb, an “oblique cross”.

This [[open-cluster]] is about 290 million years old and holds roughly 100 stars. The brightest is a yellow giant shining with about 900 times the Sun’s light. Our own Sun, seen from M 38, would be a feeble 15th-magnitude star, visible only in a large telescope.
M38.tagline: A cluster with a yellow giant as bright as 900 Suns — and a neighbour that’s only passing by.

facts.text: Both stars in HD 205117 seem to be subgiants — stars that have run low on hydrogen in their cores and are beginning to swell into giants.
facts.title: Subgiants in orbit

facts.text: The eclipses of HD 205117 dim it by only about 5% — far too little for the eye to notice, but measurable with sensitive instruments.
facts.title: A gentle dip

story: Guillaume Le Gentil discovered M 39 in 1749, and Charles Messier added it to his catalogue in 1764. It is a loose [[open-cluster]] holding about 232 times the mass of the Sun.

Look closer and many of its stars turn out to be pairs. Of its 15 brightest members, six are binary systems, and one more is suspected. One of them, HD 205117, is probably an eclipsing binary: every 113.2 days its two stars take turns passing in front of each other. M 39 also holds at least five chemically peculiar stars, with odd amounts of certain elements, and ten suspected short-period variable stars.
M39.tagline: A loose cluster where pairs are common — six of its fifteen brightest stars are binaries.

facts.text: One of M 4’s pulsars has a white dwarf partner, and a planet about 2.5 times Jupiter’s mass circles them both. Nicknamed Methuselah, it is one of the oldest planets known.
facts.title: Methuselah’s home

facts.text: In 2023, Hubble and Gaia data revealed about 800 Suns’ worth of unseen mass packed into M 4’s centre — possible evidence of a middleweight black hole, though a tight swarm of dead stars can’t be ruled out.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

facts.text: Robert Burnham Jr. compared the telescopic view of M 4 to a spinthariscope, a device that shows tiny flashes of light as radioactive particles strike a screen.
facts.title: Sparks in the eyepiece

story: Some of the oldest stars in the Milky Way live here. In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope picked out white dwarfs in M 4 — the cooling cores of dead suns — estimated at around 13 billion years old. M 4 is the nearest [[globular-cluster]] to the Solar System, which makes such faint, ancient stars easier to study.

Its path around the galaxy is a wild one. Every 116 million years or so, M 4 dives in close to the galactic centre and then swings far back out, punching through the Milky Way’s disc on the way. Each passage shakes the cluster and strips away stars, so it may once have been much more massive.
Philippe Loys de Chéseaux discovered it in 1745, and Charles Messier catalogued it in 1764. M 4 was the first globular cluster in which individual stars were seen.
M4.tagline: The nearest globular cluster — home to some of the oldest stars and one of the oldest planets known.

facts.text: In 1991 the two stars were measured 51.7 arcseconds apart, wider than in Messier’s day — fitting for two stars moving independently rather than orbiting each other.
facts.title: Drifting apart

facts.text: The nearer star, HD 238108, is itself a true binary: it has a faint white dwarf companion, an 18th-magnitude speck just 5 arcseconds away.
facts.title: A hidden third star

story: In 1764 Charles Messier went looking for a nebula that Johannes Hevelius had reported in Ursa Major. He found no nebula — only two faint stars close together — and catalogued them anyway. Robert Burnham Jr. later called M 40 “one of the few real mistakes in the Messier catalog”.

What had Hevelius seen? Probably 74 and 75 Ursae Majoris, a brighter pair a degree to the east that can blur into a single fuzzy star to the naked eye. Why Messier settled on a pair far too faint for the eye is unclear; he may have been pointing out Hevelius’s error. Friedrich Winnecke rediscovered the pair in 1863, and it became number 4 in his catalogue of double stars.
The two are not partners at all, just an optical [[double-star]]: Gaia shows one is more than twice as far away as the other.
M40.tagline: Messier’s mistake: two unrelated stars he logged while hunting for a nebula that wasn’t there.

discovered.note: Possibly seen by Aristotle around 325 BC

facts.text: M 41 may have been observed by the Greek philosopher Aristotle as early as 325 BC — long before telescopes.
facts.title: Seen by Aristotle?

facts.text: Many observers report curved lines of stars in M 41. Walter Scott Houston found they stood out strongly in his 10-inch telescope, though they look inconspicuous in photographs.
facts.title: Curves of stars

story: No [[open-cluster]] lasts for ever. The roughly 100 stars of M 41 are about 190 million years old, and astronomers estimate the cluster will drift apart by the time it reaches about 500 million. Several of its stars have already reached old age: it contains red giants and white dwarfs, the cooling remains of stars that have died.

Giovanni Hodierna recorded it before 1654. It is sometimes called the Little Beehive, for its resemblance to the Beehive Cluster, M 44. The whole cluster is moving away from us at 23.3 kilometres per second.
M41.tagline: Possibly seen by Aristotle — a star cluster with perhaps 300 million years left before it falls apart.

discovered.note: Visible to the naked eye; first recorded as a nebula in 1610

facts.text: Some scholars think the Maya saw Orion’s Sword, nebula and all, as the smouldering embers of creation, in the middle of a cosmic hearth formed by three bright stars of Orion.
facts.title: Embers of creation

facts.text: Three stars now fleeing at more than 100 kilometres per second — AE Aurigae, 53 Arietis and Mu Columbae — may have been born in the Orion Nebula’s cluster about two million years ago.
facts.title: Runaway stars

facts.text: At the nebula’s heart, four bright young stars form the Trapezium. Galileo is credited with first seeing three of them, on 4 February 1617 — yet he never mentioned the nebula around them.
facts.title: Galileo’s three stars

story: Few places have taught us more about how stars and planets are born. The Orion Nebula is the closest region of massive star formation to Earth: an [[emission-nebula]] with about 2,000 times the Sun’s mass, lit by a crowd of young stars. Since Hubble first looked in 1993, it has found discs of gas and dust — the raw material of planets — around most of the newborn stars here.

Oddly, no one seems to have recorded it before the telescope. Ptolemy and al-Sufi listed other hazy patches but not this one, and Galileo never mentioned it, though he studied the stars around it. Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc is credited with recognising it as a nebula on 26 November 1610. In 1880 Henry Draper exposed a photographic plate on it for 51 minutes — the first photograph of a nebula ever taken.
Its colours once fooled scientists. A green glow matched no known element, so some proposed a new one: “nebulium”. The truth was oxygen, glowing in a way that needs the near-perfect vacuum of space.
M42.tagline: The nearest great star factory — where we can watch planets begin to form around newborn suns.

facts.text: NU Orionis, the star system lighting M 43, is a quadruple: four stars bound together, whose ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow.
facts.title: A four-star lamp

facts.text: De Mairan is also remembered for a 1729 experiment showing that mimosa plants keep opening and closing their leaves on a daily rhythm even in darkness — an early glimpse of biological clocks.
facts.title: A man of many interests

story: The French scientist Jean-Jacques d’Ortous de Mairan found this small nebula some time before 1731, and Charles Messier catalogued it in 1769. It looks like a separate object, but it is physically part of the Orion Nebula, cut off only by a dense lane of dust — and both belong to the much larger Orion molecular cloud complex.

Its glow is a roundish bubble of hydrogen gas, ionised by NU Orionis, a system of four stars at its centre. Unlike the Trapezium stars that light the main nebula, NU Orionis is not hot enough to make oxygen glow strongly, so this [[emission-nebula]] shines mostly in the red light of hydrogen.
Dark lanes of dust wind across it and join the dust between it and M 42. To some eyes they look like smoke rising from a chimney, or bold brushstrokes in a watercolour.
M43.tagline: A nebula that looks separate but is really part of Orion’s great star factory, lit by a four-star system.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Aratus called it the “Little Mist”

facts.text: In 2012, two hot Jupiters were found in the Beehive — the first planets seen orbiting Sun-like stars in a star cluster. In 2016 one of the systems, Pr0211, turned out to have a second planet.
facts.title: Planets around Sun-like stars

facts.text: Messier added the Beehive in 1769, though no one would mistake it for a comet. He may have wanted his list to outgrow that of his rival Lacaille, whose 1755 catalogue had 42 objects.
facts.title: A padded catalogue?

facts.text: Brown dwarfs are rare in the Beehive, probably because tides from the galaxy have stripped them away from the cluster’s outer halo.
facts.title: Missing brown dwarfs

story: For thousands of years people have looked at this faint misty patch and wondered. The Greek poet Aratus called it Achlus, the “Little Mist”, in the 3rd century BC, and Hipparchus listed it as Nephelion, the “Little Cloud”. Greeks and Romans pictured a manger — Praesepe — with two donkeys, the neighbouring stars Asellus Borealis and Asellus Australis, feeding from it. Chinese skywatchers saw a ghost riding in a carriage, and gave it a grimmer name: the “Exhalation of Piled-up Corpses”.

It was among the first things Galileo studied with his telescope, and he counted 40 stars in it. We now know it is an [[open-cluster]] of at least 1,000 stars, about 600 million years old. Its age and motion match those of the Hyades, so the two clusters may share a common origin.
M44.tagline: A manger to the Greeks, a ghost to the Chinese — and home to planets around Sun-like stars.

discovered.note: Known since prehistory; shown on the Nebra sky disc around 1600 BC

facts.text: Around 2330 BC the Pleiades marked the spring equinox point. Ancient Indian and Arab calendars began with them, and a Babylonian list of stars along the Moon’s path starts with them too.
facts.title: Where the year began

facts.text: In Japan the cluster is Subaru, from a verb meaning “to cluster together”. The car maker named after it shows the stars on its badge.
facts.title: Clustering together

facts.text: With the Hyades, the Pleiades form the Golden Gate of the Ecliptic: the yearly path of the Sun across our sky runs between the two clusters.
facts.title: Golden Gate of the Ecliptic

story: Few things in the sky have meant so much to so many people. The Pleiades appear on the Nebra sky disc, a Bronze Age artefact from Germany dated to around 1600 BC — probably the oldest known picture of them. Their name likely comes from the Greek for “to sail”, because their rising marked the start of the sailing season in the Mediterranean.

Myths around the world speak of seven sisters, and often explain why only six can be seen. Some scientists suggest these stories may reach back as far as 100,000 BC, when the star Pleione sat farther from Atlas and was easier to see on its own.

The [[open-cluster]] itself is young: its hot blue stars formed within the last 100 million years, probably from a compact knot of gas that once resembled the Orion Nebula. It is the nearest Messier object to Earth and holds over 1,000 stars. In about 250 million years, the pull of its galactic surroundings will scatter them.
M45.tagline: Seven Sisters to the Greeks, Subaru in Japan, Matariki to the Māori — the most famous star cluster of all.

facts.text: The planetary nebula that seems to sit inside M 46 is probably just a chance alignment. But the star lighting up the bipolar Calabash Nebula shares the cluster’s motion and distance — a true member of the family.
facts.title: The nebula that really belongs

facts.text: M 47, about a degree away, looks like M 46’s sibling. It isn’t: M 47 is much younger and much closer to us, so the pairing on the sky is pure coincidence.
facts.title: Not a twin

story: When the stars of M 46 were born, roughly 250 million years ago, Earth’s continents were still jammed together as the supercontinent Pangaea. Ever since, this [[open-cluster]] of about 500 stars has travelled around the Milky Way as one family, with a combined mass of around 450 suns. Charles Messier logged it in 1771, and more than a century later John Dreyer summed it up as “very bright, very rich, very large”.

The family is slowly sorting itself out. In infrared light the cluster looks larger than in visible light — a sign that heavier stars are settling towards the middle while fainter, redder ones drift outwards. A thin trail of stars to the south and west may be a tidal tail, pulled loose in some past encounter.
M46.tagline: A family of five hundred suns, a quarter of a billion years old — with a stranger posing in the family photo.

discovered.note: Recorded before 1654; Messier found it again in 1771

facts.text: M 47’s stars began shining about 78 million years ago, when dinosaurs still walked the Earth — some 12 million years before the asteroid impact that ended their reign.
facts.title: Born in the age of dinosaurs

facts.text: Its brightest member, HD 60855, is a Be star: a hot, fast-spinning star that flings gas out into a disc around its middle.
facts.title: A spinning, shedding star

facts.text: The tangled history left its mark: M 47 carries two entries in the New General Catalogue, NGC 2422 and NGC 2478.
facts.title: Two numbers for one cluster

story: Charles Messier saw this cluster in 1771 and carefully recorded its position, measured from the star 2 Puppis. Then, on paper, it vanished. Anyone who looked where he said found nothing, and M 47 joined the list of “lost” Messier objects. In 1959 the Canadian astronomer T. F. Morris cracked it: swap the plus and minus signs in Messier’s note and the position lands right on a bright cluster.

Messier was not even the first to see it. The Sicilian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna had recorded it before 1654, and Caroline Herschel later found it on her own. The [[open-cluster]] itself is young and lively: around 500 stars, led by hot blue-white B-type stars, with a few red giants adding a touch of colour.
M47.tagline: The Messier object that went missing for nearly two centuries — all because of two swapped signs.

discovered.note: Messier’s position was wrong; sometimes credited to Caroline Herschel (1783)

facts.text: Astronomers dated M 48 two ways: from how far its stars have evolved, and from how fast they spin, since stars slow down as they age. Both methods give about 400–450 million years.
facts.title: Two clocks agree

facts.text: When M 48’s stars formed, around 400–450 million years ago, no animal with a backbone had yet crawled out of the sea onto land.
facts.title: Before the first footsteps

story: Charles Messier found this cluster in 1771, but the declination he wrote down was five degrees off, so for years there was nothing at the spot he gave. Some histories credit Caroline Herschel instead, who found it in 1783. Her nephew John Herschel was smitten, calling it “a superb cluster which fills the whole field”.

At roughly 400 to 450 million years old, M 48 is middle-aged for an [[open-cluster]]: older than the Pleiades, younger than the Hyades. It holds at least 438 stars, about 2,400 suns’ worth of mass in all. Its shape is broken and lumpy, perhaps from tugs by the Milky Way’s disc, and its stars now fall into three groups, each drifting its own way.
M48.tagline: A cluster Messier put in the wrong place — middle-aged, lumpy, and quietly splitting into three.

facts.text: M 49 is pulling on a small irregular galaxy, UGC 7636, which now trails a long stream of debris behind it.
facts.title: A dwarf in its grip

facts.text: X-ray images show a structure to the north of M 49 that looks like a bow shock — as if the galaxy were pushing through the Virgo Cluster’s hot gas.
facts.title: Ploughing through the cluster

facts.text: A supernova, SN 2024kce, flared in M 49’s outskirts in 2024 — possibly a rare calcium-rich type. It was still visible in June 2025 when the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory imaged the area.
facts.title: Seen by Rubin

story: In 1771 Charles Messier, combing the sky for comets, logged a faint round glow in Virgo. Without knowing it he had found the first member of the Virgo Cluster, a vast swarm of galaxies. M 49 turned out to be its most luminous member — and brighter, in true output, than any galaxy closer to us.

This [[elliptical-galaxy|giant elliptical]] is a city of old stars. Its centre hides a black hole of about 565 million suns, and around it swarm some 5,900 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] — nearly thirty times as many as the Milky Way has. On average they are about 10 billion years old. Inside one of them, astronomers found strong evidence for a black hole of its own.
M49.tagline: The first galaxy ever found in the Virgo Cluster — and still the most luminous of them all.

facts.text: M 5 holds two millisecond pulsars, one of them in a binary. If its measured mass is confirmed, it would rule out some theories of how matter behaves inside neutron stars.
facts.title: Weighing a neutron star

facts.text: Astronomers have used M 5’s stars to test whether neutrinos carry a tiny magnetic moment — a search that could shed light on hypothetical particles such as the axion.
facts.title: A neutrino test lab

facts.text: A dwarf nova has been seen in M 5: a white dwarf pulling gas from a close companion and erupting in sudden outbursts.
facts.title: A star that flares

story: In 1702 the German astronomer Gottfried Kirch was following a comet when he noticed a faint, fuzzy “star” nearby. He had found M 5, one of the grandest [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the sky. Charles Messier logged it in 1764 as one of his nebulae. It took William Herschel, in 1791, to split it into stars — he counted roughly 200.

M 5 is now known to hold 105 [[variable-star|variable stars]], 97 of them RR Lyrae stars. Because their rhythm is tied to their true brightness, these pulsing stars serve as cosmic measuring sticks. The whole cluster is also rushing away from us at more than 50 kilometres per second.
M5.tagline: A comet hunter’s chance find from 1702 — now a laboratory for pulsing stars, pulsars and neutrinos.

discovered.note: Recorded before 1711; Messier found it again in 1772

facts.text: When M 50’s stars formed, about 140 million years ago, dinosaurs ruled the Earth and flowering plants had not yet spread across it.
facts.title: A Cretaceous birthday

facts.text: Two of its stars are chemically peculiar, with strange mixtures of elements in their outer layers that set them apart from their siblings.
facts.title: Odd ones out

story: Giovanni Domenico Cassini, the astronomer famous for his work on Saturn, recorded this cluster before 1711. Six decades later Charles Messier came across it again in 1772, while following a comet — the one now known as Biela’s Comet.

Its 500-odd stars are about 140 million years old, young enough that most are still in the prime of life. Yet two have already died, leaving unusually heavy white dwarfs behind: they must have begun as hefty stars that lived fast and burned out first.
For centuries M 50 was treated as a single [[open-cluster]]. In 2025 astronomers found it is really two sub-clusters side by side, NGC 2323-a and NGC 2323-b — making it a binary cluster.
M50.tagline: A heart-shaped cluster that turned out, in 2025, to be two clusters in one.

facts.text: Stars exploded here in 1994, 2005 and 2011. The 2011 one surprised experts: its star was probably a yellow supergiant, not the red or blue supergiants thought to be the usual culprits.
facts.title: Three supernovae in 17 years

facts.text: In 2019 a flare in M 51 turned out to be a luminous red nova — a rare outburst thought to come from two stars merging. The star had been hidden by dust, visible only in infrared archives.
facts.title: Two stars become one

facts.text: In 2005 the Hubble Heritage team assembled a picture of M 51 more than 11,000 pixels wide. It became one of Hubble’s best-known pictures; the James Webb Space Telescope added its own infrared view in 2022.
facts.title: Hubble’s famous portrait

story: In 1845, at Birr Castle in Ireland, William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, turned his giant 72-inch reflector — the “Leviathan” — on a glow Charles Messier had found in 1773. He saw what no one had seen before: curving arms winding out from a bright core. M 51 became the first “nebula” known to have a spiral shape. Nobody yet knew it was a separate [[galaxy]]; that proof had to wait for Edwin Hubble.

Those arms are no accident. Its smaller companion, NGC 5195, seems to have plunged through M 51’s disc some 500 to 600 million years ago, then crossed it again between 50 and 100 million years ago. That close encounter is thought to have stirred up the bold, star-forming arms that make this a textbook [[spiral-galaxy]]. Radio maps show the two galaxies are still joined by gas.
M51.tagline: The first galaxy ever seen as a spiral — sketched by hand in 1845, and still being reshaped by its neighbour.

facts.text: Dust between us and M 52 is thicker across its southern half, so that side of the cluster looks fainter than it really is.
facts.title: Dimmed on one side

facts.text: M 52’s stars hold slightly less iron than the Sun does — a chemical fingerprint inherited from the cloud they formed in.
facts.title: A touch poorer than the Sun

story: About 160 million years ago, while dinosaurs roamed the Earth, a cloud of gas in what we now call Cassiopeia gave birth to M 52. Today this [[open-cluster]] holds around 1,200 suns’ worth of stars, crowded around a dense core. Charles Messier added it to his list in 1774; some observers today call it the Scorpion Cluster.

Its stars are a restless lot. Among them is probably a supergiant, plus eighteen candidate slowly pulsating B stars — hot stars that gently swell and shrink — and a handful of other kinds of [[variable-star|variable]]. Curiously, the cluster’s core holds almost no gas or dust. One idea is that supernovae early in its life blew the leftovers away.
M52.tagline: A cluster with an empty heart — swept clean, perhaps, by its own exploding stars.

facts.text: Clumps, ripples and long tails of stars stretch east and west along M 53’s orbit, pulled out by the Milky Way’s gravity.
facts.title: Fraying at the edges

facts.text: M 53 holds 55 RR Lyrae stars, which brighten and dim on a regular beat. Their steady rhythm makes them handy yardsticks for measuring cosmic distances.
facts.title: Clockwork stars

story: Johann Elert Bode, the Berlin astronomer, found this [[globular-cluster]] in 1775, and Charles Messier later made it number 53 in his catalogue. It turned out to be an unusual one. In most globulars, the majority of stars are a second generation, formed from gas enriched by an earlier round of stars. In M 53 most of the red giants belong to the very first generation. Its stars are also very poor in heavy elements; at one time it was thought to be the most metal-poor cluster in the Milky Way.

M 53 may have a strange relationship with its neighbour NGC 5053. A faint bridge of stars seems to link the two, wrapped in a shared envelope — signs of a tidal tussle that may be unique in our galaxy. M 53 is also a candidate member of the Sagittarius stream, a river of stars torn from a dwarf galaxy.
M53.tagline: A globular cluster of first-generation stars — perhaps joined to its neighbour by a bridge of stars.

facts.text: In 2009 a team reported evidence for an intermediate-mass black hole in M 54’s core — the elusive in-between kind, heavier than those left by single stars but far lighter than galaxy-centre giants.
facts.title: A middleweight black hole?

facts.text: The Sagittarius dwarf galaxy is being torn apart by the Milky Way’s gravity. In time, its stars and its clusters — M 54 included — may become part of our galaxy.
facts.title: Ours after all, one day

facts.text: On the scale astronomers use to rank how densely globulars are packed, from I (densest) to XII (loosest), M 54 rates III — one of the denser ones.
facts.title: Tightly packed

story: When Charles Messier recorded M 54 in 1778, he naturally took it for one of the Milky Way’s own [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], and so did everyone else for more than two centuries. Then, in 1994, astronomers discovered the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy, a small galaxy hidden behind the crowded star fields of Sagittarius — and M 54 sits at its centre.

That made M 54 the first globular once counted as ours to be reassigned to another galaxy. Some astronomers think it may actually be that dwarf galaxy’s core; others think it is an ordinary globular that sank to the middle as its orbit decayed. Either way, it is a heavyweight, shining with the light of about 850,000 suns.
M54.tagline: A globular cluster from another galaxy — possibly the very heart of a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way is swallowing.

facts.text: With so few heavy elements, M 55’s stars preserve the chemistry of the young Milky Way, from before generations of exploding stars had enriched the gas.
facts.title: A time capsule

facts.text: Lacaille, who found M 55, also gave the southern sky 14 of its modern constellations, including Telescopium, Microscopium and Fornax.
facts.title: The man who named the south

story: In 1752 the French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille was charting the southern sky from the Cape, in what is now South Africa, when he came across this ghostly ball of stars. Back in Paris, Charles Messier tried to find it from 1754 onwards, but from there it barely clears the horizon. Only in 1778 did he finally catch it and add it to his catalogue.

M 55 is a [[globular-cluster]] holding around 269,000 suns’ worth of stars. Like other globulars it is very old, and its stars are almost pure hydrogen and helium: they contain only about 1% of the Sun’s share of iron. About 55 [[variable-star|variable stars]] have been found in its central part.
M55.tagline: Found from the southern tip of Africa, then chased by Messier from Paris for more than twenty years.

facts.text: M 56 races through the Milky Way’s halo at about 177 km per second. Faint X-rays near it may come from gas heated in its wake to around 940,000 kelvin.
facts.title: A hot wake

facts.text: Only about a dozen variable stars are known here, including a Cepheid that pulses every 1.5 days and an RV Tauri star with a 90-day rhythm.
facts.title: Stellar heartbeats

story: M 56 travels around the Milky Way the wrong way, on a retrograde orbit against the galaxy’s spin. That is a strong hint it was not born here. Its properties suggest it was captured when a dwarf galaxy merged with ours — perhaps the one whose surviving core is Omega Centauri — and it is counted among the remains of the Gaia Sausage, a dwarf galaxy the Milky Way absorbed long ago.

It is a very old [[globular-cluster]]: one estimate puts it at 13.7 billion years, close to the age of the universe itself. Its stars hold only about a hundredth of the Sun’s share of heavy elements, and together they weigh around 230,000 suns. Charles Messier found it in 1779.
M56.tagline: An ancient cluster on a backwards orbit — likely a refugee from a galaxy the Milky Way swallowed.

discovered.note: Found independently weeks later by Antoine Darquier

facts.text: The blue-green glow inside the ring comes from oxygen atoms that have lost two electrons; the reddish rim, from hydrogen and nitrogen. That oxygen light only forms in extremely thin gas, with at most a few thousand atoms per cubic centimetre.
facts.title: Painted by atoms

facts.text: The nebula is probably a rugby-ball-shaped shell, thickest around its middle, which we happen to see nearly end-on.
facts.title: Not really a ring

facts.text: The central star has a surface temperature of about 125,000 kelvin — over twenty times hotter than the Sun’s — and shines some 300 times brighter. In 2025 the James Webb Space Telescope found a disc of dust around it.
facts.title: A tiny, fierce core

story: Picture a star at the very end of its life, shrugging its outer layers off into space. That is the Ring Nebula, one of the best-known [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebulae]] in the sky. The cast-off gas has been expanding for about 1,600 years, lit up by the bare core left behind — a star that no longer burns any fuel and is slowly cooling into a white dwarf.

Charles Messier found it in January 1779 while hunting comets. Weeks later Antoine Darquier came across it too and wrote that it was “as large as Jupiter” and looked like “a planet which is fading” — a description that may have helped give planetary nebulae their misleading name. Messier and William Herschel suspected it was a knot of faint stars. In 1864 William Huggins split its light into a spectrum and saw the bright lines of glowing gas: proof that some nebulae are not stars at all.
M57.tagline: A dying star’s last breath, blown into a glowing ring — a glimpse of what may one day become of our Sun.

facts.text: M 58 is one of very few galaxies known to have an ultra-compact nuclear ring — a tiny circle of star-forming regions around its centre. The YouTube series Deep Sky Videos nicknamed it the “ring bearer galaxy”.
facts.title: The ring bearer

facts.text: Of all the galaxies in Messier’s catalogue, only four are barred spirals — galaxies with a straight bar of stars across their centre. M 58 is one of them.
facts.title: One of only four

facts.text: Two stars have exploded in M 58. The first, SN 1988A, was co-discovered by Kaoru Ikeya, the Japanese comet hunter whose name is on the great sungrazing Comet Ikeya–Seki.
facts.title: A comet hunter’s supernova

story: On 15 April 1779 Charles Messier was charting a comet’s path through Virgo when he noted a very faint nebula — so faint, he wrote, that it vanished in the slightest light he used to see the wires of his micrometer. Without knowing it, he had recorded what was arguably the most distant object then known — a title it kept until the 1880s.

M 58 is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] in the Virgo Cluster, and it is running low on fuel. Like several spirals in that crowded cluster it is “anaemic”: interactions with the hot gas that fills the cluster have left it short of the cool hydrogen it needs to make new stars. At its heart sits a black hole of around 70 million suns.
M58.tagline: For a century, perhaps the most distant thing anyone had ever seen — though no one knew it.

discovered.note: Found while following a comet; Messier logged it days later

facts.text: About 2,200 globular clusters swarm around M 59 — roughly ten times as many as orbit the Milky Way.
facts.title: Thousands of globulars

facts.text: One of M 59’s two small satellites, M59cO, is a rare in-between: midway between compact ellipticals like M 32 and the even tinier ultra-compact dwarf galaxies.
facts.title: An in-between galaxy

facts.text: In May 1939 Fritz Zwicky, who helped coin the word “supernova”, found one here. The area shows no sign of young stars, a clue that it was a Type Ia: an exploding white dwarf.
facts.title: Zwicky’s supernova

story: In April 1779 the German astronomer Johann Gottfried Koehler was following a comet through Virgo when he noticed two faint glows close together. Charles Messier logged both about three days later, as M 59 and M 60. Each turned out to be an [[elliptical-galaxy]] in the vast Virgo Cluster.

M 59 looks like a smooth, flattened oval, but it hides layers. Beneath the main body lies a flatter disc of stars, and the whole thing is wrapped in a round halo. At the very centre is a black hole of around 270 million suns, inside a core that rotates the opposite way to the rest of the galaxy. That core also holds a disc of younger, bluer stars — perhaps the scar of a merger with another galaxy that set off a burst of star birth.
M59.tagline: A galaxy whose heart spins the wrong way — a clue to some ancient collision.

discovered.note: Credit often given to de Chéseaux, 1746

facts.text: BM Scorpii, the orange giant among the Butterfly’s blue stars, is a semiregular variable: its brightness slowly drifts between magnitude 5.5 and 7.
facts.title: A restless giant

facts.text: The Butterfly follows a nearly circular orbit around the Milky Way, taking about 204 million years per lap and crossing the galaxy’s midplane roughly every 29 million years.
facts.title: Bobbing through the galaxy

story: When the stars of the Butterfly Cluster were born, about 94 million years ago, dinosaurs still walked the Earth. By cosmic standards it is young: most of its bright stars are hot, blue B-type stars, and about 120 stars are thought to belong to this [[open-cluster]].

Giovanni Battista Hodierna recorded it in 1654, though credit often goes to Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux, who saw it in 1746. Robert Burnham Jr. suggested that Ptolemy may have seen it with the naked eye in the 2nd century while observing its neighbour, M 7. Charles Messier added it to his catalogue on 23 May 1764.
M6.tagline: Young blue stars in the shape of a butterfly — perhaps first glimpsed by Ptolemy.

discovered.note: Found while following a comet; Messier logged it days later

facts.text: The spiral NGC 4647 overlaps M 60’s edge; together they are listed as Arp 116. They are probably at different distances, but Hubble images hint that a gentle tidal tug may have just begun.
facts.title: A spiral photobomber

facts.text: As M 60 moves through the Virgo Cluster, the headwind of hot gas is stripping material from its outer halo.
facts.title: Losing its gas

facts.text: M 60 dominates a little group of four galaxies, the M 60 group — the closest isolated compact group of galaxies known.
facts.title: Leader of a small gang

story: In 1929 Edwin Hubble published the graph that pointed to an expanding universe: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. The fastest-moving galaxy in his sample was M 60, racing away at about 1,090 km per second — within 2% of the modern figure. His distances, though, were about eight times too small, so his rate of cosmic expansion came out roughly seven times too high.

M 60 is a giant [[elliptical-galaxy]] holding about a trillion suns’ worth of mass, nearly half of it dark matter. At its centre lies a black hole of some 4.5 billion suns, one of the largest ever found. It is quiet now, but X-ray images show a cavity carved by jets it fired in more active times. Johann Gottfried Koehler spotted the galaxy in April 1779 while watching a comet.
M60.tagline: Home to one of the biggest black holes known — and the fastest galaxy in Hubble’s famous 1929 paper.

discovered.note: Messier saw it the same night but took it for a comet

facts.text: Eight supernovae have been seen in M 61 since 1926, making it one of the most prolific galaxies known for them. Three were found by the Japanese astronomer Kōichi Itagaki, in 2006, 2008 and 2014.
facts.title: Supernova factory

facts.text: In 2026 the Vera C. Rubin Observatory revealed a faint stream of stars to the north of M 61 — the remains, perhaps, of a smaller system being pulled apart.
facts.title: A fresh discovery

story: On 5 May 1779 Barnaba Oriani, in Milan, spotted a faint glow in Virgo. Charles Messier saw it the same night but mistook it for a comet; it was six days before he realised it was a nebula. Oriani gets the credit.

M 61 is a lively [[spiral-galaxy]] with a faint bar.
