Its centre is a starburst: a cluster of about a million suns that formed only four million years ago, beside a candidate black hole of around five million suns. Unlike most spirals in the Virgo Cluster, which are short of gas, it still holds an unusual amount of cool hydrogen — fuel for the new stars and bright glowing clouds scattered across its disc.
M61.tagline: Eight exploding stars in under a century — one of the busiest supernova factories known.

facts.text: M 62 holds ten millisecond pulsars — dead stars spinning hundreds of times a second, each paired with a companion. One is eclipsed by gas streaming off its partner; another, M62H, is orbited by a body about three times the mass of Jupiter.
facts.title: Cosmic lighthouses

facts.text: M 62 is considered a promising place to hunt for an intermediate-mass black hole. Studies so far cannot rule out one of a few thousand suns lurking in its core.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

story: Few star clusters are as heavy as M 62. It packs about 1.2 million suns’ worth of stars, making it one of the most massive and luminous [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the Milky Way, and it lies fairly close to the crowded centre of our galaxy. Charles Messier spotted it on 7 June 1771, though it only appeared in his catalogue eight years later.

Its stars came in at least two waves. About four in five belong to the first generation; the rest formed later, from gas enriched by the first. The cluster is crammed with oddities: 47 candidate blue stragglers — stars rejuvenated by merging with a partner — and more than 200 RR Lyrae stars, pulsing like clockwork. It may turn out to hold more of them than any other cluster in the galaxy.
M62.tagline: Ten pulsars, a planet around a dead star and over 200 pulsating stars — all in one ball of suns.

facts.text: The warp in M 63’s gas disc suggests its dark matter halo is offset from the inner galaxy. The cause is unclear, but the warp points towards a small companion galaxy, UGC 8313.
facts.title: An off-centre halo

facts.text: M 63 belongs to the same small group of galaxies as M 51, the Whirlpool.
facts.title: The Whirlpool’s neighbour

facts.text: In May 1971 a supernova here was spotted by Glenn Jolly and, five days later, independently by Roger Clark. Its spectrum behaved oddly for its type.
facts.title: A supernova found twice

story: Pierre Méchain, Charles Messier’s colleague and fellow comet hunter, found this galaxy first; Messier confirmed it on 14 June 1779. In the mid-1800s Lord Rosse’s great telescope picked out spiral structure in it, making it one of the first galaxies in which arms were ever seen.

In ordinary light M 63 has no long, sweeping arms — just a mass of short, broken fragments. Astronomers call it a flocculent, or “woolly”, [[spiral-galaxy]]. Infrared light tells a different story: beneath the patchwork lie two smooth, symmetrical arms. Farther out, radio telescopes trace a vast disc of hydrogen gas reaching well beyond the visible galaxy, warped like the brim of a hat.
M63.tagline: A galaxy of woolly, patchy arms — hiding a neat two-armed spiral that only infrared light reveals.

discovered.note: Bode found it a month later, Messier in 1780

facts.text: The black hole at M 64’s centre weighs about 8.4 million suns — roughly twice the one at the heart of our Milky Way.
facts.title: A modest black hole

facts.text: M 64 lives a fairly isolated life, with no big galaxy nearby to blame for its strange two-way spin.
facts.title: A loner

story: In March 1779 the English astronomer Edward Pigott came across this galaxy in Coma Berenices. Johann Bode found it a month later, and Charles Messier the following year. The dark band of dust across its bright centre earned it its names: the Black Eye, the Evil Eye or, more kindly, the Sleeping Beauty.

Its real oddity cannot be seen in a telescope. M 64’s gas forms two discs of roughly equal mass that rotate in opposite directions — the inner one, home of the dark dust, turning against the outer one. Yet its roughly 100 billion stars all turn the same way. Perhaps M 64 swallowed a gas-rich companion galaxy that was orbiting backwards, or it has slowly gathered gas clouds from intergalactic space. Either way, the inner disc is busily forming new stars.
M64.tagline: A galaxy with a bruised eye — and gas that spins in two directions at once.

facts.text: Radio surveys show a source about two arcminutes from M 65’s core. Nobody has identified it, and no published paper has studied it.
facts.title: A mystery signal

facts.text: M 65 may have a central bar — often a sign of tidal disturbance — but because we see the galaxy steeply tilted, it is hard to be sure.
facts.title: A bar in disguise?

facts.text: Only one supernova has been seen in M 65: SN 2013am, found by Matsuo Sugano in March 2013.
facts.title: One explosion so far

story: Who found M 65? Charles Messier did, in 1780. But in the 19th century William Henry Smyth wrote in his popular guide, A Cycle of Celestial Objects, that Pierre Méchain had pointed it out to Messier. Kenneth Glyn Jones repeated the slip in Messier’s Nebulae and Star Clusters, and from there it spread into many other books.

Of the three galaxies in the Leo Triplet, M 65 is the calm one. This [[spiral-galaxy]] has little gas or dust left, so it makes few new stars, and old stars far outnumber young ones. Yet it hasn’t entirely escaped its neighbours. Its disc looks slightly warped, and a fairly recent burst of star birth in its arms hints at a gentle disturbance — perhaps a weak brush with the other two, which seem to have interacted strongly about 800 million years ago.
M65.tagline: The quiet one of the Leo Triplet — and the subject of a discovery mix-up that spread from book to book.

facts.text: Radio maps show a clump of hydrogen that no longer turns with the rest of the galaxy — gas apparently pulled out of one of its spiral arms during the encounter.
facts.title: A stolen clump

facts.text: Five supernovae have been reported in M 66 since 1973. One, in 1997, may not have been a true supernova at all, but a giant star’s outburst or two stars merging.
facts.title: Five explosions

story: On 1 March 1780 Charles Messier noted a nebula in Leo that he described as “very long and very faint”. He was looking at the brightest of the three galaxies now called the Leo Triplet, a small, close-knit group.

M 66 carries the scars of a past encounter with its neighbour NGC 3628. The pull of that passage piled up mass in its centre and packed much of its gas into dense molecular clouds. The result is a [[spiral-galaxy]] with oddly shaped arms and dust lanes — strange enough to be noted in Halton Arp’s Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies. Bright star clusters line its arms, where young stars light up the surrounding gas.
M66.tagline: The brightest of the Leo Triplet, its arms pulled out of shape by a close brush with a neighbour.

facts.text: In 2016 astronomers used the Kepler space telescope to time starspots on 20 of M 67’s Sun-like stars. They rotate in about 26 days — just like the Sun — a sign that our star is typical for its size and age.
facts.title: Spinning like the Sun

facts.text: A search for wobbling stars has turned up planets around five of M 67’s members.
facts.title: Planets in the family

facts.text: M 67 may once have been about ten times heavier. Over billions of years, close encounters have flung many of its lighter stars away, leaving a cluster weighted towards heavier ones.
facts.title: A shrinking cluster

story: Most open clusters scatter long before they reach a billion years. M 67 has held together for around four billion years, nearly as long as the Sun has existed. That makes it a rare survivor, and a gift to science: well over 500 stars of the same age and distance, more than 100 of them much like our Sun, with almost no dust in the way. It has become a classic laboratory for testing how stars live and age.

With so many Sun-like stars of about the right age, some astronomers wondered whether our Sun was born here and later thrown out. Computer simulations are doubtful: the outer Solar System might not have survived the ejection, and M 67 itself probably wouldn’t have either. Johann Gottfried Koehler found this [[open-cluster]] in 1779.
M67.tagline: A cluster nearly as old as the Sun, full of Sun-like stars — once suspected of being our birthplace.

facts.text: Harlow Shapley identified M 68’s first 28 variable stars in 1919–20. Today about 50 are known — mostly RR Lyrae stars, plus six SX Phoenicis stars that pulse rapidly.
facts.title: Shapley’s variables

facts.text: M 68’s orbit is so elongated that it spends much of its time far from the galaxy’s centre, out among the thinly scattered stars of the halo.
facts.title: A long way round

story: Father and son saw M 68 rather differently. Charles Messier had found it in 1780; later, William Herschel’s larger telescope showed “a beautiful cluster of stars, extremely rich”, so compressed that most of them blended together. His son John was less romantic, calling it “very loose and ragged at the borders”.

This [[globular-cluster]] is one of the most metal-poor known: its stars are almost pure hydrogen and helium, made from gas that earlier generations of stars had barely enriched. It swings around the Milky Way’s central bulge on a stretched, oval orbit that carries it far out into the halo. Astronomers suspect it was not born here at all, but captured from a small satellite galaxy. It may be undergoing core collapse, and it shows signs of slowly rotating.
M68.tagline: A pristine ball of ancient stars on a long, looping orbit — probably captured from another galaxy.

facts.text: M 69 and M 70 are not just close on the sky. They are near-twins in size and brightness, and close neighbours in space too.
facts.title: Neighbours in space

facts.text: M 69 is listed twice in the New General Catalogue, as both NGC 6637 and NGC 6634.
facts.title: Two numbers, one cluster

story: On the night of 31 August 1780 Charles Messier was searching Sagittarius for a nebula that Nicolas Louis de Lacaille had described from South Africa nearly thirty years earlier. He found a cluster and believed he had recovered Lacaille’s object. Whether Lacaille ever saw this one is unclear, but Messier entered it as M 69 — and on that same night he also found M 70.

Most [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] are poor in elements heavier than helium. M 69 is relatively rich in them, like other clusters that belong to the crowded bulge around the galaxy’s centre. It holds about 200,000 suns’ worth of stars, packed into a bright, dense core.
M69.tagline: A globular cluster rich in heavy elements — and a close neighbour of M 70 in space as well as on the sky.

facts.text: On 29 August 2006, the New Horizons spacecraft — then on its way to Pluto — took the first image with its LORRI telescope. The target was M 7.
facts.title: First light for a Pluto camera

facts.text: As of 2022, M 7 was one of the few Messier objects Hubble had never photographed. Wide clusters like it would need thousands of pictures to cover with Hubble’s narrow view.
facts.title: Too big for Hubble

story: Around AD 130, the Greek-Roman astronomer Ptolemy described a small nebula near the sting of the Scorpion. Telescopes reveal it as a scattering of bright stars: an [[open-cluster]] about 200 million years old. In Chinese astronomy it was Yú, the Fish.

Before 1654, Giovanni Hodierna counted 30 stars in it. In 1764 Charles Messier made it the seventh entry in his list of comet-like objects, and it remains the southernmost object in his catalogue. Modern surveys suggest more than a thousand stars belong to it, spread over several degrees of sky and together weighing about 735 times as much as the Sun.
M7.tagline: Recorded by Ptolemy, catalogued by Messier, and first light for the camera that later photographed Pluto.

facts.text: M 70’s stars fall into two groups with different chemical mixes — probably two generations, the younger born from gas enriched by the older.
facts.title: Two generations

facts.text: Two possible blue stragglers sit near the core — stars that look too young for the cluster, probably made when two stars merged.
facts.title: Rejuvenated stars?

story: On a July night in 1995, two observers in different states — Alan Hale in New Mexico and Thomas Bopp in Arizona — each turned a telescope towards this small globular cluster. Each noticed a fuzzy spot beside it that did not belong. It was a comet, and it grew into Hale–Bopp, the Great Comet of 1997, visible to the naked eye for about a year and a half.

M 70 itself was found by Charles Messier in 1780, on the same night as M 69. The two are close in space as well as on the sky, near-twins in size and brightness. M 70’s heart has undergone core collapse: its stars have crowded into a tiny, dense centre, a state reached by only some [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]].
M70.tagline: The cluster two observers were looking at in 1995 when a great comet drifted into view.

discovered.note: Koehler saw it around 1775; Messier catalogued it in 1780

facts.text: M 71 weighs about 53,000 suns and shines with the light of around 19,000 — modest for a globular cluster, many of which hold a few hundred thousand suns’ worth of stars.
facts.title: A lightweight

facts.text: The irregular variable star Z Sagittae belongs to the cluster, its brightness rising and falling without a steady rhythm.
facts.title: A restless member

story: The Swiss astronomer Philippe Loys de Chéseaux found this cluster in Sagitta in 1745. Johann Gottfried Koehler noted it at Dresden around 1775, and Charles Messier added it to his catalogue in 1780. Then came a long identity crisis.

For much of the 20th century M 71 was filed as a densely packed [[open-cluster]]. It looked wrong for a globular: no tightly packed centre, more heavy elements than usual, and none of the RR Lyrae stars that most globulars contain. Only in the 1970s did it switch sides. Careful measurements of its stars revealed a short “horizontal branch” on their colour–brightness chart — a fingerprint of a [[globular-cluster]]. The branch is short because M 71 is young for a globular, at 9–10 billion years.
M71.tagline: A globular cluster that spent decades disguised as an open cluster.

facts.text: M 72 has 43 known variable stars. A 2011 census of them was used to work out how far away the cluster lies.
facts.title: Measured by its heartbeats

facts.text: When M 72’s stars were already more than four billion years old, the cloud that would form our Sun and Earth had not yet collapsed.
facts.title: Older than the Sun, twice over

story: Two great comet hunters looked at M 72 and saw only a faint nebula. Pierre Méchain found it on 29 August 1780, and his countryman Charles Messier tracked it down 36 days later and added it to the catalogue. It took John Herschel’s larger telescope to show it for what it is: a “cluster of stars of a round figure”. Harlow Shapley later noted its likeness to two other globulars, M 4 and M 12.
M 72 is a [[globular-cluster]] of about 168,000 suns’ worth of stars. They are around 9.5 billion years old, more than twice the age of our Sun.
M72.tagline: Messier and Méchain saw only a faint nebula — it took John Herschel to see the stars.

facts.text: Studying chance groupings like M 73 helps astronomers recognise real, sparse clusters — the last remnants of open clusters being pulled apart by the Milky Way.
facts.title: Why it still matters

facts.text: Gaia measurements show the farthest of the four stars is more than twice as far from us as the nearest. One of them is itself a binary star.
facts.title: Far apart in depth

story: In 1780 Charles Messier recorded four faint stars in Aquarius, wrapped, he thought, in a little nebulosity. John Herschel later looked and saw no nebula at all, and doubted that it was a true cluster. Even so, M 73 kept its place in the great catalogues, including the New General Catalogue.

The argument flared up again in 2000. One team studied the stars’ colours and brightness and declared M 73 an old [[open-cluster]]; another, using similar methods, called it a chance alignment. A third argued that four such stars lining up by accident was very unlikely. In 2002 M. Odenkirchen and C. Soubiran settled it with detailed spectra: the stars lie at very different distances and move in different directions. M 73 is an [[asterism]].
M73.tagline: Four stars, one long argument: a real cluster or a coincidence? It took until 2002 to settle.

discovered.note: Méchain passed it on to Messier

facts.text: In 2002 Yoji Hirose discovered SN 2002ap, a rare Type Ic explosion of the extra-powerful kind called a hypernova. It was the brightest supernova of the year, and it helped test ideas about gamma-ray bursts.
facts.title: A hypernova

facts.text: Ben Sugerman found a light echo from SN 2003gd: the blast’s light bouncing off a sheet of dust in front of it. Such echoes are rare, and they reveal what the dust is made of.
facts.title: An echo of light

facts.text: In 2005 the Chandra X-ray Observatory found a source in M 74 that flares every two hours or so with more X-ray power than a neutron star can manage. It may be a black hole of around 10,000 suns.
facts.title: A middleweight black hole?

story: Two clean, well-defined arms wind out from the centre of M 74, making it the classic example of a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy]], home to around 100 billion stars. Because we see it face-on, professional astronomers use it to study how spiral arms form and keep their shape. Pierre Méchain found it in 1780 and passed the news to Charles Messier, who added it to his list.

In July 2022 it became one of the early targets of the James Webb Space Telescope. Since 2002 three supernovae have been seen in its arms, and in 2019 a flare appeared that may have been a giant star’s violent outburst.
M74.tagline: A textbook two-armed spiral, home to a hypernova and a mysterious flickering X-ray source.

facts.text: Astronomers have found 62 candidate blue stragglers here — stars that look too young for the cluster, probably made when two stars merged. Most of them crowd into the dense core.
facts.title: Rejuvenated stars

facts.text: Together its stars shine about 180,000 times brighter than the Sun, and the whole cluster turns slowly on its axis.
facts.title: Bright as 180,000 suns

story: Neither Pierre Méchain, who spotted M 75 in Sagittarius in 1780, nor Charles Messier, who catalogued it the same year, could have guessed its story. It lies on the far side of the galaxy’s centre, and it is one of the most densely packed [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known — class I on the scale astronomers use, the tightest category of all. Even so, its core has not yet collapsed.

It is probably an immigrant. M 75 belongs to the Gaia Sausage, thought to be the remains of a dwarf galaxy that merged with the Milky Way long ago. It still follows a wildly stretched orbit through the galaxy’s halo, completing a lap roughly every 400 million years.
M75.tagline: One of the most tightly packed globular clusters known — a refugee from a swallowed galaxy.

facts.text: It is called the Little Dumbbell for its resemblance to the brighter Dumbbell Nebula, M 27, in Vulpecula. Others call it the Barbell or the Cork.
facts.title: Named after a big sibling

facts.text: The white dwarf at its heart has a surface temperature of about 88,000 kelvin — some fifteen times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts.title: A white-hot remnant

story: One nebula or two? Pierre Méchain found this little glow in Perseus in 1780, and it became number 76 in Messier’s list. Later observers took it for two separate nebulae, so it carries two numbers in the New General Catalogue: NGC 650 and NGC 651.

Its true nature took time to pin down. William Huggins’s spectrum showed it was glowing gas, and in 1891 Isaac Roberts suggested it might be a ring like M 57, seen from the side. Heber Curtis finally classed it as a [[planetary-nebula]] in 1918. Roberts was close. As it was dying, the star first threw off a ring, which we see edge-on as the bright central bar. Soon after, it shed the rest of its outer layers in two lobes billowing from the ring’s openings, leaving a white dwarf at the centre.
M76.tagline: A dying star’s ring, seen edge-on and flanked by two lobes — once thought to be two separate nebulae.

discovered.note: Méchain passed it on to Messier

facts.text: In November 2022 the IceCube detector, buried in Antarctic ice, traced high-energy neutrinos to M 77’s core. It was only the fourth known source of neutrinos from space, after the Sun, Supernova 1987A and a distant blazar.
facts.title: Ghost particles

facts.text: M 77 leads a small group of galaxies. One of them, the edge-on spiral NGC 1055, has probably been twisted out of shape by M 77’s gravity.
facts.title: A twisted neighbour

facts.text: In visible light M 77 shows no bar, but infrared images reveal a prominent one across its centre.
facts.title: A hidden bar

story: Nebula or star cluster? Pierre Méchain, who found M 77 in 1780, called it a nebula; Charles Messier and William Herschel both thought it was a cluster of stars. It is neither. M 77 is a [[spiral-galaxy]] with a fiercely active core, one of the brightest Seyfert galaxies — a class named after Carl Seyfert, who described galaxies with such intense, star-like centres in 1943.

At its heart a supermassive black hole is feeding on gas, but we cannot see it directly: thick dust blocks the view. In 2022 astronomers mapped that hidden dust cloud in infrared light. M 77 is the prototype of its class and a key test of a big idea — that two kinds of active galaxy may be the same thing seen from different angles, with dust hiding the core in one view but not the other.
M77.tagline: A galaxy with a blazing, dust-hidden heart — and one of the first known sources of cosmic neutrinos.

facts.text: In May 2024 the European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope released a sharp image of M 78 that revealed hundreds of thousands of previously unseen objects, including bodies too small to shine as stars.
facts.title: Euclid’s deep look

facts.text: Infrared maps show the gas breaking into clumps weighing from about a third of a Sun to five Suns — the seeds of future stars.
facts.title: Seeds of stars

story: M 78 makes no light of its own. It is a cloud of dust, part of the vast Orion B molecular cloud, and it glows by reflecting the light of two hot B-type stars, like fog lit by headlamps. That makes it a [[reflection-nebula]] — the brightest of a small family of them in this corner of Orion. Amateur astronomers have nicknamed it Casper the Friendly Ghost.

Inside, a new generation of stars is forming. Infrared telescopes reveal a hidden cluster, 45 T Tauri stars still in the making, and 17 Herbig–Haro objects — glowing knots where jets from newborn stars slam into the surrounding gas. Pierre Méchain found M 78 in 1780, and Charles Messier catalogued it that same year.
M78.tagline: A ghostly fan of starlit dust — and a nursery where dozens of new stars are still taking shape.

facts.text: M 54 and M 79 are the two globular clusters in Messier’s list thought to have come from other galaxies.
facts.title: Messier’s other immigrant

facts.text: Infrared images show that most of M 79’s brightest stars are red giants — old stars that have swollen up near the end of their lives.
facts.title: Red giants rule

story: Most of the Milky Way’s [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] crowd towards the galactic centre, in Sagittarius, Scorpius and Ophiuchus. M 79, found by Pierre Méchain in 1780, sits in Lepus instead. Why is it out here?

One idea is that it is not one of ours at all. Like M 54, it may have arrived with a dwarf galaxy — in this case the Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy, which some astronomers think is having a close encounter with the Milky Way right now. Others doubt that galaxy exists at all, and M 79 may instead belong to the Gaia Sausage, the wreck of an older merger. Wherever it came from, the Milky Way is now pulling it apart: the cluster trails a long tidal tail of stars.
M79.tagline: A globular cluster far from the galaxy’s heart — possibly a migrant from a disputed dwarf galaxy.

facts.text: From mid-northern latitudes, just two star-forming nebulae are faintly visible to the naked eye: the Lagoon and the Orion Nebula.
facts.title: Only two of its kind

facts.text: The Lagoon’s Hourglass, named by John Herschel, is a different object from the Engraved Hourglass Nebula in Musca, a dying star’s shell made famous by Hubble.
facts.title: Not that Hourglass

story: Inside the Lagoon, stars are being born right now. In 2006 astronomers found four Herbig–Haro objects in its brightest region, the Hourglass — glowing knots where jets from newborn stars slam into the surrounding gas. They are direct evidence that young stars here are still gathering mass.

The whole cloud is an [[emission-nebula]], lit from within by hot young stars. One hot O-type star has carved a funnel-shaped structure into it with its ultraviolet light. Long-exposure photographs show the gas glowing pink, but to the eye it looks grey: our night vision is nearly colour-blind.

Giovanni Hodierna discovered the Lagoon in 1654. John Herschel named the Hourglass, and E. E. Barnard catalogued several dark Bok globules against its glow — dense knots of dust and gas where stars may one day form.
M8.tagline: A star factory at work — one of only two you can see with the naked eye from mid-northern latitudes.

facts.text: M 80 has an unusually large population of blue stragglers — stars that look younger than the cluster, probably made when stars merged or stole gas from a partner. Hubble found them gathered in distinct regions of the core.
facts.title: Rejuvenated stars

facts.text: T Scorpii, spotted by Arthur Auwers at Königsberg, was the first nova ever seen in a star cluster. It is still thought to be the only classical nova known for certain in a globular cluster.
facts.title: A first for novae

story: Imagine several hundred thousand stars squeezed into a ball so tight that they regularly come close to one another, or even collide. That is M 80, one of the densest [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the Milky Way. From a planet near its centre, the sky would be crowded with brilliant stars. Charles Messier found it in 1781.
Then, on 21 May 1860, one of its stars erupted. The nova T Scorpii briefly outshone the entire cluster, bright enough to be seen in binoculars, before fading back into the crowd.
M80.tagline: One of the most crowded places in the galaxy — where, in 1860, a single star briefly outshone them all.

discovered.note: Found on 31 December 1774; Méchain and Messier recovered it in 1779

facts.text: SN 1993J, found by F. García in Spain, began like a normal Type II supernova, rich in hydrogen. Then the hydrogen faded and helium took over. It was classed as Type IIb, a transitional kind, and was the second-brightest Type II of the 20th century.
facts.title: A supernova that changed costume

facts.text: In 2022 astronomers reported that a repeating fast radio burst — a flash of radio waves lasting a few thousandths of a second — may come from M 81.
facts.title: Mystery radio flashes

facts.text: The Hubble Space Telescope pinned down M 81’s distance by timing its Cepheid variable stars, using the rule linking their pulse to their brightness discovered by Henrietta Swan Leavitt.
facts.title: Measured by Hubble

story: On the last night of 1774, Johann Elert Bode in Berlin spotted two faint patches of light in Ursa Major. The brighter one now carries his name: Bode’s Galaxy. Pierre Méchain and Charles Messier found it again in 1779, and it entered Messier’s catalogue as M 81.

M 81 is a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy]], the largest in a group of galaxies that are among our nearer neighbours. It is not a gentle host. Its gravity has tugged at its companions M 82 and NGC 3077, drawing streamers of hydrogen out of all three galaxies and sending gas tumbling into the hearts of the smaller two, where it lit up bursts of star birth. At M 81’s own centre, a black hole of about 70 million suns feeds a disc of gas and fires a one-sided jet — and it may have a smaller black hole partner circling it every 30 years or so.
M81.tagline: Found on New Year’s Eve 1774 — a grand spiral whose pull set its neighbour M 82 ablaze with new stars.

discovered.note: Méchain found it again in 1779 and told Messier

facts.text: M 82 was long classed as an irregular galaxy. In 2005 near-infrared images revealed two symmetric spiral arms, hidden until then by dust and our nearly edge-on view.
facts.title: A spiral in disguise

facts.text: On 21 January 2014 lecturer Steve Fossey and four of his students at the University of London Observatory spotted a new star in M 82. SN 2014J was the closest Type Ia supernova since 1972.
facts.title: A supernova found in class

facts.text: In 2010 radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank found an object in M 82 unlike anything seen before. Its material appears to move four times faster than light — an illusion of a jet aimed close to our line of sight. No theory fully explains it.
facts.title: The unexplained object

facts.text: In 2014 astronomers studying M 82 discovered M82 X-2, the brightest pulsar then known.
facts.title: Record-breaking pulsar

story: Johann Elert Bode found M 82 alongside M 81 in 1774, describing a “nebulous patch”, “very pale and of elongated shape”. Seen almost edge-on, it does look like a cigar. But this is a galaxy in overdrive. Its centre is forming stars about ten times faster than the whole Milky Way, making M 82 the classic example of a starburst galaxy.

The trigger was its big neighbour, M 81. Close passages over the past few hundred million years funnelled gas into M 82’s core, where Hubble has counted 197 massive young star clusters. The heaviest stars there live fast and die young: in the busiest clumps a supernova goes off roughly once a decade, and together these blasts drive a “superwind” that blows gas out of the galaxy.
M82.tagline: A galaxy in overdrive: stars born at a furious pace, and a wind of gas blasting out above and below.

discovered.note: Messier added it to his catalogue in 1781

facts.text: Australian supernova hunter Robert Evans found SN 1983N here. It was the first Type I supernova detected in radio waves and the first to clearly show a large haul of freshly made iron, and it became the modern prototype of Type Ib.
facts.title: A supernova of firsts

facts.text: In April 2025 astronomers published the first clues that a supermassive black hole may lie at M 83’s centre.
facts.title: A hidden heart?

facts.text: M 83 anchors one half of the Centaurus A/M 83 Group of galaxies; the galaxies around Centaurus A form the other half, and the two subgroups barely move relative to each other.
facts.title: Two groups in one

story: On 17 February 1752, at the Cape of Good Hope, Nicolas Louis de Lacaille noted a faint glow near the border of Hydra and Centaurus. Nearly thirty years later, in March 1781, Charles Messier added it to his catalogue. Today it is called the Southern Pinwheel, for its likeness to the Pinwheel Galaxy, M 101.

M 83 is a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy]] with a weak bar, and it is busy making stars. They form most vigorously along the leading edges of its arms, just as the theory of spiral density waves predicts. In 2008 NASA’s GALEX satellite found young stars even in its far outskirts, where astronomers had thought the raw material for stars was missing. A brush with the dwarf galaxy NGC 5253 within the last billion years probably set off bursts of star birth at the centres of both.
M83.tagline: A grand southern spiral — and the home of a supernova that defined a whole class of exploding stars.

facts.text: SN 1991bg, spotted by eye by Reiki Kushida in December 1991, was an unusually faint Type Ia supernova. It became the template for a whole class, now called “91bg-like” supernovae.
facts.title: A template explosion

facts.text: M 84 has around 1,775 globular clusters — a lot by Milky Way standards, but far fewer than expected for a galaxy of its kind.
facts.title: Fewer clusters than expected

story: In 1781 Charles Messier, combing Virgo for nebulous objects, logged M 84 near what we now know is the crowded heart of the Virgo Cluster. It is a giant ball of mostly old stars — astronomers still debate whether to call it an [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical]] or a lenticular — wrapped in a massive halo of dark matter.

Radio telescopes and Hubble have found two jets shooting from its centre, and a disc of gas and stars whirling around a black hole of about 1.5 billion suns. Galaxies like this are usually quiet, with almost no new stars forming. Yet three supernovae have been credited to M 84 — although one may belong to a neighbour — a rate that is rare for its kind and may mean it hides a population of middle-aged stars.
M84.tagline: A quiet giant with a black hole of 1.5 billion suns — and a habit of unusual supernovae.

facts.text: In January 2006 a strange red flare appeared on M 85’s outskirts. M85 OT2006-1 became the first object ever identified as a luminous red nova — a kind of outburst now thought to come from merging stars.
facts.title: A new kind of outburst

facts.text: Indirect methods suggest M 85 should hold a black hole of around 100 million suns. Yet measurements of its stars’ motions hint that it may have no central massive black hole at all.
facts.title: A missing black hole?

facts.text: Big galaxies like M 85 usually have red and blue families of globular clusters. M 85 has those, plus an in-between group and an even redder one.
facts.title: Clusters of many colours

story: At first glance M 85 is a smooth, featureless [[galaxy]], somewhere between a lenticular and an elliptical. Look deeper and it is covered in scars: shells and ripples of stars in its outer parts, thought to be debris from a merger with another galaxy between 4 and 7 billion years ago. Pierre Méchain found it in 1781, on the northern outskirts of the Virgo Cluster.

That past still shapes it. Its centre holds stars under 3 billion years old, some arranged in a ring — perhaps from a late burst of star birth. The galaxy seems to be in the middle of a makeover, slowly turning from a lenticular into an elliptical. It has almost no cool hydrogen gas left, and it is still tangling with its neighbours: the spiral NGC 4394 and a small elliptical, MCG 3-32-38.
M85.tagline: Scarred by an ancient merger — and home to the first luminous red nova ever identified.

facts.text: M 86’s halo is threaded with streams of stars, thought to be the remains of small dwarf galaxies it has torn apart and absorbed.
facts.title: Eaten neighbours

facts.text: Around 3,800 globular clusters orbit M 86 — roughly twenty times as many as the Milky Way has.
facts.title: A crowd of globulars

story: Almost every galaxy beyond our immediate neighbourhood is moving away from us, carried by the expansion of the universe. M 86 bucks the trend. It has the largest blueshift of any Messier object, closing in at about 244 km per second: its own plunge through the Virgo Cluster carries it towards us fast enough to overcome the cosmic expansion.

That speed comes at a price. As M 86 ploughs through the cluster’s hot gas, the headwind strips away its own gas, leaving a long trail of X-ray-bright gas that the Chandra telescope has traced. Filaments of glowing gas also link it to the badly disrupted spiral NGC 4438, from which M 86 may have pulled gas and dust. Charles Messier found this [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical]] or lenticular galaxy in 1781.
M86.tagline: A giant galaxy heading our way — trailing a plume of hot gas as it plunges through the Virgo Cluster.

facts.text: M 87 is one of the brightest radio sources in the sky, known as Virgo A. Rockets in the 1960s also found it to be the first X-ray source known in Virgo.
facts.title: A radio beacon

facts.text: In 1978 the motions of its stars pointed to a central mass of billions of suns. In 1993 the newly repaired Hubble Space Telescope weighed the black hole again from its swirling gas disc — one of its first tests after the repair.
facts.title: Weighing the giant

facts.text: Before 1991, Otto Struve was the only person known to have seen M 87’s jet with his own eyes, through the 100-inch Hooker telescope.
facts.title: Seen by one man

story: On 10 April 2019 the world saw its first picture of a black hole: a ring of glowing gas around a dark shadow, at the heart of M 87. It took the Event Horizon Telescope — radio dishes across the Earth linked into one planet-sized telescope — to capture it, from data gathered in 2017. The black hole weighs about 6.5 billion suns, and its event horizon is wider than the orbits of all the planets around our Sun.

Long before that, M 87 kept surprising astronomers. Charles Messier logged it as a nebula in 1781. In 1918 Heber Curtis noticed a “curious straight ray” leading from its core — the first sighting of the jet of plasma that the black hole flings out at close to the speed of light. M 87 is a supergiant [[elliptical-galaxy]] of several trillion stars, wrapped in about 15,000 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], against the Milky Way’s 150 to 200.
M87.tagline: The galaxy whose black hole was the first ever photographed — a monster bigger than our whole planetary system.

facts.text: M 88 is a Seyfert galaxy, its nucleus lit by highly ionised gas. Near the centre sits a dense knot of gas with two bright peaks, fed by material streaming in along the spiral arms.
facts.title: An active heart

facts.text: The Virgo Cluster Catalogue lists 2,096 candidate member galaxies. M 88 is entry number 1401.
facts.title: One of 2,096

story: M 88 is falling. This [[spiral-galaxy]] is on a long, stretched orbit that is carrying it almost straight towards the centre of the Virgo Cluster, where the giant galaxy M 87 sits. It will make its closest approach in about 200 to 300 million years. Charles Messier found it in 1781; it is one of fifteen Messier objects that belong to this great cluster.

The journey is already costing it. As M 88 pushes through the thin, hot gas between the galaxies, the pressure is stripping hydrogen from its outer edges — so far along its western, leading side. For now its arms remain neat and regular, and can be followed all the way into the core, where inflowing gas feeds a black hole of about 80 million suns.
M88.tagline: A graceful spiral on a plunging path towards the heart of the Virgo Cluster.

facts.text: A 2006 survey estimated about 2,000 globular clusters around M 89 — roughly ten times as many as orbit the Milky Way.
facts.title: A swarm of globulars

facts.text: As M 89 moves through the Virgo Cluster’s hot gas, the headwind is stripping away some of its own gas.
facts.title: Stripped as it goes

story: Could a galaxy be a perfect sphere? M 89 may be one of the roundest known. Other galaxies of its kind that are close enough to measure easily all show some flattening; M 89 shows almost none. Either it really is a sphere, or it is an egg-shaped [[elliptical-galaxy]] that happens to point straight at us. Charles Messier found it on 18 March 1781.

Its past was livelier than its smooth face suggests. A vast structure of gas and dust surrounds it, along with traces of jets — signs that it may once have blazed as a quasar or radio galaxy. Shells and plumes of stars point to one or more mergers. And X-ray images from Chandra show two rings of hot gas in its core, the mark of an outburst just 1 to 2 million years ago. A black hole of about 480 million suns sits at its centre.
M89.tagline: Perhaps the roundest galaxy known — with the fading signs of a wilder past.

facts.text: Astronomers have found 24 variable stars in M 9, including 21 RR Lyrae stars, a Type II Cepheid and an eclipsing binary — two stars that take turns hiding each other.
facts.title: Twenty-four variables

facts.text: Many globular clusters contain blue stragglers, stars that look too young for their cluster, made when stars merge or trade mass. None has been found in M 9.
facts.title: No stragglers

story: M 9 lives in a crowded neighbourhood. It is one of the [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] closest to the centre of the Milky Way, and it lies against a dark cloud of dust catalogued as Barnard 64. Altogether its stars shine with about 120,000 times the light of the Sun.

Charles Messier found it on 3 June 1764 and called it a “nebula without stars”. Nineteen years later William Herschel turned his reflector on it and resolved individual stars, packed more and more densely towards the middle.
M9.tagline: An ancient star ball close to the heart of the galaxy, set against a dark cloud of dust.

facts.text: M 90 is approaching us, which once suggested it lay in front of the Virgo Cluster. In fact, galaxies inside the cluster move so fast in all directions that some of them are heading our way.
facts.title: A misleading blueshift

facts.text: The small galaxy IC 3583 was once thought to be M 90’s satellite. The two are now thought to be too far apart to interact at all.
facts.title: A false companion

facts.text: Around 1,000 globular clusters orbit M 90 — several times as many as the Milky Way has.
facts.title: A thousand globulars

story: In true brightness M 90 outshines even the Andromeda Galaxy, and it is one of the largest spirals in the Virgo Cluster. But it is being stripped bare. As it races through the hot gas that fills the cluster, the headwind has torn away much of its own gas, leaving long tails of glowing gas behind and even a few star-forming clouds marooned outside its disc. With little fuel left, its arms look smooth and quiet, and M 90 has become a prototype of the “anaemic” [[spiral-galaxy]].

Its heart tells a different story. Around 50,000 hot, massive stars were born there only 5 to 6 million years ago, among supergiants left by earlier bursts. Supernovae in the nucleus — perhaps as many as 100,000 — have driven “superwinds” that blow gas out of the galaxy in two jets. Charles Messier found it in 1781.
M90.tagline: A great spiral being stripped bare as it races through the Virgo Cluster — while its core still blazes.

facts.text: The Virgo Cluster as a whole is receding from us at about 1,100 km/s. M 91 is moving through it towards us at around 700 km/s, so it seems to recede at only about 400 km/s.
facts.title: Swimming against the current

facts.text: In 1997 measurements of Cepheid variables — stars whose pulsing rhythm reveals their true brightness — confirmed that M 91 really belongs to the Virgo Cluster.
facts.title: Confirmed by pulsing stars

story: For almost two hundred years, one entry in [[messier-catalog|Charles Messier’s catalogue]] pointed at empty sky. M 91 was the last of eight faint “nebulae” he found in Coma Berenices in 1781, logged as a nebula without stars, fainter than M 90. Yet nothing could be found at the position he gave.

The culprit was a bookkeeping slip. Messier had worked out its place from the galaxy M 58 when he should have used M 89. In 1969 amateur astronomer William C. Williams redid the sums from M 89 and landed on NGC 4548 — a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] that William Herschel had catalogued in 1784. The match was almost perfect.
M 91 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a vast swarm of galaxies. It is what astronomers call an anaemic spiral, with little gas left and few new stars being born.
M91.tagline: The Messier object that went missing for nearly two centuries, until an amateur cracked the case in 1969.

facts.text: As Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, the north celestial pole passes within a degree of M 92. About 12,000 years ago it was the northern sky’s ‘pole cluster’, and it will be again in roughly 14,000 years.
facts.title: Once the pole cluster

facts.text: M 92 hosts at least two generations of stars. The second is slightly richer in helium, a sign that the cluster made stars more than once.
facts.title: Two generations

facts.text: At least 17 RR Lyrae stars live in M 92. These old stars swell and shrink, brightening and fading over a cycle that lasts only hours.
facts.title: Stars with a heartbeat

story: Some 11 billion years ago, when the Milky Way was young, a great ball of stars formed that still survives today. M 92 is one of the oldest [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in our galaxy, with the mass of some 330,000 suns packed into it.

Its stars contain very little besides hydrogen and helium. Their iron content is only about half a percent of the Sun’s, a sign that they formed early, before generations of stars had enriched space with heavier elements.

Johann Elert Bode found the cluster on 27 December 1777. Charles Messier came across it again in March 1781, not knowing of Bode’s find, and gave it the number 92. In 1783 William Herschel became the first to resolve it into individual stars.
M92.tagline: One of the oldest star clusters in our galaxy — and, 12,000 years ago, the northern sky’s pole cluster.

discovered.note: Found again independently by Caroline Herschel in 1783

facts.text: M 93 lies almost on the plane of the Milky Way and takes about 243 million years to orbit the galactic centre. Since its birth it has completed only about one and a half laps.
facts.title: One and a half laps

facts.text: Astronomers have found 54 variable stars in M 93, among them Delta Scuti and Gamma Doradus stars — stars that rhythmically brighten and fade as they pulsate.
facts.title: A cluster of pulsing stars

story: The constellation Puppis is the poop deck — the stern — of the Argo, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, and M 93 rides on it. Charles Messier added this [[open-cluster]] to his catalogue of comet-like objects in 1781. Two years later Caroline Herschel, William’s younger sister and a skilled comet hunter herself, found it again, thinking that Messier had not yet listed it.
Its stars were born around 387 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs — youngsters next to the Sun, which is more than ten times older. It is sometimes called the Critter Cluster.
M93.tagline: A swarm of stars on the stern of Jason’s ship Argo, born long before the first dinosaurs.

facts.text: A 2008 study found that ordinary stars and gas could account for all of M 94’s mass, leaving little or no room for dark matter. The result is controversial and has not been confirmed.
facts.title: Where is the dark matter?

facts.text: Most spirals have a central bulge of old stars. M 94 has a ‘pseudobulge’ instead: a ring of young stars around an oval core that only looks like a bulge when seen face-on.
facts.title: A bulge that isn’t

facts.text: M 94 is one of the brightest members of the M 94 Group, which holds 16 to 24 galaxies — although only a few of them seem to be held together by gravity.
facts.title: Head of a loose family

story: In deep photographs M 94 stares back like an eye, which is why it is also called the Cat’s Eye or Crocodile Eye Galaxy. The bright ‘iris’ is a ring of intense star birth around the core, fed by gas that an oval, bar-like centre herds into it.

Further out lies a fainter outer ring. Seen in ultraviolet and infrared light, it turned out to be a lively disc of spiral arms that holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s mass in stars — and, star for star, makes new ones more efficiently than the inner disc.
Pierre Méchain discovered M 94 in 1781, and Charles Messier catalogued it two days later. At its heart sits a black hole of about 16 million suns, weighed using the James Webb Space Telescope.
M94.tagline: A galaxy with a blazing ring of newborn stars — and, puzzlingly, perhaps almost no dark matter.

facts.text: In March 2012 Paolo Fagotti and, independently, Jure Skvarc spotted supernova SN 2012aw in M 95. Later infrared images showed that the red supergiant seen at that spot beforehand had disappeared.
facts.title: A star that vanished

facts.text: The star that exploded had roughly twelve times the Sun’s mass. After the blast its light held steady on a long plateau — the hallmark of a Type II-P supernova.
facts.title: A big star’s ending

story: A straight bar of stars cuts across the centre of M 95, and around it runs a ring where new stars are being born. That ring holds some 350 million suns’ worth of molecular gas, the raw material for future stars. Inside it are knots of star clusters, each with millions of suns’ worth of stars. Some may be on their way to becoming [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] — the ancient balls of stars that orbit galaxies like our own.
Pierre Méchain found M 95 in 1781, and Charles Messier catalogued it four days later. This barred [[spiral-galaxy]] belongs to a small group of galaxies in Leo, together with M 96 and M 105.
M95.tagline: A barred spiral with a ring of star factories — and a supernova whose parent star then vanished.

facts.text: In May 1998 Mirko Villi found supernova SN 1998bu in M 96. It became the brightest supernova of that year, and a year later its debris showed about 0.4 solar masses of freshly made iron.
facts.title: An iron foundry

facts.text: M 96 is classed as a double-barred spiral: a small inner bar runs through its core, nested within a larger outer one.
facts.title: Two bars in one

facts.text: The M 96 Group is the nearest galaxy group to our own that combines bright spiral galaxies with a bright elliptical galaxy, M 105.
facts.title: A rare mix

story: Imagine the Milky Way pulled out of shape. M 96 has about the same mass and size as our own galaxy, but it is lopsided: its dust and gas are spread unevenly through weak spiral arms, and its core sits slightly off-centre. Astronomers think the tug of neighbouring galaxies is to blame.

Those neighbours include M 95 and M 105, fellow members of a group of galaxies in Leo. Pierre Méchain found M 96 on 20 March 1781, and Charles Messier confirmed it four days later. Flickers of ultraviolet light from its core hint at a supermassive black hole, and today it is one of 50 nearby galaxies studied by the LEGUS survey to learn how stars form.
M96.tagline: A lopsided twin of the Milky Way, where a 1998 supernova forged nearly half a Sun’s worth of iron.

facts.text: The whole nebula holds only about an eighth of the Sun’s mass, spread so thin that each cubic centimetre has fewer than 100 particles. The air you breathe has billions of billions.
facts.title: Almost nothing there

facts.text: The Owl’s gas is spreading into space at 27 to 39 kilometres per second — fast enough to cross from London to New York in under four minutes.
facts.title: Still expanding

story: About 8,000 years ago, a star near the end of its life began to shed its outer layers. The gas spread into three nested shells, and today they glow as a [[planetary-nebula]]. The star left behind is a scorching 123,000 degrees and is shrinking into a white dwarf. The owl’s ‘eyes’ come from the inner shell, which is not round but a barrel tilted at 45 degrees to our line of sight.

Pierre Méchain discovered it on 16 February 1781, and Messier added it to his catalogue that March, noting that its light was faint. In 1844 Admiral William Smyth recognised it as a planetary nebula. Then in 1848 Lord Rosse, observing from Ireland, drew two stars, each in a dark patch. His sketch looked like an owl’s head, and the name has stuck ever since.
M97.tagline: A dying star’s cast-off shells, shaped like an owl’s face — and named after Lord Rosse’s 1848 sketch.

facts.text: Most galaxies are moving away from us as the universe expands. M 98’s light is blueshifted instead: its motion within the Virgo Cluster carries it towards us at about 140 km/s.
facts.title: Against the flow

facts.text: About 750 million years ago M 98 may have passed close to the big spiral M 99. Today the two galaxies are far apart, both drifting within the Virgo Cluster.
facts.title: A brush with M 99

story: Tipped steeply to our line of sight, M 98 hides most of its spiral pattern. Yet it is a heavyweight: its stars add up to about 76 billion suns, and it holds more than 4 billion suns’ worth of hydrogen gas and 85 million suns’ worth of dust. Its stars whirl around the centre at up to 236 kilometres a second.

Pierre Méchain found this [[spiral-galaxy]] in 1781, along with its neighbours M 99 and M 100, and Charles Messier logged it 29 days later. All three are members of the Virgo Cluster, a huge city of galaxies.
M98.tagline: A hidden heavyweight: a spiral of some 76 billion suns, tipped steeply away from our view.

facts.text: A bridge of hydrogen links M 99 to VIRGOHI21, a gas cloud that may be a ‘dark galaxy’ with almost no stars. Its pull may have stretched M 99’s long arm — or the cloud may just be debris from another encounter.
facts.title: Stretched by a dark galaxy?

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen in M 99 since 1967, the first found by Fritz Zwicky. In 2010 it also hosted a rarer outburst, a luminous red nova, thought to mark two stars merging.
facts.title: Exploding and merging stars

story: In the spring of 1846 Lord Rosse turned his giant telescope in Ireland on a faint glow in Coma Berenices and saw it curl. M 99 became one of the first galaxies in which anyone saw a spiral pattern — long before anyone knew these spirals were whole other galaxies.

Pierre Méchain had found it on 17 March 1781 and passed it on to Charles Messier. Today we know it as a [[spiral-galaxy]] falling into the Virgo Cluster, probably for the first time. As it ploughs through the cluster’s thin, hot gas, much of its own gas is being stripped away. It is also forming stars about three times faster than similar galaxies, perhaps stirred up by a close encounter.
M99.tagline: A lopsided pinwheel with one stretched arm — among the first galaxies ever seen to spiral.

discovered.note: Found on Palomar Observatory Sky Survey plates in the 1950s

story: Even a ball of many thousands of stars can hide. Palomar 11 is an ordinary-sized [[globular-cluster]] in Aquila, but it sits behind so much dust in the plane of the Milky Way that nobody noticed it until the 1950s. It turned up on plates from the first Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, taken with the 48-inch Schmidt camera — one of 15 faint globulars the survey revealed. Here it is listed as MWSC 3171, its number in a modern catalogue of Milky Way star clusters.
MWSC3171.tagline: Palomar 11: a globular cluster in Aquila so hidden by dust that it was found only in the 1950s.

story: In 1915 Philibert Jacques Melotte, an astronomer at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, published a catalogue of star clusters drawn from photographic charts of the whole sky. Number 101 is a small [[open-cluster]] in Carina, less than a degree from IC 2602, the bright cluster known as the Southern Pleiades. The two are not related. IC 2602 is one of the nearest clusters to the Sun; Mel 101 lies far beyond it, and only shares its direction.
Mel101.tagline: A modest Carina cluster, less than a degree from the bright Southern Pleiades but far behind them.

story: The Milky Way through Carina is one of the richest parts of the sky, scattered with star clusters of many ages. Mel 105 is one of them — number 105 in the list Philibert Jacques Melotte compiled in 1915 — and it lies less than a degree from the larger cluster IC 2714. Like every [[open-cluster]], it is a family of stars born together and held together, for now, by its own gravity; in time the pull of the galaxy will scatter them.
Mel105.tagline: A small star cluster in the rich Carina Milky Way, close in our sky to the cluster IC 2714.

facts.text: Hipparcos and infrared studies measured its distance independently and got the same answer, making the cluster an important rung on the cosmic distance ladder.
facts.title: A rung on the cosmic ladder

story: To ancient skywatchers this scattering of faint stars was the tuft at the end of Leo’s tail. Then, around 240 BC, it was renamed after Queen Berenice II of Egypt, wife of Ptolemy III. Legend says she vowed her hair to the gods for her husband’s safe return from war; when the offering vanished from the temple, it was said to have been placed among the stars. Hence the constellation’s name, Coma Berenices — Berenice’s Hair.
The [[open-cluster]] is about 450 million years old, and its brighter stars are true siblings, moving through space together.
Mel111.tagline: Once the tuft of Leo’s tail, then a queen’s sacrificed hair: one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.

story: Early in the 20th century, the British amateur astronomer John Franklin-Adams photographed the entire night sky, north and south. Philibert Jacques Melotte of Greenwich combed those charts for star clusters and published his list in 1915; Mel 71 is number 71. It is an [[open-cluster]] in Puppis, the stern of the old constellation Argo Navis, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts.
Mel71.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis, listed from photographs of the whole sky taken by an amateur astronomer.

story: Monoceros, the Unicorn, has no bright stars, but the Milky Way runs right through it, and it is rich in star clusters and nebulae. Mel 72 is one of its fainter clusters, catalogued by Philibert Jacques Melotte in 1915. Like all [[open-cluster|open clusters]], it is a group of stars born together from one cloud of gas and dust. Over many millions of years such groups slowly disperse, so every cluster we see is a snapshot of a family before it scatters.
Mel72.tagline: A faint star cluster in Monoceros, the Unicorn, a dim constellation that lies across the Milky Way.

facts.text: Some 490 globular clusters orbit NGC 1023. Its little companion NGC 1023A has only about six.
facts.title: Big and small

story: Nobody has seen the black hole at the heart of NGC 1023, but its pull is clear in the way stars move around the centre: about 44 million times the mass of the Sun. NGC 1023, also called the Perseus Lenticular Galaxy, is a barred lenticular [[galaxy]] and the main member of the NGC 1023 Group, which includes NGC 925.
Halton Arp listed it as Arp 135, among galaxies with nearby fragments. One fragment is its small satellite NGC 1023A, joined to it by a bridge of hydrogen gas — a sign the two may be interacting.
NGC1023.tagline: A smooth lenticular galaxy with a giant black hole, a small companion and a bridge of gas.

story: NGC 1027 appears between two of the great glowing clouds of Cassiopeia, the Heart and Soul nebulae. The arrangement is an illusion: this [[open-cluster]] lies in the foreground, much nearer to us than either. Even the bright star in its middle is not a member. William Herschel discovered it in 1787, and it was later catalogued again as IC 1824.
NGC1027.tagline: A cluster that seems to sit between the Heart and Soul nebulae — but lies well in front of them.

story: Deep in the Milky Way fields of Cassiopeia lies NGC 103, a small [[open-cluster]] — a family of stars born together from one cloud of gas and dust, slowly drifting apart as they circle the galaxy. John Herschel recorded it in 1829 during his surveys of the northern sky. It also holds a small distinction: it is Collinder 1, the first entry in the Swedish astronomer Per Collinder’s 1931 catalogue of open clusters.
NGC103.tagline: A small cluster with a quiet claim to fame: entry number one in a well-known list of star clusters.

facts.text: 47 Tucanae holds 35 known millisecond pulsars — dead stars spinning hundreds of times a second — the second-largest haul in any globular cluster. It was the first globular cluster detected in gamma rays.
facts.title: Spinning lighthouses

facts.text: In 2017 astronomers reported signs of a black hole of about 2,200 suns at the centre, traced through the motions of its pulsars. Later timing data gave no solid evidence for it, so the question is still open.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

facts.text: In the sky 47 Tucanae sits beside the Small Magellanic Cloud, but the two are unrelated: the Small Cloud is more than fifteen times farther away.
facts.title: Not next door

story: When Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille first saw it from South Africa in 1751, he thought it was the head of a bright comet. It was in fact a [[globular-cluster]] — one of the most massive in our galaxy, holding millions of stars, many of them crowded into a small, dense core. He made it the first entry in his catalogue of southern deep-sky objects.

Its name comes from Johann Elert Bode, who in 1801 reordered Lacaille’s stars by constellation and gave it the number 47 — without ever seeing it. Its stars are about 13 billion years old, unusually old even for a globular cluster. A Hubble search of its core for planets, expected to find ten to fifteen, found none at all: planets seem to be rare where heavy elements are scarce.
NGC104.tagline: Millions of stars around 13 billion years old, with dozens of cosmic lighthouses spinning inside it.

story: John Herschel spotted this faint [[globular-cluster]] on 19 October 1835, with no idea that it belonged to another galaxy. That galaxy, the Fornax Dwarf, a small satellite of the Milky Way, is so faint and spread out that it went unnoticed until Harlow Shapley found it in 1938 — more than a century later. Today the cluster is easier to see than its parent. It is one of several globulars that orbit the Fornax Dwarf, hence its other name, Fornax 3.
NGC1049.tagline: A globular cluster found a century before anyone saw the galaxy it belongs to.

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen in NGC 1097 since 1992. The latest, SN 2023rve, was discovered by Mohammad Odeh in August 2023.
facts.title: Supernova hunting ground

facts.text: A second satellite, the dwarf galaxy NGC 1097B, was found only through the radio glow of its hydrogen gas. Little else is known about it.
facts.title: A hidden companion

story: Deep photographs of NGC 1097 show four narrow streaks shooting out from its centre, like jets from a black hole — and at first astronomers took them for exactly that. But the streaks are made of stars, with no hydrogen gas. The best explanation is that they are the shattered remains of a dwarf galaxy that NGC 1097 has cannibalised.

This barred [[spiral-galaxy]] is still feeding. At its centre a black hole of about 140 million suns is circled by a glowing ring of star-forming regions, with gas and dust spiralling inwards from the ring. Its companion galaxy NGC 1097A is close enough to have left tidal debris and distortions. William Herschel discovered NGC 1097 on 9 October 1790.
NGC1097.tagline: A barred spiral that has swallowed a dwarf galaxy, whose shredded remains streak out as four ghostly ‘jets’.

facts.text: The small galaxy NGC 1232A appears to hang beside it like a satellite, but its redshift does not match, so the two probably lie at different distances and have never interacted.
facts.title: A companion that isn’t

story: Seen face-on, NGC 1232 looks like a great eye staring back at us, which is why it is called the Eye of God Galaxy. It is considered a prototype of the many-armed [[spiral-galaxy]]: its arms are sprinkled with clusters of blue stars and glowing gas, with dark lanes of dust between. Beyond the starlight, unseen dark matter is needed to explain how its outer parts move.

The arms are not smooth. They bend abruptly, and Halton Arp suggested an encounter with another galaxy as the cause; others have proposed a collision with a dwarf galaxy, though some studies doubt it. William Herschel discovered it on 20 October 1784.
NGC1232.tagline: The Eye of God Galaxy: a face-on spiral of many arms, staring back across space.

story: Nicknamed the Patrick Starfish Cluster, NGC 1245 is a survivor. Most open clusters fall apart within a few hundred million years, but this one is nearly a billion years old. Over that time its heavier stars have sunk towards the middle while lighter ones drifted outwards, and it may have lost many of its smallest stars altogether. About 200 members remain in this [[open-cluster]]. William Herschel discovered it on 11 December 1786.
NGC1245.tagline: The Patrick Starfish Cluster: nearly a billion years old and still holding together.

facts.text: Astronomers have found 22 RR Lyrae variables in NGC 1261, along with three SX Phoenicis stars, two long-period variables and an eclipsing binary.
facts.title: A cluster of pulsing stars

facts.text: There are 18 probable blue stragglers in NGC 1261 — stars that look hotter and younger than an ancient cluster should allow.
facts.title: Too young-looking

story: Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered this [[globular-cluster]] in 1826. Its stars are about 10 billion years old, and together they weigh some 341,000 suns.

It has a curious past. Over time, the cores of globular clusters can collapse, their stars sinking into an ever denser knot. NGC 1261 shows no sign of that today, but there is evidence it may have gone through such a collapse and bounced back within the last two billion years. Its core is now unusually dim for a globular, though its stars are still strongly concentrated towards the centre.
NGC1261.tagline: A ten-billion-year-old ball of stars that may have collapsed and bounced back in recent cosmic times.

discovered.note: John Herschel’s 1836 sighting became the duplicate entry NGC 1269

facts.text: In 2007 the team behind NASA’s Galaxy Evolution Explorer held it up as an example of a “transitional galaxy”: one caught between active star birth and a quiet old age.
facts.title: Caught in transition

story: One galaxy, two NGC numbers. James Dunlop found it in 1826, and it entered the New General Catalogue as NGC 1291. John Herschel saw it again in 1836 and listed it as a new object, without realising it was the same one — so it is NGC 1269 as well. Today it is better known as the Golden Eye Galaxy.

Seen nearly face-on, it is a lenticular [[galaxy]] with a bright bulge and an unusual inner bar, circled far out by a faint ring where new stars are slowly forming. Its ringed shape is thought to be the legacy of a merger with a gas-rich galaxy long ago.
NGC1269.tagline: The Golden Eye Galaxy: a bar inside a ring, catalogued twice by mistake.

facts.text: Some 13 billion suns’ worth of molecular hydrogen seems to be falling into NGC 1275 from the surrounding cluster, feeding both its black hole and new stars.
facts.title: Raining gas

facts.text: One idea is that weak magnetic fields hold the filaments together — fields only about one ten-thousandth as strong as Earth’s.
facts.title: Held by gentle magnets?

story: Look at NGC 1275 and you are seeing two galaxies at once. Behind is the giant central galaxy of the Perseus Cluster. In front is a second galaxy, the ‘high velocity system’, plunging through the cluster at 3,000 kilometres a second. As it ploughs through the cluster’s gas it is being stripped and torn, sparking bursts of star formation.

The central giant has an active heart: its black hole and inner disc of gas weigh about 800 million suns. Rising bubbles of hot plasma from the core seem to drag out a web of glowing filaments, each holding about a million suns’ worth of gas, reaching out into the multimillion-degree gas that fills the cluster. Why these cool threads have not heated up, dispersed or collapsed into stars is a puzzle. William Herschel discovered NGC 1275 on 17 October 1786.
NGC1275.tagline: A giant galaxy at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, trailing threads of gas that may be held by magnetism.

story: Among the scattered stars of NGC 129 is a cosmic yardstick. Its brightest member, DL Cassiopeiae, is a binary system that includes a Cepheid, a pulsating [[variable-star]] that brightens and fades every eight days. A Cepheid’s rhythm gives away its true brightness, so astronomers have used DL Cas to work out how far away the whole cluster lies. A second Cepheid, V379 Cassiopeiae, may also be a member.
William Herschel discovered this large, loose [[open-cluster]] in 1788. Several of its stars have already swollen into giants.
NGC129.tagline: A scattered cluster in Cassiopeia whose brightest star beats like a clock — and works as a measuring rod.

facts.text: In 1990 Stuart Ryder spotted an odd star here and reported it as a nova. Old photographs then showed it had erupted on 31 July 1978. It was a very unusual supernova, now called SN 1978K.
facts.title: A supernova found 12 years late

facts.text: One of its two powerful X-ray sources, NGC 1313 X-1, is a rare intermediate-mass black hole: heavier than those left by single stars, far lighter than the giants in galaxy centres.
facts.title: A middleweight black hole

facts.text: Young blue stars lie scattered all across the galaxy. They were born in clusters that quickly came “unglued”, spilling their stars out into the galaxy.
facts.title: Clusters that came apart

story: Even its spin is off-centre. NGC 1313, the Topsy Turvy Galaxy, rotates around an axis that is not at its middle. It is a lopsided irregular [[galaxy]], torn by bursts of star formation that blow great bubbles in its gas. A past collision would explain all this, yet NGC 1313 has no close neighbours. Perhaps it swallowed a small companion. James Dunlop discovered it on 27 September 1826.
NGC1313.tagline: The Topsy Turvy Galaxy: lopsided, ragged and turning around a point that isn’t its centre.

facts.text: Giant galaxies like this usually sit at the centre of their cluster, as M 87 does in Virgo. Fornax A instead lies at the edge of the Fornax Cluster.
facts.title: On the edge

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen here since 1980. In 2006 Berto Monard found two, briefly visible at the same time; SN 2006dd became the brightest supernova of that year.
facts.title: Supernova factory

story: To a radio telescope, NGC 1316 is one of the loudest things in the sky: at 1400 MHz it is the fourth-brightest radio source of all. The power comes from a central black hole of around 140 million Suns, perhaps fed by the galaxies NGC 1316 has eaten.

In the late 1970s François Schweizer found ripples, loops and arcs in its outer glow, and dust lanes deep inside: the wreckage of several smaller galaxies it absorbed. The last big merger seems to have happened about 3 billion years ago. James Dunlop discovered this lenticular [[galaxy]] on 2 September 1826.
NGC1316.tagline: Fornax A: a galaxy built by swallowing others, and one of the brightest radio sources in the sky.

story: NGC 1317 lives next door to a giant, or seems to. On the sky it sits just north of NGC 1316, the powerful radio galaxy Fornax A, and the two appear to be interacting. But estimates of NGC 1317’s distance disagree widely, so nobody can be sure the pair are really close. Even if they are, the little spiral looks too small to have caused the turmoil in its big neighbour.
James Dunlop discovered this barred [[spiral-galaxy]] on 24 November 1826. It also carries a second catalogue number, NGC 1318.
NGC1317.tagline: A small barred spiral beside the giant Fornax A — perhaps a neighbour, perhaps not.

story: A small ring circles the centre of NGC 1326. It is a lenticular [[galaxy]] — a disc with little sign of spiral arms — and a member of the Fornax Cluster, in the subgroup around NGC 1316. On paper it is an ordinary early-type lenticular, yet it is very different from the others of its kind in the cluster. John Herschel discovered it on 29 November 1837, during his years observing the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC1326.tagline: A lenticular galaxy in the Fornax Cluster with a ring around its heart.

story: Heinrich d’Arrest had already earned his place in history before he found this small [[open-cluster]] on 4 February 1865. As a young assistant at the Berlin Observatory in 1846, he helped Johann Galle locate the newly predicted planet Neptune. By the 1860s he was working in Copenhagen, carefully cataloguing faint nebulae and clusters, and NGC 133 in Cassiopeia was one of his finds.
NGC133.tagline: A small cluster found by the man who helped spot Neptune.

story: Weighing a black hole precisely is hard. In 2016 a team from the United States and China used the ALMA radio telescope array to study the core of NGC 1332 in fine detail, and pinned its black hole at about 660 million times the mass of the Sun, give or take just 10 percent. It is the heaviest black hole known in the Eridanus Cluster, outweighing even the one in NGC 1399, the central galaxy of the Fornax Cluster.
NGC 1332 is an [[elliptical-galaxy]] of old, red stars, the brightest in its own small group. William Herschel discovered it on 9 December 1784.
NGC1332.tagline: A galaxy with one of the most precisely weighed black holes: about 660 million Suns.

facts.text: The cloud holds objects only a few times the mass of Jupiter, drifting free. In 2024 the James Webb Space Telescope found several but none below about 4 Jupiter masses — hinting that star-like births may not make anything smaller.
facts.title: Planets without stars

facts.text: One of them, NIRISS-NGC1333-5, weighs about 5 Jupiters yet shows signs of a disc around it, making it one of the lowest-mass objects known to have one.
facts.title: A tiny world with a disc

story: A stellar nursery caught in the act: that is NGC 1333. Inside this dusty [[reflection-nebula]], in the western part of the Perseus molecular cloud, about 150 stars have formed with a median age of only a million years — infants beside the 4.6-billion-year-old Sun. Twenty young stars are blasting out jets and outflows of gas, and many are still contracting towards adulthood. Its nickname, the Embryo Nebula, fits.
Eduard Schönfeld discovered it in 1855.
NGC1333.tagline: The Embryo Nebula: a nursery of newborn stars — and of planet-sized objects with no star at all.

discovered.note: Often credited to John Herschel, who noted Dunlop may have seen it first

facts.text: Credit often goes to John Herschel at the Cape of Good Hope, but Herschel himself noted that it might be object 590 in James Dunlop’s catalogue, published in 1828 — six years before his own observations.
facts.title: Who saw it first?

facts.text: On 20 June 2009 New Zealand amateur astronomer Stuart Parker discovered a supernova in NGC 134, SN 2009gj: the explosion of a massive star.
facts.title: An amateur’s supernova

story: Stephen James O’Meara suggested a nickname for NGC 134: the Giant Squid Galaxy. It is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] much like our own Milky Way, its arms loosely wrapped around a bright central bar. Red patches along those arms mark clouds where new stars are being born.

Seen from the side, its disc is not flat but warped, and a trail of gas is being stripped from one edge. Both hint that another galaxy once disturbed it, though that remains unproven. It belongs to a small group of galaxies that includes NGC 131 and NGC 148.
NGC134.tagline: The Giant Squid Galaxy: a Milky Way look-alike with a warped disc and a trail of stripped gas.

discovered.note: John Herschel’s 1835 sighting became the duplicate entry NGC 1340

story: William Herschel found this [[elliptical-galaxy]] in 1790. On 19 November 1835 his son John observed it, and his sighting was later treated as a separate object. Dreyer’s New General Catalogue ended up listing both: NGC 1344 for William’s observation and NGC 1340 for John’s. Today the galaxy is known to belong to the group around NGC 1399, the central galaxy of the Fornax Cluster — a family of at least 42 galaxies.
NGC1340.tagline: Two Herschels, two numbers, one galaxy.

story: Some see a stingray in NGC 1342; others see the shape of Scorpius in miniature. Hence its nicknames, the Stingray Cluster and the Little Scorpion Cluster. This [[open-cluster]] lies away from the plane of the Milky Way and is about 400 million years old. William Herschel discovered it on 28 December 1799.
Nearby is a dark cloud, LDN 1434, found by Beverly Turner Lynds in 1962 for her catalogue of dark nebulae.
NGC1342.tagline: The Little Scorpion Cluster: a stingray, or a scorpion, drawn in faint stars.

story: Two rings make NGC 1350 look like an eye in space. Its arms wind so tightly that they form a bright inner ring, and farther out a faint second ring circles it. The outer arms are so thin that more distant galaxies can be seen shining through them, and their bluish tint marks stars being born.
This [[spiral-galaxy]] appears on the outskirts of the Fornax Cluster, though whether it really belongs is uncertain. James Dunlop discovered it on 24 November 1826.
NGC1350.tagline: A ringed spiral like a cosmic eye, with distant galaxies shining through its outer arms.

facts.text: Its central star was suspected to be double in 1977, but proof took until 2017. It is a hot O-type star paired with a white dwarf — and the white dwarf is the heavier of the two.
facts.title: Two hearts

story: The Robin’s Egg Nebula is a fitting name for a cloud that shines strongly in the blue-green light of oxygen. NGC 1360 is a [[planetary-nebula]], the shed outer layers of a star near the end of its life. Reddish wisps around it are thought to be material the star threw off before its final collapse.
Friedrich Winnecke discovered it in January 1868.
NGC1360.tagline: The Robin’s Egg Nebula: a dying star’s shell, and a central ‘star’ that turned out to be two.

facts.text: In 2013 the NuSTAR X-ray telescope showed that its central black hole, about half the mass of the Milky Way’s, is spinning at close to the speed of light.
facts.title: A spinning black hole

facts.text: The Australian supernova hunter Robert Evans found two of the four supernovae seen in NGC 1365, in 1983 and 2001.
facts.title: A supernova regular

story: A great bar of stars cuts across the centre of NGC 1365, and inside it lies a second, smaller bar that turns faster than the first. The bar acts like a funnel, drawing gas and dust into a whirl of star birth and feeding the black hole at the centre. Out at its tips, the bar takes about 350 million years to turn once.
About two thirds of spiral galaxies have bars, and our own Milky Way is thought to be one of them, so this [[spiral-galaxy]] is a window on home. James Dunlop discovered it on 2 September 1826.
NGC1365.tagline: The Great Barred Spiral: a bar within a bar, feeding a black hole that spins near light speed.

facts.text: Its one known supernova, SN 1992A, was spotted by W. Liller on 11 January 1992 and independently by N. Brown the next day.
facts.title: Found twice in two days

story: About 10 billion years ago NGC 1380 swallowed another galaxy whole. The victim added roughly a fifth of its present mass, and traces of it survive in the stars of its inner halo. Today NGC 1380 is a calm lenticular [[galaxy]] near the heart of the Fornax Cluster, with about 555 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] and a central black hole of some 220 million Suns. James Dunlop discovered it on 2 September 1826.
NGC1380.tagline: A smooth lenticular galaxy that swallowed a fifth of its own mass 10 billion years ago.

story: The Milky Way has about 150 to 200 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]]. NGC 1395 has around 6,000. Many probably came from dwarf galaxies it has swallowed over time. In 1983 David Malin and Dave Carter found faint shells in its outer glow — ripples of stars that point to a smaller galaxy captured not long ago.
This [[elliptical-galaxy]] is the brightest of its subgroup in the Eridanus Cluster. William Herschel discovered it on 17 November 1784.
NGC1395.tagline: An elliptical giant with some 6,000 globular clusters — and the faint shells of a recent meal.

discovered.note: Often credited to Friedrich Winnecke, who found it in 1868; Tempel did not publish until 1882

story: Wilhelm Tempel saw NGC 1398 first, on 9 October 1861, but did not publish until 1882. Meanwhile Friedrich Winnecke came across it in Karlsruhe on 17 December 1868 while hunting for comets — and he usually gets the credit.
