Their find is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] with a double ring around its centre. It holds over 100 billion stars and lives in isolation, with no large galaxies close by.
NGC1398.tagline: A lone, double-ringed spiral whose discovery is usually credited to the second man to see it.

facts.text: When the Herschel Space Observatory, named after William Herschel, surveyed giant elliptical galaxies, most turned out to hold plenty of cold gas, the raw material of stars. NGC 1399 was one of only two exceptions.
facts.title: Out of fuel

facts.text: Near its central black hole of about 510 million Suns, stars move mostly in circles around the centre rather than in and out — more strongly than in any other galaxy measured at the time.
facts.title: Stars in circles

story: At the centre of the Fornax Cluster sits NGC 1399, a giant [[elliptical-galaxy]] wrapped in a vast, faint envelope of stars. Its gravity has made it a collector. Somewhere between 5,700 and 6,500 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] swarm around it, and many may have been taken from its neighbours: NGC 1404 seems to have given up most of its own, and NGC 1387 may have lost some too.
John Herschel discovered it on 22 October 1835.
NGC1399.tagline: The giant at the heart of the Fornax Cluster, ringed by thousands of globular clusters.

facts.text: Two Type Ia supernovae have exploded here: SN 2007on in 2007, and SN 2011iv in 2011, found by the New Zealand amateur Stuart Parker.
facts.title: Two supernovae in four years

story: Like a ship leaving a wake, NGC 1404 trails its own gas. As this [[elliptical-galaxy]] moves through the thin, hot gas that fills the Fornax Cluster, the pressure strips the galaxy’s hot gas away, and the Chandra X-ray telescope shows it streaming out behind. It may have lost other things too: astronomers have proposed that its giant neighbour NGC 1399 pulled away most of its globular clusters, leaving it about 725.
John Herschel discovered it on 28 November 1837.
NGC1404.tagline: An elliptical galaxy losing its gas — and perhaps its clusters — as it ploughs through the Fornax Cluster.

story: The stars at the heart of NGC 1407 are about 12 billion years old, born when the universe was young, and the galaxy has seen no strong burst of star birth since. This [[elliptical-galaxy]] is far from asleep, though. At its centre lies a black hole of about a billion times the mass of the Sun, and radio observations show signs of repeated outbursts.
It is the brightest member of its group in Eridanus, followed by its neighbour NGC 1400. William Herschel discovered it on 6 October 1785.
NGC1407.tagline: An ancient elliptical galaxy with a billion-Sun black hole that keeps flaring up.

facts.text: Otto Struve thought Maia varied in brightness and proposed a new class, the Maia variables. Hipparcos found no sign of it, but Kepler later caught a faint 10.3-day flicker, probably a starspot turning with the star.
facts.title: The star that named a class

story: In Greek myth Maia was one of the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. The star that carries her name is the fourth-brightest in the Pleiades, and NGC 1432 is the glow around it: a [[reflection-nebula]], dust shining by Maia’s blue-white light, one of the brighter patches of nebulosity in the cluster.
Maia itself is a blue giant with odd chemistry: too little helium on its surface, and too much manganese.
NGC1432.tagline: The glow around Maia, one of the Seven Sisters of the Pleiades.

story: Rings within rings mark NGC 1433. It is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] with a double ring structure, and close to its centre a small, irregular ring is busy making stars. Its active nucleus drives a jet of molecular gas outwards — the smallest molecular outflow ever seen in a galaxy beyond our own.
NGC 1433 belongs to the Dorado Group and is one of the 50 nearby galaxies in Hubble’s Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey. James Dunlop discovered it on 28 September 1826.
NGC1433.tagline: A ringed spiral with an active heart and the smallest molecular outflow seen beyond our galaxy.

facts.text: Close to Merope lies a bright knot, IC 349, found by E. E. Barnard in November 1890. It is bright in its own right, but almost lost in the glare of the star.
facts.title: Barnard’s knot

facts.text: John Herschel included the nebula as number 768 in his General Catalogue of Nebulae and Clusters, though he never observed it himself.
facts.title: Listed, never seen

story: For a long time it seemed obvious that the Pleiades were born from the haze around them. They were not. The dust wrapped around Merope belongs to an unrelated cloud that the cluster is drifting through by chance. Fine carbon dust scatters Merope’s light, which is why this [[reflection-nebula]] looks blue in photographs.
Wilhelm Tempel discovered it on 19 October 1859 with a 10.5 cm refractor, so it is also called Tempel’s Nebula.
NGC1435.tagline: Tempel’s Nebula: the blue haze around Merope — a cloud the Pleiades just happen to be passing through.

story: At about 7 million years old, NGC 1444 is a baby among star clusters. Its most prominent member is a triple star, Struve 446, catalogued by the double-star observer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve. The cluster belongs to Camelopardalis OB1, a loose association of hot young stars. William Herschel discovered this small [[open-cluster]] on 18 December 1788.
NGC1444.tagline: A seven-million-year-old cluster led by a triple star.

facts.text: Nearby lies the cluster King 14. The two follow similar orbits around the Milky Way, taking about 255 million years per lap, and probably formed in the same giant cloud of gas — though gravity no longer binds them together.
facts.title: A sibling cluster

story: Some of the stars in NGC 146 have not yet grown up. This young [[open-cluster]] is full of hot blue-white stars and pre-main-sequence stars — newborns still contracting, not yet shining steadily by fusing hydrogen. Among its heaviest members are two Herbig Be stars, massive youngsters still surrounded by discs of leftover gas and dust.
John Herschel discovered it in 1829 with the 18.7-inch reflecting telescope built by his father, William.
NGC146.tagline: A young cluster in Cassiopeia where some stars are still newborns.

facts.text: NGC 147 and its neighbour NGC 185 form a physical pair: two remote satellites of the Andromeda Galaxy travelling together.
facts.title: Travelling as a pair

facts.text: Its old stars vary in age and in their content of heavy elements, showing that NGC 147 enriched itself over several generations of stars before its gas disappeared.
facts.title: Generations of stars

story: John Herschel discovered this dim glow in Cassiopeia in September 1829. More than a century passed before anyone saw what it really was: in 1944 Walter Baade, using the 100-inch telescope at Mount Wilson, resolved it into individual stars and showed that it belongs to our own Local Group of galaxies.

NGC 147 is a dwarf spheroidal [[galaxy]], one of the small satellites of the Andromeda Galaxy. Its last significant burst of star birth was about 3 billion years ago. Since then it has been running down: no hydrogen gas has been detected, far less than its ageing stars should have shed, so the galaxy seems to have lost the raw material for new stars.
NGC147.tagline: A faint companion of the Andromeda Galaxy that stopped making stars around three billion years ago.

story: Little has been written about NGC 1496, a faint [[open-cluster]] in Perseus. Like other open clusters, it is a family of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas and dust and share a path around the Milky Way. Over time the galaxy’s tides pull such groups apart, until their stars blend into the crowd of the Milky Way.
NGC1496.tagline: A little-studied cluster in Perseus: a family of stars still travelling together.

facts.text: The nebula overlaps the Perseus–Pisces Supercluster, so distant galaxies can be seen shining through it. The brightest is the elliptical galaxy IC 2005.
facts.title: Galaxies behind the glow

story: Long-exposure photographs show the outline of a US state, and so this cloud became the California Nebula. By a neat coincidence, it also passes straight overhead as seen from central California, whose latitude matches the nebula’s position on the sky.
It is an [[emission-nebula]]: hydrogen made to glow by the ultraviolet light of Xi Persei, or Menkib, a hot and very energetic O-type star nearby. E. E. Barnard discovered it in 1884.
NGC1499.tagline: The California Nebula — which, by coincidence, passes straight over California.

facts.text: At least eleven of its stars vary in brightness. One, SZ Camelopardalis, is an eclipsing binary that is itself part of a visual double star.
facts.title: A nest of variables

story: A long chain of stars, Kemble’s Cascade, seems to tumble across the sky and splash into NGC 1502. The meeting is a trick of perspective: the chain and the cluster are unrelated. The Cascade is named after the Canadian amateur astronomer Father Lucian Kemble.

NGC 1502, the Golden Harp Cluster, is a young [[open-cluster]] of about 60 stars, between 5 and 15 million years old, on the outer edge of the Camelopardalis OB1 association. William Herschel discovered it on 3 November 1787.
NGC1502.tagline: The Golden Harp Cluster, where Kemble’s Cascade seems to tumble to an end.

story: Slowly, NGC 1512 is eating a neighbour. The small galaxy NGC 1510 has been caught in its grip for some 400 million years, and in the end it will be absorbed completely. The tug of war has already set off star birth in the outskirts of NGC 1512’s disc: in ultraviolet light, at least 200 young star clusters shine there.
This barred [[spiral-galaxy]] also has two rings, one around its nucleus and one farther out. It belongs to the Dorado Group. James Dunlop discovered it on 29 October 1826.
NGC1512.tagline: A ringed spiral slowly swallowing its small neighbour, NGC 1510.

story: At least 433 stars belong to NGC 1513, an [[open-cluster]] about 363 million years old. It is partly hidden behind dust from a dark cloud complex in Perseus, and its stars hold slightly less of the heavier elements than the Sun does. The whole cluster is drawing closer to us at nearly 15 kilometres per second. William Herschel discovered it in 1790.
NGC1513.tagline: A middle-aged cluster in Perseus, partly veiled by dust and drifting our way.

facts.text: In mid-infrared light a pair of faint rings appears, forming a diabolo shape. The James Webb Space Telescope has shown them to be clumpy and filamentary.
facts.title: Hidden rings

facts.text: The two central stars were once thought to orbit every 10 days or so. Years of watching showed the true period is about 9 years — one of the longest known for any planetary nebula.
facts.title: A slow waltz

story: On 13 November 1790 William Herschel met “a most singular phenomenon”. Until then he believed every nebula was a mass of stars too distant to resolve. Here was a single star wrapped in a faint glow, and he concluded that the glow was “not of a starry nature”: some nebulae, at least, were made of something other than stars.
Today we know it as the Crystal Ball Nebula, a [[planetary-nebula]]: gas thrown off by a dying star, one of a pair at its centre.
NGC1514.tagline: The Crystal Ball Nebula: the glowing shell that changed William Herschel’s mind about nebulae.

story: Some 165 stars are known to belong to NGC 1528, an [[open-cluster]] in the north-east of Perseus. It shares this stretch of the Milky Way with two other clusters, NGC 1513 and NGC 1545. William Herschel discovered it in 1790, a busy year for him in this part of the sky: he also found NGC 1513 and the Crystal Ball Nebula, NGC 1514.
NGC1528.tagline: A rich cluster of 165 stars, one of three sharing a corner of Perseus.

story: We see NGC 1532 almost exactly side-on, and that hides something. Its central bulge has a boxy shape, a sign that it is really a bar seen from the side. Bars are easy to spot in galaxies seen face-on; in an [[edge-on-galaxy]] like this one, it takes careful analysis to tell bar from bulge. Sometimes called Haley’s Coronet, this barred [[spiral-galaxy]] is also tangled with a small companion, the dwarf galaxy NGC 1531, whose pull has raised unusual plumes above its disc.
James Dunlop discovered it on 29 October 1826.
NGC1532.tagline: An edge-on spiral hiding a bar in its box-shaped bulge, tangled with a small companion.

story: Known as Cleopatra’s Eye, NGC 1535 looks remarkably like the Eskimo Nebula in Gemini, in both colour and structure. It is a [[planetary-nebula]]: the cast-off outer layers of a dying star. That star, still at the centre, is now a hot O-type star of about 66,000 kelvin with a little over half the Sun’s mass, and its fast wind is thought to have shaped the nebula into its rounded form. The gas seems to have formed in a region poor in heavy elements.
William Herschel discovered it on 1 February 1785.
NGC1535.tagline: Cleopatra’s Eye: a southern cousin of the Eskimo Nebula, shaped by the wind of a fierce star.

story: Almost all the hydrogen in NGC 1543 lies in one place: a faint outer ring, brighter in ultraviolet than in visible light. There new stars form at a gentle, steady pace — roughly one Sun’s worth every 12 years, unchanged for the last 100 million years. The rest of this barred lenticular [[galaxy]] is old and nearly empty of gas. The ring may be the scar of a collision with a dwarf galaxy as NGC 1543 passed through the middle of the Dorado Group.
Its centre holds a bar within a bar. James Dunlop discovered it on 5 November 1826.
NGC1543.tagline: An old, quiet galaxy with all its gas in one faint ring — perhaps the scar of a collision.

story: William Herschel discovered NGC 1545 on 28 December 1790. It is a looser, poorer [[open-cluster]] than its neighbour NGC 1528. The brightest star in its field is an orange giant — a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its former size — but whether it really belongs to the cluster, or just lies along the same line of sight, is uncertain.
NGC1545.tagline: A sparse cluster in Perseus whose brightest star may not belong to it.

discovered.note: James Dunlop may have seen it in 1826

story: NGC 1549 and NGC 1553 sit together at the centre of the Dorado Group, and they have begun to interact. The outer contours of NGC 1549 are twisted, and faint shells of stars surround it — signs of disturbance. It is the group’s largest [[elliptical-galaxy]], yet oddly short of globular clusters, with only about 150, few for a galaxy its size. The Spitzer Space Telescope found none of the usual infrared signature of interstellar dust.
John Herschel discovered it on 6 December 1835, though James Dunlop may have seen it in 1826.
NGC1549.tagline: The largest elliptical of the Dorado Group, just beginning to tangle with its neighbour.

facts.text: Chandra also found many point-like X-ray sources: neutron stars and black holes pulling gas off companion stars. Most lie in globular clusters, relics of the galaxy’s busy past.
facts.title: Dead stars in old clusters

story: Astronomers treat NGC 1553 as a prototype lenticular [[galaxy]], complete with an especially well-developed “lens”: a zone of nearly even brightness between its central bulge and outer disc. Yet X-ray images from Chandra reveal something hidden: a roughly symmetrical spiral in its hot gas, invisible in ordinary light, matched by a spiral pattern in glowing hydrogen.
John Herschel discovered it on 5 December 1834 with an 18.7-inch reflector. It is the second-brightest galaxy in the Dorado Group, paired with NGC 1549.
NGC1553.tagline: A textbook lenticular galaxy hiding a spiral that only X-ray eyes can see.

story: Most nebulae look the same for centuries. Hind’s Variable Nebula does not. John Russell Hind discovered it on 11 October 1852, and since then it has brightened and faded as the light reaching it from its star changes. That star is T Tauri, a young [[variable-star]] that gave its name to a whole class of newborn stars still settling down.
The nebula is also a Herbig–Haro object: the kind of glowing patch made where gas blown out by a young star strikes the cloud around it.
NGC1555.tagline: Hind’s Variable Nebula: a cloud that brightens and fades with the young star T Tauri.

facts.text: Supernova SN 2021aefx, found in NGC 1566 in November 2021, reached magnitude 12 — the brightest supernova of that year.
facts.title: Brightest of 2021

story: Its strong, symmetrical arms earned NGC 1566 the nickname Spanish Dancer. At its centre lies one of the closest and brightest Seyfert nuclei — an active core where gas spirals into a black hole of about 13 million Suns. It is also the nearest known “changing-look” galaxy: a type whose active core can flare up or fade dramatically within a few years.
This [[spiral-galaxy]] leads its own subgroup within the Dorado Group. James Dunlop discovered it on 28 May 1826.
NGC1566.tagline: The Spanish Dancer: a sweeping spiral with a restless black hole at its heart.

story: At the heart of NGC 1574 lies a black hole of about 100 million times the mass of the Sun — and it is asleep. The nucleus shows no sign of activity. Around it, a small disc of carbon monoxide gas appears to be warped. Seen nearly face-on, this lenticular [[galaxy]] has a bar wrapped in an almost complete ring. It belongs to the Dorado Group. John Herschel discovered it on 4 December 1834.
NGC1574.tagline: A lenticular galaxy with a sleeping giant at its heart.

story: Fewer than 50 stars make up NGC 1582, a sparse, loosely spread [[open-cluster]] with no strong concentration towards the middle. It is about 302 million years old. In a group this loose the Milky Way’s tides have an easy job, and over time its stars will drift apart into the galaxy. William Herschel discovered it in 1788.
NGC1582.tagline: A sparse, scattered cluster in Perseus, some 300 million years old.

story: Most spiral galaxies are speckled with bright knots of newborn stars. NGC 1617 is unusually smooth, with no sign of them. Its arms are wound so tightly that they close into a ring after only half a turn, and a weak bar crosses its centre. This [[spiral-galaxy]] belongs to the Dorado Group.
James Dunlop discovered it on 5 November 1826 — the same night he logged two other members of the group, NGC 1543 and NGC 1672.
NGC1617.tagline: A smooth, quiet spiral whose arms close into a ring after half a turn.

story: We see NGC 1647 through a veil. The cluster lies well beyond the Taurus dark cloud complex, so its light has to pass through that dust on its way to us. About 90 stars belong to this [[open-cluster]], which is some 200 million years old; its brightest ordinary stars are hot, blue-white B-type stars. William Herschel discovered it in 1784.
NGC1647.tagline: A cluster seen through the dark dust clouds of Taurus.

story: Amateur astronomers call NGC 1662 the Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster, after the warships of Star Trek. It is a loosely bound [[open-cluster]] in Orion, also listed as Collinder 55. Its age has been hard to pin down: estimates range from 100 to 800 million years, and the latest studies settle on about 400 million. William Herschel discovered it in 1784.
NGC1662.tagline: The Klingon Battlecruiser Cluster — a starship drawn in stars in Orion.

story: NGC 1664 has had time to settle down. At about 675 million years old, this [[open-cluster]] is dynamically relaxed: encounters between its stars have shared out their energy until the cluster reached a steady balance. Its stars add up to some 640 times the mass of the Sun. It was born farther from the centre of the Milky Way than the Sun is, and circles the galaxy once every 244 million years — almost three laps since its birth. William Herschel discovered it in 1786.
NGC1664.tagline: A settled middle-aged cluster that has circled the galaxy almost three times.

story: What powers the centre of NGC 1672? Its nucleus fits none of the usual categories. It is not simply a star-forming region, nor simply an active black hole, and it may be both: a Seyfert nucleus engulfed by a burst of star birth.

This barred [[spiral-galaxy]] has a large, bright bar, with four thin arms trailing from its ends, one far brighter than the others. Its membership of the Dorado Group was long debated, until recent measurements put it at the same distance as the other members. James Dunlop discovered it on 5 November 1826.
NGC1672.tagline: A barred spiral whose heart fits no category: part black hole, part star factory.

story: Three clusters in one patch of Taurus — or so it seemed. NGC 1746 gave its name to the “Cluster of Clusters”, or Taurus Triplet: a sprawling grouping that appears to hold two smaller clusters, NGC 1750 and NGC 1758. Closer study shows they are strangers. NGC 1750 is a real cluster about 200 million years old; NGC 1758 lies farther away and is older, at about 541 million years. NGC 1746 itself is most likely a chance grouping of stars, an [[asterism]].
Heinrich d’Arrest described it in 1863.
NGC1746.tagline: The ‘Cluster of Clusters’ — three star groups in one field, none of them related.

story: Beyond the edge of our own galaxy lies NGC 1747, a star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the [[magellanic-clouds]] that orbit the Milky Way. The Large Magellanic Cloud is rich in clusters like this one, thousands of them, so astronomers use it as a laboratory for how star clusters are born and age.
NGC1747.tagline: A star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy.

story: In the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the [[magellanic-clouds]], the line between kinds of star cluster blurs. NGC 1755 is usually called an [[open-cluster]], yet it is so large that it could count as a [[globular-cluster]]. Clusters like this, big and populous but much younger than the Milky Way’s ancient globulars, are a speciality of our neighbour galaxy. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.
NGC1755.tagline: A big young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, blurring the line between open and globular.

story: Stars are being born in NGC 1763, a nursery in another galaxy. Its glowing gas, catalogued as N11B, surrounds a group of young stars known as LH 10 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the [[magellanic-clouds]]. It is part of N11, a sprawling complex of star birth sometimes called the Bean Nebula. Like any [[emission-nebula]], it shines because hot young stars make its hydrogen glow.
James Dunlop discovered the region in 1826 with a 23-cm telescope, and John Herschel observed it in 1834.
NGC1763.tagline: A glowing nursery of young stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, part of the Bean Nebula.

story: Auriga is rich in star clusters, from the bright trio M 36, M 37 and M 38 to fainter groups like NGC 1778. Looking this way we gaze outwards, away from the centre of the galaxy, through the outer Milky Way. An [[open-cluster]] like this is a family of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas and dust, and still share a path around the galaxy.
NGC1778.tagline: A modest cluster in the star-rich Milky Way of Auriga.

story: To see NGC 1782 is to look out of our own galaxy altogether. It is a small, compact star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the largest of the [[magellanic-clouds]]. This neighbour galaxy holds thousands of star clusters, and because its stars all lie at about the same distance from us, it is one of the best places to compare clusters of different ages side by side.
NGC1782.tagline: A small, compact cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

story: Some 65 variable stars have been found in NGC 1786, a [[globular-cluster]] in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Fifty-three of them are RR Lyrae stars, which pulse in brightness every day or less — and RR Lyrae stars are found only among very old stars. The rest include Cepheids, eclipsing binaries and quick-pulsing Delta Scuti stars. John Herschel discovered the cluster on 20 December 1835.
NGC1786.tagline: An ancient globular cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, alive with pulsating stars.

story: Light and dark meet at NGC 1788. This [[reflection-nebula]] in Orion glows with starlight scattered by dust, but on its south-western side it ends abruptly against a [[dark-nebula]], LDN 1616. The dark cloud seems to be part of the same structure: the same dust, lit on one side and in shadow on the other. William Herschel discovered it in 1786.
NGC1788.tagline: A small reflection nebula in Orion, sharply cut off by a dark cloud.

story: Every year NGC 1792 turns about 11 Suns’ worth of gas into new stars — several times the Milky Way’s rate — and its arms are dotted with glowing star-forming regions. This flocculent [[spiral-galaxy]] has patchy, broken arms and no central bulge to speak of. Its neighbour NGC 1808 is unusually busy too, which hints that a distant encounter between the two stirred them up. The lopsided spread of hydrogen gas in NGC 1792 backs that up.
James Dunlop discovered it on 4 October 1826.
NGC1792.tagline: A spiral galaxy making stars at several times the Milky Way’s rate.

story: Is NGC 1807 a cluster at all? It is usually listed as an [[asterism]], a chance grouping of unrelated stars. Yet some astronomers have suggested that it and its neighbour NGC 1817 may be parts of one extended cluster. It lies on the border of Taurus and Orion, looking towards the galactic anticentre — directly away from the heart of the Milky Way. John Herschel recorded it in 1832.
NGC1807.tagline: A loose star grouping that may be a real cluster — or no cluster at all.

story: A ring of “hot spots” circles the core of NGC 1808: young star clusters and the remains of exploded stars. The centre was once suspected of being a Seyfert nucleus, powered by a feeding black hole, but most of its energy now seems to come from a burst of star birth, with perhaps a weak active nucleus as well. Gas blowing out of the centre has formed prominent dust lanes.
This [[spiral-galaxy]] has a warped disc and may have had a distant encounter with its neighbour NGC 1792. James Dunlop discovered it on 10 May 1826, noting a “faint nebula”.
NGC1808.tagline: A spiral galaxy with a ring of ‘hot spots’ around a furiously star-forming core.

story: Born at around the same time as the Hyades, or a little later, NGC 1817 is between 0.8 and 1.2 billion years old. Its stars of more than twice the Sun’s mass are already ageing into giants. It is unusually rich in Delta Scuti stars — sixteen of them — because the stars now leaving the main sequence fall right in the “instability strip”, the range of temperature and brightness where stars naturally pulsate.
This [[open-cluster]] lies on the opposite side of the sky from the galactic centre. William Herschel discovered it in February 1784.
NGC1817.tagline: A billion-year-old cluster full of pulsating stars, on the far side of the sky from the galactic centre.

story: In NGC 1818 the smaller stars have not finished forming. The cluster is only 25 to 40 million years old, and stars with the Sun’s mass or less are still contracting towards adulthood. This young [[globular-cluster]] in the Large Magellanic Cloud holds about 13,500 times the mass of the Sun.

Its double stars are oddly placed: they become more common farther from the centre, the opposite of the usual pattern. Close encounters in the crowded core may break pairs apart before heavier pairs have had time to sink inwards. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.
NGC1818.tagline: A young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud where Sun-like stars are still being born.

story: A table beneath the clouds — that is the idea behind Mensa, the faintest of all constellations. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille drew it in the 18th century in honour of Table Mountain above Cape Town, near where he observed. The Magellanic Clouds were sometimes called the Cape clouds, and Table Mountain is often capped by cloud, so he set a table in the sky beneath them. NGC 1848 is a star cluster in the part of the Large Magellanic Cloud that spills over into Mensa.
NGC1848.tagline: A cluster of the Large Magellanic Cloud in Mensa — the table beneath the Cape clouds.

facts.text: NGC 185 has an active nucleus usually classed as a Seyfert, though that status is questioned. If it holds, it is possibly the nearest Seyfert galaxy to Earth and the only one in the Local Group.
facts.title: A small but active heart

facts.text: A supernova remnant has been found near the centre of NGC 185 — the debris of a star that exploded in this small, quiet galaxy.
facts.title: Echo of an explosion

story: William Herschel discovered this little galaxy on 30 November 1787 and logged it as H II.707. His son John observed it again in 1833 and listed it in his General Catalogue of 1864. Between 1898 and 1900 James Keeler took its first photographs, with the Crossley Reflector at Lick Observatory.

NGC 185 is a dwarf [[galaxy]] orbiting the Andromeda Galaxy, and it bends the rules for its kind. Most of its stars formed early on, yet it kept making new ones at a slow trickle until the recent past, in its central regions. In 1951 Walter Baade spotted young blue objects in it, which turned out to be star clusters.
NGC185.tagline: A small companion of the Andromeda Galaxy — and possibly the closest Seyfert galaxy to Earth.

facts.text: In November 2021 astronomers using the Very Large Telescope reported a black hole in NGC 1850, spotted through its pull on a nearby star — claimed as the first found this way in a young, massive cluster.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

story: NGC 1850 looks like a [[globular-cluster]], but its stars are young: the main cluster is around 50 to 100 million years old and holds some 42,000 times the mass of the Sun. Beside it sits a smaller, looser cluster, NGC 1850A, only about 4 million years old, with stars of 35 to more than 50 solar masses. In the Milky Way, only Westerlund 1 is anything like it.
The pair lies in the bar of the Large Magellanic Cloud. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.
NGC1850.tagline: A young ‘globular’ in the Large Magellanic Cloud, with a still younger cluster at its side.

facts.text: One pulsar in NGC 1851 orbits an object heavier than the heaviest known neutron stars but lighter than the lightest black holes — a rare system for testing theories of gravity.
facts.title: A puzzle in the mass gap

facts.text: The MeerKAT radio telescope found thirteen new pulsars in the cluster, twelve of them millisecond pulsars spinning hundreds of times a second.
facts.title: A nest of pulsars

facts.text: The orbits of some pulsars hint that the core may hide an intermediate-mass black hole of up to 7,500 suns.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

story: NGC 1851 may not have started life as an ordinary [[globular-cluster]]. A faint halo of stars surrounds it, and its stars fall into at least two, and perhaps three, distinct populations — two of them roughly two billion years apart in age. One idea is that it is the core of a dwarf galaxy, stripped bare and captured by the Milky Way, as Omega Centauri may have been.

James Dunlop discovered it in 1826. It is about 9.2 billion years old and weighs some 551,000 suns, with one of the most concentrated cores of any globular cluster in our galaxy. It follows a highly elongated orbit around the Milky Way.
NGC1851.tagline: A dense globular cluster that may be the stripped heart of a dwarf galaxy swallowed by the Milky Way.

story: The Milky Way’s globular clusters are ancient. NGC 1854 is not. It is a young [[globular-cluster]] in the northern part of the central bar of the Large Magellanic Cloud — a big, round ball of stars formed long after our own globulars. It ended up with two catalogue numbers and is also listed as NGC 1855. Nearby lies NGC 1858, a cluster still wrapped in glowing gas. James Dunlop discovered NGC 1854 in 1826.
NGC1854.tagline: A young, bright globular cluster in the bar of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

story: NGC 1856 has the mass of a globular cluster but not the age. It is a young, massive cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the kind sometimes called a “blue globular”, because its hot, young stars are still shining. Its age has been revised: first estimated at about 80 million years, later at around 300 million. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826 with a 9-inch reflecting telescope.
NGC1856.tagline: A ‘blue globular’ in the Large Magellanic Cloud — massive, but young.

story: NGC 1857 seems to have two hearts. Its irregular shape suggests two dense cores rather than one. This rich [[open-cluster]] has around 360 member stars, is about 257 million years old and has almost the same mix of elements as the Sun. On the sky it lies close to another cluster, Czernik 20, but that is most likely a chance alignment.
William Herschel discovered it on 30 September 1780, years before his great sweeps of the sky began.
NGC1857.tagline: A rich cluster in Auriga that seems to have two hearts.

discovered.note: Catalogued as Dunlop 120; John Herschel’s 1834 observation became NGC 1858

story: When John Herschel recorded this glowing cluster on 2 November 1834, he did not connect it with Dunlop 120, an object James Dunlop had logged on 3 August 1826. Only later did astronomers realise the two were the same. NGC 1858 is a bright, irregular [[open-cluster]] wrapped in an [[emission-nebula]], in the Large Magellanic Cloud — hot young stars still lighting up the gas they formed from.
NGC1858.tagline: A glowing cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, discovered twice by two astronomers.

facts.text: In 1951 Harlow Shapley and V. M. Nail found 29 [[variable-star|variable stars]] here, 23 of them classical Cepheids. All at the same distance, they make a natural test bench for the pulsating stars used to measure the universe.
facts.title: A nest of Cepheids

facts.text: In 2025 astronomers found a planetary nebula near the cluster’s centre. Its shell is about 18,000 years old, puffed off by a star that began life with nearly four times the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: A dying star inside

story: When the stars of NGC 1866 were born, about 190 million years ago, dinosaurs were already walking the Earth. For a [[globular-cluster]] that is remarkably young. It orbits near the northern edge of the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], and with roughly 135,000 times the Sun’s mass it may be one of the most massive clusters that galaxy has built in the past three billion years.
James Dunlop discovered it from New South Wales on 3 August 1826. Hubble images and later spectra show that its stars fall into two families of slightly different ages: fast spinners and slower ones.
NGC1866.tagline: A globular cluster born while dinosaurs walked the Earth — and still rich in pulsing Cepheid stars.

story: Picture three families of newborn stars, each still wrapped in the hydrogen cloud that formed it. NGC 1871 is one of them — a young [[open-cluster]] set in an [[emission-nebula]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] — and it makes a trio with its neighbours NGC 1869 and NGC 1873. The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop found it on 5 November 1826, while sweeping the southern sky with a 9-inch reflector at Parramatta, near Sydney.
NGC1871.tagline: One of three young star clusters wrapped in glowing gas, side by side in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

discovered.note: Found again by John Herschel in 1837

story: NGC 1873 was found twice. James Dunlop logged it from New South Wales on 24 September 1826; John Herschel came across it again on 2 January 1837, during his years charting the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. It is a young [[cluster-nebula|star cluster still lit by its birth cloud]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], and one of a trio with NGC 1869 and NGC 1871.
NGC1873.tagline: Spotted from two continents a decade apart — first from Australia, then from South Africa.

facts.text: At around 6.8 billion years old, the stars of NGC 188 had already been shining for some two billion years when the Sun and Earth formed.
facts.title: Older than the Sun

facts.text: Patrick Moore numbered the 109 objects of his Caldwell catalogue from north to south. NGC 188, the closest to the north celestial pole, became number 1.
facts.title: First on the list

story: Most [[open-cluster|open clusters]] do not last. The gravity of the Milky Way tugs at their stars, and they drift apart and scatter long before they grow old. NGC 188 is a survivor. It lies above the plane of the galaxy, farther from the galactic centre than the Sun, and it has held together for billions of years.

John Herschel discovered it in the 19th century. Because it sits so close to the north celestial pole, it is nicknamed the Polarissima Cluster — ‘the most polar’ — and it heads Patrick Moore’s Caldwell catalogue as Caldwell 1.
NGC188.tagline: A family of stars that should have scattered long ago — and was already ancient when the Sun was born.

story: In 1783 William Herschel gave his sister Caroline a small telescope to sweep the sky for comets. That year she began turning up nebulae and star clusters too, among them this small [[open-cluster]] in Cassiopeia, which she logged on 27 September 1783.

Forty-six years later her nephew John came across it again, on 27 October 1829, while surveying the northern sky. NGC 189 travels around the Milky Way on a nearly circular path within the galaxy’s thin disc.
NGC189.tagline: One of Caroline Herschel’s finds, rediscovered 46 years later by her nephew John.

facts.text: John Herschel logged only a rich, coarse scatter of stars here in 1827. The glowing cloud around them was found in 1892, when Max Wolf photographed the field, and it was catalogued separately as IC 410.
facts.title: The nebula nobody saw

story: Inside the glowing [[emission-nebula]] IC 410, nicknamed the Tadpole Nebula, a crowd of infant stars is still taking shape. NGC 1893 is that [[open-cluster|cluster]], and the gas around it is the raw material it formed from. X-ray images from NASA’s Chandra observatory suggest the region holds about 4,600 young stellar objects — stars so new that most have not yet settled into the long, steady middle age our Sun is enjoying.
NGC1893.tagline: Thousands of newborn stars still inside the cloud that made them — the cluster at the heart of the Tadpole Nebula.

story: About 300 stars travel together in NGC 1907, an [[open-cluster]] in Auriga that has held on to its members for some 500 million years. That is a ripe old age for a cluster of this kind: many are pulled apart by the galaxy’s gravity long before. William Herschel added it to his catalogue in 1787. In the sky it lies just south of the brighter, better-known M 38.
NGC1907.tagline: Around 300 stars that have stayed together for half a billion years, just beside M 38 in Auriga.

facts.text: The cloud lies on the edge of the Orion–Eridanus bubble, a vast shell blown out by the massive stars of Orion. Its comet-shaped heads point back towards those stars, as if combed by a wind from that direction.
facts.title: Combed by Orion’s winds

story: In long-exposure photographs this cloud has the unmistakable profile of a fairy-tale witch. The Witch Head is a [[reflection-nebula]] just across the border in Eridanus, a faint veil of dust that shines by reflecting the light of Rigel, Orion’s brilliant blue supergiant. Its dust grains scatter blue light better than red, which gives the witch her ghostly blue tint.
She is more than a pretty silhouette. Radio telescopes detect carbon monoxide inside, a sign of cold molecular gas, and young T Tauri stars are forming deep within.
NGC1909.tagline: A witch’s profile drawn in faint blue dust, lit by Rigel and shaped by the winds of Orion’s giant stars.

story: Some of the most extreme stars in our cosmic neighbourhood live in NGC 1910, a loose group of hot, massive stars — an OB association, catalogued as LH 41 — in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]]. Among its members is S Doradus, a star so luminous and unstable that it gave its name to a whole class of erratic giants, the S Doradus [[variable-star|variables]]. Beside the group glows a hydrogen cloud known as N119.
NGC1910.tagline: A family of giant stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, home to the restless S Doradus.

story: The [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] is famous for its young, massive star clusters, but NGC 1916 is a genuine relic. It is one of only about fifteen genuinely ancient [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known in that galaxy, a ball of stars poor in heavy elements that formed many billions of years ago. It sits in the Cloud’s central bar, close in the sky to the S Doradus group NGC 1910, where patchy dust dims it unevenly and makes it harder to study.
NGC1916.tagline: A true relic: one of the oldest star clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud, buried in its central bar.

facts.text: In 1931 the Swedish astronomer Per Collinder listed NGC 1931 in his catalogue of open star clusters as Collinder 68 — a neat match of number and year.
facts.title: Catalogued in its own year

story: Shrink the Orion Nebula and move it to Auriga, and you get something like NGC 1931. Like its famous cousin, it mixes a glowing [[emission-nebula]] with dust that reflects starlight, and at its heart sits a tiny Trapezium of hot young stars. The cluster is only about 2 million years old, and most of its star formation is still hidden inside the cloud. William Herschel found it in 1793 and noted a few stars in the middle.
NGC1931.tagline: A miniature Orion Nebula in Auriga, complete with its own little Trapezium of hot young stars.

story: Wherever massive young stars are born, their ultraviolet light makes the leftover hydrogen glow. NGC 1934 is one such glow: an [[emission-nebula]] around a small star cluster in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]]. John Herschel recorded it on 23 November 1834, during his first year at the Cape of Good Hope, where he spent four years charting the far southern sky that his father had never been able to see from England.
NGC1934.tagline: Glowing hydrogen in the Large Magellanic Cloud, logged by John Herschel in his first year at the Cape.

facts.text: Its nucleus is mildly active, of a type known as a LINER. The most likely power source is gas spiralling into a supermassive black hole at the centre.
facts.title: A quietly active heart

story: Something is odd about NGC 1947. Its stars form a smooth body with no real disc, more like an [[elliptical-galaxy]] than the lenticular galaxy it is classed as. Yet lanes of dark dust cut across it, and the gas in them circles the centre at right angles to the stars — the mark of a polar-ring galaxy. With no tidal tails to suggest a violent merger, astronomers think it captured this gas and dust from a gas-rich galaxy.
NGC1947.tagline: A galaxy wearing a ring of borrowed dust, set at right angles to its stars.

story: On the night of 3 August 1826, James Dunlop had a remarkable run. From Parramatta in New South Wales he swept up several objects in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], among them NGC 1866, NGC 2014 and this one, NGC 1955. It is a young star cluster still embedded in its glowing [[emission-nebula|cloud of hydrogen]], part of a larger star-forming region in that neighbouring galaxy.
NGC1955.tagline: One of a haul of Magellanic treasures that James Dunlop logged on a single night in August 1826.

story: Young stars in NGC 1970 are still lighting up the gas they were born from — a bright [[open-cluster]] and [[emission-nebula]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]]. John Herschel recorded it on 31 January 1835. He had shipped a large reflecting telescope to the Cape of Good Hope to extend his father’s great survey of nebulae and clusters to the southern sky.
NGC1970.tagline: A young cluster and its glowing cloud, recorded from the Cape on the last day of January 1835.

story: Just north of the Orion Nebula, at the top of Orion’s Sword, lies a softer glow nicknamed the Running Man. NGC 1973 is one of its three catalogued pieces: a [[reflection-nebula]], dust that shines because it scatters the light of hot young stars nearby, chiefly 42 Orionis. William Herschel had already seen the brightest part of the cloud, but this smaller patch was first noted by the German astronomer Heinrich d’Arrest in 1862.
NGC1973.tagline: A small patch of dusty light at the northern end of Orion’s Sword, first noticed in 1862.

discovered.note: Observed again by John Herschel in 1837 and listed as NGC 1991

story: James Dunlop logged this young cluster and its glowing gas in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] on 6 November 1826. A decade later, on 2 January 1837, John Herschel observed it from the Cape, and his record was catalogued separately — so the same stars now carry two numbers, NGC 1974 and NGC 1991. Duplicates like this crop up throughout the [[ngc-ic|New General Catalogue]], which J. L. E. Dreyer compiled in 1888 from many observers’ records.
NGC1974.tagline: A Magellanic star cluster that ended up in the catalogue twice, under two different numbers.

story: Dark lanes of dust divide the nebula Sh 2-279 into three NGC pieces — NGC 1973, NGC 1975 and NGC 1977 — and together they form the shape photographers call the Running Man. NGC 1975 is one of the two smaller pieces, a [[reflection-nebula]] first noted by Heinrich d’Arrest in 1864. Studies of the area found young T Tauri stars crowded around the Orion Nebula, thinning out in a tail that reaches towards this cloud.
NGC1975.tagline: One of three dusty glows that together sketch a figure running across Orion’s Sword.

facts.text: Hubble and Spitzer have found at least seven proplyds here — young stars in planet-forming discs that are being evaporated by ultraviolet light from 42 Orionis. It was the first time a B-type star, rather than a hotter O-type, was seen doing this.
facts.title: Planet nurseries under fire

story: When William Herschel came upon this cloud in 1786, he logged it as “42 Orionis and neb” and added a double exclamation mark, the catalogue shorthand for a very remarkable object. Today it is known as the Running Man: a [[reflection-nebula]] just north of the Orion Nebula, glowing mainly with the light of the hot young star 42 Orionis scattered by dust. Darker lanes cutting through the glow give it the outline of a figure in full stride.
NGC1977.tagline: A dusty runner in Orion’s Sword, where one hot star is boiling away newborn planet-forming discs.

discovered.note: He may have seen it as early as 1783

story: At the bottom of Orion’s Sword, just south of the great Orion Nebula, young stars gather around Iota Orionis. NGC 1980 is a young [[open-cluster]] wrapped in a faint veil of glowing gas, sometimes called the Lost Jewel of Orion. William Herschel catalogued it on 31 January 1786, though he may already have seen it on 20 September 1783, while he was busy studying double stars.
NGC1980.tagline: The young star cluster around Iota Orionis, at the very tip of Orion’s Sword — ‘the Lost Jewel of Orion’.

story: Some see a crocodile here: one star for the snout, another for the tail, and two little rows of three stars for its legs. NGC 1981 is a loose [[open-cluster]] at the northern end of Orion’s Sword, separated from the Orion Nebula by the dusty Running Man region. Bright as it is, it was not William Herschel but his son John who first catalogued it, on 4 January 1827.
NGC1981.tagline: A loose ‘crocodile’ of stars at the top of Orion’s Sword, catalogued not by William Herschel but by his son.

story: Among the crowd of clusters and nebulae in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], NGC 1984 is a modest one: an [[open-cluster]] still tied to the [[emission-nebula|glowing hydrogen]] it formed in. John Herschel recorded it on 16 December 1835. Because everything in the Cloud lies at nearly the same distance from us, clusters like this make a convenient laboratory for comparing the lives of young stars.
NGC1984.tagline: A small young cluster in a glowing cloud, added to John Herschel’s southern catalogue in December 1835.

facts.text: The leading idea is that narrow jets of gas from young stars in the region blasted through the sheet of dust and gas, perhaps helped by powerful radiation from a nearby mature star.
facts.title: Who punched the hole?

facts.text: Close by lies HH 1/2, the first Herbig–Haro object ever recognised — a glowing knot where a jet from a newborn star slams into the gas around it.
facts.title: Next door to a first

story: The young variable star V380 Orionis lights up NGC 1999, a [[reflection-nebula]] in Orion with a strange black patch in the middle. For years astronomers took the patch for a [[dark-nebula]], a dense knot of dust blocking the light behind it. Then in 2009 the Herschel Space Observatory looked with infrared eyes that can see into such clouds — and still saw black. Follow-up observations confirmed it: the ‘Cosmic Keyhole’ is not dense dust at all but genuinely empty space.
NGC1999.tagline: A glowing cloud with a black keyhole in it — and the keyhole turned out to be a real hole.

story: Twenty million years is very young for a star cluster, yet NGC 2004 already holds about 23,000 times the mass of the Sun — far more than most open clusters in our own galaxy. It belongs to the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], the Milky Way’s largest satellite galaxy, which is still forming big, crowded clusters like this one. James Dunlop discovered it on 24 September 1826.
NGC2004.tagline: A heavyweight young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud — about 20 million years old and 23,000 Suns strong.

story: To celebrate its 30th anniversary in 2020, the Hubble Space Telescope released a picture that looks like a slice of undersea reef. The big red part of that ‘Cosmic Reef’ is NGC 2014, an [[emission-nebula]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], glowing around a cluster of young stars. Its smaller, bluer neighbour in the picture is NGC 2020. James Dunlop discovered NGC 2014 on 3 August 1826.
NGC2014.tagline: The red half of Hubble’s ‘Cosmic Reef’, the portrait chosen for the telescope’s 30th birthday.

facts.text: About 86 percent of the young, low-mass stars around the central hot star are still wrapped in discs of gas and dust — the raw material of planets.
facts.title: A nursery of planet-forming discs

facts.text: Radio observations with ALMA reveal two groups split by a molecular cloud: an eastern group just 200,000 to 500,000 years old, and a western one around a million years old.
facts.title: Two generations

story: Beside Alnitak, the eastern star of Orion’s Belt, a glow laced with dark dust looks like a burning fire. Alnitak seems to light it, but the two are not connected. The real power source is hidden: an O-type star called IRS 2b, buried in dust at the heart of a young cluster, whose ultraviolet light makes the gas of this [[emission-nebula]] shine.
Infrared and X-ray telescopes have uncovered several hundred young stars inside, out of an estimated 800.
NGC2024.tagline: A fire beside Orion’s Belt — though the bright star next to it has nothing to do with the flames.

story: To the naked eye, the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] looks like a torn-off scrap of the Milky Way. It is named after Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew described it during their voyage around the world in 1519–22, though it was known long before. In fact it is a separate galaxy, home to thousands of star clusters, and NGC 2037 is one of them: an [[open-cluster]] in the part of the Cloud that lies in Dorado.
NGC2037.tagline: One of the thousands of star clusters scattered through the Large Magellanic Cloud.

story: In 1826 James Dunlop, working at Parramatta in New South Wales, combed the southern sky with a 9-inch reflecting telescope and logged hundreds of nebulae and star clusters, many of them in the Magellanic Clouds. NGC 2041 was one of his finds. It is catalogued as a [[globular-cluster]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] — a dense ball of stars that belongs to another galaxy.
NGC2041.tagline: A rich cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, first spotted in 1826 with a 9-inch reflecting telescope.

story: The Milky Way’s largest companion galaxy, the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], is still making stars at a lively pace, and its clusters span every age from newborn to ancient. NGC 2042 is one of its [[open-cluster|open clusters]], lying in the sky just north-west of the Tarantula Nebula — the most active star-forming region known in our Local Group of galaxies.
NGC2042.tagline: A star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a stone’s throw in the sky from the Tarantula Nebula.

facts.text: VFTS 102, a massive star found speeding through the area, may once have been the pulsar’s companion — flung away when the supernova tore their pair apart.
facts.title: A runaway partner

facts.text: NGC 2060 is one of the few places to find OVz stars, massive stars thought to be caught at a very early stage of their lives.
facts.title: Stars at the very beginning

story: Deep in the Tarantula Nebula, beside its giant central cluster, lies NGC 2060: a loose group of stars about 10 million years old, sitting inside a bubble blown by stellar winds or old explosions. The name is often used for the [[supernova-remnant]] N157B, the debris of a star that, as seen from Earth, blew up about 5,000 years ago. In 1998 astronomers found what the explosion left behind: a pulsar spinning more than 60 times a second.
NGC2060.tagline: A star cluster in the Tarantula Nebula, wrapped in the wreck of a supernova that left a spinning pulsar.

discovered.note: The Tarantula Nebula itself was recorded by Lacaille in 1751–53

facts.text: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille recorded the Tarantula during his expedition to the Cape of Good Hope in 1751–53, describing it as a nebula with no star visible in his telescope.
facts.title: Seen from the Cape in the 1750s

facts.text: Supernova 1987A, the closest supernova seen since the invention of the telescope, went off on the outskirts of the Tarantula.
facts.title: Neighbour of a famous supernova

story: If the Tarantula Nebula were as close to us as the Orion Nebula, it would be bright enough to cast shadows. NGC 2069 is a knot in the northern loop of that vast [[emission-nebula]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], the most active starburst region known in our Local Group of galaxies. James Dunlop and John Herschel each catalogued this loop separately from the main nebula. The whole complex owes its name to glowing filaments that stretch out like a spider’s legs.
NGC2069.tagline: A loop of the Tarantula Nebula, a star factory so bright it would cast shadows if it were as close as Orion.

facts.text: In February 1987 a star on the outskirts of the Tarantula exploded. SN 1987A was the nearest supernova seen since the invention of the telescope, and southern observers could see it with the naked eye.
facts.title: A supernova on the doorstep

facts.text: In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope photographed the Tarantula in infrared light, revealing thousands of young stars that had been hidden inside its dust.
facts.title: Webb’s spider

story: Move the Tarantula to where the Orion Nebula sits and its light would cast shadows at night. That is how luminous this cloud of glowing gas is. The Tarantula is a vast [[emission-nebula]] in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the small [[magellanic-clouds|galaxies that accompany our own]]. Its spidery loops are lit mostly by one fierce star cluster at its heart, NGC 2070.

At the cluster’s core sits R136, one of the most energetic star clusters known. Among its members is R136a1, one of the most massive stars ever weighed: hundreds of times the Sun’s mass and millions of times as bright. Stars this heavy burn out within a few million years.
Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille recorded it in 1752 while mapping the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. Its other name, 30 Doradus, is the kind of number usually given to a star.
NGC2070.tagline: A nebula so luminous that, as close as Orion’s, it would cast shadows — powered by some of the heaviest stars known.

story: William Herschel started 1784 at his telescope: on 1 January he found this faint glow in Orion. NGC 2071 is a [[reflection-nebula]], a cloud of dust that shines with the reflected light of the star at its centre, HD 290861. It belongs to the same group of nebulae as the brighter M 78, along with NGC 2064 and NGC 2067. Several Herbig–Haro objects — knots lit up by jets from newborn stars — show that star birth here is still going on.
NGC2071.tagline: M 78’s quieter neighbour — a dusty mirror in Orion, found on New Year’s Day 1784.

discovered.note: Found independently by John Herschel in the 1830s

facts.text: John Herschel catalogued it in the 1830s and long had the credit. Only recently was an earlier sighting by James Dunlop, made on 3 August 1826, matched to this nebula.
facts.title: Credit, at last

story: In August 2008 the Hubble Space Telescope completed its 100,000th orbit of the Earth, and to mark the moment it photographed part of the nebula around NGC 2074. This [[emission-nebula]], near the Tarantula Nebula in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]], is a hotbed of star birth, perhaps set off by a nearby supernova. It lies on the edge of a dark molecular cloud, the raw material for still more stars.
NGC2074.tagline: The star-forming cloud Hubble photographed to celebrate its 100,000th trip around the Earth.

facts.text: Oxygen energised by a powerful star turns the western side green, hydrogen makes the outskirts red, and the centre, where both glow, looks pale yellow. Around the eyes, strongly energised hydrogen adds a blue tint.
facts.title: Colour-coded chemistry

story: Two bright white patches stare out of NGC 2080 like the eyes of a ghost. This [[emission-nebula]], just south of the Tarantula Nebula, is a busy stellar nursery, and each eye is a nest of new stars. The western one holds a young, massive star that has blown a bubble around itself; the eastern one hides a fresh cluster still swaddled in dust. Because that dust has not yet cleared, astronomers think both sets of stars formed within the last 10,000 years.
NGC2080.tagline: The Ghost Head Nebula — two pale ‘eyes’ where stars switched on within the last 10,000 years.

story: Round and densely packed, NGC 2100 looks at first glance like an ancient [[globular-cluster]]. It is in fact a young [[open-cluster]] in the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] — the kind that lasts for tens or hundreds of millions of years before gravitational tugs from other bodies scatter its stars. James Dunlop added it to his southern catalogue in 1826.
NGC2100.tagline: A round, rich young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud that is easily mistaken for a globular.

story: Orion is famous for youth: its nebulae are full of stars only a few million years old. NGC 2112 breaks the pattern. This [[open-cluster]] is roughly 2 billion years old, a survivor in a galaxy whose gravity scatters most clusters long before they reach such an age. It has nothing to do with Orion’s young nurseries — it is simply a far older group of stars seen in the same direction.
NGC2112.tagline: A two-billion-year-old star cluster in Orion, a constellation better known for its newborn stars.

story: Most of the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] lies in Dorado, but its edge spills into Mensa, a faint constellation that Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille named after Table Mountain, the flat-topped peak above Cape Town where he observed. NGC 2122 is one of the Cloud’s objects on that side of the line: an [[emission-nebula]] around a young cluster, also listed as N 180B in Karl Henize’s 1956 catalogue of Magellanic nebulae. James Dunlop found it in 1826.
NGC2122.tagline: A glowing cloud of the Large Magellanic Cloud that strays over the border into Mensa, the Table Mountain.

story: On 21 December 2010, as the Moon slid through Earth’s shadow in a total [[eclipse|lunar eclipse]], it also passed in front of NGC 2129 — an [[occultation]] seen from Japan, the North Pacific and North America. The coincidence will repeat during the December 2029 eclipse and again on 21 December 2094. The [[open-cluster]] itself is young, about 10 million years old, and dominated by two hot B-type stars that probably orbit each other.
NGC2129.tagline: A young cluster in Gemini that the Moon covered during a total lunar eclipse — and will again in 2029.

story: Among Orion’s young nebulae and clusters, NGC 2141 is a veteran. Studies put this [[open-cluster]] at roughly 1.3 to 2.5 billion years old, a great age for a group of stars that the galaxy’s tides tend to scatter. It lies towards the galactic anticentre — the direction pointing straight away from the Milky Way’s core — in the outer part of our galaxy’s disc.
NGC2141.tagline: An old, long-overlooked star cluster in Orion, looking out towards the edge of our galaxy.

story: Rich, round clusters like NGC 2157 are among the treasures of the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]]. It is crammed with stars like a [[globular-cluster]], yet Hubble images show it is only about 100 million years old. The Milky Way’s own globulars are typically more than ten billion years old, so clusters like this one let astronomers see what such dense star cities might have looked like in their youth.
NGC2157.tagline: A rich, round cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, packed like a globular but only 100 million years old.

facts.text: Among its stars is a cataclysmic variable — a white dwarf pulling gas from a close companion — only the fourth known in any open cluster.
facts.title: A rare kind of variable

story: Right beside the bright cluster M 35, NGC 2158 looks like a smaller sibling. It is nothing of the kind: it lies far beyond M 35, and at about 2 billion years old it is many times older. Some 3,000 stars are packed into it, so many that astronomers once took it for a [[globular-cluster]]. Today it is counted as a rich [[open-cluster]] that is poor in heavy elements — an in-between object. William Herschel found it in 1784.
NGC2158.tagline: M 35’s faint companion in the sky — far more distant, far older, and crammed with some 3,000 stars.

story: James Dunlop spent 1826 sweeping the southern sky from New South Wales, and the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] gave him some of his richest pickings. NGC 2164, found on 27 September that year, is one of them: a compact cluster of stars in that neighbouring galaxy, listed in some catalogues as an [[open-cluster]] and in others as a [[globular-cluster]] — a common puzzle with the Cloud’s rich clusters.
NGC2164.tagline: A compact cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, found by James Dunlop in September 1826.

discovered.note: Possibly seen by Giovanni Battista Hodierna before 1654

story: Stargazers are used to finding animals and heroes in the sky, but NGC 2169 offers a number. The brightest stars of this [[open-cluster]] in Orion fall into a pattern that looks remarkably like the digits ‘37’, earning it the nickname the ‘37’ Cluster. The Sicilian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna may have seen it before 1654; William Herschel found it independently on 15 October 1784.
NGC2169.tagline: The cluster that spells out a number: its brightest stars form the digits ‘37’.

facts.text: For its 24th anniversary in 2014, the Hubble Space Telescope released an infrared view of part of the nebula, showing knots of gas and dust being carved by the young stars.
facts.title: A Hubble birthday portrait

story: In long-exposure photographs this cloud of glowing hydrogen looks like the head of a monkey, hence its nickname, the Monkey Head Nebula. NGC 2174 is an [[emission-nebula]] lit by the young stars of the cluster NGC 2175 near its centre. Their winds and high-energy radiation push the glowing gas and dark dust into ever more complex shapes. The French astronomer Édouard Stephan discovered it on 6 February 1877.
NGC2174.tagline: A monkey’s face in glowing gas, sculpted by the fierce light of the young stars inside it.

discovered.note: Before 1654; found again independently by Karl Christian Bruhns

facts.text: Catalogues disagree: NGC 2174 and NGC 2175 have each been used for the whole nebula, its brightest knot or the cluster. The SIMBAD database uses NGC 2174 for the nebula and NGC 2175 for the cluster.
facts.title: Which number is which?

story: The stars that light up the Monkey Head Nebula belong to NGC 2175, a very young [[open-cluster]] still embedded in the cloud it formed from. At about nine million years old, its stars are infants beside our 4.6-billion-year-old Sun. Giovanni Battista Hodierna, a priest-astronomer in Sicily, seems to have spotted it before 1654. In 1970 a second, smaller cluster, NGC 2175s, was found close by.
NGC2175.tagline: The young star cluster at the heart of the Monkey Head Nebula, only about nine million years old.

story: Stars are not born alone. They form in batches inside great clouds of gas, and for a while each batch travels together as an [[open-cluster]] like NGC 2180 in Orion. Slowly, tugs from passing clouds and from the galaxy itself loosen the family until its members drift apart into the general crowd of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] — just as the Sun’s own birth siblings did long ago.
NGC2180.tagline: A small open cluster in Orion — a family of stars that will not stay together for ever.

story: Young, hot stars in Monoceros are still lighting up the dusty cloud they formed from. NGC 2182 is one of several small [[reflection-nebula|reflection nebulae]] in this complex, known as Monoceros R2, whose brightest member is NGC 2170. The dust looks blue because it scatters the blue part of starlight more readily than the red. William Herschel recorded it on 24 February 1786 as a star wrapped in a very faint, milky glow.
NGC2182.tagline: A small dusty mirror in Monoceros, lit by young stars in the Monoceros R2 star-forming cloud.

story: Every star in NGC 2186 began life at about the same time, from the same cloud, with the same mix of ingredients. That makes an [[open-cluster]] like this a natural experiment: the main difference between its members is how much mass each was born with, so astronomers can watch how mass alone shapes a star’s life. It lies in eastern Orion, close to the band of the winter [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2186.tagline: A modest open cluster in Orion — a ready-made experiment in how stars live.

story: William Herschel discovered NGC 2194 on 11 February 1784. Seventy-eight years later Heinrich d’Arrest came across it again, and J. L. E. Dreyer listed d’Arrest’s sighting in a supplement to the General Catalogue as a new object, without noticing it was already there. The [[open-cluster]] itself is rich and moderately concentrated, a few hundred million years old by most estimates, and may contain blue stragglers — stars that look younger than their neighbours.
NGC2194.tagline: A rich cluster in Orion that was accidentally catalogued a second time, almost 80 years after its discovery.

facts.text: Five variable stars have been found in the cluster, four of them eclipsing binaries — pairs of stars that take turns passing in front of one another as seen from Earth.
facts.title: Stars that eclipse each other

story: Many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] break up within a few hundred million years, but NGC 2204 has held together for about two billion. Its stars are poorer in heavy elements than the Sun, with only about 59 percent as much iron. It also has a large population of blue stragglers — stars that look too young and hot for so old a cluster, probably because older stars merged. William Herschel discovered it on 6 February 1785.
NGC2204.tagline: A two-billion-year-old cluster in Canis Major, home to stars that may be the products of stellar mergers.

story: Monoceros, the Unicorn, has no bright stars to speak of, yet it is rich in star clusters because the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] runs right through it. NGC 2215 is one of those [[open-cluster|open clusters]]. The constellation itself is a newcomer: it first appeared on star maps in the early 17th century, drawn into the dim gap between Orion, Canis Major and Canis Minor.
NGC2215.tagline: A small open cluster in Monoceros, the faint Unicorn that straddles the winter Milky Way.

story: Gathered around the bright star 10 Monocerotis, NGC 2232 is one of the nearest [[open-cluster|open clusters]] to the Sun. It belongs to the Gould Belt, a great ring of young stars that also takes in the Orion Nebula cluster, and its closeness makes it a handy place to study young stars as they settle down. Its members are richer in iron than the Sun, and several glow in the infrared with warm dust around them.
NGC2232.tagline: One of the nearest open clusters to the Sun, gathered around the star 10 Monocerotis.

story: The number in NGC 2236 comes from the [[ngc-ic|New General Catalogue]], which the Danish-born astronomer J. L. E. Dreyer published in 1888 while working in Ireland. It gathered 7,840 nebulae and clusters, most of them discovered by William and John Herschel, and its numbers still organise the deep sky today. This entry is an [[open-cluster]] in Monoceros, close to the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2236.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, one entry among the 7,840 of the New General Catalogue.

discovered.note: Catalogued in pieces during the 1800s; its central cluster was seen by John Flamsteed in 1690

facts.text: In April 2019 Oklahoma made the Rosette its official state astronomical object. The legislature passed the bill on 16 April and Governor Kevin Stitt signed it into law six days later.
facts.title: A state symbol

facts.text: The nebula was catalogued piece by piece, so its petals carry several [[ngc-ic|NGC]] numbers — 2237, 2238 and 2246 among them — while the cluster at its heart is NGC 2244.
facts.title: One flower, many numbers

story: In long-exposure photographs it blooms like a red rose, though some see a human skull and call it the Skull Nebula. The Rosette is a huge [[emission-nebula]], a cloud holding around 10,000 Suns’ worth of gas, glowing because the young stars of the cluster NGC 2244 light it from inside.

Those stars were born from the nebula itself, and now they are hollowing it out. A handful of hot O-type stars, led by HD 46223 and HD 46150, drive winds that have blown a bubble in the middle. X-ray telescopes found that bubble filled with gas at one to ten million degrees — far hotter than the 10,000 degrees typical of such clouds.
The flower is still putting out buds. About 2,500 young stars crowd the complex, and most new star birth is under way in the dark Rosette Molecular Cloud just to the south-east.
NGC2237.tagline: A cosmic rose — or a skull, to some — hollowed out by the hot young stars born inside it.

story: Most [[open-cluster|open clusters]] are cosmic mayflies, scattered within a few hundred million years. NGC 2243 has survived for something like four billion years, which makes it one of the oldest known. Its stars hold only about a third as much iron, for their hydrogen, as the Sun does — a sign that they formed from gas that earlier generations of stars had not yet enriched much. It lies well below the crowded plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2243.tagline: One of the oldest open clusters known — around four billion years old and poor in heavy elements.

facts.text: A 2023 study found that brown dwarfs here tend to form close to the hottest stars. Their fierce light may strip gas from cores that would otherwise have grown into ordinary stars.
facts.title: Brown dwarfs in the glare

facts.text: One young member shows signs of a planet-forming disc being eroded by the radiation around it, much like the proplyds seen in the Orion Nebula.
facts.title: A disc blowing away

story: Less than five million years old, the stars of NGC 2244 are cosmic infants — an [[open-cluster]] fresh from its nursery. They formed from the gas of the Rosette Nebula, which still wraps around them.

Its leaders are true heavyweights. HD 46223 has around 50 times the Sun’s mass and shines 400,000 times as brightly. HD 46150 may weigh up to 60 Suns and is brighter still — though it might really be two stars. Hot O-type stars like these pour out radiation and stellar winds that shape everything nearby.
The most obvious star in the cluster, 12 Monocerotis, is not a member at all. It is an orange giant much closer to us, lying in the foreground by chance.
NGC2244.tagline: Newborn giants at the heart of the Rosette — blazing so fiercely they stunt the stars forming around them.

story: Not every nebula makes its own light. NGC 2245 is a small [[reflection-nebula]], dust that glows only because it scatters the light of a young star at its centre. It belongs to Monoceros R1, a chain of dusty clouds and newborn stars that also includes its close neighbour NGC 2247 and the nebulae IC 446 and IC 447. Young stars and jets from newborn stars show that star birth is still under way here.
NGC2245.tagline: A small patch of reflected starlight in Monoceros, part of a young star-forming region.

discovered.note: Using Lord Rosse’s Leviathan telescope at Birr Castle

story: In 1857 Lord Rosse’s Leviathan in Ireland was the largest telescope in the world, and on 14 February that year his assistant R. J. Mitchell used it to find this faint glow in Monoceros. NGC 2247 is a [[reflection-nebula]], dust lit by a young star embedded in it, in the star-forming region Monoceros R1 alongside its neighbour NGC 2245.
NGC2247.tagline: A dusty glow in Monoceros discovered in 1857 with the giant Leviathan telescope at Birr Castle.

story: Count the stars in NGC 225 and more than half turn out not to be alone. Astronomers estimate that about 52 percent of them are in [[double-star|binary]] or multiple systems, orbiting a companion. This [[open-cluster]] is some 100 to 150 million years old, so its stars were born while dinosaurs walked the Earth — young next to the Sun, which is about 4.6 billion years old. Caroline Herschel discovered it in 1783.
NGC225.tagline: A cluster born in the age of the dinosaurs, where most stars have a partner.

story: Astronomers sort star clusters into two broad kinds. Globular clusters are ancient, dense balls of hundreds of thousands of stars that orbit in the galaxy’s halo and bulge. [[open-cluster|Open clusters]] like NGC 2250 in Monoceros are looser, usually much younger groups living in the disc of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], where new stars are still being made from gas and dust.
NGC2250.tagline: A loose open cluster in Monoceros — a very different beast from the ancient globular clusters.

story: Every [[open-cluster]] is temporary. As NGC 2251 circles the centre of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], the galaxy’s tides and the pull of passing gas clouds steadily strip away its outer stars. Over hundreds of millions of years such clusters fade into the general background of stars. In the sky, NGC 2251 has a neighbour less than a degree away: the cluster NGC 2254.
NGC2251.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, slowly coming apart as it circles the galaxy.

story: Less than a degree from the great Rosette Nebula, one of the showpieces of the winter sky, lies the much quieter NGC 2252. Being neighbours in the sky does not make them neighbours in space: objects that look close together can lie at very different distances. NGC 2252 is an [[open-cluster]] in Monoceros, in the busy band of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] where much of our galaxy’s star formation happens.
NGC2252.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, close in the sky to the famous Rosette Nebula.

story: Draw the midline of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]]’s band across the sky — the galactic equator — and NGC 2254 sits almost exactly on it. Looking there, we gaze edge-on through the flat disc of our galaxy, where its gas, dust and young star clusters are concentrated. This [[open-cluster]] in Monoceros is one of them, seen through the haze of dust that dims and reddens light travelling along the disc.
NGC2254.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, sitting almost exactly on the central line of the Milky Way.

facts.text: The space telescope named after the man who studied it photographed the nebula too. Its portrait of NGC 2261 was released in 1999.
facts.title: Hubble meets Hubble

facts.text: From October 2021 to April 2022 more than 20 amateur astronomers shared the Big Amateur Telescope to film NGC 2261 over six months, building a time-lapse of its changing face.
facts.title: An amateur time-lapse

story: Most nebulae look the same for a human lifetime. This one changes from month to month. NGC 2261 is a [[reflection-nebula]], a fan of dust lit by the young star R Monocerotis, which is itself hidden from direct view. One explanation for its shifting face is that dense clumps of dust close to the star block its light now and then, throwing moving shadows onto the cloud — like a hand passing in front of a lamp.

Edwin Hubble kept returning to it, and it now bears his name. In 1916 he photographed it with the Yerkes 24-inch reflector and compared his plates with ones F. C. Jordan had taken in 1908, flicking between them in a blink comparator to catch the changes. On 26 January 1949 he chose it again for the first light of the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar.
William Herschel had first logged it on 26 December 1783, as a considerably bright, fan-shaped glow.
NGC2261.tagline: A nebula that changes from month to month — and the one Edwin Hubble kept coming back to.

story: Join up the brightest stars of NGC 2264 and you get a Christmas tree, lit at its base by the brilliant star S Monocerotis and topped by the dark, pointed Cone Nebula. In the usual north-up view, the tree stands on its head. The [[open-cluster]] and its glowing [[emission-nebula|cloud of hydrogen]] share one catalogue number, and the same region holds the Snowflake Cluster and the Fox Fur Nebula.

Because it is relatively nearby and large, NGC 2264 is one of the best-studied star-forming regions in the sky. Young stars are still emerging from its clouds, and there may be one brown dwarf for every few ordinary stars.
NGC2264.tagline: A Christmas tree of young stars topped by the Cone Nebula — and usually pictured upside down.

story: In age, NGC 2266 is a close match for two famous clusters, the Hyades and Praesepe. In make-up it is not: its stars carry a smaller share of the heavy elements forged by earlier generations of stars. This rich, well-condensed [[open-cluster]] in Gemini was discovered by William Herschel on 7 December 1785, and it may contain a blue straggler — a star that looks younger than its neighbours.
NGC2266.tagline: A rich, compact cluster in Gemini, about the age of the Hyades but poorer in heavy elements.

story: Every [[open-cluster]], NGC 2269 included, carries its own clock. All its stars were born together, but the heaviest burn through their fuel fastest and are the first to swell into giants. By finding which stars are just beginning to leave their long, steady phase, astronomers can tell how old a cluster is. NGC 2269 lies in Monoceros, among the many clusters strung along the winter [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2269.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros — and how astronomers read a cluster’s age from its stars.

story: Its nickname, the Broken Heart Cluster, comes from the shape some observers trace in its stars. NGC 2281 is an [[open-cluster]] in the northern constellation Auriga, roughly 630 to 660 million years old — long-lived for a group of stars that the galaxy’s tides slowly pull apart. William Herschel discovered it on 4 March 1788, describing a cluster of “coarsely scattered” fairly bright stars, “pretty rich”.
