NGC2281.tagline: The Broken Heart Cluster — a family of stars in Auriga, more than 600 million years old.

story: Some objects were recorded twice and ended up with two catalogue numbers. NGC 2282 is one of them: it also appears as IC 2172 in the Index Catalogue, the supplement J. L. E. Dreyer published to extend his New General Catalogue. It is a small [[nebula]] in Monoceros, a cloud of gas and dust lit by young stars, close to the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] where new stars are born.
NGC2282.tagline: A small glowing cloud in Monoceros that made it into the catalogues twice, as NGC 2282 and IC 2172.

story: Which stars really belong to a cluster like NGC 2286, and which just happen to lie in front of it or behind? The answer is in their motion: true members drift across the sky together. ESA’s Gaia spacecraft, launched in 2013, has measured the positions and movements of more than a billion stars, letting astronomers pick out the genuine members of thousands of [[open-cluster|open clusters]] like this one in Monoceros.
NGC2286.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, and the space mission that sorts true cluster members from impostors.

story: Not every [[globular-cluster]] around the Milky Way was born here. NGC 2298, in Puppis, probably once belonged to the Canis Major Dwarf, a proposed small galaxy whose very existence is still disputed. Life beside a big galaxy is hard on small clusters: the Milky Way’s tides are pulling stars out of NGC 2298, leaving a long trail behind it. James Dunlop discovered it on 30 May 1826.
NGC2298.tagline: A globular cluster that may be a refugee from a disputed dwarf galaxy — and is slowly being torn apart.

discovered.note: Found again by John Herschel in 1828

story: William Herschel found this [[open-cluster]] in Monoceros on 4 March 1785. Almost 43 years later, on 19 January 1828, his son John came across it again — and both records made it into the catalogue, so the same stars are listed as NGC 2302 and NGC 2299. The cluster is a lightweight, with about 333 times the Sun’s mass, and roughly 80 million years old.
NGC2299.tagline: One cluster, two Herschels and two numbers: found by William in 1785 and again by his son in 1828.

story: The Great Bird Cluster takes its name from the shape some see in its stars: a bird with its wings spread wide. NGC 2301 lies right on the band of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] in Monoceros, and this [[open-cluster]] contains hot blue giants. Its brightest star is an orange subgiant, but it may not belong: it could be a foreground star that just happens to lie along the same line of sight. William Herschel discovered the cluster in 1786.
NGC2301.tagline: The Great Bird Cluster — a flock of stars on the Milky Way in Monoceros, with a possible orange interloper.

story: In Greek myth, Gemini’s twins Castor and Pollux were inseparable brothers. The stars of an [[open-cluster]] such as NGC 2304 are siblings too: born together from one cloud of gas, at the same time and from the same ingredients. Unlike the mythical twins, they will not stay together for ever — over time the galaxy’s gravity slowly pulls such families apart.
NGC2304.tagline: A small open cluster in Gemini — a family of stellar siblings in the constellation of the Twins.

story: Young star clusters are some of the best markers of our galaxy’s spiral arms, because the arms are where gas piles up and new stars are born. By mapping where clusters such as NGC 2309 lie and how old they are, astronomers can chart the structure of a galaxy they can only see from the inside. This [[open-cluster]] sits close to the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] in Monoceros.
NGC2309.tagline: A small open cluster in Monoceros, close to the plane of the Milky Way.

story: How do you describe a star cluster in a few characters? In 1930 the Swiss-American astronomer Robert Trumpler devised a code that is still in use: a Roman numeral for how strongly the stars crowd towards the centre, a number for the spread in their brightness, and a letter for how rich the cluster is. NGC 2311 is one of the many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] in Monoceros sorted this way.
NGC2311.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros, and the simple code astronomers use to describe clusters like it.

story: Far out in the Milky Way’s disc, beyond the Perseus spiral arm, NGC 2324 has kept its stars together for about 790 million years. Astronomers have identified 852 stars that very probably belong to this [[open-cluster]], among them nine confirmed giants and a blue straggler. The cluster has settled into balance, but it will not last: estimates suggest it will dissolve in about 382 million years. William Herschel discovered it on 27 December 1786.
NGC2324.tagline: A cluster far out beyond the Perseus Arm, with roughly 380 million years left before it dissolves.

story: When we look towards Gemini we are looking outwards, roughly away from the centre of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], towards the point astronomers call the galactic anticentre. NGC 2331 lies in that direction: an [[open-cluster]] seen against the outer parts of our galaxy’s disc, where stars thin out and the gas has been less enriched by earlier generations of stars.
NGC2331.tagline: An open cluster in Gemini, in the direction that points away from the heart of our galaxy.

story: NGC 2335 has company: the cluster NGC 2343 lies only about half a degree to the south-east. Both are [[open-cluster|open clusters]] in the stretch of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] that crosses Monoceros. In this part of the sky we look outwards through the galaxy’s disc, away from its crowded centre, which is one reason the Milky Way here looks fainter than it does in Sagittarius, towards the galaxy’s core.
NGC2335.tagline: One of a pair of open clusters lying side by side in the Monoceros Milky Way.

story: Clusters like NGC 2343 begin life hidden inside clouds of gas and dust. Once the hottest new stars switch on, their light and winds blow the leftover gas away, and the cluster emerges into view. What remains is an [[open-cluster]] like this one in Monoceros, with its neighbour NGC 2335 just to the north-west.
NGC2343.tagline: An open cluster in Monoceros that shares its patch of sky with NGC 2335.

story: Canis Major, the Great Dog, trots at Orion’s heels across the sky and carries Sirius, the brightest star of the night. Its stretch of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] is scattered with [[open-cluster|open clusters]], and NGC 2345 is one of them — a group of stars born together that will slowly drift apart as they circle the galaxy.
NGC2345.tagline: An open cluster in Canis Major, the Great Dog that follows Orion across the sky.

story: A single bright star, HIP 34999, dominates NGC 2353 from its southern edge. This [[open-cluster]] in Monoceros has an intriguing neighbour: about a third of a degree to the south-east lies NGC 2351, which despite its catalogue number is not a true cluster at all but an [[asterism]] — a chance grouping of unrelated stars. William Herschel discovered NGC 2353 in 1785.
NGC2353.tagline: A cluster in Monoceros with a bright star at its edge, next door to an NGC ‘cluster’ that isn’t one.

story: Canis Major is better known for Sirius and for NGC 2362, the bright cluster gathered around the star Tau Canis Majoris. Two degrees south-west of that showpiece lies NGC 2354, an [[open-cluster]] that gets far less attention. William Herschel added it to his catalogue in 1785, during the years he spent sweeping the sky for nebulae and clusters.
NGC2354.tagline: A quieter cluster in Canis Major, two degrees from the showpiece NGC 2362.

story: Its nickname, the Jedi Knight, is a nod to Star Wars. NGC 2355 is an [[open-cluster]] in Gemini about a billion years old, and it lies well above the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], where most open clusters are found. It was entered in the catalogue twice, so it also carries the number NGC 2356. William Herschel discovered it in 1784.
NGC2355.tagline: The ‘Jedi Knight’ — a billion-year-old cluster in Gemini that was catalogued twice.

facts.text: Different parts of the nebula are expanding at 10 to at least 30 kilometres per second, which puts its age somewhere between about 78,500 and 236,000 years.
facts.title: How old is the helmet?

facts.text: NGC 2361 is not a separate object: it is a bright knot of gas on one edge of the Helmet’s central ring.
facts.title: A knot with its own number

story: Picture a helmet with a wing on either side and you have Thor’s Helmet, an [[emission-nebula]] in Canis Major. The bubble is blown by WR 7, an extremely hot Wolf–Rayet star thought to be in a short-lived stage before it explodes as a supernova. Its fierce wind has swept the surrounding gas into a shell, much like the Bubble Nebula, but a nearby molecular cloud has bent it into a more complex shape with a curved bow shock. Some of the gas seems to be the star’s own, enriched by nuclear fusion.
NGC2359.tagline: A winged helmet of glowing gas, blown by a star in the brief last stage before a supernova.

facts.text: Four blue stragglers live here — stars hotter and brighter than they should be at the cluster’s age, probably because they have pulled extra matter off a companion.
facts.title: Stars that look too young

facts.text: The brightest star in the field, HD 56847, is probably not a member at all, Olin Eggen concluded in 1968. It just happens to lie along the same line of sight.
facts.title: An impostor in the field

story: On 26 February 1783 Caroline Herschel came across ‘a beautiful cluster of pretty compressed stars’ in Canis Major. Her notes were overlooked until her brother William put the cluster in his 1786 catalogue of a thousand clusters and nebulae — and named her as its discoverer. Caroline went on to find eight comets of her own.

Its stars are about 2.2 billion years old, a great age for an [[open-cluster]]; most drift apart long before. Swiss astronomers Jean-Claude Mermilliod and Michel Mayor worked out that age from the lightest stars that have already swollen into red giants. Mayor later shared a Nobel Prize for discovering the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star.
NGC2360.tagline: Caroline Herschel’s cluster: a find that waited three years for credit, among stars over two billion years old.

facts.text: NGC 2362 was once listed as a nebula. In 1930 Robert Trumpler searched it for glowing gas and found none — only stars.
facts.title: The nebula that wasn’t

facts.text: Only around 35 of its members show debris discs — rings of dust left over from the building of stars and planets.
facts.title: Dust rings

story: At four to five million years old, NGC 2362 is a young [[open-cluster]] — yet its nursery is already empty. The gas and dust that built it have gone, and star birth here has stopped.

Its brightest member, Tau Canis Majoris, is a hot O-type star that has just begun to age, attended by about 40 blue-white B-type stars still in their prime. Altogether the cluster holds more than 500 Suns’ worth of stars: 100 to 150 members, with perhaps 500 more in a halo around it. Its light has not gone to waste — the brightest members make the giant gas cloud Sh2-310 glow.
Giovanni Battista Hodierna, court astronomer in Sicily, published it in 1654. Admiral William Henry Smyth later praised its ‘bright white star’ amid ‘a rich gathering of minute companions’.
NGC2362.tagline: A cluster only a few million years old that has already blown its nursery away.

story: In 1930 Robert Trumpler, comparing the sizes and brightnesses of [[open-cluster|open clusters]], noticed that the distant ones looked fainter than they should. He had discovered interstellar dust: a fine haze that dims and reddens starlight across the [[milky-way|Milky Way]]. Clusters lying close to the galaxy’s plane, as NGC 2367 in Canis Major does, are always seen through some of it.
NGC2367.tagline: An open cluster in Canis Major — and the cluster studies that revealed the dust between the stars.

story: Spread across a patch of sky in Canis Major, NGC 2374 is an [[open-cluster]] of both bright and faint stars, with little crowding towards its centre. It is about 75 million years old and lies in the Orion Arm, the same spiral arm of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] as our Sun. Two of its stars may be blue stragglers, which look younger than their neighbours. William Herschel discovered it on 31 January 1785.
NGC2374.tagline: A scattered cluster in Canis Major, about 75 million years old, sharing the Sun’s spiral arm.

story: NGC 2383 and NGC 2384 appear almost touching in the sky, and their numbers sit side by side too. That is no accident: the [[ngc-ic|New General Catalogue]] lists its objects in order of [[right-ascension]], the sky’s east–west coordinate, so neighbouring objects often get consecutive numbers. Whether the two [[open-cluster|open clusters]] are also neighbours in space is another matter, since clusters that line up in the sky can lie at very different distances.
NGC2383.tagline: One of a close pair of clusters in Canis Major — neighbours in the sky, and in the catalogue too.

story: Many of the ‘single’ stars in an [[open-cluster]] are really pairs. A large share of stars are born with a companion, and clusters such as NGC 2384 in Canis Major are full of these binary systems, most of them too close together to separate even in big telescopes. Its neighbour in the sky, NGC 2383, lies only a few arcminutes away.
NGC2384.tagline: An open cluster in Canis Major that shares its patch of sky with NGC 2383.

facts.text: On 9 January 1982, during a total lunar eclipse, the darkened Moon passed in front of NGC 2392, and observers in England watched it happen. The next such coincidence comes in January 2066.
facts.title: Hidden by an eclipsed Moon

facts.text: The star at the centre, HD 59088, is now an extremely hot O-type star — the bare core of the old star, whose ultraviolet light makes the shells glow.
facts.title: A hot heart

story: A dying star sits at the centre of NGC 2392, wrapped in the gas it has thrown off. Once a star much like the Sun, it has shed its outer layers into two nested shells, and a fierce wind from the exposed core now drives the inner filaments outward. This is how our own Sun will end, in a [[planetary-nebula]].
William Herschel found it from Slough on 17 January 1787 and called it ‘a very remarkable phenomenon’.

Its look of a face in a fur hood earned it many nicknames: the Eskimo, the Clown Face, the Lion. In August 2020 the IAU’s star-names working group and the NED and SIMBAD databases dropped ‘Eskimo’ as offensive and recommended plain NGC 2392 instead.
NGC2392.tagline: A Sun-like star’s last breath, caught in two shells of gas — and once hidden by a Moon in eclipse.

story: A star cluster’s colours tell its age. While a cluster is young, its brightest members are hot, massive stars that shine blue-white. As it ages these burn out first, and the lead passes to cooler stars and to orange and red giants. NGC 2395 is one such [[open-cluster]], in the southern part of Gemini, away from the crowded band of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2395.tagline: An open cluster in Gemini — and what the colours of a cluster’s stars reveal about its age.

story: Not every knot of stars in the sky is a real cluster. Some are [[asterism|asterisms]], unrelated stars that only look grouped from our viewpoint. To decide whether a group such as NGC 2396 in Puppis is a true [[open-cluster]], astronomers check that its stars share the same distance and move through space together. Catalogues compiled long before such measurements were possible contain a few impostors.
NGC2396.tagline: A scattering of stars in Puppis — and the question of how to tell a real cluster from a chance alignment.

facts.text: When Kōichi Itagaki found SN 2004dj on 31 July 2004, it was the nearest and brightest supernova seen so far in the 21st century.
facts.title: A record-setting supernova

facts.text: In November 1954 a star here erupted and was later logged as a supernova. It survived: astronomers now call it an impostor, a giant star’s outburst like the 1843 Great Eruption of Eta Carinae.
facts.title: The supernova that wasn’t

story: Edwin Hubble turned the giant Hale Telescope on this galaxy and found something never seen so far away: Cepheid [[variable-star|variable stars]]. NGC 2403 became the first galaxy beyond our Local Group in which a Cepheid was discovered. These pulsing stars are cosmic yardsticks, and by 1968 they had pushed the galaxy’s distance out to almost five times the figure Hubble used in 1950.

It is a close cousin of M 33: a [[spiral-galaxy]] with short, patchy arms dotted with star-forming clouds. One of them, NGC 2404, is among the largest known, a match for M 33’s famous NGC 604 in both size and position.
NGC 2403 lives on the outskirts of the M 81 group, and it is pulling apart a dwarf companion, DDO 44, which now trails streams of stars on both sides.
NGC2403.tagline: Where Hubble found Cepheids beyond our galactic neighbourhood for the first time — and a supernova that wasn’t.

story: All the stars in an [[open-cluster]] such as NGC 2409 lie at essentially the same distance from us. Compare their brightness with that of nearby stars of the same colour and type, whose distances are known, and the cluster’s own distance falls out. Methods like this, building outwards step by step, form the cosmic distance ladder that reaches all the way to other galaxies. NGC 2409 lies in Puppis, in the southern [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2409.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis — and a rung on the ladder astronomers use to measure the universe.

story: Thousands of [[open-cluster|open clusters]] are now known in the Milky Way, and NGC 2414 in Puppis is one of them. Yet they are only the nearby part of the picture: dust in the galaxy’s disc hides most of the clusters lying farther away along the plane, so the true total must be far larger. Infrared surveys, which see through the dust, keep adding new ones.
NGC2414.tagline: One of the thousands of open clusters known in our galaxy, this one in Puppis.

facts.text: William Herschel discovered NGC 2419 on 31 December 1788 — New Year’s Eve at the telescope.
facts.title: A New Year’s Eve find

facts.text: The cluster weighs more than its light suggests. A central black hole could explain it — but so could a crowd of smaller black holes, faint stars sunk to the middle, or dark matter.
facts.title: Heavier than it looks

facts.text: Some astronomers proposed that, like Omega Centauri, it is the leftover core of a small galaxy torn apart by the Milky Way. Others dispute the idea.
facts.title: A swallowed galaxy?

story: Imagine you are an astronomer in the Andromeda Galaxy, scanning the Milky Way for its [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]]. Leoš Ondra pointed out that NGC 2419 would be your best and brightest catch: it orbits far outside our galaxy’s dusty disc, with nothing in the way.

That lonely path earned it the nickname the Intergalactic Wanderer, back when astronomers thought it might not belong to the Milky Way at all. It does, just — but one lap around the galaxy takes it about three billion years.

Out there it is a heavyweight, one of the brightest and most massive globulars our galaxy owns, at around 900,000 times the Sun’s mass. Its stars come in two families, one richer in helium than the other — something current ideas of how such clusters form struggle to explain.
NGC2419.tagline: A lonely globular on a three-billion-year orbit — the cluster astronomers in Andromeda would spot first.

facts.text: Hubble found eight candidate white dwarfs here. How far they have cooled gives an age of about two billion years — an independent check that agrees with the age of the cluster’s living stars.
facts.title: Clocks made of dead stars

facts.text: Two of its binary systems are made of two blue stragglers each, and a third pairs a blue straggler with an extremely low-mass white dwarf — clues to stars that have traded or swallowed mass.
facts.title: Blue stragglers in pairs

story: At about two billion years old, NGC 2420 is a senior citizen among [[open-cluster|open clusters]], and it lies well above the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]]. More than 500 of its stars have been counted, out of perhaps 1,000 in all, and around 41 percent of them belong to binary systems. William Herschel discovered it on 19 November 1783.
NGC2420.tagline: A two-billion-year-old cluster in Gemini, where white dwarfs keep time and blue stragglers come in pairs.

story: Puppis was once just one part of Argo Navis, the enormous ship that carried Jason and the Argonauts in Greek myth. In the 1750s Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille split the unwieldy constellation into the Keel, the Sails and the Stern — Carina, Vela and Puppis. NGC 2421 is one of the many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] scattered along the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] where it flows through the old ship’s stern.
NGC2421.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis, the stern of a giant ship that once sailed across the southern sky.

story: In the sky, NGC 2423 keeps famous company, lying close to the bright Messier clusters M 46 and M 47. The connection is only apparent: it has no real link with either. William Herschel discovered this [[open-cluster]] of some 50 to 60 stars on 19 March 1786.
NGC2423.tagline: A cluster near M 46 and M 47 in Puppis — close to them in the sky, but not in space.

story: The name Puppis means the poop deck — the raised stern of a ship — and the constellation was once the back end of the great ship Argo. The [[milky-way|Milky Way]] runs through it, making it one of the richest hunting grounds for [[open-cluster|open clusters]] in the whole sky, and NGC 2432 is one member of that crowd.
NGC2432.tagline: A small open cluster in Puppis, the ‘poop deck’ of the ancient ship Argo.

story: Astronomers cannot agree on how far away NGC 2439 is, or even whether it really exists as an [[open-cluster]]. It lies in a gap in the Milky Way’s gas and dust, so its light is dimmed less than expected, and along the same line of sight sit two separate groups of hot B-type supergiants at very different distances. Age estimates range from 20 to 300 million years. John Herschel recorded it in 1835.
NGC2439.tagline: A cluster in Puppis seen through a hole in the galaxy’s dust — if it is really a cluster at all.

facts.text: HD 62166 packs about 0.6 times the Sun’s mass into a ball only about three times as wide as the Earth, yet it shines roughly 1,100 times more brightly than the Sun.
facts.title: Small but fierce

story: At the heart of NGC 2440 lies the exposed core of a star that has run out of fuel: a white dwarf called HD 62166, with a surface temperature of about 200,000 kelvin. That makes it possibly the hottest white dwarf known — more than thirty times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Its fierce ultraviolet light makes the shells of gas the star threw off glow as a [[planetary-nebula]]. William Herschel found it on 4 March 1790 and called it “a beautiful planetary nebula of a considerable degree of brightness”.
NGC2440.tagline: A dying star’s cast-off shells, lit by one of the hottest white dwarfs known.

discovered.note: Probably seen before 1654; recorded by John Herschel in 1835

story: For centuries NGC 2451 looked like a single scattering of stars in Puppis. In 1994 astronomers suggested it was really two different [[open-cluster|open clusters]] lying along the same line of sight, and in 1996 this was confirmed. Today they are known as NGC 2451 A and NGC 2451 B, and the more distant one lies about twice as far away as the nearer. Giovanni Battista Hodierna probably saw it before 1654, and John Herschel recorded it in 1835.
NGC2451.tagline: Not one cluster but two, lined up by chance — one about twice as far away as the other.

story: Right next to NGC 2453 in the sky lies a [[planetary-nebula]], NGC 2452, and for years astronomers wondered whether the dying star belonged to the cluster. If it did, the pair would have been a valuable find, since a cluster’s age reveals the mass of the star that made the nebula. A 2019 study settled it: the nebula is closer to us and moving at a different speed, so the two are not related. NGC 2453 is an [[open-cluster]] in Puppis.
NGC2453.tagline: A cluster in Puppis with a planetary nebula beside it — a neighbour that turned out to be unrelated.

story: Inside a cluster like NGC 2455, every star’s fate was settled at birth by its mass. The heaviest burn through their fuel in a few million years and die in supernova explosions. Middleweights like the Sun last billions of years, and the smallest red dwarfs will shine for longer than the universe has so far existed. This [[open-cluster]] lies in Puppis, along the southern [[milky-way|Milky Way]].
NGC2455.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis, where every star’s fate was set by the mass it was born with.

facts.text: NGC 246 was the first planetary nebula found with a triple star system at its centre, and it is the only one known with more than two central stars.
facts.title: A first and an only

facts.text: The Rosette Nebula in Monoceros is sometimes called ‘the Skull’ too, so the nickname can cause confusion.
facts.title: Not that skull

story: Three stars live at the heart of the Skull Nebula. NGC 246 is a [[planetary-nebula]], the glowing shell thrown off by a dying star. Some amateur astronomers know it by another nickname, the Pac-Man Nebula, after the way its central stars and the star field around it are arranged.

William Herschel discovered it in 1785. At its heart is HIP 3678 A, the white dwarf left behind by the dying star, with a companion star, HIP 3678 B, travelling alongside it. In 2014 astronomers using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope found a third member: a faint red dwarf, HIP 3678 C.
NGC246.tagline: A cosmic skull — or Pac-Man — around the first planetary nebula found with three stars at its centre.

facts.text: Just beside NGC 247 on the sky lies a line of five far more distant galaxies, identified by Geoffrey and Margaret Burbidge in 1963 and known as Burbidge’s Chain.
facts.title: Burbidge’s Chain

facts.text: In 2021 amateur astronomer Giuseppe Donatiello found a tiny galaxy, Donatiello IV, which with the dwarf ESO 540-032 forms a small group around NGC 247.
facts.title: A family of its own

story: On one side of NGC 247 there is a hole. This [[spiral-galaxy]], nicknamed the Claw, has an unusually large void in its disc. Some older, redder stars live there, but none of the young blue stars that light up the rest of the galaxy.

William Herschel discovered it on 20 October 1784. NGC 247 is one of several galaxies bound by gravity to the Sculptor Galaxy, NGC 253, together forming a small core at the centre of the Sculptor Group — one of the nearest groups of galaxies to the Milky Way. Its distance has been pinned down using Cepheid variables, stars whose pulsing rhythm reveals their true brightness.
NGC247.tagline: The Claw Galaxy: a spiral with a strange gap in one side of its disc, where no young stars shine.

facts.text: The cluster lies in Puppis, the stern of the old constellation Argo Navis — the ship of Jason and the Argonauts. Lacaille himself split the ship into three, creating Puppis, Vela and Carina.
facts.title: In the stern of the Argo

facts.text: Its stars have stayed together for about a billion years. That is a long life for an open cluster; most are pulled apart by the Milky Way’s tides far sooner.
facts.title: A billion years together

story: Picture a [[globular-cluster]] with its dense core scooped out and you have the idea of NGC 2477. About 300 stars crowd this [[open-cluster]], so many that some observers rank it among the finest open clusters in the sky. It also answers to a curious nickname, the Termite Hole Cluster.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille found it in 1751, during the stay at the Cape of Good Hope in which he charted the southern sky. Robert Burnham Jr. later noted that several observers had remarked on its richness: smaller than its neighbour M 46, but richer and more compact.
NGC2477.tagline: Three hundred stars that have stayed together for a billion years, in the stern of Jason’s ship.

story: The [[milky-way|Milky Way]] flows straight through Puppis, and the constellation is crowded with star clusters as a result. Three of them, M 46, M 47 and M 93, made it into Charles Messier’s famous list. Many more, like NGC 2479, appear only in the later New General Catalogue. Each is an [[open-cluster]], a family of stars born together from the same cloud.
NGC2479.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis, a constellation crowded with star clusters including M 46, M 47 and M 93.

story: Puppis is unusual: it has no star labelled Alpha or Beta. When Lacaille lettered the stars of the great ship Argo Navis, the first letters went to stars that ended up in other parts of the ship once it was split, so the brightest star in Puppis is Zeta Puppis. Its rich stretch of [[milky-way|Milky Way]] holds many [[open-cluster|open clusters]], NGC 2482 among them.
NGC2482.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis, a constellation that has no Alpha or Beta star.

story: Star clusters are part of a great recycling loop. Their most massive stars live fast and die young, scattering carbon, oxygen and other elements back into space, where they enrich the gas that later stars and planets form from. The iron in your blood was made by stars long gone. NGC 2483, an [[open-cluster]] in Puppis lying right on the plane of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], is one more turn of that wheel.
NGC2483.tagline: A small open cluster in Puppis, lying right on the plane of the Milky Way.

story: Most stars are born in groups, but most of those groups do not last. When the hottest young stars blow away the leftover gas, the gravity holding the group together weakens, and the great majority break up within a few tens of millions of years — astronomers call it infant mortality. An [[open-cluster]] such as NGC 2489 in Puppis is one of the survivors that stayed bound.
NGC2489.tagline: An open cluster in Puppis — one of the few star families that survived its birth.

facts.text: Its stars pulse and flicker: astronomers have found fourteen Gamma Doradus variables, three Delta Scuti stars and two eclipsing binaries here.
facts.title: A cluster of pulsing stars

facts.text: Twelve blue stragglers — stars that look too young for the cluster — have been found in NGC 2506, and three of them oscillate rapidly.
facts.title: Stragglers that pulse

story: NGC 2506 lies out towards the Galactic anti-centre — the part of the sky that faces away from the heart of the Milky Way — and well above the galaxy’s flat disc. It has survived about two billion years, a great age for an [[open-cluster]].

Time has sorted its stars. Over countless close passes, lighter stars have been flung towards the edges while heavier ones settled in the middle — a process astronomers call mass segregation. Its stars are also poorer in iron than the Sun, a hint that it formed from less enriched gas.
William Herschel found it in 1791.
NGC2506.tagline: A two-billion-year survivor, sorted by time and packed with pulsing, flickering stars.

story: How old is NGC 2509? Nobody is quite sure. Estimates for this Puppis [[open-cluster]] have ranged from 1.2 billion to 8 billion years, a spread longer than the Sun’s whole life so far. Its distance was argued over too, until parallaxes measured by the Gaia spacecraft showed it lies well beyond the nearer estimates.
William Herschel found it on 3 December 1783. J. L. E. Dreyer’s New General Catalogue later summed it up as “bright, pretty rich, slightly compressed”.
NGC2509.tagline: A cluster whose age estimates range from 1.2 to 8 billion years — astronomers still can’t agree.

discovered.note: Catalogued from the Cape of Good Hope in 1751–52

facts.text: The cluster Mamajek 2, far across the sky in Ophiuchus, shares its age and chemistry. Studies of how both groups move suggest they were born in the same star-forming complex some 135 million years ago.
facts.title: A long-lost sibling

facts.text: Even in this young cluster, a couple of stars have already become red giants. Heavier stars burn through their fuel faster, so the biggest members are the first to swell up and age.
facts.title: Old before their time

story: When the stars of NGC 2516 were born, some 135 million years ago, dinosaurs ruled the Earth. They have travelled through the galaxy together ever since, though not all of them have stayed: a wide halo of stars flung out of the cluster now surrounds it.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille catalogued this [[open-cluster]] in 1751–52, during his stay at the Cape of Good Hope. Its popular name, the Southern Beehive, pairs it with the famous Beehive Cluster, M 44, in the northern sky; some also call it the Sprinter.
NGC2516.tagline: Stars born when dinosaurs ruled the Earth — with a long-lost sibling far across the sky.

discovered.note: John Herschel’s re-sighting in 1837 added the duplicate number NGC 2520

facts.text: Among its members is a single white dwarf, about three-quarters the mass of the Sun: the leftover core of a star that began with roughly three times the Sun’s mass. Heavier stars burn out sooner, so it died while its siblings shine on.
facts.title: A star that went first

story: William Herschel found this loose [[open-cluster]] in Puppis on 9 December 1784, and it became NGC 2527. His son John looked at it in 1831, then again in 1837 — and the second time took it for a new object. That slip earned it a second entry in the catalogue, NGC 2520, so one group of stars now answers to two numbers.
NGC2520.tagline: One cluster, two catalogue numbers — thanks to a slip by John Herschel.

facts.text: In the 1961 Hubble Atlas of Galaxies, Allan Sandage made it the prototype of galaxies whose pictures are dominated by dust, with arms “defined as much by the dust as by the spiral pattern”.
facts.title: Drawn in dust

facts.text: Italian amateur astronomer Giuseppe Donatiello has discovered eight faint dwarf galaxies around NGC 253 since 2021, adding to its fast-growing list of known satellites.
facts.title: A growing family

facts.text: Its central black hole is estimated at about 5 million suns, slightly heavier than Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the heart of our own Milky Way.
facts.title: A familiar black hole

story: Caroline Herschel found this galaxy in 1783, during one of her systematic searches for comets. Decades later her nephew John, observing from the Cape of Good Hope, called it “a superb object”. Today we know it as a starburst [[spiral-galaxy]], forming new stars at a furious rate.

The trigger may have been a collision: around 200 million years ago a gas-rich dwarf galaxy seems to have struck it, disturbing its disc. Near its centre the starburst has built super star clusters, one holding some 14 million suns. The winds and supernovae of its most massive stars are now blasting gas out into the halo in a ‘superwind’ that seems to be choking off further star birth.
It is the brightest galaxy of the Sculptor Group, one of the nearest groups of galaxies to our own.
NGC253.tagline: The Silver Coin Galaxy, caught in a frenzy of star birth — perhaps set off by a collision with a dwarf galaxy.

story: Puppis was once the stern of Argo Navis, the great ship of Jason and the Argonauts, until Nicolas Louis de Lacaille broke that sprawling constellation into pieces in the 1750s. The Milky Way runs right through it, and NGC 2533 is one of the many star clusters scattered along that stretch. Like every [[open-cluster]], its stars were born together from a single cloud of gas and dust.
NGC2533.tagline: A cluster in the stern of Argo, the ship of Jason and the Argonauts.

facts.text: In January 2017 astronomers caught a luminous blue variable flaring here, catalogued AT 2017be. These are massive, unstable stars given to violent outbursts — and no supernova has yet been seen in this galaxy.
facts.title: A restless giant star

facts.text: NGC 2537 sits near the galaxy IC 2233 and was long thought to be interacting with it. The two may even lie at the same distance, but neither shows the marks of a mutual pull.
facts.title: Neighbour, not partner

story: Small, blue and lumpy, NGC 2537 earns its nickname, the Bear Paw. Bright knots of newborn stars sit on a smooth, older glow, like pads on a paw print. It is a blue compact dwarf: a little [[galaxy]] that is busy making stars. Halton Arp listed it as Arp 6 in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, and William Herschel first found it on 6 February 1788.
NGC2537.tagline: A small blue galaxy with knots of newborn stars, like the pads of a bear’s paw.

facts.text: Studies of its stars have turned up eclipsing binaries, a pulsating delta Scuti star and three red giants that turn out to be pairs — one of them really a triple.
facts.title: Pairs, triples and pulsing stars

story: The bright star near the edge of NGC 2539, 19 Puppis, is an impostor: a foreground star, much nearer to us than the cluster behind it. The real cluster is a moderately rich [[open-cluster]] of several hundred stars, perhaps as much as 630 million years old. William Herschel found it on 31 January 1785.
NGC2539.tagline: A cluster of several hundred stars, with a bright impostor standing in front.

facts.text: The two groups were told apart star by star: by how fast each one moves towards or away from us, by its spectral type, and by how much intervening dust has dimmed and reddened its light.
facts.title: How to split a cluster

story: For more than two and a half centuries NGC 2546 was taken for one loose, sprawling cluster. In 2020 a team led by A. J. Alejo showed it is really two separate clusters that happen to line up in our sky, one far behind the other. The nearer, NGC 2546A, is around 180 million years old. The farther, NGC 2546B, is a youngster of under 10 million years.
Nicolas Louis de Lacaille found the pair in 1751–52 while mapping the southern sky from South Africa.
NGC2546.tagline: Taken for one cluster for over 250 years — it turned out to be two, one behind the other.

facts.text: Gaia data suggest NGC 2547 formed about 30 million years ago alongside a newly found cluster and several neighbours of similar age — perhaps all in a single, triggered burst of star formation.
facts.title: Born in one wave

facts.text: Spitzer’s spectrograph found silicate dust in the debris disc of a red dwarf here — the first time silicate had been detected in a debris disc around an M-type star.
facts.title: A first for red dwarfs

story: Around the stars of NGC 2547, planets may still be under construction. This young [[open-cluster]] in Vela, only 20–30 million years old, holds many stars ringed by debris discs: dusty rubble left over as worlds are built. Around one of them, known as ID8, the Spitzer Space Telescope saw the dust suddenly brighten and then fade over a year — the afterglow, astronomers think, of a violent impact on a planetary body.
Lacaille found the cluster in 1751 from South Africa.
NGC2547.tagline: A young cluster where planets may still be forming — and where one world may have been smashed.

story: Not every cluster is a crowd. NGC 2567 counts somewhere between 81 and 96 member stars, a modest family that has stayed together for roughly 500 million years. That is young by cosmic standards: the Sun is about nine times older. Its stars carry almost the same mix of chemical elements as the Sun does. William Herschel came across this [[open-cluster]] on 4 March 1793.
NGC2567.tagline: A modest family of fewer than a hundred stars, about half a billion years old.

story: Every star in NGC 2571 shares a birthday. An [[open-cluster]] forms when one cloud of gas and dust collapses into many stars at once, so its members are siblings of the same age and make-up. Over time the Milky Way’s tides pull such families apart. Our own Sun was probably born in a cluster like this, its siblings long since scattered around the galaxy.
NGC2571.tagline: A family of stars that all share a birthday.

facts.text: Its northern counterpart is NGC 3172, nicknamed Polarissima Borealis — the NGC object nearest the north celestial pole.
facts.title: A twin at the other end

story: The south celestial pole has no bright star to mark it, but it does have a galaxy. NGC 2573 lies closer to the pole than any other object in the New General Catalogue, which earned it the nickname Polarissima Australis, “the most polar of the south”. John Herschel found it on 29 March 1837, during his years observing from the Cape of Good Hope.
It is a weakly barred [[spiral-galaxy]] about the size of the Milky Way, though so faint that even its exact shape is still uncertain.
NGC2573.tagline: The southern sky has no bright pole star — but it does have a pole galaxy.

story: Clusters like NGC 2580 do not last for ever. Held together only by their own weak gravity, the stars of an [[open-cluster]] are slowly tugged apart by passing gas clouds and the pull of the Milky Way, until the group dissolves into the general field of stars. NGC 2580 lies in Puppis, where the band of the [[milky-way]] is thick with such star families.
NGC2580.tagline: A cluster in the thick of the Puppis Milky Way, slowly coming apart.

story: Clusters in Puppis sit against the rich star fields of the [[milky-way]], which makes it hard to tell members from passers-by. Today the Gaia spacecraft sorts them out by tracking each star’s motion across the sky. True members drift together, like a flock of birds, while foreground and background stars go their own way. NGC 2587 is one of the many clusters charted this way.
NGC2587.tagline: A Puppis cluster, picked out from the crowd by the stars’ shared motion.

facts.text: In March 2023 the ATLAS survey caught a supernova here, SN 2023dtc. It was a Type Ib: the collapse of a massive star that had already lost its outer layer of hydrogen.
facts.title: A recent explosion

story: Seen almost edge-on, NGC 2613 is a [[spiral-galaxy]] turned into a long spindle of light. Its heart hides an active nucleus — a feeding black hole — buried deep in gas and dust. Radio maps from the Very Large Array show a tail of gas trailing off one side, probably drawn out by a brush with a small companion galaxy. William Herschel found it on 20 November 1784.
NGC2613.tagline: A spiral seen almost edge-on, with a buried black hole and a tail of stolen gas.

story: Star clusters are usually pictured as born in one go. NGC 2627 seems to have had four goes: its stars show four separate peaks of star formation, with quiet spells of two to three hundred million years in between. Now about 1.4 billion years old, this [[open-cluster]] in Pyxis was found by William Herschel on 3 March 1793. Dreyer’s catalogue called it “considerably large, pretty rich, pretty compressed”.
NGC2627.tagline: A cluster built in four bursts, with quiet spells of hundreds of millions of years between.

story: Vela, the Sails, is another piece of the old ship Argo Navis, and the Milky Way flows straight through it. NGC 2645 is one of the small star clusters strewn along this stretch. Its stars were born together and still travel together, an [[open-cluster]] that will slowly scatter as the galaxy’s tides pull at it over many millions of years.
NGC2645.tagline: A small cluster in the Sails of the old ship Argo.

facts.text: In January 2011 Kōichi Itagaki and Masaki Tsuboi discovered a supernova here, SN 2011B. It was a Type Ia — the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf.
facts.title: A white dwarf blows up

story: NGC 2655 wears the scars of a busy past. A lenticular [[galaxy]] — a disc with no real spiral arms — it is crossed by lopsided dust lanes and trails long arms of stars and hydrogen gas, signs of at least one recent merger and probably more before that. At its centre is an active Seyfert nucleus. It is the brightest member of a small [[galaxy-group]] close to the north celestial pole, and William Herschel found it on 26 September 1802.
NGC2655.tagline: A galaxy scarred by mergers, leading a small group near the north celestial pole.

story: Pyxis, the Mariner’s Compass, is one of the constellations Nicolas Louis de Lacaille invented while charting the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope in the 1750s. It sits beside the old ship Argo, like a piece of the ship’s gear. NGC 2658 is an [[open-cluster]] within its borders: a family of stars born together that the Milky Way’s tides will slowly pull apart.
NGC2658.tagline: A cluster in the Mariner’s Compass, a constellation added in the 1750s.

story: Barely 8 million years old, NGC 2659 is a youngster: its stars were born long after the dinosaurs had gone. This [[open-cluster]] in Vela holds an estimated 1,800 or so stars, adding up to several hundred times the mass of the Sun. One member is a Be star — a hot star spinning so fast it flings off a disc of gas — and four more may be. John Herschel found the cluster on 3 February 1835.
NGC2659.tagline: A youthful Vela cluster with nearly two thousand stars.

story: Most open clusters fall apart within a few hundred million years, their stars scattered by the tides of the Milky Way. NGC 2660 has held together for around a billion years, which makes it an old-timer. Its most massive stars burned out long ago, and the next in line are now swelling into red giants. Old clusters like this are prized by astronomers, because they show how stars like the Sun change as they grow old.
NGC2660.tagline: A rare survivor: a cluster that has held together for about a billion years.

story: An [[open-cluster]] is a snapshot of one moment of starbirth. All the stars of NGC 2669 formed at about the same time from the same cloud, so astronomers can compare heavy and light stars of the same age — a key test of how stars live and change. That makes even modest clusters like this one in Vela useful laboratories.
NGC2669.tagline: A snapshot of one moment of starbirth in Vela.

story: The heaviest stars in a cluster burn out first, swelling into giants while their lighter siblings carry on. So astronomers can read a cluster’s age like a clock, by finding the point where its stars begin to leave their long, steady middle age. The same clock is ticking in NGC 2670, a small [[open-cluster]] in Vela, its stars all born together from one cloud.
NGC2670.tagline: A small Vela cluster whose stars keep time like a clock.

facts.text: NGC 2683 hosts about 300 globular clusters, roughly twice as many as our own galaxy — even though it is the smaller of the two.
facts.title: Rich in globulars

story: Tilted almost exactly edge-on, NGC 2683 looks like a flying saucer, and a planetarium gave it the nickname to match: the Astronaut Memorial Planetarium and Observatory dubbed it the UFO Galaxy. William Herschel, who found it on 5 February 1788, had no such word to hand.

Hidden in the saucer may be a bar. An X-shaped bulge at its centre is the kind of structure a buckling bar of stars produces. The galaxy is smaller and dimmer than the Milky Way and makes few new stars today.
NGC2683.tagline: Seen edge-on, it looks like a flying saucer — hence the UFO Galaxy.

facts.text: Wilhelm Tempel, who found it on 18 August 1882, is best known for his comets — among them Tempel 1, which NASA’s Deep Impact probe struck in 2005.
facts.title: Found by a comet hunter

story: Imagine a galaxy wearing a hoop of gas and stars at right angles to its own disc. NGC 2685 is one of the rare polar-ring galaxies, thought to form when a disc [[galaxy]] captures material from another and strings it out into a rotating ring. Here the ring seems remarkably old and stable. Allan Sandage called it “perhaps the most peculiar galaxy in the Shapley-Ames Catalog”.
NGC2685.tagline: A galaxy wearing a ring at right angles to itself — “perhaps the most peculiar” of its catalogue.

facts.text: The collapsed core of the same star lives on nearby as the Vela Pulsar, a neutron star that spins about 11 times a second.
facts.title: The star’s heart survives

story: On 1 March 1835, at the Cape of Good Hope, John Herschel came upon “an extraordinary long narrow ray of excessively feeble light”. He had found a sliver of a star’s blast wave. The Pencil Nebula is one small, bright stretch of the Vela [[supernova-remnant]], the expanding debris of a star that exploded more than ten thousand years ago. Here the shock front is still moving at roughly 644,000 km per hour, heating the thin gas it sweeps up until it glows.
NGC2736.tagline: A thin sliver of a dead star’s blast wave, still racing outwards.

facts.text: In October 2000 Tim Puckett and G. Dowdle discovered a supernova here, SN 2000ds — a Type Ib, the collapse of a massive star stripped of its outer hydrogen.
facts.title: A stripped star explodes

story: From afar NGC 2768 looks plain: a smooth, elongated [[galaxy]], classed by some as elliptical and by others as lenticular. Look closer and its centre is anything but calm. A knotted ring of dust stands at right angles to the galaxy itself, like a hoop set upright on a plate. Inside it, two tiny S-shaped jets curl outwards, flung off by gas swirling into a supermassive black hole.
NGC2768.tagline: A smooth galaxy hiding a ring of dust stood on edge, and two tiny S-shaped jets.

facts.text: SN 1993Z, a Type Ia supernova — the explosion of a white dwarf — was found here on 23 September 1993. Two days later its spectrum showed it had already peaked about four weeks earlier.
facts.title: A supernova caught late

facts.text: NGC 2775 is the leading member of a small [[galaxy-group]] named after it, the NGC 2775 Group, which also includes NGC 2777 and UGC 4781.
facts.title: Head of the family

story: The heart of NGC 2775 is a quiet place. Its central bulge holds almost no gas, and virtually no new stars are forming there; one idea is that a high rate of supernovae long ago swept the gas away. Even its nucleus is inactive.
The action is further out, in a dusty ring where stars are still being born — though at a gentle pace, with no burst of star formation.

This [[spiral-galaxy]] also carries the scars of a past meal. A small satellite galaxy seems to have looped around it several times, shedding stars at each pass and leaving faint, shell-like ripples. A neighbouring irregular galaxy, NGC 2777, trails a tail of hydrogen gas that points back towards NGC 2775, as if the two have touched.
NGC2775.tagline: A galaxy with a quiet heart, a ring of newborn stars, and the scars of a smaller galaxy it has been shredding.

story: Somewhere between the spirals and the ellipticals sit the lenticular galaxies, and NGC 2784 in Hydra is one of them. A lenticular has the flat disc and central bulge of a spiral, but no real spiral arms and little of the gas needed to make new stars, so its light comes mostly from older stars. Edwin Hubble placed this class at the fork of his famous tuning-fork diagram of [[hubble-type|galaxy types]].
NGC2784.tagline: A galaxy caught between types: a disc like a spiral, smooth like an elliptical.

facts.text: NGC 2808 is about 12.5 billion years old, nearly three times the age of the Sun. Our galaxy’s tides are slowly pulling it apart, and it trails a long tail of lost stars.
facts.title: A relic of the young universe

story: [[globular-cluster|Globular clusters]] were long thought to be the simplest things in the sky: one burst of starbirth, one generation of stars. NGC 2808 broke the rule. In 2007 a team led by Giampaolo Piotto of the University of Padua, studying Hubble images, found three generations of stars, all born within 200 million years of the cluster’s formation.

One idea is that the cluster, with more than a million stars, is heavy enough to hold on to its leftover gas for a second and third round. Another is that it is no ordinary cluster at all, but the surviving core of a dwarf galaxy — the so-called Sausage Galaxy — that collided with the Milky Way long ago.
NGC2808.tagline: A globular cluster of a million stars that broke the rules — and may be a stolen galaxy’s heart.

facts.text: Near the centre sits Burnham 1, a [[multiple-star]] found by S. W. Burnham. It has five members; the brightest, HD 5005, is a hot, highly luminous O-type star. The system has shown no appreciable change since it was first measured in 1875.
facts.title: Five suns in one

story: In photographs the shape is unmistakable: a glowing disc with a wedge cut out of it, like the hero of the 1980 arcade game. That is why NGC 281 is called the Pacman Nebula. It is an [[emission-nebula]], a cloud of hydrogen made to shine by hot young stars, including those of the cluster IC 1590 at its heart. Dark knots called Bok globules — dense pockets of gas and dust that may one day collapse into new stars — stand out against the glow.
E. E. Barnard discovered it in August 1883, calling it “a large faint nebula, very diffuse”.
NGC281.tagline: The Pacman Nebula: a glowing cloud with a bite taken out, lit by a five-star system at its heart.

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen here since 1912. The first, SN 1912A, was found by Heber Curtis and Francis Pease. Curtis went on to argue, in the 1920 ‘Great Debate’, that spiral nebulae are galaxies in their own right.
facts.title: Four supernovae

story: Most famous spirals have a couple of grand, sweeping arms. NGC 2841 has instead many short, patchy fragments, like tufts of wool. It is the prototype of the flocculent spirals, named from the Latin for a tuft of wool. In many ways it resembles our neighbour the Andromeda Galaxy.
Deep in its core, some stars and gas circle the opposite way to the rest — a hint of a recent run-in with a smaller galaxy. William Herschel found NGC 2841 on 9 March 1788.
NGC2841.tagline: The original woolly spiral — a galaxy of tufts instead of grand arms.

facts.text: Although it has shrunk to a fraction of the Sun’s size, the central star still pours out around 1,400 times as much light as the Sun.
facts.title: Small but bright

facts.text: The faint halo around NGC 2867 may really be two halos merged into one, hinting that the dying star shed its gas in an unusual way.
facts.title: A double halo

story: On 1 April 1834 John Herschel, observing from the Cape of Good Hope, thought he might have found a new planet. The next night he looked again: the little disc had not moved. Fittingly for April Fools’ Day, the ‘planet’ was nothing of the kind but a [[planetary-nebula]] — the cast-off outer layers of a dying star.

That star is now a tiny furnace. It is about a twentieth of the Sun’s width, yet its surface is around 165,000 degrees — nearly thirty times hotter than the Sun’s — and it is slowly becoming a white dwarf. As it goes, it trembles: it is a pulsating GW Virginis star, its surface rippling in complex patterns.
The gas it shed is rich in carbon, a sign that the star dredged carbon up from its core late in life.
NGC2867.tagline: John Herschel thought he had found a new planet — on 1 April. It was a dying star instead.

facts.text: NGC 288 trails tails of stars both ahead of it and behind it along its orbit: stars pulled loose from the cluster by the Milky Way’s gravity.
facts.title: Leaking stars

story: NGC 288 lies less than a degree from the south galactic pole — the point in the sky straight “below” the flat disc of the Milky Way. Looking this way, we gaze out of our galaxy rather than through its dusty disc, so the sky around it is rich in other galaxies; the bright NGC 253 is less than two degrees away.
This loosely packed [[globular-cluster]] belongs to the galactic halo, the sparse realm of old stars that surrounds the disc. William Herschel discovered it in 1785.
NGC288.tagline: A loose globular cluster almost on top of the south galactic pole, trailing streams of lost stars.

story: On 16 November 1784 William Herschel saw what he took for a double nebula here, and observers after him agreed. Only in the nineteenth century did the Third Earl of Rosse, with his giant reflectors in Ireland, see it for what it is: a single barred [[spiral-galaxy]]. The double vision left its mark. Dreyer gave it two numbers, and NGC 2905 now labels a bright knot in one of its arms.
The galaxy’s bar works like a funnel, channelling gas inwards to its core, where a burst of star formation is under way.
NGC2903.tagline: Herschel saw two nebulae here. Lord Rosse saw one spiral — but the second number stuck.

story: Open clusters like NGC 2910 live in the flat disc of the Milky Way, among the gas and dust that made them. That is why they crowd along the band of the [[milky-way]] in our sky, and why Vela, which straddles that band, is so rich in them. Older, denser globular clusters, by contrast, roam the galaxy’s halo far above and below the disc.
NGC2910.tagline: A cluster in Vela, living in the Milky Way’s busy disc.

discovered.note: Known since ancient times in the southern hemisphere; described on Magellan’s voyage of 1519–1522

facts.text: In 1913 Ejnar Hertzsprung used Leavitt’s discovery to make the first estimate of the Small Cloud’s distance. His answer was far too small — but it proved the method worked.
facts.title: First measured, far too close

facts.text: The Small Cloud is crowded with high-mass X-ray binaries — neutron stars feeding on massive companion stars — born in its recent burst of star formation.
facts.title: A nest of X-ray stars

facts.text: Hubble measurements announced in 2006 suggest the Magellanic Clouds may be moving too fast to be orbiting the Milky Way — unless our galaxy is more massive than was thought.
facts.title: Just passing through?

story: To sailors crossing the southern oceans it looked like a scrap torn from the Milky Way. Portuguese and Dutch crews called the two Magellanic Clouds the Cape Clouds, and on Ferdinand Magellan’s voyage around the world Antonio Pigafetta described them as dim clusters of stars. Long before that, they had a place in the lore of Pacific islanders and Aboriginal Australians.

In the early 1900s Henrietta Swan Leavitt at Harvard studied photographs of the Small Cloud taken in Peru. She found that its Cepheid variable stars pulse more slowly the brighter they are. Since all its stars lie at roughly the same distance, this meant a Cepheid’s rhythm reveals its true brightness — a yardstick that opened up the universe.

The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf irregular [[galaxy]] of several hundred million stars, now a satellite of the Milky Way. A bridge of gas links it to its partner, the Large [[magellanic-clouds|Magellanic Cloud]], and in 2023 astronomers reported that it is really two separate structures, one behind the other.
NGC292.tagline: The little cloud where Henrietta Leavitt found the key to measuring the size of the universe.

story: Star clusters come in two kinds. Globular clusters are ancient, tightly packed balls of hundreds of thousands of stars. NGC 2925 is the other kind: an [[open-cluster]], a loose family of stars born together in the Milky Way’s disc. Such families are only weakly bound, so over time they drift apart, their members joining the general crowd of stars in Vela and beyond.
NGC2925.tagline: A loose family of stars in the Sails of Argo.

story: NGC 2972 has a second name, NGC 2999, and both point to the same small group of stars in Vela. Duplicates like this crept into the New General Catalogue when one object was recorded twice — often with slightly different positions — and the two sightings were taken for different things. The stars themselves are an ordinary [[open-cluster]], born together and still travelling together.
NGC2972.tagline: One cluster in Vela with two NGC numbers.

story: Classed as a spiral, NGC 2976 hardly looks like one: a disc with no obvious arms and no central bulge, only dark lanes and knots of stars. It belongs to the M 81 group, and in size and brightness it falls between the Large and Small [[magellanic-clouds|Magellanic Clouds]].

Its neighbours have not left it alone. A tail of hydrogen gas pulled from its outskirts records an encounter about a billion years ago. Over that time star formation in its outer disc has dwindled, while the centre has carried on making stars at a steady pace. William Herschel found it on 8 November 1801.
NGC2976.tagline: A spiral without arms, roughed up by the giants of the M 81 group.

story: Many astronomy students know NGC 2997 by sight: it graced the cover of the first edition of Galactic Dynamics, the textbook by James Binney and Scott Tremaine. It earned the spot. Seen nearly face-on, it is a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy]] with two symmetrical arms, beaded with dusty knots where density waves squeeze gas into new stars. At the core the arms meet in a ring of hot spots that hold super star clusters.
William Herschel found it on 4 March 1793, and Dreyer called it “a remarkable object”.
NGC2997.tagline: A textbook spiral — it really was on the cover of the textbook.

facts.text: The X-ray source NGC 300 X-1 appears to be a black hole of about 17 suns paired with a Wolf–Rayet star of about 26 suns, the two circling each other every 32.8 hours.
facts.title: A black hole and a giant

facts.text: Inside one of NGC 300’s bright glowing gas clouds lies STWR 13, an oxygen-sequence Wolf–Rayet star — one of the rarest types of massive star.
facts.title: A rare kind of star

story: Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered NGC 300 on 5 August 1826. This [[spiral-galaxy]] is somewhat smaller than the Milky Way and much like the Triangulum Galaxy, and it is one of the closest galaxies to our Local Group. It probably forms a bound pair with NGC 55, the two lying in front of the Sculptor Group they were long thought to belong to.

In May 2008 amateur astronomer Berto Monard spotted a new point of light in one of its spiral arms. It was too faint for a typical supernova and too bright for an ordinary nova. Old Spitzer images revealed what had been there before: a star of about 10 suns hidden in a cocoon of dust. The outburst, NGC 300-OT, is now classed as an intermediate-luminosity red transient.
NGC300.tagline: A nearby pinwheel galaxy where a dust-shrouded star blew up in 2008 in a strange, not-quite supernova.

story: Every NGC number traces back to J. L. E. Dreyer’s New General Catalogue of 1888, which gathered nearly 8,000 nebulae and clusters in one list. Many of its far-southern entries were first recorded by John Herschel at the Cape of Good Hope in the 1830s. NGC 3033, a modest [[open-cluster]] in Vela, is one of the thousands of objects astronomers still call by Dreyer’s numbers.
NGC3033.tagline: One of thousands of entries in a catalogue that still names the sky.

story: Admiral William Henry Smyth saw NGC 3077 as if “floating in awful and illimitable space, at an inconceivable distance”. Today we know it as one of the small companions of M 81. At first glance it looks like a smooth elliptical [[galaxy]], but its wispy edges and scattered dust clouds betray a rough life alongside its larger neighbours, much like M 82.
Its centre is active too. Carl Seyfert put it on his 1943 list of galaxies with bright, active nuclei — the list that gave Seyfert galaxies their name — though it no longer qualifies today.
NGC3077.tagline: M 81’s battered little companion, “floating in awful and illimitable space”.

story: The stars of an [[open-cluster]] share more than a birthday. Formed from the same cloud, they carry the same chemical fingerprint — the same mix of iron, carbon and other elements. Astronomers hope to use such fingerprints to trace stars back to their birth clusters, even to find the Sun’s long-lost siblings. NGC 3105, a small cluster in Vela, is a family still living together.
NGC3105.tagline: A family of stars that share not just a birthday but a chemistry.

story: Picking out NGC 3114 is like finding one family in a crowded station. This sparse [[open-cluster]] lies against the dense star fields of the Milky Way, on the outskirts of the Carina complex, and so many unrelated stars crowd the view that even its size is uncertain. Studies since 1963 put its age somewhere between 60 and 200 million years, and its stars have much the same chemical make-up as the Sun.
James Dunlop catalogued it in 1826 from Parramatta, near Sydney.
NGC3114.tagline: A cluster so lost among Milky Way stars that even its size is hard to pin down.

facts.text: Even though we see it almost exactly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]], NGC 3115 was once classified as an elliptical. It is really a lenticular galaxy: a disc and a bulge of stars, but no spiral arms.
facts.title: Mistaken identity

facts.text: Only one supernova has ever been recorded in NGC 3115, SN 1935B — and even its type and brightness are unknown.
facts.title: A mystery supernova

story: Hidden in the bright core of the Spindle Galaxy is a black hole with a billion or more times the Sun’s mass. John Kormendy and Douglas Richstone announced it in 1992, after measuring how fast the stars near the centre were whirling around something unseen.

In 2011 NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory went further. It imaged hot gas flowing towards the black hole, heating up as it fell — the first clear evidence of such a flow around any black hole. The point where the heating begins marks where the black hole’s gravity takes over, and it pointed to a mass of about two billion Suns.

Today NGC 3115 is a retired galaxy. It has used up nearly all its gas, almost all its stars are very old, and its black hole has stopped growing. Some astronomers suspect that in its youth it blazed as a quasar.
NGC3115.tagline: A retired galaxy with a two-billion-Sun black hole — where astronomers first watched gas falling in.

facts.text: On 12 July 2022 NGC 3132 was one of five objects in the first official science images released from the James Webb Space Telescope.
facts.title: Webb’s debut

facts.text: The white dwarf is not alone. A bright A-type star orbits far out, near the edge of a dust cloud around it, and the whole system probably holds four stars.
facts.title: A crowded household

story: From Earth it looks like an oval ring, but NGC 3132 is really shaped more like an hourglass pointed nearly at us. Three-dimensional models show a bipolar [[planetary-nebula]] whose long axis lies only about twenty degrees from our line of sight, with a hollow centre wrapped in ring after ring of gas.
The star that made it began life with about 2.7 times the Sun’s mass. What is left is a white dwarf at around 140,000 degrees, whose intense ultraviolet light makes the surrounding gas fluoresce.
NGC3132.tagline: A dying star’s hourglass, seen nearly end-on — and one of the first pictures released from the Webb telescope.

facts.text: Two supernovae have been seen here, both Type Ia — exploding white dwarfs. Tom Boles found SN 2010af in 2010, and Giancarlo Cortini found SN 2017gla in 2017.
facts.title: Two exploding white dwarfs

facts.text: Its southern counterpart is NGC 2573, Polarissima Australis — the NGC object nearest the south celestial pole.
facts.title: A twin at the other end

story: Polaris marks the north celestial pole for the naked eye, but of all the objects in the New General Catalogue, the one closest to the pole is a faint lenticular [[galaxy]]: NGC 3172. That earned it the nickname Polarissima Borealis, “the most polar of the north”. John Herschel found it in 1831.
The title will not last for ever. Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, so the pole creeps across the sky over the centuries.
NGC3172.tagline: Of all the NGC objects, this faint galaxy lies nearest the north celestial pole.

facts.text: Six supernovae and other outbursts have been seen here since 1921. One, SN 2010dn, spotted by Kōichi Itagaki, first looked like an eruption of an unstable giant star; it was later reclassed as a rarer event, an intermediate-luminosity red transient.
facts.title: Not what it seemed

story: Neatly symmetrical and seen face-on, NGC 3184 looks like a smaller copy of the Pinwheel Galaxy, M 101 — hence its nickname, the Little Pinwheel. Its two arms keep a constant pitch as they wind outwards, tinted blue by a relatively few bright young stars born in density waves that sweep around the centre. Two of its star-forming clouds earned their own catalogue numbers, NGC 3180 and NGC 3181. William Herschel found the galaxy on 18 March 1787.
NGC3184.tagline: The Little Pinwheel: a neat, symmetrical spiral with six outbursts on record.

facts.text: The shell of NGC 3195 is expanding at about 40 kilometres every second — fast enough to cover the distance from London to New York in under two and a half minutes.
facts.title: Still swelling

facts.text: The faint star at the centre may not be alone. An analysis of data from the Gaia spacecraft suggests it is a binary system.
facts.title: A hidden partner?

story: Dying stars of modest mass end their lives by puffing away their outer layers. NGC 3195 is one of those cast-off shells, a [[planetary-nebula]] still swelling outward around the faint remains of its star — and the whole cloud is drifting towards us at 17 kilometres a second.

Sir John Herschel discovered it in 1835, during his years at the Cape of Good Hope charting the southern sky. It lies in Chamaeleon, named after the colour-changing lizard: a small constellation added in the late 1500s from the observations of Dutch navigators sailing south.
NGC3195.tagline: A dying star’s bubble in the far southern sky, still swelling at 40 kilometres a second.

facts.text: In the 1980s, radio maps of how its hydrogen gas orbits became one of the classic pieces of evidence for dark matter: the gas far out in the disc moves too fast to be held by the visible stars alone.
facts.title: Too fast to add up

facts.text: The Westerbork radio telescope detected gas floating above and below the galaxy’s disc — about 15% of all its hydrogen.
facts.title: Gas above the disc

story: To measure how fast the universe is expanding, astronomers first need distances they can trust. NGC 3198 was one of 18 galaxies chosen for the Hubble Space Telescope’s Key Project on the extragalactic distance scale, which aimed to pin down the Hubble constant to within 10%. Hubble tracked 52 Cepheids in it — pulsing [[variable-star|variable stars]] whose rhythm reveals their true brightness.
William Herschel found this [[spiral-galaxy]] on 15 January 1788.
NGC3198.tagline: A yardstick for the expanding universe — and a classic witness for dark matter.

facts.text: James Dunlop discovered NGC 3201 on 28 May 1826 and listed it in his 1827 catalogue, noting that it was ‘easily resolved into stars’.
facts.title: Dunlop’s find

facts.text: Its stars are not uniform: the redder, cooler ones gather towards the core. As of 2010 only one other globular, M 4, was known to show such a clear variation.
facts.title: Stars sorted by colour

story: Every second, NGC 3201 moves about 490 kilometres farther away from us. No other known [[globular-cluster]] has a higher speed along our line of sight. Even so, it is not fast enough to escape the Milky Way.
Its stars are about ten billion years old, more than twice the age of the Sun, and together they hold around 157,000 Suns’ worth of mass.

Because its stars are thinly packed and the cluster is far from collapsing in on itself, astronomers think its core harbours many black holes. A few have already been caught orbiting ordinary stars. A 2022 study using Hubble and Gaia found that the core may hide a sub-cluster of nearly a hundred stellar black holes, together weighing about a thousand Suns.
NGC3201.tagline: A ten-billion-year-old cluster racing away at record speed — with a hidden swarm of black holes.

facts.text: One member, HD 89856, is a variable star that repeats its cycle every 4.556 days.
facts.title: A star with a rhythm

story: In 1751–52 Nicolas Louis de Lacaille swept the southern sky from South Africa, listing the hazy objects he met along the way. NGC 3228 went into his catalogue as Lac II.7. It is a small [[open-cluster]] with a few dozen members and a slight crowding towards its centre. Its hottest star is only of type B9, a blue-white star a few times the Sun’s mass.
NGC3228.tagline: A small, bright cluster first logged by Lacaille at the Cape in 1751–52.

facts.text: At either end of the nebula sit FLIERs — fast low-ionisation emission regions, lobes of fast-moving gas that are often tinted red in false-colour pictures.
facts.title: Red-tipped knots

facts.text: Its catalogue numbers trace a century of astronomy: H IV.27 for William Herschel, h 3248 for his son John, GC 2102 in 1864, and finally NGC 3242 in Dreyer’s New General Catalogue of 1888.
facts.title: Four names in a century

story: Roughly 1,500 years ago — about when the Western Roman Empire fell — a dying star in Hydra threw off the inner layers of what we now call NGC 3242. Since then the shells have kept expanding, lit by the hot remains of the star at the centre, now a white dwarf.

Its planet-like disc earned it the name Ghost of Jupiter; others call it the Eye Nebula. Like every [[planetary-nebula]], it has nothing to do with planets. The term itself goes back to William Herschel, to whom such round glows looked like the discs of planets.
Herschel himself found this one on 7 February 1785. His son John observed it again from the Cape of Good Hope in the 1830s.
NGC3242.tagline: A ghostly planet-like disc, puffed off by a dying star around the time Rome fell.

facts.text: At its heart lies Westerlund 2, a young cluster of some of the Milky Way’s hottest and heaviest stars. Hubble’s picture of it was chosen to celebrate the telescope’s 25th anniversary in 2015.
facts.title: Hubble’s birthday portrait

story: Hidden behind dust, a whole nursery of stars is being born here. NGC 3247, also known as RCW 49, is one of the brightest and most massive star-forming clouds in our galaxy — an [[emission-nebula]] holding more than 2,200 stars. In images released in 2004, the Spitzer Space Telescope looked through its dust in infrared light and showed that at least 200 of those young stars are wrapped in dusty discs, the raw material of planets.
NGC3247.tagline: A dusty stellar nursery of over 2,200 stars, among the brightest in the Milky Way.

facts.text: NGC 3293 is linked to the nearby cluster NGC 3324: both are about 12 million years old, both keep their heaviest stars near the centre, and neither has yet settled down.
facts.title: A sibling nearby

story: Only about 12 million years old, NGC 3293 is already showing its heaviest stars at the ends of their lives. Two blue supergiants lead the pack, and a pulsating red supergiant, V361 Carinae, glows among them. More than a hundred fainter stars fill out this young [[open-cluster]] in Carina. Lacaille found it in 1751, sweeping the southern sky from South Africa.
NGC3293.tagline: A young cluster of blue supergiants with one red one glowing among them.

facts.text: NGC 330 has an unusually large share of Be stars: hot blue stars spinning so fast that they shed discs of gas from their equators.
facts.title: Spinning stars

facts.text: About a third of its massive stars have a close companion — fewer than in clusters of the Milky Way and Large Magellanic Cloud. Nobody yet knows whether its age or its scarcity of heavy elements is the reason.
facts.title: Fewer close pairs

story: NGC 330 belongs to another galaxy: the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of the [[magellanic-clouds]] that orbit the Milky Way. Dreyer’s catalogue called it a globular cluster, but it is far younger than a true globular — only about 40 million years old. It is a massive [[open-cluster]], some 54,000 times the mass of the Sun, and shines with nearly 900,000 times the Sun’s light.
James Dunlop discovered it from Parramatta, New South Wales, on 1 August 1826.
NGC330.tagline: A brilliant young cluster in another galaxy, full of stars spinning fast enough to fling off rings of gas.

facts.text: The cluster and its nebula, IC 2599, are nicknamed the Gabriela Mistral Nebula for their likeness to the profile of the Chilean poet, who won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Literature.
facts.title: A poet in the clouds

story: In July 2022 NASA unveiled the first full-colour pictures from the James Webb Space Telescope. One showed a towering wall of gas and dust, nicknamed the Cosmic Cliffs, studded with newborn stars. That wall is the edge of the glowing cloud around NGC 3324, a young [[cluster-nebula|star cluster]] near the great Carina Nebula. Hubble had photographed the same stretch years before, so astronomers could set the two views side by side.
James Dunlop first catalogued the cluster in 1826.
NGC3324.tagline: The cluster behind Webb’s Cosmic Cliffs — and a nebula with a poet’s face.

story: We live inside the Milky Way, so we cannot step outside to see its shape. Open clusters help. Their distances and ages can be measured, so astronomers use them as signposts to trace the galaxy’s spiral arms. NGC 3330, an [[open-cluster]] in Vela, is one of many such markers scattered along the southern Milky Way.
NGC3330.tagline: A Vela cluster — one of the signposts used to map our galaxy’s spiral arms.

story: Seen nearly face-on, NGC 3344 shows off its whole design: a small bar inside an inner ring, arms unwinding from that ring, and a fainter outer ring wrapped around them all. This barred [[spiral-galaxy]] lives a quiet life, with no bright galaxy close by. Even its centre is calm, lit by young stars rather than a feeding black hole. William Herschel found it on 6 April 1785.
NGC3344.tagline: A quiet, face-on spiral with rings within rings.

facts.text: One of the James Webb Space Telescope’s first images, released in 2022, showed the ‘Cosmic Cliffs’ — the edge of a young star-forming region in NGC 3324, on the north-west edge of the Carina Nebula.
facts.title: Webb’s Cosmic Cliffs

facts.text: To mark its 20th anniversary in 2010, Hubble photographed Mystic Mountain, a pillar of dust and gas here. Newborn stars hidden inside fire jets of gas from its peaks.
facts.title: Mystic Mountain

facts.text: Dust from the Great Eruption now shrouds Eta Carinae, cutting the ultraviolet light it pours into the nebula. Before the 1840s the whole nebula would have looked very different.
facts.title: A dimmer switch

facts.text: The Homunculus soaks up Eta Carinae’s light and gives it out again as infrared. At mid-infrared wavelengths it is the brightest object in the sky.
facts.title: Bright in the infrared

story: In the 1840s a star inside the Carina Nebula erupted so violently that, for a while, it was the second-brightest star in the night sky. Eta Carinae, a hypergiant of 100 to 150 Suns, survived its Great Eruption, and the gas it threw off now surrounds it as the Homunculus, a small twin-lobed cloud.

Eta Carinae is only the loudest resident of this vast [[emission-nebula]]. Its clusters include Trumpler 14, one of the youngest known at about half a million years old, and Trumpler 16, home to WR 25 — possibly the most luminous star in the galaxy. The oldest cluster, NGC 3293, lies farthest from Trumpler 14, a sign that star birth has rippled through the cloud in waves.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered it on 25 January 1752 from the Cape of Good Hope. John Herschel described a dark cloud within it as a ‘lemniscate-oval vacuity’; in 1873 the writer Emma Converse said it resembled a keyhole, and the name stuck.
NGC3372.tagline: Home of Eta Carinae, the star that erupted in the 1840s and lived — and of Webb’s Cosmic Cliffs.

story: Smooth and elongated, NGC 3377 is an [[elliptical-galaxy]] in the M 96 group in Leo. Close to its core the stars whirl faster and faster — the sign of a supermassive black hole about 80 million times the mass of the Sun. Around the galaxy swarm 400 to 500 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]]. William Herschel found it on 8 April 1784.
NGC3377.tagline: A smooth elliptical with a giant black hole and hundreds of globular clusters.

story: The stars at the centre of NGC 3384 are old.
