More than 80% of them, judging by their colour, are Population II stars over a billion years old, and among them sits a supermassive black hole of about 16 million suns. This smooth [[galaxy]] belongs to the M 96 group in Leo, and lies close in the sky to three Messier objects of the same group: M 95, M 96 and M 105. William Herschel found it in 1784. It also carries a second catalogue number, NGC 3371.
NGC3384.tagline: An old, quiet galaxy in the Leo group, sharing the sky with M 95, M 96 and M 105.

story: Not long ago, by cosmic standards, the heart of NGC 3489 lit up with new stars. Its youngest stars sit closest to the centre, around 1.7 billion years old, and the galaxy is now called post-starburst: the main show is over, though some molecular gas remains that could yet make more. Dust spirals loosely around the nucleus, where a black hole of about 6 million suns keeps up a mild active glow.
William Herschel found this lenticular [[galaxy]] in Leo on 8 April 1784.
NGC3489.tagline: A galaxy just past its last burst of starbirth, with a modest black hole at its heart.

story: Carina, the Keel of the old ship Argo, holds one of the richest stretches of the southern Milky Way. It is home to the great Carina Nebula and to Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky. NGC 3496 is one of the many open clusters strewn across this part of the sky: a family of stars born together from one cloud, still travelling together through the galaxy’s disc.
NGC3496.tagline: A cluster in the Keel of Argo, one of the richest stretches of the southern Milky Way.

story: Some clusters belong to the southern sky alone. NGC 3519 sits so far south in Carina that it never rises for observers in Europe or most of North America, so it could only have been found by someone working from the southern hemisphere. Like every [[open-cluster]], it is a family of stars born together from a single cloud, slowly drifting apart over time.
NGC3519.tagline: A cluster so far south that it never rises over Europe.

facts.text: In December 2024 the ATLAS survey found a supernova here, SN 2024aecx. First classed as one type, it turned out to be a Type Ic — a near twin of the well-studied SN 1994I.
facts.title: A supernova that changed type

story: In many ways NGC 3521 is a stand-in for our own galaxy. It is a [[spiral-galaxy]] built much like the Milky Way, with a central black hole of about 7 million suns, similar in heft to ours. Its arms are flocculent: broken into patchy tufts rather than two clean spirals. It is sometimes called the Bubble Galaxy, and William Herschel found it on 22 February 1784.
NGC3521.tagline: A patchy spiral built much like the Milky Way, down to the size of its black hole.

facts.text: Among roughly 150 stars, NGC 3532 holds seven red giants — stars swelling in old age — and seven white dwarfs, the cooling cores left once a star’s life is over.
facts.title: Stars and their ghosts

facts.text: The bright Cepheid variable x Carinae, near the cluster’s edge, is not a member. It lies between us and the cluster, pulsing away in the foreground.
facts.title: A pulsing stranger

story: On 20 May 1990, a few weeks after launch, the Hubble Space Telescope opened its eye for the first time. Its very first target was NGC 3532, a rich [[open-cluster]] in Carina.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille had catalogued it in 1752 from the Cape of Good Hope. Later John Herschel, observing from the same place, admired its many [[double-star|double stars]]. Since then it has gathered nicknames the way a fountain gathers coins: the Wishing Well, the Pincushion, the Football and the Black Arrow.
NGC3532.tagline: The very first thing the Hubble Space Telescope ever looked at — a cluster of living stars and dead ones.

facts.text: In February 2023 a supernova flared here, SN 2023bpx — a Type Ia, an exploding white dwarf. It was found by the Backyard Observatory Supernova Search.
facts.title: Found from the backyard

story: The biggest galaxy in its neighbourhood, NGC 3557 is a large [[elliptical-galaxy]] at the head of a [[galaxy-group]] of at least eleven members that bears its name. Its core is active, though the astronomers’ databases can’t agree on a label: one lists it as a Seyfert nucleus, another as a gentler LINER glow. John Herschel found it from the Cape of Good Hope on 21 April 1835.
NGC3557.tagline: The giant elliptical at the head of a group of at least eleven galaxies.

facts.text: Halton Arp discovered a supernova here, SN 1953A, in April 1953 — years before he listed the pair as Arp 105 in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
facts.title: Arp’s own supernova

story: Two galaxies locked in a collision make up NGC 3561, nicknamed the Guitar. The pair, NGC 3561A and NGC 3561B, belong to the galaxy cluster Abell 1185, and their encounter has flung out a long tail of stars and gas. Out of that debris a new dwarf galaxy seems to have formed: a small knot named Ambartsumian’s Knot, after the Armenian astronomer Viktor Ambartsumian. John Herschel found the pair on 30 March 1827.
NGC3561.tagline: Two galaxies colliding into the shape of a guitar — with a newborn galaxy in the wreckage.

facts.text: V533 Carinae is an Alpha Cygni variable whose light wavers by only about a hundredth of a magnitude. It was named as a variable star in 1999, one of 2,675 new variables found in data from the Hipparcos satellite.
facts.title: A barely-there flicker

story: Newly born by cosmic standards, NGC 3572 is a fresh brood of hot young stars near the Carina Nebula. It belongs to a wider family called Carina OB2, together with the smaller clusters Collinder 240, Hogg 10 and Hogg 11, all of them only a few million years old.

The brightest star in the area, V533 Carinae, sits in Collinder 240, which is sometimes counted as part of NGC 3572. It is a supergiant shining around 100,000 times brighter than the Sun, plain to the naked eye away from city lights.
NGC3572.tagline: A brood of hot young stars only a few million years old, near the Carina Nebula.

facts.text: NGC 3585 has about 550 globular clusters, a modest number typical of lone ellipticals. Their brightnesses hint that some of them are younger than the rest.
facts.title: A late batch of clusters

story: At the heart of NGC 3585 sits a black hole weighing a few hundred million suns. The galaxy around it is big and smooth, classed as either elliptical or lenticular, and it leads a loose [[galaxy-group]] of its own in Hydra. A reddish disc of dust lies in its core, and its outer light is lopsided — perhaps the mark of a past tidal encounter. William Herschel found it on 9 December 1784.
NGC3585.tagline: A massive galaxy with a black hole of hundreds of millions of suns at its core.

story: Look along the Milky Way in Carina and you are looking along the disc of our galaxy, through stars, gas and dust. Light from clusters such as NGC 3590 is dimmed and reddened by that dust on its way to us, and astronomers must correct for it before they can work out how bright — and how old — the stars of an [[open-cluster]] really are.
NGC3590.tagline: A cluster whose light reaches us dimmed by the dust of the Milky Way.

story: Most galaxies are wrapped in dark matter that far outweighs their stars. NGC 3607 may be an exception. The orbits of its 46 known [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] suggest it holds unusually little, though the measurement is very uncertain. It is odd in other ways too: an outer dusty disc has a second disc at right angles to it, falling in towards the centre, where a black hole of about 120 million suns waits.
William Herschel found it on 14 March 1784. Dreyer listed it as the “2nd of 3”, one of a trio of nebulae in the same field.
NGC3607.tagline: A galaxy that may be surprisingly short of dark matter.

facts.text: At the inner end of its stretched orbit, NGC 362 dives deep into the Milky Way, much closer to the galactic centre than the Sun ever comes.
facts.title: Close to the centre

facts.text: NGC 362 is visible to the naked eye under dark skies, but it is often overlooked in favour of its larger and brighter neighbour on the sky, 47 Tucanae.
facts.title: In a famous shadow

story: James Dunlop discovered NGC 362 on 1 August 1826, during his survey of the southern sky. It is a [[globular-cluster]], one of the ancient balls of stars that orbit our galaxy — yet an unusual one. Its stars contain more heavy elements than the stars of most globulars, which suggests that it formed relatively late for its kind.

It lives a dramatic life. Its orbit is highly elongated, carrying it in close to the centre of the Milky Way and then far back out again. It has an exceptionally tight core, and an unusually large share of its stars are binaries, pairs locked in orbit around each other.
NGC362.tagline: A youthful globular cluster on a looping orbit that plunges close to the heart of the Milky Way.

facts.text: Searching old Hubble and Spitzer images, astronomers found the star that exploded: a red supergiant of roughly 12 to 15 times the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: The star before the blast

story: In April 2024 a massive star in NGC 3621 blew itself apart. Found by the ATLAS survey on 11 April, SN 2024ggi brightened within days to become the brightest supernova of the year, and the nearest since SN 2023ixf the year before.

The galaxy itself is a pure disc, a [[spiral-galaxy]] with no central bulge at all. Even so, it has an active nucleus, powered by a black hole of up to three million suns. William Herschel found it on 17 February 1790.
NGC3621.tagline: Home of 2024’s brightest supernova — and a black hole in a galaxy with no bulge.

facts.text: It carries two numbers in the New General Catalogue, NGC 3626 and NGC 3632 — the same galaxy logged twice, a common slip in the 19th-century catalogues.
facts.title: Two numbers, one galaxy

facts.text: Patrick Moore included it as number 40 in his Caldwell catalogue of 1995, a list of 109 fine sights that Charles Messier’s catalogue left out.
facts.title: Caldwell 40

story: Strip the arms from a spiral galaxy and what remains is a lens-shaped disc of stars around a bright central bulge, with no spiral pattern at all — a lenticular galaxy. NGC 3626 is one of them, an unbarred example in Leo.
William Herschel found it on 14 March 1784, during his great sweeps of the sky with his home-built telescopes.

It does not live alone. NGC 3626 belongs to the NGC 3607 group, one of many small [[galaxy-group|galaxy groups]] scattered through Leo, and its neighbours in the sky include NGC 3607, NGC 3608 and a handful of other galaxies.
NGC3626.tagline: A spiral galaxy without its arms, logged twice by the catalogue-makers and living among a crowd in Leo.

facts.text: Its other nickname, Sarah’s Galaxy, is thought to honour the poet Sarah Williams (1837–1868), best known for her poem “The Old Astronomer”.
facts.title: Sarah’s Galaxy

story: Edge-on and split along its length by a broad lane of dust, NGC 3628 looks like a burger in a bun — hence the Hamburger Galaxy. It is the third member of the Leo Triplet, alongside M 65 and M 66, and the pull of its two big neighbours has drawn out a long tail of stars.
Those encounters may also have given it a bar, which we happen to see end-on. An X-shaped bulge at its centre gives it away. William Herschel found the galaxy in 1784.
NGC3628.tagline: A galaxy sliced by a thick lane of dust — the Hamburger of the Leo Triplet.

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen here, the latest, SN 2016bau, caught by Ron Arbour in March 2016 before it reached peak brightness.
facts.title: Four supernovae

story: Weather maps for a galaxy? In NGC 3631 the hydrogen gas swirls in giant eddies: two anticyclones between the spiral arms and four cyclones close beside them, all turning with the spiral pattern. Seen almost face-on, this grand-design [[spiral-galaxy]] has two main arms that branch into fainter ones, dotted with glowing star-forming clouds.
Halton Arp put it in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies for its oddly straight arm segments. William Herschel found it on 14 April 1789.
NGC3631.tagline: A face-on spiral whose gas swirls in cyclones and anticyclones, like weather.

story: Elliptical galaxies are often pictured as calm, settled balls of old stars. NGC 3640 is not. Its boxy shape and faint, patchy shells are the marks of a recent merger with a smaller, gas-poor galaxy. It also spins faster than most [[elliptical-galaxy|ellipticals]] of its brightness, and a lane of dust crosses its middle. A black hole of roughly 100 million suns sits at its core.
It leads a small [[galaxy-group]] in Leo, and William Herschel found it on 23 February 1784.
NGC3640.tagline: An elliptical still showing the scars of a recent meal.

facts.text: In December 1984 Kaoru Ikeya — the Japanese comet hunter behind the great sungrazing Comet Ikeya–Seki of 1965 — discovered a supernova here, SN 1984R.
facts.title: A comet hunter’s supernova

story: The arms of NGC 3675 wind so tightly that they close into an inner ring, then carry on for one more turn before breaking up into patchy, threadlike outer arms. Infrared pictures once seemed to show a strong bar across its middle, but later looks found none. This [[spiral-galaxy]] belongs to the Ursa Major Cluster, and William Herschel found it on 14 January 1788.
NGC3675.tagline: A tightly wound spiral in Ursa Major — with a supernova found by a famous comet hunter.

story: Well over a billion years old, NGC 3680 is an elderly [[open-cluster]]. Its hot blue stars burned out long ago. What remains are cooler, Sun-like stars, along with yellow and orange giants — stars that have used up the hydrogen in their cores and swollen up. Most open clusters break apart long before reaching this age, so survivors like this one are worth studying.
NGC3680.tagline: An elderly cluster that has outlived its hot blue stars.

story: Three arms spring from a ring at the heart of NGC 3726. The southern one is brightest, the northern one the most clearly drawn, and the third takes a sudden turn, bending sharply to the south-west. The whole pattern is a little lopsided. The bluest, youngest star-forming regions crowd along the ring itself, which circles a small bar.
This [[spiral-galaxy]] carries a massive halo of dark matter but only a modest central black hole, about 3 million suns. William Herschel found it on 5 February 1788.
NGC3726.tagline: A slightly lopsided spiral with three arms springing from a ring of young stars.

discovered.note: Found during his 1751–52 survey from the Cape of Good Hope

facts.text: NGC 3766 holds eleven Be stars — hot stars spinning so fast that they shed rings of gas around their middles.
facts.title: Spinning stars

facts.text: The Pearl Cluster is approaching us at about 15 kilometres a second, and it lies within the vast star-forming region known as the Carina molecular cloud.
facts.title: Heading our way

story: Thirty-six stars in NGC 3766 flicker in a way astronomers had not recognised before. They dim and brighten by just a few hundredths of a magnitude, over less than half a day. They are fast-spinning, pulsating B-type stars, hotter than the familiar Delta Scuti pulsators yet cooler than the so-called slowly pulsating B stars — an unusual type of [[variable-star]].

The cluster itself is young, about 14 million years old, and its heaviest stars are already living fast. Two have swollen into red supergiants, and four are Ap stars, with oddly mixed surface chemistry.
Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered it in 1751–52 during his survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC3766.tagline: A young cluster where astronomers found a new kind of flickering star — 36 of them.

discovered.note: Credited to her by William Herschel in 1787

story: William Herschel credited this cluster to his sister Caroline in 1787, although she may never have actually seen it. Whoever first glimpsed it, NGC 381 is an [[open-cluster]] of middle age: about 316 million years old, so its stars formed before the first dinosaurs. Around 350 stars are thought to belong to it. None has yet swollen into a giant.
The eclipsing binary OX Cassiopeiae was once counted as a member, but it turned out to lie far behind the cluster.
NGC381.tagline: A cluster credited to Caroline Herschel — who may never have seen it.

story: When a Sun-like star dies, it puffs off its outer layers into a glowing shell: a [[planetary-nebula]]. NGC 3918 is the brightest of these in the far southern sky, and its rich blue colour is often compared to Neptune as Voyager 2 saw it in 1989. Its shell is still expanding at around 24 km per second.
John Herschel found it from the Cape of Good Hope in March 1834. It is also known as the Southerner.
NGC3918.tagline: The brightest planetary nebula of the far south, glowing a rich Neptune blue.

facts.text: SN 2018aoz, a Type Ia supernova found here by the DLT40 survey, reached magnitude 12.7 — tying with SN 2018pv in NGC 3941 as the brightest supernova of 2018.
facts.title: Joint winner of 2018

story: Drop a stone into a pond and ripples spread outwards. Something similar happened around NGC 3923. Astronomers think that when this large [[elliptical-galaxy]] swallowed a smaller companion, the two cores sloshed back and forth, and the disturbance spread out as layers of stars, like the skins of an onion. It has up to 42 of these shells, the most of any known shell galaxy, and unusually they are faint and symmetrical. A stream of stars and a small elliptical galaxy nearby may be leftovers of that meal.
William Herschel found it on 7 March 1791.
NGC3923.tagline: A galaxy wrapped in ripples — more shells of stars than any other known.

story: Catalogues cannot agree what NGC 3928 is. Some call it lenticular, some a dwarf spiral, and others an elliptical. Its nickname, the Miniature Spiral, makes the case for a small spiral. This compact [[galaxy]] belongs to the NGC 3877 group in Ursa Major, alongside the three-armed spiral NGC 3726. William Herschel found it on 9 March 1788.
NGC3928.tagline: The Miniature Spiral — a small galaxy that catalogues can’t agree how to classify.

facts.text: In 2022 a luminous red nova, AT 2022ckk, flared here. Such outbursts are thought to mark two stars spiralling together and merging.
facts.title: Two stars become one

story: In May 2017 the amateur astronomer Ron Arbour spotted a new star in NGC 3938: a supernova, SN 2017ein. Older pictures of the galaxy seem to show the star before it died. If it was single, it weighed some 47 to 48 times the Sun’s mass; if it had a companion, perhaps 60 to 80. Five supernovae have now been seen in this [[spiral-galaxy]], one of the brightest in its corner of Ursa Major. William Herschel found it on 6 February 1788.
NGC3938.tagline: A spiral where a giant star of perhaps 50 suns or more blew up in 2017.

facts.text: Masaki Tsuboi found SN 2018pv here in February 2018. At magnitude 12.7 it tied with SN 2018aoz, in NGC 3923, as the brightest supernova of 2018.
facts.title: Brightest of the year, shared

story: The gas in NGC 3941 goes the wrong way. Its stars orbit in one direction, but a wide disc of gas turns in the other. The gas may have come from outside — in a merger, or simply falling in — already spinning the opposite way, and it has since settled calmly into two rings. This barred lenticular [[galaxy]] even has a second, smaller bar inside the first, and a black hole of about 140 million suns at its core.
William Herschel found it in 1787.
NGC3941.tagline: A galaxy whose gas spins the opposite way to its stars.

story: Pierre Méchain, Charles Messier’s colleague and fellow comet hunter, found NGC 3953 on 12 March 1781 — yet it never received a Messier number. It is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] with a ring of stars and gas encircling its bar. It belongs to the M 109 group in Ursa Major, a large gathering that may hold more than 50 galaxies.
NGC3953.tagline: Found by Messier’s colleague Pierre Méchain — yet it never got a Messier number.

story: Centaurus is a constellation of superlatives. It holds Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to the Sun, and Omega Centauri, the biggest globular cluster of the Milky Way. NGC 3960 is a quieter resident: a modest [[open-cluster]], its stars born together from one cloud and still moving through the galaxy as a group.
NGC3960.tagline: A quiet cluster in Centaurus, a constellation of superlatives.

facts.text: The central star’s surface is about 71,000 K, yet the light ionising the nebula seems to come from a source of only 45,000 K. One idea: a late thermal pulse reignited fusion and heated the star up again.
facts.title: A star reborn?

facts.text: Planetary nebulae do not last. About 30,000 years from now NGC 40 is expected to have faded away, leaving only a white dwarf about the size of Earth.
facts.title: A fleeting glow

story: Around 6,500 years ago a dying star began to hollow out a cavity in the gas around it, and about 4,200 years ago it threw out lobes to the north and south. The result is NGC 40, a barrel-shaped [[planetary-nebula]] with two extra pairs of lobes around its poles, the marks of further outbursts. Radiation from the star heats the gas to about 10,000 °C and makes it glow.
William Herschel discovered it on 25 November 1788. The star at its heart, HD 826, shines about 7,000 times as brightly as the Sun, yet it is only about half the Sun’s width.
NGC40.tagline: A dying star’s shed skin, heated to 10,000 degrees — and due to fade away within 30,000 years.

facts.text: Four supernovae have been seen in NGC 4038, in 1974, 2004, 2007 and 2013. One of them, SN 2007sr, helped astronomers measure how far away the colliding pair is.
facts.title: Supernova after supernova

facts.text: Around 53 Cepheid variables have been found in NGC 4038 — pulsing stars whose rhythm reveals their true brightness, and so their distance.
facts.title: Pulsing yardsticks

story: Two galaxies are colliding in Corvus, and NGC 4038 is the northern half of the wreck. About 1.2 billion years ago it was a normal barred [[spiral-galaxy]]. Then its neighbour NGC 4039 came close, and the two have been tearing at each other ever since.

The crash has set off a burst of star birth. As clouds of gas slam together, shock waves squeeze them into new stars — and even into new [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]]. Most globulars in our own galaxy are around 12 billion years old; these are youngsters, born in the collision.

The pair has taught astronomers how galaxies merge. Alar Toomre’s famous sequence of colliding galaxies was built in part by successfully modelling the long, curving tails thrown out by NGC 4038 and its partner.
NGC4038.tagline: The northern half of a galactic pile-up — where the crash is forging brand-new star clusters.

facts.text: In March 1921 Edwin Hubble and John Charles Duncan discovered SN 1921A in NGC 4039 — still the only supernova recorded in this half of the pair.
facts.title: Hubble’s supernova

facts.text: The Chandra X-ray Observatory found clouds in the colliding pair rich in neon, magnesium and silicon, with 16 times the Sun’s share of magnesium and 24 times its silicon — elements needed to build planets.
facts.title: Ingredients for planets

story: Six hundred million years ago, NGC 4039 and its neighbour NGC 4038 passed right through each other. Once a separate [[spiral-galaxy]], NGC 4039 has been reshaped by the encounter. Starting around 300 million years ago, stars were flung out of both galaxies, and today they stream far into space in two long, curving tails. Those tails, like an insect’s feelers, give the pair its name: the Antennae.

The story is not over. Within 400 million years the cores of the two galaxies will collide and become one. Simulations suggest the pair will end as a single giant [[elliptical-galaxy]] — a fate that may one day await our Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy too.
NGC4039.tagline: Half of the Antennae: a spiral that passed right through its neighbour, and will one day merge with it.

story: In early 1998 the bright X-ray glow from the heart of NGC 4051 simply switched off. The BeppoSAX satellite saw it go dark; by August it was back to normal. The source is a feeding black hole in this Seyfert [[galaxy]], and a lightweight one: about 1.7 million suns, less than half the mass of the one in our own galaxy.
William Herschel found NGC 4051 on 6 February 1788. It belongs to the Ursa Major Cluster.
NGC4051.tagline: A galaxy whose X-ray glow switched off for months in 1998.

story: Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of the 88 constellations, yet one of the most famous: it appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea and Samoa. Its patch of the [[milky-way]] is packed with star clusters, from the celebrated Jewel Box to small groups such as NGC 4052, an [[open-cluster]] of stars born together.
NGC4052.tagline: A cluster in the Southern Cross, the smallest and best-known of southern constellations.

story: Two stars in NGC 4103 are locked together. AI Crucis is a pair of massive stars so close that they circle each other every 1.42 days, near enough for gas to stream from one onto the other. Several suns’ worth of material has already changed hands, and the transfer, along with a strong wind from the hotter star, is slowly lengthening their orbit.
The [[open-cluster]] around them is young — estimates range from 6 to 30 million years — and none of its stars has yet become a red giant. James Dunlop found it in 1826.
NGC4103.tagline: A young cluster where one star is slowly feeding on its partner.

facts.text: John Russell Hind also discovered ten asteroids, among them Iris and Flora, and gave his name to Hind’s Crimson Star, R Leporis.
facts.title: The discoverer’s other finds

story: In May 2016 a robotic telescope at Lick Observatory in California caught a white dwarf blowing up in NGC 4125. Over the next few days the supernova, SN 2016coj, brightened to magnitude 13, the brightest of the whole year. The [[elliptical-galaxy]] that hosted it was found on 4 January 1850 by the English astronomer John Russell Hind.
NGC4125.tagline: Home of 2016’s brightest supernova, in a galaxy found by an asteroid hunter.

story: NGC 4147 may be an immigrant. This small [[globular-cluster]] sits far out in the Milky Way’s halo, isolated from its fellows, along the path of the Sagittarius stream — the trail of stars torn from the Sagittarius Dwarf galaxy. It may have been captured from that galaxy. S-shaped tidal arms stretch away from it to the north and south.
Its core holds as many as 23 blue stragglers: stars that look too young for their surroundings, probably made when two older stars merged. William Herschel found it on 14 March 1784.
NGC4147.tagline: A small, lonely globular cluster that may have been captured from another galaxy.

story: The Milky Way’s globular clusters are relics, most of them well over 10 billion years old. NGC 419 is a youngster by comparison: about 1.45 billion years. It lies in the Small Magellanic Cloud, one of the [[magellanic-clouds]] orbiting our galaxy, and holds some 64,000 times the mass of the Sun. James Dunlop discovered it on 2 September 1826, and Dreyer later described it as pretty large and bright, growing brighter towards the middle.
NGC419.tagline: A ‘globular’ cluster in a neighbour galaxy, billions of years younger than the Milky Way’s own.

facts.text: Radio searches have found no nucleus for either of the merging galaxies. But in 2009 the Chandra X-ray Observatory picked up X-rays from a black hole out in the tidal tail.
facts.title: A black hole in the tail

story: Two galaxies have nearly become one in NGC 4194, the Medusa merger. Loops, arcs and a tidal tail spill from its centre, and Halton Arp listed it as Arp 160 in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies. At its heart, the gas-rich Eye of Medusa, gas squeezed by the collision is turning into stars at a furious pace: about eight suns’ worth a year in the central region, several times the rate of the whole Milky Way.
William Herschel found it on 2 April 1791.
NGC4194.tagline: Two galaxies become one in the Medusa merger, with a furious burst of starbirth at its eye.

facts.text: In 1954 Paul Wild discovered a supernova here, SN 1954A, at magnitude 9.8 — a Type Ib, the collapse of a massive star.
facts.title: A bright supernova

facts.text: One of its satellites, MADCASH-2, is an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy that, unusually, has formed stars in more than one burst: about 400 million and 1.5 billion years ago.
facts.title: A tiny companion

story: Larger and brighter than the Small Magellanic Cloud, NGC 4214 is a dwarf [[galaxy]] in the middle of a starburst. Its two biggest star-forming regions sit at the centre: one holds a super star cluster rich in Wolf–Rayet stars, hot giants blowing off their outer layers, and the other is younger than 3 million years. Two older super star clusters, both 200 million years old, weigh about 260,000 and 1.5 million suns.
William Herschel found it on 28 April 1785.
NGC4214.tagline: A dwarf galaxy bigger than the Small Magellanic Cloud, in the middle of a starburst.

facts.text: Two streams of stars in its halo are small satellite galaxies being torn apart and swallowed. It also hosts about 700 globular clusters, nearly five times as many as the Milky Way.
facts.title: Eating the neighbours

story: Seen almost edge-on, NGC 4216 earns its nickname, the Silver Streak. It is one of the largest and brightest spirals in the Virgo Cluster, intrinsically brighter than the Andromeda Galaxy. Like most spirals in the cluster it is short of hydrogen gas, which leaves it anaemic and slow to make new stars, and pillar-like structures in its disc may be marks of its crowded surroundings.
William Herschel found this [[spiral-galaxy]] on 17 April 1784.
NGC4216.tagline: The Silver Streak: an edge-on giant of the Virgo Cluster that feeds on dwarf galaxies.

story: Even the big catalogues make mistakes. The ESO catalogue and the SIMBAD database both pin the name NGC 4230 on a different cluster, ESO 171-SC14. The real NGC 4230 is a loosely scattered [[open-cluster]] in Centaurus, found by John Herschel on 5 April 1837 while he was observing from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC4230.tagline: A loose cluster whose name the big databases pin on the wrong stars.

facts.text: Three radio sources sit in its quiet core. They may be the remains of supernovae — or two may be pockets of star birth and the third a Sun-like star in our own galaxy, lying in front.
facts.title: Three radio puzzles

facts.text: NGC 4236 belongs to the M 81 group, alongside the bright spiral M 81 and the starburst galaxy M 82, but it keeps its distance from the group’s busy centre.
facts.title: On the edge of the family

story: Built like the Large Magellanic Cloud — a loose, barred disc with only a hint of spiral arms — NGC 4236 is the type astronomers call a Magellanic [[spiral-galaxy]].
Stars are being born right across its disc, and it is dotted with bright clouds of glowing hydrogen. Only its core is quiet, with very little star formation, while its halo stays active.

William Herschel discovered it in April 1793. Two centuries later Patrick Moore made it Caldwell 3; his list runs from north to south, so the low number marks it as one of the most northerly objects in the catalogue.
NGC4236.tagline: A loose, Magellanic-style spiral on the edge of the M 81 family, with three radio puzzles at its core.

facts.text: NGC 4244 belongs to the Canes Venatici I group, also called the M 94 group — one of the galaxy families closest to our own Local Group.
facts.title: A neighbouring family

facts.text: In the sky it shares its patch with the barred spiral NGC 4151 and the irregular galaxy NGC 4214, close to the yellow naked-eye star Beta Canum Venaticorum.
facts.title: Good company

story: Turn a pinwheel side-on and all you see is a thin line. NGC 4244 is a loosely wound [[spiral-galaxy]] seen just that way, its arms hidden and its disc reduced to a sliver. Galaxies caught [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]] like this let astronomers study a spiral in profile: how thin its disc is, and what lies above and below it.
At its centre sits a nuclear star cluster, a dense knot of stars packed into the galaxy’s core, wrapped in a faint halo.
William Herschel discovered it in 1787, in the constellation of the Hunting Dogs.
NGC4244.tagline: A spiral galaxy turned exactly side-on, with a dense knot of stars hidden at its heart.

facts.text: Scottish amateur astronomer Tom Boles discovered a supernova here in November 1999, SN 1999ev — the collapse of a massive star.
facts.title: An amateur’s find

story: NGC 4274 is built like a set of nested hoops. A small ring circles the nucleus. Farther out, its bright, dusty inner arms overlap to form a second ring, and beyond that a set of fainter outer arms makes a third. Inside, a small bar lies almost at right angles to the main bar — a bar within a bar. This [[spiral-galaxy]] leads its own small [[galaxy-group]] in Coma Berenices. William Herschel found it on 13 March 1785.
NGC4274.tagline: Three rings and two bars — a spiral built like a set of nested hoops.

facts.text: The Spitzer Space Telescope found glowing carbon-rich molecules called PAHs here. They are rare in ellipticals, where hot gas is thought to destroy them.
facts.title: Molecules that shouldn’t survive

story: Most elliptical galaxies hold little cold gas. NGC 4278 has a massive disc of hydrogen, probably taken from a dwarf galaxy it swallowed, and threads of dust spiral down to its core. There a black hole of about 300 million suns flickers: its ultraviolet glow brightened 1.6 times in six months in 1994–95, and its X-rays rose fivefold within three years. Two tiny S-shaped radio jets curl out from the centre.
William Herschel found this [[elliptical-galaxy]] on 13 March 1785.
NGC4278.tagline: An elliptical with a gas disc, a flickering black hole and two tiny S-shaped jets.

story: The outskirts of NGC 4293 look ruffled. Its outer disc of stars is disturbed, a sign that something has tugged at it, and new stars now form only in a small region at its very centre. A member of the Virgo Cluster, this [[galaxy]] sits on the border between lenticular and spiral, with a bar and faint, tightly wound arms. At its heart a black hole of about 60 million suns feeds slowly, giving off a dim glow.
William Herschel, who found it on 14 March 1784, described it as “large, extended, resolvable”.
NGC4293.tagline: A ruffled Virgo Cluster galaxy whose starbirth has shrunk to its very centre.

story: For centuries sailors in southern seas found their way by the Southern Cross: follow its long arm about four and a half times its length and you are close to the south celestial pole. NGC 4337 is one of the open clusters within the Cross’s borders, a family of stars born together in the Milky Way’s disc and still travelling through the galaxy as a group.
NGC4337.tagline: A small cluster inside the Southern Cross, the sailors’ guide to the south.

facts.text: Two Cepheid variable stars, R and T Crucis, appear among the cluster’s stars but are not members. R Crucis lies well outside the cluster’s edge and much nearer to us.
facts.title: Passers-by

story: For a while, a giant star in NGC 4349 seemed to have a companion. The star, catalogued as NGC 4349 No. 127 and about three times the Sun’s mass, shows a regular to-and-fro in its speed that was once read as the tug of an orbiting brown dwarf. It turned out to come from the star itself — a reminder of how careful planet hunters must be.
James Dunlop found this [[open-cluster]] in 1826.
NGC4349.tagline: A cluster where a ‘brown dwarf’ turned out to be the star’s own wobble.

story: William Herschel found NGC 436 on 3 November 1787, one of the many star clusters he swept up in the Milky Way band through Cassiopeia. A century later John Dreyer’s New General Catalogue summed it up as a small, irregular, fairly compressed cluster. It is an [[open-cluster]], a family of stars born together, and sits less than a degree from the much brighter NGC 457.
NGC436.tagline: A small, compact cluster sitting in the shadow of a brighter neighbour, NGC 457.

story: The core of NGC 4365 spins at right angles to the rest of the galaxy — strong evidence that [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxies]] grow by swallowing others. This giant formed its stars early and ran out of gas for new ones about 12 billion years ago, and its shape has hardly changed since. Now it is helping itself to a neighbour: a stream of globular clusters links it to the compact galaxy NGC 4342, which it seems to be stripping of clusters and stars.
William Herschel found it on 13 April 1784.
NGC4365.tagline: A giant elliptical with a sideways-spinning core, stealing star clusters from a neighbour.

facts.text: Just to the east runs the Dark Doodad, a long, thin streak of dust silhouetted against the Milky Way — one of the more whimsically named objects in the southern sky.
facts.title: The Dark Doodad

facts.text: Its peculiar chemistry has been likened to that of NGC 5694, a remote globular cluster in Hydra that may have been captured from another galaxy.
facts.title: A chemical twin

story: Old stars are usually poor in heavy elements, and the stars of NGC 4372 are poorer than most: they hold only a tiny trace of iron. Yet, oddly, they are richer than the Sun in magnesium and titanium. That highly peculiar recipe sets this [[globular-cluster]] apart from most of its kind.
The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop found it in 1826, working from New South Wales. It lies in Musca, the Fly, one of the small southern constellations introduced in the late 1500s.
NGC4372.tagline: An ancient star cluster with a bizarre chemical recipe, beside a dark streak called the Dark Doodad.

facts.text: Three brighter patches in the galaxy were catalogued as objects of their own: NGC 4399, NGC 4400 and NGC 4401.
facts.title: Three patches, three numbers

facts.text: In 1974 Allan Sandage and Gustav Tammann used individual stars resolved in NGC 4395 and other nearby galaxies to measure how fast the universe is expanding.
facts.title: Measuring the universe

story: Active galaxies are usually powered by black holes of millions or billions of suns. The one in NGC 4395 may weigh only a few thousand to a few hundred thousand, among the smallest ever measured at a galaxy’s centre — perhaps a rare intermediate-mass black hole. It lives in an unlikely home: a faint dwarf [[spiral-galaxy]] with no central bulge at all, and one of the nearest and least luminous Seyfert galaxies known.
William Herschel found it on 2 January 1786.
NGC4395.tagline: A faint dwarf spiral hiding one of the smallest black holes ever measured in a galaxy’s heart.

facts.text: On 1 January 2021 a Type Ia supernova, SN 2021J, was spotted here by the ALeRCE alert system. It was a bright one, at around magnitude 12.
facts.title: A New Year’s Day supernova

story: Hubble photographed NGC 4414 in 1995 to measure its distance from its Cepheid variable stars, and returned in 1999 to make a full-colour portrait for the Hubble Heritage project. The picture shows a flocculent [[spiral-galaxy]]: no grand arms, just short, fleecy segments, dusty and laced with young blue stars. It has no sign of past run-ins with other galaxies, yet it is rich in gas, with hydrogen reaching far beyond its visible disc.
William Herschel found it on 13 March 1785.
NGC4414.tagline: A fleecy, dusty spiral that posed for Hubble twice.

story: Galaxies are not supposed to have corners, but the bright central bulge of NGC 4429 is hexagonal. Inside it lie a small disc of dust and possibly a cold disc of stars, perhaps built from gas that fell inwards after a merger long ago — so long ago that no sign of disturbance remains. Seen almost edge-on, this lenticular [[galaxy]] may now be losing much of its gas, swept away as it moves through the hot gas of the Virgo Cluster.
William Herschel found it on 15 March 1784.
NGC4429.tagline: A galaxy with a hexagonal bulge, slowly losing its gas to the Virgo Cluster.

facts.text: Deep images seem to show a long tidal tail streaming from NGC 4435. Some studies suggest it is really foreground dust in our own Milky Way — galactic cirrus — lying in front of it by chance.
facts.title: Tail or trick of the light?

story: NGC 4435 is one of the two Eyes, a pair of galaxies in Markarian’s Chain also known as Arp 120 — and the calmer of the two. This barred lenticular [[galaxy]] is interacting with its partner, NGC 4438. The Spitzer Space Telescope found a relatively young population of stars at its centre, about 190 million years old, perhaps born when the encounter squeezed gas and dust into its core.
NGC4435.tagline: The calmer of the two Eyes in Markarian’s Chain, its centre lit by a burst of starbirth.

facts.text: Filaments of glowing gas link NGC 4438 to the giant elliptical M 86, and gas and dust inside M 86 may have been stripped from NGC 4438 during a past encounter.
facts.title: A third party

story: The more battered of the two Eyes, NGC 4438 has a twisted disc trailing long tidal tails, so distorted that astronomers cannot agree whether to call it a spiral or a lenticular. Its gas and dust have been dragged out towards its partner, NGC 4435: the mark of a close pass, and of the pressure of the Virgo Cluster’s hot gas as it ploughs through at high speed. Something heats its centre — a starburst or a feeding black hole — and astronomers are still working out which.
NGC4438.tagline: The battered Eye of Markarian’s Chain, torn by collisions and stripped by the cluster.

story: Open clusters change colour as they age. When young they are lit by a few hot blue-white stars; as those burn out, the light turns yellower and the brightest members become orange and red giants. Astronomers read the age of clusters such as NGC 4439, in the Southern Cross, from that shifting palette — a family portrait in which the colours give away the year.
NGC4439.tagline: A small cluster in Crux whose colours tell its age.

facts.text: Around NGC 4449 lies an envelope of hydrogen gas about 14 times wider than the visible galaxy, twisted and distorted by encounters with its neighbours.
facts.title: A vast hidden cloud

facts.text: It hosts an ultraluminous X-ray source, NGC 4449 X7. Three supergiant stars, each about eight times the Sun’s mass, are candidates for its visible counterpart.
facts.title: An X-ray powerhouse

story: Imagine the [[magellanic-clouds|Large Magellanic Cloud]] in overdrive. NGC 4449 has the same loose, barred shape as our neighbour, but it is making stars twice as fast. Photographs show it splashed with the pink glow of hydrogen, the tell-tale sign of massive young stars, and studded with young clusters — one of them right at its centre.

Encounters with other galaxies have probably stoked that fire, and they are still going on. In 2012 astronomers found two small galaxies being torn apart and absorbed by NGC 4449: a faint, shredded dwarf rich in dark matter, and a flattened clump of stars trailing two tails of young stars that may be the core of a gas-rich galaxy.
William Herschel discovered it on 27 April 1788.
NGC4449.tagline: A Large Magellanic Cloud in overdrive — making stars at twice the pace while it swallows two smaller galaxies.

story: Dust swirls in a ragged, patchy disc around the centre of NGC 4459, wrapped around an inner ring, and some of it seems to be forming new stars. At the very centre sits a black hole of about 70 million suns. Its event horizon would span nearly three times the distance from the Earth to the Sun. This lenticular [[galaxy]] is a member of the Virgo Cluster, and William Herschel found it on 14 January 1787.
NGC4459.tagline: A Virgo Cluster galaxy with a ragged dust disc and a black hole of 70 million suns.

story: NGC 4463 may hold a rare prize. The young [[planetary-nebula]] He 2-86 — the glowing shell thrown off by a dying star — is thought to belong to this [[open-cluster]] in Musca. Planetary nebulae inside clusters are scarce, and they are valuable: because a cluster’s age can be measured, it tells astronomers how massive the dying star was when it was born. John Herschel found the cluster in 1835.
NGC4463.tagline: A cluster in Musca that may hold a rare prize: a dying star’s glowing shell.

story: Deep inside NGC 4473, two discs of stars spin in opposite directions. They may have formed from gas that fell in from outside, or in mergers with gas-rich galaxies. This [[elliptical-galaxy]] in Markarian’s Chain hosts nearly 400 [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], perhaps gathered in a series of small mergers. Using Hubble, Douglas Richstone and colleagues at the University of Michigan found a black hole of about 100 million suns at its centre.
William Herschel found it on 8 April 1784.
NGC4473.tagline: A smooth elliptical hiding two discs of stars that spin in opposite directions.

story: A strong, sharply drawn bar crosses the centre of NGC 4477, set inside a broad, lens-shaped glow. Around it lie a ring-like rim and two wide, faint arcs: the remains of a double-ring pattern, now so old and washed out that it has nearly faded away. This barred lenticular [[galaxy]] has an active Seyfert nucleus and belongs to Markarian’s Chain in the Virgo Cluster. William Herschel found it on 8 April 1784.
NGC4477.tagline: A barred galaxy in Markarian’s Chain with rings that have faded with age.

facts.text: In August 2011 Giancarlo Cortini and Stefano Antonellini found a luminous red nova here, AT 2011kp — the outburst thought to mark two stars spiralling together and merging.
facts.title: Two stars merge

story: NGC 4490 and its small companion, NGC 4485, have already had their closest brush and are now rushing apart. The encounter has set NGC 4490 ablaze with new stars, and a stream of stars and gas still links the pair, dotted with knots where hot blue stars are forming. It is one of the closest interacting pairs of galaxies to us, and even has a double nucleus. Halton Arp listed the two together as Arp 269.
William Herschel found NGC 4490, the Cocoon Galaxy, on 14 January 1788.
NGC4490.tagline: The Cocoon Galaxy and its small partner, rushing apart after a close encounter.

story: Is NGC 4494 a galaxy without dark matter? In X-rays it is surprisingly faint, nearly a hundred times dimmer than similar galaxies, which suggests it has little hot gas or dark matter. One team called it “naked”; others found a dark matter halo of unexpectedly low density. Another study put dark matter at about 60% of its mass. The argument goes on.
This [[elliptical-galaxy]] was probably built in a merger with a gas-rich galaxy: a neat, settled ring of dust circles its core. William Herschel found it in 1785.
NGC4494.tagline: A ‘naked’ galaxy? Astronomers still argue over how much dark matter it has.

facts.text: In 2018 a survey caught a “luminous red nova” here, AT 2018bwo. Such outbursts are thought to happen when two stars merge. Before the flare, the star at that spot was a yellow supergiant.
facts.title: Two stars become one?

story: Most spiral galaxies have a bright central hub. NGC 45 barely has one at all. It is a loose, dim [[spiral-galaxy]] with no clearly defined arms, its light spread so thinly that astronomers class it as a galaxy of low [[surface-brightness]]. New stars form here only slowly. It shares its patch of sky with the Sculptor Group of galaxies but most likely lies well behind it. John Herschel discovered it on 11 November 1835.
NGC45.tagline: A shy spiral with no bulge to speak of — and the scene of a possible stellar merger in 2018.

story: Tilt a spiral galaxy until you look along its disc and the arms vanish into a slim blade of light. NGC 4517 lies at nearly that angle, so we see it almost [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]]. William Herschel found this [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]] in 1784. It belongs to the Virgo II Groups, a chain of galaxy groups strung out from the southern edge of the Virgo Supercluster, and it carries a second catalogue number too: NGC 4437.
NGC4517.tagline: A spiral galaxy turned almost exactly side-on, so its whole disc shrinks to a thin streak.

discovered.note: Seen again in 1785 and catalogued a second time as NGC 4560

facts.text: Its core hides a black hole of roughly 450 million Suns. It was the first black hole weighed by measuring how molecular gas rotates around it with a radio interferometer — the CARMA array in California.
facts.title: A black hole weighed by its gas

facts.text: In March 1994 a carbon–oxygen white dwarf exploded here. It was caught about two weeks before peak brightness, and Hubble’s picture of it — a bright point beside the dusty disc — became a classic.
facts.title: Supernova 1994D

facts.text: The orbits of globular clusters in its outer halo suggest unusually little dark matter: less than half the mass out there seems to be the invisible kind.
facts.title: Light on dark matter

story: Lenticular galaxies sit between spirals and ellipticals: a disc and a bright bulge, but no real spiral arms. NGC 4526 is one of the brightest known, seen nearly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]] with a dark band of dust across its middle. It lies in the Virgo Cluster.
William Herschel found it on 13 April 1784, then observed it again in December 1785 — and so it entered the New General Catalogue twice, also as NGC 4560.
NGC4526.tagline: A dusty Virgo galaxy whose black hole was the first weighed by tracking the swirl of its molecular gas.

facts.text: Found by Stephen Knight on 13 April 1991, this white-dwarf explosion was brighter and stranger than a normal Type Ia. It has been studied so closely that similar events are now called “91T-like”.
facts.title: Supernova 1991T

facts.text: The first supernova seen here, in 1915, was found by Heber Curtis — who five years later argued in the Great Debate that spiral nebulae are galaxies like our own.
facts.title: Heber Curtis’s supernova

story: Deep in its centre, NGC 4527 hoards about 2.5 billion Suns’ worth of molecular hydrogen — the raw material of new stars. A burst of star formation has begun there, though it still seems to be in its earliest, gentle phase. William Herschel discovered this [[spiral-galaxy|spiral galaxy]] on 23 February 1784. It belongs to the M 61 Group, on the outskirts of the Virgo Cluster.
NGC4527.tagline: Host of Supernova 1991T, the overbright explosion that became the template for a whole class.

facts.text: Erik Holmberg listed it in 1937 as a double with NGC 4535A. The companion is actually about seven times farther away — the two only line up by chance.
facts.title: A pair that isn’t

story: Its light is spread so thinly that NGC 4535 has been nicknamed “the Lost Galaxy”: low [[surface-brightness]] lets it fade into the sky. Yet it is a handsome barred spiral, whose two inner arms branch into many as they wind outwards. William Herschel found it on 28 December 1785. It belongs to the Virgo Cluster.

In 1999 the Hubble Space Telescope picked out Cepheids here — [[variable-star|variable stars]] whose rhythm of brightening and fading reveals their true power. They gave a distance that matched other members of the cluster.
NGC4535.tagline: Faint enough to be called “the Lost Galaxy”, yet Hubble used its pulsing stars to measure its distance.

facts.text: Dmitry Tsvetkov found a Type Ia supernova here on 2 March 1981. It peaked at magnitude 12 six days later, then faded from view over the next two months.
facts.title: Supernova 1981B

story: A ring of intense star birth circles the bar at the heart of NGC 4536, marking it as an HII galaxy — one in the middle of a strong burst of star formation. It has no classical bulge, and X-rays from its core hint at a modest black hole of perhaps ten thousand to a million Suns. William Herschel discovered it on 24 January 1784. Though it lies about 10° south of the Virgo Cluster’s centre, it belongs instead to the M 61 Group.
NGC4536.tagline: A barred spiral with a ring of star birth at its heart, and a supernova that reached 12th magnitude.

facts.text: Rebecca Jones discovered SN 1941A here on 24 February 1941. Older photographs showed it had already been visible since 5 February.
facts.title: Rebecca Jones’s supernova

facts.text: NGC 4559 is an intermediate spiral, halfway between barred and unbarred, with a weak inner ring around its centre.
facts.title: Neither barred nor unbarred

story: A restless star in NGC 4559 keeps crying wolf. AT 2016blu, a luminous blue variable, was caught erupting in 2012, again in 2014, and then almost every year from 2016 to 2026. Each outburst looks like a supernova, yet the star survives.
Luminous blue variables are among the heaviest and most unstable stars known; Eta Carinae, in the Carina Nebula, is the most famous.
William Herschel discovered this [[spiral-galaxy]] on 11 April 1785. It belongs to the Coma I group of galaxies.
NGC4559.tagline: Home to a restless giant star that has erupted almost every year since 2016 — and survived each time.

facts.text: About 240 globular clusters orbit NGC 4565 — more than the Milky Way has.
facts.title: More clusters than ours

facts.text: Besides the Needle, it is called the Flying Saucer and Berenice’s Hair Clip, after its constellation, Coma Berenices — the hair of Queen Berenice.
facts.title: Berenice’s Hair Clip

facts.text: It lies close to the North Galactic Pole, so we see it by looking straight out of the Milky Way’s disc, through very little of our own galaxy’s dust.
facts.title: Looking out of our galaxy

story: More luminous than even the Andromeda Galaxy, NGC 4565 is a giant [[spiral-galaxy]] that we happen to see exactly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]]. That view hides its shape, so its centre long puzzled astronomers. Infrared studies with the Spitzer Space Telescope settled the question: NGC 4565 has a central bar, as the Milky Way does, with a pseudobulge inside it and an inner ring.

Its disc is gently warped, probably by tugs from its satellite galaxies. Radio maps made with LOFAR found a faint halo whose shape follows the warp, which is at least 130 million years old, and a bridge of hydrogen gas joining it to the small galaxy IC 3571 shows the two met recently in cosmic terms.
William Herschel discovered it on 6 April 1785.
NGC4565.tagline: A giant spiral brighter than Andromeda, seen perfectly side-on — with a bar hidden in its middle.

facts.text: The pair were long called the Siamese Twins because they look joined. In August 2020 NASA said it would stop using that name, as part of an effort to avoid discriminatory terms.
facts.title: A retired nickname

story: Two spiral galaxies overlap on the sky like a butterfly’s open wings: NGC 4567 is one, NGC 4568 the other. This is no chance alignment. Maps of their hydrogen gas show the pair are starting to collide, and stars are forming fastest where the two discs overlap. William Herschel discovered both in 1784. They belong to the Virgo Cluster.
NGC4567.tagline: One wing of the Butterfly — a spiral in the first stages of a slow collision with its neighbour.

facts.text: Four stellar explosions have been seen in the Butterfly pair since 1990. The first, SN 1990B, was found by Saul Perlmutter and Carlton Pennypacker; Perlmutter later shared a Nobel Prize for showing the universe’s expansion is speeding up.
facts.title: Four supernovae

story: The collision has only just begun. NGC 4568 and its partner NGC 4567 are still in an early phase of their encounter, their [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]] shapes largely intact. In about 500 million years they should coalesce into one [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxy]], a smooth ball of stars with no trace of the arms we see today. William Herschel found the pair in 1784.
NGC4568.tagline: The Butterfly’s other wing — destined to merge with NGC 4567 into a single elliptical galaxy.

facts.text: Placed beside Phi Cassiopeiae, the Sun would shine at only magnitude 17.3 — a target for large telescopes — while Phi Cassiopeiae itself can be seen with the naked eye.
facts.title: Our Sun at that distance

facts.text: The cluster’s next brightest star is V466 Cassiopeiae, a red supergiant that changes in brightness.
facts.title: A red supergiant too

story: Few clusters have collected as many nicknames as NGC 457. Observers call it the Owl Cluster, the E.T. Cluster after the film’s friendly alien, the Dragonfly, the Kachina Doll and the Phi Cassiopeiae Cluster. William Herschel discovered it and catalogued it as VII 42.

This [[open-cluster]] is young, about 21 million years old, and around 60 stars are known to be true members. The bright star Phi Cassiopeiae marks one of the ‘eyes’. Nobody is yet sure whether it belongs to the cluster. If it does, it would be one of the most luminous stars known, outshining even Rigel.
NGC457.tagline: A young star cluster with many names — and an ‘eye’ that may be one of the most luminous stars known.

story: A bright bar with a knot of light at each end dominates NGC 4596. It is a barred [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] — a disc galaxy without well-formed spiral arms — though two faint, diffuse arms do curl from the ends of the bar to form an inner ring before fading into the outer disc. William Herschel found it on 15 March 1784. It belongs to the Virgo Cluster, and its centre holds a supermassive black hole of about 78 million Suns.
NGC4596.tagline: A smooth disc galaxy crossed by a strong bar, with a black hole of 78 million Suns at its heart.

story: Imagine the Large Magellanic Cloud — the brightest of the Milky Way’s companion galaxies — lifted out of our neighbourhood and set down in Ursa Major. NGC 4605 is about the same size and gives out about the same amount of light. It is a dwarf barred spiral, and its family ties are uncertain: it may belong to the M 81 Group or to the M 101 Group. William Herschel found it in 1790.
NGC4605.tagline: A small barred spiral in Ursa Major, close in size and brightness to the Large Magellanic Cloud.

facts.text: One of its stars, BZ Crucis, is a variable Be star: a hot star rotating so rapidly that it throws off a disc of gas, which makes its light change.
facts.title: A spinning member

facts.text: The Coalsack in front of the cluster is part of the Emu in the Sky, traced in dark dust clouds along the Milky Way by Aboriginal Australians — the Coalsack forms the emu’s head.
facts.title: Head of the Emu

story: Despite its name, the Coalsack Cluster has nothing to do with the Coalsack. That famous dark cloud of dust lies in front; NGC 4609 sits far beyond it, and the two only line up by chance.

The cluster is about 83 million years old, so its stars were born while dinosaurs still walked the Earth — they would not die out for another 17 million years. It is a sparse [[open-cluster]]: only 33 probable members have been identified, with just one red giant among them. Its stars are slightly richer in iron than the Sun.
The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered it on 12 May 1826, while cataloguing the southern sky from New South Wales.
NGC4609.tagline: A cluster named after the Coalsack that actually lies far beyond it — born when dinosaurs still walked the Earth.

facts.text: In January 2021 the ATLAS survey caught a luminous red nova here, AT 2021biy — most likely from a pair of stars, the heavier 17 to 24 times the Sun’s mass. Its glow held on a plateau for 210 days, the longest yet seen.
facts.title: A record-breaking afterglow

facts.text: Its small companion, the dwarf elliptical NGC 4627, sits close by. Halton Arp listed the two in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies as an example of a double galaxy.
facts.title: A peculiar pair

story: At the heart of the Whale Galaxy, stars are being born and dying at a furious pace. So many massive stars have exploded as supernovae in its central starburst that together they are blowing gas right out of the galaxy’s disc. This superwind has wrapped the whole galaxy in a giant corona of hot gas that glows in X-rays.

Because we see this barred [[spiral-galaxy]] [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]], professional astronomers use it to study the gas and stars that live outside a galaxy’s flat plane — exactly where that wind is blowing.
William Herschel discovered it on 20 March 1787. Its slightly bent, wedge-like outline reminds some people of a herring, but the name that stuck is the Whale.
NGC4631.tagline: A whale-shaped galaxy blowing a hot wind out of its own disc, powered by countless exploding stars.

facts.text: NGC 4636 hosts far more globular clusters than other galaxies of its size that do not sit at the centre of a galaxy cluster.
facts.title: Crowded with globulars

story: Elliptical galaxies are supposed to be quiet: old stars, little gas, little dust. NGC 4636 breaks the pattern. It glows about 50 times more brightly in far-infrared light than its stars can explain — a sign of dust, probably swallowed in a recent merger with a gas-rich galaxy. At its centre, a cavity in the warm gas is ringed by a dense shell, most likely pushed outwards by its active black hole. William Herschel found it on 23 February 1784.
NGC4636.tagline: An elliptical galaxy whose active black hole has blown a hollow cavity in the gas at its centre.

facts.text: Most spirals in the Virgo Cluster have lost much of their hydrogen gas. NGC 4651, out on the cluster’s fringe, is still rich in it — the gas even reaches beyond its visible disc.
facts.title: Still rich in gas

story: Off one side of NGC 4651 sticks a faint shape like an open umbrella. It is made of streams of stars: the wreckage of a much smaller galaxy torn apart by NGC 4651’s gravity. That shape earned the [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]] its nickname and a place in Halton Arp’s Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, as Arp 189. Radio maps also show a clump of gas with a dwarf galaxy that may have been born in the same encounter. William Herschel found it on 30 December 1783.
NGC4651.tagline: A spiral holding an “umbrella” of stars — the torn remains of a smaller galaxy it pulled apart.

story: As NGC 4654 moves through the Virgo Cluster, the thin hot gas between the galaxies pushes against it like a headwind. Its hydrogen is squeezed on one side and drawn into a tail on the other. That alone cannot explain its lopsided spread of stars, though. Astronomers suggest it also brushed past its neighbour NGC 4639 about 500 million years ago. Despite the buffeting, it still makes stars at the usual rate for a [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]] of its type. William Herschel found it on 12 April 1784.
NGC4654.tagline: A Virgo spiral whose gas is being swept into a tail as it ploughs through the cluster.

facts.text: On 21 March 2005 astronomers found a luminous blue variable here — a rare, unstable and very massive star — caught in a “super-outburst”.
facts.title: A star in super-outburst

story: Most [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]] galaxies look like straight needles. NGC 4656 has a crook at one end, which has earned it the names Hockey Stick, Fish Hook and Crowbar; the bent end was catalogued separately as NGC 4657. The warp is thought to come from encounters with its neighbours NGC 4631, the Whale Galaxy, and NGC 4627. Together they form the NGC 4631 Group. William Herschel found it in 1787.
NGC4656.tagline: A galaxy bent into a hockey stick by a gravitational tussle with its neighbour, the Whale.

discovered.note: Recorded at a wrong position; seen again in 1786

story: William Herschel found this galaxy on 23 February 1784, but wrote down a position 10′ away, where there is nothing. Seeing it again on 30 April 1786, he recorded it correctly — and took it for a different nebula. John Herschel logged it too, in 1828. It ended up with three NGC numbers, 4624, 4664 and 4665, until John Dreyer noted in 1912 that they were all the same object. The galaxy itself has a bright bar, with two faint arms that curl into a ring around it.
NGC4664.tagline: One galaxy, three catalogue numbers — thanks to a misplaced position in William Herschel’s notes.

facts.text: In 2002 the Hubble Space Telescope photographed the Mice in detail. The same picture shows more than 3,000 far more distant galaxies scattered across the background.
facts.title: Hubble’s view

story: Two galaxies in the Coma Cluster are in the middle of a collision, and the pull of each on the other has drawn out long, thin tails of stars and gas. Those tails gave the pair its name: the Mice. They should keep colliding until they merge into one.
Their colours are odd too. One tail starts blue and ends yellowish — the reverse of the usual pattern in a spiral’s arms. William Herschel found the pair in 1785.
NGC4676.tagline: Two colliding galaxies trailing long tails of stars, like a pair of mice.

story: Many rich clusters of galaxies are ruled by one giant. In the Centaurus Cluster it is NGC 4696, the brightest member — a big [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxy]] surrounded by many smaller dwarf ellipticals. Like most giants of its kind, it is believed to hide a supermassive black hole at its centre. James Dunlop discovered it on 7 May 1826, while cataloguing the southern sky from Parramatta in New South Wales.
NGC4696.tagline: The brightest galaxy in the Centaurus Cluster, surrounded by a swarm of dwarf galaxies.

facts.text: The prolific Japanese supernova hunter Kōichi Itagaki discovered SN 2018imd in NGC 4697 on 14 November 2018 — a Type Ia supernova, the only one yet recorded here.
facts.title: Itagaki’s supernova

facts.text: Astronomers still disagree about how far away NGC 4697 is: different measurements vary by more than a factor of two.
facts.title: Uncertain distance

story: Three times since 1950, a total lunar eclipse and an [[occultation]] of this galaxy have happened together: the darkened Moon slid in front of NGC 4697 in April 1950, April 1996 and April 2015. The next time will be on 4 April 2080, seen from the Pacific Ocean, including Hawaii.

Behind that coincidence lies an [[elliptical-galaxy]] with a heavy heart. At its centre sits a black hole of about 130 million Suns, weighed by the ALMA telescope array, which tracked a disc of gas whirling around it.
William Herschel found NGC 4697 on 24 April 1784. It gives its name to a group of galaxies — one of many that together form a southern extension of the Virgo Supercluster.
NGC4697.tagline: A galaxy the eclipsed Moon keeps covering — in 1950, 1996 and 2015, and next in 2080.

facts.text: On 5 March 1948 Edwin Hubble himself discovered a supernova in NGC 4699 — the first of three seen here so far.
facts.title: Edwin Hubble’s supernova

facts.text: Supernova 1983K brightened from magnitude 17 to 14 in four days. Its changing spectrum suggested the star had been surrounded by a shell of material before it exploded.
facts.title: A star wrapped in a shell

story: Look into the bright centre of NGC 4699 and there is a second, smaller disc inside it, wound with its own tightly wrapped spiral arms. Around it lie a bar, a ring and many glowing clouds of star birth, while a faint, thick outer disc stretches far beyond. William Herschel found this [[spiral-galaxy|spiral galaxy]] in 1786. It belongs to the Virgo II Groups, an extension of the Virgo Cluster.
NGC4699.tagline: A galaxy with a smaller spiral disc tucked inside its bulge — and a supernova found by Edwin Hubble.

facts.text: In July 2016 an automated survey spotted a new point of light near NGC 4725 and flagged it as a possible supernova. It was the dwarf planet Makemake, drifting past far out in our own Solar System.
facts.title: Not a supernova

story: A single ring of star formation encircles the bar of NGC 4725, slightly off-centre and moving in non-circular paths. Look closer and there are two bars, one inside the other — a feature found in about a third of barred spirals. The galaxy is the brightest of the Coma I Group and is being disturbed by its neighbour NGC 4747, which trails a tidal plume towards it. William Herschel found it on 6 April 1785.
NGC4725.tagline: A ringed spiral where, in 2016, a would-be supernova turned out to be the dwarf planet Makemake.

facts.text: NGC 4753 has an estimated 1,070 or so globular clusters — roughly seven times as many as the Milky Way.
facts.title: A thousand globulars

story: Lanes of dust wind round and round the centre of NGC 4753, as if it had been wrapped in string. The favoured explanation is that this [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] swallowed a gas-rich dwarf galaxy. Over several orbits the debris smeared out into a disc, which twisted as it settled; it is thought to be half a billion to a billion years old. Studying the twist showed that most of the galaxy’s mass lies in a halo of dark matter. William Herschel found it on 22 February 1784.
NGC4753.tagline: A smooth galaxy wrapped in a twisted ribbon of dust — perhaps the remains of a swallowed dwarf.

story: Side by side on the sky, NGC 4754 and NGC 4762 make an odd couple: one a barred [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]], the other a lenticular seen [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]]. For all their closeness, the two are not thought to be interacting. Both belong to the Virgo Cluster. William Herschel found NGC 4754 on 15 March 1784.
NGC4754.tagline: Half of an odd couple in Virgo: a barred disc galaxy beside the edge-on NGC 4762.

discovered.note: Observed from the Cape of Good Hope in 1751–52

facts.text: Across the bar of the cluster’s A-shaped pattern, three stars in a row are nicknamed the traffic lights for their different colours. One is DU Crucis, a red supergiant; another, BU Crucis, is an eclipsing binary.
facts.title: The traffic lights

facts.text: DS Crucis, the brightest star in the cluster’s area, is probably not a member at all but a supergiant lying in the foreground.
facts.title: A bright outsider

facts.text: The Jewel Box’s distance is tricky to pin down, because the dark Coalsack Nebula nearby dims some of its light.
facts.title: Hard to measure

story: Fourteen million years ago — long after the dinosaurs, but before the first humans — a cloud of gas in Crux gave birth to the stars of the Jewel Box. That makes it one of the youngest known [[open-cluster|open clusters]]. Its brightest members are supergiants, among the most luminous stars in the Milky Way.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille found it in 1751–52 from the Cape of Good Hope, using a telescope only half an inch across. To the naked eye it looks like a hazy star, which is why it carries a star’s name, Kappa Crucis — but Lacaille was the first to see that it was a group of many stars.
John Herschel gave it its popular name, and between 1834 and 1838 he recorded the positions of just over 100 of its stars.
NGC4755.tagline: Young supergiants in Crux, named a jewel box by John Herschel for their contrasting colours.

story: Seen from the side, a galaxy hides its true shape. NGC 4762 was first taken for a barred spiral; astronomers now see four parts in it — a central bulge, a bar, a thick disc and an outer ring — making it a [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] viewed [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]]. Its disc is lopsided and warped. One idea is that it swallowed a smaller galaxy whose remains settled into the disc and reshaped it. Its centre is an active nucleus of the type astronomers call a LINER.
NGC4762.tagline: A disc galaxy seen side-on, its warped, lopsided disc perhaps the scar of an old merger.

story: Many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] drift apart within a few hundred million years. NGC 4815 has lasted about half a billion — close to the age of the Hyades in Taurus — and its heaviest stars have already swollen into red giants. Some 15 red giants are probable members, along with five blue stragglers: stars that look too young for the cluster, probably made when two stars merged or swapped material. John Herschel found it in 1834, from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC4815.tagline: A half-billion-year-old southern cluster, about the age of the Hyades, already home to red giants.

facts.text: Its orbit is so stretched that it carries the cluster close to the Galactic Centre. Repeated passes by the crowded central bulge have probably stripped away a large part of its original mass.
facts.title: A plunging orbit

facts.text: A 2012 survey found 19 RR Lyrae stars, six SX Phoenicis stars and two eclipsing binaries in NGC 4833 — a cluster full of stars that pulse or wink.
facts.title: A census of variables

story: Even among [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], NGC 4833 is old. After correcting for the dust that reddens its light, astronomers found evidence that it is around two billion years older than the globulars M 5 and M 92. It is massive and poor in heavy elements, and its stars show signs of more than one generation, born at different times.

Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille found it during his 1751–52 stay in South Africa and catalogued it in 1755. It took the larger telescopes of James Dunlop and John Herschel to resolve it into individual stars.
NGC4833.tagline: One of the galaxy’s elder clusters, on a plunging orbit that has probably cost it much of its mass.

story: Not every cluster has a famous story. NGC 4852 is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in the rich Milky Way fields of Centaurus — a family of stars born together from one cloud of gas and dust, still travelling through space as a group. Over time the tides of the Galaxy will pull them apart and scatter them among the field stars.
NGC4852.tagline: A modest family of sibling stars in the Milky Way star fields of Centaurus.

facts.text: SN 1976G was found by Miklós Lovas and, two days later, independently by Paul Wild in Switzerland. SN 2010eb, a Type Ia, was spotted in 2010 by the South African amateur Berto Monard.
facts.title: Two supernovae

story: Seen almost face-on, NGC 488 shows a pattern astronomers treat as a textbook case: many thin, tightly wound arms around a large, bright central bulge. It is considered a prototype of the multi-arm [[spiral-galaxy]]. Its very centre is a surprise: the nucleus is twice as rich in heavy elements as the bulge around it, chemically set apart from its surroundings.
William Herschel discovered it on 13 December 1784. It gives its name to a small, isolated group of at least seven galaxies.
NGC488.tagline: A model many-armed spiral, its tightly wound arms wrapped round a huge bulge.

facts.text: About 15,800 globular clusters orbit NGC 4889 — more than the 12,000 of the giant galaxy M 87, but only half as many as its neighbour NGC 4874.
facts.title: A swarm of star clusters

facts.text: Dreyer’s New General Catalogue of 1888 accidentally listed it twice, as NGC 4884 and NGC 4889. Later revisions caught the slip, and the second number stuck.
facts.title: Counted twice

facts.text: Charles Messier never listed it, though it is intrinsically bright and near some of his objects in the sky. In 1995 Patrick Moore made it number 35 in his Caldwell catalogue.
facts.title: Missed by Messier

story: At the core of NGC 4889 sits one of the most massive black holes on record: around 21 billion times the mass of the Sun by the best estimate, some 5,200 times heavier than the one at the centre of the Milky Way. Its event horizon alone may be two to twelve times as wide as the orbit of Pluto.

The galaxy around it is a supergiant [[elliptical-galaxy]], probably built from many smaller galaxies that merged. Its stars, nearly all old, swarm in random orbits rather than a neat spinning disc, which keeps it egg-shaped. It may once have blazed as a quasar; now its black hole is quiet, having apparently eaten everything within easy reach.
It shares the centre of the Coma Cluster, a swarm of some 2,000 galaxies, with its rival NGC 4874. William Herschel, helped by his sister Caroline, recorded it in 1785.
NGC4889.tagline: A supergiant galaxy at the heart of the Coma Cluster, hiding one of the heaviest black holes ever weighed.

facts.text: In 2023 ALMA found a mysterious point of radio light near the galaxy’s centre, named Punctum — Latin for ‘dot’. A 2025 paper said it most resembles a magnetar, though magnetars are usually much fainter at those wavelengths.
facts.title: Punctum

facts.text: ‘NGC 4945’ is the title of a song by Brett Domino, on the album Funk.
facts.title: A song of its own

story: Visible light cannot escape the dusty heart of NGC 4945, yet it holds one of the nearest active galactic nuclei to Earth. X-rays and infrared get through: in hard X-rays only NGC 4151 outshines it, and in 1979 astronomers picked up a powerful water maser — a natural microwave laser — from its centre.

The core is doubly busy. Beside the active nucleus a starburst is under way, and so many stars have exploded there that their winds have probably hollowed out a cone-shaped cavity. A hot wind carries away about 1.6 Suns’ worth of gas every year.

Seen exactly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]], NGC 4945 is thought to resemble our own Milky Way. It was the first galaxy beyond the Local Group whose halo stars could be picked out one by one — and that halo seems to turn the opposite way to the disc, a sign it was built from a swallowed galaxy about as massive as the Large Magellanic Cloud.
NGC4945.tagline: A Milky Way look-alike seen edge-on, with a dust-hidden active core, a starburst — and a song named after it.

story: John Herschel came across NGC 4976 on 31 March 1835, during his four-year survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. It is classed as a peculiar [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxy]] — a smooth, rounded swarm of stars, but with something in its shape or structure that departs from the textbook pattern.
NGC4976.tagline: A southern elliptical galaxy that doesn’t quite fit the standard mould.

facts.text: NGC 5005 and the nearby spiral NGC 5033 form a true physical pair. They tug on each other only weakly, and are not yet close enough to be pulled out of shape.
facts.title: A gentle partnership

facts.text: Claudio Bottari discovered SN 1996ai in NGC 5005 on 16 June 1996. It was a Type Ia supernova, the kind that comes from an exploding white dwarf.
facts.title: A 1996 supernova

story: Something in the heart of NGC 5005 is flickering. X-ray telescopes have found a point-like source of hard X-rays in its nucleus that varies in brightness — the signature of hot, squeezed gas swirling just outside a supermassive black hole.

That matters because of a long argument. NGC 5005 has a LINER nucleus, a type that glows with weakly ionised gas, and astronomers have debated for years what powers such cores: a feeding black hole, or bursts of star birth? In this [[spiral-galaxy]], at least, the X-rays show that a supermassive black hole is there.
William Herschel discovered NGC 5005 on 1 May 1785.
NGC5005.tagline: A dusty spiral whose flickering X-ray heart gives away a supermassive black hole.

facts.text: William Herschel found it on 14 March 1784. After checking it at a magnification of 240, he logged it as a cluster of extremely small stars, “beyond doubt”.
facts.title: “Beyond doubt”

facts.text: It holds ten RR Lyrae variable stars. Walter Baade found nine of them in 1928; Helen Sawyer Hogg added the tenth in 1946.
facts.title: Ten pulsing stars

story: Some of the Milky Way’s [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] were not born here, and NGC 5053 is a suspect. Its stars are poor in heavy elements — as late as 1995 it was thought the most metal-poor globular in the Galaxy — and their chemistry looks more like the Sagittarius Dwarf galaxy’s than our own halo’s. Together with its orbit, that suggests it was stripped from that dwarf.
It is a loose, low-mass cluster trailing a stream of debris, and it lies less than a degree from M 53 on the sky. A tidal bridge links the two, hinting at a past encounter.
NGC5053.tagline: A sparse, ancient star cluster that may have been stolen from another galaxy.
