story: In April 1996 a white dwarf in NGC 5061 blew itself apart. Reaching magnitude 13, SN 1996X was the brightest supernova of that year. One of its discoverers was Robert Evans, an Australian minister who found dozens of supernovae by eye, having memorised the look of hundreds of galaxies.
The galaxy itself is an [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical]] with a Seyfert nucleus — a compact, active core — and it heads a group of about ten galaxies. William Herschel found it on 28 March 1786.
NGC5061.tagline: An elliptical galaxy in Hydra that hosted the brightest supernova of 1996.

story: No supernova has yet been seen in NGC 5068, but in April 2020 the ATLAS survey caught something stranger: a luminous red nova. These outbursts are thought to happen when two stars in a close pair spiral together and merge, throwing off a cool, reddish glow brighter than an ordinary nova. The galaxy itself is a [[spiral-galaxy|barred spiral]] that we see face-on, discovered by William Herschel on 10 March 1785.
NGC5068.tagline: A face-on spiral where, in 2020, two stars probably merged in a flash of red light.

facts.text: In 1997 astronomers measured the motions of nine satellite galaxies around NGC 5084. Their result was the highest mass derived for any disc galaxy at the time.
facts.title: Weighed by its satellites

story: Seen almost exactly [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]], NGC 5084 doesn’t look like a record-holder. Yet this [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] is one of the largest and most massive in the Virgo Supercluster. Its disc spins at about 330 kilometres per second, and estimates of its mass start at around a trillion Suns. Large amounts of hydrogen gas along its warped disc suggest it has absorbed several smaller galaxies. William Herschel found it on 10 March 1785.
NGC5084.tagline: A heavyweight disc galaxy — one of the largest and most massive in the Virgo Supercluster.

story: Half a degree away on the sky lies the spiral NGC 5078, and the two are thought to be at the same distance — true neighbours, each roughly the size of the Milky Way. NGC 5101 is a [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]], a disc of stars without spiral arms, and both belong to the ten-strong NGC 5061 group. William Herschel found it on 28 March 1786. A supernova was seen here in 1986.
NGC5101.tagline: A disc galaxy in Hydra with a Milky Way-sized neighbour just half a degree away.

story: Its nickname, Iota’s Ghost, comes from the bright star Iota Centauri, which sits close to it on the sky. NGC 5102 is a [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] in the Centaurus A/M 83 Group — near enough that astronomers can gauge its distance from its brightest red giant stars, and catch single novae flaring up. The first confirmed one was found by the ATLAS survey on 5 June 2026. John Herschel discovered the galaxy on 21 April 1835.
NGC5102.tagline: Nicknamed Iota’s Ghost for the bright star beside it — and close enough to catch its novae.

facts.text: In July 2021 the Event Horizon Telescope — the network that photographed the black hole in M 87 — released a sharp radio image of Centaurus A’s jet as it leaves the black hole.
facts.title: A portrait of the jet

facts.text: The Australian amateur Robert Evans found SN 1986G in the dust lane on 3 May 1986. It showed that Type Ia supernovae are not all identical, and can differ in how they brighten and fade.
facts.title: A supernova that broke the mould

facts.text: In 2010, after years of observations, the Pierre Auger Observatory pointed to Centaurus A as a source of the highest-energy cosmic rays reaching Earth.
facts.title: Cosmic-ray suspect

facts.text: Some of its apparent globular clusters may be the stripped cores of galaxies it consumed. One, VHH81-01, seems to hold a black hole of around 800,000 Suns.
facts.title: Cores of eaten galaxies

story: In 1949 three radio astronomers in Australia — John Bolton, Bruce Slee and Gordon Stanley — traced a source of radio waves to NGC 5128, making it one of the first radio sources ever matched to another galaxy. Centaurus A is still the closest radio galaxy to Earth. Its power comes from a black hole of about 55 million Suns, which fires jets of particles; radio images taken a decade apart show the inner jet moving at about half the speed of light.

Five years after the radio discovery, Walter Baade and Rudolph Minkowski suggested that its odd look was the scar of a collision: a giant [[elliptical-galaxy]] swallowing a smaller spiral. Models still back the idea. Its dusty disc is busy making stars — Hubble found young blue stars along it, and over 100 star-forming regions have been counted.
James Dunlop discovered it on 29 April 1826 from his home in Parramatta, New South Wales.
NGC5128.tagline: The nearest radio galaxy: a cosmic collision with a black hole firing jets at half the speed of light.

story: A family of suns that started life together: that is the simple story of an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] like NGC 5138, in the southern Milky Way of Centaurus. Because its stars share one birthday and the same raw material, clusters like this let astronomers see how stars of different masses age at different speeds.
NGC5138.tagline: A family of stars that began life together, in the southern Milky Way of Centaurus.

discovered.note: Catalogued as a star by Ptolemy around AD 150; Halley first saw it was not a star

facts.text: In 2008 astronomers reported signs of a black hole of 40,000 Suns at its centre. Later work disputed it; a 2024 study of seven fast-moving stars argued for one of at least 8,200 Suns, but that too has been questioned.
facts.title: A black hole at the heart?

facts.text: Of all the globular clusters in the Local Group of galaxies, only Mayall II in the Andromeda Galaxy is brighter and more massive than Omega Centauri.
facts.title: Second only to Mayall II

facts.text: Ian Douglas’s 2012 novel Singularity builds its plot on Omega Centauri being a dwarf galaxy’s remains, and the Perry Rhodan spin-off series Atlan sends its hero there.
facts.title: In science fiction

story: For most of history, Omega Centauri was a star. Around AD 150 Ptolemy listed it in his Almagest as a star on the centaur’s back, and in 1603 Johann Bayer gave it a star’s Greek letter. Then in 1677 Edmond Halley, observing with a telescope from the island of Saint Helena, saw that it was no star at all. In 1826 James Dunlop recognised it as a ‘beautiful globe of stars’.

That globe holds some 10 million stars, about 4 million Suns’ worth of mass: the heaviest [[globular-cluster]] in the Milky Way. In the core, stars sit on average about forty times closer together than the Sun and its nearest neighbour. From a planet there, the night sky would be crowded with brilliant stars.

Unlike a typical globular, its stars span a range of ages and chemistry, which suggests that Omega Centauri is the leftover core of a small galaxy swallowed long ago. Kapteyn’s Star, one of the Sun’s near neighbours, is thought to have come from it.
NGC5139.tagline: Ten million stars that Ptolemy took for one — perhaps the heart of a galaxy the Milky Way swallowed.

story: Scattered along the southern Milky Way in Centaurus are dozens of small star clusters, and NGC 5168 is one of them: an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] of stars that formed together from the same cloud. Held only loosely by their shared gravity, its members will slowly drift apart and blend into the field of stars around them.
NGC5168.tagline: One of the many small star clusters scattered along the southern Milky Way in Centaurus.

facts.text: A very similar planetary nebula, N66, lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud — and it too has a Wolf-Rayet-type star at its heart.
facts.title: A twin in another galaxy

story: With its tangled S-shape, NGC 5189 looks more like a barred spiral galaxy than the cast-off shell of a star. Well into the 1960s it was taken for an ordinary [[emission-nebula|emission nebula]]; only in 1967 did Karl Henize, from its spectrum, call it “quasi-planetary”. Today it is classed as a [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]].

The S, with matching knots on opposite sides, long hinted that two stars were at work. The Southern African Large Telescope finally found the partner: a white dwarf circling the rare Wolf-Rayet-type central star every 4.04 days. Hubble images show the S is two dense clumps moving in opposite directions, perhaps thrown out in a recent outburst.
NGC5189.tagline: A dying star’s cloud twisted into an S, shaped by a hidden companion on a four-day orbit.

facts.text: In 2016 astronomers using NASA’s Chandra X-ray telescope reported two huge arcs of hot gas pushed out by the black hole at the centre of NGC 5195, sweeping cooler hydrogen ahead of them — one of the closest examples of a black hole blasting out gas this way.
facts.title: A black hole’s burps

story: Just behind the Whirlpool Galaxy, M 51, hangs a smaller partner, and it is no bystander. The pull of NGC 5195 has helped sharpen the Whirlpool’s famous [[spiral-galaxy|spiral arms]], while the encounter has left NGC 5195 itself so distorted that astronomers struggle to classify it at all. A dusty bridge joins the two; that dust is seen in silhouette against NGC 5195’s centre, which shows the smaller galaxy lies farther away.
Pierre Méchain, Charles Messier’s colleague, discovered it on 20 March 1781.
NGC5195.tagline: The Whirlpool’s small companion — its pull helped carve the famous spiral, and its black hole is burping gas.

story: Dwarf elliptical galaxies are among the most common in the universe, yet among the hardest to notice: small, dim swarms of mostly old stars. NGC 5206 is one of them, with a twist — it is strongly nucleated, with a dense, bright knot of stars packed into its centre. John Herschel found it in 1834, during his survey of the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC5206.tagline: A small, faint galaxy with a dense, bright knot of stars packed into its core.

facts.text: On 4 May 1985, during a total lunar eclipse, the darkened Moon passed in front of NGC 524 as seen from South Africa and Antarctica.
facts.title: Hidden by a red Moon

facts.text: SN 2000cx, a peculiar Type Ia supernova found here in July 2000, reached magnitude 13.1 — the brightest supernova seen anywhere that year.
facts.title: Brightest of the year

story: A lenticular galaxy is an in-between: it has a disc like a spiral’s, but little sign of arms. NGC 524 is one, yet deep in its bulge, gas traces a faint spiral pattern of its own. It is the largest [[galaxy]] in a small group that keeps company with NGC 488 and its neighbours. William Herschel discovered it on 4 September 1786.
NGC524.tagline: A smooth, lens-shaped galaxy that once slipped behind the eclipsed Moon.

story: Some spiral galaxies owe their sweeping arms to the pull of a passing neighbour. NGC 5247 seems to have managed alone: a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]] with no sign of disturbance by other galaxies. Its two main arms each wrap halfway round the centre, then split in two. We see it nearly face-on. William Herschel found it on 7 February 1785, and two supernovae from collapsing massive stars have been seen here since 2012.
NGC5247.tagline: A grand-design spiral that shaped its two great arms with no sign of a neighbour’s meddling.

facts.text: The distance to NGC 5248 is debated. Its redshift points to one figure, but 17 independent measurements place it much closer.
facts.title: How far away?

facts.text: Patrick Moore made it number 45 in his Caldwell catalogue of 1995. He used his own surname, Caldwell-Moore, because the letter M was already taken by Messier.
facts.title: Patrick Moore’s pick

story: Halfway between barred and unbarred, NGC 5248 is an intermediate [[spiral-galaxy]]: a compact disc of stars whose central bar is only weakly formed.

It gives its name to a small family of galaxies, the NGC 5248 Group. That group is one of the Virgo III groups, a chain of galaxy groups strung out to the east of the Virgo Supercluster — the vast gathering of galaxies whose outskirts also hold our own Local Group.
William Herschel discovered it on 15 April 1784, one of the many hundreds of galaxies he found in his systematic sweeps of the sky with home-built telescopes.
NGC5248.tagline: A spiral with only half a bar, in a family of galaxies strung out beside the Virgo Supercluster.

facts.text: In 1895 Williamina Fleming, one of Harvard’s women “computers”, found a supernova here that reached magnitude 8.
facts.title: Williamina Fleming’s supernova

facts.text: SN 1972E, found by Charles Kowal, peaked at magnitude 8.5. Of all the supernovae seen in the 20th century, only SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud appeared brighter.
facts.title: Runner-up of the century

story: Buried in a giant dust cloud at the heart of NGC 5253 is a newborn cluster of more than a million stars, up to 7,000 of them hot, massive O-type stars. It is only about 3 million years old, yet together its stars outshine a billion Suns. This small, irregular galaxy is a dwarf starburst, making stars at least ten times faster than comparable regions of the Milky Way. It belongs to the group around M 83. William Herschel found it on 15 March 1787.
NGC5253.tagline: A small galaxy that hosted two of the brightest supernovae of modern times, and hides a cluster of a million stars.

facts.text: One member, HD 119682, is a hot Be star that gives out X-rays, flickering within hours. By chance it appears inside the radio lobes of a supernova remnant in the same direction, to which it is unrelated.
facts.title: An X-ray star

story: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille swept up this cluster in 1751–52 from the Cape of Good Hope, during his pioneering survey of the southern sky, and listed it as Lacaille I.7. Four of its brighter stars line up in a striking row. NGC 5281 is a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]], about 45 million years old, and two of its brightest stars have already moved on from the steady middle age of their lives.
NGC5281.tagline: A young southern cluster first logged by Lacaille, with an X-ray-bright star among its members.

facts.text: The motions of stars in its core hint that it might host a black hole. If so, it weighs no more than about 6,000 Suns — less than one per cent of the cluster’s mass.
facts.title: A black hole, but a small one

facts.text: NGC 5286 may be associated with the Monoceros Ring, a long stream of stars that could itself be the shredded remains of another dwarf galaxy.
facts.title: Linked to a stream?

story: Long ago, a dwarf galaxy fell into the Milky Way and was torn apart. Astronomers call its scattered remains the Gaia Sausage, and NGC 5286 is thought to be one of the [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] it brought with it. Today the cluster circles through our galaxy’s halo.
At about 12.5 billion years old, it may be one of the oldest clusters in the Milky Way. Its stars were already ancient when the Sun was born.
The Scottish astronomer James Dunlop, working in Australia, discovered it and listed it in his catalogue of southern nebulae and clusters.
NGC5286.tagline: One of the Milky Way’s oldest clusters — and an immigrant, brought in by a dwarf galaxy that was torn apart.

story: At the centre of NGC 5315 is a star that has lost its hydrogen. It is a Wolf-Rayet-type star, class WC4, with a surface at around 76,000–79,000 kelvin, and its light sets the surrounding gas glowing. This [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]] is slightly oval, with a complex structure and a broken ring. Its chemistry holds a puzzle: no extra share of the heavy elements such stars usually forge late in life. One explanation is a companion star that cut that phase short. Ralph Copeland discovered it in 1883.
NGC5315.tagline: A small planetary nebula around a hydrogen-stripped star blazing at nearly 80,000 kelvin.

story: James Dunlop found NGC 5316 in 1826 while charting the southern sky from Parramatta. Some 570 probable members make up this [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in the Carina–Sagittarius Arm of the Milky Way. They are about 100 million years old, with almost exactly the Sun’s mix of chemical elements. The brightest star is the odd one out: it holds noticeably more barium than its siblings.
NGC5316.tagline: A hundred-million-year-old cluster in Centaurus whose brightest star is unusually rich in barium.

story: Inside NGC 5322 lie the remains of another galaxy. A flat disc of stars at its centre turns the opposite way to the rest of this [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxy]] — most likely all that is left of a gas-rich satellite it swallowed. A thin disc of dust, seen edge-on, crosses the core. The black hole there, of a few hundred million Suns, feeds quietly on gas and fires two symmetric radio jets out at right angles to that dust. William Herschel found the galaxy on 19 March 1790. It leads a small group of its own.
NGC5322.tagline: An elliptical galaxy with a disc of stars spinning the wrong way — the remains of a swallowed companion.

story: NGC 5363 holds about a hundred times more dust than its own ageing stars could have made. The clue to where it came from lies in faint shells of stars around the galaxy, the ripples left by a merger. This [[hubble-type|lenticular galaxy]] seems to have swallowed another galaxy, taking in its dust and gas, which then sparked a fresh round of star birth. At its centre is an active nucleus and a black hole of about 375 million Suns. William Herschel found it on 19 January 1784.
NGC5363.tagline: A smooth galaxy holding a hundred times too much dust — loot from a galaxy it swallowed.

story: On 7 May 1826 James Dunlop, mapping the southern sky from Parramatta, described this cluster as “a curiously curved line of small stars, of nearly equal magnitudes”. John Herschel later called it “a very coarse cluster”. NGC 5460 is a loose [[open-cluster|open cluster]], somewhere between about 110 and 160 million years old. Several of its stars are chemically peculiar, showing too little helium on their surfaces, and one may be rich in mercury and manganese.
NGC5460.tagline: A loose southern cluster that James Dunlop called “a curiously curved line of small stars”.

facts.text: It holds 97 blue stragglers, stars that look younger than their neighbours. It was the first globular where an eclipsing blue straggler was found, and in 2019 another was found with a hot white dwarf companion.
facts.title: Blue stragglers

facts.text: The cluster is home to V19, the brightest anomalous Cepheid known — a rare type of pulsating star.
facts.title: A record Cepheid

story: Over billions of years, the Milky Way’s tides have been pulling NGC 5466 apart. In 2006 astronomers found the evidence: a thin stream of stars torn from the cluster, stretching perhaps 45° to 60° across the sky. What remains is a loose [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], unusually thinly packed for its brightness, with stars about 12 billion years old and very little of the heavy elements later generations would gain. William Herschel found it on 17 May 1784.
NGC5466.tagline: An ancient, loosely packed globular cluster shedding a stream of stars 45° or more long.

facts.text: NGC 55 and the spiral NGC 300 probably form a pair bound by gravity. Long counted as members of the Sculptor Group, both now appear to lie in front of it.
facts.title: A partner in the south

facts.text: Robert Burnham called NGC 55 “one of the outstanding galaxies of the southern heavens”, likening it to a smaller version of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
facts.title: A southern showpiece

story: Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered this galaxy on 7 July 1826. NGC 55 is a barred [[spiral-galaxy]] of the Magellanic type, built along the lines of the Large Magellanic Cloud, and it holds about 20 billion suns’ worth of mass.

In September 1897 the famous New York comet hunter Lewis Swift, observing from Echo Mountain in California with a 16-inch refractor, spotted its faint eastern end and took it for a new find — even though John Herschel had already drawn it. That is how part of NGC 55 ended up with a second catalogue number, IC 1537.
NGC55.tagline: The String of Pearls — a southern galaxy that a famous comet hunter once mistook for a new discovery.

facts.text: Most star clusters break up within about 50 million years. NGC 559 has already held together dozens of times longer than that.
facts.title: A survivor

facts.text: When the stars of NGC 559 were born, some 1.8 billion years ago, life on Earth was still almost entirely microscopic.
facts.title: Older than it looks

story: Astronomer Stephen J. O’Meara looked at this cluster in Cassiopeia and saw a jewelled goblet in the instant before it vanishes, like a ghost. He named it the Ghost’s Goblet. The fading impression, he said, comes from the many faint stars at its centre — and from the cluster’s great age.

William Herschel discovered it in 1787, and Patrick Moore later included it as number 8 in his Caldwell catalogue. At about 1.8 billion years old, it is an elder among [[open-cluster|open clusters]], most of which break apart long before they reach such an age.
NGC559.tagline: The Ghost’s Goblet: an ancient star cluster that looks ready to vanish like a phantom’s cup.

story: Hot, blue B-type stars fill NGC 5606, marking it as a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]] — perhaps only a few million years old, though estimates range up to about 30 million. Data from the Gaia spacecraft show some of its stars already drifting off into the surrounding field, a process astronomers call “melting”. One member, HD 126357, is a Beta Cephei star that pulses in brightness. James Dunlop found the cluster on 8 May 1826, a short hop from Alpha Centauri on the sky.
NGC5606.tagline: A young cluster of hot blue stars near Alpha Centauri, already starting to “melt” into the field.

story: Some star clusters are born in pairs. NGC 5617 and its neighbour Trumpler 22 move through space at the same speed, share the same age and chemistry, and appear to be held together by gravity — a primordial binary cluster, formed side by side. Both are some 70 to 90 million years old, and in both the heaviest stars have settled towards the centre. James Dunlop found NGC 5617 on 8 May 1826, about a degree from Alpha Centauri.
NGC5617.tagline: Half of a true double cluster — born alongside its twin, Trumpler 22, and still bound to it.

story: Where was NGC 5634 born? For a while astronomers thought this [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]] came from the Sagittarius Dwarf, a small galaxy now being torn apart by the Milky Way. Newer work points elsewhere: it may have arrived with Gaia–Enceladus, a galaxy ours swallowed billions of years ago, or with the Helmi stream, another band of stars left by an ancient merger. Every candidate points the same way — it was probably born outside the Milky Way. William Herschel found it in 1785.
NGC5634.tagline: A distant globular cluster that probably formed in another galaxy — but which one is still debated.

facts.text: Stuart Parker, an amateur astronomer in New Zealand, found a Type Ia supernova here on 13 February 2013. It reached magnitude 11.3, the brightest supernova of that year.
facts.title: Supernova 2013aa

story: Two broad, symmetric arms make NGC 5643 a grand-design [[spiral-galaxy|spiral]], seen almost face-on. Its heart is active but hidden: a thick wall of gas and dust blocks our direct view of the nucleus, yet Hubble images show a V-shaped cone of glowing gas lit by the central black hole, lined up with a radio jet. Near the centre, an X-ray source thought to be a black hole of about 30 Suns outshines the core in X-rays. James Dunlop found the galaxy on 10 May 1826.
NGC5643.tagline: A face-on spiral with a hidden black hole, and the brightest supernova of 2013.

story: Among the nearly 300 stars of NGC 5662 is V Centauri, a Cepheid: a pulsating giant star that swells and shrinks in a steady rhythm. Because a Cepheid’s rhythm reveals its true brightness, one that belongs to a cluster is precious — the cluster helps calibrate the yardstick astronomers use to measure other galaxies. V Centauri sits far from the cluster’s centre but is still very likely a member. Nicolas Louis de Lacaille discovered this [[open-cluster|open cluster]] on 17 May 1752 from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC5662.tagline: A rich southern cluster with a pulsing Cepheid among its members — one of astronomy’s yardsticks.

facts.text: NGC 5694 sits just below the tail of a constellation that no longer exists: Noctua, the Owl, made from faint stars now divided among Libra, Hydra and Virgo.
facts.title: Under the Owl’s tail

facts.text: Astronomers have compared its odd chemistry with that of NGC 4372, a dust-dimmed globular in Musca with a similarly peculiar recipe.
facts.title: A chemical cousin

story: Born nearly 12 billion years ago, NGC 5694 is one of the oldest [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known in the Milky Way. It may not have been born in the Milky Way at all.

Its chemistry is highly peculiar. The share of so-called alpha elements, such as magnesium, in its stars sits at nearly solar levels — a recipe unlike that of the galaxy’s typical old globulars. Astronomers take it as a sign that NGC 5694 formed in another galaxy and was captured by the Milky Way later, an adopted member of our galaxy’s family of clusters.
William Herschel discovered it on 22 May 1784.
NGC5694.tagline: An ancient, remote cluster with a foreign chemistry — perhaps captured from another galaxy.

story: Circinus, the Compasses, is one of the small constellations Nicolas Louis de Lacaille invented to fill gaps in the southern sky, and the Milky Way runs right through it. NGC 5715 is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in that river of stars: a group of siblings formed from the same cloud of gas, still sharing a path around the Galaxy.
NGC5715.tagline: A small cluster in Circinus, the Compasses — one of Lacaille’s little southern constellations.

story: Most of the stars that seem to crowd around NGC 5749 are impostors: only about three in ten of the brighter ones in its area really belong. The true members make a sparse, young [[open-cluster|open cluster]] about 27 million years old, with a total mass of only some 21 Suns. Measurements of polarised starlight suggest a cloud of dust lies within it. James Dunlop found it in 1826.
NGC5749.tagline: A sparse young cluster in Lupus whose stars add up to only about 21 Suns.

facts.text: Two barium stars live here: giants enriched in barium, probably passed to them by a companion that is now a white dwarf. In 2013 that made NGC 5822 only the second cluster known to host them.
facts.title: Barium stars

story: Most open clusters scatter long before they reach a billion years. NGC 5822, at about 900 million, is still holding together — a rich [[open-cluster|open cluster]] of some 1,700 Suns’ worth of stars with almost exactly the Sun’s chemistry. The stars now leaving their long, steady middle age form a broader band than expected, probably because they spin at different speeds. Right beside it lies another cluster, NGC 5823, and the two may be related. John Herschel found it on 3 July 1836.
NGC5822.tagline: A 900-million-year-old cluster in Lupus, one of the few known to hold barium stars.

facts.text: Circinus is one of the constellations Lacaille created for the southern sky, many of them named after tools of science and art, such as the telescope, the microscope and the air pump.
facts.title: Instruments among the stars

facts.text: James Dunlop, a Scottish-born astronomer, catalogued hundreds of southern clusters and nebulae from Parramatta, and many of the Caldwell objects in the far south are his finds.
facts.title: A Scot in Australia

story: NGC 5823 refuses to stay inside the lines. It lies in Circinus but spills across the border into neighbouring Lupus — two constellations that could hardly be more different in age. Lupus, the Wolf, dates from antiquity and was listed by Ptolemy. Circinus, the drawing compass, was invented by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in the 1750s.
Like every [[open-cluster]], it is a family of stars born together from the same cloud of gas, which will slowly drift apart as the pull of the galaxy works on them.
James Dunlop discovered it in 1826, while cataloguing the southern sky from Parramatta in New South Wales.
NGC5823.tagline: A star cluster straddling the border between an ancient wolf and an 18th-century drawing compass.

discovered.note: Also found independently by John Herschel (1831) and E. E. Barnard (1882)

story: Three astronomers each thought they had discovered NGC 5824: James Dunlop in 1826, John Herschel in 1831 and E. E. Barnard in 1882. The cluster’s bigger story came much later. The Milky Way’s tides are stripping stars from this [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], and the Triangulum stellar stream, a faint band of stars in a distant part of the sky, is thought to be part of its leading tail. Its trailing tail has been traced across about 50° of sky.
NGC5824.tagline: A compact globular cluster whose lost stars may stretch across the sky as far as Triangulum.

story: [[elliptical-galaxy|Elliptical galaxies]] are smooth, rounded swarms of stars, with little of the gas and dust that spirals use to build new ones. NGC 584 is one of these, and gives its name to a small group that also includes NGC 596, NGC 600, NGC 615 and NGC 636. William Herschel found it on 10 September 1785. It was later catalogued a second time, so it also carries the name IC 1712.
NGC584.tagline: A smooth elliptical galaxy that ended up with two catalogue names.

facts.text: Hubble has found more than 1,200 globular clusters around NGC 5846. Seven of them shine in X-rays, among the brightest X-ray sources in the galaxy.
facts.title: Twelve hundred globulars

story: Hot, thin gas surrounds NGC 5846, glowing in X-rays. Near its centre, NASA’s Chandra telescope found two bubbles in that gas, filled with radio emission and edged with bright rims — the mark of outbursts from a black hole of about a billion Suns. Their push seems to be squeezing and cooling the gas into knots. This giant, round [[elliptical-galaxy|elliptical galaxy]] heads its own group of galaxies. William Herschel found it on 24 February 1786.
NGC5846.tagline: A giant elliptical whose billion-Sun black hole has blown bubbles in the hot gas around it.

story: A star less than a quarter of the Sun’s width, yet 830 times as bright, sits near the middle of NGC 5882 — though not quite at the centre. Around it, the layers it cast off form two shells: an inner oval full of bubble-like shapes, and a rounder outer shell expanding faster and studded with clumps. A faint glow reaches three times the size of the main [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]]. Its gas has the Sun’s chemistry except for twice the nitrogen. John Herschel found it on 2 July 1834, from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC5882.tagline: Two nested shells of glowing gas around a tiny star that shines 830 times brighter than the Sun.

story: Its stars hold less than one per cent of the Sun’s share of iron, but plenty of elements such as oxygen and magnesium, which massive stars forge quickly. That chemical fingerprint says NGC 5897 formed early, before the Milky Way had settled into a disc with spiral arms. It is a loose [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], thinly packed even at its centre, and some of its stars seem younger than the rest — a hint of more than one round of star birth. William Herschel found it in 1785.
NGC5897.tagline: A loose, ghostly globular cluster that formed before the Milky Way had a disc.

facts.text: NGC 5907 ULX-1 is a neutron star spinning once every 1.13 seconds, and speeding up. At its peak it shines more than 1,000 times brighter than the theoretical limit for such an object — one of the brightest X-ray sources of its kind.
facts.title: An overachieving neutron star

facts.text: It is also NGC 5906: in 1850 George Johnstone Stoney, Lord Rosse’s assistant, recorded the fainter strip beyond the dust lane as a separate object.
facts.title: Two numbers

story: Seen [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on]], NGC 5907 is a thin sliver of light — hence its names, the Splinter and the Knife Edge. For a long time it was the textbook example of a warped spiral living alone. Then faint loops of stars were found around it, the remains of a torn-apart dwarf galaxy whose pull may have bent the disc. Deeper images suggest a single, knee-shaped stream rather than the double loop first reported. William Herschel found the galaxy on 5 May 1788.
NGC5907.tagline: The Splinter Galaxy: a razor-thin spiral hosting one of the brightest neutron stars ever found.

story: James Dunlop found NGC 5925 in 1826, one of the many clusters he logged along the southern Milky Way. This [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Norma is thought to be around 316 million years old — old enough that its heaviest, most brilliant stars have long since burned out, leaving gentler, longer-lived suns behind.
NGC5925.tagline: A cluster in Norma some 300 million years old — its brightest stars long since gone.

story: Most [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] are made of stars nearly empty of heavy elements, relics of the Milky Way’s youth. NGC 5927 is different: it is relatively metal-rich, and may hold more than one generation of stars. Metal-rich globulars like it tend to belong to the inner Galaxy, formed from gas already enriched by earlier stars. James Dunlop found it in 1826, and John Herschel observed it in 1834.
NGC5927.tagline: A globular cluster unusually rich in heavy elements, perhaps holding more than one generation of stars.

story: Like every [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], NGC 5946 is a tight ball of ancient stars, born when the Milky Way was young and still circling the Galaxy’s centre billions of years later. It lies in Norma, towards the crowded inner regions of the Milky Way, and it carries a second catalogue number too: IC 4550.
NGC5946.tagline: An ancient ball of stars in Norma, catalogued twice — as NGC 5946 and as IC 4550.

story: NGC 5986 has had a hard life. Its irregular, highly eccentric orbit carries it through the inner halo of the Milky Way, and it seems to have lost some 60–80% of its original mass along the way. Even so it remains a relatively massive [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], with at least four or five distinct populations of stars, each with its own chemical make-up. James Dunlop discovered it on 10 May 1826; John Dreyer later called it “a remarkable object”.
NGC5986.tagline: A massive globular cluster that has lost most of the stars it was born with.

story: About 400 million years ago, a cloud in the Milky Way gave birth to the stars of NGC 5999. That makes this [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Norma more than three times the age of the Pleiades: its hottest, shortest-lived stars are gone, and the survivors are steadier suns. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.
NGC5999.tagline: A middle-aged cluster in Norma, more than three times as old as the Pleiades.

facts.text: Its brightest star, MQ Trianguli Australis, is a blue straggler — hotter and bluer than a star of the cluster’s age should be. Such stars are thought to have gained extra mass from a companion or a merger. It is the only one found here.
facts.title: A straggler in the family

facts.text: Seven of its stars are spectroscopic binaries: pairs so tight that no telescope can split them, revealed only by the to-and-fro shift of the lines in their light.
facts.title: Built in pairs

facts.text: To astronomers, every element heavier than helium is a “metal”. NGC 6025’s stars hold more of them than the Sun does — more, even, than the well-studied Hyades cluster in Taurus.
facts.title: Richer than the Hyades

story: A ruler-straight border runs right through this family of stars. When Eugène Delporte drew the official constellation boundaries for the International Astronomical Union, his line split NGC 6025 down the middle: its northern stars belong to Norma, its southern ones to Triangulum Australe. The stars, of course, never noticed.

They are a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]], born between 40 and 69 million years ago — around the time the dinosaurs died out, or a little later. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille found it in 1751, during his expedition to the Cape of Good Hope to chart the southern sky. Fittingly, half of it now lies in Norma, the carpenter’s square, one of the constellations Lacaille himself invented.
NGC6025.tagline: A young star cluster cut in two by a line on the sky — half in Norma, half in the Southern Triangle.

story: Its stars carry the same proportion of iron as the Sun — a sign that NGC 6031 formed from gas enriched much like the cloud our own Sun came from. This [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Norma is about 250 million years old, give or take a hundred million. James Dunlop found it in 1826.
NGC6031.tagline: A star cluster in Norma with essentially the Sun’s chemistry.

facts.text: It holds BMP J1613-5406, one of only a few planetary nebulae known to belong to a star cluster. Because the cluster’s age is known, astronomers can tell that the star which made it was unusually massive.
facts.title: A cluster’s planetary nebula

story: John Herschel called NGC 6067 “a most superbly rich and large cluster”, and the numbers bear him out: it is 15 to 20 times as rich as the Pleiades, at about the same age of roughly 100 million years. It lies in the Norma Star Cloud, in the Norma Arm of the Milky Way. Two of its members are Cepheids, [[variable-star|variable stars]] that pulse in brightness every 3.8 and 11.3 days. James Dunlop found the cluster in 1826.
NGC6067.tagline: A rich southern cluster with two Cepheids and a rare planetary nebula among its members.

facts.text: Leavitt found her rule using Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble applied it to Cepheids in the “spiral nebulae” and proved they are galaxies far beyond our own.
facts.title: A rule that measured the universe

facts.text: James Dunlop, a Scottish astronomer working at Parramatta near Sydney, recorded the cluster in 1826 while sweeping the southern sky for nebulae and star clusters.
facts.title: Found from Parramatta

story: At the heart of this cluster, one star breathes. S Normae is a Cepheid [[variable-star|variable]]: a yellow supergiant that swells and shrinks in a steady rhythm, brightening and fading every 9.75 days or so. Around it gather 40 or more fainter siblings, all born from the same cloud.

Cepheids matter because their rhythm gives away their true brightness. In 1912 Henrietta Swan Leavitt, one of Harvard’s women “computers”, showed that the slower a Cepheid pulses, the more luminous it really is. Compare that with how bright the star looks, and you know how far away it is.

That makes S Normae precious. Spectra show it moves through space together with the rest of the cluster, so it is a genuine member, not a chance passer-by. Its neighbours give an independent check on its distance — and Cepheids in clusters like this one are used to calibrate the yardstick that reaches out to other galaxies.
NGC6087.tagline: A star cluster with a heartbeat — its brightest member swells and fades like clockwork, every ten days.

facts.text: Apus means “footless”. The first bird-of-paradise skins to reach Europe had their feet removed, and people came to believe the birds never landed, spending their whole lives on the wing.
facts.title: A bird without feet

facts.text: Dunlop’s catalogue of southern nebulae and clusters, published in 1828, listed more than 600 objects. Its entries are still written with a Greek delta for Dunlop, so this cluster is Δ68.
facts.title: Δ68

story: Black holes are invisible, but they leave fingerprints. Astronomers studying NGC 6101 have concluded that this [[globular-cluster]] holds an unexpectedly large number of them — the crushed remains of its most massive stars, still lurking among the survivors.

Those survivors are among the oldest stars in the [[milky-way|Milky Way]], packed together into a ball that circles the galaxy farther from its centre than the Sun does. They have been orbiting together since long before the Sun and Earth existed.

James Dunlop found the cluster in 1826 from Parramatta, near Sydney, and listed it as number 68 in his catalogue of southern nebulae and clusters. It sits in Apus, the Bird of Paradise — a constellation that has only been on star maps since around 1600, when Dutch navigators brought home the southern stars.
NGC6101.tagline: An ancient star ball in the Bird of Paradise that may be hiding a crowd of black holes.

story: At around 870 million years old, NGC 6115 has outlasted most of its kind. Passing gas clouds and the Galaxy’s tides break up many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] long before they near a billion years, so this one is a survivor. John Herschel found it in 1834, in the southern constellation of Norma.
NGC6115.tagline: A cluster in Norma nearly 900 million years old — a survivor among its kind.

facts.text: Lacaille named 14 new southern constellations, most after tools of science and art: the telescope, the microscope, the air pump, the painter’s easel and the chemist’s furnace among them.
facts.title: A sky full of instruments

facts.text: From the Cape, Lacaille recorded the positions of nearly 10,000 southern stars. His great catalogue was published in 1763, a year after his death.
facts.title: Ten thousand stars

story: Picture a French abbé at the Cape of Good Hope in 1751, charting the southern stars night after night. Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille had come to map the sky that Europe could not see, and along the way he noted a few dozen fuzzy patches that were not single stars at all. NGC 6124 was one of them.

It is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Scorpius, a family of about 125 stars. Like every open cluster, its members were born together from a single cloud of gas and dust, so they share the same age and the same make-up. Over many millions of years the galaxy’s gravity will tug them apart, until they drift off as separate stars across the Milky Way — just as the Sun’s own birth siblings are thought to have done long ago.
NGC6124.tagline: A swarm of more than a hundred stars, first logged by a French abbé charting the southern sky from Africa.

discovered.note: Found again by James Dunlop in 1826

facts.text: On 20 September 2016 Argentinian amateur Victor Buso photographed NGC 613 just as a star in it was starting to explode, catching the birth of supernova SN 2016gkg. Hubble images taken earlier show the star before it died: probably a yellow supergiant.
facts.title: The luckiest picture

story: In 1912 a photograph showed what eyes had missed: NGC 613 is a spiral. Today we know it as a barred [[spiral-galaxy]], with a broad bar across its centre, dust lanes along the bar’s leading edges and new stars forming at its tips. Radio telescopes later found a strong source in its core, where a black hole of tens of millions of solar masses probably lies.
William Herschel discovered it on 9 December 1798, and James Dunlop found it again from Australia in 1826.
NGC613.tagline: A barred spiral where an amateur caught a star in the very first moments of exploding.

story: James Dunlop added NGC 6134 to his catalogue in 1826, one of hundreds of southern clusters and nebulae he recorded from Parramatta, near Sydney. It is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Norma, set against the dense star fields of the southern Milky Way: a family of stars born together, slowly going their separate ways.
NGC6134.tagline: A southern cluster from James Dunlop’s pioneering 1826 survey, set in the star fields of Norma.

story: Some [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] roam the outer halo of our Galaxy. NGC 6139 lives in the busy inner Milky Way, less than half as far from the Galactic centre as the Sun is. It is a compact, tightly packed ball of ancient stars in Scorpius. James Dunlop discovered it in 1826.
NGC6139.tagline: An ancient star cluster in Scorpius, orbiting deep in the inner Milky Way.

story: Just a degree from the bright cluster M 4 lies its fainter neighbour on the sky, NGC 6144. Between us and it drift the dusty clouds of the Rho Ophiuchi complex, which partly hide it. It is a loosely packed [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]], with an unusually low density of stars in its core, and it hosts a handful of X-ray sources. William Herschel found it in 1784.
NGC6144.tagline: A loose globular cluster seen through the dusty clouds of Rho Ophiuchi, a degree from M 4.

story: John Herschel found NGC 6152 in 1834, in his first year of mapping the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. It is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Norma, the Carpenter’s Square — one of the small constellations Nicolas Louis de Lacaille created in the 1750s to fill gaps in the southern sky.
NGC6152.tagline: A cluster in Norma, the Carpenter’s Square, found in John Herschel’s first year at the Cape.

facts.text: The nebula owes its nickname to its neighbours on the sky: it lies near the Fighting Dragons of Ara, the glowing cloud also known as NGC 6188.
facts.title: Why “Dragon’s Egg”?

facts.text: In 2024 astronomers found that HD 148937 is really two stars, one strangely young-looking and strongly magnetic. The best explanation: two stars merged in a violent event that also threw out the surrounding nebula.
facts.title: Born from a stellar merger

story: Look at the Dragon’s Egg and you might think of a dying Sun-like star puffing off its outer layers. It isn’t one. NGC 6164 is the northern lobe of a two-lobed [[emission-nebula|emission nebula]], blown out by HD 148937 — a young, hot O-type star of about 40 Suns, wrapped in a magnetic field. The same star sets the gas glowing. John Herschel found the nebula on 1 July 1834.
NGC6164.tagline: The northern half of the Dragon’s Egg — gas thrown off by a young, magnetic giant star.

facts.text: A 2024 study found that one of the two stars at the centre formed when two stars merged — and that the merger is what blew out these glowing lobes.
facts.title: A collision’s aftermath

story: NGC 6165 is the southern half of a matched pair of glowing lobes, with NGC 6164 to the north and a faint halo around both. At the centre sits the star that made them, HD 148937: only three to four million years old and some 40 times the Sun’s mass. The shape mimics a [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]], but this star is young and heavy, and it is expected to explode as a supernova within another three to four million years. John Herschel found the nebula in 1834.
NGC6165.tagline: The southern lobe of the Dragon’s Egg, around a star expected to explode in a few million years.

story: James Dunlop came across NGC 6167 in 1826, on one of the richest stretches of the southern Milky Way. Norma is crowded with [[open-cluster|open clusters]] because, in that direction, we look along spiral arms of our Galaxy where stars are still being born. NGC 6167 is one of those families of stars, travelling together around the Galaxy.
NGC6167.tagline: One of the many star clusters crowding Norma, where we look along the Milky Way’s spiral arms.

story: Is it a cluster at all? A 2013 catalogue listed NGC 6169 as a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]] about 32 million years old. But in 2020 a study using the Gaia spacecraft’s precise measurements of star positions and motions found that its stars are not physically linked — which would make it an [[asterism]], a chance grouping on the sky. It lies near the star Mu Normae. John Herschel recorded it in 1834.
NGC6169.tagline: A star cluster that may not be one at all — Gaia suggests its stars only line up by chance.

story: Scorpius is best known for its red heart, Antares, and its curling tail, but its southern reaches are scattered with star clusters set against the Milky Way. NGC 6178 is one of them: an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] of stars that share a birthplace and an age, still travelling together through the Galaxy.
NGC6178.tagline: A small family of sibling stars in the southern reaches of Scorpius.

facts.text: Nearby on the sky, the two-lobed nebula NGC 6164–6165 is nicknamed the Dragon’s Egg because it lies close to these Fighting Dragons.
facts.title: A dragon and its egg

story: Sculpted ridges of glowing gas give NGC 6188 its many names: the Rim Nebula, the Firebird and the Fighting Dragons of Ara. It is a stellar nursery, an [[emission-nebula|emission nebula]] shaped by massive young stars born inside it, some only a few million years old. The spark for this burst of star birth was probably an earlier generation of stars exploding as supernovae.
Beside it lies the bright young cluster NGC 6193, whose stars light part of the cloud as a [[reflection-nebula|reflection nebula]]. John Herschel found the nebula in 1836.
NGC6188.tagline: The Fighting Dragons of Ara — a star-forming cloud carved by the young stars it has just made.

story: Southern Scorpius holds a scatter of star clusters against the glow of the Milky Way, and NGC 6192 is one of them. Like every [[open-cluster|open cluster]], it is a group of stars born together from one cloud of gas, so they share an age and a chemical make-up and differ mainly in mass. That makes such clusters natural test beds for how stars live and age.
NGC6192.tagline: A cluster of sibling stars in the Milky Way fields of southern Scorpius.

facts.text: Photographs of the glowing gas next door, NGC 6188, show dark, twisting shapes that astrophotographers call the Fighting Dragons of Ara — clouds being sculpted by the cluster’s light and winds.
facts.title: Fighting Dragons

facts.text: Ara OB1 is an OB association: a loose gathering of hot, young O and B stars born around the same time. It spreads over about a square degree of sky — roughly five times the area of the full Moon.
facts.title: A family the size of five Moons

story: At the centre of NGC 6193 sit two systems of O-type stars — the hottest, most massive kind there is — almost touching on the sky. Around them blaze at least 20 more hot, blue-white B stars. Together they flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light, and the neighbouring cloud NGC 6188 glows in response.

This young [[open-cluster|open cluster]], nicknamed the Firebird, is the core of Ara OB1, a much larger, looser family of massive young stars spread across this part of the sky. Stars this heavy burn out in just a few million years, and the biggest are likely to end as supernovae.
James Dunlop recorded the cluster from Parramatta in 1826. Its constellation, Ara, is the Altar — in Greek myth, the altar on which the gods swore allegiance before their war against the Titans.
NGC6193.tagline: The Firebird Cluster: a nest of giant blue stars setting the clouds of the Altar aglow.

story: Lying almost on the midline of the Milky Way, NGC 6200 is an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Ara, the Altar. One of its stars is a Beta Cephei variable: a hot, massive blue star whose surface swells and shrinks every few hours, making its light pulse gently. John Herschel found the cluster in 1834.
NGC6200.tagline: A cluster in Ara, the Altar, with a star that pulses in brightness every few hours.

story: James Dunlop found NGC 6204 on 13 May 1826. It lies close to the galactic equator — the midline of the Milky Way’s disc — in Ara, which the ancient Greeks pictured as the altar where the gods swore their oath before battling the Titans. Like other [[open-cluster|open clusters]], its stars were born together and will slowly drift apart.
NGC6204.tagline: A star cluster on the midline of the Milky Way, in Ara, the altar of the gods.

story: Most [[open-cluster|open clusters]] never see their billionth birthday: passing clouds and the Galaxy’s tides scatter their stars long before. NGC 6208 has reached about 1.17 billion years, which makes it one of the oldest open clusters known. James Dunlop found it in 1826, in Ara.
NGC6208.tagline: One of the oldest known open clusters — still holding together after more than a billion years.

discovered.note: Recorded as a star by Joseph Lalande in 1799

facts.text: A faint halo nearly twice the size of the main nebula surrounds it, with four arm-like extensions and at least three faint, circular ripples within it.
facts.title: A rippling halo

story: Shells, lobes, knots and arches crowd NGC 6210, the Turtle. Astronomers count five different directions in which its central star has thrown out material, and those outflows have changed course sharply since the gas began to glow, around 3,500 years ago. So tangled a shape has led to the idea that three stars, passing material between them, sculpted this [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]].
It sits unusually high above the plane of the Milky Way. Joseph Lalande recorded it as a star in 1799; Wilhelm Struve recognised it as a nebula in 1825.
NGC6210.tagline: The Turtle: a dying star’s cloud whose outflows have swung in new directions again and again.

story: NGC 6216 is one of the many [[open-cluster|open clusters]] dotted along the southern Milky Way in Scorpius, in the direction of the inner Galaxy. Its stars are siblings, born from the same cloud at the same time. Over hundreds of millions of years, encounters with gas clouds and the pull of the Galaxy will loosen their hold on one another.
NGC6216.tagline: A family of stars in Scorpius, in the direction of the crowded inner Galaxy.

story: Hercules is home to two of the finest globular clusters in the sky, M 13 and M 92. NGC 6229 is the little-known third, fainter because it lies much farther out, in the remote halo of the Milky Way. Its stars come in two distinct generations, and it may be the surviving core of a small spheroidal galaxy that the Milky Way captured and stripped. William Herschel found this [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]] on 12 May 1787.
NGC6229.tagline: Hercules’s third globular — the remote one, possibly the core of a lost dwarf galaxy.

discovered.note: Recorded before 1654 as “Luminosae”; seen again by Halley in 1678

facts.text: Some call it the Northern Jewel Box, for its likeness to NGC 4755, the Jewel Box in Crux — even though it is itself a southern cluster, just a little less far south.
facts.title: The Northern Jewel Box

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy this patch is usually identified with Shengong, a dressing room — though older sources pin the name on faint stars nearby.
facts.title: A dressing room in the sky

facts.text: NGC 6231 was used to count how often B-type stars come in pairs: about half of them do. That is common, but not as common as among the even heavier O-type stars. The cluster also holds three rare Wolf–Rayet stars.
facts.title: Twins are common

story: Low in the curl of the Scorpion’s tail, a little knot of stars looks like the head of a comet, with a faint tail streaming northward. Observers call it the False Comet. The head is NGC 6231, a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]]; the tail is a trail of other young clusters, fanning out where the Prawn Nebula glows.

The stars in that head are babies, just 2 to 7 million years old, and some are giants. Zeta¹ Scorpii, part of the same wider family, is one of the most luminous stars known in our galaxy. Its naked-eye partner, Zeta², only looks brighter because it is a near neighbour of ours: the pairing is a trick of perspective.

Giovanni Battista Hodierna recorded the cluster before 1654, calling it Luminosae in a book published that year in Palermo. Edmond Halley found it again in 1678, and Lacaille saw it from the Cape in 1751–52.
NGC6231.tagline: The head of a false comet in Scorpius — a cluster of blazing young giants, among the most luminous stars known.

story: Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, is rich in [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]], because it looks towards the centre of the Milky Way, around which these ancient balls of stars swarm. NGC 6235 is one of them: a tight sphere of very old stars, born when the Galaxy was young and still orbiting its heart today.
NGC6235.tagline: One of the many ancient star balls in Ophiuchus, towards the centre of the Galaxy.

story: Racing away from NGC 6242 at about 112 kilometres per second is GRO J1655-40, a microquasar: a black hole feeding on a companion star and firing out jets. Its motion suggests it was born in this cluster and kicked out by a supernova explosion some 220,000 years ago. The [[open-cluster|open cluster]] itself is about 78 million years old. Nicolas Louis de Lacaille discovered it in 1752, from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC6242.tagline: A star cluster that may have flung a black hole into space in a supernova 220,000 years ago.

story: Stars are rarely born alone. Most form in groups inside great clouds of gas, and NGC 6249, in Scorpius, is one such group that has stayed together: an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] of siblings that share a birthday. In time the Galaxy’s pull will scatter them, as it scattered the cluster in which the Sun was probably born.
NGC6249.tagline: A group of sibling stars in Scorpius, still travelling together through the Galaxy.

story: At just 14 million years old, NGC 6250 is young enough that three of its seven hot B-type stars still light up nearby clouds of dust as [[reflection-nebula|reflection nebulae]]. It also holds some chemical oddities: two magnetic stars with peculiar surface chemistry, and two candidate Lambda Boötis stars, whose surfaces are strangely poor in heavy elements. John Herschel discovered it on 1 July 1834.
NGC6250.tagline: A young cluster whose hot blue stars still light up nearby wisps of dust.

story: In Ara, the Altar, lies NGC 6253, an [[open-cluster|open cluster]]. Its stars share one origin: they condensed from the same cloud of gas at the same time, and they still move through the Galaxy together, held by their combined gravity. Clusters like this act as clocks for astronomers, because all their stars began ageing at once.
NGC6253.tagline: A star cluster in Ara, the Altar — siblings still moving together through the Galaxy.

story: NGC 6259 appears twice in the New General Catalogue — it is also listed as NGC 6222, a reminder of how easily 19th-century observers could log the same object twice. Behind both numbers is a single [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Scorpius: a family of stars born together, still travelling as a group.
NGC6259.tagline: One cluster, two catalogue numbers: NGC 6259 is also listed as NGC 6222.

story: Scorpius lies towards the heart of our Galaxy, and the Milky Way there is thick with star clusters. NGC 6268 is one of them: an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] whose stars condensed together from a single cloud of gas and dust. Clusters like it help astronomers trace the spiral arms of the Milky Way, where new stars are still being made.
NGC6268.tagline: A cluster of stars that formed together from one cloud, in the rich Milky Way of Scorpius.

story: Charles Messier never listed it, and Patrick Moore left it out of his Caldwell catalogue too — yet NGC 6281 is the brightest star cluster in Scorpius missing from both the [[messier-catalog|Messier]] and [[caldwell-catalog|Caldwell]] lists. Informally it is called the Moth Wing Cluster. James Dunlop described it as a “curiously curved line of pretty bright stars, with many stars mixt”. All told, this [[open-cluster|open cluster]] holds about 214 Suns’ worth of stars.
NGC6281.tagline: The Moth Wing Cluster — the brightest cluster in Scorpius left off both the Messier and Caldwell lists.

facts.text: HD 194598, a metal-poor star relatively near the Sun, may be a recent runaway from NGC 6284 — a star thrown out of the cluster.
facts.title: A runaway?

story: Over billions of years, the heavier stars in a [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]] sink towards the middle, and the core can shrink into an extremely dense knot — a “core collapse”. In 2023 sharp Hubble images of NGC 6284 showed just such a steep spike of stars at its centre, and gave the first high-quality census of its stars’ colours and brightness. William Herschel found it on 22 May 1784.
NGC6284.tagline: A globular cluster whose core has collapsed into a dense, spiky knot of stars.

story: William Herschel was working through the rich skies of Ophiuchus in late May 1784, and on the 21st he found NGC 6287 — one of several [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] he swept up there within a few nights. Like its neighbours, it is a dense ball of very old stars orbiting the heart of the Milky Way.
NGC6287.tagline: One of several globular clusters William Herschel found in Ophiuchus in a single week of May 1784.

discovered.note: Once wrongly credited to Lewis Swift (1885)

story: For years some catalogues credited NGC 6293 to Lewis Swift, who was said to have found it in 1885. The records show otherwise: William Herschel had already logged it on 24 May 1784, as number 12 in his sixth class, reserved for rich, compressed clusters of stars. Like many [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] towards the centre of the Galaxy, its distance is still poorly known.
NGC6293.tagline: A globular cluster once credited to Lewis Swift — William Herschel had found it a century earlier.

story: At the centre of NGC 6300, gas falling towards a black hole heats up and pours out X-rays. That active core makes this barred [[spiral-galaxy|spiral galaxy]] a Seyfert galaxy, and its black hole is thought to be fairly modest — about 300,000 times the Sun’s mass, against the millions or billions found in many other galaxies. James Dunlop discovered it on 30 June 1826, from Parramatta in New South Wales.
NGC6300.tagline: A barred spiral in Ara with an X-ray-bright heart, fed by a central black hole.

facts.text: Its nuclear fires have gone out. The central star is predicted to fade by about one per cent every year as it cools towards a white dwarf.
facts.title: Fading by the year

facts.text: The nebula’s bright north-west lobe seems to have been blown out in an eruption about 1,900 years ago — roughly when Hadrian ruled Rome.
facts.title: An eruption in Roman times

facts.text: After astronauts repaired and upgraded Hubble in 2009, the Bug Nebula was among the first images released to show what the refreshed telescope could do.
facts.title: Hubble’s comeback picture

story: Two glowing wings burst from a dark, dusty waist. NGC 6302 — the Bug, or the Butterfly — is a [[planetary-nebula]] with one of the most complex shapes ever seen. At the tip of one wing, gas rushes outward at more than 600 kilometres per second: fast enough to cross from Earth to the Moon in about eleven minutes.

The star behind it all was once about five times the mass of the Sun. Having cast off most of itself, it is now a white dwarf in the making, with a surface hotter than 200,000 degrees — among the hottest stars known. For years it stayed hidden: it shines mostly in ultraviolet, and a thick belt of dust blocks the view. Hubble’s new Wide Field Camera 3 finally caught it in 2009.
That belt is strange stuff. It holds crystalline silicates, water ice and quartz — and perhaps carbonates, minerals that on Earth usually form in water, though that claim is still disputed.
NGC6302.tagline: A dying star so hot it hid from Hubble, wrapped in a dusty belt and flinging out wings of gas.

story: William Herschel found NGC 6304 in 1786 with his 18.5-inch reflector, whose mirror was made not of glass but of speculum, a polished alloy of copper and tin. This [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]] lies near the Milky Way’s central bulge, the crowded hub of old stars at the heart of our Galaxy.
NGC6304.tagline: A globular cluster near the Galaxy’s central bulge, found with Herschel’s metal-mirrored telescope.

facts.text: Wilhelm Tempel discovered it in 1876. He is best remembered for comets: one of his finds, Comet Tempel–Tuttle, is the parent of the Leonid meteor shower.
facts.title: Found by a comet hunter

story: Many [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebulae]] are round, or stretched along a single axis. NGC 6309 has two: two pairs of lobes point in different directions, wrapped inside a round outer shell that formed first. Together they give it a square-cut shape and its names, the Box Nebula and the Exclamation Mark Nebula. Its hot central star has a helium-rich atmosphere and shines about 1,800 times as brightly as the Sun.
NGC6309.tagline: A dying star that blew out two pairs of lobes, giving its nebula a square-cut, boxy look.

story: With a strong inner core of stars, NGC 6316 is one of the [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the direction of the Milky Way’s centre. It was long thought to be quite rich in heavy elements; newer studies find somewhat less, yet it still counts as a “metal-rich” globular, unlike the ancient, metal-poor clusters of the outer halo. William Herschel found it on 24 May 1784, the same night as NGC 6293.
NGC6316.tagline: A tightly cored globular in Ophiuchus, rich in heavy elements by the standards of its kind.

story: Every star in NGC 6322 began in the same cloud of gas, at the same moment in cosmic terms. Ever since, they have travelled together around the centre of the Milky Way — an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Scorpius that will slowly come apart as the Galaxy’s tides tug its members away one by one.
NGC6322.tagline: A family of stars in Scorpius that began together in one cloud and still travel as a group.

story: On 24 May 1835, John Herschel, observing from the Cape of Good Hope, came across NGC 6325 — 51 years to the day after his father William found NGC 6293 and NGC 6316 in the same patch of sky. It is a [[globular-cluster|globular cluster]] in Ophiuchus, a ball of ancient stars with a moderately concentrated core, in the direction of the Galaxy’s centre.
NGC6325.tagline: A globular cluster John Herschel found 51 years to the day after his father’s finds close by.

facts.text: In July 2025, marking three years of science, the James Webb Space Telescope looked inside one of the paw’s “toe beans”. It found smaller beans within, where veiled young stars are switching on — one has thrown out gas fast enough to drive a shockwave.
facts.title: Webb’s toe beans

story: Round, glowing pads of gas give NGC 6334 its name, the Cat’s Paw Nebula. Behind the playful look is a busy stellar nursery. Its dust hides clumps of gas up to 3,000 times the Sun’s mass, and X-rays reveal ten distinct young star clusters forming inside this [[emission-nebula|emission nebula]]. A thin filament links it to its neighbour NGC 6357; the two may be parts of one vast complex.
John Herschel discovered it on 7 June 1837, from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC6334.tagline: A paw print of glowing gas, where Webb found newborn stars inside the “toe beans”.

story: Most old [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] hide two or more generations of stars, the later ones built partly from material the first generation shed. NGC 6342 seems to be an exception. Its stars are rich in heavy elements for so ancient a cluster, yet they appear to have formed together, in a single burst.
William Herschel found it on 28 May 1786 — the same night he came across the globular cluster NGC 6440 and the planetary nebula NGC 6445.
NGC6342.tagline: A metal-rich globular cluster whose stars all seem to have been born in one go.

facts.text: Most globular clusters are poor in elements heavier than helium. NGC 6352 has more than most, a sign that the gas it formed from had already been enriched by earlier generations of stars.
facts.title: Old, but not pristine

facts.text: It travels close to the flat disc of the Milky Way, about half as far from the galaxy’s centre as the Sun is.
facts.title: An inner orbit

story: About 12.7 billion years ago, when the universe was still young, a great cloud of gas collapsed to make the stars of NGC 6352. Then, only about ten million years later, a second generation followed.

Astronomers can still tell the two populations apart, a reminder that a [[globular-cluster]] is not the simple, single-birth family it was once thought to be. By cosmic standards the gap between them is a blink: ten million years out of nearly thirteen billion is like three weeks in an 80-year human life.

Unusually for such an old cluster, its stars are relatively rich in heavier elements, and its orbit suggests it belongs to the galaxy’s bulge or disc rather than the distant halo. James Dunlop discovered it on 14 May 1826, from Parramatta in New South Wales.
NGC6352.tagline: Two generations of stars, born almost 13 billion years ago and only ten million years apart.

story: Deep in the bulge — the crowded, star-packed hub of the Milky Way — lies NGC 6355. William Herschel found it on 24 May 1784. For a time it was thought to be an [[open-cluster]], a loose family of stars; later work showed it to be a [[globular-cluster]], ancient and tightly bound.
It is also a core-collapse cluster. Over billions of years, close encounters between its stars let the heavier ones sink inward, squeezing its centre into an extremely dense knot.
NGC6355.tagline: A globular cluster in the Milky Way’s crowded hub, first mistaken for a looser kind of star cluster.

story: Little more than a degree from M 9 lies a neighbour that few observers visit. William Herschel found NGC 6356 on 18 June 1784. It is a compact [[globular-cluster]], its stars crowding ever more tightly towards the middle.

What sets it apart is its chemistry. Compared with most globular clusters, its stars carry a generous share of elements heavier than helium — the ash of earlier generations of stars, inherited from the gas the cluster formed from.
NGC6356.tagline: M 9’s quieter neighbour in Ophiuchus: a compact ball of ancient stars, rich in heavy elements.

facts.text: Pismis 24-1, in the nebula’s cluster Pismis 24, was once thought to be perhaps the most massive star known, close to 300 times the Sun’s mass. It turned out to be at least three stars — each still around 100 solar masses.
facts.title: Not quite the heaviest star

facts.text: Chandra’s X-ray images revealed two more young clusters beside Pismis 24, each with roughly 800 stars.
facts.title: Hidden crowds

facts.text: In 2013 a petition with 19,000 signatures asked for it to be renamed the “Madokami Nebula”, after an anime heroine it was said to resemble. The name did not stick.
facts.title: The rename that failed

story: Scientists working on the Midcourse Space Experiment looked at this cloud in infrared light and saw two pictures in one. The bright western part resembled a dove; the eastern part, a skull. They called it the War and Peace Nebula. Others know it as the Lobster Nebula.

Inside this [[emission-nebula|glowing cloud]] is one of the busiest sites of massive-star birth in our part of the Milky Way. Hot O-type stars blow bubbles in the gas, while young stars lie wrapped in expanding cocoons of gas. A thread of gas links it to the Cat’s Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, and the two may form one vast complex.
NGC6357.tagline: A star factory with a dove at one end and a skull at the other — home to some of the galaxy’s heaviest stars.

story: Far down in the southern sky, close to the border of Ara and Apus, NGC 6362 was first recorded by James Dunlop on 30 June 1826, from Parramatta in New South Wales. It is an irregularly shaped [[globular-cluster]], ancient like all its kind.

Among its old stars are a number of blue stragglers: stars hotter and bluer than any star of the cluster’s age ought to be. They are thought to form when two stars merge, or when one feeds on its partner and is rejuvenated.
NGC6362.tagline: A loose, ragged globular cluster far south in Ara, home to stars that refuse to look their age.

story: A [[globular-cluster]] is usually a tight ball of stars, but NGC 6366 is one of the loosest: it is rated XI on the Shapley–Sawyer scale, where XII is the most scattered. It is rich in heavy elements for its type, resembles M 71 and NGC 6342 in make-up, and its stars all seem to have formed at the same time.
Friedrich Winnecke found it on 12 April 1860. The German astronomer is best remembered for comets: Comet Pons–Winnecke carries his name.
NGC6366.tagline: One of the loosest globular clusters, found in 1860 by an astronomer better known for comets.

facts.text: On 15 June 2011 the Moon passed in front of the Little Ghost during a total lunar eclipse, as seen from north-east Africa, Arabia and South Asia.
facts.title: Swallowed by an eclipse

story: Round, faint and pale, it earns its name. William Herschel found the Little Ghost in 1784. It is a [[planetary-nebula]]: the outer layers of a dying star, cast off and now glowing in the light of the hot white dwarf left behind.

That central star is unusual. Its spectrum resembles an oxygen-rich Wolf–Rayet star, a sign of fierce winds and extreme heat, and Gaia data hint that it may have a companion. In Hubble’s portrait, glowing oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen are shown in blue, green and red.
NGC6369.tagline: A pale, ghostly ring in Ophiuchus — the cast-off shell of a dying star with an unusual heart.

story: Five of the seven brightest stars in NGC 637 change in brightness. This compact young [[open-cluster]], only 5 to 15 million years old, holds four β Cephei stars — hot, massive stars that pulse over a matter of hours — one of the highest counts known for any open cluster. William Herschel discovered it on 9 November 1787.
It also holds a puzzle. Plotted by colour and brightness, its stars show a gap along the main sequence, the band where ordinary stars lie, and missing data does not explain it.
NGC637.tagline: A young, compact cluster unusually rich in pulsating stars — and with a puzzling gap among its stars.

discovered.note: Also listed in the NGC as NGC 6383

story: Catalogues can blink. This cluster in Scorpius appears in the New General Catalogue twice — as NGC 6374 and as NGC 6383 — most likely through a clerical error. John Herschel was the first to record it.

It is a young [[open-cluster]], somewhere between 4 and 20 million years old, with stars still forming in the last few million years. Its brightest member, the hot O-type binary HD 159176, floods the region with ultraviolet light and makes the surrounding gas glow. It probably belongs to the same family of young stars, Sagittarius OB1, as NGC 6530 in the Lagoon Nebula and M 21.
NGC6374.tagline: A young cluster listed twice in the New General Catalogue, lit by a brilliant pair of hot stars.

facts.text: It was once proposed that NGC 6388 was captured from another galaxy. The chemistry of its stars says otherwise: it formed within the Milky Way.
facts.title: Born at home

facts.text: Chandra found 61 X-ray sources near its core. Five look like X-ray binaries, where a dead star pulls gas from a companion.
facts.title: X-ray nest

story: About two million suns’ worth of stars make NGC 6388 one of the most massive [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the Milky Way. They are some 11.5 billion years old. James Dunlop found it on 13 May 1826 with a nine-inch reflector; John Herschel was the first to resolve it into stars.

Its stars come in more than one population, and some shine brighter than expected. That once raised a tantalising idea: a black hole of intermediate mass at the centre. Later studies ruled out anything heavier than about 2,000 Suns, but a smaller one remains possible.
NGC6388.tagline: One of the Milky Way’s heaviest globular clusters — and a place astronomers have searched for a hidden black hole.

story: Every [[open-cluster]] begins as a family. Its stars condensed from the same cloud of gas at about the same time, so they share an age and a recipe. NGC 6396 is one such family in Scorpius, where the [[milky-way]] runs thick towards the galaxy’s centre. Like all open clusters it is only loosely bound: in time, passing clouds and the pull of the galaxy will scatter its members on their own paths.
NGC6396.tagline: A loose family of stars in Scorpius, where the Milky Way runs thick towards the galaxy’s centre.

facts.text: In 2006 Hubble found that the faintest stars in NGC 6397 suddenly run out. Below about 0.083 times the Sun’s mass, it seems, a ball of gas cannot ignite fusion in its core — and never becomes a true star.
facts.title: The smallest possible star

facts.text: Hubble’s deep pictures of NGC 6397 also caught many globular clusters belonging to galaxies far behind it — ancient star balls seen through another.
facts.title: Clusters behind the cluster

story: How old is the Milky Way? In 2004 astronomers turned to NGC 6397 for an answer. With the Very Large Telescope in Chile they measured beryllium in two of its stars — an element that slowly builds up in the galaxy, like sand in an hourglass. Adding the cluster’s own age gave an estimate for the whole galaxy: about 13.6 billion years, nearly as old as the universe itself.

Around 400,000 stars crowd into this [[globular-cluster]], and its core has collapsed into an extremely dense knot. In 2021 astronomers reported a hidden concentration of mass there, perhaps black holes. By 2022 the culprits looked more like hundreds of heavy white dwarfs, with essentially no black holes at all.
Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered the cluster in 1752, from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC6397.tagline: Ancient stars that helped date the Milky Way — and showed how small a star can be.

story: On 13 May 1826, at Parramatta in New South Wales, James Dunlop recorded the globular clusters NGC 6388 and NGC 6441 — and this loose [[open-cluster]] in Scorpius. Unlike those ancient, tightly packed balls of stars, NGC 6400 is a modest, open group, only weakly gathered towards its centre: the kind of cluster that slowly drifts apart over the ages.
NGC6400.tagline: Logged by James Dunlop on the same May night in 1826 as two great globular clusters.

facts.text: During the total lunar eclipse of 15 June 2011, the darkened Moon passed in front of NGC 6401 as seen from Europe, North Africa and south-west Asia. It will happen again during the eclipse of June 2076.
facts.title: Hidden by an eclipsed Moon

story: William Herschel found it in 1784 and filed it as a bright nebula. His son John came to the same verdict: their telescopes could not split the glow into stars. NGC 6401 is in fact a [[globular-cluster]] about 13 billion years old, orbiting in the bulge at the heart of the Milky Way.
It is massive enough that it may be trapped in the galaxy’s central bar. Seen from Earth it lies only a few degrees from the Galactic Centre, and thick dust reddens its light.
NGC6401.tagline: An ancient globular cluster near the galaxy’s centre, mistaken for a nebula by two Herschels.

story: Stars in an [[open-cluster]] are siblings. They formed together from one cloud of gas, so they are nearly the same age and made of the same mix of elements. That makes clusters such as NGC 6425 natural laboratories: by comparing their members, astronomers can see how stars of different masses age at different speeds. It lies in Scorpius, against the rich star fields near the heart of the [[milky-way]].
NGC6425.tagline: A small open cluster in Scorpius — a family of stars that shares a birthday.

facts.text: By 2022, thirteen pulsars had been found in NGC 6440 — spinning neutron stars, the collapsed cores of long-dead massive stars. The cluster is rich in X-ray sources too.
facts.title: A pulsar nest

story: Old star clusters are usually poor in elements heavier than helium, because they formed before many generations of stars had enriched the galaxy. NGC 6440 bucks the trend. It is one of the most metal-rich [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known, close to the Sun’s own mix, and lies towards the Milky Way’s central bulge.
William Herschel found it on 28 May 1786, the same night as the planetary nebula NGC 6445, which lies just to the north.
NGC6440.tagline: A globular cluster almost as rich in heavy elements as the Sun — and a nest of pulsars.

facts.text: It contains a planetary nebula, JaFu 2 — one of only four known inside the Milky Way’s globular clusters.
