facts.title: A rare guest

facts.text: At least four millisecond pulsars spin inside it. One, PSR J1750−37A, swings round a companion on a highly elongated orbit.
facts.title: Pulsars

facts.text: A 2021 study suggested that its core may hide an intermediate-mass black hole of up to about 13,000 times the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: A black hole at the core?

story: James Dunlop logged it on 13 May 1826 as “a small, well-defined rather bright nebula”. In fact NGC 6441 is one of the most massive and luminous [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] in the Milky Way, with some 1.6 million suns’ worth of stars, deep in the galaxy’s bulge.
It is also unusually busy with pulsating stars: dozens of RR Lyrae variables with oddly long periods, plus several Cepheids. Its giants hint at two or even three distinct generations of stars.
NGC6441.tagline: The Silver Nugget: a heavyweight globular cluster with pulsars, a planetary nebula and perhaps a black hole.

facts.text: NGC 6818, also in Sagittarius, goes by the same nickname. Both are planetary nebulae, so the name can cause confusion.
facts.title: Two Little Gems

story: A dying star does not always leave a neat ring. NGC 6445, also called the Box Nebula, has a bright inner ring with open lobes flaring out on either side: a bipolar [[planetary-nebula]], and one of the largest known.

Its gas is rich in helium and nitrogen, a sign that the star which shed it was more massive than most. William Herschel found it on 28 May 1786, the same night as the globular cluster NGC 6440, which lies just to the south.
NGC6445.tagline: A boxy planetary nebula, one of the largest known — and not the only Little Gem in the sky.

story: Look towards Scorpius and you are looking across the crowded, dusty disc of our galaxy, towards its centre. NGC 6451 is an [[open-cluster]] in that direction: a group of stars born together and still loosely held by their mutual gravity. Clusters like it orbit within the disc of the [[milky-way]], and over many millions of years they slowly dissolve into the general field of stars.
NGC6451.tagline: A modest star cluster in Scorpius, seen through the dusty plane of the Milky Way.

story: John Herschel found NGC 6453 on 8 June 1837, while observing from the Cape of Good Hope. It is a [[globular-cluster]] lying close to the Galactic Centre, so its light reaches us through thick clouds of dust that dim and muddle the view.
On the sky it sits at the edge of M 7, a bright open cluster far closer to us. The pairing is pure perspective: a nearby open cluster in front, a remote ball of ancient stars far behind.
NGC6453.tagline: A faint globular cluster near the galaxy’s centre, sitting on the sky beside the bright cluster M 7.

story: Sagittarius is where the [[milky-way]] is at its richest, because here we look towards the galaxy’s centre. Scattered across these star fields are many open clusters, and NGC 6469 is one of the quieter ones. Its stars were born together from a single cloud, and they still travel as a loose group — for now. Over time, the galaxy’s tides will pull the family apart.
NGC6469.tagline: A scattering of stars in Sagittarius, one of many clusters along the Milky Way’s brightest stretch.

story: Astronomers once counted NGC 6496 among the clusters of the Milky Way’s disc, but that has been questioned. It may instead belong to the halo, swinging through the galaxy on a steeply inclined orbit — as NGC 6624 and M 69 may also do.

It is a fairly metal-rich [[globular-cluster]], open and uncrowded for its kind. Few searches for variable stars have been made here; one, by Moe Abbas and Andrew Layden of Bowling Green State University, turned up thirteen.
NGC6496.tagline: A globular cluster that may not be what it first seemed: a halo wanderer on a steeply tilted orbit.

facts.text: Its one known satellite, KK 242, holds about three million suns’ worth of stars. It sits on the border between two kinds of dwarf galaxy: irregular and spheroidal.
facts.title: A single companion

story: Most galaxies live in groups and clusters. NGC 6503 lives on the edge of nothing. It sits at the border of the Local Void, a vast, nearly empty region of space, and may mark the far tip of a long chain of galaxies reaching out into it.

It is a dwarf [[spiral-galaxy]], tilted almost edge-on to us. A ring of young stars circles its centre, perhaps around a bar seen end-on, and its hydrogen gas spreads well beyond the visible disc. Arthur von Auwers found it on 22 July 1854.
NGC6503.tagline: A small spiral galaxy on the shore of the Local Void, one of the emptiest regions near us.

story: Stars are rarely born alone. Most form in groups inside great clouds of gas, and the Sun itself probably began life in a cluster that has long since dispersed. NGC 6507 is one such group in Sagittarius, an [[open-cluster]] still held together by its own gravity. In time it too will drift apart, its members scattering among the countless field stars of the [[milky-way]].
NGC6507.tagline: A little-known open cluster in Sagittarius — the kind of family most stars, perhaps even the Sun, start out in.

story: Ophiuchus is crowded with [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] — seven of them made it into Messier’s catalogue alone. NGC 6517 is one of the many that did not. Like the rest of its kind it is a dense ball of very old stars, held tightly by gravity, that formed early in the galaxy’s history and has been orbiting the Milky Way’s centre ever since.
NGC6517.tagline: An ancient globular cluster in Ophiuchus, a constellation unusually rich in them.

story: Beside NGC 6520 lies Barnard 86, the Ink Spot: a [[dark-nebula|dark cloud]] of dust silhouetted against the Large Sagittarius [[star-cloud|Star Cloud]]. The two look like partners, the cluster perhaps born from the cloud. But their speeds along our line of sight differ by about 30 kilometres per second, so they may simply be lined up by chance.

The cluster itself is a young [[open-cluster]]. Estimates put it at 150 to 190 million years old, though some of its hot blue stars suggest nearer 60 million. Together its members weigh a few hundred times as much as the Sun.
NGC6520.tagline: A young star cluster paired on the sky with a dark cloud called the Ink Spot — a pairing that may be chance.

facts.text: Twenty variable stars and six pulsars have been found among its members, and their chemistry shows later generations of stars polluted by earlier ones.
facts.title: A busy population

story: Thick dust usually hides the heart of our galaxy. Baade’s Window, named after the astronomer Walter Baade, is a rare patch where the veil thins and we can peer into the central bulge. NGC 6522 sits right in it. This [[globular-cluster]] may be the oldest star cluster in the Milky Way, more than 12 billion years old.

That means it formed some four billion years before the galaxy’s central bar appeared. For a while it may have been caught up in the bar; today it trails behind it on its orbit around the core. William Herschel found it on 24 June 1784.
NGC6522.tagline: Possibly the oldest star cluster in the Milky Way, seen through a rare clear window towards the galaxy’s core.

story: Two globular clusters share Baade’s Window, a rare clear gap in the dust towards the galaxy’s centre: NGC 6522 and, just to its south-west, NGC 6528. William Herschel found both in 1784.
NGC 6528 is unusually rich in heavy elements for a [[globular-cluster]]. Its chemistry closely matches that of NGC 6553, a few degrees away, which suggests the two were born in similar surroundings.
NGC6528.tagline: NGC 6522’s neighbour in Baade’s Window, and a chemical twin of the globular cluster NGC 6553.

discovered.note: Hodierna saw the nebulosity; Loys de Chéseaux saw the cluster in 1746

facts.text: Giovanni Battista Hodierna recorded the Lagoon’s glow before 1654. In 1746 Philippe Loys de Chéseaux saw only a cluster; a year later Guillaume Le Gentil realised it was both a cluster and a nebula.
facts.title: Cluster or nebula?

facts.text: By 2019, 652 stars had been confirmed as members of NGC 6530, out of more than 2,700 likely ones.
facts.title: A growing headcount

story: Most of the stars in NGC 6530 are babies. Star formation in this [[open-cluster]] began up to 15 million years ago, but the bulk of its members formed within the last one or two million years, near its centre. Hundreds are T Tauri stars: young suns still settling down, flickering as they draw in leftover gas.

The trigger may have been a collision. About four million years ago the cluster’s parent cloud seems to have ploughed into the plane of the galaxy, squeezing its gas into stars. Now the young family may be coming apart, spreading out to the north and south.
NGC6530.tagline: The newborn star cluster inside the Lagoon Nebula — most of its stars only a million or two years old.

discovered.note: Long credited to John Russell Hind (1852)

facts.text: Most globular clusters contain RR Lyrae stars, which pulse in brightness in less than a day. NGC 6535 has none that are known — one of several quirks of this little cluster.
facts.title: Missing pulsators

story: History books credit John Russell Hind with finding NGC 6535, in 1852. But the historian Wolfgang Steinicke uncovered evidence that William Herschel saw it on 24 August 1780 — making it possibly his first discovery of all, months before he found Uranus.

It is a small, sparse [[globular-cluster]], about 12.75 billion years old and light for its kind, yet it holds more than one generation of stars. It is also unusually heavy for the little light it gives out, and some astronomers suspect a black hole at its centre.
NGC6535.tagline: A small, sparse globular cluster that may have been William Herschel’s very first discovery.

facts.text: The lobes are expanding so fast that they reached their present size in only about 3,700 years — a blink in the life of a star.
facts.title: Young lobes

story: At the heart of the Red Spider lies one of the hottest white dwarfs known. Its surface is probably at 150,000 to 250,000 degrees, and perhaps far hotter. It drives a wind at about 300 kilometres per second, and where that wind slams into slower gas it raises colossal rippling waves. Those shocks shape the nebula’s lobes into the spider’s form.

Edward Pickering found this [[planetary-nebula]] on 15 July 1882. Hubble and JWST have since found hot dust close to the central star, and the S-shaped twist of the lobes hints that a smaller companion star is stirring things up.
NGC6537.tagline: The Red Spider: a dying star so hot and fierce that its winds raise colossal waves in the surrounding gas.

story: A great cloud of dust lies between us and NGC 6539, reddening and dimming its light. Behind it, in the outer reaches of the Milky Way’s bulge, sits a [[globular-cluster]] richer in heavy elements than most of its kind.

The Danish astronomer Theodor Brorsen found it in 1856; he is better known for comets, several of which bear his name. In 1990 astronomers discovered a millisecond pulsar here — the collapsed core of a dead star, spinning hundreds of times a second.
NGC6539.tagline: A dust-veiled globular cluster in Serpens, found by a comet hunter and home to a millisecond pulsar.

facts.text: Oddly, the middle of the cluster looks less reddened by dust than its edges. One explanation: two layers of dust lie between us and NGC 654, with a third behind it.
facts.title: Through layers of dust

story: At the centre of NGC 654 shines a yellowish supergiant, a huge evolved star that may or may not belong to the cluster around it. The cluster itself is very young, about 15 million years old, though its stars seem to have formed over a spread of at least 20 million years. Among its 80 or so members are three Be stars.

NGC 654 is thought to be part of Cassiopeia OB8, a loose family of clusters and supergiants of similar age in the Perseus Arm, together with M 103, NGC 659 and NGC 663. William Herschel discovered it in 1787.
NGC654.tagline: A young cluster around a yellow supergiant, seen through three veils of dust.

story: William Herschel swept it up on 24 May 1784 with his 18.7-inch telescope and noted it as “pretty faint, not large, crookedly extended, easily resolvable”. For a long time NGC 6540 was thought to be an [[open-cluster]]. Only later was it recognised as a [[globular-cluster]], an ancient ball of stars.
It lies close to the Galactic Centre on the sky, in Sagittarius. Among its stars is a peculiar X-ray source whose nature is still uncertain.
NGC6540.tagline: William Herschel called it “crookedly extended”. It was long taken for an open cluster — it is a globular.

discovered.note: Found independently by James Dunlop the same year

facts.text: Cacciatore smuggled his name into the sky. Two stars in Delphinus are called Sualocin and Rotanev — read them backwards and you get Nicolaus Venator, the Latin form of Niccolò Cacciatore.
facts.title: A name written backwards

facts.text: Cacciatore worked at Palermo under Giuseppe Piazzi, who in 1801 discovered Ceres — the first asteroid, now counted as a dwarf planet.
facts.title: Piazzi’s assistant

facts.text: The cluster also hosts three W Ursae Majoris stars — pairs so close that they touch, sharing one outer envelope — and nine rapidly pulsing SX Phoenicis stars.
facts.title: Stars that touch

story: On 19 March 1826, at the Palermo Observatory in Sicily, Niccolò Cacciatore spotted a round glow in the southern constellation of Corona Australis. Three and a half months later, on the other side of the world, James Dunlop found it again independently from Australia.

The glow is a [[globular-cluster]] holding more than half a million times the Sun’s mass, around 12.9 billion years old. It orbits deep in the crowded inner regions of the Milky Way, and its core is thought to have collapsed into a tight, dense knot. It is also one of the most metal-poor clusters near the galaxy’s centre: its stars contain very little besides hydrogen and helium.
Among its residents are 94 blue stragglers — stars that look too young for their age, probably rejuvenated by stealing mass from a companion or by merging with it.
NGC6541.tagline: A star city nearly 13 billion years old, found by a Sicilian astronomer who hid his own name among the stars.

facts.text: The Cat’s Eye lies almost exactly at the north ecliptic pole, the point straight “above” the plane of Earth’s orbit. The celestial pole slowly wanders, but this one barely moves, so the nebula will mark it for all of human history.
facts.title: Marking the ecliptic pole

facts.text: In 2001 the Chandra X-ray Observatory found gas inside the nebula at about 1.7 million degrees, heated where the star’s fast wind slams into material it shed earlier.
facts.title: A million-degree bubble

facts.text: Measuring how fast the nebula grows between Hubble images suggests its bright inner part is no more than about a thousand years old.
facts.title: Young, by nebula standards

story: On 29 August 1864, William Huggins, an English amateur with an observatory at his London home, pointed a spectroscope at the Cat’s Eye. Starlight would have spread into a continuous rainbow. Instead he saw just a few bright lines — the signature of glowing gas. For the first time, a [[planetary-nebula]] had been shown to be a cloud of luminous gas, not a swarm of stars.

Today we know what Huggins was looking at. A dying star has been shedding its outer layers in shells, and Hubble’s images reveal knots, jets, bubbles and a dartboard of rings around it. The star is still losing around twenty trillion tonnes of material every second, carried off on a wind racing at about 1,900 kilometres per second.
William Herschel discovered the nebula on 15 February 1786.
NGC6543.tagline: The nebula that proved some nebulae are pure glowing gas — and marks the pole of Earth’s orbit.

facts.text: In 1999 a millisecond pulsar, PSR J1807−2459, was discovered in the cluster, locked in orbit with a companion star.
facts.title: A pulsar with a partner

story: Just south-east of the Lagoon Nebula lies one of the smaller [[globular-cluster|globular clusters]] known, and one of the closest to the plane of the Milky Way. William Herschel found NGC 6544 in 1784.

Its orbit is a puzzle. It circles the galaxy in the same direction as most stars, but on an unusual path and moving fast across our sky, and nobody is sure whether it was born here or captured. In 2021 a faint cluster, VVV CL160, was found with a similar position, chemistry and motion — perhaps a travelling companion.
NGC6544.tagline: A tiny globular cluster beside the Lagoon Nebula, perhaps travelling with a newly found companion.

story: An [[open-cluster]] is a clock. Its stars were all born at about the same time, but the most massive burn through their fuel fastest and are the first to die. By finding the heaviest stars still shining, astronomers can tell how old a cluster is. NGC 6546, a little-studied group in Sagittarius, keeps time this way like any other, against the crowded star fields of the [[milky-way]].
NGC6546.tagline: A little-studied star cluster in Sagittarius — and, like every open cluster, a clock.

story: Just over a degree from the Lagoon Nebula lies NGC 6553, a [[globular-cluster]] that breaks the usual pattern. Most such clusters are poor in heavy elements; this one is relatively rich in them, and its stars are loosely spread even at the centre.

It also formed in at least two episodes. Stars from the different generations carry different amounts of sodium and aluminium, chemical fingerprints of that drawn-out history. In make-up it closely resembles NGC 6528, a hint that the two were born in similar surroundings.
NGC6553.tagline: A loose, metal-rich globular cluster near the Lagoon, built in more than one burst of star birth.

story: Close to Alnasl, the star at the tip of the Teapot’s spout in Sagittarius, lies a [[globular-cluster]] that rarely gets a second look. NGC 6558 is an ancient swarm of stars in the direction of the galaxy’s centre, where it shares the sky with dense star clouds and drifting dust. John Herschel found it on 3 August 1834, while charting the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope.
NGC6558.tagline: A small, rarely visited globular cluster near the spout of the Sagittarius Teapot.

story: We live inside the Milky Way, so we cannot see its shape from outside. Open clusters help. They are found in the galaxy’s disc and trace its spiral arms, so by measuring where they lie, astronomers can sketch the structure of our home. NGC 6568 is one of these markers, a loose [[open-cluster]] in Sagittarius, its stars born together from a single cloud of gas.
NGC6568.tagline: One of the many open clusters strewn through Sagittarius — the markers astronomers use to map our galaxy.

story: Sagittarius holds more globular clusters than any other constellation, and for good reason: these ancient swarms gather around the centre of the Milky Way, which lies in this direction. NGC 6569 is one of the crowd, a [[globular-cluster]] that sits close on the sky to its fellow globular NGC 6558. William Herschel found it in 1784.
NGC6569.tagline: One of the many ancient globular clusters crowding Sagittarius, towards the heart of the galaxy.

facts.text: The central star burns at about 68,000 degrees and shines some 5,700 times brighter than the Sun.
facts.title: The star at its heart

story: Blue Racquetball, Emerald Nebula, Green Nebula, Turquoise Orb: every one of its nicknames is about colour. Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve found NGC 6572 in 1825.

It is a young [[planetary-nebula]]. Its star began shedding gas only a few thousand years ago, so the shell is still dense and bright. That gas is racing outward at about 15 kilometres per second, and as it thins, the nebula will dim. Inside are two lobed shells, slightly out of line, with a ring of gas round the waist.
NGC6572.tagline: The Emerald Nebula: a young, bright planetary nebula that has only just begun to fade.

story: The colours of a cluster’s stars tell its age. Young clusters sparkle with hot blue-white stars; those massive stars die young, so older clusters glow with yellow and orange suns instead. NGC 6583 is a small [[open-cluster]] in Sagittarius, one of many strewn along the [[milky-way]] towards the galaxy’s centre, its stars bound loosely together since birth.
NGC6583.tagline: A small open cluster in Sagittarius, whose star colours, like any cluster’s, record its age.

story: Watch NGC 6584 for a few nights and many of its stars would brighten and fade. It holds at least 69 [[variable-star|variable stars]], most of them RR Lyrae stars that pulse in a rhythm of less than a day. Astronomers prize such stars as yardsticks, because their true brightness is known.

It is an old, metal-poor [[globular-cluster]] in the faint southern constellation Telescopium. Like others of its kind, its stars are rich in elements such as oxygen and magnesium compared with iron — a sign of gas enriched early on by exploding massive stars.
NGC6584.tagline: A far-southern globular cluster in Telescopium, alive with dozens of pulsating stars.

story: On 28 August 1867 Truman Safford found a faint glow in Sagittarius. As a child he had been famous for working out enormous sums in his head; as an adult he became a professional astronomer. NGC 6589 is a [[reflection-nebula]]: dust that shines by scattering the light of nearby stars, which gives such clouds their bluish tint.
It has a near twin, the similar nebula NGC 6590, and the pair lie beside the red glow of the emission nebula IC 1284. Edward Barnard listed it again in 1905, so it is also IC 4690.
NGC6589.tagline: A small blue cloud in Sagittarius, first spotted by a man once famous as a boy for doing sums in his head.

story: Caroline Herschel discovered NGC 659 in 1783. Her brother William later described it as “a beautiful cluster of pretty large stars … considerably rich”. Today it is sometimes called the Yin-Yang Cluster.

It sits almost next to NGC 663 on the sky, and the two are probably related: both are counted among the young clusters of the Cassiopeia OB8 association, alongside M 103 and NGC 654. An [[open-cluster]] like this is a family of stars born together, slowly drifting apart.
NGC659.tagline: The Yin-Yang Cluster: a Caroline Herschel find that her brother called “a beautiful cluster”.

discovered.note: Found again by Lewis Swift (1885) and Edward Barnard (1905)

story: Some objects are hard to keep track of. John Herschel found this [[reflection-nebula]] on 14 July 1830. Lewis Swift found it again on 12 July 1885, and Edward Barnard a third time in August 1905. Along the way it gathered three catalogue numbers: NGC 6590, NGC 6595 and IC 4700.

It is a cloud of dust lit by nearby stars, scattering their light like haze around a streetlamp. With its neighbour NGC 6589 it sits beside IC 1284, where hydrogen gas glows red, energised by hot young stars.
NGC6590.tagline: Discovered three times and catalogued under three numbers: a dusty cloud that kept being found anew.

facts.text: HD 168112 is another pair of heavyweights whose fierce winds crash together. It and HD 167971 both shine unusually brightly in X-rays.
facts.title: Colliding winds

story: A short hop north of the Eagle Nebula, M 16, NGC 6604 is still busy making stars. Only about 6.5 million years old, this [[open-cluster]] sits at the heart of a glowing hydrogen cloud, S54, and forms the densest part of a wider family of stars moving together through space. William Herschel found it on 15 July 1784.

Its brightest system, HD 167971, is three massive stars in one. Two of them orbit so tightly that they touch, eclipsing each other as they go. The system ranks among the most luminous in the Milky Way.
NGC6604.tagline: The Eagle Nebula’s young neighbour, home to one of the most luminous stars in the galaxy.

story: Near the border of Serpens and Scutum, in a rich stretch of the Milky Way, lies NGC 6605. John Herschel recorded this [[open-cluster]] in 1826, years before he sailed to the Cape of Good Hope to chart the southern sky. Its stars were born together and still drift through the galaxy as a loose group. From a dark site far from city lights it is just within reach of the naked eye.
NGC6605.tagline: A scattered star cluster on the edge of naked-eye visibility, found by John Herschel in 1826.

story: Inside NGC 6624 two dead stars are locked in a frantic dance. The X-ray source 4U 1820−30 is a neutron star and a white dwarf so close that they orbit each other every 11.5 minutes. The neutron star feeds on its partner’s gas, and the stolen matter glows fiercely in X-rays.

Measurements with NASA’s NICER instrument suggest the neutron star spins 716 times a second, matching the fastest-spinning neutron star known. The cluster also holds six pulsars. William Herschel found this [[globular-cluster]] on 24 June 1784.
NGC6624.tagline: A globular cluster hiding a pair of dead stars that whirl round each other every 11.5 minutes.

story: Scutum is one of the few constellations named in honour of a real person. Johannes Hevelius created it in 1684 as Sobieski’s Shield, for the Polish king John III Sobieski. NGC 6625 is an [[open-cluster]] within its borders, one of many in this rich stretch of the [[milky-way]]. Its stars were born together from the same cloud and still travel loosely as a group.
NGC6625.tagline: A star cluster in Scutum, the constellation named for a Polish king’s shield.

facts.text: NGC 663 holds at least five blue stragglers — stars that look too young for the cluster, probably formed when two stars merged into one.
facts.title: Stars that merged

facts.text: A candidate member, LS I +61° 235, is a Be star with an X-ray-emitting companion that orbits it about once every three years.
facts.title: An X-ray partner

story: Only 20 to 25 million years old, NGC 663 is already seeing its heaviest stars come to the end of their hydrogen-burning lives. Among its roughly 400 stars are about 24 Be stars — hot blue stars whose spectra show bright emission lines of hydrogen, a sign of gas thrown off into a disc around them. That is an unusually high number for one [[open-cluster]].

It belongs to a loose family of young stars called Cassiopeia OB8, along with M 103 and other clusters of similar age and distance, in the Perseus Arm of the Milky Way. NGC 663 is likely the most massive cluster in that family, and possibly in the whole Perseus Arm.
NGC663.tagline: A young cluster crowded with rare Be stars — and perhaps the heaviest star cluster in its spiral arm.

discovered.note: Found in 1745–46; rediscovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783

facts.text: The eighth-magnitude double star HD 169959 appears to sit among the cluster’s stars, but it only lies along the same line of sight and is not a true member.
facts.title: An impostor in the crowd

story: Philippe Loys de Chéseaux spotted this cluster in 1745 or 1746. Nearly four decades later Caroline Herschel found it again on her own, and it went into her brother William’s catalogue. Bright enough to glimpse with the naked eye, NGC 6633 is an [[open-cluster]] about 550 million years old.
It has gathered nicknames: the Wasp, Captain Hook, and — paired with its neighbour IC 4756 — Tweedledum to that cluster’s Tweedledee.
NGC6633.tagline: Tweedledum to IC 4756’s Tweedledee: a bright cluster first seen in the 1740s and found again by Caroline Herschel.

story: Beside Kaus Borealis, the star that marks the top of the Teapot’s lid in Sagittarius, sits a [[globular-cluster]] few people notice. NGC 6638 is a compact ball of ancient stars, one of the roughly 150 globular clusters that swarm around the centre of the Milky Way. William Herschel came across it in 1784, sweeping the sky with his 18.7-inch reflector.
NGC6638.tagline: A compact globular cluster tucked beside the top of the Sagittarius Teapot’s lid.

facts.text: During the total lunar eclipse of June 2094, the darkened Moon will pass in front of NGC 6642 as seen from New Guinea, northern Australia and the Pacific.
facts.title: A date with an eclipse

story: Blue stragglers are stars that look younger than they have any right to be: hotter and bluer than the rest of their ancient cluster, probably rejuvenated by a merger or by stealing gas from a partner. NGC 6642 has many of them. It is also short of low-mass stars — the ones that tend to drift to a cluster’s edge, where the galaxy’s pull can strip them away.
William Herschel found this [[globular-cluster]] in 1784.
NGC6642.tagline: A globular cluster short of small stars and full of blue stragglers — due to be hidden by an eclipsed Moon in 2094.

story: Compared with the ancient globular clusters, open clusters live fast. Most come apart within a few hundred million years, their stars slipping away one by one into the galaxy at large. NGC 6645 is an [[open-cluster]] in the northern part of Sagittarius, a group of stars that formed together from one cloud and, for now, still holds together.
NGC6645.tagline: An open cluster in northern Sagittarius — one of the short-lived families of the Milky Way’s disc.

story: Every open cluster starts life wrapped in the gas it was born from. Its hottest young stars soon clear that gas away with their light and winds, and what is left is a group of bare stars travelling together. NGC 6647 is one such [[open-cluster]] in Sagittarius, set against the crowded star fields of the [[milky-way]] towards the galaxy’s centre.
NGC6647.tagline: A star cluster in Sagittarius, long since freed from the cloud of gas that gave it birth.

story: Cepheid variables pulse with a rhythm that reveals their true brightness, which makes them one of astronomy’s key yardsticks. Finding one in a cluster of known age is a prize, and NGC 6649 has one: V367 Scuti. This [[open-cluster]] is young, about 40 to 60 million years old, and rich, with more than a thousand members, two red supergiants among them.
Two smaller clusters lie close by, and the three may form a triple system. William Herschel found NGC 6649 on 10 July 1787.
NGC6649.tagline: A rich young cluster in Scutum with a pulsing Cepheid among its members — and two smaller clusters for company.

facts.text: One source, NGC 6652B, may be a transitional millisecond pulsar — a dead star that switches between being powered by its spin and by gas pulled from a partner. Catching it changing state would confirm it.
facts.title: Caught between two lives?

story: One pulsar in NGC 6652 spins more than 500 times a second, circling a companion that is probably a white dwarf; it is likely the source of the gamma rays coming from the cluster. Another swings round its partner every 9.25 days on an extremely stretched orbit.
James Dunlop found this [[globular-cluster]] on 3 September 1826. Today the Chandra X-ray Observatory has picked out eleven X-ray sources in it, among them neutron stars feeding on companion stars.
NGC6652.tagline: A globular cluster with pulsars spinning hundreds of times a second — and one that may switch between lives.

story: NGC 6664 lies right in the plane of the Milky Way, against a dense background of fainter stars, close to Alpha Scuti on the sky. William Herschel found it on 16 June 1784, and his son John later observed it too.

Its standout member is EV Scuti, a yellow supergiant that is also a Cepheid [[variable-star|variable]], swelling and shrinking so that its brightness rises and falls in a steady rhythm. The [[open-cluster]] lies near NGC 6649 on the sky, another cluster with a Cepheid of its own.
NGC6664.tagline: A loose cluster near Alpha Scuti, with a pulsing yellow supergiant among its stars.

story: Scutum is tiny, but it holds one of the brightest stretches of the Milky Way: the Scutum [[star-cloud|Star Cloud]], where thinner dust lets us see far into the galaxy. NGC 6683 is an [[open-cluster]] in this rich region, a group of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas and still travel side by side around the galaxy’s centre.
NGC6683.tagline: An open cluster in Scutum, a small constellation that holds one of the Milky Way’s brightest patches.

story: Pavo, the Peacock, is one of the southern constellations drawn up in the late 1500s from the observations of the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. Every star you can see in it belongs to our own galaxy. NGC 6684 does not: it is a separate [[galaxy]], a whole island of stars lying far beyond them.
NGC6684.tagline: A galaxy far beyond the stars of Pavo, the Peacock, in the deep southern sky.

story: Scutum’s most famous cluster is the Wild Duck, M 11, but this little constellation holds several more. NGC 6704 is one of them, an [[open-cluster]] set in the bright band of the [[milky-way]]. Its stars share a birthplace and an age, and they still move through space together, a family that has not yet scattered.
NGC6704.tagline: A lesser-known open cluster in Scutum, home constellation of the famous Wild Duck Cluster.

story: On the evening of 13 November 1984, David Levy discovered his first comet, less than a degree from NGC 6709. He went on to find many more, including Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9, which crashed into Jupiter in 1994.
The cluster itself is an [[open-cluster]] of some 300 stars in Aquila, about 141 million years old — much the same age as the Pleiades.
NGC6709.tagline: A cluster as old as the Pleiades, beside which David Levy found his very first comet.

discovered.note: Probably; found again by William Herschel in 1784

facts.text: Its pulsar PSR J1853−0842A is a “black widow”: its fierce radiation is slowly evaporating a companion of only a few hundredths of the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: A black widow

facts.text: Pulsars slow down as they age, yet this one appears to be speeding up. That is only possible because it sits inside a globular cluster, whose gravity tugs on it.
facts.title: Speeding up

story: Its plunges through the Milky Way’s disc have cost NGC 6712 dearly. Each pass let the galaxy’s tides strip away more of its stars, and this [[globular-cluster]], about 12 billion years old, may once have been far more massive.

Guillaume Le Gentil probably saw it first, on 9 July 1749, and called it a “true nebula”, unlike the star cluster M 11 nearby. William Herschel found it again in 1784, still as a round nebula; only in the 1830s did John Herschel describe it as a globular cluster.
NGC6712.tagline: A battered globular cluster that has lost much of itself to the galaxy — and hosts a black widow pulsar.

story: Stars in an [[open-cluster]] share a birthday, but not a fate. The heaviest shine brilliantly and burn out within a few million years; the lightest are dim red dwarfs that will still be glowing long after the Sun has died. NGC 6716, in Sagittarius, holds such a mix of stars, born from one cloud and still travelling together through the galaxy’s disc.
NGC6716.tagline: An open cluster in Sagittarius: a family of stars sharing a birthday, but not a fate.

story: The Palomar globular clusters take their name from the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey of the 1950s, whose photographs revealed many faint, remote clusters. NGC 6717 is listed among them as Palomar 9 — yet William Herschel had already seen this [[globular-cluster]] on 7 August 1784.
It lies just south of the star Nu² Sagittarii. A bright knot of stars on its north-eastern edge was given a catalogue number of its own, IC 4802.
NGC6717.tagline: A globular cluster with two names: found by William Herschel, yet also listed among the faint Palomar clusters.

story: Near the border of Sagittarius and Corona Australis hangs the Chandelier Cluster, NGC 6723. James Dunlop found this [[globular-cluster]] on 2 June 1826, from Parramatta in New South Wales.

In wide photographs it shares the frame with the dark dust clouds and blue [[reflection-nebula|reflection nebulae]] of the Corona Australis star-forming region: an old star cluster beside a nursery where stars are being born today. The pairing is only a line of sight; the two lie at very different distances.
NGC6723.tagline: The Chandelier Cluster, an ancient globular that shares the sky with the dusty clouds of Corona Australis.

facts.text: Its discoverer, Julius Schmidt, spent decades drawing the Moon. His great map of the lunar surface, published in 1878, was the most detailed of its day.
facts.title: The Moon mapper

facts.text: The dark Corona Australis cloud is still making stars. R CrA and T CrA are two of its youngsters, and infrared telescopes reveal many more hidden in the dust.
facts.title: A nursery in the Southern Crown

story: Deep in a dark cloud of gas and dust in Corona Australis, a star is still in its infancy. R Coronae Australis has not yet settled down to burning hydrogen steadily in its core, as the Sun does, and its home is one of the closest places where stars are forming today.

Light spilling from the young star bounces off the surrounding dust, painting a glowing fan — a [[reflection-nebula]] — that opens towards another youngster, T Coronae Australis. Because its star is restless, NGC 6729 is restless too: it is one of the rare variable nebulae, whose look changes over the years.
Johann Friedrich Julius Schmidt, the German astronomer who ran the observatory in Athens, discovered it in 1861.
NGC6729.tagline: A fan of starlit dust around a star still being born, in one of the nearest stellar nurseries.

story: The Herschels swept the skies for nebulae, yet NGC 6741 slipped past them. Bright but tiny, it was easy to overlook, and it was only spotted in 1882, by Edward Pickering.

It is a [[planetary-nebula]] — a misleading name, coined because such round shells reminded early observers of the discs of the giant planets. In fact it is the cast-off outer layers of a dying star, glowing in the light of the hot core left behind.
NGC6741.tagline: A small, bright planetary nebula that slipped past the great sky surveyors until 1882.

story: Lyra, the Lyre, is a small constellation with famous residents: Vega, one of the brightest stars in the night sky, and the Ring Nebula, M 57. NGC 6743 is a much quieter neighbour, an [[open-cluster]] whose stars were born together from one cloud of gas and still share a path around the centre of the galaxy.
NGC6743.tagline: A quiet open cluster in Lyra, the small constellation of Vega and the Ring Nebula.

facts.text: The galaxy’s first recorded supernova, SN 2005at, was found on 15 March 2005 by R. Martin and the South African amateur Berto Monard.
facts.title: The first supernova

facts.text: Its nucleus is a mild active galactic nucleus, glowing with the light of weakly ionised gas — far tamer than a quasar, but more than an ordinary core.
facts.title: A quietly active heart

facts.text: It is sometimes called the Pavo Galaxy, after the Peacock, one of the southern constellations added to star maps around 1600 from the observations of Dutch navigators.
facts.title: The Pavo Galaxy

story: We can never photograph the Milky Way from outside: we live inside it. NGC 6744 is the next best thing. It is one of the largest spirals nearby and one of the closest look-alikes of our own galaxy, with an elongated core, fluffy, patchy arms busy with star formation, and even a small, distorted companion that resembles one of our [[magellanic-clouds|Magellanic Clouds]].
James Dunlop found it on 30 June 1826 from Parramatta, in Australia — the same night he found the Great Peacock Globular, nearby in Pavo.

In September 2024 the BlackGEM survey caught a new point of light in the galaxy. At first it looked like an odd nova, but it turned out to be a faint Type Iax supernova — probably the closest of its kind ever seen.
NGC6744.tagline: If you could fly out of the Milky Way and look back, you might see something very like this.

facts.text: Its nickname comes from Pavo, the Peacock. The constellation’s brightest star is itself called Peacock — a name given in the late 1930s for the Royal Air Force’s navigation almanac.
facts.title: Named for a peacock

facts.text: The cluster may also carry a second catalogue number, NGC 6777 — an old entry that probably describes the same object, though nobody can be quite sure.
facts.title: A double identity

story: Only three globular clusters outshine it: Omega Centauri, 47 Tucanae and M 22. NGC 6752 — the Great Peacock Globular — is an ancient ball of stars about 11.8 billion years old, and its centre is packed so tightly that astronomers think its core has collapsed.

In a crowd that dense, stars meet. Many of its members are binaries, and it holds blue stragglers — stars that look too young and too blue for their age, probably made when smaller stars collided and merged. The Chandra X-ray Observatory has picked out six X-ray sources in its crowded core.
James Dunlop found it from Parramatta on 30 June 1826, describing a bright nebula that could be resolved into a [[globular-cluster|cluster]] of many stars, highly compressed at the centre.
NGC6752.tagline: The fourth-brightest globular cluster in the sky, found by a Scot in Australia one winter night in 1826.

story: Seen together, NGC 6755 and NGC 6756 look like a matched pair, half a degree apart. Appearances deceive. The two clusters have different ages and lie too far from each other to be bound together, so this is a chance alignment rather than a true binary cluster.

The [[open-cluster]] NGC 6755 is about 250 million years old. William Herschel found it on 30 July 1785. A search of its field turned up 71 variable stars, among them 31 eclipsing binaries — pairs of stars that pass in front of each other.
NGC6755.tagline: Half of a double cluster in Aquila — though the two partners are not really a pair.

story: A star from our own galaxy sits almost on top of NGC 676. The 10th-magnitude star BD +04 244 lies just 5 arcseconds from the galaxy’s nucleus — a chance alignment of a near neighbour with a galaxy far beyond. Behind it, NGC 676 is a lenticular [[galaxy]] with a Seyfert nucleus: its core glows brightly as gas falls towards a central black hole.
William Herschel discovered it on 30 September 1786. Marat Arakelian later included it in his catalogue of 621 galaxies with high [[surface-brightness]].
NGC676.tagline: A galaxy with an active heart — and a foreground star photobombing its core.

story: About 71 million years ago, NGC 6760 passed through the disc of the Milky Way. Astronomers suspect that its passage may have helped trigger the birth of a young open cluster, Ruprecht 127 — an ancient [[globular-cluster]] playing midwife to a new generation of stars.
At least two millisecond pulsars spin inside it. John Russell Hind, better known for finding asteroids, discovered the cluster in 1845.
NGC6760.tagline: An old globular cluster whose plunge through the Milky Way’s disc may have helped a new cluster form.

story: Some five billion years from now, the Sun will do what the star in NGC 6790 has recently done. That star began life with about the Sun’s mass. After swelling into a giant it shed its outer layers, and what remains is a white dwarf of about 0.6 Suns, with a surface near 73,500 degrees.
The [[planetary-nebula]] it lights is young, roughly 6,000 years old, and still compact and bright. Hubble images show elongated shells of gas around the central star.
NGC6790.tagline: A young planetary nebula whose star began life much like the Sun — a preview of our own fate.

facts.text: When NASA’s Kepler planet-hunting telescope released its first images in April 2009, NGC 6791 was one of two objects highlighted.
facts.title: Kepler’s first look

facts.text: Some of its faintest white dwarfs seemed to be only 6 or 4 billion years old, out of step with the cluster’s 8 billion. Astronomers have since proposed a solution that fits an age of about 8 billion years.
facts.title: Out-of-step white dwarfs

story: Old usually means poor. The oldest stars formed before the galaxy had built up much iron and other heavy elements, so they contain little of them. NGC 6791 breaks the rule. At roughly 8 billion years old, it is one of the oldest [[open-cluster|open clusters]] known, yet its stars hold more than twice the Sun’s share of iron.
Add an unusually large crowd of stars, and it is no surprise that this is one of the most studied clusters in the sky. Friedrich Winnecke found it in 1853.
NGC6791.tagline: One of the oldest and most metal-rich star clusters in the galaxy — a cluster that breaks the usual rules.

story: Vulpecula, the Little Fox, is one of the constellations Johannes Hevelius added to the sky in the late 17th century; he pictured the fox carrying a goose. Within its borders, close on the sky to the star pattern known as the Coathanger, lies NGC 6802, a small [[open-cluster]] of stars that were born together and still travel as a group.
NGC6802.tagline: A faint open cluster in the Little Fox, close on the sky to the famous Coathanger.

facts.text: The discovery suggests planets are about as common in clusters as around lone stars, and can form and survive in surroundings far more crowded than the Sun’s.
facts.title: Planets in a crowd

facts.text: The cluster probably once held 8 O-type and 125 B-type stars — hot, massive suns that have all long since left the main sequence.
facts.title: Lost giants

story: Two stars in NGC 6811 have worlds of their own. NASA’s Kepler mission caught Kepler-66b and Kepler-67b crossing the faces of their Sun-like stars: the first planets smaller than Jupiter, and the first transiting planets, found in an [[open-cluster]]. Both are smaller than Neptune, and because the cluster is so well measured, they are among the few planets whose age is accurately known.

The cluster is about a billion years old and may have started with some 6,000 stars; a few hundred confirmed members remain. They ring a seemingly empty centre, which earned it the name “Hole in the Cluster”. John Herschel found it in 1829.
NGC6811.tagline: A billion-year-old cluster with a hole in its middle — and the first transiting planets found in an open cluster.

facts.text: NGC 6445, another planetary nebula in Sagittarius, shares the nickname Little Gem.
facts.title: One of two Little Gems

story: When a star like the Sun nears its end, it puffs its outer layers into space. NGC 6818 shows the result: a bright, enclosed bubble of gas inside a larger, fainter cloud, laced with knotty filaments. William Herschel found this [[planetary-nebula]] in 1787.

A wind streaming from the central star shapes it. As that wind ploughs through slower gas thrown off earlier, it stretches the nebula into an oval and lights up bright spots in the bubble’s outer layers.
NGC6818.tagline: A small, glowing bubble in Sagittarius, blown by the wind of a dying Sun-like star.

story: Caroline Herschel found this cluster on 12 May 1784, in the years she spent sweeping the sky alongside her brother William. She went on to discover eight comets and became the first woman to be paid for scientific work.

NGC 6819, the Foxhead, is a rich [[open-cluster]] about 2.5 billion years old. That is old for its kind: most open clusters dissolve long before reaching such an age. It sits on the border of Cygnus and Lyra.
NGC6819.tagline: Caroline Herschel’s Foxhead: a rich, old open cluster on the border of Cygnus and Lyra.

facts.text: Its hydrogen gas lies in a disc, but that disc is tipped at about 60° to the galaxy’s stars — a puzzle astronomers have yet to solve.
facts.title: A tilted mystery

facts.text: Hubble described its five brightest star-forming clouds, including ones known as the Bubble and the Ring. More than 150 such glowing clouds are now catalogued.
facts.title: Bubbles and rings

facts.text: NGC 6822 has spent most of its life alone, but it probably passed close to the Milky Way 3 to 4 billion years ago — around the time it began making most of its stars.
facts.title: A brush with our galaxy

story: In 1925 Edwin Hubble published a paper with a modest title: “N.G.C. 6822, a Remote Stellar System”. In this faint smudge in Sagittarius he had found eleven Cepheid variable stars, and their pulsing told him how far away they were. The answer placed it far beyond Harlow Shapley’s estimate for the size of the entire universe.

It was the first system beyond the Magellanic Clouds to have its distance measured, and it helped settle the “Great Debate”: the faint spiral nebulae scattered across the sky turned out to be whole galaxies of their own. Hubble went on to do the same for Andromeda and the Triangulum Galaxy.

Edward Emerson Barnard had discovered it in 1884 with a six-inch refractor. Today we know it as a barred irregular [[galaxy]] in the Local Group, much like the Small Magellanic Cloud — and the closest galaxy to us that is not a satellite of the Milky Way.
NGC6822.tagline: The small galaxy that helped Edwin Hubble show the universe is far bigger than anyone thought.

story: The stars at the centre of NGC 6823 are only about two million years old, and its outskirts hold even younger ones. Their fierce light is pushing back the surrounding cloud, the [[emission-nebula]] NGC 6820, sculpting great pillars of gas and dust like Hubble’s famous Pillars of Creation.

William Herschel found the cluster on 17 July 1785; the fainter nebula waited until Albert Marth spotted it on 7 August 1864. The cluster forms the core of Vulpecula OB1, a wider family of young, hot stars.
NGC6823.tagline: A two-million-year-old cluster carving pillars into the cloud of gas it was born from.

facts.text: The name stands for Fast Low-Ionisation Emission Region: a dense knot of gas, travelling outward fast and glowing with less ionised gas than its surroundings.
facts.title: What a FLIER is

facts.text: Its nickname, the Blinking Planetary, comes from a trick of the human eye. Plenty of other planetary nebulae “blink” in just the same way; this one simply got the name.
facts.title: Not the only blinker

story: When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel, it swells into a red giant and gently puffs its outer layers into space. Its exposed, intensely hot core then lights them up from inside. NGC 6826 is caught in exactly that stage: a glowing shell around a hot O-type star, catalogued as HD 186924.

William Herschel found it in 1793. He had coined the term [[planetary-nebula|planetary nebula]] for objects like this, because their small round discs reminded him of a planet — and he knew planets well, having discovered Uranus.
The most curious features are two bright patches on either side, known as FLIERs. They appear to be relatively young, and they are moving outward at supersonic speed.
NGC6826.tagline: A dying star in a glowing shell, flanked by two mysterious knots racing outward faster than sound.

story: Nicknamed the Poodle Cluster, NGC 6830 is an [[open-cluster]] of about 150 stars in Vulpecula, the Little Fox. William Herschel found it on 19 July 1784, and his son John observed it again on 12 July 1830.
Its constellation holds a landmark of modern astronomy: the first pulsar ever discovered, found by Jocelyn Bell Burnell in 1967.
NGC6830.tagline: The Poodle Cluster: some 150 stars in the Little Fox, the constellation where the first pulsar was found.

story: Dust between us and NGC 6834 steals more than four-fifths of its light. Behind that veil lies a young [[open-cluster]] of about 260 stars, some 65 million years old, discovered by William Herschel on 17 July 1784.
Among its members are four Be stars — hot, rapidly spinning stars that fling off discs of gas, which glow in the red light of hydrogen. Fifteen of its blue-white B-type stars vary in brightness.
NGC6834.tagline: A young Cygnus cluster dimmed by dust, with fast-spinning stars shedding rings of gas.

story: Caroline Herschel found the Kite Cluster on 23 July 1783. More than two centuries later it sat inside the patch of sky that NASA’s Kepler telescope watched for years — one of only four star clusters in that field.

Kepler’s data let astronomers listen to its stars ringing, tiny vibrations that reveal their insides, and so date this [[open-cluster]] at about 430 million years. Dozens of its stars pulsate, many more are spotted like the Sun, and the cluster slowly leaks its members into space, losing about two stars every million years.
NGC6866.tagline: The Kite Cluster: found by Caroline Herschel, and one of four clusters inside the Kepler telescope’s gaze.

story: NGC 6871 has many siblings. It was born in the same giant cloud of gas as at least six other open clusters, which now go their own way, no longer bound to it by gravity. Fewer than 50 stars make up this small, young [[open-cluster]], most of them hot blue and white stars.
Even this little family is coming apart: NGC 6871 itself appears to be disintegrating.
NGC6871.tagline: A small young cluster in Cygnus, one of at least seven siblings born from the same giant cloud.

story: Through Cygnus the summer Milky Way splits in two. The dark lane between, the Great Rift, is not empty space but clouds of dust that hide the stars behind them. NGC 6883 is one of the many open clusters scattered along this stretch of sky: an [[open-cluster]] of stars that formed together and still move as one.
NGC6883.tagline: An open cluster in Cygnus, where dark rivers of dust split the summer Milky Way in two.

facts.text: Hevelius called the constellation Vulpecula cum Ansere, the little fox with the goose. The goose has long since flown from the name, but the brightest star, Anser, keeps its memory.
facts.title: Where the goose went

facts.text: It lies near M 27, the Dumbbell Nebula — the first planetary nebula ever discovered, found by Charles Messier in 1764.
facts.title: Next door to the Dumbbell

story: Some stars spin so fast they come close to flinging themselves apart. 20 Vulpeculae is one of them: a hot Be star, whirling so quickly that it sheds gas from its equator into a glowing disc around itself. Around it lies NGC 6885, an [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in the summer Milky Way.
William Herschel recorded it in 1784. Its catalogue history is tangled: some lists treat it and its neighbour NGC 6882 as one cluster, others as two separate ones.
It lies in Vulpecula, the Little Fox, a constellation created in the late 1600s by the Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius — who originally drew the fox with a goose in its jaws.
NGC6885.tagline: A scattered star family around a fast-spinning blue star, in the constellation of the Little Fox.

facts.text: At higher magnification some observers see a shape like the € symbol in it, which has earned it the nickname “Euro Sign Nebula”.
facts.title: The Euro Sign Nebula

facts.text: A Wolf–Rayet star has lost its outer hydrogen, exposing layers that were once buried deep inside. The result is one of the hottest, fiercest types of star there is.
facts.title: A star turned inside out

story: Around 250,000 years ago, the star now called WR 136 swelled into a red giant and began shedding its outer layers in a slow, dense wind. Since then it has changed completely. Stripped down to its blazing hot interior, it has become a Wolf–Rayet star, driving a far faster wind that is ploughing into the material it shed before.

Where the two winds collide, a glowing shell forms: the Crescent Nebula. Two shock waves run from the collision, one outward and one back towards the star, and the inward one heats the gas inside to temperatures high enough to shine in X-rays.

William Herschel discovered this [[emission-nebula]] in 1792. Wolf–Rayet stars are thought to be in the last stage of life before they explode as supernovae, so the Crescent may one day be torn apart by its own star.
NGC6888.tagline: A bubble blown by a doomed star, as its fierce wind smashes into the debris of its own past.

story: Ralph Copeland found NGC 6891 not by its shape but by its light. On 22 September 1884, at Dun Echt Observatory near Aberdeen, he was examining the sky through a spectroscope on a 6.1-inch refractor, and its spectrum gave it away as glowing gas.

This [[planetary-nebula]] is built in layers: a bright inner nebula, an attached middle shell, and a detached outer halo expanding faster than the rest. Inner shells pointing in different directions show that the dying star threw off its gas in several separate episodes.
NGC6891.tagline: A planetary nebula unmasked by its spectrum in 1884, built from shells thrown off in several bursts.

facts.text: Its central star shows some of the broadest lines of highly ionised oxygen — atoms missing five of their eight electrons — seen in any planetary nebula. Oxygen stripped of seven electrons has been detected too: signs of extreme heat.
facts.title: Stripped atoms

story: The star at the heart of the Blue Flash Nebula began life only a little heavier than the Sun. Making this [[planetary-nebula]] cost it nearly half its mass. What remains is a naked core of about 0.6 Suns, blazing at some 150,000 degrees, with a spectrum like an oxygen-rich Wolf–Rayet star.
Around it, an inner shell sprouts cone-like extensions tipped by knots that glow strongly in the light of nitrogen. William Herschel found it in 1784, in Delphinus.
NGC6905.tagline: The Blue Flash Nebula: the cast-off shell of a Sun-like star whose naked core burns at 150,000 degrees.

story: On the sky NGC 6910 sits just beside Sadr, the star at the heart of the Northern Cross. In reality Sadr is a foreground star; the cluster lies far behind it, beyond the dark dust of the Great Rift, perhaps alongside the glowing Gamma Cygni Nebula, IC 1318.

This young [[open-cluster]] is the core of a larger family of hot stars, Cygnus OB9. Its members include a blue supergiant, a hot O-type giant and four beta Cephei variables — pulsating hot stars, unusually many for one cluster. William Herschel found it on 17 October 1786.
NGC6910.tagline: The Inchworm: a young cluster beside Sadr on the sky, but far behind it, beyond the Great Rift.

facts.text: Its stars show a split subgiant branch, a sign that the cluster may contain more than one population of stars rather than a single generation born all at once.
facts.title: More than one generation?

facts.text: There is some evidence that NGC 6934 is shedding stars into a tidal tail, stripped away by the Milky Way’s gravity as it swings through the galaxy.
facts.title: A trailing tail

story: Most of the Milky Way’s stars circle its centre in a flat, orderly disc. NGC 6934 does not. This [[globular-cluster]] follows a stretched, highly eccentric orbit tipped at 73° to the galaxy’s plane, swooping in towards the centre and then far back out again.

It may share a common origin with another globular cluster, NGC 5466. Inside, astronomers have counted 85 variable stars, 79 of them RR Lyrae stars — old pulsating stars that brighten and fade in less than a day, and whose rhythm makes them handy distance markers.
William Herschel found the cluster on 24 September 1785. Even so, as late as 2018 it was described as poorly studied — one of the sky’s ancient star cities still waiting for its close-up.
NGC6934.tagline: An ancient star cluster on a wild, plunging orbit through the Milky Way — and full of pulsing stars.

story: Two hazy patches sit side by side near the border of Cepheus and Cygnus. One is NGC 6939, a cluster of stars in our own galaxy. The other is NGC 6946, the Fireworks Galaxy, a whole spiral galaxy far beyond, famous for its many supernovae. Their meeting is pure perspective.
NGC 6939 is old for an [[open-cluster]], between 1 and 1.3 billion years, and lies well above the plane of the Milky Way. William Herschel found it in 1798.
NGC6939.tagline: An old star cluster that shares a field of view with the Fireworks Galaxy, far beyond it.

story: Of all the open clusters in Vulpecula, NGC 6940 is considered the finest. It has hundreds of members and is about a billion years old, old enough that its leading stars have swollen into red giants. More than 20 are known, and the brightest, FG Vulpeculae, slowly brightens and fades over about 80 days.

Some of its stars are close pairs whose tight orbits keep them spinning fast, so they stay magnetically active and glow in X-rays despite the cluster’s age. William Herschel found this [[open-cluster]] in 1784.
NGC6940.tagline: The finest cluster in Vulpecula — a billion-year-old crowd led by a slowly flickering red giant.

facts.text: SN 2017eaw was found on 14 May 2017 by Patrick Wiggins, an amateur astronomer in Utah. Its star turned out to be a red supergiant about 15 times the mass of the Sun.
facts.title: An amateur’s supernova

facts.text: For SN 2004et, astronomers found the doomed star on older images — only the seventh time a supernova had been traced back to the star that exploded.
facts.title: Caught before it blew

story: Stars keep exploding in this galaxy. In 1917 George Willis Ritchey spotted a new star in this face-on spiral: a supernova, the first of ten seen here in a century. That is about ten times the Milky Way’s rate, even though our galaxy has twice as many stars, and for a time no galaxy had shown more — until NGC 3690 overtook it.

The reason is a boom in star birth. NGC 6946 is a starburst [[galaxy]], forming new stars at a furious pace, and its most massive stars die young and violently. Its arms are full of oddities, from the giant “Red Ellipse” bubble to Hodge’s Complex, once thought to be a young star cluster and now suspected to be a small galaxy seen against it.

Then there is the star that disappeared. In 2009 a yellow hypergiant here brightened to over a million times the Sun’s luminosity, then faded away. Hubble finds no sign that it survived: it may have collapsed into a black hole without a proper explosion.
NGC6946.tagline: A galaxy where stars keep exploding — and where one giant star may have quietly vanished into a black hole.

facts.text: Its long, sweeping shape with a bright star at one end gives it the nickname Witch’s Broom. It also goes by the Lacework Nebula and the Filamentary Nebula.
facts.title: Many names

facts.text: Each glowing strand is a shock front less than one fifty-thousandth as thick as the shell’s radius — so thin that we only notice it when we look along it.
facts.title: Thinner than thin

story: Somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 years ago, a star about 20 times the mass of the Sun blew itself apart in Cygnus. For a time it outshone Venus, bright enough to see in daylight. Our ancestors, living around the end of the last Ice Age, could have watched it blaze and fade.

The wreckage is still flying outward. Its glowing edges form the Cygnus Loop, a [[supernova-remnant]], and the Western Veil is one long strand of it. William Herschel found it on 5 September 1784, noting that it “passes thro’ 52 Cygni” and runs nearly two degrees. That star is only a bystander, far in the foreground.

Why does it look like a wisp of rope rather than a cloud? The shock front is a vast, thin shell, and we only see it brightly where we look along its surface edge-on — like the rim of a soap bubble. Ripples in the shell make the strands seem to twist around each other.
NGC6960.tagline: The Witch’s Broom: a strand of wreckage from a star that blew apart around the end of the last Ice Age.

facts.text: Between the Eastern and Western Veils lies a fainter wisp found on photographs in 1904 by Williamina Fleming. As was the custom of the day, credit went to her boss, Edward Pickering: it is still called Pickering’s Triangle.
facts.title: Fleming’s triangle

facts.text: The Cygnus Loop shines far beyond visible light: it is a strong source of both radio waves and X-rays, from gas the blast has heated.
facts.title: Loud in radio and X-rays

story: Compare pictures of the Eastern Veil taken years apart and you can see it move. Between 1997 and 2015 the Hubble Space Telescope did exactly that, catching the debris of an exploded star as it ploughs outward at around 1.5 million kilometres per hour.

The star, roughly 20 times the Sun’s mass, blew up 10,000 to 20,000 years ago. Its expanding shell, the Cygnus Loop, now spreads across a patch of sky many times wider than the full Moon, and NGC 6992 is the brightest arc of this [[supernova-remnant]]. Heated by the blast, atoms of oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen glow in its tangled filaments. Together with NGC 6995 to the south, it forms the Network Nebula.
William Herschel came across it on 5 September 1784 and described “branching nebulosity” whose streams divide and then unite again towards the south.
NGC6992.tagline: The brightest arc of a supernova’s wreckage — still expanding fast enough for Hubble to watch it move.

story: On the sky, NGC 6997 sits inside one of the best-known clouds of the northern Milky Way: the North America Nebula, NGC 7000, named for its likeness to the continent’s outline, Gulf of Mexico and all. That great [[emission-nebula]] glows red as its hydrogen is energised by hot stars. The cluster’s stars, born together, are scattered across the glow like a handful of sparks.
NGC6997.tagline: A small star cluster set within the glow of the North America Nebula.

discovered.note: Named the North America Nebula by Max Wolf in 1890

facts.text: The star’s name follows the map. “Islas de Bajamar”, the low-tide islands, was the original Spanish name for the Bahamas, just off Florida — many of them are easiest to see from a ship at low tide.
facts.title: Islands at low tide

facts.text: The dark cloud in front dims the Bajamar Star almost 10,000 times. Without it, the star would shine at magnitude 3.6 — nearly as bright as Albireo, and easy to see with the naked eye.
facts.title: Hidden in plain sight

facts.text: The Bajamar Star and another hot star, nicknamed the Toronto star, both seem to have been flung out of a group dubbed the Bermuda cluster about 1.5 million years ago.
facts.title: Runaways from Bermuda

story: In 1890 the German astrophotographer Max Wolf took a long-exposure photograph of a patch of Cygnus and saw a familiar shape emerge: a glowing continent. He named it the North America Nebula. William Herschel had noted “faint milky nebulosity” here back in 1786, but only the camera revealed its outline.

For decades nobody knew what made it shine. In 1922 Edwin Hubble suggested nearby Deneb, but Deneb is not hot enough. By 1958 George Herbig realised the culprit had to be hidden behind a dark lane of dust. In 2004 Fernando Comerón and Anna Pasquali found it in infrared: a fierce O-type star of over 40,000 degrees, just off the nebula’s “Florida coast”. In 2026 the IAU named it the Bajamar Star.

The same dark lane splits one great [[emission-nebula|cloud of glowing hydrogen]] in two: the North America and Pelican nebulae are parts of a single cloud. The stretch shaped like Mexico, the Cygnus Wall, is where stars are forming most intensely.
NGC7000.tagline: A glowing continent in Cygnus, lit by a hidden star that was only tracked down in 2004.

facts.text: Delphinus, the Dolphin, is a small constellation with a big myth: in Greek legend a dolphin was set among the stars for rescuing the poet Arion — or, in another telling, for finding Poseidon his bride.
facts.title: Among the Dolphin’s stars

facts.text: The galactic halo is mostly dark matter, with thin gas and a sprinkling of ancient star clusters. NGC 7006 is one of its outlying residents, far beyond the busy disc where the Sun lives.
facts.title: Residents of the halo

story: Wrapped around the Milky Way’s flat, spinning disc is the halo: a vast, roughly spherical region of dark matter, thin gas and scattered ancient star clusters. NGC 7006 lives far out in that halo, a [[globular-cluster]] some five times farther from us than the centre of the galaxy.

From a planet orbiting one of its stars, the Milky Way would not be a band of light across the sky but a whole galaxy, seen from outside. The cluster has even found its way into fiction. Edgar Rice Burroughs, creator of Tarzan, used NGC 7006 as a signpost in his science-fiction story “Beyond the Farthest Star”: the people of the planet Poloda use it to work out roughly where Earth lies.
William Herschel discovered the cluster in 1784.
NGC7006.tagline: A far-flung star cluster in the galaxy’s halo — used as a signpost to Earth by the creator of Tarzan.

facts.text: The 19th-century astronomer William Henry Smyth counted it among Struve’s nine “Rare Celestial Objects” — a select club of the sky’s most curious sights.
facts.title: One of Struve’s rarities

facts.text: The whole nebula is moving towards us at about 45 kilometres per second — fast enough to cross the Atlantic in about two minutes.
facts.title: Heading our way

facts.text: Beyond its famous handles, the nebula has a faint halo, several shells, jet-like streams and small knots and filaments, all arranged in three dimensions.
facts.title: Layers upon layers

story: In the 1840s Lord Rosse, working with some of the largest telescopes yet built, saw thin extensions poking out on either side of a small nebula in Aquarius, like Saturn’s rings seen edge-on. He gave it the name we still use: the Saturn Nebula.

Those “handles”, or ansae, turn out to be knots of gas moving outward from a dying star — though, oddly, not in straight lines away from it. This [[planetary-nebula]] is made of the cast-off outer layers of a low-mass star. What remains at the centre is a hot white dwarf of about 55,000 degrees, whose ultraviolet light makes oxygen atoms in the nebula fluoresce green.

William Herschel had discovered it some sixty years earlier, on 7 September 1782, from his garden at Datchet near Windsor, using a telescope of his own design. It was one of the first finds of his great survey of the sky.
NGC7009.tagline: A dying star’s nebula that looks like a ringed planet — named by Lord Rosse in the 1840s.

facts.text: New stars are still forming in the Iris. It holds the densest gathering of young stellar objects in the Cepheus Flare, a sprawl of dark clouds in this part of the sky.
facts.title: A nursery in the dust

facts.text: Outflows from the young central stars have carved a two-sided, cone-shaped cavity in the cloud, and their light is breaking molecules apart along its glowing walls.
facts.title: Hollowed out by its stars

facts.text: The nebula is also rich in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — flat, honeycomb-patterned carbon molecules much like those found in soot and smoke on Earth.
facts.title: Smoky chemistry

story: There are footballs in the Iris Nebula. Not real ones: in 2007 the Spitzer Space Telescope found buckyballs here, cage-shaped molecules of 60 carbon atoms arranged like the panels of a football. It was the first firm detection of neutral fullerenes in interstellar space, and they rank among the largest molecules ever found there.

The surprise was where they sat. Fullerenes were thought to be built in the hot, dense outskirts of old stars, yet here they lie in a cold, thin cloud bathed in ultraviolet light. One idea is that the starlight strips larger carbon molecules of their hydrogen, then folds them into cages that shrink until they reach the tidy 60-atom ball.
That light comes from HD 200775, a pair of young stars at the centre of this [[reflection-nebula]]; their glow bounces off the surrounding dust. William Herschel discovered the nebula in 1794.
NGC7023.tagline: A dusty flower in Cepheus where a space telescope found carbon molecules shaped like footballs.

facts.text: In 2019 the helium hydride ion — thought to be the first molecule to form in the universe, about 100,000 years after the Big Bang — was detected in space for the first time, here.
facts.title: The first molecule

facts.text: Its outer halo holds about three Suns’ worth of cast-off gas. Mass loss like this showed that stars a few times heavier than the Sun can shed enough to avoid exploding as supernovae.
facts.title: Escaping a supernova

facts.text: The nebula is rich in carbon, and there is evidence that it contains nanodiamonds — specks of diamond only billionths of a metre across.
facts.title: Carbon and diamonds

story: Around six centuries ago, a star three or four times heavier than the Sun began to shed its outer layers. NGC 7027 is the result: a [[planetary-nebula]] so young and compact that astronomers once thought its central star was still too cool to light it up. Hubble showed otherwise. It is a planetary nebula at the very start of its life.
Édouard Stephan found it in 1878 with the 80-centimetre reflector at Marseille Observatory. Nicknamed the Jewel Bug and the Magic Carpet, it is by far the most studied planetary nebula.
NGC7027.tagline: One of the youngest planetary nebulae known — where the universe’s first kind of molecule was finally found.

story: William Herschel found this small [[open-cluster]] on 21 September 1788. It lies in Cygnus, and that matters: when we look towards the Swan, we are looking along the length of our own spiral arm of the Milky Way, so clusters, nebulae and star fields pile up one behind another. NGC 7031 is one of the many in that crowded view.
NGC7031.tagline: A small open cluster in Cygnus, where we look along the length of our own spiral arm.

story: Cygnus is home to Deneb, the Swan’s tail and one of the most luminous stars the naked eye can see. NGC 7039 is a far humbler resident of the constellation: an [[open-cluster]], a family of ordinary stars that formed together from a single cloud of gas and still travel through the [[milky-way]] as a group.
NGC7039.tagline: A modest open cluster in Cygnus, the constellation of the brilliant supergiant Deneb.

story: Cygnus has a famous dark resident: Cygnus X-1, the first object widely accepted as a black hole. NGC 7062 is one of the constellation’s quieter sights, an [[open-cluster]] whose stars formed together from one cloud of gas. Bound loosely by their own gravity, they still share a path around the centre of the [[milky-way]].
NGC7062.tagline: An open cluster in the Swan, the constellation that gave us the first widely accepted black hole.

story: When Per Collinder studied NGC 7063 in 1931, he believed it held only 10 to 12 stars. In 2021 a new study counted 75 members. The cluster had not grown, of course; our ability to tell true members from unrelated stars along the same line of sight had.
John Herschel found this small [[open-cluster]] on 19 August 1828, near the star 69 Cygni.
NGC7063.tagline: A cluster that grew from a dozen stars to 75 — not by making stars, but by better measurement.

story: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel used a star in Cygnus, 61 Cygni, to make the first measurement of the distance to any star beyond the Sun. NGC 7067 shares the constellation: an [[open-cluster]], a group of stars born together from one cloud of gas, still travelling as a family through the disc of the [[milky-way]].
NGC7067.tagline: An open cluster in Cygnus, the constellation where a star’s distance was first measured.

story: At the head of Cygnus shines Albireo, a [[double-star]] of gold and blue and one of the best loved in the sky. Elsewhere in the Swan lies NGC 7082, an [[open-cluster]] — a family of stars that formed together and still drift through the galaxy as a loose group, set against the rich star fields of the summer Milky Way.
NGC7082.tagline: A scattered open cluster in Cygnus, the Swan with a gold-and-blue double star for its head.

story: The brightest stars of Cygnus form the Northern Cross, laid along the band of the Milky Way. Scattered among them are dozens of star clusters, and NGC 7086 is one: an [[open-cluster]] whose stars share a birthplace and an age. Over time the galaxy’s tides will loosen the group, and its members will drift apart.
NGC7086.tagline: An open cluster in Cygnus, whose brightest stars form the Northern Cross.

story: Cygnus holds some of the most active star-forming regions of the northern Milky Way, where giant clouds of gas are still turning into stars. NGC 7128 is an [[open-cluster]] in this crowded constellation, a group of stars that formed together from one cloud. Its members share an age and a chemical make-up, so they help astronomers test how stars evolve.
NGC7128.tagline: A small open cluster in Cygnus, one of the busiest star-making regions of the northern sky.

story: Dust covers this part of Cepheus so thoroughly that one study concluded no part of the field is free of it. That uneven veil has made NGC 7142 hard to measure. Even so, it seems to be about as old as M 67 and NGC 188, which makes it one of the oldest [[open-cluster|open clusters]] known.

Old clusters should have lost their hot blue stars long ago. NGC 7142 has a surprising number of them — blue stragglers, probably rejuvenated by mergers or by stealing gas from companions. It lies near the reflection nebula NGC 7129.
NGC7142.tagline: One of the oldest open clusters known, hidden behind patchy dust — and full of blue stars that shouldn’t be there.

facts.text: It has been suggested that the bright stars Lambda Cephei and 68 Cygni are runaways, flung out at high speed from this same region.
facts.title: Runaways

story: NGC 7160 lives inside a giant bubble. The Cepheus Bubble, a dusty shell spanning about ten degrees of sky, was blown out by the winds and light of massive stars that later died as supernovae. This young [[open-cluster]], 10 to 19 million years old, may once have been their companion, along with Mu Cephei — Herschel’s Garnet Star — and Nu Cephei.
The gas it formed from is already gone. Yet one small, cool member is still feeding from a disc of material, perhaps one in which planets could form.
NGC7160.tagline: A young cluster inside the Cepheus Bubble, a vast shell blown by stars that have since exploded.

facts.text: NGC 720 hosts nine ultraluminous X-ray sources — as of 2003, the most found in any galaxy of its smooth, early type.
facts.title: X-ray hotspots

facts.text: Its stars change in age from the centre outwards. Astronomers have proposed that NGC 720 swallowed a smaller galaxy about 4 billion years ago.
facts.title: A past merger

story: In 2000 the Chandra X-ray Observatory noticed something odd about NGC 720. This [[elliptical-galaxy]] is wrapped in a flattened halo of hot gas, and the halo is tilted differently from the starlight we see. The mismatch fits the idea that most of the gravity comes from unseen dark matter, though some alternative theories of gravity can explain it too. Counting that hidden mass, the galaxy weighs about three trillion Suns.
Its centre holds stars about 13 billion years old, and some 1,500 globular clusters swarm around it. William Herschel discovered it on 3 October 1785.
NGC720.tagline: An elliptical galaxy whose tilted halo of hot gas betrays a hidden mass.

story: For decades, SS Lacertae dimmed every 14.4 days as one of its two stars passed in front of the other. Then, in the middle of the 20th century, the eclipses stopped. The culprit is a third star, circling the pair every 679 days. Its pull slowly tilts their orbit, so that from Earth they no longer line up.

The tilt cycles round in about 600 years, bringing two spells of eclipses that each last about a century. SS Lacertae belongs to NGC 7209, an [[open-cluster]] of some 150 stars that William Herschel found on 19 October 1787.
NGC7209.tagline: Home of SS Lacertae, a pair of stars that stopped eclipsing each other in the mid-20th century.

story: Rings within rings mark NGC 7217. Three main rings of stars circle its core, the outermost holding most of its gas and new stars, and Hubble found still smaller rings inside the innermost — signs that its centre has gone through several bursts of star formation.

Something else hints at a turbulent past: some of its stars orbit the centre in the opposite direction to the rest. A merger with one or two smaller, gas-rich galaxies may explain it, perhaps turning a lenticular galaxy into the [[spiral-galaxy]] we see today. Now it floats alone, with no large companions. William Herschel found it in 1784.
