NGC7217.tagline: A ringed spiral galaxy with stars orbiting the wrong way — clues to a merger long ago.

story: Cepheus holds a star that changed astronomy: Delta Cephei, whose regular pulsing John Goodricke discovered in 1784. Its kind, the Cepheids, later let astronomers measure the distances to other galaxies. NGC 7226 is a far humbler resident of the constellation, an [[open-cluster]] whose stars were born together and still drift through the [[milky-way]] as a group.
NGC7226.tagline: An open cluster in Cepheus, the constellation of the star that gave Cepheid variables their name.

story: Some clusters are catalogued once; this one twice. It carries two numbers in the New General Catalogue, NGC 7234 and NGC 7235, a duplicate entry for the same group of stars. Whatever the label, it is an [[open-cluster]] in Cepheus: stars that share a birthplace in one cloud of gas and still travel together through the disc of the Milky Way.
NGC7234.tagline: An open cluster in Cepheus that carries two numbers in the New General Catalogue.

facts.text: The decade of monitoring also turned up one possible transiting planet: a small, regular dip in a star’s light as something passes in front of it. It has yet to be confirmed.
facts.title: A planet candidate

facts.text: Its hottest remaining star is a B5 giant, already ageing. Any more massive stars the cluster was born with have long since burnt out.
facts.title: Lost its heavyweights

story: For a decade, astronomers kept returning to NGC 7243, measuring how each star’s light changed from night to night. By 2016 they had found 37 eclipsing binaries — pairs of stars that take turns passing in front of each other — along with 26 stars that pulse.

This [[open-cluster|open cluster]] is about 250 million years old: its stars were born around the time the first dinosaurs appeared on Earth. A 2003 study counted 211 likely members, with a combined mass of roughly 350 to 520 Suns.
William Herschel discovered it on 26 September 1788. It lies in Lacerta, the Lizard, a small constellation squeezed in between Cygnus and Andromeda by Johannes Hevelius in the late 1600s.
NGC7243.tagline: A quiet-looking cluster that a decade of watching revealed to be full of eclipsing and pulsing stars.

story: Lacerta, the Lizard, is a small constellation with one famous oddity. BL Lacertae was catalogued as a variable star until astronomers realised it is the blazing core of a distant galaxy, with a jet pointed almost straight at us. NGC 7245 is a much closer, quieter resident: an [[open-cluster]] within our own galaxy, its stars born together from one cloud.
NGC7245.tagline: An open cluster in Lacerta, the little Lizard with a famous impostor star.

story: Every star in an [[open-cluster]] shares a birthplace: the members of NGC 7261 formed together from a single cloud of gas and dust, and have travelled through the Milky Way as a group ever since. Its neighbour in the sky is far more famous. A little over a degree away shines Delta Cephei, whose steady pulsing gave its name to the Cepheid [[variable-star|variable stars]] — the yardsticks Edwin Hubble used to prove that other galaxies lie far beyond our own.
NGC7261.tagline: A little-known family of stars in Cepheus, a short hop from the star that gave Cepheid variables their name.

facts.text: Karl Ludwig Harding, who found the Helix — most likely before 1824 — is better known for discovering Juno in 1804, only the third asteroid ever found.
facts.title: Juno’s discoverer

facts.text: Dust glowing in infrared around the white dwarf seems to be topped up by thousands of comets on stretched orbits, perhaps from a cloud like the Sun’s own Oort cloud.
facts.title: Comets around a dead star

facts.text: A 2025 X-ray study suggested the white dwarf may be swallowing the remains of a Jupiter-like planet. A 2024 study hinted at another, smaller planet, but that is far from certain.
facts.title: A planet’s last meal?

story: Look at a photograph of the Helix and it seems to look back. Its glowing rings have earned it nicknames like the “Eye of God” and the “Eye of Sauron”. What it really shows is the end of a star.

A low- to intermediate-mass star shed its outer layers here, beginning around 10,600 years ago. What remains is a white dwarf of about 120,000 degrees, only a few times wider than Earth, whose ultraviolet glare makes the cast-off gas glow. This is a [[planetary-nebula]] — the fate that awaits the Sun.

Look closer and the Helix is full of “cometary knots”, some 40,000 of them, each with a bright head facing the star and a tail streaming away. Leave off the tail and each knot is about as big as our whole Solar System. The Helix was the first planetary nebula in which such knots were found.
NGC7293.tagline: The “Eye of God”: a dying star’s cast-off layers, studded with some 40,000 comet-like knots.

story: Lacerta, the Lizard, is one of the sky’s latecomers. Johannes Hevelius, the great astronomer of Gdańsk, made it up in the late 1600s from faint stars squeezed between Cygnus and Andromeda. The Milky Way runs through it, and with it a scattering of star clusters. This small [[open-cluster]] is one of them: a group of stars born together and still travelling side by side. Catalogues know it by two numbers, NGC 7295 and NGC 7296.
NGC7295.tagline: A small star cluster in Lacerta, the Lizard — a constellation pieced together from faint stars in the 1680s.

facts.text: SN 2014C began as a hydrogen-poor Type Ib explosion, then over the course of a year turned into a hydrogen-rich Type IIn — an unusual “metamorphosis” for a supernova.
facts.title: A supernova that changed

facts.text: A photographic plate taken at Yerkes Observatory in 1903 shows a faint point of light here that may have been an earlier supernova.
facts.title: An old plate’s secret

facts.text: The first confirmed supernova here, SN 1959D, was found at Palomar by Milton Humason and Howard Gates. Humason began by driving mule trains up Mount Wilson and became Edwin Hubble’s key collaborator.
facts.title: From mule driver to astronomer

story: Its centre spins the wrong way. In most spiral galaxies the central bulge turns along with the disc around it, but in NGC 7331 the two rotate in opposite directions. Its core also sits slightly off-centre, with one side of the disc reaching farther out than the other.

For years it was called “the Milky Way’s twin”, for its similar size and structure. The comparison has faded since we learned that our galaxy has a central bar, and NGC 7331 has none. The faint galaxies that seem to huddle around it are not companions either: they lie far in the background, lined up by chance.

William Herschel discovered this [[spiral-galaxy]] on 6 September 1784. Five supernovae have been confirmed in it since. In July 2025 the GOTO survey found one that climbed to magnitude 11.9, the brightest supernova of the year, and in September 2026 ATLAS caught another.
NGC7331.tagline: A spiral whose heart spins the wrong way — and the host of the brightest supernova of 2025.

facts.text: Fourteen of the cluster’s known variable stars are pre-main-sequence stars — so young that they are still contracting and have not yet settled into steady hydrogen burning.
facts.title: Stars still growing up

story: It takes a long-exposure photograph to see the wizard: a figure of glowing hydrogen that gives this [[emission-nebula]] its name. Inside it lies NGC 7380, a young [[open-cluster]] somewhere between about 4 and 12 million years old. Caroline Herschel discovered it in 1787, and her brother William added it to his catalogue as H VIII.77.
At the cluster’s heart is DH Cephei, two massive O-type stars in a tight orbit. Their ultraviolet light makes the gas glow, pushes it outwards and squeezes neighbouring clouds into forming new stars.
NGC7380.tagline: A cloud shaped like a wizard, found by Caroline Herschel and stirred up by a pair of giant stars at its heart.

facts.text: In 2018 astronomers reported that Hubble had imaged SN 2001ig’s surviving companion star in ultraviolet light — the first companion of a Type IIb supernova ever seen.
facts.title: A survivor caught on camera

facts.text: In 2002 the Chandra X-ray Observatory found two ultraluminous X-ray sources here, shining more brightly than known stellar processes easily explain. One brightened tenfold in just 20 days.
facts.title: Two X-ray puzzles

story: Astronomers call NGC 7424 a ‘grand design’ [[spiral-galaxy]] for its well-defined arms, and it is similar in size to our own Milky Way. Its bar glows reddish with older stars, while the loose arms shine blue with clusters of massive young ones.

In December 2001 Robert Evans, the Australian amateur famed for hunting supernovae, found one on the galaxy’s outer edge. SN 2001ig was a rare Type IIb: hydrogen showed in its light at first, then faded, leaving lines of oxygen, calcium and magnesium.
NGC7424.tagline: A ‘grand design’ spiral in Grus, where Hubble photographed the star that survived a supernova.

story: About 140 stars make up NGC 744, a small [[open-cluster]] in Perseus. John Herschel discovered it on 28 November 1831. The whole cluster is moving towards us at around 25 kilometres per second — fast enough to cross from London to Paris in under 15 seconds.
NGC744.tagline: A small cluster of about 140 stars, heading our way.

facts.text: Its core is classed as a Seyfert nucleus, where gas falling towards a central supermassive black hole shines brightly.
facts.title: An active heart

facts.text: Automated searches have caught two supernovae here, SN 1990U and SN 2009jf. Both were massive stars that had lost their outer layers before they exploded.
facts.title: Two stripped stars

facts.text: In size and shape it closely resembles NGC 1300 in Eridanus, one of the best-known barred spirals of all.
facts.title: A famous look-alike

story: Picture the emblem on Superman’s chest: a bold S. NGC 7479 draws something like it across the sky — a bright central bar with a curving spiral arm at each end — which is how it earned its nickname.

Behind the shape lies a collision. The galaxy’s arms are lopsided, and it is forming stars at a furious rate: in its core, in its outer arms and right along its bar, where most of the stars are less than 100 million years old. Astronomers blame a recent merger with a smaller galaxy.

Radio telescopes add a twist. In radio light, the arms open in the opposite direction to the arms we see in visible light — a feature not seen in any other galaxy. William Herschel discovered this [[spiral-galaxy|barred spiral]] in 1784.
NGC7479.tagline: A galaxy shaped like the S on Superman’s chest, still shaken by swallowing a smaller neighbour.

facts.text: Its stars form two halos that turn in opposite directions: the outer halo rotates one way, the inner halo the other.
facts.title: Two halos, two directions

facts.text: NGC 7507 has only about a tenth as many globular clusters as comparable ellipticals — a population more like a spiral galaxy’s.
facts.title: Short on globulars

story: Nearly every big galaxy seems to sit inside a heavy cocoon of invisible dark matter. NGC 7507 is an odd one out. This massive, almost perfectly round [[elliptical-galaxy]] behaves as though its stars account for nearly all of its mass — something today’s standard theory of the universe finds hard to explain. William Herschel found it on 30 October 1783. It leads a fairly lonely life, with one partner, the barred spiral NGC 7513.
NGC7507.tagline: A perfectly round galaxy that seems to have almost no dark matter — a puzzle for cosmology.

story: Around ten million years old, NGC 7510 is a youngster among [[open-cluster|star clusters]]: its stars began to shine long after the dinosaurs had died out. It lies in the Perseus Arm, the next spiral arm of the Milky Way out from our own, and its brightest member is a hot, blue B-type giant. Interstellar dust between us and the cluster dims and reddens its light — the effect astronomers call [[extinction]] — so it looks fainter than it really is.
NGC7510.tagline: A young cluster in Cepheus, about ten million years old, lying in the next spiral arm out from ours.

facts.text: NGC 752 has a blue straggler — a star that looks too hot and young for such an old cluster, probably formed when two stars merged.
facts.title: A straggler

facts.text: The cluster includes DS Andromedae, a pair of stars that take turns passing in front of each other, dimming the light we receive.
facts.title: Stars that eclipse

story: Open clusters rarely live long, but NGC 752 has held together for about 1.34 billion years. Time has thinned out its brightest stars: the heaviest have already evolved away, leaving mostly modest stars still burning hydrogen, along with red giants. Some 302 stars are now counted as members of this [[open-cluster]].

Caroline Herschel discovered it in 1783, and her brother William catalogued it in 1786. But the Sicilian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna may have described it before 1654, more than a century earlier.
NGC752.tagline: An elderly star cluster, 1.34 billion years old, perhaps glimpsed by Hodierna and found again by Caroline Herschel.

facts.text: Stars as massive as BD+60°2522 burn through their fuel in only a few million years — a blink compared with the Sun’s lifetime of around ten billion.
facts.title: Living fast

facts.text: It is also number 162 in Stewart Sharpless’s 1959 catalogue of glowing hydrogen clouds, compiled from the photographs of the Palomar Sky Survey.
facts.title: Sharpless 162

story: A single star is inflating this bubble. BD+60°2522 is young, hot and enormous — around 44 times the mass of the Sun — and it drives a fierce wind of particles out into space. Where that wind meets the surrounding gas, it sweeps up a thin, glowing shell: the Bubble Nebula.

The bubble cannot grow freely. Nearby lies a giant molecular cloud, a dense reservoir of cold gas that holds back the expansion — and the star’s ultraviolet light makes that cloud glow too, turning it into part of the same [[emission-nebula]].
William Herschel discovered it in November 1787. In 2016 the Hubble Space Telescope marked 26 years in orbit with a detailed portrait of it.
NGC7635.tagline: A single star, some 44 times the Sun’s mass, blowing a bubble of glowing gas into space.

facts.text: Much of its blue-green colour comes from oxygen atoms that have lost two electrons, glowing as the central star’s ultraviolet light strikes them.
facts.title: Why it looks blue

facts.text: Its two shells are stretched spheroids — rugby-ball shapes — tilted to our line of sight, with the inner shell more elongated than the outer.
facts.title: Shaped like rugby balls

story: Some 3,000 years ago, a dying star in Andromeda began throwing off its outer layers. Today they form the Blue Snowball: a [[planetary-nebula]] built of a bright inner shell, a fainter outer one and a faint round halo enclosing both, threaded with knots and a jet-like streak.

At the centre sits what is left of the star: a hot subdwarf with a surface of around 100,000 degrees. It holds only about 60 per cent of the Sun’s mass, yet shines more than 5,000 times as brightly. Its wind still blows, and where it slams into gas shed earlier, the nebula glows in X-rays.
William Herschel discovered it on 6 October 1784. A century later the New General Catalogue described it with unusual enthusiasm as a “magnificent planetary or annular nebula”.
NGC7662.tagline: A snowball of glowing gas around a star of 100,000 degrees, blown out over the last 3,000 years.

story: William Herschel found NGC 7686 in Andromeda in 1787, and catalogues describe it as a modest [[open-cluster]] of about 80 stars. Not everyone agrees. In 1961, Johnson and colleagues plotted the colours of its stars against their brightness. Members of a true cluster usually trace a tidy band on such a diagram, because they share an age and a distance. Here the team found only a uniform scatter, and concluded that NGC 7686 is not really a cluster at all — just stars that happen to lie in the same direction.
NGC7686.tagline: Catalogued as a star cluster since 1787 — but one study concluded it is no cluster at all.

facts.text: In 2003 two supernovae shone in NGC 772 at the same time: SN 2003hl, found in August, and SN 2003iq, discovered seven weeks later by Jean-Marie Llapasset.
facts.title: Two supernovae at once

story: One arm of NGC 772 is far longer and stronger than the others, curling outwards like the tip of an unfurling fern — hence its nickname, the Fiddlehead Galaxy. The likely cause is its satellite galaxies, including the small elliptical NGC 770, whose gravity tugs at the big spiral.
It is a large [[spiral-galaxy]]. Halton Arp included it in his Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies as Arp 78. William Herschel discovered it on 29 November 1785.
NGC772.tagline: The Fiddlehead Galaxy: one giant arm curls out like a fern frond, pulled by its small companions.

story: Star clusters often keep company. NGC 7788 shares a small patch of the Cassiopeia Milky Way with two others: NGC 7790, about half a Moon’s width away, and the tiny Harvard 21, a little farther off. Each is an [[open-cluster]], a group of stars born together from one cloud. Whether the three are true neighbours in space or simply line up from where we stand, they show how thickly clusters are sown along the plane of our galaxy.
NGC7788.tagline: One of three small star clusters huddled together in a rich patch of the Cassiopeia Milky Way.

facts.text: Two of its red giants are unusually rich in lithium, an element such stars normally destroy. Mixing deep inside them, or a past encounter with a companion star, may explain it.
facts.title: A lithium mystery

story: Caroline Herschel spent many nights sweeping the sky for comets and nebulae with a small telescope her brother William built for her. In 1783 she came upon this rich cloud of faint stars in Cassiopeia, and William entered it in his catalogue as H VI.30. It now bears her name: to many observers its loops of stars and dark lanes swirl like the petals of a rose seen from above.

At 1.4 to 1.7 billion years old, NGC 7789 is middle-aged for an [[open-cluster]]. It has a prominent crowd of red giants and an unusually large number of blue stragglers — stars that look younger than their siblings, probably rejuvenated by a companion.
NGC7789.tagline: Caroline Herschel’s rose: a rich, billion-year-old cluster whose loops of stars look like petals.

facts.text: A recent study suggests NGC 7790 and its neighbour Berkeley 58 may form a binary cluster, with matching motions, ages and speeds. Four Cepheids could belong to the pair.
facts.title: A double cluster?

story: Few star clusters contain even one Cepheid [[variable-star]], the pulsing stars astronomers use to measure distances across the universe. NGC 7790 has three: CEa Cas, CEb Cas and CF Cas. Because cluster members share an age and a distance, Cepheids like these help calibrate that cosmic yardstick. The [[open-cluster]] itself is young, 60 to 80 million years old, and lies in the Cassiopeia Milky Way close to NGC 7788.
NGC7790.tagline: A young cluster with three Cepheid variables — and perhaps a twin, Berkeley 58.

facts.text: Its X-ray source P13 was thought to hold a black hole. It turned out to be a pulsar spinning once every 0.42 seconds, circling a giant companion star every 64 days.
facts.title: A pulsar in disguise

facts.text: In 2008 Berto Monard found supernova SN 2008bk here. Its parent star, a red supergiant, had been observed just 547 days before it exploded.
facts.title: Seen before it blew

story: Some spirals have clean, sweeping arms. NGC 7793 has tufts. Astronomers call it a flocculent [[spiral-galaxy]], from the Latin for a tuft of wool: its arms are short, loose and broken, around a tiny bulge with a star cluster at its heart. James Dunlop found it from New South Wales on 14 July 1826. It is one of the five brightest galaxies of the Sculptor Group, one of the nearest [[galaxy-group|groups of galaxies]] to our own.
NGC7793.tagline: A tufted, patchy spiral in Sculptor, home to a pulsar once mistaken for a black hole.

facts.text: Its one known supernova, SN 2021rhu — the explosion of a white dwarf — was flagged in July 2021 by ALeRCE, a system that uses machine learning to sort the night sky’s changes.
facts.title: Found by a machine

facts.text: It is UGC 8 and PGC 218. Both catalogues run in order around the sky, and this galaxy sits just past their starting line at zero hours of right ascension.
facts.title: Low numbers

story: Behind NGC 7814 lies a crowd. Photographs of this [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on spiral]] show the sky around it packed with faint, remote galaxies, much like the famous Hubble Deep Field.

Astronomers have put that backdrop to work. Light from the distant galaxies must pass through NGC 7814’s halo on its way to us, and it arrives redder than it set out, because dust scatters blue light more than red. Measuring the change reveals how much gas and dust the halo holds.
Seen exactly side-on, it is also one of the few bright galaxies whose disc shows a modest warp and twist in visible light. William Herschel discovered it in 1784.
NGC7814.tagline: A side-on galaxy that works as a filter: light from distant galaxies behind it reveals the dust in its halo.

story: More than two thousand years ago the Greek astronomer Hipparchus recorded a hazy patch between Perseus and Cassiopeia. A telescope splits it into two rich clusters side by side, and NGC 869 is the western one. Each is an [[open-cluster]] of young, mostly blue-white stars.

Its name, h Persei, hides a puzzle. It is a [[bayer-designation|Bayer letter]], from Johann Bayer’s star atlas of 1603, and nobody is quite sure what he meant by it. Some argue that Bayer never saw the patch as two, and that his χ meant the whole Double Cluster and h a nearby star. Yet his chart of Cassiopeia does show the clusters as hazy patches.
NGC869.tagline: The western half of the Double Cluster, known since Hipparchus — and named by a small mystery.

facts.text: Julius Schiller’s 1627 star atlas Coelum Stellatum Christianum, put together with Johann Bayer’s help, labelled the pair Nebulosa Duplex: the double nebula.
facts.title: The double nebula

story: The two halves of the Double Cluster are not a chance line-up. NGC 884, the eastern half, and its partner NGC 869 are true neighbours in space, both part of Perseus OB1, a loose association of hot young stars. They formed about 14 million years ago — long after the dinosaurs died out, but long before the first humans.
To the naked eye the pair shows as a brighter knot in the winter Milky Way, a sight recorded since the days of Hipparchus.
NGC884.tagline: The eastern half of the Double Cluster: a family of young stars born 14 million years ago.

facts.text: NGC 891 appeared in the end credits of the TV series The Outer Limits, which is why it is sometimes called the Outer Limits Galaxy.
facts.title: The Outer Limits Galaxy

facts.text: John Carpenter’s 1974 film Dark Star features a piece called “When Twilight Falls on NGC 891”, and Edgar Froese’s album Aqua, from the same year, has a track named after it.
facts.title: Music of the sliver

facts.text: NGC 891 was chosen as the first-light image of the Large Binocular Telescope in 2005, and again for the Lowell Discovery Telescope’s Large Monolithic Imager in 2012.
facts.title: First light

story: If you could travel far out and look back at the Milky Way edge-on, it might look much like NGC 891. The two galaxies are similar in brightness and size, and some astronomers have noted how much our galaxy, seen from the Southern Hemisphere, resembles it. Like the Milky Way, it probably has a central bar.

Up close it is less tidy. Filaments of dust rise from its disc into the halo, perhaps flung out by exploding stars or pushed by starlight. Faint streams of stars loop around it — the remains of a smaller galaxy being torn apart and absorbed. William Herschel discovered this [[edge-on-galaxy|edge-on spiral]] on 6 October 1784.
NGC891.tagline: Our own Milky Way’s look-alike, seen edge-on — and a galaxy that found its way into songs and sci-fi credits.

facts.text: Robert McNaught, later famous for the Great Comet of 2007 that bears his name, discovered a supernova here in 1994. Another, SN 2006ce, was found by amateur Berto Monard in 2006.
facts.title: A comet hunter’s supernova

story: Something stirred NGC 908 up. This [[spiral-galaxy]] is forming stars at a furious pace — a starburst — and two of its three arms are oddly shaped, dotted with clusters of young stars. Both are signs of a close encounter with another galaxy, yet no culprit is anywhere to be seen.
William Herschel discovered it on 20 September 1786. It is the main galaxy of a small group with NGC 899, NGC 907 and IC 223.
NGC908.tagline: A spiral galaxy in a frenzy of star birth, shaken up by an encounter with a vanished partner.

facts.text: No supernova has been seen in NGC 925 yet, but in 2023 the ATLAS survey caught a luminous red nova here — the kind of outburst thought to happen when two stars merge.
facts.title: A merger’s flash

story: Everything about NGC 925 is a little off-balance. Its bar sits off-centre, and its southern spiral arm is much stronger than the ragged northern one — traits typical of Magellanic spirals, named after the Large Magellanic Cloud. New stars are forming all along the bar.

Attached to the galaxy by a streamer is a cloud of hydrogen holding ten million times the mass of the Sun. It could be a small satellite galaxy, debris from an old encounter or untouched gas left over from the early universe; nobody yet knows. William Herschel discovered this barred [[spiral-galaxy]] on 13 September 1784.
NGC925.tagline: A lopsided spiral with an off-centre bar and a mysterious cloud of hydrogen on a leash.

facts.text: The spiral NGC 941 appears close by, but the two galaxies are not interacting. Both belong to a small group linked with the larger group around M 77.
facts.title: Neighbours that never touch

story: A bright bar, a round nucleus and a ring of stars at the bar’s ends: to some eyes NGC 936 looks like a TIE fighter from Star Wars, so it has been called Darth Vader’s Galaxy or Darth Vader’s Starfighter. It is a barred lenticular [[galaxy]]. In 1986 John Kormendy measured the motions in its disc and found it stable, which is why it looks so smooth.
William Herschel discovered it on 6 January 1785 and, seeing a round glow, classed it as a [[planetary-nebula]].
NGC936.tagline: Darth Vader’s Galaxy: a bar, a ring and a bright core shaped like a TIE fighter.

story: Not every star cluster is real. John Herschel recorded NGC 956 on 23 December 1831 as a cluster of stars. In 2008 a study concluded it is only a chance alignment — stars at different distances that happen to line up, an [[asterism]] rather than a true [[open-cluster]]. A real cluster’s stars share a birthplace, an age and a path through space. These share only a direction.
NGC956.tagline: A ‘cluster’ that turned out to be a trick of perspective.

story: Less than 11 million years old, NGC 957 is a young, loosely bound [[open-cluster]] in Perseus — its stars were born long after the dinosaurs had gone. Loose clusters like this are gradually pulled apart by the Milky Way’s tides, their stars scattering into the galaxy. It also carries the name Collinder 28 and lies on the sky less than two degrees from NGC 884, half of the Double Cluster. John Herschel recorded it in 1831.
NGC957.tagline: A loose, young cluster on the sky next to the Double Cluster.

discovered.note: Its nature recognised by Knut Lundmark and Philibert Melotte in 1926

facts.text: In 2024 astronomers found WLM-CB1, a candidate contact binary of two massive stars touching each other — the first such pair seen in surroundings so poor in heavy elements.
facts.title: A first-of-its-kind star pair

facts.text: Hubble observations suggest that about half of all the stars in WLM formed in a burst that began some 13 billion years ago.
facts.title: Born in a burst

story: Max Wolf found this faint smudge in Cetus in 1909, but it took Knut Lundmark and Philibert Melotte, in 1926, to recognise what it was. Hence its triple-barrelled name: the Wolf–Lundmark–Melotte galaxy, or WLM. It is a small, barred irregular [[galaxy]] on the outer edge of the [[galaxy-group|Local Group]], far enough out to have been spared mergers with other galaxies. That makes its stars a ‘pristine’ sample, useful for comparison with busier galaxies.
PGC143.tagline: A lonely dwarf galaxy at the edge of the Local Group, named after the three astronomers who found and explained it.

story: Galaxies are rarely square, but Sextans A comes close. This small dwarf irregular [[galaxy]], on the outskirts of the Local Group, owes its shape to a chain reaction. Massive, short-lived stars exploded as supernovae; their blasts set off new star formation, which led to more supernovae, until an expanding shell had formed. Young blue stars now line its edges, and from Earth that ring of fresh stars looks roughly square.
PGC29653.tagline: A small dwarf galaxy with a strangely square shape, carved by waves of exploding stars.

discovered.by: Mike Irwin, Peter Bunclark, Mick Bridgeland and Richard McMahon

story: Even in 1990 the Milky Way still had companions waiting to be found. That year Mike Irwin, Peter Bunclark, Mick Bridgeland and Richard McMahon discovered the Sextans Dwarf, the eighth known satellite [[galaxy]] of our own. Like other dwarf spheroidals it is faint and diffuse, little more than a thin haze of stars. Its stars are old and poor in heavy elements — some of them strikingly so.
PGC88608.tagline: A faint, ghostly satellite of the Milky Way, found only in 1990 and full of old, primitive stars.

discovered.note: Earliest known mention: a 1954 paper listing it as the “Wilson Dwarf”

facts.text: Five planetary nebulae have been found in Sextans B, making it one of the smallest galaxies known to host them. It also has a massive globular cluster.
facts.title: Small but well stocked

facts.text: In November 2024 the ATLAS survey caught the first confirmed nova in this galaxy, now known as AT 2024aawe.
facts.title: A first nova

story: Sextans B sits right on the border of our Local Group, and may lie just beyond it. It first appeared in print in 1954, listed as the “Wilson Dwarf”. This small irregular [[galaxy]] pairs up with its neighbour Sextans A and has made its stars in gentle spells, separated by shorter pauses when star formation stopped. Its stars and gas contain very little of the elements heavier than helium.
UGC5373.tagline: A dwarf galaxy on the edge of the Local Group — one of the smallest where planetary nebulae have been found.

facts.text: One study suggested Leo I hides a black hole of about three million solar masses, comparable to the one at the Milky Way’s centre. Another found room for one of at most a few hundred thousand.
facts.title: A heavy heart?

story: Albert Wilson found Leo I in 1950 on plates from the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey. It sits just 12 arcminutes from Regulus, the brightest star in Leo — hence its nickname, the Regulus Dwarf — and the star’s glare still makes it hard to study. This dwarf spheroidal [[galaxy]] is one of the farthest satellites of the Milky Way.

It is also thought to be the youngest of the Milky Way’s dwarf spheroidal satellites. Most of its stars formed between 6 and 2 billion years ago, and star formation dropped off suddenly about a billion years ago — around the time it last swung close to the Milky Way and probably lost its gas.
UGC5470.tagline: A dwarf galaxy hiding in the glare of Regulus, one of the most distant satellites of the Milky Way.

facts.text: As the larger star of the inner pair keeps swelling, it is expected to begin pouring gas onto its partner within a few tens of millions of years.
facts.title: Due for a swap

facts.text: Chinese astronomers placed Acamar in Tiān Yuán, the Celestial Orchard, an asterism of twelve stars in Eridanus. It is the Orchard’s sixth star.
facts.title: The Celestial Orchard

story: Ptolemy’s Almagest, in the 2nd century, listed Acamar among the very brightest stars in the sky, and al-Sufi did the same in 964. Today it is a modest third-magnitude star. One suggestion is that its inner pair went through a long outburst, lasting perhaps a thousand years, as one star spilled gas onto the other.

That inner pair is remarkable in itself: two white stars, each more than twice the Sun’s mass, whirling round each other every four days. They are so close that tides pull them out of round, and as they turn, the light we see rises and falls. W. H. Wright detected the pair in their spectrum in 1905; in 2025 the GRAVITY instrument at the Very Large Telescope split them directly. A third white star, Theta² Eridani, completes this [[multiple-star]].

The name is a copyist’s slip. Arabic Ākhir an-nahr, ‘the end of the river’, became Acamar when ‘rn’ was misread as ‘m’. For the Greeks the river really did end here: Achernar, which carries the same Arabic name, never rose above their horizon.
acamar.tagline: The old end of the celestial river — a fine double whose inner pair may once have blazed far brighter.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star; first reported in Europe by Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser

facts.text: Precession kept Achernar so far south in ancient times that Ptolemy could not have seen it from Alexandria. It is the only first-magnitude star missing from his Almagest; Europe learned of it from Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser on the first Dutch voyage to the East Indies.
facts.title: Missing from Ptolemy

facts.text: Achernar is slowly moving north in our sky. Between the 8th and 11th millennia AD it will be visible as far north as Germany and southern England.
facts.title: Heading north

facts.text: The Wardaman people of Australia call Achernar Gawalyan, the echidna. To the Boorong people of Victoria it was Yerrerdetkurrk.
facts.title: The echidna

story: Achernar spins so fast that it is squashed: its equator is about 35% wider than its poles. As of 2015 it was the least spherical star known in the Milky Way, as flattened as the dwarf planet Haumea. The spin makes its poles far hotter than its waist — over 17,000 K against under 13,000 K — and a wind streams off the poles. Around its middle it throws off a disc of gas that grows, shrinks and sometimes falls back into the star.

It is a blue [[star]] six to seven times the Sun’s mass and about 3,000 times as bright — the hottest and bluest of the ten brightest stars in our sky. A smaller white companion circles it every seven years. Its name comes from the Arabic for ‘the end of the river’, the last star of Eridanus.
achernar.tagline: The end of the river — a hot blue star spinning so fast it bulges at the waist.

facts.text: Lying about a degree from the [[ecliptic]], it can be covered by the Moon and, very rarely, by a planet. Venus passed in front of it on 9 December 1906, and Jupiter on 13 May 1971.
facts.title: Hidden by planets

facts.text: Beta Scorpii is one of the stars on Brazil’s flag, where it stands for the state of Maranhão. A US Navy ship, USS Graffias, was also named after it.
facts.title: On the flag of Brazil

facts.text: One of the fainter stars in the family has an odd surface: unusually rich in manganese and strontium, yet surprisingly poor in other metals.
facts.title: Strange chemistry

story: Pairs within pairs: what looks like one star to the eye, and two in a small telescope, is really a family of six. The two heaviest, 15 and 10 times the Sun’s mass, whirl around each other every 6.8 days. Together they circle a third star every 610 years, while the fainter half of the visible pair turns out to be a triple of its own.

These are young stars, only around 6 to 12 million years old — born long after the dinosaurs died out. They belong to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, a loose family of thousands of young stars spread across the southern sky.
The name Acrab comes from al-‘Aqrab, Arabic for “the Scorpion” — once the name of the whole constellation. Its other old name, Graffias, comes from a Greek word for a crab.
acrab.tagline: A star named after the whole Scorpion — with six suns hidden inside it, nested in pairs within pairs.

discovered.note: Seen double by a Jesuit priest — the second binary ever recognised

facts.text: Acrux appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea. On Brazil’s flag it stands for the state of São Paulo, and it also features on the cover of the Brazilian passport.
facts.title: Five flags and a passport

facts.text: The heaviest star, about 17 times the Sun’s mass, is expected to swell into a red supergiant like Betelgeuse or Antares and then explode as a supernova.
facts.title: Destined to explode

facts.text: In Portuguese it is the Estrela de Magalhães, the “Star of Magellan”. Johann Bayer originally labelled it Zeta Centauri; Lacaille gave it the name Alpha Crucis in 1756.
facts.title: The Star of Magellan

story: Seven stars hide in the single point of light at the bottom of the Southern Cross. Its two brightest members are hot blue-white stars that take roughly 1,300 years to circle each other, and each of them is itself a close pair. A third, more distant member is a pair too, with a small red dwarf in tow. Together they make Acrux the 13th-brightest star in the night sky.

In 1685 a Jesuit priest noticed that it was double, making it only the second star system ever recognised as a [[double-star|binary]]. Its name is much more recent: the American astronomer Elijah Hinsdale Burritt coined “Acrux” in the 19th century by squeezing together its catalogue label, Alpha Crucis.

It lies so far south that it never rises north of latitude 27°. Yet because Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, the ancient Greeks and Romans could see it, counting it as part of the Centaur, and astronomers in ancient India named it Tri-shanku.
acrux.tagline: The brightest star of the Southern Cross, flown on five national flags — and home to seven suns.

facts.text: A seventh-magnitude companion sits close beside Adhara, but the main star is about 250 times brighter, so only large telescopes can split the pair.
facts.title: A companion lost in the glare

facts.text: Adhara appears on the national flag of Brazil, where it stands for the state of Tocantins.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Adhara is the seventh star of Hú Shǐ, the Bow and Arrow, a pattern that spans Canis Major and Puppis.
facts.title: The Bow and Arrow

story: Some four and a half million years ago, Adhara passed much closer to the Sun and blazed at about magnitude −4, as bright as Venus often appears. No star has looked so bright in our sky since, and none will for at least five million years.

Today it is a hot blue giant [[star]], shining with about 38,700 times the Sun’s light from a surface at around 22,000 K. That heat makes it the brightest source of extreme ultraviolet light in our night sky. No star does more to strip electrons from the thin hydrogen gas near the Sun, so it plays a big part in shaping the nearby Local Interstellar Cloud. It is massive enough to end as a supernova — and one study suggests it may itself be the product of two stars merging.
Its name comes from the Arabic for ‘the virgins’, a group it formed with Wezen, Aludra and a fainter neighbour.
adhara.tagline: Once the brightest star in Earth’s sky, by far — and still the strongest source of extreme ultraviolet we see.

facts.text: Albaldah lies close to the ecliptic, so the Moon can pass in front of it. On 17 February 2035 Venus will hide it, as seen from parts of Antarctica and southern Australia.
facts.title: Venus will cover it in 2035

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Albaldah belongs to Jiàn, ‘Establishment’, an asterism of six stars in Sagittarius. It is the third of them.
facts.title: Third Star of Establishment

story: Albaldah means ‘the town’, from the Arabic balda. A 17th-century star calendar compiled in Cairo called it the brightest of the town — Lucida Oppidi in its Latin translation. Long before that, the Akkadians may have counted it, with Zeta and Sigma Sagittarii, as Gu-shi-rab-ba, the Yoke of the Sea.

Heavy stars live fast. With nearly six times the Sun’s mass, Albaldah has already burned through the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a yellow-white bright giant — in only about 67 million years. The Sun, by comparison, is about 4.6 billion years old and still nowhere near that stage.

Look closer and it is a [[multiple-star|triple system]]. Two companions orbit within a fraction of an arcsecond of the main star, far too close for any amateur telescope, and nothing is yet known about their orbits.
albaldah.tagline: ‘The town’ in Arabic: a heavy, fast-living giant near the Teapot that Venus will hide in 2035.

facts.text: Albireo is heading our way. In about 3.87 million years it should become the brightest star in the night sky, peaking at around magnitude −0.5 some 4.6 million years from now.
facts.title: Tomorrow’s brightest star

facts.text: In 2023 the Gaia team found that the orange star is being tugged far harder than its known companion can explain. That companion may be a tight pair of its own — or a compact, collapsed star.
facts.title: A heavyweight in hiding

facts.text: In 2022 astronomers found another small star circling the orange giant every 371 days. It has only about 8.5% of the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: A new member in 2022

story: Nobody is sure the two stars of Albireo belong together. If they do orbit each other, a single lap takes at least 100,000 years. Some astronomers think they are a chance alignment instead, the two stars drifting in slightly different directions — and not even the Hipparcos and Gaia space missions have settled the question.

The [[star-colour|colours]] tell you what they are. The brighter, orange star is a cool giant many times wider than the Sun. The blue one is far hotter, with a surface of about 13,200 kelvins, and spins at least 250 kilometres a second at its equator.

Even the name is a puzzle. The 19th-century scholar Christian Ludwig Ideler traced “Albireo” to a garbled phrase, ab ireo, in a medieval Latin translation of Ptolemy — later given an extra “l” as though it were Arabic. Medieval Arabic-speaking astronomers had their own name for it: “the hen’s beak”.
albireo.tagline: A name born from a translator’s slip — and, millions of years from now, the brightest star in our sky.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers called the Pleiades Mǎo, the Hairy Head. Alcyone is its sixth star, Mǎo Xiù liù.
facts.title: The Hairy Head

facts.text: Lunar occultations once hinted that Alcyone had very close companions. A 2021 interferometric study concluded that it is a single star.
facts.title: Alone after all

facts.text: Because Alcyone is flattened by its spin, its poles are hotter than its equator. Averaged over the whole star, its surface is about 12,300 kelvins.
facts.title: Hotter at the poles

story: In 1846 the German astronomer Johann Heinrich von Mädler proposed that the stars of the Milky Way all circled one central body: Alcyone. He was wrong, but the star at the heart of his idea is remarkable enough. It is the brightest member of the Pleiades, the [[open-cluster]] named for the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione in Greek myth, and Alcyone was one of them.

Alcyone is a blue-white giant about 1,750 times as luminous as the Sun, and it spins so fast that it bulges: its equator is more than ten times the Sun’s radius, its poles only eight. The spin has flung off a disc of gas that circles its equator, making it a Be star, with bright emission lines in its spectrum. A 2017 study of Kepler space telescope data caught it flickering by just a thousandth of a magnitude, with a 2.3-day rhythm that is probably its rotation.
It is also a puzzle. The Pleiades are about 130 million years old, yet Alcyone looks younger — under 100 million. It may be a blue straggler, or the models may simply struggle with stars like it.
alcyone.tagline: The brightest of the Seven Sisters — a spinning, flattened giant once hailed as the centre of the Milky Way.

facts.text: Edmond Halley studied a record of the Moon covering Aldebaran, seen in Athens in AD 509. In 1718 he concluded the star had shifted since then — one of the clues that led him to discover that stars move.
facts.title: The star that moved

facts.text: Aldebaran lies close to the Moon’s path, so the Moon sometimes passes in front of it in an [[occultation]]. A run of 49 such occultations took place between 2015 and 2018.
facts.title: Hidden by the Moon

facts.text: Between 420,000 and 210,000 years ago Aldebaran was the brightest star in our sky, peaking at magnitude −1.54.
facts.title: Once the brightest

story: Aldebaran is a [[star]] in its final stages. More than six billion years old, it has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 45 times the Sun’s width, though it has only a little more mass. Its surface has cooled to about 3,900 K — the source of its orange glow — yet its sheer size lets it pour out over 400 times the Sun’s light. It turns slowly, once every 520 days.

Its name is Arabic for ‘the follower’: it seems to chase the Pleiades across the sky. It sits right in front of the Hyades star cluster, but is unrelated and far older. A faint companion star, far too dim for the eye, travels with it.
Its long history of measurements made it one of the benchmark stars used to calibrate the Gaia mission, and it was used before that to calibrate instruments on the Hubble Space Telescope.
aldebaran.tagline: The Bull’s fiery eye — an orange giant that only pretends to belong to the Hyades.

facts.text: Mars’s north pole points to the middle of the line joining Alderamin and Deneb — so the two serve as pole stars of a sort for the red planet.
facts.title: A pole star for Mars

facts.text: Ulugh Beg grouped it with Alfirk and Alkidr, two other stars of Cepheus, as al-Kawākib al-Firq, “the Stars of the Flock”.
facts.title: Stars of the Flock

facts.text: The Japanese light novel series Alderamin on the Sky takes its name from the star.
facts.title: A novel’s namesake

story: Alderamin is a contraction of the Arabic al-dhirā‘ al-yamīn, “the right arm”, of King Cepheus. It is waiting for a bigger role. As Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, the north celestial pole wanders among the stars, and around AD 7500 Alderamin will take over as the North Star.

It spins at least 246 km per second at its equator, turning once in under 12 hours; the Sun takes almost a month. The spin flattens it, so its equator is about 27 per cent wider than its poles, and leaves the equator near 6,600 kelvin against 8,600 at the poles.

This white [[star]] is just beginning to leave its long hydrogen-burning life and will probably become a red giant. Surprisingly for such a fast spinner, it gives off about as much X-ray light as the Sun, a sign of strong magnetic activity. It also pulses very faintly in two different ways at once.
alderamin.tagline: The king’s right arm — a white star spinning in under 12 hours, and a future North Star.

facts.text: As Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, the north celestial pole will pass within 5° of Alfirk. That makes it a candidate pole star of the far future, a title it would share with Iota Cephei.
facts.title: A future pole star

facts.text: Beta Cephei stars pulsate rather like Cepheid variables, but the engine is different: their beat is driven by iron deep inside the star, which traps and releases heat like a valve.
facts.title: Driven by iron

story: Every 4 hours and 34 minutes, Alfirk pulses, its light rising and falling by about a tenth of a magnitude. It became the model for a whole family of hot, massive [[variable-star|variable stars]] that beat in the same way — the Beta Cephei variables.

The pulsing star is young, just a few million years old, and many times heavier than the Sun — yet it turns lazily, once every 51 days or so. A smaller Be star circles it every 81 years, so close that it was only resolved in 1972, using speckle imaging.
Its name comes from the Arabic al-firqah, “the flock” of sheep. The 15th-century astronomer Ulugh Beg grouped it with Alderamin and Alkidr as “the stars of the flock”.
alfirk.tagline: A star that swells and shrinks every four and a half hours — the model for a whole class of pulsating stars.

facts.text: In 1911 Keivin Burns noticed Algenib’s spectral lines shifting back and forth. In 1953 D. Harold McNamara showed why: the whole star is pulsating.
facts.title: Caught by its spectrum

facts.text: Hot stars usually spin fast, but Algenib’s spectrum shows almost no rotation. Either it turns unusually slowly, or we are looking down on one of its poles.
facts.title: Slow spinner — or pole-on

facts.text: Chinese astronomers grouped Algenib with Alpheratz in the asterism Bìxiù, the Wall. Algenib is its first star.
facts.title: First Star of the Wall

story: Every 3.6 hours Algenib swells and shrinks. The change in its light is tiny — about a tenth of a magnitude — but it marks the star as a Beta Cephei [[variable-star]], one of a family of hot, massive stars that throb in and out. Slower rhythms ride on top of the fast one, so astronomers call it a hybrid pulsator.

Behind the pulse is a blue-white heavyweight of nearly nine solar masses, five and a half times the Sun’s width and about 6,000 times as luminous, with a surface hotter than 22,000 kelvins. Its [[spectral-type]], B2 IV, marks a subgiant: running low on hydrogen in its core and starting to leave the main sequence. In 2025 interferometers found a close companion, about which almost nothing is yet known.

Its name was once shared with Alpha Persei — a muddle the IAU settled in 2016 by naming Perseus’s star Mirfak. In Hindu astronomy, Algenib and Alpheratz together form the 26th nakshatra, or lunar mansion, Uttara Bhādrapadā.
algenib.tagline: A blue-white heavyweight at a corner of the Great Square, swelling and shrinking every 3.6 hours.

facts.text: William Herschel found Algieba was double in 1792. Even with 190 years of measurements, the orbit is uncertain: a 2025 estimate gives about 553 years per lap.
facts.title: An orbit still unpinned

facts.text: In 1959 Algieba was mistakenly published as an eclipsing binary. The cause was a typographical slip: the paper meant a different star, Y Leonis.
facts.title: A typing error

facts.text: Just 5′ away on the sky lies AD Leonis, a flaring red dwarf. It has nothing to do with the pair and is far closer to us.
facts.title: An unrelated neighbour

story: Both stars of Algieba are giants that have left the prime of their lives behind. Around 2 billion years old, each has been through a sudden “helium flash” and now quietly burns helium in its core. The brighter shines about 250 times as brightly as the Sun, its partner about 63 times.

In 2009 astronomers announced a planet circling the brighter star every 429 days, only a little farther out than Earth is from the Sun. It is a gas giant at least ten times the mass of Jupiter — perhaps even heavy enough to be a brown dwarf, a failed star, rather than a true planet.
The name is a small mix-up. It comes from the Arabic al-Jabhah, “the forehead”, yet the star sits in the Lion’s mane — which suits its old Latin name, Juba.
algieba.tagline: Two ageing giants in the Lion’s mane — and a planet at least ten times heavier than Jupiter.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Montanari first recorded its variability, and John Goodricke found the period in 1783

facts.text: Hebrew folklore called it Rōsh ha Sāṭān, “Satan’s Head”, and a 16th-century Latin name was Caput Larvae, “the Spectre’s Head”.
facts.title: Satan’s Head

facts.text: About 7.3 million years ago Algol passed close to the Solar System and shone at around magnitude −2.5 — far brighter than Sirius looks today.
facts.title: A brilliant past

facts.text: Joel Stebbins turned an early selenium-cell photometer on Algol, making the first photoelectric study of a variable star. It revealed the faint second dip, when the bright star hides its partner.
facts.title: First photoelectric light curve

story: Every few days the Demon Star loses about two-thirds of its light. Algol is two stars in a tight orbit seen edge-on: when the larger, cooler, fainter partner passes in front of the hot main star, Algol fades for about ten hours, then recovers. A third star circles the pair every 680 days. It is the namesake of a whole class of [[variable-star|eclipsing variables]].

Its name, from the Arabic raʾs al-ghūl, means “head of the ogre”, and it marks the severed head of Medusa in Perseus’s hand. Whether ancient stargazers knew it winked is unproven. Geminiano Montanari noted its changes in 1667, and in 1783 the British amateur John Goodricke found the period and proposed a dark body passing in front of it, winning the Copley Medal.
Algol also posed a riddle. Heavier stars age faster, yet here the lighter star is the more evolved. The answer is that it was once the heavier one, and poured much of its gas onto its partner.
algol.tagline: The Demon Star that winks every three days — two suns eclipsing each other in plain sight.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy the four bright stars of Corvus form Zhěn, the Chariot, one of the lunar mansions. Algorab is its third star.
facts.title: Third Star of the Chariot

facts.text: A 2006 search found no dusty disc around Algorab. A 2014 study did detect warm dust — but it was interstellar, not a disc of its own.
facts.title: Dust, but not its own

story: Algorab may be young or old, and astronomers cannot yet tell which. It shines about 69 times as brightly as the Sun — too bright for a settled star of its mass. Either it is a 260-million-year-old [[star]] running out of hydrogen in its core, or a newborn just 3.2 million years old, still shrinking towards adulthood. The same light tells two very different life stories.

Its name is simple: Arabic al-ghurāb, ‘the crow’, the bird of Corvus itself. In medieval Europe it was one of the fifteen Behenian stars of astrological magic, each paired with a gemstone and a plant, and the US Navy later named a ship, USS Algorab, after it.

In 1823 James South and John Herschel noticed a faint companion beside it. In two centuries the two have not shifted against each other, and they drift through space together — but their apparent ages differ, so they may not be true partners. Another faint star moving with Algorab may be its real companion.
algorab.tagline: The Crow’s own star — and a puzzle: an ageing star of 260 million years, or a newborn of three million?

facts.text: A Dutch ship named Alhena rescued many people from the stricken Italian liner Principessa Mafalda in October 1927.
facts.title: A rescue ship

facts.text: Alhena lies too far south of the ecliptic for the Moon to cover it, and planets usually pass several degrees north. But from August 2143 Venus will make a series of close passes, every eight years.
facts.title: Venus is coming

story: Alhena is a white [[star]] beginning to grow old. It is running low on hydrogen in its core and has started to swell into a subgiant — already about six times the Sun’s width, with 3.4 times its mass and 200 times its light, from a surface at about 9,200 K.

It hides a partner. Shifts in its spectrum reveal a companion about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, probably a yellow star like the Sun but heavier, swinging round it every 12.6 years on a very stretched orbit.
Its name comes from the Arabic al-han‘ah, ‘the brand’ on a camel’s neck; another old name, Almeisan, means ‘the shining one’. In China it is the third star of Jǐng, the Well.
alhena.tagline: The white star at the Twins’ feet — with a hidden partner on a 12-year orbit.

facts.text: In China Alioth is the fifth star of the Northern Dipper, and is also called Yù Héng, the Star of the Jade Sighting-Tube.
facts.title: The jade sighting-tube

facts.text: Alioth is one of the 57 navigational stars, and was long used by sailors in the maritime trade to fix their position at sea.
facts.title: A sailor’s star

story: Alioth hides an odd personality behind its plain white light. It is a ‘peculiar’ A-type [[star]] whose magnetic field — 100 times stronger than Earth’s — sorts the elements in its atmosphere into patches, including a dark band of chromium. Its magnetic poles lie almost at right angles to its spin axis, so as the star turns every 5.1 days, different patches swing into view and its spectral lines shift and change.

In 2008 a study suggested the five-day rhythm came from a hidden companion about 15 times Jupiter’s mass. Astronomers now think it is simply the star’s rotation, and no companion has been found. Alioth belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, a loose family of stars, including most of the Plough, that travel through space together.
Its name comes from the Arabic alyat al-hamal, ‘the sheep’s fat tail’. In India it was Añgiras, one of the Seven Rishis.
alioth.tagline: The brightest star of the Plough — a magnetic star whose strange spectrum shifts every five days.

facts.text: Since 1943 astronomers have used Aljanah’s spectrum as one of the fixed anchor points against which other stars are [[spectral-type|classified]].
facts.title: A yardstick star

facts.text: A 13th-magnitude star 78 arcseconds away shares Aljanah’s motion through space. If the two are bound, a single orbit would take at least 50,000 years.
facts.title: A distant follower

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the ninth star of Tiān Jīn, the Celestial Ford, a chain of nine stars strung across Cygnus.
facts.title: Ninth star of the Celestial Ford

story: Here is a glimpse of the Sun’s far future. Aljanah is only about 10% heavier than the Sun but roughly twice its age — some nine billion years old — and it has already been through its red-giant phase. A sudden helium flash ignited helium in its core, which it now fuses quietly, swollen to 11 times the Sun’s width and glowing a warm [[star-colour|orange]].

It does not travel alone. A hidden partner, never seen but given away by a wobble in Aljanah’s spectrum, swings around it every 53 years on a stretched-out orbit, closing to about the Earth–Sun distance and then pulling out about as far as Neptune is from the Sun.

Its name is Arabic for “the wing”: it marks one of the Swan’s outstretched wings. For centuries it was called Gienah, but so was a star in Corvus, so in 2017 the IAU settled on Aljanah, another rendering of the same Arabic word, for this one.
aljanah.tagline: A nine-billion-year-old orange giant — a preview of what the Sun will one day become.

facts.text: In Japan and Korea Alkaid is known as Hagunsei and Mukokseong, ‘the military breaking star’ — names that came from ancient China.
facts.title: The military breaking star

facts.text: A fossil starfish, Alkaidia, is named after the star.
facts.title: A starfish namesake

story: Alkaid is a hot young [[star]], only about six million years old and just starting its main-sequence life. With about five times the Sun’s mass, it spins at around 240 km/s, bulging slightly at the equator. Its surface, between about 16,300 K at the equator and 17,700 K at the poles, gives it a crisp blue-white colour.

Most stars of the Plough travel together through space as the Ursa Major moving group. Alkaid does not — it simply lies in the same direction. Since 1943 its spectrum has been one of the standards by which other stars are classified. Astronomers have looked closely for planets or companions, and found none.

Its name comes from the Arabic qā’id banāt na‘sh, ‘the leader of the daughters of the bier’. The four stars of the bowl were a funeral bier; the three handle stars were the mourning maidens, with Alkaid at their head.
alkaid.tagline: The tip of the Plough’s handle — a hot young star that does not travel with its neighbours.

facts.text: In Babylonian star catalogues, Almach and the stars of Triangulum formed a constellation called the Plough. Astrologers considered the star “honourable and eminent”.
facts.title: The Babylonian Plough

facts.text: The bright star is a massive giant that may be close to the end of its giant phase, though its surface chemistry lacks some of the signs astronomers would expect.
facts.title: Near the end of the giant road

facts.text: One medieval Arabic star catalogue listed it as “the fifth ostrich”, rendered in Latin translation as Quinta Struthionum.
facts.title: The fifth ostrich

story: In 1778 Johann Tobias Mayer discovered that Almach is double: a bright giant with a much fainter partner. Then the partner kept splitting. In 1842 Wilhelm Struve found it was itself a close pair, and spectra taken in the late 1950s showed that one of those is a pair too. What looks like a single star to the eye is a [[multiple-star|family of four]].

The innermost two are hot blue-white stars racing around each other every 2.67 days — and in 2026 observers found that they eclipse one another. That pair circles a third star every 64 years on a very elongated orbit, and the whole trio takes around 5,000 years to go round the giant.
The name comes from the Arabic al-‘anāq, the caracal, a desert lynx. Medieval astronomers writing in Arabic also called it the foot of the chained woman — Andromeda herself.
almach.tagline: Named after a desert lynx — a bright giant whose faint companion kept splitting until it was three stars.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the first star of Hè, the Crane, and that name gave rise to another English name for it: Ke.
facts.title: A name from China

facts.text: Alnair is one of the 58 stars selected for celestial navigation. Confusingly, a mid-20th-century almanac also gave the name Alnair to a different star, Zeta Centauri.
facts.title: A navigator’s star

story: Alnair is Arabic for ‘the bright one’, short for a longer name meaning ‘the bright one of the fish’s tail’. Arab astronomers counted the stars of the Crane as part of the Southern Fish; the Crane is a much younger constellation, and Alnair first appeared in a star atlas in Johann Bayer’s Uranometria of 1603.

It is a hot blue-white [[star]] about four times the Sun’s mass and roughly 520 times as bright, spinning at 215 km/s or more at its equator. It is young, perhaps 100 million years old, and belongs to the AB Doradus moving group — a family of young stars that travel through space together. Unlike so many bright stars, it has no known companions.
alnair.tagline: The bright one of the Crane — a fast-spinning blue-white star from a young family of stars.

facts.text: Just under a degree to the north is Gamma¹ Sagittarii, a pulsating Cepheid variable also known as W Sagittarii. It only looks close: the two stars are not related.
facts.title: A Cepheid next door

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Alnasl, Delta, Epsilon and Eta Sagittarii form Jī, the Winnowing Basket, one of the lunar mansions. Alnasl is its first star.
facts.title: The Winnowing Basket

story: Alnasl means ‘the arrowhead’, from the Arabic al-naṣl; another old name, Nushaba, means the same. To modern stargazers it is the tip of the spout of the Teapot, the [[asterism]] traced by the brightest stars of Sagittarius.

Older skywatchers saw birds. A 17th-century star calendar from Cairo calls it the first of the ostriches going down to the water: with Delta, Epsilon and Eta Sagittarii it formed a flock stooping to drink from the river of the Milky Way, while a second flock climbed back up. The Akkadians saw a swallow in some of the same stars.

The star is an orange giant, twice the Sun’s mass and twelve times its width. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it now fuses helium there, on the stage astronomers call the horizontal branch. Its surface is about 4,900 kelvins, some 900 degrees cooler than the Sun’s.
alnasl.tagline: The arrowhead of the Archer — and the tip of the Teapot’s spout.

facts.text: Alnilam is wrapped in a molecular cloud, NGC 1990, which it lights up as a faint [[reflection-nebula]].
facts.title: Lighting up a cloud

facts.text: Since 1943 Alnilam’s spectrum has been one of the fixed reference points for classifying stars — the standard for type B0Ia.
facts.title: A standard for blue supergiants

story: Alnilam is one of the most powerful stars you can see without a telescope. Estimates of its output range from about 275,000 to more than 500,000 times the Sun’s — its exact distance is hard to pin down. It is a blue supergiant [[star]] of roughly 30 to 40 solar masses, with a surface near 27,000 K, and only a few million years old.

In 2025 observations with the Very Large Telescope found it spinning close to its break-up speed, flattened so that it is 51% bigger around the equator than over the poles. Such a fast spin suggests that Alnilam was born when two stars merged. Its wind blows at up to 2,000 km/s, carrying off mass about 20 million times faster than the Sun loses it.
Its name comes from the Arabic al-niẓām, ‘the string of pearls’ — the Belt itself. Arab astronomers also called the Belt ‘the golden grains’; in China it was a weighing beam.
alnilam.tagline: The middle pearl of Orion’s Belt — a blue supergiant hundreds of thousands of times brighter than the Sun.

discovered.note: Companion reported in 1819; the star itself has been known since antiquity

facts.text: Alnitak is bathed in the glow of IC 434, the glowing [[emission-nebula|curtain of gas]] against which the dark Horsehead Nebula is silhouetted.
facts.title: Beside the Horsehead

facts.text: In China the belt formed the Three Stars mansion, one of the 28 mansions of the sky, in the White Tiger of the west. Alnitak was its first star.
facts.title: First of the Three Stars

story: Stars of the rare class astronomers call O are the hottest and bluest of all, and none in our night sky shines brighter than Alnitak. Its main star is a blue supergiant up to 33 times the Sun’s mass, pouring out some 21,000 times as much light. Stars like this live fast. In about a million years it will balloon into a red supergiant wider than Jupiter’s orbit, then explode — probably leaving a black hole behind.

It does not shine alone. In 1819 the German amateur astronomer George Kunowsky reported a fainter companion, which takes more than 1,500 years to complete an orbit. A third star, hugging the primary much more tightly, was confirmed only in 1998 by a team from Lowell Observatory, after hints in the 1970s.
The name comes from the Arabic an-niṭāq, “the girdle”. The belt itself has worn many names: the Golden Grains, the Scale of Justice and, in China, the Weighing Beam.
alnitak.tagline: The brightest of the hottest, bluest stars in our sky — at the end of Orion’s Belt and bound for a supernova.

facts.text: Alniyat is only 8 to 10 million years old. When it formed, the dinosaurs had already been gone for more than 55 million years.
facts.title: Younger than the dinosaurs’ end

facts.text: Chinese astronomers grouped Alniyat with Antares and Tau Scorpii as Xīn, the Heart. Alniyat is the Heart’s first star.
facts.title: First Star of the Heart

story: Arab astronomers saw two arteries beside the Scorpion’s heart: Sigma and Tau Scorpii, flanking red Antares. Alniyat, from al-niyāṭ, ‘the arteries’, is the northern one. To the Boorong people of north-western Victoria the two flanking stars were the wives of Djuit, the red star between them, and in Hawaii Alniyat was Au-haele, one of a line of three with Antares.

Up close it is a [[multiple-star|family of four]]. A blue-white giant of about 18 solar masses and a smaller partner whirl round each other every 33 days, too close to split in any telescope. A third star circles them over more than a century, and a fourth lies far beyond.

The giant also pulses as a Beta Cephei [[variable-star]], its surface temperature swinging by thousands of degrees with each beat of about six hours. The whole family belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, a vast group of young stars.
alniyat.tagline: One of the two ‘arteries’ beside the Scorpion’s heart — a young family of four stars, led by a pulsing giant.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Alpha, Beta and Sigma Arae form Chǔ, the Pestle. From this, R. H. Allen and later Patrick Moore gave Alpha Arae the name Choo.
facts.title: The Pestle

facts.text: An 11th-magnitude star appears about 50 arcseconds away, but the two are unrelated: their closeness in the sky is a coincidence of line of sight.
facts.title: A chance neighbour

story: Alpha Arae spins almost as fast as a star can. Its equator races round at about 470 kilometres a second, close to the speed at which it would begin to break apart. The spin squeezes the star into a pronounced bulge at its equator and throws off gas, so this blue-white [[star]] is wrapped in a disc of its own material: a Be star, with bright emission lines in its spectrum.

In 2003 and 2005 astronomers examined it with the Very Large Telescope Interferometer. They found a dense disc circling its equator, its gas orbiting the way planets circle the Sun — faster close in, slower farther out — while a wind of about 1,000 kilometres a second blows from its poles. There are also hints of a close companion.

The star has about 9.6 times the Sun’s mass and shines 5,800 times as brightly, from a surface of some 18,000 kelvins. Its light wanders between magnitudes 2.76 and 2.90, with quick, regular flickers and slower, irregular outbursts.
alpha-arae.tagline: The Altar’s spinning top: a blue-white star whirling so fast it is close to flying apart.

discovered.note: Found to be double; the star itself has been known since antiquity

facts.text: Proxima is a flare star that can brighten without warning. In August 2015 it flared to 8.3 times its normal brightness in blue light, the largest outburst on record.
facts.title: A flaring neighbour

facts.text: To the Boorong people of north-western Victoria, Alpha and Beta Centauri are two brothers who speared Tchingal, the Emu — the dark Coalsack Nebula.
facts.title: The two brothers

facts.text: Ptolemy listed it in the 2nd century, when it could still be seen from Alexandria in Egypt. The slow wobble of Earth’s axis has since carried it out of view from there.
facts.title: Lost from Alexandria

facts.text: Rigil Kentaurus may have a planet about as massive as Saturn in its habitable zone, though astronomers are not yet certain it is a planet.
facts.title: A planet in waiting

story: Two suns much like our own circle each other every 79 years, swinging between roughly the distance of Saturn from the Sun and that of Pluto. Rigil Kentaurus is a little heavier and brighter than the Sun; Toliman a little smaller and cooler. Together they make the third-brightest star in the night sky, outshone only by Sirius and Canopus.

Far out from the pair drifts a third member, the faint red dwarf Proxima Centauri — the closest star of all to the Sun. Robert Innes found it in 1915 and named it from the Latin for “nearest”. It has at least two planets, one of them Earth-sized and in the zone where liquid water could exist, though it is probably not habitable.
In December 1689 Jean Richaud, watching a passing comet from Puducherry in India, noticed that the bright star was double. It was only the third [[double-star|binary star]] ever found.
alpha-centauri.tagline: Our nearest stellar neighbours: two Sun-like stars and a little red dwarf with an Earth-sized planet.

facts.text: Alphard is on the flag of Brazil, standing for Mato Grosso do Sul — and it lent its name to the Toyota Alphard minivan.
facts.title: On a flag and on the road

facts.text: In ancient China it belonged to the great “red bird” of the southern sky, and it is the first star of Xīng Xiù, the Star mansion.
facts.title: Part of the Red Bird

story: Some stars are known by the company they keep. Alphard is known for having none. Arab astronomers called it al-fard, “the individual”, because no other bright star lies near it; a later catalogue named it Soheil al Fard, rendered in Latin as “the bright solitary one”. Tycho Brahe preferred Cor Hydræ, the heart of Hydra.

Alphard has left the prime of life. About three times the Sun’s mass and some 420 million years old, it has run out of hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant almost 58 times the Sun’s width. Its surface is cooler than the Sun’s, which gives it its orange colour.

Its light holds a puzzle: a mild excess of barium, which in other stars usually points to a white dwarf companion that once spilled material onto them. Its surface also quivers in rhythms of hours to days, much like the Sun’s, which lets astronomers probe its interior.
alphard.tagline: The Solitary One — a lone orange giant at the heart of Hydra, the sea serpent.

facts.text: Under the name Alphecca it was one of the Behenian fixed stars, a short list of stars prized by medieval astrologers.
facts.title: A Behenian star

facts.text: As the brightest star of the Northern Crown, it lent its name to Alphekka Meridiana, the brightest star of the Southern Crown.
facts.title: Namesake in the south

facts.text: Alphecca moves through space with the Ursa Major Moving Group, a loose family of stars sharing a common motion.
facts.title: Family ties

story: Alphecca is the bright gem in a small arc of stars, the Northern Crown. Its Arabic name is short for nayyir al-fakka, “the bright one of the broken ring”; in Latin it was Gemma, “jewel”. In one myth the crown is Ariadne’s wedding diadem, and a Latin name drawn from Virgil’s Georgics, Gnosia Stella Coronae, recalls her home at Knossos on Crete.

It is really two stars, circling every 17.4 days in an orbit we see almost exactly edge-on, so each takes a turn passing in front of the other. That makes it an [[variable-star|eclipsing binary]] like Algol, though the dimming is far subtler. The main star is white, about 2.6 times the Sun’s mass; its partner is a yellow star slightly smaller than the Sun.

That small partner is fierce: it gives out 30 times the Sun’s peak X-ray output, as expected for a young star. Around the white star, extra infrared light reveals a disc of dust, perhaps a planetary system in the making, like the one thought to surround Vega.
alphecca.tagline: The jewel of the Northern Crown — two stars that take turns hiding each other every 17 days.

facts.text: With Caph in Cassiopeia and Algenib in Pegasus, Alpheratz is one of the “Three Guides” that mark the prime meridian of the heavens.
facts.title: One of the Three Guides

facts.text: William Herschel recorded a faint companion on 21 July 1781. It is a chance alignment: that 11th-magnitude star lies far behind Alpheratz.
facts.title: Herschel’s false companion

facts.text: Old astrologers believed Alpheratz blessed those born under its influence with honour and riches.
facts.title: A lucky star

story: For centuries this star belonged to two figures at once. Ptolemy treated it as shared by Andromeda and Pegasus, and Johann Bayer gave it two labels, Alpha Andromedae and Delta Pegasi. Its name comes from the Arabic surrat al-faras, “navel of the horse”, yet when the official constellation boundaries were published in 1930 it went to Andromeda alone, marking the chained princess’s head.

To the eye it is one star, but it is two, circling each other every 97 days. Vesto Slipher caught the motion in its spectrum between 1902 and 1904; the fainter partner was only resolved in 1988–89 with an interferometer at Mount Wilson.

The main star, a hot blue-white star of about 3.6 solar masses, has a strange atmosphere. It is the brightest known mercury-manganese star, laced with far too much mercury, manganese, gallium and xenon. In its unusually calm outer layers some elements sink while starlight pushes others up, and the mercury gathers into clouds near the equator that slowly drift across the surface.
alpheratz.tagline: The star two constellations shared — the horse’s navel that became the princess’s head.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; found to be an eclipsing binary in 2000

facts.text: The eclipses were announced in 2000. Observers on the ground and NASA’s Galileo spacecraft, then at Jupiter, caught the star’s variations independently.
facts.title: Spotted from Jupiter

facts.text: With Kappa Velorum and two stars of Carina it forms the False Cross, a pattern so like the Southern Cross that it has caused errors in navigation by the stars.
facts.title: The False Cross

facts.text: In China it was Tiān Shè sān, the Third Star of the Celestial Earth God’s Temple.
facts.title: A temple star

story: Every 45 days, one star slips in front of another. Alsephina is really two white suns, each about two and a half times the Sun’s mass, whose orbit we see almost edge-on. That makes it the brightest known eclipsing [[variable-star|variable]]. A third, smaller star circles the pair once every 143 years.

Both stars spin so fast that they bulge at the equator. Their poles are hotter than their waists — about 10,100 kelvin against 9,700 for the larger star — so they would look brighter from above. We happen to see them side-on.

The name comes from the Arabic al-safīnah, “the ship”, once used for the whole of Argo Navis, the Argonauts’ vessel. By 1660 it had settled on this one star in Andreas Cellarius’s illustrated atlas Harmonia Macrocosmica. Precession will bring the south celestial pole close to it around AD 9000.
alsephina.tagline: The brightest eclipsing star known — two spinning, flattened suns that take turns to hide each other.

facts.text: In 1983 a group of Japanese scientists beamed a radio message towards Altair, hoping to reach anyone who might be listening.
facts.title: Calling Altair

facts.text: The Koori people of Victoria know Altair as Bunjil, the wedge-tailed eagle. The two stars beside it are his wives, the black swans.
facts.title: Bunjil the eagle

facts.text: Altair brightens and dims by a few thousandths of a magnitude, with several rhythms each under two hours long. It was classed as a Delta Scuti variable in 2005.
facts.title: A gentle flicker

story: Altair spins once in under eight hours; the Sun takes about 25 days. That whirl, faster even than Jupiter’s, flattens the star so that its equator is more than 20% wider than its poles. The poles are hotter and brighter than its middle, an effect called gravity darkening. In 2007 Altair became the first ordinary, hydrogen-burning [[star]] besides the Sun to have the details of its surface imaged, using the CHARA array of telescopes.

It is a young star of about 100 million years, with 1.8 times the Sun’s mass and 11 times its light. Its name comes from the Arabic al-nasr al-ṭā’ir, ‘the flying eagle’. In the Chinese and Japanese legend it is the Cowherd, Niulang or Hikoboshi, with the two stars beside him as his children — kept apart from his wife, Vega, by the river of the Milky Way.
altair.tagline: A star that spins once in under eight hours — so fast it has been squashed into a flattened ball.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Hú Shǐ èr, the Second Star of the Bow and Arrow, an asterism drawn from stars of Canis Major and Puppis.
facts.title: Bow and Arrow

facts.text: Two US Navy vessels, a stores ship and a cargo ship, were named USS Aludra after the star.
facts.title: Two ships

story: Aludra comes from the Arabic al-adhraa, “the virgin”. Arab astronomers grouped it with three neighbours in Canis Major — Adhara, Wezen and Omicron² — as the Virgins.

It has packed a whole life into less than 10 million years. Born with about 22 times the Sun’s mass, Aludra probably swelled into a red supergiant and has since shrunk back, shedding much of its mass along the way. Now a blue supergiant some 54 times the Sun’s width and over 100,000 times as luminous, it is in the final stages of its life.
