It is still losing about one solar mass every 8.3 million years to its wind, and it varies slightly over 4.7 days, an Alpha Cygni [[variable-star]]. Since 1943 its spectrum has been the standard for its [[spectral-type|spectral class]], the B5 supergiants.
aludra.tagline: The Great Dog’s tail — a blue supergiant that has probably already been a red one.

discovered.note: First measured as a double in 1755

facts.text: Serpens is the only constellation split in two, its head and tail on either side of Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer. A medieval Arabic catalogue called Alya simply “the serpent’s tail”.
facts.title: A constellation in two pieces

facts.text: A Sun-like star appears in the same part of the sky, but it is an impostor: much closer to us than the pair, and moving in a different direction.
facts.title: An impostor nearby

story: Matched in almost every way, the two white stars of Alya — each about twice the Sun’s mass — share a slow orbit. Both are hotter, brighter versions of the Sun, still steadily burning hydrogen: they give off 24 and 13 times the Sun’s light, with surfaces of around 8,000 and 7,600 kelvins.
They are in no hurry. Since the first measurements in 1755, their separation and angle on the sky have barely changed. One orbit probably takes something like 10,000 years.
The name comes from the Arabic ’alyah, the fat tail of a sheep. In China it belonged to the Left Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, where it stood for the ancient state of Xu.
alya.tagline: Twin white stars at the end of the Serpent’s tail, wearing a name that means “the fat tail of a sheep”.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star known to medieval Arab astronomers

facts.text: Medieval Arab astronomers pictured a boat here, not a bird. They called the star Nayyir al-Zawraq, “the bright one of the skiff”, Latinised as Cymbae.
facts.title: The bright one of the skiff

facts.text: When Chinese astronomers adopted the European southern constellations, Phoenix became Huǒ Niǎo, the Firebird, and Ankaa its sixth star.
facts.title: The Firebird

story: A phoenix rises from its own ashes, and this star’s name is a late arrival too. Ankaa, from the Arabic al-ʽanqāʼ, “the phoenix”, was attached to it only sometime after 1800, borrowed from the constellation itself — a southern figure first drawn after Dutch voyages at the end of the 16th century.

Ankaa is an orange giant, a [[star]] that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen. It is not alone. Regular shifts in its spectrum reveal a companion circling it every 3,849 days, about 10.5 years. The two are too close to see separately, which makes Ankaa a spectroscopic [[double-star|binary]].
ankaa.tagline: The phoenix’s brightest star — an orange giant with a partner on a ten-year orbit.

discovered.note: Companion first reported in 1819 but doubted; seen by James William Grant in 1844

facts.text: Research published in 2018 showed that the Ngarrindjeri people of South Australia noticed Antares changing in brightness and wove it into their oral traditions as Waiyungari, the “red man”.
facts.title: Remembered as the red man

facts.text: Venus last passed directly in front of Antares on 17 September 525 BC. The next time will be on 17 November 2400.
facts.title: Venus’s rare visit

facts.text: Early 20th-century astronomers saw its spectrum shifting and suspected an orbit. It turned out to be the star’s atmosphere pulsing; by 1928 they reckoned its size changes by about 20%.
facts.title: A breathing star

facts.text: Antares lights up part of the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex in front of it. The glowing patch is sometimes called the Antares Nebula.
facts.title: Lighting the clouds

story: Put Antares where the Sun is and its surface would reach somewhere out in the asteroid belt, engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. It is a [[variable-star|pulsating]] red supergiant, between 13 and 16 times the Sun’s mass, late in its life — a star that will one day explode as a supernova.

Its colour gave it its name. Antares comes from the Greek for “rival to Ares” — or, more bluntly, “not Ares” — because its reddish glow looks so like Mars. The name already appears in Ptolemy’s writings; Mesopotamian astronomers had called it the heart of the Scorpion.

A small, hot companion hides in its glare. Johann Tobias Bürg first reported it in 1819, during an occultation, but few believed him. James William Grant saw it from India in 1844, and Ormsby Mitchel found it again in 1846.
antares.tagline: Mars’s red rival — a supergiant so vast it would swallow the planets out to the asteroid belt.

facts.text: In 1635 Jean-Baptiste Morin turned a telescope on Arcturus during the day and saw it — the first recorded daylight sighting of any star other than the Sun and supernovae.
facts.title: Seen in broad daylight

facts.text: Comparing his positions with Ptolemy’s, Edmond Halley found that Arcturus, Sirius and Aldebaran had shifted since ancient times — the discovery that the ‘fixed’ stars move.
facts.title: The star that would not stay put

facts.text: Arcturus crosses the sky faster than any other first-magnitude star except Alpha Centauri. In antiquity it sat closer to the middle of its constellation.
facts.title: Fast across the sky

story: Arcturus is a [[star]] in old age. Around seven billion years old — older than the Sun — it has run out of hydrogen in its core and puffed up to about 25 times the Sun’s width. With roughly the Sun’s mass, it is a glimpse of the red giant our own star will one day become. Its cool surface glows orange, and it pours out about 170 times the Sun’s light, much of it as invisible infrared.

It is also just passing through. Arcturus has only about a third of the Sun’s share of heavy elements, a mark of an older generation of stars, and it races past us at about 122 km/s with a loose band of old stars called the Arcturus stream. It is almost at its closest to us now.
Its name is Greek for ‘Guardian of the Bear’: it follows the Great Bear around the pole. Ptolemy described its colour as slightly red, and Chaucer named it Alramih.
arcturus.tagline: The brightest star of the northern sky — an ancient orange giant just passing through our neighbourhood.

discovered.note: Found on the same night as Umbriel

facts.text: Once every 42 years, when Uranus’s moons orbit edge-on to us, they can pass in front of one another. On 19 August 2007, Umbriel was seen crossing in front of Ariel in a rare mutual [[occultation]].
facts.title: Moons in front of moons

facts.text: John Herschel suggested names for Uranus’s four then-known moons in 1852, at Lassell’s request — though it is unclear whether Herschel or Lassell actually picked them.
facts.title: Who chose the names?

facts.text: Ariel’s mass is roughly the same as that of all the water on Earth — our planet’s entire hydrosphere.
facts.title: The weight of our oceans

story: Ariel takes its name from two airy spirits: the leading sylph in Alexander Pope’s The Rape of the Lock, and the sprite who serves Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest. William Lassell discovered it on 24 October 1851, the same night as its neighbour Umbriel.

Made of roughly equal parts ice and rock, Ariel has the freshest-looking face of Uranus’s large [[planetary-moon|moons]]. Its old cratered plains are cut by scarps, canyons and ridges, signs of more recent geological activity than on its siblings. Tidal heating is the likely cause, perhaps from an ancient orbital resonance with Titania that has since broken.

Like Uranus itself, Ariel is tipped on its side relative to the Sun, so each pole spends 42 years in sunlight and then 42 in darkness. When Voyager 2 flew by in 1986 it was midsummer in the south, and only about 35% of the moon could be imaged.
ariel.tagline: Named after a spirit of the air — the Uranian moon with the freshest-looking face.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers grouped Arneb with three other stars of the Hare as Cè, the Toilet. Arneb is “the First Star of Toilet”.
facts.title: The First Star of Toilet

facts.text: Since 1943 Arneb’s spectrum has been one of the fixed anchor points astronomers use when sorting other stars by type.
facts.title: A yardstick star

facts.text: The US Navy named an attack cargo ship after the star: USS Arneb (AKA-56).
facts.title: USS Arneb

story: Arneb has lived fast. With 12 or 13 times the Sun’s mass, it is only about 13 million years old, yet it has already burned through the hydrogen in its core, ballooned into a red supergiant, and is now shrinking and heating up again — a late-life detour astronomers call a blue loop.

Even after shrinking it is huge, about 105 times the Sun’s width: set in the Sun’s place, its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mercury. At around 7,300 K, that surface glows the yellowish white typical of an [[spectral-type|F-type]] [[star]].
The name is simply Arabic for “hare”, matching the Latin Lepus.
arneb.tagline: A yellow-white supergiant that has already been red — the bright heart of the Hare.

facts.text: In the Calendarium of Al Achsasi al Mouakket the star was Thalath al Sadirah — “the third returning ostrich”.
facts.title: The third returning ostrich

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the first star of Dǒu, the Dipper — a group of six stars, five of which also belong to the Teapot.
facts.title: First star of the Dipper

story: The Teapot’s handle hides a family of three. Ascella’s two main stars are near-twins, each almost twice the Sun’s mass, whirling around each other about once a month — closer together than Mercury is to the Sun. A third, heavier star circles the pair every 21 years, making it a [[multiple-star|triple system]].

Their future could be dramatic. In about 500 million years the twins will swell into giants and end up sharing a single envelope of gas. They may then merge into one white dwarf, or settle down as a tight pair of them.

Ascella is Late Latin for “armpit”. Data from the Hipparcos satellite once suggested that about 1.2 million years ago it passed close enough to be the brightest star in Earth’s sky, but a 2023 study found its closest approach was much more distant.
ascella.tagline: Three stars in the Teapot’s handle — two of them twins that may one day merge.

facts.text: With Delta and Kappa Velorum and Epsilon Carinae it makes the False Cross. Navigators who took it for the Southern Cross went astray.
facts.title: A misleading cross

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Hǎi Shí èr, the Second Star of the Sea Rock.
facts.title: Sea Rock

story: Aspidiske means “little shield” in Greek, a translation of the Arabic turais; the Latin version is Scutulum. It rides on the old ship Argo, in the part now called Carina, the keel, and marks one corner of the False Cross.

It is a white supergiant about seven times the Sun’s mass, swollen to roughly 50 times its width and shining 4,900 times as brightly. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, it is now crossing quickly towards the red supergiant stage — a short-lived phase in which few stars are caught.

It is not quite heavy enough to explode. Instead it will most likely end as a white dwarf of about the Sun’s mass, much like Sirius B. Before then, precession will carry the south celestial pole close by, making Aspidiske a South Star around AD 8100.
aspidiske.tagline: The little shield of the ship Argo — a white supergiant and a future south pole star.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the third star of the Left Wall of the Purple Forbidden Enclosure, the walled region around the celestial pole, where it represents the Second Premier.
facts.title: The Second Premier

facts.text: When the IAU named the pair in 2017, Zeta Draconis became Aldhibah, “the female wolf”, and this star became Athebyne.
facts.title: The female wolf

story: Arab stargazers saw a small drama in this part of the sky. Athebyne and its neighbour Aldhibah, Zeta Draconis, were two wolves lying in wait for a camel’s foal — a faint star guarded by the Mother Camels. Athebyne’s name is a rendering of al-dhi’bayn, “the two wolves”.

The star is a [[star-colour|yellow]] giant of nearly three times the Sun’s mass. Heavier stars burn faster, so it ran out of core hydrogen after only about 650 million years; the Sun, about 4.6 billion years old, is still going. Athebyne has swollen to about 10 times the Sun’s width and shines 65 times as brightly.
A small orange dwarf, a K-type star, orbits it at least 140 times as far as Earth is from the Sun, taking at least a thousand years per lap.
athebyne.tagline: One of the Dragon’s two wolves, lying in wait for a camel’s foal.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star of the far southern sky

facts.text: Atria appears on the flag of Brazil, where it represents the state of Rio Grande do Sul.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: When Chinese astronomers adopted the European southern constellations, Atria became the third star of Sān Jiǎo Xíng, the Triangle.
facts.title: The Triangle

story: Placed where the Sun is, Atria would reach to, or almost to, the orbit of Venus: it is about 139 times the Sun’s width. Born only about 48 million years ago with some 6.4 times the Sun’s mass, it has already left the main sequence and swollen into an [[star-colour|orange]] giant — or perhaps a supergiant, as astronomers disagree. It shines with about 4,600 times the Sun’s light from a surface at around 4,600 K.

It also behaves oddly for such a star, flaring and giving off more X-rays than expected. A hidden companion may explain it: a young, magnetically active, Sun-like star circling Atria every 130 years or more.
Its name is simply a contraction of its catalogue label, Alpha Trianguli Australis.
atria.tagline: The bright corner of the Southern Triangle — an orange giant that would reach almost to Venus.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star; named Avior by HM Nautical Almanac Office in the late 1930s

facts.text: On its own, Avior’s blue-white companion would shine at magnitude 3.9, easy to see with the naked eye. Here its light merges with the orange giant’s.
facts.title: A hidden blue star

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Avior is the first star of Hǎi Shí, the Sea Rock, a pattern it forms with stars of Carina.
facts.title: The Sea Rock

story: Avior’s name was made up in the late 1930s. HM Nautical Almanac Office was compiling The Air Almanac for the Royal Air Force, and two of its 57 navigation stars had no classical names. The RAF insisted that every star must have one, so new names were invented: Alpha Pavonis became Peacock, and Epsilon Carinae became Avior. Donald Sadler, the office’s superintendent, told the story in his memoirs — but never explained what Avior means.

Its light comes from two stars too close to separate by eye. The brighter is an orange giant [[star]] that has left its youth behind and varies slowly. Its companion is a hot blue-white star, which may have a partner of its own; if so, that pair may eclipse each other every 785 days, dimming the system slightly.
avior.tagline: A star christened by the RAF — an orange giant whose name nobody ever explained.

discovered.note: Measured its record motion; it had already appeared on Harvard plates in 1888 and 1890

facts.text: Barnard’s Star is approaching at about 110 kilometres a second. Around AD 11,800 it will pass closest to the Sun — and still be too faint to see without a telescope.
facts.title: Heading our way

facts.text: Barnard’s Star e has at least 0.19 times Earth’s mass, making it the lightest exoplanet yet found from the wobble it gives its star.
facts.title: A featherweight planet

facts.text: In the 1970s the British Interplanetary Society’s Project Daedalus designed an uncrewed, fusion-powered probe to fly to Barnard’s Star.
facts.title: Target of a starship study

story: No star crosses our sky faster. In 1916 Edward Emerson Barnard measured its motion: 10.3 arcseconds a year, the highest of any known star. In a human lifetime it slides about a quarter of a degree — half the [[angular-size|apparent width]] of the full Moon. It is the nearest star in the northern half of the sky, and the nearest single star after the three of Alpha Centauri.

Yet it is far too faint to see with the naked eye. Barnard’s Star is a [[spectral-type|red dwarf]] with 16% of the Sun’s mass and about a fifth of its width, giving out barely a third of a percent of the Sun’s light. It is ancient, too — 7 to 12 billion years old — though it can still surprise: in 1998 it let off a powerful flare.

For decades it was a cautionary tale. From 1963 Peter van de Kamp claimed giant planets around it, until in 1973 other astronomers showed the signal was an artefact, linked to work on his telescope’s lens. Real planets were finally confirmed in 2024–2025: four small worlds, each less massive than Earth, all orbiting closer to the star than its habitable zone.
barnards-star.tagline: The star that moves fastest across our sky — an ancient red dwarf with four tiny planets.

facts.text: To the Inuit, Betelgeuse and Bellatrix high in the southern sky after sunset marked the coming of spring and longer days. They called the pair Akuttujuuk, ‘those placed far apart’.
facts.title: Those placed far apart

facts.text: In 1963 Bellatrix was one of the bright stars chosen to define the UBV brightness system, its magnitude fixed at 1.64. A 1988 survey then found that it varies slightly — awkward for a standard star.
facts.title: An unreliable standard

facts.text: The Wardaman people of northern Australia know Bellatrix as Banjan, the sparkling pigment used in ceremonies led by Rigel, the Red Kangaroo Leader.
facts.title: The sparkling pigment

story: Bellatrix is a hot blue [[star]] about 8.4 times the Sun’s mass and six times its width, with a surface at around 22,000 K — nearly four times hotter than the Sun’s. Heavy stars live fast. At about 28 million years old, it should run out of core hydrogen within another seven million years, then swell and cool. It may end in a supernova.

Its name is Latin for ‘female warrior’, and it was borrowed. The medieval writers Abu Ma’shar and Johannes Hispalensis used it for Capella; astronomers in 15th-century Vienna moved it to Orion. It was also called the Amazon Star.

It is no sibling of the Belt stars, either. Once thought to belong to their family, the Orion OB1 association, it turned out to be much closer to us than the rest — the nearest of Orion’s major stars.
bellatrix.tagline: The Female Warrior at Orion’s shoulder — a hot blue star with a borrowed name.

facts.text: Its old European name, Ke Kwan or KeKouan, comes from a French rendering of the Chinese Qí Guān, the Imperial Guards, a group in which Beta Lupi is the fourth star.
facts.title: A name via France

facts.text: Beta Lupi shifts across the sky by more than 50 milliarcseconds a year — a high proper motion that hints at a fast sideways speed through space.
facts.title: On the move

story: Just over a degree from Beta Lupi lies the wreck of the supernova of 1006, the brightest exploding star in recorded history. Beta Lupi may one day explode too. At about 8.8 times the Sun’s mass it sits close to the dividing line: it might die as a supernova, or settle down as a white dwarf.

For now it is a hot giant, around 24,000 K at the surface and about 25 million years old, nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life on its way to becoming a red supergiant. It also pulsates: it is a [[variable-star|Beta Cephei variable]] with several rhythms at once, the strongest repeating about every five and a half hours.
It belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest family of massive stars to the Sun, born together and still moving through space as a group.
beta-lupi.tagline: A pulsing blue-white giant beside the wreck of history’s brightest supernova.

facts.text: The combined light of the trio varies slightly, but nobody yet knows which of the three stars is responsible.
facts.title: Which one flickers?

facts.text: In 1988 speckle observations suggested the faintest star was itself double. Later infrared observations could not confirm it, so for now the count stays at three.
facts.title: A fourth that faded

story: Three stars in a nearly straight line, each more than a thousand times as bright as the Sun — and all three of the same unusual kind. Every member of Beta Monocerotis is a Be star: a hot blue-white star spinning fast and wrapped in a disc of glowing gas around its equator.

The heaviest, about seven times the Sun’s mass, shines some 3,200 times as brightly as our star. Its two companions are close behind, at about six times the Sun’s mass each. All three drift together across the sky and share almost the same speed along our line of sight — a real family, not a chance line-up.
William Herschel discovered the trio in 1781. To the naked eye they merge into one point of light, the brightest star in Monoceros, the Unicorn.
beta-monocerotis.tagline: Three hot, fast-spinning stars in a row — the brightest star of the Unicorn, all three of the same unusual kind.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; John Herschel noted its changes in brightness from 1836

facts.text: In 1920 Albert Michelson and Francis Pease measured Betelgeuse’s apparent width with an interferometer on the Mount Wilson telescope — the first star beyond the Sun whose disc was measured.
facts.title: The first star measured

facts.text: Betelgeuse probably has a small companion orbiting close in. Its discoverers named it Siwarha, Arabic for ‘her bracelet’; the name became official in September 2025.
facts.title: Her bracelet

facts.text: John Herschel saw Betelgeuse outshine Rigel in 1837 and 1839. Such swings may explain why Johann Bayer labelled it alpha, ahead of the usually brighter Rigel.
facts.title: Outshining Rigel

facts.text: Born among the stars of Orion’s Belt in the Orion OB1 association, Betelgeuse was flung out. It now ploughs through space at 30 km/s, piling up a bow shock of gas ahead of it.
facts.title: A runaway

story: If Betelgeuse took the Sun’s place, its surface would reach beyond the asteroid belt, engulfing the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. It is a red supergiant of between ten and twenty solar masses, less than 10 million years old — a star that has lived fast. Within about 100,000 years it should explode as a supernova, shining as brightly as a half Moon for more than three months, with no harm to life on Earth.

Late in 2019 it began to fade, and by February 2020 it had lost about two-thirds of its light. Hubble observations suggest why: the star threw out a vast burst of gas, which cooled into dust and veiled part of its face. It is a restless [[variable-star|variable star]] anyway, pulsing on a main period of about 400 days.
Its name is a medieval slip. The Arabic yad al-jawzā’, ‘the hand of al-Jawzā’’ (Orion), was misread in the 13th century — one letter for another — and Europe ended up with Betelgeuse.
betelgeuse.tagline: A red supergiant so vast it would swallow the orbit of Mars — and one day it will explode.

facts.text: Up close, Callisto’s high points are tipped with small, sparkly frost deposits, surrounded by a smooth, low-lying blanket of dark material.
facts.title: Sparkling frost

facts.text: In Greek myth Callisto was a nymph who hunted with the goddess Artemis. She was turned into a bear and placed among the stars as the Great Bear.
facts.title: A nymph turned into a bear

facts.text: Callisto is nearly as wide as the planet Mercury but has only about a third of its mass, because it is roughly half ice.
facts.title: Almost a Mercury

story: Callisto keeps a record of almost everything that ever hit it. Its surface is the oldest and most heavily cratered in the Solar System, nearly covered in [[crater|craters]], with no volcanoes or drifting plates to wipe them away. Giant bull’s-eye scars called multi-ring basins mark the biggest impacts, and chains of craters trail across the ice.

It is the outermost of the four [[galilean-moons|Galilean moons]], and the quietest. Unlike Io, Europa and Ganymede, it is not locked in an orbital resonance, so Jupiter’s tides barely warm it, and the rock and ice inside it never fully separated. Even so, the Galileo spacecraft found hints of an ocean of liquid water deep below the surface.

Its distance from Jupiter has one great advantage: it lies just outside the planet’s main radiation belt. That has long made Callisto the favourite site for any future crewed base in the Jupiter system.
callisto.tagline: The most heavily cratered world known — a battered ball of ice and rock, and the safest harbour at Jupiter.

facts.text: In 1153 the scholar Ibn Rushd travelled from Córdoba to Marrakesh to see Canopus, which never rose at home. He used the way its visibility changes with latitude to argue that the Earth is a sphere.
facts.title: A star that proved the Earth is round

facts.text: In 1592 the explorer Robert Hues listed Canopus as one of only three first-magnitude stars he had seen on his voyages that can never be seen from England. The others were Achernar and Alpha Centauri.
facts.title: Never seen from England

facts.text: Seen only rarely from Middle Eastern latitudes, Canopus gave its Arabic name, Suhail, a second meaning: something seldom seen.
facts.title: A rare sight

story: Canopus is a [[star]] in a late, restless stage of life. It has used up the hydrogen in its core, swollen to about 71 times the Sun’s width, and now burns helium instead. Nine or ten times the Sun’s mass, it shines with more than 10,000 times the Sun’s light from a surface at about 7,400 K — hot enough to look white.

Sirius only beats it because Sirius is so close to us. Over the past four million years Canopus has been the brightest star in our sky three times, and in about 480,000 years, once Sirius has drifted away, it will take the crown back for around 510,000 years.

Its name honours Canopus, the pilot of King Menelaus’s ship on the voyage to recover Helen of Troy — fitting for the leading star of the great ship Argo Navis, where it marked the steering oar. In India it is Agastya, after a revered sage. Chinese astronomers called it the Old Man of the South Pole, and in Arabic it is Suhail.
canopus.tagline: The second-brightest star in the sky — a white bright giant named after a legendary ship’s pilot.

facts.text: In 1919 John Anderson and Francis Pease split Capella’s giants with an interferometer at Mount Wilson — the first interferometric measurement of any object beyond the Solar System.
facts.title: The interferometrist’s friend

facts.text: Capella is one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky. Rocket flights picked it up in 1962 and 1963; the X-rays come mainly from the hot corona of one of the giants.
facts.title: A star that shines in X-rays

facts.text: Building J at Monte Albán in Mexico, built around 275 BC, faces the point where Capella rose. Its first dawn rising came within a day of the Sun passing directly overhead there.
facts.title: Aligned with a temple

story: To the eye Capella is one star. It is really four. Most of its light comes from two yellow giants, each about two and a half times the Sun’s mass, whirling round each other every 104 days — barely farther apart than Venus is from the Sun. Both have used up the hydrogen in their cores and swollen; the larger is about 12 times the Sun’s width. Far beyond them travels a second pair: two faint red dwarfs.

Its name is Latin for ‘little she-goat’: the goat Amalthea, who suckled the infant Zeus. Goat lore around these stars goes back to Mesopotamia, and Bedouin astronomers saw Auriga as a herd of goats. In classical times it was seen as a portent of rain.
In 1899 William Wallace Campbell at Lick Observatory saw two sets of spectral lines swinging back and forth in its light, proving it was a [[double-star|double]].
capella.tagline: One golden point, four stars — two yellow giants locked in a 104-day embrace and a distant pair of red dwarfs.

facts.text: With Alpheratz and Algenib it is one of the “Three Guides”: a line from Caph through Alpheratz runs south to where the Sun crosses the celestial equator at the equinoxes.
facts.title: The first Guide

facts.text: In 1572 a brilliant new star — the supernova now called Tycho’s Star — blazed out about five degrees north-west of Caph.
facts.title: Tycho’s Star

facts.text: In China Caph is the legendary charioteer Wang Liang himself, and the other stars of his asterism are his four horses.
facts.title: The charioteer himself

story: Caph is Arabic for “palm”. Long ago the whole W of Cassiopeia was al-Kaff al-Khadib, “the stained hand”, a hand dyed with henna, belonging to a vast figure whose head was the Pleiades. Over time the name shrank to this one star.

Caph is a yellow-white giant that has just finished burning hydrogen in its core. Once an A-type star of about twice the Sun’s mass, it is cooling and expanding on its way to becoming a red giant — a brief stage, so stars like it are uncommon. It pulses every 2.5 hours, a Delta Scuti [[variable-star]], and the fourth-brightest of its kind after Denebola, Vega and Altair.

It also spins fast, at about 92 per cent of the speed that would break it up, turning more than once a day. Its equator bulges about 24 per cent wider than its poles, and the poles are some 1,000 kelvin hotter. We see it almost pole-on.
caph.tagline: The tip of Cassiopeia’s W — a fast-spinning white giant that pulses every two and a half hours.

discovered.note: Possibly seen as two points of light by Cassini as early as 1678

facts.text: James Pound first recorded Castor as double in 1718, though Cassini may have seen it as two points of light as early as 1678.
facts.title: Split in 1718

facts.text: Over a human lifetime you can watch the orbit unfold: the two bright stars were about 2″ apart on the sky in 1970, and about 6″ in 2026.
facts.title: Drifting apart

facts.text: Arabic star lore called it the head of the foremost twin. In China it was the second star of the North River, alongside Pollux.
facts.title: The foremost twin

story: [[multiple-star|Six suns]] hide inside Castor’s single point of light. Two bright white stars, both heavier and brighter than the Sun, each have a small red dwarf whipping around them every few days. Farther out, a third pair of red dwarfs, Castor C, completes its orbit in less than a day, and that pair in turn circles the others over several thousand years.

Castor C is a lively couple. Its two near-identical red dwarfs eclipse one another, while starspots and sudden flares make their light flicker — every red dwarf in the system is a flare star. Since 2018 astronomers have suspected that a brown dwarf at least 49 times Jupiter’s mass circles them every 50 years.

Castor is named after one of the twin sons of Zeus and Leda in Greek myth. With his brother Pollux he gives Gemini, Latin for “twins”, its name. Oddly, Castor carries the Alpha label even though Pollux shines half a magnitude brighter.
castor.tagline: One of the Heavenly Twins — with six stars, in three pairs, hidden inside its single point of light.

facts.text: The US Navy named a Crater-class cargo ship after the star, using one of its other names: USS Cheleb (AK-138).
facts.title: USS Cheleb

facts.text: Cebalrai belongs to the galaxy’s thin disc. It follows a nearly circular path around the Milky Way that never takes it far from the galaxy’s midplane.
facts.title: A calm orbit

story: Cebalrai is younger than the Sun — about 2.75 billion years old, 60% of the Sun’s age — yet it is already a giant. Stars with more mass race through their lives, and this one has used up its core hydrogen and swollen to about 12 times the Sun’s width, shining 58 times as brightly from a cool [[star-colour|orange]] surface near 4,560 K.
It is gently restless. Its surface probably moves in and out on a 142-day rhythm, picked up as a shifting speed in its spectrum, and its brightness changes by just two hundredths of a magnitude.
Its name comes from the Arabic kalb al-rā‘ī, “the shepherd’s dog”, the source too of variants such as Cheleb and Kelb Alrai.
cebalrai.tagline: The shepherd’s dog — an orange giant younger than the Sun.

facts.text: Its 2006 maximum reached magnitude 3.8, the brightest for over a century. Less than ten years later, the 2015 maximum barely reached 6.5 — perhaps the faintest ever seen.
facts.title: Brightest in a century

facts.text: Flamsteed catalogued a star as Bayer’s Chi Cygni when Chi was probably too faint to see, so he had in fact recorded another star. Nobody noticed until 1816.
facts.title: A star that went missing

facts.text: By measuring how fast layers of its atmosphere rise and fall, astronomers weighed Chi Cygni at about 2.1 times the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: Weighed by its own pulse

story: In 1686 the German astronomer Gottfried Kirch was searching that part of the sky for observations of Nova Vulpeculae when he noticed that a star marked on Bayer’s atlas, Chi Cygni, was missing. He kept watching, and on 19 October 1686 it reappeared at 5th magnitude. He had found one of the most extreme [[variable-star|variable stars]] in the sky.

At its extremes Chi Cygni has climbed to magnitude 3.3 and sunk to 14.2, over cycles of about 409 days — yet its total energy output changes far less. It is a pulsating red giant near the end of its life, swelling from about 350 to 480 times the Sun’s radius. As it cools, molecules form that soak up visible light, and more of its glow shifts into the infrared.

It is also an S-type star, its spectrum marked by zirconium oxide and by technetium — an element with no stable form, which must have been forged inside the star itself. And it was the first Mira variable in which a magnetic field was detected.
chi-cygni.tagline: A star whose brightness can swing more than ten-thousand-fold — one of the widest ranges of any pulsating star.

facts.text: Some books say Scarborough suggested the name to Edmond Halley. That story first appears in a report published in 1801 and seems to have no other support.
facts.title: Halley’s name?

facts.text: Cor Caroli marks the northern point of the Great Diamond, a large asterism also known as the Diamond of Virgo.
facts.title: Top of the Diamond

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the first star of Cháng Chén, the Imperial Guards — the source of another name, Chang Chen.
facts.title: The Imperial Guards

story: “Charles’s Heart” — the name comes from the turbulent England of the 1600s. In 1660 Sir Charles Scarborough, physician to Charles II, claimed the star shone with unusual brightness on the night the king returned to England. Yet the first star map to show the name, Francis Lamb’s chart of 1673, labels it “the heart of Charles the martyred king” — meaning his father, Charles I, executed in 1649.

The star itself is just as unusual. Its brighter member has a magnetic field about 5,000 times as strong as Earth’s, and an atmosphere oddly rich in silicon, mercury and europium, as some elements sink under gravity while others are pushed up by the pressure of light. Its magnetism is thought to create enormous spots, so its brightness changes as it turns, every 5.47 days. It is the prototype of a whole class of [[variable-star|variable stars]].
Its fainter partner is an ordinary yellow-white star. The two take roughly 8,000 years to complete one orbit.
cor-caroli.tagline: A star named for a king’s heart — and a magnetic oddball with an atmosphere full of rare metals.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers saw Cursa and three nearby stars — two in Eridanus and one in Orion — as Yù Jǐng, the Jade Well. Cursa is its third star.
facts.title: The Jade Well

facts.text: An 11th-magnitude star 2 arcminutes away looks like a partner, but it is only an optical companion, lined up by chance.
facts.title: A chance companion

story: Orion has a footstool. Cursa takes its name from the Arabic Al Kursiyy al Jauzah, “the chair (or footstool) of the central one” — the central one being Orion. The name once belonged to a small group of stars beside the hunter’s foot: Cursa, two fainter stars of Eridanus and Tau Orionis.
Cursa is a hot white [[star]] near 8,360 K that has used up the hydrogen in its core. It spins at 196 kilometres per second or more — nearly 100 times the speed of the Sun’s equator.

Its light is not quite steady: it [[variable-star|varies]] between magnitudes 2.72 and 2.80, and a particularly strong flare-up was reported in 1985. Its path through space suggests it may belong to the Ursa Major family of stars, though its colours hint that it could be an interloper.
cursa.tagline: Orion’s footstool — a fast-spinning white star at the head of the River.

facts.text: Henry Madan, a science master at Eton, took the names from Book XV of Homer’s Iliad, where Ares summons Dread (Deimos) and Fear (Phobos).
facts.title: Fear and Dread

facts.text: No one knows how Mars got its moons. They may be captured asteroids, or the pieces of a single parent body shattered between one and 2.7 billion years ago.
facts.title: Born from one body?

facts.text: The escape velocity of Deimos is only 5.6 m/s, about 20 km/h — so a well-thrown ball would leave it for ever.
facts.title: Throw a ball into space

story: Long before anyone saw them, writers gave Mars two moons. In Gulliver’s Travels, published in 1726, Jonathan Swift had the astronomers of Laputa discover a pair of them, and Voltaire repeated the idea. Then, in August 1877, Asaph Hall, searching specifically for Martian moons, found Deimos. Its only two named features are craters called Swift and Voltaire.

Deimos is a tiny grey lump of carbon-rich rock, its craters softened by a blanket of loose dust. From Mars it would look almost like a star, yet at its brightest it would shine like Venus does for us. It rises in the east and takes about two and a half days to cross the sky, and from time to time it slides across the Sun as a small black dot — a miniature [[transit]].
Unlike Phobos, which is falling inward, Deimos is slowly moving outward. One day it is expected to escape Mars altogether.
deimos.tagline: Mars’s smaller moon — named for dread, imagined by satirists, and slowly drifting away.

facts.text: Delta Cephei was only the second star of its kind to be found. Eta Aquilae had been caught varying a few weeks earlier, on 10 September 1784.
facts.title: Beaten by weeks

facts.text: Its wide companion is itself a pair of hot stars. Their light heats the gas blown off by Delta Cephei, making the surrounding cloud glow in infrared.
facts.title: A glowing cloud

facts.text: A small star about a tenth of Delta Cephei’s mass also circles it every six years, coming within about twice Earth’s distance from the Sun.
facts.title: A hidden partner

story: On 19 October 1784 a young deaf astronomer, John Goodricke, began watching Delta Cephei, and kept at it most nights until late December. Its light rose and fell in a regular rhythm, brightening quickly and fading more slowly. The star went on to give its name to the Cepheids, a whole class of pulsating [[variable-star|variable stars]].

That rhythm turned out to be one of the most useful things in astronomy. At Harvard, Henrietta Leavitt found that a Cepheid’s period reveals its true brightness, so comparing it with how bright the star looks gives its distance. Edwin Hubble later used Cepheids to show that other galaxies lie far beyond the Milky Way. Delta Cephei, one of the nearest Cepheids, helps calibrate that scale.

The star itself is restless. About five times the Sun’s mass and some 1,900 times as luminous, it swells and shrinks with every pulse, and its wind blows away roughly a Sun’s worth of gas every million years, building a cloud around it.
delta-cephei.tagline: The star that gave Cepheids their name — the cosmic yardstick that measured the universe.

facts.text: Earth’s wobbling axis will bring the north celestial pole within about 7° of Deneb around AD 9800.
facts.title: A future pole star

facts.text: The north pole of Mars points to a spot halfway between Deneb and the star Alderamin.
facts.title: Mars’s pole star

facts.text: Deneb has gathered many names. The German poet Philippus Caesius called it Os rosae, and also Uropygium — the parson’s nose.
facts.title: The parson’s nose

story: Deneb looks modest beside Vega, yet it is in another league. It is a white supergiant of about 19 solar masses, shining with somewhere between 55,000 and 196,000 times the Sun’s light — its distance is so uncertain that nobody knows exactly. Put in the Sun’s place, it would reach at least to the orbit of Mercury, perhaps to Earth’s. It may be the most distant of the 30 brightest stars.

It began as a hot blue star of about 23 solar masses and has already used up its core hydrogen. A strong wind strips away roughly an Earth’s worth of gas every 500 years, and within a few million years it will explode as a supernova. Meanwhile it flickers irregularly: Deneb is the prototype of the Alpha Cygni [[variable-star|variable stars]].
Its name comes from the Arabic for ‘tail’, from dhanab al-dajājah, ‘the tail of the hen’.
deneb.tagline: The tail of the Swan — a supergiant tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Olin J. Eggen discovered its eclipses in 1956

facts.text: Medieval astrologers counted it among the fifteen Behenian stars, linking it with the gemstone chalcedony and the herb marjoram.
facts.title: A Behenian star

facts.text: The brighter star turns at about 105 kilometres per second, in time with the orbit — unusually fast for a star with its peculiar, metal-rich spectrum.
facts.title: Spinning in step

facts.text: Lying just south of the ecliptic, it can be hidden by the Moon in an [[occultation]]; such events were observed in 1951, 1962 and 1988.
facts.title: Hidden by the Moon

story: Every 24½ hours, Deneb Algedi blinks. Two stars circle each other so tightly, and so nearly edge-on to us, that each passes in front of the other in turn. It is the nearest known [[variable-star|eclipsing binary]].

Its secrets came out in stages. Vesto Slipher found from its spectrum in 1906 that it was double; Clifford Crump worked out the orbit in 1921 from 69 measurements at Yerkes Observatory; and only in 1956 did Olin Eggen, at Lick Observatory, catch the eclipses.

The pair has a tangled past. The brighter star, about twice the Sun’s mass, is heavier than models predict, and its smaller partner is bloated — signs that gas once flowed between them. The name is Arabic for “the tail of the goat”: the fish-like tail of the Sea Goat.
deneb-algedi.tagline: The Sea Goat’s tail — the nearest known eclipsing binary, blinking every 24½ hours.

facts.text: Denebola shares its motion through space with more than sixty stars, including the open cluster IC 2391. They may once have been born together.
facts.title: A scattered family

facts.text: Ancient Chinese astronomers made it the first star of the “Seat of the Five Emperors”, a five-star asterism.
facts.title: Seat of the Five Emperors

story: Denebola is short for Deneb Alased, Arabic for “tail of the lion”. Medieval writers linked it with the weather: Ulugh Beg called it al-Ṣarfah, “the Changer”, and al-Biruni wrote that its rising ends the heat and its setting ends the cold.

It is a young white [[star]], less than 400 million years old, with 75 per cent more mass than the Sun and 15 times its luminosity. It spins fast — about 128 km per second at its equator, against the Sun’s 2 — enough to squash it into a flattened ball. It also flickers very slightly, about ten times a day, as a Delta Scuti [[variable-star]].

Around it orbits a disc of cold dust at about −153 °C, lying roughly as far from the star as Pluto is from the Sun; the Herschel Space Observatory imaged it. Our own Solar System formed from such a disc, so Denebola, like Vega, is a place where planets might be found.
denebola.tagline: The Lion’s tail — a young, fast-spinning white star ringed by a disc of cold dust.

facts.text: Two small trojan moons, Helene and Polydeuces, share Dione’s orbit, riding 60° ahead of it and 60° behind.
facts.title: Two moons along for the ride

facts.text: Dione’s ridge Janiculum Dorsa rises about 1.5 km, and the crust sags beneath it in a way most easily explained by liquid water below.
facts.title: A ridge that bends the crust

facts.text: Apart from being somewhat smaller and denser, Dione is very like Rhea: both have bright ice cliffs, and both have leading and trailing sides that look quite different.
facts.title: Rhea’s smaller sibling

story: When Voyager 1 photographed Dione in 1980, one side of the moon was laced with bright, wispy streaks. Nobody knew what they were. The favourite idea was frost or ash from ancient eruptions, sprayed out along cracks. Then, in December 2004, Cassini took a close look. The wisps were not deposits at all, but bright cliffs of ice, some several hundred metres high, lining enormous fractures in the crust.

Saturn’s fourth-largest [[planetary-moon|moon]] is roughly half rock and half ice. It orbits Saturn at almost the same distance as our Moon orbits Earth, yet goes round ten times as fast, because Saturn is so much more massive. It also keeps its neighbour busy: for every orbit Dione makes, Enceladus makes two, and that steady rhythm helps heat Enceladus and power its geysers. Dione may even hide an ocean of its own.
dione.tagline: An icy moon whose mysterious ‘wispy’ streaks turned out to be cliffs of ice.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers called it Tǔsīkōng, the Master of Constructions — “Superintendent of Earthworks” in R. H. Allen’s rendering. It stands alone in its own asterism.
facts.title: Superintendent of Earthworks

facts.text: The Latin form of its name, Rana Secunda (“second frog”), gave the name Rana to another star, Delta Eridani.
facts.title: A frog that named a star

story: Its Arabic name means “the second frog”. The first frog is Fomalhaut, and the two sit in a dark, sparse stretch of sky. Diphda has a second name, Deneb Kaitos, “the southern tail of the whale”, and despite its “beta” label it is the brightest star in Cetus — half a magnitude brighter than Menkar, the “alpha”.

Diphda was born as a hot blue-white star of about three and a half solar masses. It has since swollen into an orange giant some 18 times wider than the Sun and 150 times as luminous. Now it quietly fuses helium in its core, a stage that will last more than 100 million years.

It is not as calm as it looks. Diphda throws flares that brighten it for several days at a time — far longer than the Sun’s, which last hours. In 2005 the XMM-Newton observatory found it shining in X-rays about 2,000 times more strongly than the Sun, enough for Chandra to take its picture.
diphda.tagline: The second frog — a “beta” star that outshines its constellation’s “alpha”.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Otero spotted its outburst in June 2000

facts.text: In 1981 Voyager 2 watched Dschubba through Saturn’s rings. Its light was dimmed even in the apparently empty gaps, showing that there is very little empty space anywhere in the main rings.
facts.title: Seen through Saturn’s rings

facts.text: Dschubba belongs to the Upper Scorpius group: thousands of young stars with an average age of about 11 million years.
facts.title: A young family

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Fáng Xiù sān, the Third Star of the Room, an asterism shared with Acrab and its neighbours.
facts.title: The Room

story: For generations Dschubba was a steady star in the arc of the Scorpion’s head; its name comes from the Arabic for “the forehead of the scorpion”. Then in June 2000 Sebastian Otero noticed it was a tenth of a magnitude brighter than normal. Since then it has climbed to at least magnitude 1.6, altering the familiar look of Scorpius.

The cause is spin. Dschubba is a hot blue-white subgiant turning so fast that it throws off glowing gas from its equator into a disc. That makes it a Gamma Cassiopeiae [[variable-star]], like the star at the centre of Cassiopeia’s W. A companion swings around it every 10.5 years on a very elongated orbit, and at its close pass in July 2011 Dschubba peaked again, near magnitude 1.65.
Astronomers once used its spectrum as the standard for its class, but it is now considered too unusual and changeable for the job.
dschubba.tagline: The Scorpion’s forehead — a steady star that flared up in 2000 and changed the shape of Scorpius.

facts.text: Dubhe is the official state star of Utah.
facts.title: Utah’s star

facts.text: Dubhe varies by about a thousandth of a magnitude — far too little to see. Astronomers have found ten different oscillations in it, with periods from 6.4 hours to 6.4 days.
facts.title: A faint flutter

story: Dubhe is the odd one out in the Plough. Most of the pattern’s stars travel through space together as the Ursa Major moving group; Dubhe does not. It differs in colour, too: an orange giant [[star]] of 3.7 solar masses and 280 million years, it has used up its core hydrogen and swollen to 27 times the Sun’s width, shining with 340 times the Sun’s light.
Close beside it, too near to see apart, a hot white star circles it every 44.5 years. Another close pair of stars a few arcminutes away belongs to the same system, making four stars in all.

Its name comes from the Arabic for ‘bear’, from a phrase meaning ‘the back of the Greater Bear’. The ancient Egyptians called it Ak, ‘the Eye’. In India it was Kratu, one of the Seven Rishis, and in China Tiān Shū, the Celestial Pivot.
dubhe.tagline: The Plough’s outer pointer — an orange giant that shows the way to the North Star.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Elnath is the fifth star of the Five Chariots, a pattern it shares with Capella and other stars of Auriga.
facts.title: Five Chariots

facts.text: Elnath lies close enough to the Moon’s path to be occulted. Most of these events are visible only from the Southern Hemisphere, but they occasionally reach as far north as southern California.
facts.title: Hidden by the Moon

story: Elnath lives on a border. Ptolemy counted it as part of both Taurus and Auriga, and Johann Bayer gave it two labels, Beta Tauri and Gamma Aurigae. Only when constellation boundaries were fixed in 1930 did it settle in Taurus, at the tip of the Bull’s northern horn. Its name is Arabic for ‘the butting’ — the Bull’s horns.

It is a blue-white giant [[star]], about 700 times as luminous as the Sun and nearly five times its width. Its light carries a chemical oddity. It is a mercury-manganese star, with unusually strong signs of some heavy elements: plenty of manganese, but little calcium and magnesium. Its mercury lines are weak, though, so some astronomers file it under other peculiar types.
elnath.tagline: The tip of the Bull’s horn — a star once shared with the Charioteer, with an odd taste for manganese.

facts.text: Regular shifts in its spectrum were once blamed on an orbiting planet. They turned out to come from the star itself — a warning for planet hunters studying other giants, such as Aldebaran.
facts.title: A planet that wasn’t

facts.text: Ursula K. Le Guin set her novel Planet of Exile on the third planet of Eltanin.
facts.title: Le Guin’s world

facts.text: Arab astronomers saw Eltanin and four neighbours as the Mother Camels, a group later known in Latin as the Quinque Dromedarii.
facts.title: The Mother Camels

story: Eltanin passes almost straight overhead in London, which made it the ideal target for a great prize of 17th- and 18th-century astronomy: measuring a star’s parallax. Robert Hooke tried. In 1728 James Bradley tried too, and failed — but the star’s tiny yearly shifts revealed something else. Bradley had discovered the aberration of light, caused by the Earth’s motion around the Sun. George Airy later called Eltanin “the birth-star of modern astronomy”.

Its name comes from the Arabic for “the great serpent”, and despite its gamma label it is the brightest star in Draco. It is an orange giant about twice the Sun’s mass, some 50 times wider and 600 times as luminous.
Eltanin is heading our way. In about 1.5 million years it will pass much closer and, for a time, become the brightest star in the night sky — nearly as bright as Sirius is now.
eltanin.tagline: London’s zenith star — where the hunt for a parallax revealed that Earth is moving.

facts.text: William Herschel discovered Enceladus on 28 August 1789, during the first use of his 40-foot telescope, then the largest in the world.
facts.title: Found on first light

facts.text: Together, the geysers of Enceladus blast about 200 kilograms of material into space every second.
facts.title: 200 kg every second

facts.text: Features on Enceladus are named after characters and places in Richard Burton’s 1885 translation of The Book of One Thousand and One Nights.
facts.title: Names from the Arabian Nights

story: Enceladus is one of the most reflective objects in the Solar System, coated in fresh, clean snow. Even at noon its surface stays near −198 °C. Yet when Cassini began flying close by in 2005, it found this small, frozen [[planetary-moon|moon]] hard at work: from fractures near its south pole, more than 100 geysers shoot jets of water vapour and ice into space.

The jets come from an ocean of liquid water beneath the ice, kept warm by tides as Enceladus and its neighbour Dione tug on each other in a steady rhythm. Cassini flew through the spray and tasted it — salt, hydrogen and signs of hot water reacting with rock on the sea floor. Some scientists think microbes like those around Earth’s deep-sea vents could live there.
Some of the spray falls back as snow, now hundreds of metres deep. The rest escapes to supply most of Saturn’s faint, wide E ring.
enceladus.tagline: A snow-white moon that sprays its hidden ocean into space from geysers at its south pole.

facts.text: Enif is a classic target for the Pulfrich effect: swing a telescope gently from side to side and a faint nearby star seems to sway like a pendulum against the bright one.
facts.title: The swinging star

facts.text: Its spectrum shows an excess of strontium and barium, heavy elements that may be built up by slow neutron capture in the star.
facts.title: Extra strontium and barium

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Wēi Sù sān, the Third Star of the Rooftop, an asterism shared with Alpha Aquarii and Theta Pegasi.
facts.title: The Rooftop

story: Enif comes from the Arabic for “nose”: it marks the muzzle of Pegasus, the winged horse, and despite its epsilon label it is the constellation’s brightest star. Another old name, Fom al Feras, became Os Equi, “the horse’s mouth”, in Latin.

This is an orange supergiant of 11 to 12 solar masses, some 183 times the Sun’s width and about 8,500 times as luminous. In the Sun’s place it would reach past the orbit of Venus. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, it is almost certainly fusing helium now. It may end as a heavy oxygen–neon white dwarf, or in an electron-capture supernova.

Enif usually wavers only gently, but it once surprised observers by appearing very briefly at magnitude 0.7, far above normal — suggesting that supergiants may unleash huge flares. It may even have turned from whitish-yellow to its present colour within the last 2,000 years, though no historical record confirms it.
enif.tagline: The winged horse’s nose — an orange supergiant once caught in a startling flash.

facts.text: Seen from Epsilon Eridani, the Sun would be a 2.4-magnitude star in the constellation Serpens.
facts.title: Our Sun, seen from there

facts.text: Ptolemy listed it in his Almagest as the star that leads a group of four in the River — the first of them to cross the sky each night.
facts.title: Ptolemy’s leading star

facts.text: Epsilon Eridani may belong to the Ursa Major moving group, stars that share a path through the galaxy — and perhaps a birth in the same cluster.
facts.title: A family resemblance

story: Young stars are restless, and Epsilon Eridani is no exception. About a billion years old, it is smaller and cooler than the Sun — an orange [[spectral-type|K-type]] star — but its magnetic activity is higher and its stellar wind about 30 times as strong. It spins once every 11.2 days at its equator.

It has a family. A giant planet, Epsilon Eridani b, circles it — first announced in 2000 and long debated, but now accepted by most astronomers. Farther out lie a belt of warm dust and a cold ring like our Kuiper belt, with a gap between them that hints at more unseen planets. As one of our nearest Sun-like neighbours it has been a target in the search for alien radio signals since Frank Drake’s Project Ozma in 1960, and a favourite of science fiction.

In 2015 the star and planet were named Ran and AEgir, after the Norse sea goddess Rán and her husband Ægir, god of the ocean. The names were proposed by eighth-grade pupils at Mountainside Middle School in Colbert, Washington.
epsilon-eridani.tagline: A young, restless Sun-like star next door, with a giant planet, dust belts and Norse sea gods for names.

facts.text: Its atmosphere holds only about half the Sun’s share of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium — a sign that it formed from less-enriched gas.
facts.title: Half the Sun’s metals

facts.text: Seen from Earth, its surface turns at only about 8 kilometres a second. Stars tend to slow down as they swell into giants.
facts.title: A slow spinner

story: Its names are directions. Algenubi and Ras Elased Australis both mean ‘the southern star of the lion’s head’: Genubi is Arabic for ‘south’, Australis is Latin.

Looks deceive here. Epsilon Leonis appears much fainter than Regulus, but only because it lies more than three times as far away. Its absolute [[magnitude]] — how bright it would look from a standard distance — is −1.49, well ahead of Regulus. It is a yellow giant of about four solar masses that has finished burning hydrogen in its core and swollen to 21 times the Sun’s radius, shining 282 times as brightly.
epsilon-leonis.tagline: The southern star of the Lion’s head — more powerful than Regulus, though it looks far fainter.

facts.text: On Pukapuka in the Cook Islands the system is Na ponga-ponga-iyu-o-te-kiole, “the nostrils of the rat”. In June 2026 the IAU gave the shortened form, Pongaponga, to the main star of the northern pair.
facts.title: The nostrils of the rat

facts.text: In 2022 researchers using data from NASA’s TESS satellite found that the fainter star of the northern pair is a Gamma Doradus variable, pulsing with a main period of 0.415 days.
facts.title: A gentle pulse

story: Stand on a planet beside one half of the Double Double and the other half would blaze in your sky, about as bright as a quarter Moon, its two stars less than a degree apart.

Each pair is a [[double-star|binary]] in its own right. The stars of one take something like 1,200 years per orbit, the other perhaps half that, and the two pairs circle each other over hundreds of thousands of years. Since the first precise measurements in the 1980s, both have turned only a few degrees.

There are more members still. A fifth star, found in 1985 by speckle imaging, whips around one star of the southern pair. It has been seen only a few times, so no orbit can yet be worked out, but its rapid motion suggests it goes round in a few decades.
epsilon-lyrae.tagline: Two pairs of stars in a slow dance — named in 2026 after “the nostrils of the rat”.

discovered.note: First firm record; its Great Eruption began in 1837

facts.text: The Boorong people of north-western Victoria told of a reddish star, Collowgullouric War, wife of the Crow (Canopus). In 2010 astronomers showed this was Eta Carinae during its 1840s eruption.
facts.title: Old Woman Crow

facts.text: In 1843 the Reverend W. S. Mackay wrote from Calcutta that the star had become ‘fully as bright as Canopus, and in colour and size very like Arcturus’.
facts.title: “Very like Arcturus”

facts.text: After sinking out of sight, Eta Carinae has slowly brightened since about 1940. By 2014 it was again a 4th-magnitude star, visible to the naked eye.
facts.title: Coming back

story: On the evening of 16 December 1837, John Herschel, observing from South Africa, was astonished to see a star in the ship Argo outshining Rigel. It was Eta Carinae, and its ‘Great Eruption’ had begun. By March 1843 only Sirius outshone it. Then, over the following decades, it faded from naked-eye view, hidden by dust from its own outburst.

The gas it threw off now forms the Homunculus, a two-lobed [[nebula]] wrapped around the star. At its heart are at least two stars on a 5.54-year orbit. The primary was born with perhaps 150 to 250 times the Sun’s mass and has already lost at least 30; its companion is a hot star of 30 to 80 solar masses. Together they shine over five million times as brightly as the Sun.
Astronomers expect the primary to explode as a supernova — soon, by the standards of stars. Until then it holds a strange record: it is the only star known to produce ultraviolet laser light.
eta-carinae.tagline: The star that briefly outshone all but Sirius, then vanished — a doomed giant waiting to explode.

facts.text: The name Achird first appears in the Skalnaté Pleso Atlas of the Heavens, published in 1950. No one knows where it came from, yet the IAU made it official in 2017.
facts.title: A name without a past

facts.text: Achird shows a repeating wobble every 868 days or so that could come from a planet at least 22 times Earth’s mass. It is unconfirmed, and might instead be a long-term activity cycle.
facts.title: A planet in waiting?

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it belongs to Wang Liang, an asterism named after a famous charioteer of the Spring and Autumn period.
facts.title: The charioteer

story: Look at Achird and you are seeing roughly what our own Sun would look like from out there. It is almost a copy of the Sun: just 3% heavier and 13% more luminous, with a very similar surface temperature. Both it and its partner contain only about half as much of the heavier elements as the Sun does.

Its companion is a smaller, cooler star with just over half the Sun’s mass and only 8% of its light. The two swing around each other in roughly 470 years on an oval orbit, closing to a little beyond Neptune’s distance from the Sun before drifting out to three times as far.

William Herschel discovered the pair in August 1779. Any planet here would have to stay close to home: one circling the brighter star could only keep a stable orbit within about 9.5 times Earth’s distance from the Sun.
eta-cassiopeiae.tagline: A near-twin of the Sun with a small orange partner — and a name nobody can trace back before 1950.

facts.text: Eta Persei mysteriously picked up the name Miram in the 20th century, from no known source. The IAU nonetheless made it official in 2017.
facts.title: A name from nowhere

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the first star of Tiān Chuán, the Celestial Boat, an asterism that includes Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus.
facts.title: The Celestial Boat

facts.text: With Delta, Psi, Sigma, Alpha and Gamma Persei it forms a group of stars that has been called the Segment of Perseus.
facts.title: Segment of Perseus

story: Swap the Sun for Eta Persei and Mercury and Venus would vanish inside it. This ageing supergiant has swollen enormously and now pours out around 7,500 times as much light as the Sun, from a surface cooler than the Sun’s — around 4,100 kelvins, which gives it its warm orange glow.
Its light reaches us dimmed: dust between the stars steals almost half a magnitude of its brightness on the way.
Catalogues list several companions near it on the sky, but only one, an eighth-magnitude star, appears to lie at the same distance. Whether any of them really belongs to Eta Persei is still unclear.
eta-persei.tagline: An orange supergiant thousands of times brighter than the Sun, with a name whose origin no one knows.

discovered.note: Possibly also seen by Simon Marius

facts.text: On 7 January 1610 Galileo saw Io and Europa merged as a single point of light. The next night they had separated, and Europa was seen on its own for the first time.
facts.title: One light, then two

facts.text: Europa was a Phoenician princess courted by Zeus, who became queen of Crete. Simon Marius gave the moon her name, crediting the idea to Johannes Kepler.
facts.title: Named for a princess

facts.text: Europa has a very thin atmosphere made mostly of oxygen. It comes not from life but from Jupiter’s radiation breaking apart the surface ice.
facts.title: Air made by radiation

facts.text: In September 2022 NASA’s Juno spacecraft flew within about 320 km of Europa’s icy surface, the closest look since the Galileo mission.
facts.title: A close pass by Juno

story: Europa looks like a cracked eggshell. Its pale surface is criss-crossed by tan streaks and cracks, yet it has almost no craters or mountains, making it the smoothest solid object known in the Solar System. Something keeps renewing it. Beneath the ice lies an ocean of liquid water, kept from freezing by the flexing of Jupiter’s tides, and the ice above may slowly shift like Earth’s drifting plates.

That ocean makes this [[planetary-moon|moon]], a little smaller than our own, one of the most promising places to search for life. Sea salt seems to stain parts of the surface, hinting that the water touches a rocky sea floor. Hubble has spotted signs of water vapour plumes venting into space — a chance to sample the ocean without ever landing.
No spacecraft has landed yet. NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024, is on its way to make dozens of close passes, and Europe’s Juice will fly by twice.
europa.tagline: A cracked shell of ice over a hidden ocean — one of the best places to look for life beyond Earth.

facts.text: Fang belongs to the Upper Scorpius group, part of the Scorpius–Centaurus association of thousands of young stars. It is only 12 to 14 million years old.
facts.title: Born with the Scorpion’s stars

facts.text: Both stars of the inner pair spin quickly — at least 87 and 108 kilometres a second — while they circle each other on a circular orbit.
facts.title: Spinning as well as orbiting

story: Unusually for an official star name, Fang is Chinese. Fáng Xiù, ‘the Room’, is one of the lunar mansions of Chinese astronomy, made from the stars of the Scorpion’s head, and Fang is its first star.

Look closer and it becomes three stars. Two hot, blue-white stars race round each other every 1.57 days, so close that their centres are only about 15 times the Sun’s radius apart. Gravity stretches each one out of round, and the light of the pair wobbles slightly as they turn. A faint third star keeps its distance. The brighter of the inner pair has 12 to 13 times the Sun’s mass and shines like about 22,000 Suns.

Harvard’s Edward Pickering announced the pair in 1899. Two years later Solon Bailey found their 1.57-day period, and in 1927 Otto Struve and Christian Elvey worked out the precise orbit of this [[double-star|double]] that no telescope can split.
fang.tagline: A star with a Chinese name: a tight, egg-shaped pair of hot stars at the Scorpion’s head.

facts.text: In 1837 the companion was reported to vary between magnitudes 6.3 and 8.5, and in 1951 the main star was said to flicker slightly. Neither change has ever been confirmed.
facts.title: Suspected, never confirmed

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Delta Cygni belongs to Tiān Jīn, the Celestial Ford, along with Deneb and other stars of the Swan. It is the Ford’s second star.
facts.title: The Celestial Ford

story: Around AD 11,250, Fawaris will probably be a pole star. Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, carrying the celestial pole round a wide circle among the northern stars, and that circle passes within three degrees of Delta Cygni. For at least four centuries it should take over the role Polaris plays today.

The name is older. Al-Fawāris, ‘the Riders’, was an Arabic grouping of four stars across the Swan’s outstretched wings — the crossbar of the Northern Cross. In 2018 the IAU gave it to Delta Cygni’s brightest star.

That star has company. Fawaris is a blue-white star of about three solar masses, spinning at least 135 kilometres a second — around 60 times faster than the Sun — and nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life. A yellow-white companion circles it once every 780 years, and a faint orange star travels with both, making a [[multiple-star|triple system]].
fawaris.tagline: The western end of the Northern Cross’s crossbar — and a pole star of the far future.

facts.text: Fomalhaut shares its path through space with two companions, the orange dwarf TW Piscis Austrini and the red dwarf LP 876-10, though they appear about 8° apart in our sky.
facts.title: Far-flung family

facts.text: Since 1943 Fomalhaut’s spectrum has served as one of the standard references against which other stars are classified.
facts.title: A measuring stick

story: Fomalhaut is a young white [[star]], a few hundred million years old, about twice the Sun’s mass and 17 times as bright. Around it lies a vast ring of dust with a sharp inner edge, sometimes called ‘Fomalhaut’s Kuiper belt’. The dust must be constantly topped up: collisions between icy bodies — perhaps 2,000 kilometre-sized comets a day — keep grinding out fresh grains.

In 2008 Hubble images showed a speck just inside the ring, hailed as the first planet candidate ever imaged in visible light. It was named Dagon, after a Semitic god often shown as half-man, half-fish. But the speck spread out and faded, and studies in 2019 and 2023 concluded it was probably an expanding cloud of debris from a collision between two large bodies.
The star’s name comes from the Arabic for ‘the mouth of the fish’: it marks the mouth of Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish.
fomalhaut.tagline: A lonely bright star ringed by dust — and home of a ‘planet’ that turned out to be a cloud of wreckage.

facts.text: On Brazil’s flag Gacrux stands for the state of Bahia. The line through Gacrux and Acrux matches the meridian of the sky over Rio de Janeiro at 8:30 am on 15 November 1889, when the new republic was formally ratified.
facts.title: A flag with a moment in it

facts.text: The Aranda and Luritja people of Central Australia see Gacrux as part of Iritjinga, the Eagle-hawk, a four-sided pattern with nearby stars of the Cross and Centaurus.
facts.title: The Eagle-hawk

facts.text: Gacrux is one of the Southern Cross stars on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea.
facts.title: Four flags more

story: Gacrux is the nearest M-type red giant to the Sun. Only half again as massive as the Sun, it has swollen to about 73 times its width and shines with some 830 times its light. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, giving the reddish-orange glow that sets it apart from the blue-white stars of the Cross. Like many giants it swells and fades a little, a semi-regular [[variable-star]].
Its atmosphere holds a puzzle: it is rich in barium. That usually means a companion once dumped processed material on it before fading into a white dwarf — yet no such companion has been found.

Precession let the ancient Greeks and Romans see it, and Ptolemy counted it as part of Centaurus. Yet it had no Western name until navigators, by the 1940s, shortened Gamma Crucis to Gacrux. In Brazil it is also called Rubídea, ‘ruby-like’.
gacrux.tagline: The ruby head of the Southern Cross — the nearest red giant of its kind to the Sun.

facts.text: The Aranda and Luritja people around Hermannsburg in Central Australia saw it, with Delta Centauri, Delta Crucis and Gacrux, as Iritjinga, the Eagle-hawk.
facts.title: The Eagle-hawk

facts.text: Its proper name, Muhlifain, shares an Arabic root with Muliphein in Canis Major — two different stars, easily confused.
facts.title: Two names, one root

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Kù Lóu qī, the Seventh Star of the Arsenal, the same ten-star asterism that includes Menkent.
facts.title: Seventh star of the Arsenal

story: To the naked eye Gamma Centauri is one star. It is really a pair of near-twins: two white stars, each about 2.8 times the Sun’s mass and around 100 times as luminous, circling each other every 84.5 years. Their orbit is wide — some 93 times the Earth–Sun distance, more than twice as far as Pluto is from the Sun. Astronomers have tracked the pair since 1897.

Both are [[spectral-type|A-type]] subgiants, just starting to swell into giants. And they are probably not alone. Tau Centauri shares their path through space, with a 98 per cent chance that it is gravitationally bound to them, which would make this a wide triple system.
gamma-centauri.tagline: One point of light, two white stars — and probably a far-flung third in Tau Centauri.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the eighth star of Tiān Qūn, the Circular Celestial Granary, a ring of thirteen stars in Cetus.
facts.title: A granary in the sky

facts.text: Astronomers searched the bright star for the infrared glow of a surrounding dust disc, the kind that can betray leftover planet-building debris, but found none.
facts.title: No dust found

story: Three stars make up Gamma Ceti. The brightest is a hot white star; close beside it sits a smaller yellow-white companion that glows in X-rays. Far out, a dim orange dwarf shares their path through space — so remote that only its matching motion and distance tie it to the pair.

The family is young by stellar standards, about 300 million years old, and seems to travel with a loose stream of stars linked to the Ursa Major Moving Group, the family that includes most of the stars of the Plough.
Its name comes from the Arabic al-kaf al-jadhmā’, “the cut-short hand”. That title once belonged to five stars of Cetus, the Whale, before settling on this one.
gamma-ceti.tagline: A white star, a yellow-white partner and a distant orange dwarf, under a name meaning “the cut-short hand”.

discovered.note: Later observed by William Herschel in 1779

facts.text: In July 2026 the IAU named the fainter star Dhanishta, after one of the 27 nakshatras, or lunar mansions, of Indian astronomy. Its asterism matches the Dolphin.
facts.title: Named in 2026

facts.text: Early measurements put the two stars 12″ apart; by 2019 the gap had shrunk to under 9″ as they move along their long orbit.
facts.title: Closing in

story: Here the heavier star is already showing its age. About twice the Sun’s mass, it has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into an orange subgiant. Its lighter partner is still a steady yellow-white star, about 1.8 billion years old. Observers have likened the colours to orange and lime.

Their orbit is extremely elongated. In one lap of about 3,250 years they swing from roughly 40 times Earth’s distance from the Sun out to 600 times. Christian Mayer first found the pair double, and William Herschel observed it on 27 September 1779.
In 1999 astronomers suggested that a planet of at least 0.7 Jupiter masses might be tugging the brighter star every 1.44 years. The wobble is there, but the planet has never been confirmed.
gamma-delphini.tagline: An orange star and a lime-tinted partner on a 3,000-year orbit, newly named after an Indian lunar mansion.

facts.text: Neither Regor nor the Arabic al-Suhail al-Muhlif has been approved by the IAU, making Gamma Velorum the brightest star without an official proper name.
facts.title: No official name

facts.text: The fainter star of the visible pair is itself a close binary with a 1.48-day orbit, so the system is a [[multiple-star|multiple star]] of at least four. Several hundred young stars are scattered around it.
facts.title: At least four stars

story: Gamma Velorum holds the nearest and brightest Wolf–Rayet star — a massive [[star]] that has blown away its outer layers, baring its fierce, hot interior. Born with about 35 times the Sun’s mass, it has shed all but about nine. Its partner is a blue supergiant of some 30 solar masses, and the two whirl round each other every 78.5 days. Their winds collide so violently that they accelerate particles, and the Fermi telescope has seen gamma rays rise and fall in step with the orbit. Both stars will probably end as supernovae.

Its bright emission lines, where most stars show dark ones, earned it the nickname ‘the Spectral Gem of Southern Skies’. Its modern name, Regor, is Roger spelled backwards — a tribute to the astronaut Roger Chaffee, who died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967.
gamma-velorum.tagline: The Spectral Gem of the southern skies — home of the nearest Wolf–Rayet star, and a tribute to an astronaut.

facts.text: Chinese records say that in 365 BC the astronomer Gan De saw a small reddish star beside Jupiter. It may have been Ganymede, glimpsed with the naked eye — though the colour is a puzzle.
facts.title: A sighting in 365 BC?

facts.text: Before settling on mythological names, Simon Marius tried calling the moons the Mercury, Venus, Jupiter and Saturn of Jupiter. Ganymede was the ‘Jupiter of Jupiter’.
facts.title: The ‘Jupiter of Jupiter’

facts.text: Ganymede’s magnetic field gives it auroras. In 2015 Hubble showed that they sway less than expected — the damping effect of a salty ocean hidden under the ice.
facts.title: Auroras that betray an ocean

story: If Ganymede circled the Sun instead of Jupiter, we might well call it a [[planet]]. It is the largest moon in the Solar System, wider than Mercury, though lighter, being roughly half rock and half water. It is also the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field, probably stirred up in a liquid, iron-rich core.

Under its icy crust lies an ocean that may hold more water than all of Earth’s oceans combined. The surface tells two stories: dark, ancient regions crowded with craters about four billion years old, and lighter terrain, covering two-thirds of the moon, scored with long grooves and ridges.

Galileo first saw it in January 1610 as one of three ‘stars’ beside Jupiter. Simon Marius named it after Ganymede, the Trojan prince Zeus carried off to be cupbearer to the gods — the only male among the four [[galilean-moons|Galilean moons]]. Europe’s Juice spacecraft, launched in 2023, is set to become the first ever to orbit a moon other than our own.
ganymede.tagline: The largest moon in the Solar System — bigger than Mercury, with its own magnetic field and a hidden sea.

discovered.note: Discoverer of its variability; the star itself is visible to the naked eye

facts.text: Since 1943 the Garnet Star has been one of the ‘dagger stars’ — standards for classifying other stars. Today it defines the M2- Ia class of red supergiants.
facts.title: A yardstick for red supergiants

facts.text: Some catalogues call it Erakis, but that name probably comes from a mix-up with Mu Draconis, once known in Arabic as al-Rāqis.
facts.title: Erakis, by mistake

facts.text: Infrared observations suggest a wide ring of dust and water around the star, beginning at about twice the star’s own radius.
facts.title: A ring of dust and water

story: William Herschel saw in it ‘a very fine deep garnet colour’, and the name stuck: the IAU made Garnet Star official in 2024. Few stars visible to the naked eye are larger. Recent estimates put it at roughly 760 to over 1,200 times the Sun’s radius; set in the Sun’s place, it would swallow the orbit of Mars and the asteroid belt.

This red supergiant shines more than 100,000 times as brightly as the Sun, and it wanders erratically between magnitudes 3.4 and 5.1, with rough rhythms of about 860 and 4,400 days. John Russell Hind noticed the changes in 1848, and observers have tracked this [[variable-star]] almost without a break since 1881. It is also a runaway, ploughing through space at about 80 kilometres a second.
