Its end is near, as stars go. It has begun fusing helium into carbon, and it is wrapped in a shell of gas it threw off some 2,000 to 3,000 years ago. When its core finally collapses it will explode as a supernova, most likely leaving behind a black hole.
garnet-star.tagline: Herschel’s Garnet Star: one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye, glowing like a dark red gem.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Gienah is the first star of Zhěn, the Chariot — a group formed by the four bright stars of Corvus.
facts.title: The Chariot

facts.text: The Calendarium of Al Achsasi al Mouakket listed it as Djenah al Ghyrab al Eymen, translated into Latin as Dextra ala Corvi — the Crow’s right wing.
facts.title: Dextra ala Corvi

story: Gienah’s atmosphere is sorting itself out. In this calm, hot star the elements slowly separate — some sinking, others drifting upwards — and the surface ends up with far more mercury and manganese than normal. Astronomers call it a mercury-manganese star.

It is a [[star-colour|blue-white]] giant of about four times the Sun’s mass and width, with a surface near 12,000 K, twice as hot as the Sun’s. A much smaller, cooler star of about 0.8 solar masses circles it, perhaps once every 158 years.

The name comes from an Arabic phrase in Ulugh Beg’s star catalogue meaning “the right wing of the crow” — though on modern charts it marks the left wing. Epsilon Cygni was also called Gienah, so the IAU gave the name to this star in 2016, and the Swan’s star became Aljanah.
gienah.tagline: The Crow’s brightest star — whose calm atmosphere is unusually rich in mercury.

facts.text: Canada’s small MOST space telescope found Gomeisa varying by mere thousandths of a magnitude, in rhythms of a little over three cycles a day. That makes it a slowly pulsating B star.
facts.title: A heartbeat from space

facts.text: Gomeisa was listed as a variable star in 1977, yet several later studies found no change in its brightness. Its clearest changes are in the hydrogen glow of its disc.
facts.title: Variable on paper

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Gomeisa, Procyon and Epsilon Canis Minoris form Nán Hé, the South River. Gomeisa is its second star.
facts.title: The South River

story: Gomeisa spins like a top. Its equator races round at more than 200 kilometres a second, and it may turn once a day — the Sun takes almost a month. Flung out by that spin, a thin disc of hot gas circles its equator, reaching out to about three times the star’s radius and glowing with hydrogen light. That makes Gomeisa a Be star: a blue-white [[star]] of about three and a half solar masses, still burning hydrogen in its core.

What spun it up? Gomeisa probably has a hidden partner of under half the Sun’s mass, on an eccentric 170-day orbit. One idea is that it is the stripped core of a star that once poured gas — and spin — onto Gomeisa. If confirmed, the pair would join a very rare class of Be stars with hot subdwarf companions.

Its name is gentler: Arabic al-ghumaisa’, ‘the bleary-eyed woman’, short for a phrase meaning ‘the girdle of the bleary-eyed one’. The same short name was also used in Arabic for brilliant Procyon nearby.
gomeisa.tagline: Procyon’s little companion in the sky: a whirling blue-white star wrapped in a disc of its own gas.

facts.text: The Boorong people of Victoria saw Hadar and Alpha Centauri as two brothers who speared Tchingal, the Emu — the dark Coalsack Nebula beside the Southern Cross.
facts.title: Two brothers and an emu

facts.text: Joan Voûte spotted the faint third star in 1935. In 1967 a shifting spectrum hinted that the main star was itself double, which was confirmed in 1999.
facts.title: One star becomes three

facts.text: The Mursi people of Ethiopia call Hadar Waar. It forms a pattern with Alpha Centauri and two stars of the Southern Cross.
facts.title: Waar

story: Hadar looks like one star, but it is three. Two blue giants, each 10 to 12 times the Sun’s mass, swing around each other every 357 days on a long, stretched orbit. A third, smaller star circles farther out. All three are hot stars of the same B1 [[spectral-type]], shining blue-white.

The two giants are heavy enough to end their lives as supernovae; the third will swell into a red giant and fade into a white dwarf. The brightest star also pulses gently — a [[variable-star]] of the Beta Cephei kind — though the changes are far too small to notice by eye.
Its name comes from Arabic. Its other name, Agena, probably comes from the Latin for ‘knees’: it marks the left knee of the centaur.
hadar.tagline: The inner Pointer to the Southern Cross — three hot blue stars, two of them heavy enough to explode.

facts.text: James Blish’s 1953 novel A Case of Conscience is set largely on Lithia, an imaginary planet of Hamal that is home to an alien race.
facts.title: A world in a novel

facts.text: Hamal’s declination is almost exactly the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer, so seen from that line on Earth it passes straight overhead.
facts.title: Overhead on the Tropic

facts.text: Geoffrey Chaucer knew it as Alnath, Arabic for “the butting horns”. That name has since moved to Beta Tauri, now called Elnath.
facts.title: Chaucer’s name for it

story: Why do horoscope columns start with Aries? Between about 2000 and 100 BC the Sun stood in this constellation at the March equinox, the start of northern spring. Hamal, its brightest star, shone near what was then a key point in the sky. Precession has since moved the equinox into Pisces, but the habit stuck.

The name comes from the Arabic for “head of the ram”. It is an orange giant that has used up the hydrogen in its core: about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, some 15 times wider and 91 times as luminous. Since 1943 its spectrum has been one of the fixed reference points astronomers use to classify other stars.

In 2011 a team led by Byeong-Cheol Lee in South Korea reported a likely [[planet]] circling it every 381 days, at least 1.8 times the mass of Jupiter. Its orbit would take it a little farther from Hamal than Earth is from the Sun.
hamal.tagline: The Ram’s head — the reason horoscopes still begin with Aries.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Hassaleh is the first star of the Five Chariots, a pattern in Auriga that also includes Mahasim.
facts.title: First of the Five Chariots

facts.text: Dust between us and Hassaleh dims it by about 0.6 magnitudes. Without it, the star would look about 1.7 times as bright.
facts.title: Dimmed by dust

facts.text: Since 1943 its spectrum has served as one of the stable reference points that astronomers use to classify other stars.
facts.title: A yardstick star

story: Geoffrey Chaucer knew this star. In his Treatise on the Astrolabe of 1391 it appears as Alkab, one of the star markers on the instrument. Alkab was short for an Arabic phrase meaning “the ankle of the rein holder” — the Charioteer, Auriga.
Its modern name is a puzzle. Hassaleh first turned up in Antonín Bečvář’s 1951 star atlas, and despite extensive searching no one has found its origin or linked it to any language.

The star itself is an [[star-colour|orange]] giant, cooler than the Sun at about 4,160 K. Loops of plasma at around 3 million K in its outer atmosphere give off faint X-rays. In 2007 astronomers announced two possible brown dwarfs circling it, but they have never been confirmed; the signal may instead come from slow pulsations of the star itself.
hassaleh.tagline: An orange giant Chaucer knew — now carrying a name no one can explain.

discovered.note: Named after Hind, who described its colour in 1845

facts.text: At its dimmest, R Leporis is a candidate for the reddest star visible — though that claim is questioned, and near maximum its colour is far less striking.
facts.title: Reddest of all?

facts.text: In 1848, three years after describing R Leporis, John Russell Hind discovered that the Garnet Star in Cepheus varies in brightness.
facts.title: Hind’s other red star

story: In 1845 the British astronomer John Russell Hind turned his telescope on a star in Lepus and found it glowing ‘like a drop of blood on a black field’. It has carried his name ever since: Hind’s Crimson Star, or R Leporis.

Its colour comes from carbon. R Leporis is a carbon star, a cool giant whose atmosphere is so rich in carbon that it filters out the blue part of the star’s light. The effect is strongest when the star is dimmest. It pulsates as a Mira-type [[variable-star]], swinging between about magnitude 5.5 and 11.7 over roughly 427 days, and is reddest near minimum.
From its pulsation period, astronomers estimate it shines about 13,200 times as brightly as the Sun. There may also be a much slower cycle, about 40 years long, on top of its usual rhythm.
hinds-crimson-star.tagline: ‘Like a drop of blood on a black field’ — one of the reddest stars in the sky, at its reddest when faintest.

discovered.by: William Cranch Bond and George Phillips Bond
discovered.note: Seen independently by William Lassell two days later

facts.text: William Bond and his son George found Hyperion in the United States in September 1848. William Lassell, in England, saw it two days later — and beat them to publication.
facts.title: Two discoveries, two days apart

facts.text: Hyperion was the first moon ever discovered that is not round, and it is still one of the largest irregularly shaped bodies known.
facts.title: The first lumpy moon

facts.text: Hyperion is named after the Titan god of watchfulness and observation, an elder brother of Cronus. Lassell suggested the name.
facts.title: God of watchfulness

story: Hyperion looks like a giant sponge. Deep, sharp-edged craters riddle its surface, each with dark, reddish material pooled in the bottom. The reason is what it is made of: mostly water ice, packed so loosely that about 40% of the moon is empty space. Impacts tend to crush the surface rather than blast it out, and with gravity this weak, most of the debris never falls back.

It also tumbles. Hyperion is the only regular [[planetary-moon|moon]] known not to keep one face turned to its planet, and its spin is chaotic: its axis wobbles so much that its orientation soon becomes impossible to predict. Its lumpy shape, its stretched orbit and regular tugs from giant Titan all play a part. It may be a fragment of a larger moon, shattered by an ancient impact.
hyperion.tagline: A tumbling, sponge-like moon that is about 40 percent empty space.

facts.text: In Arthur C. Clarke’s novel 2001: A Space Odyssey, the alien Star Gate waits on Iapetus, spelled Japetus. The film moved the scene to Jupiter.
facts.title: A Star Gate in fiction

facts.text: Iapetus orbits far beyond Titan, yet still keeps one face toward Saturn. No other tidally locked moon in the Solar System orbits so far from its planet.
facts.title: The most distant locked moon

facts.text: Geological features on Iapetus are named after characters and places from the French epic poem The Song of Roland.
facts.title: Names from The Song of Roland

story: In 1671 Giovanni Domenico Cassini found a new moon west of Saturn. But when it swung round to the eastern side, it vanished. The same thing happened the next year. Cassini guessed why: one half of the moon is bright and the other dark, and it always keeps the same face turned to Saturn. He was right. Only in 1705, with a better telescope, did he catch it on the eastern side, two [[magnitude|magnitudes]] fainter.

Iapetus is still the strangest-looking of Saturn’s large moons. Its leading side is as dark as coal, its trailing side bright with ice. A ridge runs three-quarters of the way around its equator, giving it the look of a walnut. And from its tilted, faraway orbit, it is the only large moon from which [[saturns-rings|Saturn’s rings]] would be clearly seen, rather than edge-on.
iapetus.tagline: A two-faced moon, coal-dark on one side and snow-bright on the other, with a ridge around its waist.

facts.text: Imai flies on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea as part of the Southern Cross. On Brazil’s flag it is one of 27 stars and stands for the state of Minas Gerais.
facts.title: On five flags

facts.text: In Portuguese it is sometimes called Pálida, “the pale one” — a fair name for the faintest star of the Cross.
facts.title: The pale one

facts.text: The Aranda and Luritja people of Central Australia saw Imai, Gacrux and two stars of Centaurus as a four-sided figure, Iritjinga, “the Eagle-hawk”.
facts.title: The Eagle-hawk

story: For the Mursi people of Ethiopia, this star is a calendar. When Imai stops appearing in the evening sky at dusk, the Omo River is said to rise high enough to flatten the imai grass along its banks, before subsiding again. The Mursi follow a series of southern stars to track the river’s floods, among them Mimosa, Hadar and Alpha Centauri. In 2018 the IAU adopted the name Imai.

It is a hot [[star-colour|blue-white]] [[star]], about 20,400 K at the surface and 8,100 times as luminous as the Sun. It spins fast — at least 210 kilometres per second — and is beginning to evolve away from the main sequence towards becoming a giant.
Imai belongs to the Lower Centaurus Crux, a group of massive stars that formed together 16 to 20 million years ago.
imai.tagline: The Southern Cross’s faintest star — a river calendar for the Mursi people of Ethiopia.

discovered.note: Found with the other three Galilean moons; named by Simon Marius

facts.text: In 1676 Ole Rømer noticed that Io’s [[eclipse|eclipses]] behind Jupiter came early or late depending on how far Earth was from Jupiter. The difference was light’s travel time — the first measurement of the speed of light.
facts.title: Timing the speed of light

facts.text: Io’s features are named after gods of fire, volcanoes, the Sun and thunder, characters from the myth of Io, and places from Dante’s Inferno.
facts.title: Names from Dante’s Inferno

facts.text: Gas from Io’s volcanoes feeds a vast doughnut of charged particles around Jupiter, the Io plasma torus, bathing the moon in fierce radiation.
facts.title: A ring of radiation

facts.text: Io has less water, by atomic ratio, than any other known object in the Solar System.
facts.title: Bone dry

story: Picture a moon painted yellow, red, white and black — the colours of sulfur, laid down by eruption after eruption. Io, innermost of the four [[galilean-moons|Galilean moons]], has more than 400 active volcanoes, making it the most geologically active world in the Solar System. Some fling plumes of sulfur hundreds of kilometres above the surface, lava flows run for hundreds more, and some of its mountains stand taller than Everest.

The fire comes from a tug of war. Io is caught between Jupiter and its sibling moons Europa and Ganymede, whose regular pulls keep its orbit slightly stretched. As Io swings closer to Jupiter and away again, the giant planet’s gravity flexes it, and the friction heats its interior. Unlike most moons of the outer Solar System, Io is made of rock rather than ice.

Nobody suspected any of this until 1979, when Voyager 1 sent back pictures of a young face with no obvious impact craters and a plume rising above its edge — the first active volcanoes ever seen beyond Earth.
io.tagline: The most volcanic world in the Solar System — a moon squeezed by Jupiter until lava pours out.

facts.text: Arabic astronomers called this star and Alpha Cancri Al Zubanāh, “the claws” of the crab — the source of Alpha Cancri’s modern name, Acubens.
facts.title: The crab’s claws

facts.text: The giant’s surface is about 4,950 kelvins, while its partner’s is nearly twice as hot, around 9,260 — the reason the pair shows such a strong [[star-colour|colour]] contrast.
facts.title: Where the colours come from

story: The yellow giant here carries the chemical fingerprint of a vanished companion. It is a mild “barium star”, its atmosphere enriched with elements forged inside a more evolved kind of giant. The likely explanation: another star once dumped that material onto it, then faded into a white dwarf that has never been seen.

Its partner is a hot white star spinning so fast — at least 170 kilometres a second at its equator — that it has flung off a shell of material around itself. The two drift through space together, but they are so far apart that no orbit has been measured.

In Bali the whole constellation of Cancer is called Yuyu, a Javanese word for the freshwater crab of the rice fields, attested for at least 1,300 years. In 2026 the IAU gave that name to the brighter star.
iota-cancri.tagline: A yellow giant and a fast-spinning white star, named in 2026 after the freshwater crab of Javanese skies.

facts.text: The blue giant’s surface is around 32,500 kelvins, and it pours out about 68,000 times the Sun’s energy — though it is only about nine million years old.
facts.title: Young and blazing

facts.text: Its combined spectrum was long listed as a standard for its class, O9 III — a reference point against which other hot giant stars are compared.
facts.title: A textbook star

facts.text: The fainter visible companion varies in brightness and is probably a young star, still not fully settled into adult life.
facts.title: A star still settling

story: Something does not add up at the heart of Iota Orionis. Its two main stars — a blue giant about 23 times the Sun’s mass and a partner about 13 times — whirl around each other every 29 days on a very elongated orbit. Yet the smaller star seems to be about twice as old as the bigger one, and stars born together should be the same age.

The likely answer is a capture. Perhaps two pairs of stars once met, each gave up one member to form this mismatched couple, and the other two were flung away as runaway stars. Today the pair’s stellar winds slam into each other, making the system a strong source of X-rays.

It belongs to NGC 1980, a young [[open-cluster|open cluster]] in Orion. Its old Arabic name, Nair al Saif, means “the Bright One of the Sword”. The more familiar Hatysa first appeared in Antonín Bečvář’s 1951 star atlas, and no one has found an older source for it.
iota-orionis.tagline: A blue giant with a partner twice its age — a mismatched couple probably forged in a stellar encounter.

facts.text: A 10th-magnitude companion lies 37.5 arcseconds from Iota¹ Scorpii. At the supergiant’s distance that gap is enormous — and the true separation may be larger still.
facts.title: A distant companion

facts.text: Luminosity class Ia is reserved for the most luminous supergiants. The Sun, by comparison, is class V: an ordinary main-sequence dwarf.
facts.title: Top of the class

story: The ‘Ia’ in Iota¹ Scorpii’s [[spectral-type|classification]], F2 Ia, puts it in the top tier of stars: a supergiant brighter even than ordinary supergiants. With some 12 solar masses, it shines about 35,000 times as brightly and has swollen to about 120 times the Sun’s radius. Set in the Sun’s place, it would reach well beyond the orbit of Mercury.

Its surface, at around 7,000 kelvins, glows yellow-white, hotter than the Sun’s. And much of its light never reaches us: gas and dust along the way dim it by about two-thirds of a magnitude, so without them it would look nearly twice as bright.
iota1-scorpii.tagline: An ultra-luminous yellow-white supergiant in the Scorpion’s tail, shining like 35,000 Suns through a veil of dust.

facts.text: In 1973 the Scottish writer Duncan Lunan claimed signals recorded in the 1920s by two Norwegian physicists came from an ancient alien probe orbiting Earth, sent from a planet of this star. Time magazine reported it. Lunan later withdrew the idea — then revoked his withdrawal.
facts.title: The Black Knight affair

facts.text: The IAU approved Izar for the brighter star in 2016 and, in April 2026, Pulcherrima for its companion. Izar comes from an Arabic word for a kilt-like garment.
facts.title: Two names, two stars

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the first star of Gěng Hé, the Celestial Lance, together with Sigma and Rho Boötis.
facts.title: The Celestial Lance

story: At Izar, two stars at very different stages of life share one orbit. The brighter is an orange giant more than four times the Sun’s mass, its core hydrogen already spent, shining about 650 times as brightly as the Sun. Its partner is a hot white star, still burning hydrogen in its core and spinning fast — at least 123 kilometres a second.

One day they will swap roles. By the time the companion reaches the giant’s present stage, the giant will have shed its outer layers as a [[planetary-nebula]] and shrunk into a dim white dwarf — leaving the former junior partner to shine as the giant.
There may be more to the family. A distant brown dwarf, and another star much farther out still, seem to share the pair’s motion across the sky, so this may turn out to be a system of four.
izar.tagline: A giant and a young companion destined to swap roles — and a star once blamed for an alien probe.

facts.text: Jupiter is so massive that the balance point it shares with the Sun lies just outside the Sun’s surface.
facts.title: Pulling on the Sun

facts.text: The word “jovial” comes from Jupiter: medieval astrologers believed the planet brought on a happy, merry mood.
facts.title: Jovial by name

facts.text: Add 40% more mass and Jupiter would actually get smaller, squeezed by its own gravity. It is about as wide as a planet of its kind can be.
facts.title: As big as it gets

facts.text: The IAU names Jupiter’s newly found moons after the god’s lovers, favourites and descendants.
facts.title: Moons named for lovers

story: Jupiter was probably the first planet to form, just a million years after the Sun and tens of millions of years before Earth. It outweighs all the other planets put together two and a half times over. As it grew it may have wandered in towards the Sun and back out again — a journey some scientists think cleared the way for Earth and the other rocky planets to form from the rubble.

It spins in about ten hours, so fast that its middle bulges outwards. Its stripes are bands of cloud, with storms where they meet; the largest, the [[great-red-spot|Great Red Spot]], has been recorded since 1831. Deep inside, hydrogen is squeezed into a liquid metal that drives the strongest magnetic field of any planet. Jupiter even gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun, as its interior slowly contracts — by about a millimetre a year.
At least 115 moons circle it. The four largest, the [[galilean-moons|Galilean moons]], show up in ordinary binoculars, and Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury.
jupiter.tagline: The oldest, biggest planet — a giant that may have shaped the whole Solar System, and is still shrinking.

facts.text: The Kamilaroi and Euahlayi Aboriginal peoples of New South Wales call this star Gidjirrigaa, the budgerigar.
facts.title: The budgerigar

facts.text: Kappa Scorpii is one of the stars on the flag of Brazil, where it represents the state of Paraíba.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Wěi Xiù qī, the Seventh Star of the Tail, a lunar mansion made from the Scorpion’s curving tail.
facts.title: Seventh star of the Tail

story: Kappa Scorpii has borne an ancient name: Girtab, the Sumerian word for “scorpion”, which survived through Babylonian star catalogues. It first belonged to a group of four stars in the tail, this one among them. A 1971 NASA catalogue listed the star instead as Mula, after an Indian nakshatra in the same part of the sky.

It is really two hot blue-white stars, too close together to separate in a telescope, circling each other every 195 days. The larger, about 11 times the Sun’s mass and nearly 7 times its width, is a Beta Cephei [[variable-star]]: it pulses about five times a day, roughly every 4.8 hours. It also spins quickly, turning once in only 1.9 days. Its partner, of about 10 solar masses, is only a little smaller.
kappa-scorpii.tagline: Two hot blue giants in the Scorpion’s tail, carrying the Sumerian word for “scorpion”.

facts.text: The Babylonian star compendium MUL.APIN lists Kaus Australis as MA.GUR8, ‘the Bark’ — an old word for a boat.
facts.title: The Bark

facts.text: The Kalapalo people of Mato Grosso in Brazil link it with stars in the Scorpion’s tail as Taugi kusugu, ‘Taugi’s fishing basket’.
facts.title: Taugi’s fishing basket

facts.text: In China it is the third star of Jī, the Winnowing Basket, a pattern made with three other stars of Sagittarius.
facts.title: The Winnowing Basket

story: Kaus Australis spins at 95% of the speed that would tear it apart — the highest rate ever measured for a star in the Milky Way. The spin squashes it so that it is about a third bigger around the equator than over the poles. The poles, at about 11,700 K, are far hotter than the equator, at about 7,400 K, and a disc of gas spun off its middle surrounds it.

Such a spin is hard to explain for a lone star. More likely it was spun up long ago when gas poured onto it from a partner. Today it is a [[star]] of about 3.8 solar masses, shining 500 times as brightly as the Sun, with a smaller, Sun-like companion first seen in 1993.
Its name mixes Arabic qaws, ‘bow’, with Latin australis, ‘southern’ — the southern part of the Archer’s bow.
kaus-australis.tagline: The brightest star of the Teapot — spinning closer to break-up than any other star measured in our galaxy.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers counted it as the second star of Dǒu, the Dipper, the same group in which Ascella is the first.
facts.title: Second star of the Dipper

facts.text: On 17 December 2021 Mercury passed less than an arcminute from Kaus Borealis, as seen from Earth.
facts.title: A close call with Mercury

story: Medieval Arabic astronomers called it the keeper of the ostriches. Al Tizini named it Rāʽi al-Naʽāʼim, watching over two flocks of stars nearby: the Going Ostriches and the Returning Ostriches. Its modern name is plainer, joining the Arabic qaws, “bow”, to the Latin borealis, “northern” — the top of the Archer’s bow.

It is an [[star-colour|orange]] giant of about 1.8 times the Sun’s mass, swollen to 11 times its width, with a surface near 4,770 K. It turns lazily: its equator moves at least 3.8 kilometres per second, about twice the Sun’s rate.
Lying just south of the [[ecliptic]], it is sometimes covered by the Moon and, rarely, by a planet. Venus last passed in front of it on 19 November 1984; before that, Mercury did so in 1865.
kaus-borealis.tagline: The top of the Archer’s bow — once the keeper of the ostriches.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Kaus Media is the second star of Jī, the Winnowing Basket, a group of four stars around the Teapot’s spout.
facts.title: The Winnowing Basket

facts.text: In Hindu astrology this star is also called Purvashada, the name of one of the nakshatras, the lunar mansions.
facts.title: A lunar mansion

story: The Archer’s bow is drawn with three stars, and Kaus Media holds the middle — its name joins the Arabic qaws, “bow”, to the Latin media, “middle”. Kaus Borealis marks the bow’s northern tip and Kaus Australis its southern end.

It is an [[star-colour|orange]] giant about three times the Sun’s mass. Though only some 260 million years old, it has already left the main sequence and is most likely fusing helium into carbon in its core.

It may not be alone. It has been listed as having a white dwarf companion — the dense, burnt-out core of a star that has already finished its life. Three much fainter stars, of magnitudes 13 to 15, also appear within a minute of arc of it.
kaus-media.tagline: The middle of the Archer’s bow — an orange giant that may hide a white dwarf.

facts.text: Ancient Egyptian astronomers called Kochab and Mizar “the Indestructibles” lighting the north — stars that never set.
facts.title: The Indestructibles

facts.text: The name’s meaning is uncertain. It may come from Arabic al-kawkab or Hebrew kōkhāv, both simply “star”, but more likely from Rucaba, an old name for a star in Ursa Major.
facts.title: Just “star”?

facts.text: In China it is Běi Jí èr, the Second Star of the North Pole asterism, representing the emperor.
facts.title: The emperor’s star

story: Long before Polaris took the job, Kochab helped mark north. Around 2500 BC, as Thuban drifted away from the celestial pole, a plumb line hung between Kochab and Mizar in the Big Dipper pointed to true north — something the ancient Egyptians knew well. From about 1700 BC until just after AD 300, Kochab and its neighbour Pherkad circled the pole as twin pole stars.

It is an orange giant some 44 times the Sun’s width and about 540 times as luminous, with a surface near 4,100 kelvin. Astronomers still debate its exact stage of life, and estimates of its mass range from about 1.3 to 2.5 Suns. Its age is put at roughly three billion years.
Kochab also brightens and fades slightly over about 4.6 days, and a giant [[planet]] some six times Jupiter’s mass has been reported circling it every 522 days.
kochab.tagline: A pointer to true north for the ancient Egyptians — and now a Guardian of the Pole.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; W. W. Campbell found its companion from its spectrum in 1899

facts.text: Its other old name, Rutilicus, is a corruption of the Latin titillicus, “armpit”. The US Navy gave that name to a cargo ship, USS Rutilicus (AK-113).
facts.title: The armpit

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the first star of the Right Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, representing Hézhōng — which R. H. Allen rendered as Ho Chung, “in the river”.
facts.title: In the river

facts.text: Astronomers compare it with the main star of Capella: a similar giant, but warmer and brighter.
facts.title: Capella’s warmer cousin

story: Kornephoros is Greek for “the club bearer”, a fitting name for the brightest star of Hercules. In July 1899 the American astronomer W. W. Campbell noticed that its speed along our line of sight kept changing, and concluded that an unseen companion was tugging on it. In 1977 Antoine Labeyrie and colleagues finally resolved the pair, using speckle interferometry on the Hale Telescope at Palomar.

The two stars circle each other about every 410 days on a stretched orbit. The main star is a [[star-colour|yellow]] giant of nearly three times the Sun’s mass, swollen to 16 times its width; its partner is a little lighter than the Sun.

Kornephoros was once a hot B-type star much like Zubeneschamali in Libra. Now about 420 million years old, it probably fuses helium in its core. It is not heavy enough to explode, so it will end as a white dwarf, like Sirius B but less massive.
kornephoros.tagline: The club bearer — Hercules’ brightest star, a giant with a hidden partner.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers counted Kraz as the fourth star of Zhěn, the Chariot, made from the four bright stars of Corvus.
facts.title: Fourth star of the Chariot

facts.text: Kraz is listed as a suspected variable star, wandering between magnitudes 2.60 and 2.66 — far too small a change to notice by eye.
facts.title: A suspected variable

story: Nobody knows what Kraz means. The name first appears in 1951, in the star atlas Atlas Coeli by the Czech astronomer Antonín Bečvář, and its origin and meaning remain a mystery. The IAU made it official anyway in 2018.

The star itself is a [[star-colour|yellow]] bright giant of about 3.3 times the Sun’s mass. Though only some 300 million years old — around a fifteenth of the Sun’s age — it has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to nearly 16 times the Sun’s width, shining 175 times as brightly from a surface near 5,300 K.
It is also rich in heavy elements, with about 1.4 times the Sun’s share of what astronomers call metals.
kraz.tagline: A yellow giant in the Crow whose name nobody can explain.

discovered.note: Named by John Birmingham in 1876, after Angelo Secchi’s description of its spectrum

facts.text: The vast shell of material around La Superba shows that it once lost mass as much as 50 times faster than it does today.
facts.title: A once-stronger wind

facts.text: Its brightness wanders by about a magnitude over roughly 160 days, with slower swings on top. Periods of 194 and 186 days have also been suggested.
facts.title: Rhythms within rhythms

facts.text: The IRAS infrared satellite found La Superba surrounded by one of the most prominent dust shells in its whole-sky survey.
facts.title: Seen by IRAS

story: In the 19th century the Jesuit astronomer Angelo Secchi called this star’s spectrum ‘superba’. In 1876 the Irish astronomer John Birmingham turned the word into a name, and the IAU adopted La Superba officially in 2018. It is Italian for ‘the magnificent’.

It is one of the [[star-colour|reddest]] stars known, and the reason is carbon. La Superba is a carbon star: deep churning has dredged carbon up from its interior into its atmosphere, where molecules soak up blue and violet light. At about 2,760 kelvins it is also one of the coolest stars known, and it is the brightest of the rare J-stars, rich in carbon-13.

Placed where the Sun is, its surface would reach beyond Earth’s orbit. Near the end of its life, it is shedding gas fast and is wrapped in a vast shell of material it has already thrown off. Soon, as stars count time, it should cast off its outer layers as a [[planetary-nebula]], leaving its core behind as a white dwarf.
la-superba.tagline: One of the reddest stars in the sky — a cool carbon giant, nearly ready to shed its skin.

facts.text: Larawag is one of the stars on the flag of Brazil, where it represents the state of Ceará.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: Patrick Moore gave its Chinese name as Wei, but that seems a misreading: Wěi, the Tail, is a whole asterism, and this star is its second star.
facts.title: A misread name

story: Larawag’s name comes from the Wardaman people of Australia’s Northern Territory, for whom it means “clear sighting”. The International Astronomical Union adopted it in 2017, bringing an Aboriginal Australian name into the official catalogue of the stars.

Larawag is an orange giant about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass and 13 times its width. Having finished with the hydrogen in its core, it now fuses helium there, which places it among the red clump giants, a common stage for orange giants. Its surface glows at about 4,500 kelvin, cooler than the Sun’s.
It also has company. In 2018 astronomers found a much smaller, fainter star moving with it through space, which makes Larawag a [[double-star|binary]].
larawag.tagline: An orange giant in the Scorpion’s tail, with a Wardaman name meaning “clear sighting”.

facts.text: In Bayer’s atlas of 1603, “Zeta Centauri” was Acrux, then counted as part of the Centaur. Lacaille gave the letter to this star in his catalogue of 1756.
facts.title: A borrowed letter

facts.text: It has also been called Alnair, from the Arabic for “the bright star of the body of the Centaur” — a name first used for Acrux and now officially given to Alpha Gruis.
facts.title: A name passed around

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the first star of Kù Lóu, the Arsenal, a group of ten stars in Centaurus.
facts.title: The Arsenal

story: Every eight days or so, two hot [[star-colour|blue-white]] stars whirl around each other in Zeta Centauri, too close for any telescope to split. Astronomers know the [[double-star|pair]] from the spectrum alone, where each star’s lines shift back and forth as they swing towards and away from us.

The brighter star has nearly eight times the Sun’s mass and six times its width, and spins at least 235 kilometres per second at its equator. At about 40 million years old it is young by the Sun’s standards, yet already easing off the main sequence into a subgiant.
In the Marshall Islands it is Ļeepwal, the third of the ten sons of Lōktañūr — the star we call Capella. In 2024 the IAU adopted the name, spelled Leepwal.
leepwal.tagline: Two hot stars locked in an eight-day orbit — named in the Marshall Islands as a son of Capella.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Lesath is the ninth star of Wěi, the Tail — the long curl of stars that forms the Scorpion’s tail.
facts.title: Ninth star of the Tail

facts.text: A US Navy Crater-class cargo ship, USS Lesuth (AK-125), was named after the star, using one of its older spellings.
facts.title: USS Lesuth

story: Lesath’s name is a scholar’s mistake. The Arabic las‘a, “the bite of a poisonous animal”, suits a star in a scorpion’s sting — but it was a miscorrection by Scaliger, a European astronomer who knew Arabic. The earlier name, Alascha, came from al-laṭkha, “the foggy patch”: the star cluster M 7 nearby.

With brighter Shaula, it has been a pair in many skies. The Babylonian star list MUL.APIN names the two as Sharur and Shargaz; in Coptic they were Minamref; and the Boorong people of north-western Victoria saw them as Karik Karik, the Falcons.

The star itself is a hot [[star-colour|blue-white]] subgiant of about 11 times the Sun’s mass and six times its width, with a surface near 23,000 K. It gives out some 12,000 times as much light as the Sun.
lesath.tagline: One of the Scorpion’s two stinger stars — with a name born of a scholar’s mistake.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Mahasim is the fourth star of the Five Chariots, a pattern in Auriga that also includes Hassaleh.
facts.title: Fourth of the Five Chariots

facts.text: Versions of Mahasim, “the wrist”, were also used for Eta Aurigae and for Lambda Herculis, far away in Hercules.
facts.title: One name, three stars

story: Mahasim’s surface is a patchwork. This hot white star has a strong magnetic field and an atmosphere strangely rich in silicon, with the unusual elements gathered in patches. As it turns, they swing into and out of view, nudging its brightness up and down by less than a tenth of a magnitude — making it a [[variable-star|variable star]].
The star has more than three times the Sun’s mass, nearly five times its width and over 200 times its luminosity. A fainter, cooler F-type star keeps it company.

Its name is a late arrival. Some authors say the star had no traditional name at all; the IAU adopted Mahasim in 2017 from a passing mention by the star-name historian Richard Hinckley Allen. It is Arabic for “the wrist” — the Charioteer’s.
mahasim.tagline: A magnetic star with a patchy, silicon-rich surface, at the Charioteer’s wrist.

facts.text: In ancient Indian astronomy Markab and Beta Pegasi are the chief stars of Purva Bhadrapada, the 25th nakshatra — one of the lunar mansions the Moon passes through each month.
facts.title: A mansion of the Moon

facts.text: Chinese astronomers paired Markab with Beta Pegasi in Shì, the Encampment. Markab is its first star.
facts.title: The Encampment

facts.text: The same Arabic word gave the name Markeb to a star in Vela. It is spelled differently to avoid confusion with this one.
facts.title: A namesake in the south

story: Markab holds up one corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, yet for an Alpha star it is surprisingly modest: two other stars in the winged horse outshine it. It is a hot white [[star]], around 10,000 K at the surface, that has used up the hydrogen in its core and begun to swell. It is now nearly five times the Sun’s width and 165 times as luminous.

It spins hard, too — at least 130 kilometres per second at its equator, more than 60 times the Sun’s rate. Astronomers have not even settled its exact [[spectral-type|class]]: it has been listed as a subgiant, a main-sequence star and a giant.

The name is usually traced to the Arabic for “the saddle of the horse”. It may instead be a garbled copy of Mankib, “the shoulder of the horse”, a name that first belonged to its neighbour Scheat, Beta Pegasi.
markab.tagline: A corner of the Great Square of Pegasus — a fast-spinning white star that has begun to swell.

facts.text: The fainter companion has 7.7 times the Sun’s mass and a surface of around 19,000 K — slightly hotter than its brighter partner.
facts.title: No lightweight partner

facts.text: Markab and Markeb are the same Arabic word. The IAU approved Markab for Alpha Pegasi in 2016 and Markeb for this star in 2017, keeping the two apart.
facts.title: Two names, one word

facts.text: Chinese astronomers placed Markeb in Tiān Shè, the Celestial Earth God’s Temple, together with Gamma and Delta Velorum. It is known as the temple’s fifth star.
facts.title: Fifth star of the temple

story: Southern navigators learned to be wary of this part of the sky. Markeb is one of four stars that make up the False Cross, a pattern so like the Southern Cross that mixing them up has caused errors in navigating by the stars. Its name comes from the Arabic markab, “something to ride”, and is spelled Markeb to keep it apart from Markab in Pegasus.

What looks like one [[star-colour|blue-white]] point is really a [[double-star|pair]] of hot stars, circling each other every 117 days at a little more than the Earth–Sun distance. The brighter one has about 13 times the Sun’s mass and 12 times its width, and shines some 13,000 times more brightly. It is running low on hydrogen in its core and beginning to turn into a subgiant.

Markeb’s light even reveals a passing cloud. Over the years, absorption lines from the gas between us and the star have strengthened and weakened, probably because a small, dense cloud is drifting across our line of sight.
markeb.tagline: One corner of the False Cross, the star pattern that has led southern navigators astray.

facts.text: A 2023 study suggests Mars may once have had a ring, made from a moon about 20 times heavier than Phobos — and that Phobos itself could be a remnant of it.
facts.title: A lost ring?

facts.text: NASA’s InSight lander recorded more than 450 marsquakes and related events, helping to show that Mars has an iron core that is at least partly molten.
facts.title: Marsquakes

facts.text: Its smooth northern lowlands and cratered southern highlands may be the scar of a giant impact by a Pluto-sized body about four billion years ago.
facts.title: A planet of two halves

facts.text: The Phoenix lander found Martian soil to be slightly alkaline and laced with perchlorate, at levels toxic to humans.
facts.title: Toxic soil

story: Mars owes its colour to rust: iron oxide dust coats the ground and hangs in the thin air, which is mostly carbon dioxide at less than a hundredth of Earth’s pressure. Up close the dust can look butterscotch, golden or brown. With an axis tilted much like Earth’s, Mars has seasons, and its day lasts just 24.6 hours.

It is a world of extremes. Olympus Mons, the tallest of its extinct volcanoes, rises about two and a half times higher than Everest, and Valles Marineris is one of the largest canyons in the Solar System. Billions of years ago water carved valleys and vast flood channels here, and may even have filled oceans. Whether life ever arose is still an open question.

No planet beyond Earth has had more robot visitors. Mariner 4 flew past in 1965; in 1971 Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, and Mars 3 made the first landing. Probes have worked there without a break since 1997, sometimes more than ten at once.
mars.tagline: A rusty desert of giant volcanoes, perhaps a lost ring — and more robot visitors than any other planet.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers grouped Matar with five other stars of Pegasus as Lì Gōng, the Resting Palace. Matar is its fourth star.
facts.title: The Resting Palace

facts.text: Two more yellow G-type stars lie farther out from the main pair. Nobody yet knows whether they really belong to the system.
facts.title: More family, perhaps

story: Matar’s name promised rain. It comes from the Arabic Sa‘d al-Maṭar, ‘the lucky star of rain’, and the US Navy later named a cargo ship, USS Matar, after it.

It is really [[double-star|two stars]]. The brighter is a yellow giant of about three and a half solar masses that has swollen to more than 24 times the Sun’s radius and shines about 331 times as brightly. A smaller, hotter main-sequence partner circles it every 813 days on a slightly stretched orbit.
As the giant expanded, its spin slowed, the way a twirling skater slows by spreading her arms. It now turns only about once every 818 days — close to the time its partner takes to go round it.
matar.tagline: ‘The lucky star of rain’: a yellow giant in Pegasus that has slowed its spin to a crawl.

facts.text: In 1889 Antonia Maury, one of Harvard Observatory’s women ‘computers’, noticed Menkalinan’s spectral lines doubling and merging. It was only the second spectroscopic binary ever found, after Mizar.
facts.title: The second binary of its kind

facts.text: In traditional Chinese astronomy Menkalinan is the third star of the Five Chariots, a pattern it shares with Capella and Elnath.
facts.title: Five Chariots

story: Menkalinan looks like one [[star]] but is two: a pair of white [[spectral-type|A-type]] stars, both hotter and brighter than the Sun, circling each other every four days. Their orbit is tilted so that every 47.5 hours one partly hides the other, and the light dips — but only by a few hundredths of a magnitude. Both are ‘metallic-line’ stars, whose odd spectra make them look like ageing subgiants, though both are still in the prime of life.
The pair is heading our way. Menkalinan and the Sun are closing in on each other as they orbit the galaxy, and in about a million years it should become the brightest star in our night sky.

Its name comes from the Arabic for ‘shoulder of the rein-holder’ — the Charioteer’s shoulder. Like most stars of the Plough, it is thought to belong to the Ursa Major moving group, a family of stars sharing one path through space.
menkalinan.tagline: Two white stars that eclipse each other every two days — and a future brightest star in the sky.

facts.text: Arabic star lore grouped Menkar with six other stars of Cetus as al-Kaff al-Jidhmah, “the part of a hand”.
facts.title: Part of a hand

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Menkar is the first star of Tiān Qūn, the Circular Celestial Granary, a group of 13 stars in Cetus.
facts.title: The Circular Granary

facts.text: The US Navy named a Crater-class cargo ship after the star: USS Menkar (AK-123).
facts.title: A ship named Menkar

story: If Menkar took the Sun’s place, its surface would reach past the orbit of Mercury. This bloated [[star-colour|red]] giant is about 100 times the Sun’s width, and although its surface is a cool 3,700 K, all that glowing area gives off more than 1,700 times the Sun’s light.

It is near the end of its life. Menkar has used up first the hydrogen and then the helium in its core. Astronomers expect it to become unstable, like its famous neighbour Mira, before puffing off its outer layers as a [[planetary-nebula]] and leaving behind a white dwarf.
The name is Arabic for “nostril” — the Sea Monster’s. Despite its Alpha label, Menkar is not the brightest star in Cetus: Beta Ceti, also called Diphda, outshines it.
menkar.tagline: The Sea Monster’s nostril — a dying red giant big enough to swallow Mercury’s orbit.

facts.text: Menkent is often called a southern counterpart of Pollux in Gemini, the closest giant star to the Sun: both are orange, helium-burning giants.
facts.title: Pollux of the south

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Kù Lóu sān, the Third Star of the Arsenal, an asterism of ten stars spread across the Centaur.
facts.title: Third star of the Arsenal

story: Menkent’s name is a blend: the Arabic mankib, “shoulder”, run together with a clipped form of “kentaurus”. It marks the shoulder of the Centaur, a constellation better known for its brilliant pair of Pointers, Alpha Centauri and Hadar.

This is an orange giant of about 1.3 solar masses, 11 times the Sun’s width and 56 times as luminous. Having finished with hydrogen in its core, it now fuses helium into carbon, which makes it what astronomers call a red clump [[star]]. Its surface, near 4,850 kelvin, is cooler than the Sun’s.
Menkent is also a visitor. Its relatively quick drift across the sky suggests it was born in the outer disc of the [[milky-way|Milky Way]] and is only passing through the Sun’s neighbourhood.
menkent.tagline: The Centaur’s shoulder — an orange giant just passing through our part of the galaxy.

facts.text: In 1943 Merak was listed as a spectral standard for white A1 stars, a reference against which the light of other stars was measured.
facts.title: A yardstick for white stars

facts.text: In China it is Tiān Xuán, the Star of Celestial Rotating Jade, and the second star of the Northern Dipper.
facts.title: Celestial Rotating Jade

story: Merak is one half of the most famous signpost in the northern sky, the Pointers of the Big Dipper, or Plough. Its name comes from the Arabic al-marāqq, “the loins” of the bear. Hindu astronomers knew it as Pulaha, one of the Seven Rishis, the sages of these seven stars.

It is a white [[star]] about 2.7 times the Sun’s mass and 68 times as luminous, some three-quarters of the way through its hydrogen-burning life. Around it orbits a disc of cold dust at about 120 kelvin, like the discs found around Vega and Fomalhaut.

Merak is also part of a real family. With four other Dipper stars it belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, stars born together about 500 million years ago and still travelling through space side by side. Much of the Dipper is not a chance line-up at all.
merak.tagline: One of the Big Dipper’s Pointers — a white star from a family that still travels together.

facts.text: Mercury’s axis barely tilts, so the floors of some polar craters never see sunlight. Water ice is strongly suspected to be hiding there.
facts.title: Ice on the planet nearest the Sun

facts.text: Mercury’s [[crater|craters]] are named after artists, musicians, painters and authors; its mountains after the word “hot” in different languages; its valleys after abandoned cities of antiquity.
facts.title: Craters for artists

facts.text: Mercury is smaller than Jupiter’s moon Ganymede and Saturn’s moon Titan — though it outweighs them both.
facts.title: Smaller than two moons

story: On Mercury, one day from sunrise to sunrise lasts 176 Earth days — two of its years. The planet spins exactly three times for every two trips around the Sun, so each side bakes in sunlight for a whole Mercurian year, then freezes through a night just as long. At the equator, days reach 420 °C and nights plunge to −170 °C.

Inside, it is mostly metal: its iron-rich core fills more than half the planet’s volume, against less than a fifth for Earth. Perhaps a giant impact stripped away much of its rocky mantle, or perhaps the young Sun’s heat drove it off. NASA’s MESSENGER probe found surface chemistry that argues against both ideas, and the European–Japanese BepiColombo mission, arriving in 2026, will test them further.

As the core cooled, the whole planet contracted, wrinkling its crust into long ridges. The ancient Greeks realised by about 350 BC that the morning and evening “stars” were one object; the Romans named it after their swift messenger god, because it moves across the sky faster than any other planet.
mercury.tagline: A scorched iron world where one day lasts two of its years — the Sun’s swift messenger.

facts.text: It was once called the First Star in Aries, because it was at one time the nearest visible star to the equinox point, where the Sun crosses the celestial equator each March.
facts.title: The First Star in Aries

facts.text: In Hindu astrology, Mesarthim and Sheratan are the Ashvins, the twin gods of the Rigveda who act as doctors to the divine.
facts.title: The heavenly physicians

facts.text: In 2016 a study found a likely red dwarf on a close orbit around the brighter star, which would make the system a triple.
facts.title: A third member?

story: On paper, the two stars of Mesarthim are twins: both about 2.7 times the Sun’s mass, both around 10,000 kelvins at the surface, both only about 34 million years old. Look at their light in detail, though, and they could hardly be more different.

The brighter is a magnetic “Ap” star whose atmosphere is loaded with silicon, strontium and chromium; its brightness wavers very slightly every 2.61 days as it turns. Its companion has the opposite quirk — it is unusually poor in iron and similar elements — and spins at more than 200 kilometres a second.

Even the name is a mistake. The star once shared the name Sheratan with its neighbour Beta Arietis. Medieval manuscripts garbled that into “Sartai”, which Johann Bayer wrongly explained as a Hebrew word for “servants” — and later scholars ran with it.
mesarthim.tagline: Twin stars with opposite chemistry — and a name that grew out of a scholar’s mistake.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star of the far southern sky

facts.text: Edmond Halley made it the alpha star of Robur Carolinum, Charles’s Oak, a constellation he created to honour King Charles II. The constellation is no longer used.
facts.title: Halley’s royal oak

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the fifth star of Nán Chuán, the Southern Boat, a pattern within Carina, the Keel.
facts.title: The Southern Boat

story: Nobody is quite sure what Miaplacidus means. The name first appeared on star maps in 1856, in Elijah Burritt’s atlas Geography of the Heavens. The second half looks like Latin placidus, ‘placid’; the 19th-century star-name scholar William Higgins guessed that the first part comes from the Arabic miyāh, ‘waters’. Neither part is certain.

The star itself is a white giant [[star]] of about 3.8 solar masses. At around 260 million years old it has used up its core hydrogen and expanded to almost six times the Sun’s width, yet it still spins fast. It shines with about 220 times the Sun’s light from a surface at about 9,150 K. Unlike Vega or Fomalhaut, it shows no sign of a dusty debris disc.
miaplacidus.tagline: A bright southern star with a name nobody can quite explain — the leading light of the Diamond Cross.

facts.text: With Herschel crater on its face, Mimas looks very like the Death Star of Star Wars — yet the film came out in 1977, three years before Voyager 1 photographed the moon.
facts.title: A Death Star in orbit

facts.text: When Cassini mapped Mimas’s daytime temperatures in 2010, the warm and cool regions formed a shape just like Pac-Man.
facts.title: A Pac-Man made of heat

facts.text: The whole surface of Mimas is slightly smaller than the land area of Spain or California.
facts.title: Smaller than Spain

story: One giant [[crater]] dominates Mimas. Named Herschel after the moon’s discoverer, it spans almost a third of the moon’s width, with walls about 5 km high and a central peak rising 6 km from the floor. On Earth, a crater on the same scale would be wider than Australia. The blow that made it must have nearly shattered Mimas: the ground on the far side is broken up, as if the shock wave rang through the whole moon.

Mimas is the smallest body known to have been pulled into a round shape by its own gravity, and it is made mostly of water ice. Careful tracking of how it moves has revealed a surprise: a young ocean of liquid water beneath its cratered crust, formed within the last 25 million years and perhaps only a few million years ago.
Small as it is, Mimas shapes Saturn’s [[saturns-rings|rings]]. Its repeated pulls sweep particles out of the Cassini Division, the dark gap between the two broadest rings.
mimas.tagline: A small ice moon with one enormous crater — and an uncanny likeness to the Death Star.

facts.text: Mimosa is one of the Southern Cross stars on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea. On Brazil’s flag it stands for the state of Rio de Janeiro.
facts.title: On five flags

facts.text: Precession once placed Mimosa far enough north for the ancient Greeks and Romans to see it from latitudes north of 40°. They counted it as part of Centaurus.
facts.title: Once a Greek star

facts.text: Asteroseismology — reading a star’s insides from its pulsations — gives Mimosa an age of 11 million years. It is the most massive star whose age has been found this way.
facts.title: A record age

story: Mimosa is a newcomer. The system is only 8 to 11 million years old, yet its main [[star]] — a blue giant 15 times the Sun’s mass — has already used up the hydrogen in its core. Heavy stars live fast: in roughly 6 million years it may explode as a supernova. Its surface, at about 27,000 K, glows blue-white, and a fierce wind streams off it at 2,000 km/s or more.

It does not live alone. A smaller star circles it every five years, too close to separate in a telescope, and a third, still-young star, announced in 2007, glows in X-rays. The giant is also a [[variable-star|variable star]], pulsing gently with three rhythms, each a little over four hours long. Its name may come from the mimosa flower, or from the Latin for ‘actor’.
mimosa.tagline: The second star of the Southern Cross — a young blue giant that may explode in a few million years.

facts.text: Arab astronomers called the three belt stars the Belt, the Line, and the Golden Grains; in modern Arabic they are the Accurate Scale Beam, and in Chinese mythology the Weighing Beam.
facts.title: Many names for the Belt

facts.text: The Chinese asterism Shēn, the Three Stars, began with the belt alone; Betelgeuse, Bellatrix, Saiph and Rigel were added later. Mintaka is its third star.
facts.title: Where Shēn began

story: Mintaka, from the Arabic for “belt”, is the westernmost of the three stars of Orion’s Belt. It sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises almost due east and sets almost due west wherever you are on Earth.

That single point of light holds five stars. At its heart a hot blue giant and a smaller partner whirl around each other every 5.7 days, eclipsing slightly as they go. A third star circles them about every 150 years, and a separate pair keeps company nearby. All five are hotter and heavier than the Sun.

Mintaka made history in 1904. At Potsdam, Johannes Hartmann noticed that one calcium line in its spectrum stood still while the others swayed back and forth with the stars’ orbit. That calcium had to lie in a cloud between us and the star — the first detection of the gas between the stars.
mintaka.tagline: The westernmost star of Orion’s Belt — five suns in one point of light, and proof that space is not empty.

facts.text: When William Herschel described the deep colour of the Garnet Star in Cepheus, he compared it with ‘the periodical star ο Ceti’ — Mira.
facts.title: Herschel’s yardstick for red

facts.text: Chinese and Korean records from 1596, 1070 and 134 BC may describe Mira, and some lines by Hipparchus might too. None is certain.
facts.title: Seen before Fabricius?

facts.text: In 1925 Francis Pease used an interferometer at Mount Wilson to measure Mira’s size. It was then the second-largest star known, after Antares.
facts.title: Measured in 1925

story: In August 1596 the pastor David Fabricius picked a third-magnitude star in Cetus as a reference while tracking a planet. Within weeks it had brightened; by October it had vanished. He took it for a nova — until he saw it again in 1609. In 1638 Johannes Holwarda worked out that it returned every eleven months, and in 1662 Johannes Hevelius named it Mira, ‘the wonderful’.

Mira is a red giant near the end of its life, hundreds of times wider than the Sun. It pulsates, and since most of its light is infrared, small changes in its temperature make huge changes in what our eyes see: at its best it can reach magnitude 2, at its faintest about 10, and its deep red at minimum pales to orange as it brightens. It is the prototype of the Mira [[variable-star|variables]], of which thousands are now known.

It is not alone. A white dwarf, Mira B, pulls gas from the giant across a bridge of matter seen by the Chandra X-ray Observatory. And in 2007 NASA’s GALEX ultraviolet telescope revealed a vast, comet-like tail of shed gas trailing behind Mira as it speeds through space.
mira.tagline: ‘The Wonderful’ — a pulsing red giant that swells, fades from sight and returns roughly every eleven months.

facts.text: Just seven arcminutes from Mirach lies the small galaxy NGC 404, nicknamed Mirach’s Ghost for the way it hovers in the bright star’s glare.
facts.title: Mirach’s Ghost

facts.text: In Micronesia the star was Kyyw, “the Porpoise”, and the name also served for one of the months.
facts.title: The Porpoise

facts.text: The Babylonian star catalogue MUL.APIN lists it as KA.MUSH.I.KU.E, “the Deleter”.
facts.title: The Deleter

story: Mirach’s name is a copying slip. The Arabic mīzar, “girdle”, was garbled to mirat in a Latin translation of Ptolemy’s Almagest, and the Alfonsine Tables of 1521 described the star as super mizar. The girdle sits at the left hip of the chained princess Andromeda.

It is a red giant late in its life, about two and a half times the Sun’s mass. With the hydrogen in its core long gone, it has bloated to some 86 times the Sun’s width and shines nearly 1,700 times as brightly. It may vary slightly, and a 2023 study found hints of a brown dwarf circling it.

Since 1943 its spectrum has been one of the anchor points for classifying other stars. Chinese astronomers used it as their standard “black” star — in this sense a deep red, set against Antares, the standard red.
mirach.tagline: The red giant at Andromeda’s hip — and the classic signpost to the Andromeda Galaxy.

facts.text: Kuiper named it after Miranda in Shakespeare’s The Tempest. Uranus’s earlier moons were named for fairies and spirits; Miranda was the first human.
facts.title: A human among fairies

facts.text: Miranda’s whole surface area is roughly equal to that of the US state of Texas — where, fittingly, it was discovered.
facts.title: A Texas-sized moon

story: When Voyager 2 sped past Uranus in January 1986, the team expected Miranda to look like Saturn’s Mimas: a plain, cratered ball. Instead it was a patchwork of grooved, chevron-shaped regions called coronae, jumbled terrain and Verona Rupes, a cliff about 20 km high that may be the tallest in the Solar System. With only a day before the pictures went to the press, the scientists were at a loss to explain it.

Decades later, several explanations still compete. One idea is that Miranda was once caught in an orbital resonance with Umbriel, which stretched its orbit, heated its interior and left it with an unusually tilted path. Only its southern half has ever been seen up close: during the flyby, the north lay in darkness.

Gerard Kuiper discovered Miranda, the smallest and innermost of Uranus’s five round [[planetary-moon|moons]], in 1948 at McDonald Observatory in Texas — the first new moon of Uranus found in nearly a century.
miranda.tagline: A small moon that looks stitched together from scraps — with what may be the tallest cliff in the Solar System.

facts.text: In Native Hawaiian astronomy Mirfak is Hinaliʻi. The name commemorates a great tsunami and marks the beginning of the migration of Maui.
facts.title: Hinaliʻi

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made Mirfak the third star of Tiān Chuán, the Celestial Boat, a pattern made from stars of Perseus.
facts.title: The Celestial Boat

story: Mirfak is a supergiant [[star]] in the later stages of its life, six to seven times the Sun’s mass and swollen to about 54 times its width. It shines with some 4,000 times the Sun’s light from a surface at about 6,400 K, a yellow-white glow. Its spectrum looks much like Procyon’s, yet it is far more luminous. The Yerkes system of 1943, which ranks stars by luminosity as well as type, tells the two apart, and Mirfak has been one of its reference stars ever since.

It sits in the zone of temperature and brightness where pulsing Cepheid variables live, so it helps astronomers understand them — though Mirfak itself barely flickers. A suspected giant planet was ruled out in 2025: the wobble it seemed to cause kept changing, and is more likely the star’s own oscillations.
Its name is Arabic for ‘elbow’, from mirfaq al-thurayyā, ‘the elbow of the Pleiades’.
mirfak.tagline: The heart of Perseus — a yellow-white supergiant shining from the middle of its own star cluster.

facts.text: Mirzam is one of the stars on the flag of Brazil, where it stands for the state of Amapá.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: The Dunhuang Star Chart from China shows it as Yeji, the “Pheasant Cock” — drawn about 10 degrees too far north.
facts.title: A misplaced pheasant

facts.text: Mirzam lies inside the Mirzam Tunnel, a corridor of thin interstellar gas near the far edge of the Local Bubble, the cavity the Sun is travelling through.
facts.title: Its own tunnel

story: Its name means “the Herald” in Arabic, probably because it climbs above the horizon just ahead of Sirius, announcing the brightest star in the sky. But the herald once outshone its master. Around four million years ago Mirzam was the brightest star in Earth’s night sky — more than seven times as bright as Sirius is now.

It is a hot blue-white giant of 12 to 13 solar masses, its surface near 24,700 kelvin, over four times hotter than the Sun’s. Only 12 to 14 million years old, it has already begun to swell, and it is heavy enough to end its life as a supernova.
Mirzam also breathes. Its outer layers pulse in three overlapping rhythms, each about six hours long, making it a Beta Cephei [[variable-star]]. The change is far too slight for the eye to notice.
mirzam.tagline: The Herald that rises before Sirius — and was once brighter than Sirius is today.

discovered.note: Observed at Benedetto Castelli’s request; Mizar and Alcor have been a naked-eye pair since antiquity

facts.text: In 1996, 107 years after their discovery, the two stars of Mizar A were finally imaged directly, using the Navy Prototype Optical Interferometer.
facts.title: Seen at last

facts.text: In traditional Indian astronomy Mizar is Vashistha, one of the Saptarishi — the seven sages whose stars make up the Plough.
facts.title: One of the seven sages

facts.text: Steely Dan name-check Mizar in their song “Sign In Stranger”, from the album The Royal Scam.
facts.title: A rock-song star

facts.text: Mizar, Alcor and many of the other bright stars of the Plough belong to the Ursa Major Moving Group, a family of stars drifting through space together.
facts.title: Travelling together

story: In 1617 Benedetto Castelli asked Galileo to turn a telescope on Mizar, and Galileo made a detailed record of what he saw: two stars where the eye sees one. It may have been the first double star known to Europeans through a telescope.

Its next first came from Harvard. During Antonia Maury’s work classifying stellar spectra, the brighter star’s light turned out to come from two stars circling every 20½ days, far too close to see apart. It was the first [[double-star|spectroscopic binary]] ever discovered, and its orbit was published in 1890. In 1908 the fainter star proved to be a close pair as well.

Alcor completes the family. Arab sky-watchers called the two the horse and rider. To the Mi’kmaq, in the story of the great bear and the seven hunters, Mizar is Chickadee and Alcor is his cooking pot.
mizar.tagline: The Plough’s horse and rider — and the very first star shown to be a binary from its light alone.

facts.text: By coincidence the Moon and the Sun look almost the same size in our sky, which is why the Moon can cover the Sun completely in a total solar [[eclipse]].
facts.title: A perfect fit

facts.text: Thanks to [[libration]], a slight rocking of the Moon as seen from Earth, we can see about 59% of its surface over time.
facts.title: More than half

facts.text: The Soviet Luna 2 became the first spacecraft to strike the Moon in 1959, and Luna 9 made the first soft landing in 1966.
facts.title: The first visitors

facts.text: The word moon comes from Old English mōna, and further back from an ancient root meaning “month” — possibly linked to a verb for measuring time.
facts.title: A word for time

story: The Moon was probably born in violence. The leading theory says a Mars-sized world, named Theia, struck the young Earth and blasted material into orbit, where it gathered into the Moon roughly 4.4 to 4.5 billion years ago. That would explain why Earth and Moon rocks have nearly identical isotopic make-up — and simulations from 2023 suggest remnants of Theia may still lie deep inside Earth.

Since then Earth’s tides have locked the Moon so that it always turns the same face to us, and have slowly pushed it outwards; long ago it loomed far larger in our sky. The dark [[mare|maria]], or “seas”, are vast plains of lava that welled up until about 1.2 billion years ago, mostly on the near side. For all its brilliance at night, its surface is about as reflective as asphalt.

It remains the only world beyond Earth that people have visited. Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and by 1972 six Apollo missions had put twelve astronauts on its surface. In 2026 the crew of Artemis II flew around it.
moon.tagline: Born in a collision, as dark as asphalt, and the only world beyond Earth where people have walked.

facts.text: Seen from a planet near Arcturus, Muphrid would shine at about magnitude −2.4, more than twice as bright as Sirius looks from Earth.
facts.title: The view from Arcturus

facts.text: The Calendarium of Al Achsasi al Mouakket called it Ramih al Ramih, translated into Latin as Lancea Lanceator — possibly “the lance of the lancer”.
facts.title: The lance of the lancer

facts.text: A companion orbiting every 494 days has been suspected from Muphrid’s spectrum, but speckle interferometry has not confirmed it.
facts.title: A partner unconfirmed

story: Muphrid’s closest stellar neighbour is Arcturus — not just in our sky, but in space. The two lie at almost the same distance from us, and each would shine brightly in the other’s sky. From a planet near Muphrid, Arcturus would blaze at magnitude −5.2, about twice as bright as Venus appears to us.

Muphrid is a yellowish [[star]] of about 1.7 times the Sun’s mass and around 2.7 billion years old. It is starting to evolve away from the main sequence and has grown to about 2.7 times the Sun’s width. It is also unusually rich in iron, close to the upper limit for stars like it in the Milky Way’s disc.
Its name comes from the Arabic for “the single one of the lancer”. The Boorong people of north-western Victoria knew it as Weetkurrk, the singing bush lark.
muphrid.tagline: Arcturus’s next-door neighbour — in our sky and in space.

facts.text: Naos dims by a mere 0.02 magnitude every 1.78 days. The cause seems to be bright patches at the base of its wind, carried round as the star turns.
facts.title: A patchy surface

facts.text: Its mix of spectral features — evolved, yet spinning fast — is so unusual that only eight such stars are known in the Milky Way.
facts.title: One of eight

facts.text: Arab astronomers called it Suhail Hadar, one of several bright southern stars that shared the name Suhail.
facts.title: Another Suhail

story: Few naked-eye stars are as extreme. Naos is a rare [[spectral-type|O-type]] blue supergiant with a surface around 40,000 kelvin, so hot that most of its light pours out as ultraviolet we cannot see. Counting all of it, Naos shines hundreds of thousands of times as brightly as the Sun.

It is shedding itself fast. A wind blowing at 2,500 km per second carries off more than a millionth of its mass each year — about ten million times the Sun’s rate. It spins at over 220 km per second, close to breaking up, and it is a runaway, racing through space, perhaps flung out when a companion exploded as a supernova. It is heavy enough to end as one itself.

Its name is Greek for “ship”, fitting for the brightest star of Puppis, the stern of the ship Argo. In 1896 Williamina Fleming at Harvard found puzzling lines in its spectrum; they were later traced to helium that had lost an electron.
naos.tagline: One of the hottest stars the eye can see — a runaway blue supergiant racing through the Milky Way.

discovered.note: Predicted by Urbain Le Verrier (and independently by John Couch Adams)

facts.text: Galileo’s drawings from December 1612 and January 1613 show a ‘star’ near Jupiter that matches Neptune’s position. It barely moved, so he never knew what he had seen.
facts.title: Galileo saw it first

facts.text: At Cambridge, James Challis had searched using Adams’s predictions and recorded Neptune twice without recognising it. He blamed out-of-date star maps.
facts.title: The one that got away

facts.text: Le Verrier tried to have the planet named after himself. The idea met stiff resistance outside France, and Neptune, the Roman god of the sea, won the day.
facts.title: Le Verrier’s planet

facts.text: Neptune takes 164.8 years to circle the Sun. It completed its first full orbit since its discovery only in 2011.
facts.title: A very long year

story: Uranus was misbehaving. Decades after its discovery it was straying from its predicted path, as if something unseen were tugging on it. In Paris, Urbain Le Verrier calculated where that something must be and wrote to Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory. On 23 September 1846, the evening the letter arrived, Galle — helped by the student Heinrich d’Arrest and a fresh star chart — found the new [[planet]] within a degree of the predicted spot. In England, John Couch Adams had made similar calculations.

Neptune is an ice giant, a little smaller than Uranus but denser and more massive, tinted blue by methane. For a world so far from the Sun it is restless. Its winds reach 2,100 km/h, the strongest of any planet. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989 — still the only spacecraft to visit — it found a Great Dark Spot, a storm comparable to Jupiter’s [[great-red-spot|Great Red Spot]]. A few years later, Hubble found it had vanished.
neptune.tagline: The planet found by mathematics before anyone knew where to look — home to the fastest winds of any planet.

facts.text: Nihal’s disc spans just 3 thousandths of an arcsecond, yet astronomers have measured it — and from that worked out its true width.
facts.title: Measuring a giant

facts.text: The occasional spelling Nibal seems to come from nothing more than a misreading of Nihal.
facts.title: Nibal by mistake

story: Nihal has lived fast. With 3.5 times the Sun’s mass, it needed only about 240 million years to burn through the hydrogen in its core. It has since swollen into a [[star-colour|yellow]] bright giant nearly 16 times the Sun’s width.

It has a fainter companion that may be in orbit around it. Astronomers measured the pair with adaptive optics on the AEOS telescope at Haleakala in Hawaii, and the companion itself seems to change in brightness: it is listed as a suspected variable star.
The name is Arabic for “quenching their thirst”. Chinese astronomers, less poetically, made it the second star of Cè, the Toilet — Arneb is the first.
nihal.tagline: A yellow bright giant in the Hare, whose Arabic name means “quenching their thirst”.

facts.text: The astronomer James B. Kaler calls the name Kuma “of obscure origin”; one source has suggested it means “at last”.
facts.title: A name of obscure origin

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the second star of Tiān Bàng, the Celestial Flail, together with Rastaban, Eltanin, Xi Draconis and Iota Herculis.
facts.title: The Celestial Flail

story: Side by side, two white stars of almost equal brightness travel through space together. They share the same distance, the same motion across the sky and the same speed along our line of sight, though they are so far apart that no orbital movement has ever been seen.

They even share a chemical quirk. Each is an “Am” star, with abnormally strong lines of metals in its light. One of them also hides a small companion, never seen directly but betrayed by the tug it gives every 38 days on a nearly circular orbit.

Arabic astronomers counted it among Al ‘Awā’id, “the Mother Camels” — five stars of the Dragon’s head, later called the Quinque Dromedarii. Its modern name, Kuma, first appeared in Antonín Bečvář’s 1948 Skalnaté Pleso Atlas of the Heavens.
nu-draconis.tagline: Two matched white stars in the Dragon’s head — once among the “Mother Camels” of Arabic star lore.

facts.text: Nunki lies just south of the ecliptic, where the Moon and planets travel. On 17 November 1981 Venus passed in front of it — the last time a planet hid it.
facts.title: Covered by Venus

facts.text: Johann Bayer’s star atlas Uranometria placed Nunki in the fourth magnitude class, though by modern measurement it is a second-magnitude star.
facts.title: Bayer’s low ranking

facts.text: The Calendarium of Al Achsasi al Mouakket named it Thanih al Sadirah, the “second returning ostrich”.
facts.title: The second returning ostrich

story: Nunki looks like one star, but it is two hot blue-white stars, each more than six times the Sun’s mass, swinging around each other every 135 days. Their surfaces are near 18,500 kelvin, more than three times hotter than the Sun’s, and their stretched orbit brings them closer together than Venus is to the Sun.

The pair is about 30 million years old, and its future is dramatic. In some 25 million years the larger star will swell into a red giant and pour gas onto its partner. The two should then merge into one star of over 10 solar masses — enough to explode. That makes Nunki the nearest star expected to end as a core-collapse supernova.

Its name is far older than the science. Nunki is Sumerian, the name of the holy city Eridu, “Divine Place of the Earth”. R. H. Allen popularised it for this star, though it probably first belonged to stars in the region of Vela.
nunki.tagline: Two hot blue stars in the Teapot’s handle — and the nearest star expected to end as a supernova.

discovered.note: Found on the same night as Titania

facts.text: On 4 May 2007, during Uranus’s equinox season, Oberon was seen passing in front of Umbriel, an event that lasted about six minutes.
facts.title: Moon passes moon

facts.text: Voyager 2 photographed Oberon in January 1986, mapping about 40% of its surface. No spacecraft has been back since.
facts.title: One flyby, 40% mapped

story: Oberon is the outermost of Uranus’s five large [[planetary-moon|moons]] and the most heavily cratered, its dark, slightly red surface shaped mostly by asteroid and comet impacts. Long chasms crack the crust where the young moon’s interior expanded and stretched it. Inside, it is probably a rocky core under an icy mantle, perhaps with a thin layer of liquid water where the two meet.

Its distant orbit sets it apart. For part of each orbit Oberon lies outside Uranus’s magnetic bubble, where the solar wind strikes it directly. It is also the only large Uranian moon whose trailing side is not darkened; on the others, the planet’s charged particles are thought to be to blame.

William Herschel discovered Oberon on 11 January 1787, the same night as Titania — fittingly, as Oberon is Titania’s husband, king of the fairies in A Midsummer Night’s Dream. For nearly fifty years, no telescope but Herschel’s own saw either moon.
oberon.tagline: King of the fairies — the outermost of Uranus’s large moons, old, dark and battered.

facts.text: Astronomers use Okab as a telluric standard: its spectrum lets them measure, and remove, the fingerprints Earth’s own atmosphere leaves on starlight.
facts.title: A standard for Earth’s air

facts.text: The 2MASS survey seemed to show extra infrared light around Okab, hinting at a dusty disc. In 2009 the signal was traced to overloaded detectors.
facts.title: A false alarm

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Okab is the sixth star of the Left Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, a chain of eleven stars, each standing for an old state of China.
facts.title: Wall of the Heavenly Market
