story: Okab spins at more than 300 kilometres a second at its equator, and the spin has reshaped it. Its equator bulges to about 2.8 times the Sun’s radius while its poles reach only 2.2. The spin also sorts the heat: the poles, closer to the star’s centre, glow at about 11,000 kelvins, while the stretched equator cools to about 8,700. We see this white [[star]] almost exactly edge-on.

Close in, something glows in the infrared. Interferometers in 2008–2011 picked up emission within an Earth–Sun distance of the star, and a 2017 study proposed hot dust — perhaps debris from a collision between orbiting bodies, or a giant comet vaporising in the heat.
Its name comes from Deneb el Okab, Arabic for ‘the tail of the eagle’, a title it once shared with Epsilon Aquilae. In Chinese star lore the same two stars stood for the ancient states of Wu and Yue.
okab.tagline: The tail of the Eagle: a white star spinning so fast it is hotter at its poles than at its equator.

facts.text: About a degree to the north, 32 Cygni is another eclipsing pair made of a large, cool evolved star and a small, hot companion — the same kind of arrangement.
facts.title: A neighbour of the same kind

facts.text: Depending on the catalogue it is ο¹ Cygni, ο² Cygni or 31 Cygni — and, as a variable star, V695 Cygni.
facts.title: Many names, one star

story: About once every ten years, a hot blue-white star and a huge orange supergiant line up, one eclipsing the other, and the light of 31 Cygni dips slightly. These eclipses are precious: they let astronomers weigh the supergiant directly, a rare opportunity for a star of its kind. The answer is about 6.7 times the Sun’s mass, believed accurate to around 2%, though the orbit still has some loose ends.
Farther out, a seventh-magnitude blue-white star completes the system — a hot B-type star still burning hydrogen in its core.

Its name is a tangle. Over the centuries the Greek letter omicron has been pinned on two or three different stars here — 30, 31 and 32 Cygni — so astronomers prefer to call it by its Flamsteed number, 31 Cygni.
omicron1-cygni.tagline: An orange supergiant eclipsed by a hot blue partner about once a decade — a rare chance to weigh a giant.

facts.text: The Boorong people of north-western Victoria saw this star and Alniyat as the wives of Djuit, the star Antares.
facts.title: Wives of Djuit

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Paikauhale, Antares and Alniyat make up Xīn, the Heart. Paikauhale is its third star.
facts.title: Third star of the Heart

facts.text: It belongs to the Upper Scorpius group, thousands of young stars that formed together and share a path through space.
facts.title: A family of thousands

story: In Hawaiian, Paikauhale means to go gadding about from house to house — a vagabond with no home. The star stands in a line of three with Hōkū-ʻula, Antares, and Au-haele. Arab astronomers saw it and Alniyat as al-niyāṭ, “the arteries”, flanking the Scorpion’s heart.

It is a young, hot [[star-colour|blue-white]] star of 15 times the Sun’s mass, about 28,900 K at the surface and some 25,000 times as luminous, and only around 5 million years old. In about 6 million years it is expected to swell into a red supergiant hundreds of times the Sun’s width, much like the Antares it now sits beside.

It is also a puzzle. It spins slowly, once every 41 days, and has a magnetic field that astronomers have mapped across its surface. Its X-rays are unusually energetic, perhaps from clumps of hot gas falling back onto the star.
paikauhale.tagline: The Hawaiian wanderer beside Antares — a young blue star that will become a red supergiant.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star; named Peacock by HM Nautical Almanac Office in the late 1930s

facts.text: Some German sources of the 19th and early 20th centuries listed the star as ‘Rediculus’. In Marshallese it is called Likin-Buwame.
facts.title: Rediculus

facts.text: Peacock probably belongs to the Tucana–Horologium association, a group of stars about 45 million years old moving through space together.
facts.title: A young family

story: The star’s plain English name dates only from the late 1930s, when The Air Almanac was being prepared for Royal Air Force navigators. Alpha Pavonis had no traditional name, and the RAF wanted every star in the almanac to have one, so it was simply called Peacock — a translation of Pavo. Older names did exist: Arab astronomers paired it with Alpha Indi as al-ṣuradān, the Two Shrikes.

It is a hot blue-white [[star]] of about six solar masses, shining 2,200 times as brightly as the Sun from a surface at 17,700 K. A close companion, never seen directly, circles it every 11.75 days. One puzzle: a star like this should keep the deuterium it was born with, yet Peacock has almost none. Perhaps it formed from deuterium-poor gas, or burned it up while it was still forming.
peacock.tagline: A hot blue-white star with an RAF-issue name — and a strange shortage of deuterium.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers paired Phact with Epsilon Columbae as Zhàng Rén, the Grandfather. The Western name Chang Jin comes from it.
facts.title: The Grandfather

facts.text: A faint star 13.5 arcseconds away makes Phact look double, but it is only an optical companion: Phact itself is believed to be a single star.
facts.title: A companion by chance

story: Phact wears a ring of glowing gas. It is a Be star: a hot [[spectral-type|B-type]] star surrounded by a disc of gas whose hydrogen shines in bright emission lines. Like nearly all such stars it spins fast — at least 176 kilometres per second, and perhaps around 457 at its equator.
Its light may also waver by a few hundredths of a magnitude, as Gamma Cassiopeiae — the best-known of these restless, disc-bearing stars — does. That makes it a suspected [[variable-star|variable]].
The name comes from the Arabic fākhitah, “ring dove”. It was first used for the constellation Cygnus and only later moved to this star — a happy fit, since Columba is the Dove.
phact.tagline: The Dove’s brightest star — a fast spinner wrapped in a glowing disc of gas.

facts.text: Phecda’s spectrum has served since 1943 as one of the stable reference points by which astronomers sort other stars into classes.
facts.title: A standard since 1943

facts.text: In China it is Tiān Jī, the Star of Celestial Shining Pearl, and the third star of the Northern Dipper.
facts.title: Celestial Shining Pearl

story: Phecda is the thigh of the Great Bear — its name comes from the Arabic fakhth al-dubb, “thigh of the bear”. Hindu astronomers knew it as Pulastya, one of the Seven Rishis.

It is a white [[star]] 2.4 times the Sun’s mass and about 333 million years old, spinning at some 386 km per second at its equator. The spin flattens it: its equator is about half as wide again as its poles. The poles, near 10,500 kelvin, are far hotter than the equator, near 6,750. A shell of gas around it adds bright emission lines to its spectrum.

Phecda has a hidden partner, a smaller orange star of about 0.8 solar masses whose pull makes it wobble every 20.5 years. It is also part of a real family: with four other Dipper stars it belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, and it lies fairly close in space to Mizar and Alcor.
phecda.tagline: The Dipper’s spinning corner — a white star whose poles run thousands of degrees hotter than its equator.

facts.text: Stickney crater carries the maiden name of Angeline Stickney Hall, Asaph Hall’s wife, who urged him to keep searching when he was close to giving up.
facts.title: Named for a determined wife

facts.text: Around 1958, Iosif Shklovsky studied Phobos’s odd orbit and suggested it might be hollow — even artificial. Later measurements found nothing so strange.
facts.title: Hollow Phobos

facts.text: The unusual Kaidun meteorite, which fell on a Soviet military base in Yemen in 1980, may be a piece of Phobos — but nobody can yet prove it.
facts.title: A piece of Phobos on Earth?

story: Stand on Mars and watch Phobos: it rises in the west, races across the sky in about four hours and sets in the east, twice each Martian day. It orbits closer to its planet than any other known moon, circling every 7 hours 39 minutes — faster than Mars itself turns.

Phobos is a small, irregular lump of dark, carbon-rich material, one of the least reflective objects in the Solar System. One impact [[crater]], Stickney, takes up a large part of its surface; the blow that made it nearly shattered the moon. Phobos may be a rubble pile held together by a thin crust, and it is doomed. Mars’s tides are drawing it inward by about 2 cm a year, and in tens of millions of years it will be torn apart or crash.
Asaph Hall found it on 18 August 1877 with the 26-inch ‘Great Equatorial’ at the US Naval Observatory, then the world’s largest refracting telescope, a few days after finding Deimos.
phobos.tagline: A dark, lumpy moon racing round Mars faster than Mars spins — and slowly falling towards it.

discovered.note: Outer companion found in 1779; the star itself known since antiquity

facts.text: Polaris was the first classical Cepheid to have its mass measured from an orbit. A 2024 study put it at about five times the Sun’s mass.
facts.title: Weighed by its partner

facts.text: In 2024 a team using the CHARA Array tentatively imaged large bright and dark patches on its surface, changing over time.
facts.title: Spots on a supergiant

facts.text: The supergiant appears much younger than its two companions — strange, since the stars of a triple system would normally have formed together.
facts.title: An age puzzle

facts.text: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, so the pole drifts among the stars. Polaris will be closest to the pole soon after 2100, then slowly drift away from it.
facts.title: A temporary title

story: The whole northern sky seems to wheel around Polaris, because it sits almost exactly above Earth’s North Pole. Its height above your horizon roughly matches your latitude, which made it a lifeline for navigators. Yet it is not the brightest star in the sky, as many people think — it ranks only about 47th.

It is also a star with secrets. Polaris is the nearest Cepheid, a [[variable-star|pulsing supergiant]] of the kind astronomers use to measure the cosmos. But its pulses have behaved oddly: after 1966 they shrank sharply, and they now seem to be growing again — a reversal not seen in any other Cepheid. Research even suggests it is about 2.5 times brighter than when Ptolemy observed it.

Polaris is a triple. William Herschel found its outer companion in August 1779 with a reflecting telescope of his own; a much closer partner, circling about every 30 years, was only confirmed in the early 20th century. In 2006 the Hubble Space Telescope showed all three.
polaris.tagline: The North Star: not the brightest, not quite at the pole, and a stranger star than it looks.

facts.text: Sigma Octantis is the faintest star shown on any national flag. On Brazil’s flag it stands for the Federal District, home of the capital.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

facts.text: For the Revised Harvard Photometry of 1908, astronomers used Sigma Octantis as a reference for measuring southern stars, while Polaris and Lambda Ursae Minoris served in the north.
facts.title: A yardstick for brightness

story: The north has Polaris, bright enough to steer by. The south has Sigma Octantis — Polaris Australis — barely visible to the naked eye. It sits about a degree from the south celestial pole, so as the sky turns, every other southern star appears to wheel around it. But it is so faint that navigators use the Southern Cross to find the pole instead.

Up close it is a white subgiant, about 4.4 times the Sun’s radius and 44 times as luminous, near the end of its hydrogen-burning life at around 900 million years old. It also pulses as a Delta Scuti [[variable-star]], brightening and fading by about three hundredths of a magnitude every 2.33 hours.

Its reign is temporary. Precession — the slow wobble of Earth’s axis — is carrying the pole away from it. The name Polaris Australis was first used in the 1700s, and it is the southernmost named star.
polaris-australis.tagline: The southern pole star — so faint it is no use for navigation, yet it flies on Brazil’s flag.

facts.text: Pollux has a magnetic field of under one gauss — one of the weakest ever detected on a star. It may be the faded remnant of a much stronger field from its youth.
facts.title: A whisper of magnetism

facts.text: Pollux lies too far north of the Moon’s path to be hidden by it today. The last lunar occultation visible from Earth was on 30 September 117 BC.
facts.title: Out of the Moon’s reach

facts.text: In Shelley’s 1818 poem Homer’s Hymn to Castor and Pollux, the star is “mild Pollux, void of blame”.
facts.title: Mild Pollux

story: Castor and Pollux are the heavenly twins of Greek and Roman myth, but the stars are anything but identical. Castor is a family of six stars; Pollux is a single orange giant — the closest giant [[star]] to the Sun. It began life as a hot white star rather like Sirius. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, it has swollen to about nine times the Sun’s width, with about twice its mass, and its surface has cooled to about 4,800 K.

In 2006 astronomers announced a planet circling it every 590 days, at least 2.3 times as massive as Jupiter. A public vote named it Thestias. The winning idea was Leda, the twins’ mother, but that name was already taken, so it became Thestias, after her father Thestius. Some doubt remains: the star’s own magnetic activity might mimic the planet’s signal.
pollux.tagline: The nearest giant star to the Sun — an orange twin that is nothing like its brother Castor.

facts.text: Porrima lies near the [[ecliptic]], so the Moon can pass in front of it, and on rare occasions a planet. In June 2011 Saturn passed just a quarter of a degree south of it.
facts.title: Saturn’s near miss

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the second star of the Left Wall of the Supreme Palace Enclosure, standing for the First Eastern Minister — the “High Minister of State”.
facts.title: The High Minister of State

story: As alike as twins — same type, same brightness, each a little hotter and brighter than the Sun — the two stars of Porrima circle each other every 169 years on a stretched orbit. For most of that time they move slowly. Near their closest approach they whip around each other in just a few years; one such close pass came in 1836, the next 169 years later.
Their X-ray glow, a gauge of their magnetic activity, suggests they are about 1.14 billion years old — roughly a quarter of the Sun’s age.

Porrima, also known as Antevorta, was one of the Camenae, the Roman goddesses of prophecy. Arabic astronomers saw this star as part of the Barker, a group of five stars in Virgo; a medieval catalogue called it “the angle of the barker”.
porrima.tagline: Twin stars named after a Roman goddess of prophecy, on a 169-year orbit that swings them close, then far apart.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; its white-dwarf companion was first seen by John Martin Schaeberle in 1896

facts.text: To the Babylonians Procyon was Nangar, the Carpenter — an aspect of the god Marduk, who built and ordered the sky.
facts.title: The Carpenter

facts.text: In Macedonian folklore Procyon and Sirius were wolves, circling hungrily around Orion — which they saw as a plough pulled by oxen.
facts.title: Wolves round a plough

facts.text: Procyon B has less mass than Sirius B, yet it is bigger. In the crushed matter of a white dwarf, less mass means a larger star.
facts.title: Lighter but larger

story: Its name is Greek for ‘before the dog’: for observers in the north, Procyon rises shortly ahead of Sirius, the Dog Star. It is one of our nearest stellar neighbours, a [[star]] somewhat bigger than the Sun — 1.5 times its mass, twice its width and seven times as bright. It has nearly finished fusing the hydrogen in its core. Within 10 to 100 million years it will swell to 80–150 times its present size and glow orange or red.

Like Sirius, it has a ghostly partner. Friedrich Bessel suspected an unseen companion in 1844 from Procyon’s wobble, and Arthur Auwers calculated its orbit in 1862. John Martin Schaeberle finally saw it in 1896, right where predicted, with Lick Observatory’s great 36-inch refractor. Procyon B is a white dwarf, the cooling core of a star that died about 1.2 billion years ago. The two circle each other every 41 years.
procyon.tagline: The Little Dog’s bright eye, rising just before Sirius — with a faint white dwarf in tow.

facts.text: Proxima is on average about 33 times denser than the Sun, and the gravity at its surface is roughly 160 times Earth’s.
facts.title: Small but dense

facts.text: As it slowly turns hydrogen into helium, Proxima will grow smaller and hotter, becoming a ‘blue dwarf’, then end as a white dwarf — without ever becoming a red giant.
facts.title: A future blue dwarf

story: In 1915 Robert Innes, at the Union Observatory in Johannesburg, found a faint red star near Alpha Centauri sharing its motion across the sky. It turned out to be the nearest star of all after the Sun, and its name, Proxima, is Latin for ‘nearest’. It belongs to the Alpha Centauri system, circling the bright pair once in about 550,000 years.

Proxima is a [[spectral-type|red dwarf]] with an eighth of the Sun’s mass and a seventh of its diameter — only about one and a half times the width of Jupiter. More than 85% of its energy comes out as infrared. Its whole interior churns, driving a strong magnetic field and violent flares that can reach 27 million kelvins. The same churning keeps fresh hydrogen flowing into its core, so it will keep shining for about four trillion years — hundreds of times the present age of the universe.

In 2016 astronomers found Proxima b, a planet at least as massive as Earth, orbiting every 11.2 days within the star’s habitable zone. Given the flares, whether it could support life is highly uncertain. A second, smaller planet, Proxima d, circles even closer.
proxima-centauri.tagline: The nearest star to the Sun: a tiny, flaring red dwarf with an Earth-mass planet in its habitable zone.

facts.text: Relative to the Sun, the system moves at about 22.5 kilometres a second — around 80,000 kilometres an hour.
facts.title: Fast travellers

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the sixteenth star of Kuí Sù, the Legs, a long asterism that winds through Pisces and Andromeda.
facts.title: Sixteenth of the Legs

story: What looks like a simple pair of white stars is really three. The brighter of the two is itself a close [[double-star|binary]]: two A-type stars, hotter and brighter than the Sun, that take 14.44 years to go once around each other. Its wide partner, only slightly fainter, is another A-type star.

All three travel through the galaxy together. Their path around the Milky Way is nearly circular, keeping them within a narrow band of distances from the galactic centre, much like the Sun’s own orbit. Stars like these, hotter than the Sun, burn through their fuel faster and live shorter lives.
psi1-piscium.tagline: A wide pair of white stars in Pisces — and the brighter one is secretly two.

facts.text: In August 2007 R CrB began a fade to an unprecedented minimum. By mid-2017 it had spent ten years below its normal brightness, reaching a record faint magnitude of 15.2.
facts.title: A decade in the dark

facts.text: R Coronae Borealis and RY Sagittarii are the only stars of their class bright enough to be seen with the naked eye.
facts.title: One of only two

facts.text: Hubble images show clouds of dust around R CrB. Puffs condense close to the star and, seen to one side of it, look like little cometary knots.
facts.title: Puffs of soot

story: Most of the time R Coronae Borealis sits quietly near the limit of naked-eye vision. Then, without warning, it fades — sometimes to below 15th magnitude, thousands of times fainter — and may stay hidden for months or years before it slowly recovers. It is a ‘reverse nova’, the prototype of a whole class of [[variable-star|variable stars]].

The culprit is soot. R CrB’s atmosphere is about 90% helium, with less than 1% hydrogen and most of the rest carbon. Every so often carbon condenses into soot-like dust above the star, blocking its light, until radiation pressure blows the cloud away. That odd make-up was a first: in 1935 it became the first star shown, from its spectrum, to have a different chemical composition from the Sun.

How such a star forms is a puzzle. A favourite idea is that two white dwarfs, one of carbon and oxygen and one of helium, merged into one; another is a very late helium flash in a dying star. Edward Pigott discovered its fades in 1795.
r-coronae-borealis.tagline: The ‘reverse nova’: a soot-shrouded star that vanishes for months when it chokes on its own carbon.

facts.text: Just five degrees away shines Rasalhague, the brightest star in Ophiuchus. They may be the closest pair of “alpha” stars anywhere in the sky.
facts.title: Two alphas side by side

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Dìzuò, the Emperor’s Seat, standing alone at the centre of its own asterism within the Heavenly Market enclosure.
facts.title: The Emperor’s Seat

facts.text: Despite its Alpha label, Rasalgethi is only the fifth-brightest star in Hercules.
facts.title: Alpha in name only

story: If Rasalgethi took the Sun’s place, its surface would reach beyond Earth’s orbit, though not quite as far as Mars. It is a red giant near the end of its life, burning hydrogen and helium in shells around an exhausted core of carbon and oxygen. Its bloated surface swells and shrinks, so its light rises and falls over weeks, months and years.

It is slowly losing itself to space. Like most stars at this stage, it is shedding gas into a thin envelope that stretches far beyond where Neptune would be. It is also the second-nearest star of its kind to the Sun. Its visible companion is really two stars: a yellow giant and a smaller partner that circle each other every 51.6 days.
The name comes from the Arabic ra’s al-jāthī, “head of the Kneeler”. In antiquity Hercules was drawn upside down on maps of the constellation, so the star at his head is this one.
rasalgethi.tagline: The head of the Kneeler — a dying red giant so swollen it would engulf the Earth.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers named it Hòu, a senior assistant to the emperor, sometimes said to be an astrologer.
facts.title: The emperor’s assistant

facts.text: Because it is flattened and hottest at the poles, Rasalhague would look brighter seen pole-on. From our tilted view it appears almost a fifth dimmer than its true output.
facts.title: Dimmer from the side

story: Rasalhague’s name means “the head of the serpent collector” in Arabic: it marks the head of Ophiuchus, the giant who grips a snake. Just five degrees away shines Rasalgethi, the head of Hercules, so two mythical heads almost touch.

The main star is white, about twice the Sun’s mass, and it spins at least 240 km per second at its equator — close to 90 per cent of the speed that would tear it apart. The spin squashes it, so its equator bulges about 20 per cent wider than its poles. The poles are hotter too, near 9,400 kelvin against 7,600 at the equator.

Rasalhague is also a [[double-star|binary]]. A smaller orange dwarf of about 0.8 solar masses circles it every 8.6 years. The orbit was only pinned down in 2011 using adaptive optics, and the two made their closest approach in April 2012.
rasalhague.tagline: The serpent-bearer’s head — a white star spinning so fast it is close to flying apart.

facts.text: Rastaban sits on or near the instability strip where stars such as Cepheids pulsate, yet it varies by only about a hundredth of a magnitude — confirmed by Gabriel Cristian Neagu using TESS and Hipparcos data.
facts.title: Barely flickering

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the third star of Tiān Bàng, the Celestial Flail, made of the four stars of the Dragon’s head and Iota Herculis.
facts.title: The Celestial Flail

facts.text: Its chromosphere, the layer above the visible surface, is unusually active, giving off X-rays and far-ultraviolet light.
facts.title: A glowing upper atmosphere

story: Rastaban means “the head of the dragon” in Arabic, a name it has shared with its neighbour Eltanin, Gamma Draconis. Arab stargazers also counted it among the Mother Camels, five stars of Draco guarding a camel’s foal — a group later called Quinque Dromedarii, the five dromedaries. Another old name, Alwaid, comes from the Arabic for “the old mother camels”.

The star sits on the border between bright giants and supergiants, and its spectrum is a standard for that [[spectral-type|class]]. It has about six times the Sun’s mass and roughly 40 times its width, and shines some 950 times as brightly. At about 65 million years old it is churning material from deep inside up to its surface for the first time, in what astronomers call the first dredge-up.
A very faint companion, about 11 magnitudes dimmer, circles it perhaps once every four thousand years.
rastaban.tagline: The Dragon’s head — a yellow star poised between giant and supergiant.

facts.text: Regulus lies less than half a degree from the [[ecliptic]] — the closest of all the bright stars — so the Moon often covers it. Venus last passed in front of it on 7 July 1959 and will again on 1 October 2044.
facts.title: Closest to the Sun’s path

facts.text: When the asteroid 166 Rhodope passed in front of Regulus in 2005, observers in Italy filmed it. The tiny bending of the star’s light matched the predictions of general relativity.
facts.title: Einstein in an asteroid’s shadow

story: Regulus spins once every 15.9 hours; the Sun takes about 25 days. Its equator whirls round at about 320 km/s — 96.5% of the speed at which it would start to fly apart. The spin squashes it into a flattened shape, and its poles shine hotter and, area for area, five times brighter than its waist.

It is a [[multiple-star|multiple star]] of at least four. The bright one has a dim partner, probably a white dwarf, that circles it every 40 days, and a wider pair of small orange and red stars travels with them. That white dwarf hints at a strange history: the main star may have grown by taking gas from its companion.

Its name is Latin for ‘little king’, and royalty follows it through history. The Babylonians called it Sharru, ‘the King’, and in Persia it was one of the four royal stars. Its Arabic name, Qalb al-Asad, means ‘the heart of the lion’.
regulus.tagline: The little king at the Lion’s heart — a star spinning so fast it is close to flying apart.

facts.text: Rhea was the Titaness who married Cronus — the Greek counterpart of Saturn — and bore the first generation of Olympian gods.
facts.title: Mother of the gods

facts.text: In 2008 Cassini’s instruments hinted that Rhea might have rings of its own, the first known around a moon. Later searches with Cassini’s cameras found no sign of them.
facts.title: The rings that weren’t

facts.text: Rhea is almost exactly the size of Uranus’s moon Oberon, but Oberon is denser, so it is the heavier of the two.
facts.title: Oberon’s near-twin

story: Rhea is a world of ice and old craters. Saturn’s second-largest [[planetary-moon|moon]] is roughly three-quarters water ice and one-quarter rock, and its surface temperature swings between about −174 °C and −220 °C. Like its smaller neighbour Dione, it is streaked with bright cliffs of ice, and it always keeps the same face turned to Saturn.

It is the smallest body in the Solar System confirmed to have the balanced, rounded shape that gravity alone would give it, and its surface area is about that of Australia. In 2010 Cassini, swooping close, detected a whisper-thin atmosphere of oxygen and carbon dioxide — the oxygen freed from the ice by Saturn’s radiation.
Giovanni Domenico Cassini discovered Rhea on 23 December 1672 with a telescope more than 10 metres long, made by Giuseppe Campani. It was only the third moon of Saturn ever found.
rhea.tagline: Saturn’s second-largest moon — a cold, cratered ice world wrapped in a whisper of oxygen.

facts.text: Rigel is almost always brighter than Betelgeuse, yet Bayer labelled it Beta in 1603. Perhaps Betelgeuse was having a rare bright spell — or Bayer simply listed first-magnitude stars from north to south.
facts.title: Why Beta?

facts.text: Rigel’s spectrum is a defining point of the classification sequence for supergiants, a reference that other stars are measured against.
facts.title: A yardstick for supergiants

facts.text: Rigel is an important navigation star, easy to find and visible from all the world’s oceans except the far Arctic, north of about 82° latitude.
facts.title: A sailor’s star

story: Rigel shines somewhere between 61,500 and 363,000 times as brightly as the Sun — the wide range shows how hard such a star is to pin down. It is a blue supergiant of 18 to 24 solar masses that, in just seven to nine million years, has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen. It will end as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole behind.

Its surface is restless. Rigel’s light flickers irregularly as its unstable atmosphere pulsates, and its spectrum shows gas surging outwards — and occasionally falling back — in great looping structures thought to be shaped by magnetic fields. Its wind carries away mass about ten million times faster than the Sun’s.
Rigel does not shine alone. Its faint companion is really three stars, each three to four times the Sun’s mass, and the whole family may take some 24,000 years to circle its common centre.
rigel.tagline: Orion’s blazing blue foot — a supergiant tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun, bound for a supernova.

facts.text: A second name, Ksora, appeared in Antonín Bečvář’s 1951 star atlas. The star-name scholar Paul Kunitzsch could find no clue to where it came from.
facts.title: A mystery name

facts.text: Chinese astronomers made it the third star of Gé Dào, the Flying Corridor, a path of six stars through Cassiopeia.
facts.title: The Flying Corridor

facts.text: Alpha Sagittarii also bore the name Ruchbah. The IAU kept Ruchbah for this star and gave Alpha Sagittarii the variant Rukbat.
facts.title: Another Ruchbah

story: Ruchbah is a [[star]] at a turning point. It has just used up the hydrogen in its core — astronomers reckon it is only about 4% past the end of its main-sequence life — and at around 600 million years old it is beginning to swell, already nearly four times the Sun’s width.

Something cold surrounds it. The star gives off extra infrared light, the glow of dust at about 85 K circling roughly 88 times farther out than the Earth is from the Sun — well beyond the reach of our own Kuiper belt. It suggests a debris disc.

It was once listed as an eclipsing binary, dipping slightly every 759 days, but modern measurements show no changes larger than a hundredth of a magnitude. Its name is Arabic for “knee” — the knee of Queen Cassiopeia.
ruchbah.tagline: The queen’s knee in Cassiopeia’s W — a star ringed by cold, distant dust.

facts.text: In China it is the Eleventh Star of the Left Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, standing for the ancient state of Song.
facts.title: The state of Song

facts.text: The US Navy cargo ship USS Sabik, of the Crater class, was named after the star.
facts.title: A ship’s name

story: Sabik comes from the Arabic al-sābiq, “the preceding one” — though nobody is quite sure what it was meant to precede.

It is really two white [[star|stars]], both still burning hydrogen in their cores: the brighter about 2.25 times the Sun’s mass, its partner about twice. They circle each other every 87.8 years on an extremely elongated orbit. At their farthest they are about twice as far apart as Neptune is from the Sun; at their closest they come within about twice the Earth–Sun distance.
Their last close pass came in 2024. Watched with the Very Large Telescope, it finally pinned down the orbit and the stars’ masses. The pair is thought to be about 500 million years old.
sabik.tagline: Two white stars on a wildly stretched orbit, swinging close together every 88 years.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Sadalmelik joins Theta and Epsilon Pegasi in Wēi, the Rooftop, one of the lunar mansions. It is the Rooftop’s first star.
facts.title: First Star of the Rooftop

facts.text: Sadalmelik was also once called Rucbah, a name it shared with Delta Cassiopeiae. The IAU settled the matter in 2016: Delta Cassiopeiae is now Ruchbah.
facts.title: A borrowed name

facts.text: NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory found Sadalmelik giving off far fewer X-rays than Sun-like stars do — a shortfall common among early G-type giants.
facts.title: Quiet in X-rays

story: From almost anywhere on Earth, Sadalmelik rises close to due east and sets close to due west. It lies within a degree of the celestial equator — one of only two stars with ancient proper names that do. The name comes from the Arabic sa‘d al-malik, ‘the lucky star of the king’, though how the star earned it is lost to history.

Like Sadalsuud, its neighbour in Aquarius, it is a yellow supergiant: about 53 million years old, swollen to around 70 times the Sun’s radius and shining some 3,900 times as brightly, from a surface cooler than the Sun’s. It sits in the Cepheid instability strip, where stars of its temperature and power tend to pulse like Cepheids, yet it is not classed as a [[variable-star]]. Instead, a massive wind streams off it, reaching supersonic speed in its outer atmosphere.
sadalmelik.tagline: ‘The lucky star of the king’, sitting almost exactly on the celestial equator.

facts.text: Since 1943 Sadalsuud’s spectrum has been one of the fixed anchor points against which astronomers classify other stars. It is also a standard for measuring how fast stars move towards or away from us.
facts.title: A yardstick for starlight

facts.text: Sadalsuud, Sadalmelik and Eta Pegasi form a trio moving through space together, at right angles to the plane of the Milky Way.
facts.title: Leaving the galactic plane

facts.text: NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory detected X-rays from Sadalsuud’s hot outer atmosphere — among the first ever caught from a yellow supergiant of its kind.
facts.title: X-rays from a supergiant

story: Sadalsuud means ‘luck of lucks’, from the Arabic sa‘d al-su‘ūd. In old Egyptian, Persian and Islamic lore the star was tied to the end of winter, when gentle, steady spring rains began — good fortune for anyone who farmed. Along the Euphrates its name was Kakkab Nammax: the Star of Mighty Destiny.

Behind the name is a yellow supergiant of [[spectral-type]] G0 Ib, 48 times the Sun’s width and about 2,000 times as luminous, with a surface temperature close to the Sun’s. It is only about 56 million years old, but at five or six solar masses it has already used up its core hydrogen and is probably fusing helium into carbon. Too light to explode, it will most likely end as a heavy white dwarf, comparable to Sirius B.
sadalsuud.tagline: ‘Luck of lucks’: the brightest star of Aquarius, a yellow supergiant astronomers use as a yardstick.

facts.text: Since 1943 Sadr’s spectrum has been one of the fixed anchor points astronomers use to classify other stars.
facts.title: A yardstick star

facts.text: In China it is Tiān Jīn yī, the First Star of the Celestial Ford, an asterism that also takes in Deneb.
facts.title: The Celestial Ford

story: Sadr sits where the beams of the Northern Cross meet, and its name fits: Arabic ṣadr, “chest”, the breast of Cygnus the swan. The same word gave Schedar in Cassiopeia its name. A later catalogue called it Pectus Gallinæ, “the hen’s chest”.

This is an enormous star, about 14.5 times the Sun’s mass and some 180 times its width. If it replaced the Sun, its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Venus. It shines over 33,000 times as brightly as the Sun, yet its surface, near 5,790 kelvin, is almost exactly as hot as the Sun’s. Only about 12 million years old, it is heavy enough to end as a supernova.

It is restless too. Its spectrum shifts slowly over 100 days or more, and it lies close to the zone where stars pulsate like Cepheid [[variable-star|variables]]. It appears wrapped in a faint glowing cloud, IC 1318, the Gamma Cygni nebula.
sadr.tagline: The heart of the Northern Cross — a yellow-white supergiant set among glowing clouds of gas.

facts.text: The Wardaman people of northern Australia see Saiph as the Guman digging stick, used by Black-headed Python to make a canyon.
facts.title: The Python’s digging stick

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Saiph is the Sixth Star of Shēn, the Three Stars — an asterism that also takes in Betelgeuse, Rigel, Bellatrix and the three belt stars.
facts.title: Sixth of the Three Stars

story: Saiph’s name is a case of mistaken identity. It comes from the Arabic saif al-jabbar, “sword of the giant”, a name that first belonged to another of Orion’s stars, Eta Orionis. A 17th-century catalogue gave it a more fitting label: Genu Dextrum Gigantis, the “right knee of the giant”.

It is a blue supergiant [[star]] that has already used up the hydrogen in its core. Smaller and less luminous than Rigel but hotter at its surface, it still shines around 57,000 times as brightly as the Sun. Estimates of its mass run from about 15 to 28 Suns, and one study puts its age at just 6.2 million years.

A fierce wind streams off its surface, carrying away the equivalent of the Sun’s entire mass every 1.1 million years. Like many of Orion’s great stars, Saiph is destined to collapse and explode as a supernova.
saiph.tagline: Orion’s other foot — a blue supergiant hotter than Rigel, destined to end as a supernova.

facts.text: In Iran the star name Sar Gaz — a possible source of ‘Sargas’ — was used to time farmers’ shares of irrigation water.
facts.title: Timing the water

facts.text: Sargas appears on the flag of Brazil, where it represents the state of Alagoas.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

story: Sargas is a giant [[star]] of about three solar masses, shining with some 1,400 times the Sun’s light from a yellow-white surface at about 6,300 K. It spins so fast that it is flattened: about 36 times the Sun’s width across the equator but only 26 times from pole to pole. A spin like that is unusual for a giant, and astronomers think Sargas may have formed when the two stars of a binary merged.

It is not alone, though. In 1991 the Hipparcos satellite found a companion, Theta Scorpii B, only half an arcsecond away. An older report of a fifth-magnitude companion was probably mistaken: later observers could not find it.
The name Sargas may be Sumerian in origin, or Persian for ‘arrowhead’.
sargas.tagline: The Scorpion’s yellow-white tail star — a giant spun into a flattened shape, perhaps by a stellar merger.

facts.text: Around Saturn’s north pole the clouds form a six-sided jet stream, first seen in Voyager images in the early 1980s and studied for years by Cassini. Each side is wider than Earth.
facts.title: A hexagon at the pole

facts.text: Saturn’s south pole has a warm polar vortex, a vast hurricane-like storm. It is the only known example of such a vortex in the Solar System.
facts.title: A warm storm at the south pole

facts.text: After thirteen years in orbit, Cassini ended its mission on 15 September 2017 by diving into Saturn on purpose, so that it could never crash into and contaminate Enceladus or Titan.
facts.title: A planned plunge

facts.text: The Romans named the seventh day of the week after the planet: Saturday comes from Sāturni diēs, ‘Saturn’s day’.
facts.title: Saturn’s day

story: Galileo was baffled. In 1610 his small telescope showed Saturn with two mysterious lumps, one on either side. Two years later they had vanished. It took Christiaan Huygens, with a better telescope in the 1650s, to see the truth: a thin, flat ring circling the planet without touching it. Those [[saturns-rings|rings]] are made mostly of water ice, in pieces from dust grains to boulders, and when Earth passes through their plane they all but disappear — which is what fooled Galileo.

Beneath them lies a [[planet]] made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, with no surface to stand on. It is the only planet less dense than water: in a large enough ocean, Saturn would float. A day lasts only about ten and a half hours, a spin fast enough to squash the planet visibly, and its winds reach 1,800 km/h. Deep inside, droplets of helium may be raining down — and perhaps even diamonds.
About once every Saturnian year — roughly 30 of ours — a Great White Spot erupts. The latest, in 2010, grew until it wrapped around the whole planet, watched from orbit by the Cassini spacecraft.
saturn.tagline: A planet light enough to float, crowned with rings of ice and a six-sided storm at its pole.

facts.text: The gas and dust Scheat sheds form a shell that, around the Sun, would reach well beyond the orbit of Saturn.
facts.title: A shell beyond Saturn

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Scheat and Markab form the Encampment, and Scheat is its second star, Shì Xiù èr.
facts.title: The Encampment

story: Of the four stars of the Great Square of Pegasus, Scheat is the odd one out: a red giant among blue-white stars. Its name may come from the Arabic al-sāʿid, “the upper arm”, or from saʿd, and the same name was once given to Delta Aquarii, now called Skat.

Scheat has swollen to about 109 times the Sun’s width and shines 1,640 times as brightly, yet its surface is only about 3,600 kelvin — cool enough for molecules of titanium oxide to form in its atmosphere. In the Sun’s place, it would reach beyond the orbit of Mercury.

In 1847 Johann Friedrich Julius Schmidt discovered that it varies. Scheat is a semiregular [[variable-star]] that brightens and fades over about 43 days, and it is slowly shedding gas and dust into an expanding shell.
scheat.tagline: The Great Square’s red corner — a cool, swollen giant that slowly pulses.

facts.text: In China it is Wáng Liáng sì, the Fourth Star of Wang Liang, named after a famous charioteer of the Spring and Autumn period.
facts.title: The charioteer’s star

facts.text: Schedar passes straight overhead in cities such as Edinburgh, Copenhagen and Moscow.
facts.title: Overhead in Edinburgh

facts.text: Schedar gives out about 18 times as much light as Caph, but it lies much farther away, so the two look almost equal in our sky.
facts.title: Brighter than it looks

story: Cassiopeia was the boastful queen of Ethiopia, and Schedar marks her breast: its name comes from the Arabic ṣadr, “chest”. On Gerardus Mercator’s celestial globe of 1551 she is chained to a chair as punishment, with Schedar near her left breast. Al-Sufi and Ulugh Beg called the star “the lady in the chair”.

Schedar spent most of its 100 to 200 million years as a hot blue-white star. Now it is an orange giant some 43 times the Sun’s width, almost certainly fusing helium in its core and shining about 800 times as brightly as the Sun. Like most giants it turns slowly, about once every 102 days.

Johann Bayer labelled it alpha, yet it and Caph are so evenly matched that which looks brighter depends on the colour of light you measure. Calculations from NASA’s WISE telescope give Schedar the edge as Cassiopeia’s brightest [[star]].
schedar.tagline: The queen’s breast — an orange giant in Cassiopeia’s W that once shone blue-white.

facts.text: The Babylonian star compendium MUL.APIN lists Shaula and its neighbour Lesath as Sharur and Shargaz. The Boorong people of Victoria saw the same pair as Karik Karik, the Falcons.
facts.title: Sharur and Shargaz

facts.text: Shaula appears on the flag of Brazil, where it stands for the state of Rio Grande do Norte.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

story: Shaula, the Scorpion’s sting, is three stars in one. The main star is a hot blue giant of 14.5 solar masses. A second blue star of 10.6 solar masses circles it every 1,053 days, while a small, still-forming young star whips round in just six days. All three orbit in the same plane — a strong sign that they were born together, only 10 to 13 million years ago.

The main star flickers by about a hundredth of a magnitude, a [[variable-star]] of the Beta Cephei type, and it is heavy enough to end its life as a supernova. Its name comes from the Arabic al-shawlā’, ‘the raised tail’. In Indian astronomy it belongs to Mula, ‘the root’, a lunar mansion symbolised by a bundle of tied roots.
shaula.tagline: The sting in the Scorpion’s tail — three stars born together, one of them bound for a supernova.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers grouped Sheratan with Hamal and Mesarthim as Lóu, the Bond. Sheratan is its first star.
facts.title: The Bond

facts.text: The Spitzer Space Telescope searched for the infrared glow of a dusty disc around Sheratan, like those around Vega and Fomalhaut, but found none.
facts.title: No dust found

story: Sheratan’s faint companion is a near-match for the Sun. The two stars swing around each other every 107 days on a stretched orbit, too close to split in an ordinary telescope. The Mark III Stellar Interferometer at Mount Wilson resolved them, letting astronomers weigh both: the leader is a hot white A-type star, the follower a G2 dwarf — the same [[spectral-type|type]] as our Sun.

The brighter star spins at least 73 kilometres per second, which smears out the lines in its spectrum, and it may have a mildly peculiar chemistry. As it ages and swells towards a red giant, it is expected to pour gas onto its Sun-like partner.

The name comes from the Arabic for “the two signs”. Several thousand years ago Sheratan and its neighbour Mesarthim, Gamma Arietis, marked the spring equinox, where the Sun crosses the celestial equator heading north.
sheratan.tagline: A hot white star in the Ram’s horn, with a faint partner much like our Sun.

discovered.note: Seen as triple in 1776; the star itself known since antiquity

facts.text: Sigma Orionis E is unusually rich in helium and has an abnormally strong magnetic field — features astronomers pieced together between 1956 and 1979.
facts.title: A magnetic oddity

facts.text: Masses worked out from the stars’ orbits come out larger than stellar models predict for stars like these, a mismatch that is still being studied.
facts.title: Heavier than expected

facts.text: One young star in the cluster, Haro 5-34, has five gaps in its disc, seemingly arranged in a resonant chain.
facts.title: Five gaps in a row

story: At the heart of Sigma Orionis is a triple of hot, young, massive stars, each 11 to 18 times the Sun’s mass. The inner two swing around each other every 143 days on a highly elongated orbit; the third circles them every 157 years. Oddly, the two orbits are tilted almost at right angles to each other.

Around them lies a young [[open-cluster|cluster]], recognised only in 1996, where stars began forming about 3 million years ago. It holds several hundred small members: red dwarfs, brown dwarfs and even objects of planetary mass. In 2024 the ALMA telescope saw rings and gaps in the dusty discs around some young stars — patterns often linked to forming planets. The fierce light of Sigma Orionis may be eroding those discs.
The star has been known since antiquity, yet Ptolemy left it out of his Almagest. In 1776 Christian Mayer saw that it was triple, and observers have been finding more members ever since.
sigma-orionis.tagline: A family of hot young stars at the heart of a cluster teeming with brown dwarfs and planet-mass objects.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; its white-dwarf companion was first seen by Alvan Graham Clark in 1862

facts.text: In 1868 William Huggins measured Sirius’s motion from the shift of the lines in its spectrum — the first star ever to have its velocity measured. His figure was too large, and had the wrong sign: Sirius is approaching us.
facts.title: The first star clocked for speed

facts.text: Precession and Sirius’s own motion will carry it to within 1.6° of the south celestial pole around AD 66,270, when it will take a turn as the southern Pole Star.
facts.title: A southern Pole Star to come

facts.text: Sirius will brighten slightly over the next 60,000 years, then slowly fade. Even so, it should remain the brightest star in our sky for about 210,000 years, until Vega takes over.
facts.title: Brightest for ages yet

facts.text: Medieval Scandinavians called it Lokabrenna, ‘burning done by Loki’ or ‘Loki’s torch’. In Sanskrit it is Mrgavyadha, the deer hunter.
facts.title: Loki’s torch

story: Nothing in the night sky outshines Sirius except the Moon and a few planets — it is almost twice as bright as Canopus, the runner-up. It earns that partly through power: a white [[star]] about twice the Sun’s mass, it gives out 25 times as much light. The rest is closeness. Sirius is one of our nearest neighbours, and it is slowly drifting nearer still.

It does not travel alone. Every 50 years it is circled by Sirius B, a white dwarf — the exposed core of a star that was once the heavier of the pair. That star burned through its fuel, swelled into a red giant, shed its outer layers and collapsed about 120 million years ago. Friedrich Bessel deduced the unseen partner in 1844 from the wobble in Sirius’s path; Alvan Graham Clark first saw it in 1862.

Its name comes from the Greek for ‘glowing’ or ‘scorching’. In Egypt its first dawn appearance each year heralded the Nile flood, and it was worshipped as the goddess Sopdet. The Greeks blamed it for the sweltering ‘dog days’, while Polynesian navigators steered by it across the Pacific.
sirius.tagline: The brightest star in the night sky — a dazzling Dog Star with a tiny, crushed companion at its side.

facts.text: Spica is thought to be the star that gave Hipparchus the data that led him to discover precession — the slow wobble of Earth’s axis that shifts all the stars’ positions over centuries.
facts.title: The clue to precession

facts.text: Each of Spica’s two stars reflects a little of the other’s light. In 2016 that made them the first stars ever to have their reflectivity measured — just a few per cent.
facts.title: Starlight bouncing between stars

facts.text: Venus last passed in front of Spica on 10 November 1783. The next time will be 2 September 2197.
facts.title: Hidden by Venus

story: Spica looks like a single blue-white point, but it is a [[double-star|pair]] of hot stars whirling round each other every four days. They are so close that each pulls the other into an egg shape, and the pair brighten and fade slightly as they turn. The larger is a blue giant of more than ten solar masses, shining some 20,000 times as brightly as the Sun and pulsing every four hours or so. It is one of the nearest stars heavy enough to end as a supernova — though not for several million years.

Its name is Latin for the ear of wheat held by Virgo, the harvest maiden; on a Sumerian star list from Uruk it is ‘the Seed-Furrow’. In 2026 astronomers found a third star circling the pair and nicknamed it Arista — the bristle, or awn, of the wheat ear.
spica.tagline: The Virgin’s ear of wheat — two blue stars so close that each pulls the other into an egg shape.

discovered.note: Named after its entry in F. G. W. Struve’s double-star catalogue

facts.text: Double stars from F. G. W. Struve’s catalogue carry the prefix Σ or STF. His Catalogus Novus of 1827 listed more than 3,000 double stars.
facts.title: Struve’s sigma

facts.text: Spectral types B0.5 and B1 mean surface temperatures well above 20,000 kelvins — several times hotter than the Sun’s.
facts.title: Hot and short-lived

story: Some stars get myths; this one got a catalogue number. Struve 747 is entry 747 in the double-star catalogue of Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve, who combed the sky for pairs with the great Fraunhofer refractor at Dorpat — today Tartu, in Estonia — in the 1820s. The Greek letter Σ, for Struve, still marks the pairs in his catalogue.

Both stars are blue-white B-type stars on the main sequence, far hotter and more massive than the Sun. Stars like these burn through their hydrogen quickly and live only a few tens of millions of years at most, so this pair is young by cosmic standards.
struve-747.tagline: Two hot blue-white stars in Orion’s Sword, known simply by their number in a great 19th-century survey.

facts.text: The name Suhail was used for at least three other stars: Canopus, Gamma Velorum and Zeta Puppis. Canopus kept its own name, and Zeta Puppis became Naos.
facts.title: Four Suhails

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is Tiānjì, the Judge for Estimating the Age of Animals, standing alone in its own asterism.
facts.title: Judge of animals’ ages

story: Suhail is a common Arabic boy’s name, and Arab skywatchers gave it to several bright southern stars, Canopus among them. This one was Suhail al-Wazn. As a star used in modern celestial navigation, its name was shortened to plain Suhail.

It is an orange [[star]] about seven times the Sun’s mass, with a surface near 3,800 kelvin, and only about 32 million years old — heavy stars live fast. Though it is classed as a supergiant, it is probably an aging giant with a dead core of carbon and oxygen, burning helium and hydrogen in shells around it. Its deep, churning outer layers generate a magnetic field.

Its fate hangs on its weight. Stars like it usually end by puffing off a [[planetary-nebula]] and leaving a white dwarf. But Suhail may be just heavy enough for an electron-capture supernova, like the one that made the Crab Nebula, leaving behind a neutron star.
suhail.tagline: A cool orange supergiant in the Sails — one of four bright stars that shared the name Suhail.

discovered.note: Discovered in outburst; seen earlier as an unremarkable 10th-magnitude star

facts.text: Old records hint that T Coronae Borealis may also have been seen in 1217 and 1787, long before anyone knew what a recurrent nova was.
facts.title: Seen in 1217?

facts.text: John Birmingham, who caught the 1866 eruption, also gave La Superba in Canes Venatici its name, in 1876.
facts.title: Birmingham’s other star

story: In May 1866 the Irish astronomer John Birmingham spotted a new 2nd-magnitude star in the Northern Crown. It was an unremarkable 10th-magnitude star caught in a nova outburst — and in February 1946 it did it again. That second eruption was found independently by three observers, one of them a 15-year-old schoolboy from Wales, Michael Woodman. The name Blaze Star has been used since 1866, and the IAU made it official in 2025.

T Coronae Borealis is a pair: a red giant and a white dwarf circling each other every 228 days. Gas from the giant piles up on the white dwarf until it ignites in a runaway nuclear explosion, and the system brightens about 3,000-fold. Two eruptions 80 years apart make it a recurrent nova, a rare kind of [[variable-star]], and suggested it flares on roughly that schedule.

In 2015 it began a sustained brightening like one seen in 1938, eight years before its last eruption, and a dip in 2023 resembled one just before 1946. Predictions of an imminent outburst have come and gone; as of October 2026 the Blaze Star is still waiting.
t-coronae-borealis.tagline: The Blaze Star: a sleeping recurrent nova that astronomers expect to flare to naked-eye brightness.

facts.text: In 2023 Stefan Ziegenbalg reported a faint emission nebula centred just 7 arcminutes from Tarazed. The star is unlikely to be what makes it glow.
facts.title: A nebula found in 2023

facts.text: The Calendarium of Al Achsasi al Mouakket called it Menkib al Nesr, translated into Latin as Humerus Vulturis — “the eagle’s shoulder”.
facts.title: The eagle’s shoulder

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Tarazed, Altair and Alshain form Hé Gǔ, the River Drum. Tarazed is its third star.
facts.title: The River Drum

story: Many cultures have told stories about Altair and the two stars that flank it. In the Chinese tale of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, Tarazed and Alshain are the children of the Cowherd, Altair, and the Weaver Girl, Vega. The Koori people of Victoria saw them as the black swan wives of Bunjil, the wedge-tailed eagle.

Tarazed is the brighter of the two flanking stars. It is an [[star-colour|orange]] bright giant about 92 times the Sun’s width — in the Sun’s place it would reach past Mercury’s orbit — and shines over 2,100 times as brightly. Though only about 270 million years old, it has already used up its core hydrogen and now burns helium into carbon.
Its name comes from the Persian for “the scale beam” or “the balance”, once used for all three stars; Alshain comes from the same phrase.
tarazed.tagline: Altair’s orange companion — in Chinese legend, a child of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl.

facts.text: From a planet of Tau Ceti, the Sun would be an ordinary 2.6-magnitude star in the constellation Boötes.
facts.title: Our Sun, seen from there

facts.text: Tau Ceti is heading our way: in about 43,000 years it will pass closest to the Sun, before moving off again.
facts.title: Coming closer

facts.text: A 17th-century star calendar from Cairo called it ‘the third of the ostriches’, one of five stars of Cetus seen as hen ostriches.
facts.title: The third ostrich

story: Of all the Sun’s near neighbours, Tau Ceti is the closest single star of the Sun’s own [[spectral-type|class G]]. It is close kin, but not a twin: it has about 78% of the Sun’s mass and 79% of its radius, gives out just over half as much light, and holds only about a third as much iron. That shortage hints at age — most estimates put it near 9 billion years old, against the Sun’s 4.6.

A steady, Sun-like star made an obvious target in the hunt for life. In 1960 Frank Drake pointed a radio dish at Green Bank, West Virginia, towards Tau Ceti for Project Ozma, the first modern search for alien signals. Several candidate planets have been proposed since, but none has been confirmed beyond doubt — and with more than ten times as much dust as the Solar System, any planet there would suffer far more impacts than Earth.
Fiction has been kinder. Ursula K. Le Guin set her novel The Dispossessed on a pair of worlds in the Tau Ceti system.
tau-ceti.tagline: The nearest lone Sun-like star — older than the Sun, and a favourite of SETI and science fiction.

facts.text: Tejat lies less than a degree south of the ecliptic, so the Moon sometimes passes in front of it — and, very rarely, a planet does too.
facts.title: In the Moon’s path

facts.text: Two arcminutes away lies a faint pair of stars catalogued as Tejat’s companion. They are an unrelated double, far in the background.
facts.title: A companion that isn’t

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Tejat leads Jǐng, the Well, an asterism of eight stars in Gemini that includes Alhena.
facts.title: First Star of the Well

story: In its last bright act, Tejat has swollen into a red giant more than 100 times wider than the Sun. Its core has run out of fuel, leaving an inert heart of carbon and oxygen, while hydrogen and helium still burn in thin, nested shells around it. Its surface, at about 3,800 kelvins, is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the bloated star shines more than 1,500 times as brightly.

Stars at this stage rarely sit still. Tejat drifts in brightness by a few tenths of a magnitude, with a rough 72-day rhythm and a slower swing lasting about 2,000 days, making it a slow, irregular [[variable-star]].

Its name is a mystery. Tejat comes from an old southern Arabic word, tiḥyāt, whose meaning has been lost. Other names have attached themselves over the centuries: Calx, Latin for ‘heel’; Pish Pai, Persian for ‘foreleg’; and Nuhatai, from an Arabic word for a camel’s hump.
tejat.tagline: A swollen red giant at the Twins’ feet, near the end of its life — with a name whose meaning is lost.

facts.text: Two tiny moons, Telesto and Calypso, travel along Tethys’s orbit, one 60° ahead of it and one 60° behind, at balance points known as Lagrange points.
facts.title: Two moons share its orbit

facts.text: Although it is mostly ice, Tethys outweighs all the known moons smaller than itself put together.
facts.title: Heavier than all smaller moons

facts.text: Cassini honoured King Louis XIV by calling the four moons he found Sidera Lodoicea, ‘the stars of Louis’. The modern names came from John Herschel in 1847.
facts.title: The stars of Louis

story: Tethys is about as close as a moon gets to a giant snowball. Its density is the lowest of any major moon in the Solar System, just under that of water, so it must be almost pure ice with only a little rock. And it gleams: its surface is one of the most reflective known, sandblasted clean by ice grains from Saturn’s E ring, which the geysers of Enceladus keep supplying.

Two great scars mark it. Odysseus is an impact [[crater]] spanning more than a third of the moon’s width, and Ithaca Chasma, a rift valley about 100 km wide, runs for more than 2,000 km. The two may be related. Both take their names from Homer’s Odyssey.
Giovanni Domenico Cassini found Tethys in 1684 with a giant aerial telescope — a lens mounted high on a pole, with no tube — in the grounds of the Paris Observatory.
tethys.tagline: Saturn’s ice-white moon, marked by a giant crater and a canyon named for Odysseus’s home.

facts.text: Johann Bayer made Thuban the Alpha of Draco in 1603, yet today it is 3.7 times fainter than Eltanin, the Dragon’s brightest star.
facts.title: Bayer’s puzzling Alpha

facts.text: Astronomers use Thuban as a reference: it is a standard star for the A0 III [[spectral-type]], against which other white giants are compared.
facts.title: A standard white giant

facts.text: Thuban’s partner sits just a few thousandths of an arcsecond from it. The Navy Precision Optical Interferometer finally detected it directly.
facts.title: Seen at last

story: When the pyramids of Giza were built, the sky turned around Thuban. Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, and from 3942 BC until 1793 BC this star in Draco was the naked-eye star nearest the [[celestial-sphere|north celestial pole]]. In 2830 BC it sat less than a sixth of a degree from the pole — closer than Polaris is today.

The wobble has since carried the pole away towards Polaris, leaving Thuban a modest star in the Dragon’s tail. But the cycle turns: in AD 20,346 Thuban will again be the pole star. Its name comes from the Arabic thu‘bān, a great serpent. Chinese astronomers called it Yòushū, the Right Pivot — fitting for a star the sky once turned upon.

Thuban is a white giant, about 120 times as luminous as the Sun, that has stopped fusing hydrogen in its core. A fainter partner circles it every 51 days, and NASA’s TESS satellite has caught the two eclipsing each other.
thuban.tagline: The pole star of the pyramid builders — a modest star in the Dragon that will guide the north again in AD 20,346.

discovered.note: Naked-eye star; Alan Cousins announced its variability in 1952

facts.text: At around 150 times the Sun’s radius, Tiaki would reach almost to the orbit of Venus if it sat at the centre of our Solar System.
facts.title: If it replaced the Sun

facts.text: Chinese astronomers saw a crane here too: Beta Gruis is Hè èr, the Second Star of the Crane — the source of its old English name, Ke.
facts.title: Second Star of the Crane

story: Tiaki carries a name from the Tuamotu islands of French Polynesia, adopted by the International Astronomical Union in 2017. It has changed constellations too: medieval Arab astronomers counted it as the last star in the tail of the Southern Fish, before it became part of the Crane.

It is a red giant late in life, about 2.4 times the Sun’s mass but swollen to some 150 times its width. Its surface is only about 3,500 kelvin, just over half as hot as the Sun’s, which gives it a dull red [[star-colour|colour]]. Even so it pours out about 3,200 times the Sun’s energy, much of it as infrared: at near-infrared wavelengths it is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky.

Tiaki also changes. Alan Cousins announced in 1952 that it is a [[variable-star]]. It brightens and fades by about 0.4 magnitude, sometimes on a regular 37-day rhythm, sometimes slowly and irregularly.
tiaki.tagline: A cool red giant in the Crane, glowing brightest in infrared, with a Polynesian name.

facts.text: The two stars of Tianguan circle each other every 133 days on circular orbits, a little farther apart than Earth is from the Sun.
facts.title: A year of 133 days

facts.text: Watching from Croatia’s Hvar Observatory in 1981–1986, astronomers saw what looked like eclipses. Later studies, including Hipparcos data, could not confirm them.
facts.title: Eclipses that vanished

story: In July 1054 Chinese astronomers recorded a ‘guest star’ near Tianguan, bright enough to be seen in daylight for 23 days. It was a star exploding as a supernova, and its wreckage is the Crab Nebula, M 1, a [[supernova-remnant]] about a degree from Tianguan in our sky. Tiānguān itself means the Celestial Gate — a frontier gate within the Net, one of the Chinese lunar mansions.

Tianguan is a pair too close for any telescope to split, revealed only by the shifting lines in its spectrum. The main star is a giant of more than 11 solar masses, spinning fast and wrapped in a disc of gas thrown off from its equator — a Be star. A one-armed spiral wave runs through that disc, which may be wobbling under the pull of the companion. That companion has about the Sun’s mass and may be a white dwarf feeding on the gas, which would explain the hard X-rays the system gives off.
tianguan.tagline: The Celestial Gate at the tip of the Bull’s horn — beside which a ‘guest star’ blazed in 1054.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; F. G. W. Struve reported its companion in 1826

facts.text: Zeta Herculis gives its name to a moving group: stars scattered across the sky, including Zeta Reticuli and Phi² Pavonis, that travel through space together.
facts.title: A family on the move

facts.text: Tianji, with different meanings, is also the Chinese name for Phecda in the Big Dipper and for Suhail in Vela.
facts.title: One name, three stars

story: Two stars much like our Sun circle each other in Zeta Herculis. The companion is about the Sun’s size and mass. The brighter one is heavier, about 1.45 times the Sun’s mass, and has begun to run out of core hydrogen, so it has grown to nearly three times the Sun’s width and shines more than seven times as brightly. Its surface, at around 5,760 K, is almost exactly as hot as the Sun’s.

They take 34.45 years to complete one orbit, on average about 15 times the Earth–Sun distance apart. F. G. W. Struve reported the [[double-star|pair]] in 1826, so astronomers have now followed it around nearly six full orbits.
In May 2026 the IAU gave the brighter star a name, Tianji, after the Chinese star group Tiān Jì, “Celestial Discipline”, in which it is the second star.
tianji.tagline: Two Sun-like stars in the Keystone of Hercules, followed for nearly six orbits since 1826.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Secchi found the first emission lines ever seen in a star

facts.text: Apollo crews used it as a navigation star. In 1967 it was nicknamed Navi — “Ivan” backwards — for Apollo 1 astronaut Virgil Ivan “Gus” Grissom. Despite the popular story, Grissom did not name it himself.
facts.title: An astronaut’s star

facts.text: Chinese astronomers saw it as one of four horses pulling the chariot of the charioteer Wangliang; later it became his whip. In 2025 the IAU named it Tiansi, after the Heavenly Quadriga.
facts.title: From horse to whip

facts.text: A naked-eye neighbour, HR 266, is itself a quadruple star and seems to travel with Gamma Cassiopeiae. Together the system may hold eight stars, one of the highest counts known.
facts.title: A crowded family

story: In 1866 the Italian astronomer Angelo Secchi turned a spectroscope on this star and saw something new: bright emission lines, the first ever seen in a star. Gamma Cassiopeiae became the first known Be star and the model for a whole class of restless, eruptive [[variable-star|variables]].

The cause is spin. This blue-white star of about 17 solar masses turns at some 450 km per second, so fast that its equator bulges far wider than its poles. Shining like 19,000 Suns, it flings gas into a hot disc around its waist — the source of the bright lines and of its fits of brightening and fading. In the late 1930s it rose above magnitude 2, outshining Schedar and Caph, then dropped to 3.4.

It is also unusually bright in X-rays. In 2026 the XRISM observatory showed that the hot gas moves with a companion: a white dwarf a little smaller than Earth, circling every 203.5 days and feeding on the big star’s gas.
tiansi.tagline: The middle of Cassiopeia’s W — a whirling star with a hidden white dwarf and an astronaut’s nickname.

facts.text: Titan is wider than the planet Mercury, yet has only about 40% of its mass: Titan is mostly ice, while Mercury is iron and rock.
facts.title: Bigger than Mercury, but lighter

facts.text: Seen from Titan, Saturn would look more than ten times as wide as our Moon does from Earth — if only the thick haze would let you see it.
facts.title: Saturn fills the sky

facts.text: Computer simulations suggest a mid-sized moon collided with Titan a few hundred million years ago, and that the debris may have gathered to form the moon Hyperion.
facts.title: Hyperion’s parent?

story: On Titan the air is thicker than on Earth and the sky is a dim orange haze. It rains here — not water but liquid methane. Wind and rain have shaped rivers, dunes and deltas, and near the poles lie lakes and seas, all at about −179 °C. Titan is the only moon with a dense atmosphere, and the only world besides Earth known to have stable bodies of liquid on its surface.

Saturn’s largest [[planetary-moon|moon]] is second in size only to Jupiter’s Ganymede. Christiaan Huygens discovered it in 1655 with a telescope he built with his brother Constantijn — the first moon of Saturn ever found. He called it simply Saturni Luna, ‘moon of Saturn’; the name Titan came from John Herschel in 1847.

On 14 January 2005, the European Huygens probe, carried there by Cassini, parachuted through the haze and landed on a plain strewn with rounded pebbles of ice — still the most distant landing ever made. NASA’s Dragonfly, a flying rotorcraft, is due to follow.
titan.tagline: A moon with orange skies, methane rain, rivers and seas — the most Earth-like world we know, at −179 °C.

discovered.note: Found on the same night as Oberon

facts.text: The name Titania is ancient Greek for ‘daughter of the Titans’, and its adjective, Titanian, is the same as that of Saturn’s moon Titan.
facts.title: Daughter of the Titans

facts.text: When Titania passed in front of a star, the starlight cut off sharply, showing that any atmosphere it has must be extremely thin.
facts.title: A test with starlight

facts.text: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus, in January 1986. Its pictures mapped about 40% of Titania’s surface.
facts.title: Mapped only once

story: On 11 January 1787, six years after discovering Uranus, William Herschel spotted two moons circling it. The larger was Titania. Herschel later reported four more moons, but they turned out to be illusions. The names came only in 1852, from his son John: Titania is the queen of the fairies in Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

The largest [[planetary-moon|moon]] of Uranus is made of roughly equal parts ice and rock, probably divided into a rocky core and an icy mantle, perhaps with a layer of liquid water where they meet. Its surface is cut by enormous canyons and cliffs, cracked open as the interior expanded long ago. Frozen carbon dioxide on the ground hints at a whisper-thin atmosphere.
titania.tagline: Queen of the fairies and the largest moon of Uranus — a world split by enormous canyons.

discovered.note: Sketched three of the stars on 4 February 1617

facts.text: A 2012 study suggested an intermediate-mass black hole, more than 100 times the Sun’s mass, may lurk in the Trapezium. It would explain why its stars move so fast relative to one another.
facts.title: A hidden black hole?

facts.text: About half the stars in the cluster are wrapped in dwindling discs of gas and dust — the likely raw material for planets.
facts.title: Planets in the making

story: On 4 February 1617 Galileo sketched three stars at this spot in Orion’s Sword. Oddly, he drew nothing of the great glowing cloud around them — the Orion Nebula. A fourth star was spotted by several observers in 1673, and by 1888 eight had been counted.

These are newborn stars, formed straight out of the nebula they now light up. The five brightest are each some 15 to 30 times the Sun’s mass, and their fierce light is responsible for much of the nebula’s glow. Infrared cameras, which see through the dust, reveal many more stars hidden in the cloud, along with brown dwarfs and low-mass runaway stars.
The Trapezium is a tight [[open-cluster|open cluster]], perhaps the core of the much larger Orion Nebula Cluster of about 2,000 stars.
trapezium.tagline: Galileo saw three stars here and missed the nebula around them — the young powerhouse of Orion.

facts.text: Triton is larger than any known dwarf planet, Pluto included, and is the seventh-largest moon in the Solar System.
facts.title: Bigger than Pluto

facts.text: The name Triton, after the son of Poseidon, was first proposed by Camille Flammarion in 1880. Until 1949 it was simply ‘the satellite of Neptune’.
facts.title: A name from Flammarion

facts.text: Because it orbits backwards, Neptune’s tides are slowly dragging Triton inward. In billions of years it may be torn apart, perhaps to become a ring around Neptune.
facts.title: A doomed orbit

story: Triton goes the wrong way. It circles Neptune backwards, against the planet’s spin — the only large moon in the Solar System to do so. That is a strong clue that it was not born there. Triton was probably a dwarf planet from the Kuiper belt, the icy realm beyond Neptune, until Neptune’s gravity captured it.

When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989 it found one of the youngest surfaces in the Solar System, coated with frozen nitrogen and almost free of craters. Geysers sent dark plumes kilometres high, leaving streaks across the ice. This [[planetary-moon|moon]] has a thin nitrogen atmosphere with ice clouds and an organic haze, and it may hide an ocean beneath its crust.
William Lassell, a brewer by trade, found Triton on 10 October 1846 — just 17 days after Neptune itself — with a telescope he had built, after John Herschel urged him to look for moons.
triton.tagline: A captured world circling Neptune backwards, with nitrogen geysers and a surface of frozen nitrogen.

discovered.note: Known since antiquity; Olin J. Eggen announced its pulsations in 1956

facts.text: In 2017 astronomers found a magnetic field around Tureis, making it only the second Delta Scuti star known to have one.
facts.title: A magnetic pulsator

facts.text: Extra infrared light hints at a disc of dust around the star, at about 85 K — roughly 50 times the Earth–Sun distance from it.
facts.title: A cold ring of dust

story: Every 3 hours and 23 minutes, Tureis swells and shrinks, brightening and dimming as it goes. Olin Eggen announced the pulsations in 1956, making it one of the first known [[variable-star|Delta Scuti stars]], and records going back to 1946 show the rhythm keeping steady time. At about 6,650 K it is one of the coolest stars of its kind.

Its chemistry is odd too. Its spectrum shows weak calcium but strong lines of other metals, and it has more than twice the Sun’s share of heavy elements. It is the prototype of the Rho Puppis stars: aged stars with this peculiar mix. Most such stars have a partner, but Tureis seems to be alone.
Its name is Arabic for “little shield”, once shared with Iota Carinae, now called Aspidiske. About 394,000 years ago Tureis passed about as close to us as Procyon is today; it is now moving away.
tureis.tagline: A pulsing star that keeps time every 3 hours 23 minutes — the model for a whole class.

discovered.note: Found on the same night as Ariel

facts.text: Around Uranus’s 2007 equinox, Umbriel was seen passing in front of Titania twice, on 15 August and 8 December.
facts.title: Shadow play in 2007

facts.text: Early in its history Umbriel may have been in a 1:3 orbital resonance with Miranda, stretching Miranda’s orbit and helping to heat that moon from within.
facts.title: A heater for Miranda?

facts.text: After Oberon, Umbriel is the most heavily cratered moon of Uranus, with impact craters up to 210 km across.
facts.title: Battered

story: Umbriel is the ‘dusky melancholy sprite’ of Alexander Pope’s poem The Rape of the Lock, and its name echoes the Latin umbra, ‘shadow’. It suits the moon. Umbriel has the darkest surface of Uranus’s large moons, an old, heavily cratered landscape of ice mixed with a good deal of rock.

One feature breaks the gloom: a ring of bright material on the floor of the [[crater]] Wunda, the most prominent mark on the moon. Canyons hint that Umbriel was once active inside, and it may have been resurfaced early on, wiping out an even older face.
William Lassell discovered Umbriel on 24 October 1851, the same night as Ariel. Only Voyager 2 has seen it up close, in January 1986, mapping about 40% of its surface.
umbriel.tagline: The darkest of Uranus’s big moons, named after a gloomy sprite and marked by one bright ring.

facts.text: Arabic star lore placed it in al-Nasaq al-Yamānī, “the Southern Line”, a string of stars across Serpens and Ophiuchus that includes Yed Prior and Zeta Ophiuchi.
facts.title: The Southern Line

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the seventh star of the Right Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, where it stands for Shu, one of the old states of China.
facts.title: The state of Shu

story: Serpens is the only constellation split in two: Ophiuchus, the serpent-bearer, grips the snake in the middle, with its head on one side and its tail on the other. Unukalhai shines in the head half. Its name is Arabic for “the serpent’s neck”, and in Latin it was Cor Serpentis, “the heart of the serpent”.

It is an [[star-colour|orange]] giant of about 1.6 times the Sun’s mass. It has used up the hydrogen in its core and probably now fuses helium there, swollen to 13.5 times the Sun’s width with a surface near 4,700 K. Its spectrum shows unusually strong bands of cyanogen, a molecule of carbon and nitrogen, which marks it out as a “CN star”.
unukalhai.tagline: The serpent’s neck — brightest star of the only constellation cut in two.

discovered.note: Catalogued as a star by John Flamsteed in 1690

facts.text: Uranus had been logged as a star long before Herschel. John Flamsteed recorded it at least six times from 1690, cataloguing it as 34 Tauri.
facts.title: Seen, but not recognised

facts.text: In 1789 the chemist Martin Klaproth named his newly discovered element uranium in honour of the new planet.
facts.title: A namesake element

facts.text: Uranus’s rings were discovered in 1977, when a star blinked on and off as it passed behind them — an [[occultation]]. They are so dark they reflect only about 2% of the light that hits them.
facts.title: Rings found by starlight

facts.text: Voyager 2 flew past in January 1986 and remains the only spacecraft to visit. US planetary scientists have named a Uranus orbiter and probe a top priority for 2023–2032.
facts.title: One visit, ever

story: On 13 March 1781, in the garden of his house in Bath, the musician and astronomer William Herschel noticed something odd. Under higher magnification one ‘star’ grew larger, as a planet would, while the real stars stayed points. He reported a comet.
