Others worked out its nearly circular orbit and realised it was something far bigger: a new [[planet]], the first found with a telescope, doubling the size of the known Solar System at a stroke.

Herschel wanted to call it Georgium Sidus, ‘George’s Star’, after King George III, who rewarded him with a yearly stipend. Most of Europe preferred Johann Bode’s suggestion: Uranus, the Greek god of the sky and father of Saturn. Britain’s Nautical Almanac Office held out until 1850.

Uranus is an ice giant, its blue-green tint coming from methane, and its axis is tipped so far over that it rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets about 42 years of unbroken sunlight, then 42 years of night. Its atmosphere is the coldest of any planet’s, dropping to about −224 °C.
uranus.tagline: The planet that rolls around the Sun on its side — first taken for a comet, then nearly named after a king.

facts.text: R. H. Allen gave it the Chinese name Yang Mun, “the South Gate”. But in Chinese astronomy that gate is made by two stars of the Centaur.
facts.title: The South Gate that wasn’t

facts.text: Its Chinese name is in fact Qí Guān shí, the Tenth Star of the Imperial Guards, an asterism spread across Lupus.
facts.title: An imperial guard

story: The Sumerians had a name for this constellation, UR.IDIM, written Uridimmu in later Akkadian. In 2024 the International Astronomical Union revived it as Uridim, the official name of the Wolf’s brightest star.

It is a blue-white giant about ten times the Sun’s mass, shining 18,000 times as brightly with a surface near 24,550 kelvin. In 1956 Bernard Pagel and colleagues found that it pulses: every 7 hours and 6 minutes it brightens and fades by about 5 per cent, a Beta Cephei [[variable-star]]. A fainter companion of about 2.25 solar masses was found in 2023, on an orbit expected to take about a decade.

Uridim belongs to the Upper Centaurus–Lupus group, a family of stars some 16 to 20 million years old within the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest gathering of massive young stars to the Sun. Stars of this family blew the Local Bubble, the cavity of hot gas the Sun now travels through. Uridim itself is one of the nearest candidates to explode as a supernova.
uridim.tagline: The Wolf’s brightest star — a pulsing blue giant that carries a revived Sumerian name.

facts.text: Vega comes from the Arabic an-nasr al-wāqi’, ‘the falling eagle’. Its neighbour Altair is the flying one.
facts.title: The falling eagle

facts.text: Earth’s slowly wobbling axis pointed near Vega around 12,000 BC and will do so again around AD 14,000. It is the brightest of all the northern pole stars.
facts.title: Pole star past and future

facts.text: In the Chinese legend of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl, Vega is Zhinü, kept apart from Altair by the river of the Milky Way. Once a year magpies form a bridge so the lovers can meet — Japan’s Tanabata festival.
facts.title: The Weaver Girl

facts.text: Friedrich von Struve published a parallax for Vega, one of the first attempts to measure a star’s distance. He later doubted it, yet his first value was close to today’s.
facts.title: An early distance

story: Vega spins so fast — about 236 km/s at its equator — that it bulges into a flattened ball, hotter at the poles than around its middle. We happen to look almost straight down on one of those poles. With 2.1 times the Sun’s mass, it is only a tenth of the Sun’s age, yet it will also live only a tenth as long: both stars are now about halfway through their lives.

Astronomers have called it arguably the most important star in the sky after the Sun. In 1850 it became the first star ever photographed, on a daguerreotype at Harvard. In 1872 Henry Draper photographed its spectrum, the first such picture to show absorption lines. For many years it helped define [[magnitude]] zero, the starting point of the brightness scale.

Infrared telescopes found that Vega gives off more heat than a bare star should. The excess comes from a disc of dust, ground out by collisions like those in our Kuiper belt. JWST has since shown the disc to be remarkably smooth, with no sign of giant planets carving it.
vega.tagline: The star that set the brightness scale — the first ever photographed, and a pole star past and future.

facts.text: Venera 1 flew past Venus in 1961, the first interplanetary spaceflight. In 1970 Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to land on another planet.
facts.title: First across the gulf

facts.text: In Old English Venus was Ēarendel, “ray of light”, as well as the morning and evening star. It is the brightest natural point of light in our sky.
facts.title: Ray of light

facts.text: High in its clouds, conditions are the most Earth-like found anywhere else in the Solar System. Possible signs of life reported there in 2020 have spurred new research and missions.
facts.title: Life in the clouds?

facts.text: Venus has only about a thousand craters, most of them pristine — a sign that its whole surface was renewed by lava some 300 to 600 million years ago.
facts.title: A young face

story: Almost Earth’s twin in size and mass, Venus would kill you several ways at once. Its air is mostly carbon dioxide, so dense that the pressure at the surface is 92 times Earth’s and the gas there behaves like a hot fluid. A runaway greenhouse effect holds the ground at about 464 °C, making Venus the hottest planet of all — hotter even than Mercury. Above it all, clouds of sulphuric acid wrap the whole planet.

It also spins slowly, and backwards: one day from sunrise to sunrise lasts about 117 Earth days, roughly half its year. Radar maps show a world shaped by volcanoes — more than 85,000 have been mapped — and fresh looks at old Magellan images have caught signs of eruptions under way. Almost all its features are named after women from history and myth.

Venus even changed our place in the cosmos. Through a telescope it shows [[phase|phases]] like the Moon, and by 1613 those phases had been presented as decisive evidence that the planets circle the Sun, not the Earth.
venus.tagline: Earth’s twin in size, but a crushing, scorching furnace beneath clouds of sulphuric acid.

facts.text: With Zavijava, Porrima, Zaniah and Minelauva, Vindemiatrix formed the Arabic star group Al-ʽAwwāʼ, “the Barker”.
facts.title: Part of the Barker

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it is the fourth star of the Left Wall of the Supreme Palace Enclosure, representing the Second Eastern General.
facts.title: The Second Eastern General

story: Vindemiatrix means “the grape-harvestress”. The ancient Greeks called the star Protrygeter, and its first appearance in the dawn sky was taken as the signal to start picking grapes. The name came down to us through Latin, with medieval variants such as Provindemiator and Protrigetrix.

Today it is a [[star-colour|yellow]] giant of 2.7 times the Sun’s mass, about 700 million years old. It has used up its core hydrogen and settled into what astronomers call the red clump: helium fuses into carbon at its centre, wrapped in a shell where hydrogen still burns. It has grown to 12 times the Sun’s width and shines 82 times as brightly.
Since 1943 its spectrum has been one of the fixed anchor points that astronomers use to sort other stars by type.
vindemiatrix.tagline: The grape-harvester — a yellow giant whose dawn rising once called the vintage.

discovered.note: First known record, as a 7th-magnitude star

facts.text: VY Canis Majoris has been described as ‘Betelgeuse on steroids’. Its closest analogue is NML Cygni, another extreme cool hypergiant, in Cygnus.
facts.title: ‘Betelgeuse on steroids’

facts.text: At its estimated size, VY Canis Majoris has almost 3 billion times the Sun’s volume — yet only about 17 times its mass.
facts.title: Billions of Suns inside

facts.text: It sits at the tip of the glowing cloud Sh 2-310 and is thought to belong to the young star cluster NGC 2362.
facts.title: Child of a stellar nursery

story: If VY Canis Majoris took the Sun’s place, its surface would stretch beyond the orbit of Jupiter. Light would need about six hours to travel once around it, against 14.5 seconds for the Sun. With a radius estimated at around 1,420 times the Sun’s — close to the limit of how large a cool [[star]] can grow — it is one of the largest stars known, and one of the most luminous in the Milky Way.

It is tearing itself apart. Strong convection and magnetic fields in its tenuous outer layers drive huge, randomly aimed outbursts — like the Sun’s coronal mass ejections, but far larger — that have flung arcs and knots of gas into a complex cloud around it within the last thousand years. In that cloud astronomers have found molecules ranging from titanium oxide to table salt.

Its history is full of illusions. Since 1847 observers have called it crimson, and in the 19th century they saw up to six ‘companions’ around it — now known to be bright patches in its surrounding nebula. It was also one of the first radio masers ever discovered.
vy-canis-majoris.tagline: One of the largest stars known: a swollen red hypergiant that would engulf the orbit of Jupiter.

facts.text: Turning at about 28 km/s at its vast equator, Wezen may take about a year to spin once.
facts.title: A year-long day

facts.text: An Arabic catalogue calls Wezen Thalath al Adzari, ‘the third virgin’ — one of a group of stars in the Great Dog’s hindquarters known as the Virgins.
facts.title: The third virgin

facts.text: Wezen appears on the flag of Brazil, where it stands for the state of Roraima.
facts.title: On Brazil’s flag

story: If Wezen were as close to us as Sirius, it would shine as brightly as a half Moon. It is a supergiant [[star]] 14 to 15 times the Sun’s mass, around 190 times its width and 35,000 times as luminous. Curiously, its surface temperature of about 5,800 K is almost the same as the Sun’s.

It is only about 12 million years old, yet it has already stopped fusing hydrogen in its core. Over the next 100,000 years it will swell into a red supergiant, forging heavier and heavier elements in its core, until an iron core collapses and it explodes as a supernova.

Its name comes from the Arabic al-wazn, ‘weight’. The writer Richard Hinckley Allen thought it alluded to the star’s struggle to rise above northern horizons; the astronomer Jim Kaler noted how well it suits so massive a star.
wezen.tagline: A yellow-white supergiant so powerful that, as close as Sirius, it would shine like a half Moon.

facts.text: Infrared observations suggest the brighter star may be ringed by a cold dust belt like our Kuiper belt, holding at least 2.4 times the mass of our Moon.
facts.title: A Kuiper belt?

facts.text: Any planet circling the brighter star would need to stay within about 3.8 times Earth’s distance from the Sun to keep a stable orbit.
facts.title: Room for planets

facts.text: A search for exoplanets found a slow, steady drift in the brighter star’s motion — most likely the pull of its companion.
facts.title: Spotted by planet hunters

story: Picture a Sun-like star in its youth. Xi Boötis A is a little smaller and dimmer than our star, and only about 200 million years old — and it shows. Its surface is magnetically active and blotched with starspots, which make its light waver as it turns, roughly every ten days.
Its companion is a cooler orange dwarf with two-thirds of the Sun’s mass and just 6% of its light. The pair follow a wide, very elongated orbit that takes about a century and a half.
Together they are two of the closest young Sun-like stars to us, and they make up the nearest naked-eye star in Boötes.
xi-bootis.tagline: A young, spotted cousin of the Sun with an orange partner — and perhaps a Kuiper belt of its own.

facts.text: Alula comes from an Arabic phrase meaning “the first spring” — as in a leap — a name it shares with Nu Ursae Majoris. Australis is Latin for “southern”.
facts.title: The first spring

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy it belongs to Sān Tái, the Three Steps, a chain of star pairs in the Great Bear; it is the star of the Second Lower Step.
facts.title: The Three Steps

facts.text: The system varies in brightness by about 0.01 magnitude. The fainter star is thought to be responsible, showing emission lines that the brighter one lacks.
facts.title: A tiny flicker

story: In 1780 William Herschel noticed that this star in the Great Bear’s hind paw was double. By 1804 he had watched the two stars move enough to present them as a likely true pair, bound by gravity. Then, in the late 1820s, the French astronomer Félix Savary used their motion to calculate a full orbit — the first ever worked out for a visual double star. One lap takes just under 60 years.

Since then the family has kept growing. Each of the two stars is itself a close pair. One of the hidden partners may be a white dwarf, betrayed by an excess of barium in its companion’s atmosphere. In 2012 the WISE infrared satellite added a fifth member: a cold brown dwarf far out from the rest. Only one quintuple system is known to be closer to us.
xi-ursae-majoris.tagline: Five suns in the Great Bear’s paw — and the first double star to have its orbit worked out.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Yed Prior is the ninth star of the Right Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure, where it represents the ancient state of Liang.
facts.title: The state of Liang

facts.text: With Unukalhai and Zeta Ophiuchi it belonged to al-Nasaq al-Yamānī, “the Southern Line”, an Arabic star group of seven stars.
facts.title: The Southern Line

story: Two stars hold the serpent’s head. Yed Prior and Yed Posterior mark the left hand of Ophiuchus, gripping the snake Serpens — yed comes from the Arabic yad, “hand”. Yed Prior gets its name because it leads its partner across the sky. Yet the two are neighbours only by chance: Yed Posterior is much closer to us.

Yed Prior is a [[star-colour|red]] giant late in life, on what astronomers call the asymptotic giant branch. It has swollen to about 54 times the Sun’s width with only 1.5 times its mass, so its outer layers are far less dense than the Sun. Its surface glows at a cool 3,733 K, and it holds more than twice the Sun’s share of heavy elements.

Its light hints at something lopsided. It is strongly polarised, more so in blue light than red, and the effect changes over time — perhaps from an uneven shell of dust thrown off by the star, or from hot spots on its surface.
yed-prior.tagline: The Serpent-bearer’s hand — a red giant paired with a star that is no relation.

facts.text: Chinese astronomers placed Zaurak in Tiān Yuàn, the Celestial Meadows, a sweep of sixteen stars in Eridanus and Cetus. Zaurak is its first star.
facts.title: First of the Celestial Meadows

facts.text: The US Navy named a Crater-class cargo ship, USS Zaurak, after this star.
facts.title: A ship named after it

story: Zaurak means ‘the boat’ — it is one of the Arabic words for one — and it floats in Eridanus, the celestial river. The star is a red giant near the end of its life. Its core is spent, and it now burns hydrogen and helium in separate shells around it, having swollen and cooled to a warm orange-red.

It is so typical of its kind that astronomers use it as a reference: Zaurak is a standard star for the M0 III [[spectral-type]], against which other red giants are compared. In 1960 observers found it flickering by a few hundredths of a magnitude, and in 1977 it was officially listed as a [[variable-star]] — though nobody is sure what kind.

Nor is it alone. Data from the Gaia spacecraft revealed a small star, about a tenth of the Sun’s mass, travelling with Zaurak far out, and another red dwarf may hide much closer in, lost in the giant’s glare.
zaurak.tagline: ‘The boat’ of the celestial river: an ageing red giant that astronomers use as a standard for its kind.

discovered.note: Measured by William Herschel in 1779; Christian Mayer listed an earlier observation

facts.text: Earth’s slowly wobbling axis shifts the celestial equator among the stars. Zeta Aquarii sat right on it in 2004; before then it was a southern star, and now it is a northern one.
facts.title: Crossing the line

facts.text: Arabic astronomers counted it among al-Akhbiya, the Tents, with Gamma, Pi and Eta Aquarii. In China the same four stars formed the Tomb.
facts.title: The Tents and the Tomb

story: In 1942 Kaj Strand noticed that the two stars of Zeta Aquarii were not moving quite as they should. Something unseen was tugging on them: a third star. For decades astronomers argued over which star it circled, and two teams even claimed to have photographed it — claims later dismissed as bogus.

It was finally imaged directly in 2009, by the Southern Astrophysical Research Telescope, and later observations confirmed that it orbits the brighter star every 26 years. It has about 0.6 times the Sun’s mass.

The two bright stars are yellow-white F-type stars, one still on the main sequence and the other a slightly more evolved subgiant. William Herschel measured them in 1779, but Christian Mayer listed an earlier sighting, so nobody knows who first spotted the pair.
zeta-aquarii.tagline: A hidden third star astronomers argued over for decades — in a system that crossed the equator in 2004.

facts.text: Am stars usually spin slowly. In their calm atmospheres some elements sink while others are lifted, so certain metals look far more abundant than they really are inside the star.
facts.title: Why Am stars look odd

facts.text: The two stars sit about 44″ apart on the sky and are believed to be a genuine, physically linked pair rather than a chance alignment.
facts.title: A real pair

story: Three stars hide in this wide pair. The brighter, Zeta¹ Lyrae, is itself a close [[double-star|spectroscopic binary]]: two stars too near each other to see apart, revealed only by the regular shifting of the lines in their spectrum. Its main star is an “Am” star, whose light shows unusually strong lines of certain metals.

Its companion, Zeta² Lyrae, is an F-type subgiant — a star that is moving on from the long, steady hydrogen-burning stage our Sun is in now. The two are believed to be physically bound, travelling through space as one system.
In 2026 the IAU gave both stars names taken from cultural star patterns in Lyra: Kautoki for the brighter star’s primary, and Urquchillay for its companion.
zeta-lyrae.tagline: A triple star in the Lyre whose two visible members received their names only in 2026.

facts.text: Dust soaks up much of its light. Without it, Zeta Ophiuchi would shine at magnitude 1.5 — the brightest star in Ophiuchus and the 23rd-brightest in the whole night sky.
facts.title: Hidden by dust

facts.text: Its fast spin stretches the star, so its surface runs from about 39,000 K at the poles to 30,700 K at the equator.
facts.title: Hot poles, cooler waist

facts.text: In 1979 astronomers spotted bumps travelling across the helium lines in its spectrum, probably caused by the star pulsating. Stars that show them are now called Zeta Ophiuchi stars.
facts.title: Moving bumps

facts.text: In April 2010 the asteroid 824 Anastasia passed in front of the star in an [[occultation]], briefly hiding it from observers along the asteroid’s shadow path.
facts.title: Hidden by an asteroid

story: A runaway star is ploughing through the dust of Ophiuchus, and it leaves a wake. Zeta Ophiuchi moves so fast that it heaps up a glowing arc ahead of it — a bow shock, like the wave at a ship’s prow — captured in infrared by NASA’s WISE telescope.

Why is it running? It may once have had a partner, a heavier star that exploded as a supernova and set it loose. A pulsar, PSR B1929+10, could be that star’s collapsed core: it was flung out of the same family of young stars, on a matching track.

It is the nearest [[spectral-type|O-type]] star to the Sun: more than 20 times the Sun’s mass, around 34,000 K at the surface, and spinning perhaps once a day — close to the speed that would tear it apart. Within a few million years it will balloon into a red supergiant wider than Jupiter’s orbit, then explode in turn.
zeta-ophiuchi.tagline: The nearest O-type star — a runaway star pushing a glowing wave through the dust.

facts.text: Zeta and its neighbour Omicron Persei once shared the Arabic name Atik, ‘the collarbone of the Pleiades’. The IAU gave the name to Omicron, so Zeta goes by its Greek letter.
facts.title: The collarbone of the Pleiades

facts.text: A 9th-magnitude star beside Zeta Persei drifts across the sky at the same rate and in the same direction. The two may be a true pair, though a very wide one.
facts.title: A partner on the move

story: Imagine losing a whole Sun’s worth of gas every 4.3 million years. That is the rate at which a fierce wind is stripping Zeta Persei away. This blue-white [[star]] is a supergiant some 26 times the Sun’s width, 13 to 16 times its mass and about 47,000 times as luminous, with a surface of 20,800 kelvins. Its spectrum shows unusually high levels of carbon.

It does not travel alone. Zeta Persei belongs to the Perseus OB2 association, also called the Zeta Persei association: 17 massive, highly luminous blue stars moving through space on similar paths. They probably formed together from the same cloud of gas, and they are about the same age.
zeta-persei.tagline: A blue supergiant blowing itself away — and the namesake of a family of massive stars travelling together.

facts.text: In Chinese astronomy Zosma sits in the Right Wall of the Supreme Palace Enclosure, where it represents the First Western Minister — the “Higher Minister of State”.
facts.title: A minister of state

facts.text: Arabic tradition also called it Dhur or Duhr, from the word for “back” — another name that describes exactly where it sits in the Lion.
facts.title: The Lion’s back

story: Spin a star fast enough and it stops being round. Zosma turns so quickly — about 280 kilometres per second at its equator, well over 100 times the Sun’s rate — that it bulges at the middle. Its polar radius is only about 84% of its equatorial one.

Underneath the spin is a hot white [[star]] a little over twice the Sun’s width, a size measured directly with an interferometer, and more than 15 times as luminous. Heavier stars live faster: in roughly 600 million years Zosma will swell into an orange or red giant, then fade as a white dwarf of carbon and oxygen.

The name is ancient Greek for “girdle”, for its place on the Lion’s hip. Zosma may also have famous siblings: its path through space suggests it belongs to the Ursa Major Moving Group, a family of stars around 500 million years old that includes most of the Big Dipper.
zosma.tagline: A white star on the Lion’s back, spinning so fast that it bulges at the middle.

facts.text: From about 7 to 9 November each year the Sun itself passes in front of the star, hiding it completely.
facts.title: Lost in the Sun

facts.text: Its other old name, Kiffa Australis, is a partial Latin translation of the Arabic for “the southern pan” of the scales. Older texts also used Lanx Australis.
facts.title: The southern pan

facts.text: KU Librae, 2.6 degrees away, moves through space with the system, but its different chemistry makes it unlikely to be bound to it by gravity.
facts.title: A fifth member?

story: One point of light, four stars. Zubenelgenubi has a fainter partner that travels with it through space, and each of the two is itself a close pair, too tight for amateur telescopes to split. The four probably formed together, some 200 million years ago, with the stars of the Castor Moving Group — a [[multiple-star|multiple star]] system.

The bright pair holds a puzzle. Its two stars have nearly equal masses, yet one spins three times faster than the other. Their spin axes may be badly misaligned, or the faster star may be the product of two stars that merged.

The name is Arabic for “the southern claw”, coined before Libra was a constellation of its own, when these stars were the claws of the Scorpion. Lying almost on the [[ecliptic]], it can be hidden by the Moon, and very rarely by a planet: Venus covered it in 1947, and Mercury will next do so in 2052.
zubenelgenubi.tagline: The Scorpion’s southern claw — one point of light, four stars.

facts.text: Its hot surface gives a simple, clean spectrum, which makes it ideal for studying the thin gas and dust that lie between the star and us.
facts.title: A clear window

facts.text: It was also known as Kiffa Borealis, from the Arabic for “the northern pan” of the scales, and in Latin as Lanx Borealis.
facts.title: The northern pan

facts.text: In about 200 million years it will run out of hydrogen in its core and become a giant much like Kornephoros, Beta Herculis, which started out with a similar mass.
facts.title: A future giant

story: Is it green? Earlier generations of observers described Zubeneschamali as the only naked-eye star with a greenish tint. Most modern eyes see white or bluish, as you would expect of a hot [[spectral-type|B-type]] star, and there is no accepted explanation for the green.

Its brightness may have changed too. Eratosthenes found it brighter than Antares; Ptolemy, some 350 years later, called the two equal. Perhaps Antares brightened, or perhaps this star varies — today it changes by only a few hundredths of a magnitude.

The star is about 4.8 times the Sun’s width and 410 times as luminous, with a surface near 12,000 K, and it spins more than 100 times faster than the Sun. Its name is Arabic for “the northern claw”, from the days when Libra was seen as the claws of the Scorpion.
zubeneschamali.tagline: The Scorpion’s northern claw — long described as the only green star seen by the naked eye.
